Foreverloops is an innovative sandbox and tool that takes a new approach to producing rythmic musical loops, combined with video clips and/or changing still images.
Audio-visual loops can be built by constructing cog chains, each cog having trigger points which can be linked to your choice of sample, still image or video clip. It comes with a good selection of video clips, images and a comprehensive .wav sample library, but you are not limited to just these as it recognises a wide variety of audio, image and video formats, (meaning you can use your own content).
This software seems to be aimed both at people who have no experience with music production and existing creators who like to experiment with new approaches. I think that used to its full potential, some quite complex sequences are possible. Combined with the ability of the software for using any existing user content, the results should be very rewarding.
Strengths
Very intuitive, a new user can dive right in and start creating. The devs are also creating a youtube channel and set of instructional videos so a good body of reference material is being established for users of the software.
Educational. Associating bars and loops with Gears and trigger points makes the process of building a music loop easy to understand.
Fun.  foreverloops comes with a library of > 200 samples and theyre pretty good ones, adding and swapping samples to hear the cumulative effect is a blast.
Flexible.  You can use your own .wav sample library and images/video clips in your creations, making foreverloops a powerful tool with unlimited potential.
Projects can be exported as audio-/video sessions.
Comprehensive, The program recognises a wide variety of audio, image and video formats.

Not recommended.  I hoped this would be something of a cross between Minecraft and Factorio — and it is, kinda — but without the charm or appeal of either one.
The survival mechanics are cranked up to an excessive degree.  You're in a hostile environment, so your suit has to spend power keeping you warm (or sometimes cool), and also powering your light and your scanner and etc.  It recharges slowly during the day, but VERY slowly, and days feel incredibly short.
So at least in the beginning, you're going to need a recharge every couple of minutes.  That ties you to your central power hub, which the game states is irreplacable, meaning you literally cannot explore very far (or deep), nor set up base in a place of your choosing.
The grind is similarly cranked way up.  It doesn't just offer you automation, it forces it on you.  For example: While the ore smelter will take ore from (and put bars into) a neighbouring "hopper" (chest), there's no way to manually load said hoppers, as far as I can tell.  It wants you to use conveyor belts to automate everything, but conveyors cost tin and copper bars, which need smelting.  Just getting the initial conveyor network set up can be a royal pain depending on how far (and how uphill/downhill) your mines are.
Research is a total mess.  The game will happily let you research advanced devices without researching the components that go into those devices — like inventing the car before you've invented wheels and motors.  If those were your last research points … congrats, you're screwed.  At least until you find more things to scan — which might be impossibly far from your base without some basic suit upgrades, which you can't afford because you haven't found the materials, etc etc.
And finally, the graphics.  This might be a question of taste, but personally, I'm amazed they managed to take Minecraft and make it even MORE ugly.  Same blocky world, but with a very limited colour palette, almost everything in the dark, and constant snow.  Not pleasant.
I only played for a couple of hours — not long enough for enemies to show up, whenever that happens — but I simply wasn't having much fun.  YMMV.
Not worth $40.

While you can create music and manipulate video with Foreverloops, it is not an all-purpose music creation/video editing tool. At this point it is a creative toy, although quite a powerful one. Very easy to use, a beginner can jump right in and create in a very short amount of time.
The gear system is unique in music creation as far as I can tell. Most music creation is done linearly. From what I have experimented with in a short amount of time, this makes the software easy to use but the end result is fairly repetitive since it is simply a continuous loop.
The ability to add your own sound, video, and photo clips makes this software able to create endless variations of multimedia projects.
Pros:
Very user-friendly and easy to use
Instant results
Unlimited potential for unique projects
Fun!
Potential for live manipulation to vary the loop pattern (This will take some preparation and skill)
Con:
Fairly short video and audio loops make the results repetitive unless used as mentioned above to vary the loops

For one dollar, most would expect a game of horrible proportions, however this game is truly astonishing as it defies any expectations one might have negative to it.
To start with the basics, let me discuss the gameplay.
You play as a Shiba Inu which is commonly refered to as a shibe, shobe, shib, or doge. You are constantly running through a lush beautiful enviorment that is automatically generated yet feels perfected every time.  The mere title screen blows me away with music worthy of a tremendous price tag. Because the terrain wasn't manually made it keeps thing fresh and new to the player, intriguing the mind by having to constanly figue out how to get past the next obstacle.  The setting is placed in a big city reminicant of very popular tourist destinations such as New York City. There are humans (specifically woman) roaming the streets at all times were from them you get one of the 2 collectables in the game, pantsu. Pantsu is magical underwear which grants protection against banana peels scattered between buildings. You can jump from high places on to these sometimes multiple at once to propell the Shiba Inu up to the next building to collect doge coins on top. Collecting this unique currency grants access to many costumes you can equip to the doge, giving the player a sense of accomplishment. It's not all easy though, as there are 3 enemies that can be defestating to the high score you're trying to set, bringing the challenge factor into each run. First is the chicken who when hit causes a swarm of them to fly left and right on the ground killing you instanly. Similar to the chicken, there is the flock of birds. If you disrupt their peacefull group they will slowly target you and charge fast in that direction. The 3rd and final variation of the enemy types are the cats. The cats sit on piles of junk and garbage almost in the sense of taunting you to come close. Do not be fooled by this though, as they will bestow upon you the curse of cattos; the deadliest thing in the world that destroys the host body in mere miliseconds.
Next I want to discuss technical perfoemance.
This game runs like a dream never dropping down from the smooth 30 fps it retains. Although one minor concern is on full screen mode as loading some menus the frame rate drops by a bit. Although it barely made an impact on the game as a whole. Another factor that quite possibly contributes to this would be the overall performance of the laptop I currently play this on. Lets just say, well... it's not the most powerfull computer or one chosen for gaming by FAR. I do not know the specifications of the resolution, but it looks very sharp and clean almost up to par with more expensive AAA titles currently avalible on steam.

What happens when you combine Dracula, Frankenstein, and H.P. Lovecraft?  You get Amnesia, far and away the best survival horror game I've ever played.  The reason it's so terrifying is simple:  you are completely defenseless, except to go run and hide when you're seen by whatever's lurking in the dark.  I won't mention the plotline or go into any of the  gameplay since there are tons of reviews that do just that.  I guess I'll just mention some of the other, maybe smaller details, that drew me in.
The atmosphere in this is perfect:  dark, cold, lonely, and uncertain.  One thing I appreciate is that it's a return to the classical style of horror (19th Century, creepy old castle, ghostly sounds, roaring fireplaces, etc.).  You could say these things are cliche's, and in a lot of ways, they are.  You're wandering around in a creepy, haunted castle; it doesn't get much more cliche than that, but it's done so well it doesn't matter.  The sounds are so immersive and the environments are so eerie that there is a constant layer of dread throughout the entire game.  It just goes to show how tried and true these conventions are if they're put in capable hands.
Another thing I love is that it doesn't rely on jump scares, something I've always found to be cheap.  If something is out to get you, you know it's coming, which makes it, I think, even more horrifying.  You have time to run, but how much?  Can it run faster than you?  Will it find you in your hiding spot?  These guys really understand how to make a horror game, and even a good horror story.  It relies more on what isn't seen, rather than bombarding you with monsters and stuff jumping out and screaming "Boo" that you eventually grow numb to, and eventually get tired of, which is becoming more and more of a cliche these days.  Good horror is dependent upon subtlety, which is rare to find.
In short, if you love the classical style of horror and want something that truly will terrify you, then Amnesia is a must.  Games like this don't come around very often, and they're definitely not to be overlooked, especially this one.

Kotor 2 was a mixed bag for a lot of fans of the first game. The game is a lot more cerebral then it`s predecessor.
The original Kotor was a nice game with a ``Gather your friends and save the galaxy`` plotline. In this game you`re dealing with the fallout of the actions of the previous game. It`s a lot darker of a storyline and it has a nice climax when it ends.
The voice acting is simply breathtaking and the storyline itself top notch. Just bare in mind that Kotor 2 was rushed on release and as such a large portion of content was cut out. Thankfully modders have restored most of it since then, so I recommend googling Kotor 2 restored content mod if you want to fully experience this game how the developers intended.

Hi, welcome to my short review about Arma 3.
First of all, I claim that I DO NOT have a great PC so this is all based of my opinions and not videos.
Variety:
This game is amazing at providing variety. You can do normal missions from the campaign or CO-OP ones, you can play some Arma 3 Life, play some modded scenarios. King of the Hill, Gun Game are all available for everyone.
Graphics and Gameplay:
This game looks great even on lower settings. However, the game is CPU-heavy so I personally did not get 60FPS at all. Even at 30FPS, I enjoyed the game a lot. A lot of this game's popularity (in my opinion) comes from the extreme realism which I admire a lot. All of the features that make the game more realistic really put you into the shoes of the soldier you are playing as, or whatever character you are. The advanced leaning is worth noting as it makes that engagement even more tactical. Radios are perfect if you have a nice squad with your friends however I personally use direct communication due to me not having anyone to play with.
Overall, this game is very fun to play and I reccomend it to anyone especially when it's on sale.

I've thought of buying this game for quite a while and initially I chose not to, because of all the reviews. I bought it because it didn't seem so bad in one of the YouTuber's videos (although it is really odd that his ads are everywhere in the game - I don't think I've ever seen something like that before and it kind of makes you think. Go figure.).
But now to pros and cons:
PROS
1. This game has quite some potential - the engine provides quite some room for expansion, and the topic is pretty interesting.
2. The coaches are pretty nicely made.
3. I had no trouble setting up the controls.
4. Rain looks really great.
5. The check-in system is really fun.
6. FPS is stable on max settings, at least for me - no problems here with i7 Intel Processor and GTX 960M.
CONS
1. It feels like Early Access all the time.
2. There are A LOT OF bugs - from grass on the streets, rain falling through briges, passengers thinking that you're off road when you're not etc. etc.
3. AI Cars are AWFUL, and I really mean awful - they can even stop in the middle of a highway, causing accidents - with you or another AI car hitting them, they can't figure how to get out of a traffic jam and whenever something unexpected happens, they can't cope with it at all. It really breaks the game for me - I want to feel like a good driver and I constantly have to break the rules and do something really dangerous to avoid accident or simply to move forward.
4. GPS that doesn't help you at all frequently - it is supposed to show you which lane to choose but it displays all of them, so that you have to rapidly change the lane on the highway, even 2 or 3 at once, causing a very dangerous situation.
5. Passengers disappearing when boarding the bus, only to reappear inside - it breaks the immersion a lot.
6. Sometimes I can't check the passengers in and have to restart the route.
7. Passenger models aren't that great - still way better than OMSI 2, but not great.
8. Fog in the rear mirrors - I constantly have this fog in the rear mirrors, which makes it impossible to see fast moving cars when changing lanes.
9. Many graphic glitches - LoD problems and problems with displays inside the car - unless you zoom at least once, the temperature and speed displays are glitched. Also, at times, road signs are blurry.
10. AI cars constantly disappear or suddenly appear in front of you, many times causing accidents.
My verdict - while it is not that bad, it feels beta right now. I cannot recommend this game in its present state, although I do hope that they will fix it in the future. It certainly has potential, but I don't like it when paying customers are doing what beta-testers should be doing.

This game isn't for everyone, but oh man, if it turns out you're one of the people it IS for, then prepare to spend weeks of your life in this game.  Builders, perfectionists, architects & problem solvers - read on, this game is for you.
You toil endlessly creating complex systems to do some work for you so you can go back to toiling endlessly, but with a goal to achieve.  Sounds like torture?  Skip it.  Sounds like fun?  Buy it.
It's like Factorio got moved into MineCraft.  A 3D block environment where you dig and mine, but not to gather resources.  You dig and mine so that you can place down machines to gather the resources for you.  Then you build a transportation system to move those resources to your base to be turned into more machines.  So you can dig and mine deeper, to place more machines to gather more resources.  Thats the "Craft" piece of the game.
The "Fortress" piece is about defending against the waves of attackers.  Fortress isn't really an apt desription, I'd say its more of a camp with a heart that you defend with craploads of guns.  Again, you don't do the defending so much as your machines do the defending for you.  Granted, the waves of attackers are a bit simplistic - very much like the waves in a tower defense game, they mindlessly hover toward the exit (in this case not an exit, but the core machine in your base).  If they reach it, they attack and you 'lose'.
The game has several tiers, each reachable only by solving the previous tier; and a little bit of the tier itself that you're trying to reach.  Problematic enough to cause some frustration along with the satisfaction of having overcome that obstacle.  Several times as you try to get to the next tier, you find the machines you have access to come up a bit shy and you need to temporarily resort to doing things by hand again for the earliest parts of of 'leveling up' to the next tier.  How you go about solving it is all part of the fun, and there isn't just one right answer either.
This sort of problem solving, improving and perfecting is found throughout the game.  For me, it was an everflowing cycle of frustrating problems and dopamine reward.  Like I said, it's not for everyone, but if it is for you, then easily expect triple digits of playtime next to FortressCraft on your Steam profile.

Take a classic NES action-platformer like Mario, Megaman, Ducktales, Castlevania, or Ninja Gaiden. Remove the unnecessary arcade game holdovers and sloppy design from just not yet knowing how to make games.
No score. High scores were for bragging and putting A S S or F U K in the high score names. No lives. Lives and continues were to get the player to stop playing or put in another quarter every few minutes. The punishment for death is instead a Dark Souls-like dropping of currency that you may be able to reacquire. No untelegraphed deaths or leaps of faith. It's always intuitive where you need to go and what you need to do, the challenge is in acting at the right time and observing patterns.
Clean up the gameplay, but keep some aesthetic attributes. Chiptune music and pixel graphics accurate to NES graphics (with minor exceptions and enhancements). The color pallet is accurate to the NES and sprites are drawn in a similar way to the NES's limitations. There are minor visual enhancements like parallax scrolling (background and foreground moving at different speeds) that couldn't exist on NES. Widescreen, high resolutions, and no need for slowdowns or sprite flickering when there are more than five enemies on-screen because the NES had a bare-bones amount of RAM.
On top of that three unique playable characters each with their own story. That's Shovel Knight for you: a NES classic filtered by thirty years of hindsight. Worth every penny, worth every second of play.

Fernbus Simulator is a good game and has a lot of potential in it.
It has a great ground: the graphics is awesome, the map is huge, the cities are lovely. There are some bugs, but the team is working to clear them, and hands out patches regularly.
Pros:
-awesome graphics (the lights are the best!)
-detailed simulation (of the bus, and other tasks of the driver)
-you can walk through and around your bus
-realistic passengers (complaining literally for everything, just like in real life, so now it is not a bug, it's a feature)
-lovely cities (including some famous local sights, and many unique bus stations)
-you can plan your routes just like you want them
-good control settings (you can customize your controls very easily, much better than in other simulators)
-dynamic weather: pretty, but changes weather types a bit often
-dynamic events (not really appears for me, only the police stops, but I have spent only 15 hours in the game, and discovered just a small part of Germany)
-catchy soundtracks
Cons:
-AI is not the best, if you have a dense traffic setting, you can encounter some never ending traffic jams, but if you set it to low, there will be only a few cars on the roads
-a bit hard to follow the navigation: it shows precisely the lanes you need to follow, but don't give enough time to you to notice the next junction or exit
-career mode is really short: it would be great if you can start your own coaching company where you can manage every stuff (there are many contractors for Flixbus in real life as well)
-only two buses (hopefully there will be more later, or at least some great mods)
All in all the game is great, and hopefully the developpers will keep updating it. It is a simulator, where everything should work like in real life, which makes it inevitable to have some bugs or missing features in the beginning, but I believe that with the feedbacks and the continous work, it can be absolutely awesome.

FortressCraft Evolved! scratched all the itches I had playing other sandbox games. I don't care about survival and crafting; that isn't what this game is about. It is about exploring and designing your own systems and gradually opening up more options to make things more efficient. Constant revisioning and redesigning my systems is the best thing about it. The search for efficiency is my motivator throughout. I like playing this game in an information vacuum because I don't care how the other players are doing it; I want to work through it on my own.
With the nature of the development there is a fair bit of jank in the game but it is coherent enough to let me forget it after I learned the basics. It is a hard sell to friends that are used to very complete tutorials. This is not a game that holds your hand and it expects you to do some research on your own. I'm fine with that because it is a good game. Any less and it would have sat in my back log.
Finally, you can really tell the game is a labor of love and if I were the developer, I would be very, very proud of this achievement.

Although the game has a great design, has deep gameplay and shows a lot of promise, I cannot recommend it in its current state. It currently makes an unpolished and buggy impression, which may be acceptable for an early access game, but not for a game that has been officially released.
For example, it took me several hours just to get my interface working. It turns out that the game seems to assume a 16:9 aspect ratio of your monitor. When I tried to load the game with my monitor's native resolution, which has a 4:3 aspect ratio, the interface was completely buggy. For example, windows were overlapping that were not supposed to, so that I could not see the entire interface. The game does not provide any warning when selecting an unsupported resolution.
Other bugs that I have encountered include items on conveyor belts not being rendered at all under certain conditions (thereby making them invisible) and turrets not firing at the enemy, but instead making jittery movements. Also, I have encountered several bugs in the user interface. Additionally, the game crashes frequently when doing certain things, such as scanning for ore.
Because this game has a great design and shows a lot of promise, I hope that the developer will fix these issues. Afterwards, I will gladly change my rating to a positive one.
Meanwhile, if you are interested in resource management games with complex assembly lines, I would recommend buying the game Factorio instead. Even though it is officially still in early access, it is already a lot more polished than FortressCraft. However, the main disadvantage of Factorio is that you are limited to two dimensions (i.e. the surface of the planet), whereas in FortressCraft you can also build in the third dimension, digging deep into the planet.

This game will either be really fun, or rather boring depending on what type of games you like. If you like building complex machinery chains to automate everything then this will be a good game for you. If you like fast paced, action games... This probably will not be your cup of tea.
That being said lets go over some of my thoughts on this game
Self contained machinery, automation, building, and resource gathering that plays much like a minecraft modpack based around a single tech mod.
The graphics, while based around cubes for the terrain, is actually pretty good. It has vastly improved since I got this game a year+ ago.
Caving is just fun in this game. There are massive cave systems that put other digger/builder games like minecraft to shame. Example, there is a cave with a ravine right next to my starting base that is almost deeper than the entirety of the building area minecraft allows (at least vertically).
Some aspects of the game are rather grindy, even on the "fast" paced version. Ore collection and smelting takes time, and as you get later into the progression tree you unlock things to speed this up.
Unfortunatly the cost to create everything also gets pretty high.
Energy production is really small unless you are playing on the fast version, Solar panels are almost worthless unless you choose to have eternal day.
The "expected" time to reach the endgame (OET) is not bad, but the charge time is really long. Although this gives you a good reason to make a well fortified base!
Overall those detractor points are rather insignificant to me, as they just extend the time until I "beat" the game and then get bored. Heck.... I haven't even gotten to the end game yet and I'm almost 50 hours in!
This game is well worth the money to me and DjArcas is great developer that is active within the community!

A great game that demonstrates about the battles of Gettysburg, that allows we to change history, by altering strategies, and creating new opportunities. The game is played on real-time. There is no base building in this game, or unit building in this game, in this game you get new units/reinforcements as in history, thus this game have no unit building at all.
What is quite different with regular RTS is that this game have few types of units : infantry, skirmishers, cavalry, and artillery. There is only few differences between Union and Confederates units, the Confederates are better at charging, where the Union are better at shooting. This game use "truesight", which the shooting range of a unit is defined by whether it can see its enemies or not, and unit on elevated/higher position can shot farther than units at lower position. Also, hills and terrain contours play a lot of effect in this game, as ridges and hills could afford a defensible place to shot down, and units could also take cover behind the hills from pounding artillery or from other units. Aside from elevation, terrain also play a key, units located on wooded terrain will be protected better from enemy fire.
Units fight by firing each other, and get to melee/hand-to-hand combat. Because of the similarities of unit statistics, the important thing is not the units itself, but how the player positions the units. Some units do have "veteran" status, like the Union Iron Brigade, but the most important thing is where you place the unit.
This game is very recommended for RTS players, most notably people who are interested in American Civil War and gunpowder era.

Take a classic NES action-platformer like Mario, Megaman, Ducktales, Castlevania, or Ninja Gaiden. Remove the unnecessary arcade game holdovers and sloppy design from just not yet knowing how to make games.
No score. High scores were for bragging and putting A S S or F U K in the high score names. No lives. Lives and continues were to get the player to stop playing or put in another quarter every few minutes. The punishment for death is instead a Dark Souls-like dropping of currency that you may be able to reacquire. No untelegraphed deaths or leaps of faith. It's always intuitive where you need to go and what you need to do, the challenge is in acting at the right time and observing patterns.
Clean up the gameplay, but keep some aesthetic attributes. Chiptune music and pixel graphics accurate to NES graphics (with minor exceptions and enhancements). The color pallet is accurate to the NES and sprites are drawn in a similar way to the NES's limitations. There are minor visual enhancements like parallax scrolling (background and foreground moving at different speeds) that couldn't exist on NES. Widescreen, high resolutions, and no need for slowdowns or sprite flickering when there are more than five enemies on-screen because the NES had a bare-bones amount of RAM.
On top of that three unique playable characters each with their own story. That's Shovel Knight for you: a NES classic filtered by thirty years of hindsight. Worth every penny, worth every second of play.

If you're asking yourself "Should I get Ultimate General: Gettysburg?" the answer is a resounding YES! I don't normally write reviews on here, but I just had to take the time for UG:G becasue it's such a well designed game, and such a breath of fresh air for the strategy genre.
I won't bore you with multiple long paragraphs on how great the game is, but I will say this: if anything about this game sparks your interest, from a trailer, to a gameplay video, to a recommendation, then GET IT. $15 is an amazing price for this game. I normally wait for games to go on sale beforte purchasing them, but I bought UG:G at full price, and have absolutely no regrets about doing so.
Combat *seems* simple, and for the most part it is, yet there is such a depth and complexity to it that you'll still be mastering new techniques dozens of hours into the game. Gameplay is fun and engaging, and you're never left feeling like you've been cheated by the AI. Speaking of which, both individual units' AI, and the the enemy general's AI are extraordinary. There are nine different diffuculty settings for AI matches/campaigns, each with differing strategies and characteristics, so there's massive replay value, even for purely offline play.
Ultimate General: Gettysburg is the first of hopefully many Ultimate General games. I'm happy to show my support for  UG:G, and I'm excited to see what's next.

So my first impressions of this game are pretty good so far. It's a vast improvement over the 1st in both gameplay and acting but even then the combat is fairly easy to grasp but tricky to to actually do when fighting more than one enemy. It's been set in a beautiful world however filled with different types of enemies and some side quests to keep you entertained should you decide to do them. I enjoy watching the clips which are well animated and sword fight early on in the game between an Orc and armour clad Knight was pretty entertaining to watch thanks to the way it was animated.
VOICE ACTING
The voice acting is good in some places and not so good in others with the main character neither being the best or worst of the lot but in the long run he talks in a grumpy whisper ALL the time with little or no emotion shown in his lines and, truth be told, listening to him speak caused me to turn on subtitles and skip the dialogue.
Which leads me to my next issue. The Subtitles are poorly written, whether or not this was done in some kind of translation or just by sheer lack of proofreading what is actually said is sometimes a little different to whats written. This wouldn't be a problem if not for the grammer and placement issues I noticed so even though the actors make perfect sense the subtitles sometimes don't.
GAME WORLD
RPG's like this need a strong world to back it up, one that looks good and encourages me to explore and yes it is absolutely beautiful and the enemies in it are often well animated and nice to look at (all except the Groms which annoy me) but I felt no drive to go exploring too far off the road for fear of the extremely tough enemies that randomly plague the wilderness. This game has no leveled zones and, unlike Skyrim on consoles, the world does not level with you. At level 2 you could fight something very capable fo turning you into mince in less than ten seconds so choose your battles wisely. The first town you start in is located in the Sahvanna which is nice and has some enemies often not seen in RPG's like Baboons, Rhinos and other such enemies.
COMBAT
Combat is easy to pick up. You learn it step by step in the tutorial sections so if you cant block from the get go, worry not because you still need to learn how. Melee comes first then Archery and finally Magic which people (including me) say is a strong point in the game thanks to the customizable spells. Archery and Magic are all auto aim but Melee is a different story, You need to think tactically to some degree though most enemies are a hack and slash affair.
What surprised me was the stealth system of the game. You can sneak up behind enemies and stab them in the back with a pretty simplistic animation but this only works on humanoids so far as I know. Though I did notice a fair amount of enemies seem to be have their backs turned in the worst places such as beside a cliff. Why would you be staring into a wall of rock when your back is so exposed to an assisination from behind. It's alnost like they invite you to get that free kill!
SKILLS
So there's a variety of crafting skills from alchemy to blacksmithing which work but its really hard to explain their function. Lockpicking in this game is quite simple but rewarding and the minigame used to pick the locks is both easy but clever.
MUSIC
This game has a really good soundtrack. The ambience to the scores during cutscenes are great in my opinion and really bring something good to this beautiful world filled with boring people. You can even buy an intrument and some song sheets though I never got to see if you could play them or not as I wasn't wasting money on it.
As I play through the game I plan on adding more to my review.

If you're looking to make the clothes beneath your stomach nice and damp, go somewhere else....
....but if you're looking for a nice atmospheric game that will grip you with its story, and make you want to explore and experience: this is the game for you.
Cause this game is ALL about your feeling of "What the hell is going on?", and by looking around you and finding pages from your diary you slowly uncover what has happened in this castle. Speaking of castle, it IS a rather spooky castle: I found myself jumping more from the creeks and the wind working on the old structure than the actual monsters, and some rooms are just messed-up fun.
This game also has a great community for mods and custom maps, so this game has high replayability and length (some of the custom content might even manage to scare you...)
There are some let-downs though, the most notable being the tediousness of the puzzles. If this game had any more puzzles, I'd call it Portal 3. The monsters not really being more than an inconvenience is also a minus, and a system were you slowly lose your sanity by not being close to light is just annoying: it ruins the atmosphere to have to lift your lantern every 3 meters.
Overall it's a nice, tense experience. Having a mod community is ALWAYS a big plus for me. But it's not a great horror game.
It may work nicely as your first horror game, if you're too afraid to try others.

A great case of an oldie but a goodie. With the newly added addition of The Restored Content Mod, this game truly is restored. KotOR II is one of the best cRPGs I've ever played. Its beautiful background and stunning music backs up the amazing voice acting and brilliant scripts that carry this game far further than any Star Wars title ever could on the silver screen.
As a Star Wars game, its is quite removed from the movies (taking place 3000 years before A New Hope), but nevertheless the parallels between film and videogame are stronger than ever. This game puts the magnifying glass over the force, expounding upon it in great detail throughout the story. If you've ever wanted to play as a jedi, then this game is one best places to start,
Player agency is at an all time high in this game. While it may not be as free roaming as the earlier Fallout games, this title will give you decisions that shape the game as you play. Most importantly, this game deals with the concept of "morality" better than any game I have played since. KotOR II changes the way you think about black and white choices, with there always being more to a situation than just the upfront value of A or B. It is that simple factor that makes this game what it is. It is a collection of choices wrapped in excellent storytelling, a beautiful background, and a masterful concert of talented musicians.
TL;DR
Choices, Morality, Music. Great game for in-depth RPGs

A simple, terrifying game. The controls are different from any other game, but for any avid video gamer are easy and fairly intuitive. The graphics are not top-of-the-range but are more than sufficent for conveying the dark and dreary atmosphere for Brennanberg castle. The shadows particularly are oppressive.
The developers are very aware as well that less is more and the game if well balanced between periods of calm and periods of horror that will keep you on the edge of your seat the whole time. The concept of not having a weapon of any shape or form helps to add to the terror when an unnatural roar comes echoing down a corridor and you know its time to flee or die.
Whilst the story is not wholly original, its enough to drive the game forward just to see and discover what in the world is happening.
Replay-wise, once you play it, you know what to expect. However I bought this game many years ago and this is only my second-playthrough. With games like this its best to step away from it long enough to forget the details (whether small or large) and then come back to it. I've always kept safe on the Library shelf.

This recommendation was a tough call. I ended up choosing no for some very key things in the game that just made it painful to play. But first the pros.
>Good theme, like, they couldn't have done it better. The blend between nature and technology was blended perfectly and it does feel like it is part of a bigger universe.
>Nice controls (more on that).
>Frankly great graphics (again, more on that later).
>Good menus.
And now the cons. In the cons I will not be discussing Uplay. The DRM does cost you a few minutes in the beginning and (for other games) can be a huge pain. However, in this game, all you need to do is log in once when you first boot it up and it doesn't really bug you much after that.
So, cons
>For someone with a lower-end machine, this game will kill you. As I said, great graphics, but what it did to me was reduce the framerate down to almost nothing and made the game almost unplayable due to button lag. My pc isn't terrible, either. It can play almost all games above 60fps and only goes this low for games like Next Car Game (which is an excellent game), and even for that it still gets 15-20fps.
>Multiplayer is a pain, unlike the previous ones where it was a huge part of the experience.
>Lack of content, which other people have commented on.
>"Season pass," which is required to add what content the game should have had in the begining. Plus DLC, which I am generally against unless it's something like the gods and kings expansion pack. Basically, its just Ubisoft being Ubisoft.
And thats pretty much it. If you are someone who has seen trials videos and wants to get in on it, pick Trials Evolution Gold Edition. It is better in most ways and equal when it isn't. If you have been a fan of the trials series ever since it started, go on right ahead. The main con for me is circumstantial, so if you are really dedicated you can have fun with the game despite the other flaws.
Edit: Forgot about the "More on controls." Basically the only thing that I was going to say on that was that the game implemented a trick system that really doesn't contribute to the game at all. A few challenges may use it but most of the time it just gets in the way, especially during the tutorial levels.

So, after reading alot of reviews of the Trials series and this game in particular, i feel obligated to write one on my own.
Many people had a huge problem with Ubisoft and their way to market their games, in fact those people hate on Trials Fusion just because it uses Uplay. The game is published by Ubisoft, i do not know why you would think they wouldnt put it on their own PC distribution service and account control service.
Yes Uplay is sometimes broken, but those times are not THAT often, it happens  here and there, and Ubisoft doesnt seem to give a♥♥♥♥♥♥ But really, i dont want to review the Publisher or the Developers, which both chose to run this game on the platform.
The Game Itself:
- a very skillbased "racing" game, where the point is more or less to drive through a track with no mistakes, only after that the time really matters
- has alot of content (though the price with the DLC is pretty high, compared to a triple a title it matches though)
-> User created content pushes the game forward to a pretty high replay value (which mostly explains my playtime)
Most negative aspects about it:
- lack of content of the original game (no dlcs) compared to evolution
- no ways of communication directly through the game
- the multiplayer is pretty lagged out (though it is much better than evolution)
Overall, they needed too long for the game to be at this state (which is a pretty definitve version on how a trials game needs to feel like), it felt like a beta for about a year into it. The developers did not abandon the game though and continued to give (free) content for the players to enjoy. With this in mind, i can only say it is one of my most beloved games today, for its high skillcap and active community, which still produces some great quality tracks.

After almost 20 hours of continuously playing I'm finally done. This has really been that one game, that has finally revived my hunger for actually playing games. Where to start, you start as a warrior named war (hence the pun :D) fighting against 2 factions, heaven and hell to regain balance. As most people I started by reading some reviews, then I stumbled across this one review which said '' please don't play this game on easy, you'll regret as hell'' so I followed his advice, took normal, now that I'm done I highly regret not playing on apocalyptic (hardest difficulty). So please, don't be as foolish as me and play this game on apocalyptic mode and just enjoy it. Now to some pros and cons
Pros:
- The story is just amazing IMO, you're a horseman, you're one of the 4 horsemen who serve as the law, balance and order between Hell, Heaven and Earth. I really recommend you see all cutscenes and just follow the story and never miss a shot, cause man you'll regret like hell.
- The voice actors are just amazing, the way they talk, how they talk and just everything, there's always something new to expect in each cutscene.
- Dialogue is amazing, not just the voice actors.
- The best way to put the combat is that it's hack and slash, use combos, any kind of combos you desire, buy, explore and slaughter.
- Terrain and environment is good, it ranges from different areas and ''worlds'' to explore, everything from new york (if I'm not mistaken) to huge deserts where hostile threats are yet to be found.
- As the game progresses you'll obtain new items, upgrades, special moves, and character upgrades (different tokens, health and wrath)
- Creativity is shown, the economy here isn't the typical gold, or dollars, here you deal with 3 different type of souls, money1, wrath2 and health3. Blue1, yellow2 and green3 ( Number behind indicates which colour is for which thing.)
- Graphics are good. cutscenes are good, nothing bad which I've noticed
- Music is quite good, it fits the situations you're in perfectly, it's basically this Synchronisation that's highly appealing and creates this dramatic effect.
Cons:
- Game might crash when you alt+tab and enter back to the game, so if you must alt+tab, remember to save right before you do.
- too many puzzles at certain times, but look at the bright side, if you like challenges and like to exercise your brain, this will be no con to you.
- Some bosses are just too easy, it isn't overwhelmingly easy, but they just don't feel as hard as they should have ( might be cause I played in normal and not apocalyptic, silly me :C)
Conclusion: I would just like to say that I had a really good time playing this, at times I got shivers down my neck and goose bumps by the story alone. This is one of the best games I've played in a long while, I got this constant thrill and at times my adrenaline was just soo high. If you are considering on purchasing this, stop hesitating and just buy this. It's really worth it, if you are a tf2 trader, go to market and buy the franchise pack for 5 keys, it's worth every single penny, I promise. that's all I had to say.

When this game came out, it was often described as a mix between God of War and Legend of Zelda, with the implication that it wasn't all that original.  While this was true, with the clarity of hindsight we can see that Darksiders took those ideas and made a great game out of them.  The combat is fluid and satisfying, the puzzles are clever and challenging.  The one downside, in my opinion, is the story and the main character: a brooding, growling, unjustly prosecuted white guy who finds an answer in killing everyone in his way - in the clarity of hindsight, we can see just how unhelpful this kind of fantasy is.  If you can overlook this particular aspect of the game, you'll find that the rest is a textbook example of good game design that stands the test of time.

Early Access Alpha, People, ALPHA!
I love this game, I've been looking for an off-line Wurm for some time, and this doesn't disappoint. I host my own server, just for me, with x2 skill gain and am really enjoying building up my little 'community' bit by bit, a potters house, a miners house, a farmers house, a ranchers house, and so on.
It is an early access game, in Alpha - that is it is un-optimised (optimisation would ideally be finished in beta stress testing), it is not full of content yet (there is content but it's more to test the mechanics) and even not all the mechanics are in game yet (an alpha should start with the core mechanics, test them through content, then add more content/mechanics, test those, and so forst). If this is not the sort of game you want to play, with possible roll-backs, world-breaking bugs, crashes - then don't buy this game. Certainly don't buy it, then whinge about the state of it - the fact that it is Alpha is smeared everywhere! If you want to play the game, but not in the alpha state, then buy the game to support the developers to finish it then go away for a year!

You'll be sniping the Nazi's and the Red as you take on this WWII Sniper shooter!
I've enjoyed playing through the game the minute I purchased it! The game can be played in two ways as I see it, Normal mode, where bullet drop won't affect your aim when sniping or Realism mode, where you'll have to make each shot count and hope to God you didn't mess up. The game still is enjoyable either way and offers stealth. You'll be able to access a slow motion bullet time when aiming, that triggers an epic bullet follow kill x ray cam. It'll show the bullet entering and cracking the bones/organs you hit on the target, on top of that the game has a fully fledged stealth system, traps you can set up in case things go south and you can set up your loadout before each mission. The game is fair in length and will take a few days to tackle. It is a great game for Third Person shooter/sniping game lovers.
Bottom Line: Great way of implementing sniping in a game, good graphics, enjoyable gameplay.

Decided to give the game a chance after all positive reviews, and it was worth it. Overall well-executed and solid (not what you would expect of Two Worlds franchise, huh?) Though it has it downsides, of that below. But short summary - yes, the game is good.
Two Worlds 2 in many ways reminds me of Gothic series. Free roaming, ability to climb rocks, ability to beat strong enemies, loot and steal everything, sensible NPCs and a right feel of progression. Not exactly there, but this is the best experience in open-world RPGs I've got since those times. On top of that, excellent graphics and animations (oh, pity that with such great combat animations game has such crappy combat mechanics!) and good story and side quests - you feel involved and always have a reason to intervene.
Bad things. 1) The redundant key entering and invasive registration form (do not fill that, it's unnecessary!). Almost ragequite after some unsuccesful registration attempts; thankfully, continued. No drm-client, at least. 2) The game claims to be open-world, but in fact you are limited to plot zones, though they are large and free to roam. And there is next to nothing to explore outside of key locations. So it's more correct to perceive this game as story-driven RPG, but without rails and corridors. 3) Game is exploitable in a lot of ways. Kiting, click spamming, paralizing, poor aggro handling, patrol limits - all of that makes combat unchallengeable and boring. Having tons of health of the enemies doesn't help with boring. Heard there are mods that improve combat and difficulty level, but haven't tried them.
Overall, the game was fun. Little grindy, but I don't mind to kite mobs a little - loot is good as a reward. Good controls, freedom to go, believable world, good story and quests. Good thing I have an addon, can experience the game a little more.
And, of course, 10/10 for being eaten by umbrella!

Very promising - There is a surprising amount of content to explore given that this is an early access game.
PROS:
- Many of the complex systems are already in place (such as terraforming, construction, logging, etc.) which is good as this is a crafting game at  heart.
- The huge crafting and skill systems require specialization as you have a finite number of skill points to allocate (on most servers).
- This is great for encouraging player interaction and community building. The idea of having a town blacksmith that you need to go to for swords and armor, a logger to cut your trees, etc. is a lot of fun and not something a lot of games like to encourage. You're not a god, you can't do everything on your own.
CONS:
- Combat is promising and deep but not very satisfying at the moment.
- Long server load times (seriously, be patient).
- The engine needs optimization. This isn't up to the Life is Feudal dev team but it does affect their game.
- Occasional bugs and some people experience frequent crashing.
CONCLUSION:
If the dev team can continue building on what they have without falling into the typical early access pitfalls then this game will be the next big thing. All it will need is a promotion from a YouTuber to blow up.

You can conquer the world with many different factions, not just roman, but that's mostly for "historical fiction" and entertainment; playing as roman, you will play as one of three powerful patrician families, the Julii (main enemy: the gauls and germans), the Scipii (main enemy, the iberians and carthaginians) and the Brutii (main enemy: the hellenistic kingdoms and Parthia). If you get too powerful, you'll have to eventually face the envy and paranoia of the Senate, launching a relentless civil war that will threaten everything you have built at that point and will turn the Republic into your personal Empire, but that's the end of the game.
Or you can install a Total Realism mod, and just play as Rome itself (not patrician families), skipping the whole "civil war" part and conquering the WHOLE map with the colors of Rome. Your choice.
Anyway, the game is a mid-00's flawless RTS classic. Engaging grand campaign map and fun as hell RTS battles. Roma Invicta Est! And then there's the Barbarian Invasion expansion pack: same mechanics, but new factions (Dark Ages factions, huns, goths, vandals, saxons, franks, etc) and a new grand campaign map with the Western Empire (weak) and the Eastern Empire (decent) ruling everything, until you smash them with a barbaric horde, that is. Just as good as Rome.
Rome II and Attila are nothing more than decent remakes with better graphics, but the original Rome/BI is still fresh and fun.

How to properly experience Rome Total War.
Step one: Start a new game playing as the Romans, doesn't matter the family.
Step two: Decide how fast you want to get going by using cheats or not, usually depends onthe mood I'm in.
Step three: Create an unstoppable army, or two, or 20, depends how fast you want the world to tremble at your feet.
Step four: Send forth your armies into the lands of the barbarians, take their cities and sack them, burn them down, kill them all.
Step five: Once the barbarians have been eradicated completely from the map, head for Greece, the home of the intelects.
Step six: Send your armies to enslave the Greek peoples, beat them off their high horses and kill them slowly and painfully.
Step seven: Once Greece has been pacified sucsessfuly, wait till you have a plauge in one of your cities, you will soon see why.
Step eight: once you do have a plauge in one of your cities, get unimprtant agents like diplomats there, keep them for a bit, them send them to the south, in places like Memphis, Alexandria, or Carthage, large cities.
Step nine: watch as thousands die from your own little biological terrorist attack, take it in.
Step ten: Send your armies to finish off Carthage, Egypt and Numidia, enslave their peoples too, and make sure to kil the pharoh.

So after quite a bit of time playing this game, modded, unmodded, singleplayer, multiplayer, etc. I feel its about time I write a review.
+ Gigantic maps full of scenery and towns and cities
+ Constant dev support and new content releases (free DLC even)
+ Very high quality campaigns with replayability
+ Dozens of guns and vehicles
+ Sandbox type map creation and mission creation
+ Steam workshop
+ Enormous and mostly friendly community
+ Lots of gamemodes (Roleplay, Invade and Annex, Intel Recovery, Hostage Recovery, etc.)
+ Extremely detailed models and guns, replicating real world counter parts
+ Difficult FPS that thankfully pushes away immature and whiny players
+ Teamwork based game (Going lone wolf style will result in failure unless the mission is designed for it)
+ Modding from third party websites in additon to the Workshop (Armaholic for example)
-
- Extremely clunky and buggy engine. It looks nice but its outdated. A 64bit edition was released recently, fixing FPS issues and other problems but the game is still very clunky. (You can vault through objects, flip cars by touching sidewalks, and bullet physics dont always work as they should)
- Unbalanced. You'll find a lot, if not the majority of gamemodes in this game are co-op, PVP gamemodes have heavy restrictions on many weapons and gear as well. This is because between the 3 factions (BLUFOR, OPFOR, and Independant) there are many inconsistencies and balancing problems that make certain weapons and gear so powerful that it renders many others useless. For example: if you own the Apex DLC, you get access to the Special Operations (VIPER) gear. This includes: a bullet resistant helmet with built in thermal and nightvision, a underarmor clothing that is bullet resistant (more so than some vests) and is thermal-proof (this means you will not show up under any thermal scope) and a automatic rifle that switches firemodes from 5.56 rounds to .50 BW rounds based on what mag you have in it. By paying for one DLC you get access to these weapons, while non-dlc owners do not. The AI however, are not DLC locked, and have access to this gear and will use it and the other high tier weapons and armor that you may not have access to.
- The recent DLC: Jets. Now this part is personal preference, but the newest DLC called "Arma 3: Jets" is, to put bluntly, a donation DLC. By this I mean you're buying it, not because of what content it provides, but because you want to support BI. Now this is perfectly ok with me and all to you if that's what you wish to do with your money. Many of the DLC in this game (such as Helicopters) are in that same boat of content vs. price. Now you're probably asking "Why?" and here is why: the steam workshop. I'm a fan of BI and have purchased the entire Arma franchise with all DLC back to Operation Flashpoint, and why? Because it was good quality. The newest DLC releasing however, has not been. The Jets DLC features 3(?) new fighter jets and a static aircraft carrier to be placed in the world using the editor. Along with this came a free platform update, overhauling the flying mechanics, radar system, and more for all players, DLC purchasers and not. The problem with this, is that through the Steam Workshop you can find (in my opinion) better planes and a MUCH better Aircraft Carrier with all the features of the DLC one and more. And the best part is all of these are free. Now as I said, this last point here is entirely personal opinion and I know people who love the new jets and aircraft carrier, however I'm not a fan.

Synopsis: Before I say why I'm against this game, it isn't because it isn't fun, because it can be fun with friends, but it just isn't worth your money.
Alright, let's get the pros out of the way.
Pros:
- Scary at first.
- Interesting creatures to play as.
- Good maps, but the maps do have some cons.
- A LOT OF FUN WITH FRIENDS.
Cons:
- Seems like an outdated game. (just to me with the new types of games releasing).
- Characters have no depth to them and nothing to put them apart besides appearance.
- Maps aren't adjusted with many secrets. (what I mean is not enough to give survivors an advantage).
- Guns didn't make the game better, it just held it back.
- Updates were few and far between for awhile.
- Seekers seem like they have too much power sometimes. (making it seem like a game that really the seeker chooses who to keep alive until the end instead of actually finding them last).
- Too expensive after the state this game was in for the longest time.
Conclusion: I'm not going to lie, this was a good game FOR ITS TIME. However, with new games releasing, it doesn't hold up all that much. Even though I haven't played the new updates, the addition of guns makes it more like The Hidden then what Dead Realm was going for. For this game to get my recommendation, it needs to go back to its roots and upgrade the factors that made it such a good game when it was released.

Very promising - There is a surprising amount of content to explore given that this is an early access game.
PROS:
- Many of the complex systems are already in place (such as terraforming, construction, logging, etc.) which is good as this is a crafting game at  heart.
- The huge crafting and skill systems require specialization as you have a finite number of skill points to allocate (on most servers).
- This is great for encouraging player interaction and community building. The idea of having a town blacksmith that you need to go to for swords and armor, a logger to cut your trees, etc. is a lot of fun and not something a lot of games like to encourage. You're not a god, you can't do everything on your own.
CONS:
- Combat is promising and deep but not very satisfying at the moment.
- Long server load times (seriously, be patient).
- The engine needs optimization. This isn't up to the Life is Feudal dev team but it does affect their game.
- Occasional bugs and some people experience frequent crashing.
CONCLUSION:
If the dev team can continue building on what they have without falling into the typical early access pitfalls then this game will be the next big thing. All it will need is a promotion from a YouTuber to blow up.

I can't quite understand how this game is so loved, perhaps the following for civil war era RTS games has carried it perhaps i've missed something while playing it. Forewarning this review is exclusively of my experiences with the single player, the multiplayer may have been fantastic, but i'll never know.
I'll start of by saying I'm quite a fan of RTS games. But this game absolutely wastes its potential in my mind, through a bunch of frustrating issues, that for me obviously were deal breakers.
The AI.
The issue isn't so much the enemy AI, altough it completely does broken crap all the time, as your own unit's AI being absolutely frustrating. Please explain to me how a 1000 strong unit can't destroy an exposed enemy artillery unit, or as to why it doesn't take literal seconds.
Attack commands don't work as you would expect. Move commands also don't work as expected.
Enemy AI routing is stupid. I've encircled you with the entirety of my army. Spent the billion minutes it takes in game to take the long way round your army with a sizeable handful of troops and a few cannons. I've decidedly turned the battle into my favour. Not only have your men realised how screwed they are, but now you're men have fled, and quite rightly so. The day is mine. Watch them flee!
Then take hardly any damage. AS THEY LITERALLY RUN THROUGH YOUR LINES! No matter they've fled the battlefield? Apart from they bloody didn't. They've gone a 100 meters past your line. Decided that they day isn't quite lost and turned around to now shoot your exposed back. In a wonderous example of turning the battle now into their favour. This is futher compounded as more and more troops "rout" en masse to this new superb position, taking less casualties than if they had been ordered too. To now decimate the men you've sent to encircle them.
Routing a cannon unit means they rout with the cannon. Why? Because when fleeing the enemy the first thing you do is hook up you cannon, load up your equipment, and ride away into the game equivalent of a sunset (which as previously mentioned is most likely your exposed flank)
Your cannon's will not hit anything. That 2000 strong infantry unit? Nope. Might as well ask them to hit the moon. They will however happily destroy the ground around them. Remember how decimating an accurate cannon shot was in total war? Well these are nothing like that.
Flanking.
Why bother? Attacking an infantry's flank in this game provides you with no discernible advantage. No massive drop in moral or men. They just fight on like they normally would and usually get the advantage of you having not fired on them while you took the effort to flank. Just don't.
Graphics and UI.
Quite fine. The units are more like sprites with their unit strength above. If you were expecting men individually rendered you'll be dissappointed.
The topological map is a nice touch. However due to the camera angle it can be visually hard to judge whether you are sitting in a defilade or not.
Illogical crap.
Can't for the life of me work out how to target enemy generals. They just stand there around their dying men then retreat to their other soldiers like they're trotting through a rose garden.
The Default controls are some of the worse I've ever seen. Why is everything a group move. WHY CAN'T I TARGET THAT UNIT? I CAN SEE IT. I JUST CAN'T CLICK ON IT. STOP TARGETING THE INFANTRYMEN TARGET THE CANNONS. I'm pretty sure if i was a real general i'd have shot whoever commands half these units. Two Worlds II is another one of those promising games that take you absolutely nowhere.
Gameplay is pretty solid, a 7/10 to say the least, combat feels good and responsive, actions are quickly performed, movement is smooth and you won't feel like it takes four hours to walk from point A to point B, even though the game world is large enough. There is a decent amount of habilities, magic spells, weapons and armors to buy and upgrade, but they are bound to level, meaning that they'll only appear on the game world once you reach a certain level, so if you want to relive the thrill of finding that overpowered legendary item in a chest deep down a cave full of perilous monsters, forget that. All you're gonna get are some lockpicks, a medium healing potion and a wizard's hat. And that is if you're a warrior. 'Cause if you play a mage, the game will make sure that there's a warrior helm in that chest, just so you won't be able to use what you find, a very common issue in modern RPGs.
The game world is pretty large, composed of some three major islands, each one of them themed around something like middle-east, asian, and european designs of builduings, flora and fauna. There are plenty of quests to be done and there's a fair amount of NPCs, but none of them are memorable or even good at all. You're going to do a lot of running around, a little bit of riding around on a horse and even less sailing around, because you only get a boat too goddamn late, and that is another issue with modern RPGs. What the ♥♥♥♥ is wrong with giving the player a ship from the start, so he or she can have some fun sailing around the islands? Anyway, It seems like there's a lot to do, but there isn't, really.
Which brings us to the last point of this review and, by far, the worst thing in this game, not to mention the reason for me to not recomend Two Worlds II to anyone: The game suffers from a all-too-common rushed ending. The first major island will take you quite a long time to complete, since there's a lot to do and see. The second one, a little bit less. The third you can almost skip completely, since there's very little to do on it. The plot is also extremely rushed, with a huge deus ex machina right at the ending, throwing everything you've been doing on the main quest since the start out of the window.
All in all, this game dosen't deserve more than a 5/10 and I would only recomend it if you, like me, have played pretty much every other RPG on existence. You might have some fun with it, but you would probably rather play something else instead.

The good things about the game, which have been pointed out in the positive reviews, I generally agree with.  The main bad thing about it is the developers' lack of historical research on Civil War armies and battles.  They claim (and have designed the game to reflect) that Union soldiers were better-drilled, better trained, and more effective in ranged combat with the musket than the Confederates.  Anyone who's read anything about the battles of Fredericksburg, Chickasaw Bluffs, Spotsylvania, Kennesaw Mountain, and Cold Harbor, among others, can tell you that's untrue.   Confederate infantry was absolutely lethal in ranged combat.   At Cold Harbor Lee's infantry and artillery shot over 7,000 Federals in about 20 minutes, inflicting a total of 12,500 casualties in the entire battle while losing a scant 1,450 themselves.
The developers completely miss the fact that both armies were composed almost entirely of volunteers and conscripts who had been civilians before the war--thus neither side had a real advantage in training.  Proficiency in combat came with experience, and here the Confederates generally had the advantage because instead of raising new regiments to replace losses as the Union did, they fed replacements into existing units so the fresh fish could learn their trade from the veterans in the ranks.
Finally, the developers claim that the Union had more advanced weaponry than the Confederates at the Battle of Gettysburg--supposedly this resulted in their superiority in ranged fire, both with infantry and artillery.  Also untrue.  A modest amount of reading on their part would have revealed what pretty much any student of the Civil War knows--both sides used pretty much the same weapons (except for the Union's repeating rifles and carbines, which were very small in number).  The fact is that at Gettysburg, both Union and Confederate infantry were variously equipped with model 1842 Springfield smoothbore muskets and model 1855 and 1861 Springfield rifled muskets, as well as the British model 1853 Enfield rifled musket (very similar in performance to the Springfield).  Artillery was about the same--both sides mainly used a mixture of 12-pounder Napoleon smoothbore cannon, 3-inch Ordnance Rifles, and 10-pounder Parrott Rifles.  The Union had a higher percentage of rifled guns, but this didn't prove to be too much of an advantage, as rifled projectliles had a tendency to burrow into the ground without doing much damage--the 12-pounder Napoleon smoothbore was actually better in terms of the damage it could do to infantry formations.
These mistaken premises really hurt the game, as they force the Confederate player to charge in situations where it normally wouldn't have been advisable (and charging in this game is pretty useless for both sides, in my experience--the Confederates don't seem to have the advantage in melee combat that the developers advertise).  They also enable the Union player to win simply by forming an intelligent line, placing artillery, and pretty much sitting back and watching the fireworks.
This is a game that wishes it could be Sid Meier's Antietam and Sid Meier's Gettysburg.  It could have been if the developers had gone into more depth with unit tactics, put more realism into the game mechanics, and done the necessary historical research.  You know there's something fishy when a single AI infantry brigade routs 4 artillery batteries in a frontal assault, uphill, with no support while taking minimal casualties, but when you try it with three brigades in a flank attack you get butchered.  There are other similar problems with the mechanics that have already been noted in the reviews.

One of my favorite games. I usually have a dislike for realistic shooter, be they first or third person. I usually want to have some more fantasy or sci fi feel to them, but this game, while based as much as yo0u can in history without actually making a game on historic accounts, is quite fun. The game is built so that you can traverse most of the maps completely in stealth, and a large part of the challenge comes from that element, to map out how your enemies are moving about, when and where to strike to get away cleanly before the next kill.
You have a few game mechanics to help you on your way. Most notably is the sound overlap. In vertain maps there is things like bombers flying over dropping bombs on the town nearby or a PA system shouring out orders. During these sound overlaps you can shoot someone without anyone noticing, unless they can actually see your target go down.
The difficulty level is a nice ladder to climb. To start with you don't have an kind of physics affecting your bullet. Whatever you point your crosshair at you will hit. With each difficulty physics are introduced more and more, with visual aids in your scope to none, and heavily affected by gravity and winds. It is however very satisfying when you manage to get a headshot on an enemy 300 meters (328 yards) away, with wind changing the horizontal position and gravity the vertical without any help at all from the computer.
Last but not least the bullet cam should be mentioned. At random times (very few forced ones, and frequency can be set in Settings) you get to follow your bullt from exiting your rifle until it tears the flesh and shatters the bones of your opponent. You also get to see an X-ray of the area affected by the bullet, and how it passes through the body of your victim.
There are of course a few drawbacks as well. The AI could be smarter on the more difficult settings. If you would stand, talking to a guy, turn away to light a smoke or something, and then turn back and he just vanished, you might get a little bit concerned. Specially in wartime. Not here though.
The only addons available are either actual hacks, or DLC's. There is no community modding at all, and I hear this was a concious choice of the developer, which I think is too bad. They should compete with quality, not monopoly for their addons. Community modding can bring so much more value to a game than a developer could after the initial release.
All in all a fun game with a "long enough" single player campaign, Co-op and multiplayer options.

Your enjoyment of Amnesia: The Dark Descent hinges almost entirely on what you expect to get out of it.
As a horror game, certainly what it’s advertised and probably considered by most to be, it shockingly comes across as rather...uninteresting. It does an amazing job setting a tense, foreboding atmosphere, layering on copious amounts of disturbing exposition and twisted imagery. And then sort of throws it away when it attempts to bring it all to boiling point and scare you out of your wits, relying on a sluggish, rather dimwitted monster which is rather less than frightening and scare tactics which all too quickly become  predictable.
The sense of dread I felt when I first awoke in the mysterious castle that makes up Amnesia, was lost after just a few hours, as it became dreadfully easy to guess exactly when and how the game would attempt to scare me, no matter how much I kept hoping that it would reject my expectations. Picking up key items, opening a particularly unappealing door, or finding a note; Amnesia’s list of triggers is short and used liberally, making for an experience that quite frankly left me a bit annoyed at how little it managed to get to me. I was practically begging to be scared by the end, but aside from a few very brief standout sections Amnesia almost does more to set you at ease than it does to freak you out.
I say all this, and yet, Amnesia is still immensely compelling as something completely atypical of what I would have guessed: a traditional adventure game. Behind the gruesome imagery and very effective atmosphere, the excellent puzzle designs and exploration were what kept me intrigued and wanting to come back to the game. Though they’re often simple in design, there’s a rewarding logic to each puzzle that makes them unexpectedly enjoyable to solve. Frictional Games manages to make blind exploration and continual backtracking interesting and continually stimulating, with each area you visit being visually distinct and engaging, and often holding within contextual exposition that creates a great sense of place and causes the castle to feel far larger than just the areas you explore.
When you’re not solving puzzles, the disorganized narrative compels you forward, leaving you vague notes that give just enough information to make you want to learn more while rarely telling you the whole story until the very end. Finding the details of this plot are often disturbing and thoroughly unpleasant, leaving me feeling rather mixed about my protagonists actions but nonetheless complacent as I couldn’t leave this story unfinished. The flashbacks/hallucinations that your character often witnesses gives a look into how the castle used to operate, horribly inhumane and driven by some mysterious supernatural element, but all the same a place I wanted to learn more about if only so I could make sense of my character’s madness.
This madness is perhaps the game’s strongest achievement, distorting the world around you and causing you to see things that may very well not be there. Staying too long in the dark wears on your sanity, requiring you to ransack every room you come across so you can be sure to have enough oil for your lantern and tinderboxes to light candles and torches. I was a bit disappointed that these resources came in such large supply, as it made darkness less of a threat and more of an occasional hindrance to your view, but the mechanic was still engaging enough to cause me to pay more attention to the environment and as a result find things I may otherwise have missed.
It’s a little funny to me that despite being let down by the aspect that I expected would have prevented me from even finishing the game, what I found underneath it proved more than enough to push me through the game. If you’re hoping Amnesia will leave you terrified and sleeping with the lights on, you’ll most likely be let down by the underdeveloped, somewhat lazy frights found here. But if you can appreciate the game without those prerequisites, there’s an eerie and twisted adventure game waiting to swallow you whole into its brilliantly realized darkness.
