The game is unlike anything else on the market, it is becoming and will become a cult classic just like I predicted when I reviewed this game a few days after the release (the Nazi Zombie expansion packs attest to that)  There are only three major negatives about this game that I can think of:
1) It is not as immersive and complex as the first game;
2) The enemy AI could be improved, but its not terrible;
3) The game could be harder.
I've been playing this game practically non-stop since it came out.
There are certainly some trade-offs for the negatives. The graphics have been improved over the first game, obviously. The Asura engine is now one of my favorite engines, it shined in Aliens Vs. Predator and it's pretty good here. Except I don't understand why the last AVP game had Directx 11 support and this game doesn't. That is kind of inconsistent on the part of Rebellion. The bullet ballistics are still pretty good although they have been made easier since the first game. After a pretty fast learning curve you will be able to snipe targets away pretty easily. So I do kind of wish that it could be harder to snipe targets, for the better kill satisfaction. The graphics are pretty decent, I just with the anti-aliasing applied to every jaggy out there.
The X-ray slow-mo camera. You can shoot your enemy's gonads off, you can shoot their jaw off, you can destroy their rib cages, their kidneys, their heart, their lungs, their eyes. The skull can also be destroyed in many ways even when the enemy is wearing a helmet. You just never get tired of it. I am frankly surprised that other shooting games haven't attempted this before and it is 2012!
The physics of the game are pretty good. There is plenty of destruction to go around. What I also loved is that if you make your character sit and then start slowly rotating the camera view either left or right, you will actually see your character chance stance by turning the torso and moving the legs. It just FEELS that you are controlling someone. Compare that with Skyrim's third person view. When you do the same thing in that game, your character will just start levitating in air without shuffling legs or changing the body position.
The bullet ballistics are good but can get predictable. If you miss your first shot from afar, you can immediately adjust your aim to shoot either slightly to the left or to the right, depending on where the last bullet hit.
The online co-op campaign, something that is missing in so many games, thanks for not having an emblem for that, gamespot. My buddy and I spent hours carefully going through the 11 NON-RECYCLED AND VARIOUS missions. Not only that, there is a horde mode, or the Kill Tally mode, (only 2 players), with 10 waves and an increasing amount of enemies plus enemy trucks, jeeps, halftracks and tiger tanks (last wave only). There are 3 maps for that, each with plenty of locations to hide and hold your ground. You can plant trip wires, mines, dynamite. You can also self ignite enemy vehicles by shooting their fuel tank. You can also kill two or three enemies at a time with one bullet and even kill them with ricochet when they are hiding. There is also a bombing run mode, where you and your partner attempt to collect auto parts for fixing a vehicle and extracting. It is much harder than Kill Tally. There is also an overwatch mode (3 maps only) wherein you and your partner can either play as a sniper or the attacker conducting the ground assault. Finally, there is team deathmatch, with 2 new additional maps that were just added by Rebellion a couple of days ago.
The story is okaish but damn is it made up, straight out of Inglorious Basterds. You are an American (of course) sniper in Berlin in April 1945 (yeah right), killing Germans and....Russians (with American bullets, ooookay), who is supposed to stop the Russian launch of captured V-2 rockets with poisonous gas on London as a prelude for the Cold War. It's preposterous if you have any respect for history.
There is a lack of stealth in the game. I mean you could do it in about half the missions but it's more fun just shooting ze Germans and ze Russkies. Whenever you decide to go stealth, make sure to snipe targets during a loud sound as to not alert nearby enemies. You can also search your slain enemies for the ammo and supplies. You can also pick them up and hide them. As you progress, you find new weapons that you can later use in multiplayer but there aren't that many of them.
The sound is good. There are distant explosions in the background, there are low and high altitude planes flying. There isn't a single civilian in the entire game though.
The enemies could use some work. They aren't terrible though. They shoot, they take cover, they change positions, they zigzag, they throw grenades, they pick up and treat their fallen comrades. The snipe from afar and CHANGE THEIR SNIPING POSITIONS. The only real thing that I would have liked is for them to stick to their cover for longer times if they are being shot at by the sniper. The slowing down of time is neat, but it makes the game super easy. That technique is meant for the controller, since you can't aim as well with the two sticks.
Finally, this is a great game if you are looking for something fresh. I can only hope that Rebellion adds a map editor. There are just so many scenarios to invent here.  The game is somewhat innovative, fun and pretty solid.
All in all, awesome game. Go ahead and support Rebellion. They have redeemed themselves after AVP.

Retro refined for every generation.  Too often, retraux games abuse being old-fashioned as an excuse for their flaws, whether it be a cheesy artstyle or an uneven challenge.  Shovel Knight, on the other hand, is meticulously crafted, having learned its gameplay lessons from each and every era.  The visuals and titular hero's jumping mechanics might be from the NES, but the lives system is done away in favor of a modern checkpoint system designed to curb frustration and help master its oldschool challenges.  And then it goes the extra mile, with touches like leaving in the option to discard that help in favor of more rewards.  The RPG elements used to raise your stats are a well-balanced grind to reward your efforts while infusing the world with enjoyable exploration.  The level designs, boss fights, and subweapons have all learned from the best while putting in their own spin to be memorable.
Crazier still, long after buying Shovel Knight, it keeps finding new ways to impress.  When I thought a legitimate flaw in the base gameplay was the action-halting fishing mechanic, Plague Knight comes along to eschew the whole thing.  Once I felt the chiptune soundtrack might be wearing out early, every track got remixed for Spectre Knight's DLC.  Both for free and turning out to add layers to every corner of the world.  The game continues refining itself, already three times bigger than it has any business being.
More than anything, Shovel Knight uses simplicity as a tool rather than a crutch.  The faceless character designs exude personality through their distinct silhouettes, colors, and tireless animation.  The sountrack is such a tight fit to every environment like a moody, catchy glove.  The story gets showing over telling so well, it can make guest characters give you the warm and fuzzies where you'd expect a cringe minefield.  Driven by limitless ambition and never satisfied with mere gimmicks, Shovel Knight goes far beyond resembling the classics to joining their ranks as one of the greats.

Have you ever bought a game before, and then suddenly got a sequel for free, and then a prequel for free, and then get told that one more game is on the way? All because a bunch of people bet their wallets on the inherent goodness and competence of humanity, like, three or four years ago?
That's not what happened here in technicality, but in functionality, that is 100% what happened.
And yes, it was all good: three whole unique, polished, and memorable campaigns of NES-style platforming, all well-stocked with memorable characters, interesting and fun stages, bonus challenges and secrets, and an extensive, well-crafted OST.
And no, it doesn't rely on le ebin nostalgia- this is probably the only good modern, Mega Man-styled game you'll play in a very long time. Even then, it resembles Mega Man only in structure- the items, combat and level design work entirely different, making Shovel Knight a thing of its own.

I play every 4x/base building game that comes out. In almost every game, I find myself wishing that X would be automated in some way. Such as, hiring bots, employees, or machines to do marketing, sales, shipping... whatever the task happens to be in the context of the game, and I'm invariably let down every, single, time. No developer has ever gotten this workflow right. In fact, some even argue that too much automation takes away "work" from the game. I've hand delivered X item to X person 100 times now; Why do I have to keep doing this same damn mission over and over Elite Dangerous? I literally can't hire a space mailman to deliver packages? I gotta do it myself? Jesus.
Thankfully, FortressCraft: Evolved has none of that grindy crap and they did automation properly. I spent a 1100hrs playing this game. I've been on Steam for 6 years and never bothered to write a review before. You need to buy this game.
The entire purpose of this game is to automate production. You build a machine that poops out other machines, which poops out crafted items. Automate all the things!! In one sense, that does make it feel like Factorio, and it has blocks like Minecraft. But boiling this game down to simply those observations shows how little you actually understand. FortressCraft has snap-to production building like Big Pharma and tower defense like Clash of Clans. Unlike Minecraft, there actually is a goal to achieve in FortressCraft. Quite simply, this is the best game of 2016 and I doubt you've played anything like it before.
If there were any downsides to this game, I'd say it will take longer to win than you think it will. You will lose a few times because you don't know how much power all the guns take. So, you try to half♥♥♥♥♥it and get power. But, then you find out you need 10x power you though was required, and your production chain is a mess. So, you have to rip things up and move them around. Some  people don't like ripping everything up and redoing their base design. But, that's part of the experimentation and learning process everyone goes through when they play this game.
The "winning condition" is to power the orbital transmitter, and the expansion goal is building a machine that will drill down to planetary magma. Pro Tip, you can not power the damn thing with just 10 generators you started out using in the beginning of the game. Don't be "that guy" who complains the game is taking days to power the Orbital Transmitter because you are using coal you found in the beginning of the game.
If you find yourself complaining FCE should build products like Factorio, then the problem is that you are not automating properly. See, as long as you have the technology in Factorio, you can build products without setting up the proper production chain, and that's cheating. In FCE, you need to place the wire maker down, and supply it with copper, or you will have no wire. No Factorio style cheating here. What I'm getting at is that the game isn't badly designed. You are simply being lazy and spolied. If you can't be bothered to place your own machines and conveyor belts, then you can just go play any LEGO game where you mindlessly click on some self assembling blocks and be done with it.
Additionally, the limited graphic style of Factorio means it's all 2d. But in FCE, you build 3 dimensional. This creates interesting tasks to do for people that like to do things "just so" in a quest for perfection. The most inefficient automation is always better than manual effort, and multiple solutions will all work, so don't worry about perfection. The thing to remember is if the game feels "tedious" then you're not automating enough. Like if you find yourself shooting enemies with your pistol, that means you haven't built enough gun or missile defense. So, stop trying to gun down bosses with the god damn pistol. If all those guns you made drain your power, then guess what? Yeah, the next thing you need to do is build more power. In fact, it's the consumption of power that drives the game foward. More power creates more enemies, which require more guns, which creates more loot drops, used in machines which requires more power, etc.
There is enough stuff to do that you shouldn't be sitting there watching machines tick away. That's means you're wasting time. Yes, that landscape clearing machine does work slowly. It's supposed to. You're not supposed to sit there and stare at it like a tea pot. Give it power, and go do something else for ten minutes. Mine more coal, research something, harvest some crystals, and by the time you get done with that the base will be clear. This is what makes you fell like real game progress is being made. You will literally be absorbed into 10 things going on at once before the sun comes up. If you're bored because "things take to long" then what you need to do is multitask.
Unlike every other "something-Craft" game, there is no "build order" to follow by rote memorization, or a plan to spend your power efficiently. Such as; make 10 tin, then make exactly 2 hoppers, then make 2 lasers... No no no no. This isn't StarCraft. Consume all the power you can. When you run out, just build more generators. Build thousands of missiles, burn hundreds of coal a second. Consumption. This game is a consumption simulator. It doesn't matter that a quarry is less efficient than an excavator. Because the whole point of this game is to build all the machines, power them, and have them do stuff automatically! What I said will take the average player 100hrs before it finally clicks, "Oh, build lots of everything. I get it now".
The developer made sure you can play the game "to the end" without needing the expansion. The thing is, much like a Star Wars movie, you've just watched Star Wars, and your NOT going to see Empire Strikes Back... are you crazy? You have to see Empire! So, in that sense, Frozen Factory is a "must have".

Rome Total War was the first game that I was ever obsessed with, being early in high school when it came out in 2004. I actually first saw the game engine on the History Channel’s show Decisive Battles, which used the game to depict the Battle of Cannae, among others.
The slaughter that can be witnessed and commanded on the RTS battlefield in this game came at a pivotal time, when Lord of the Rings rewrote the book on grand fantasy movies. You saw these huge battles on screen in movies, and now you could command them yourself.
From experience the central mechanics of a game obviously must grab you to hold interest, but I also believe that the little details can be just as important in showing the player how much the developers love their work. Those that struck me in this game were the hilarious descriptions and attributes of the generals, which adds flesh to the polygons you command.
Here you could find that your general could be a bold Caesar, or an insane Caligula (literally one of the attributes can describe a character as painting his butt blue and running around the palace naked). These attributes can affect what your generals say in their speeches before a battle; I would always make insane generals my frontline commanders, just so I could hear them say ridiculous things before a battle.
The game is fun, has plenty charm, and an epic soundtrack; still plenty of bugs, but they can be worked around. Try roleplaying your generals in battle, and your faction leader in the campaign map based upon their respective attributes.

DNF has been forever in the making & has finally arrived. DNF might lack story & character depth [that's for sure] & the graphics might look 5 years OLD, but DNF surely can be a lot of fun b/c when DNF is on, DNF is on point. When it's not, well...it's not.
DNF is a shooter, but it often tries to be more than a shooter - also having a puzzle-physics elements & tons of interactivity w/ objects in the game-world.
The on & off early part of the SP portion might throw the player for a loop, but don't quit yet - the game gets better once you leave The Lady Killer casino...A LOT better. Later on, a few levels are pointless [the strip club] or often repetitive [the get gas 3 times for the truck mission] - which unfortunately also drag the game's quality down a quite a bit.
The MP feels like a throwback to the good old days of DN3D; Quake 2 + 3 glory; and UT days, which is welcome - but, if only there were more maps & game modes.
DNF certainly might not be worth the original $60 price-tag, but DNF surely is worth the $20 or less that it is often going for now.

I tried liking this game, I really did, but it caught a nasty case of modern shooter syndrome and ultimately turned me off from playing it again. The beginning was great! I couldn't ask for anything more from Duke when you're making popcorn or screwing around with the interactive stuff. That's what made Duke different from most other shooters, not what happens in the end. I wish it took more cues from the earlier Duke game, Manhatten Project, and left his Ego meter as a health meter with health pick-ups, not this. That and ammo is almost instantly replenished. This is not the game I expected, and didn't exactly want. I honestly wanted to like this game, but there's so many flaws that now I don't even recognize Duke. His one-liners are often repeated and reflect a disinterested voice actor rather than capturing the true voice of Duke. All I can say is that the developer who picked it up last gave it their best shot and shouldn't be judged by this failure. The ship had already sank.

I bought this game looking for a good Civil War fix and was sadly disappointed.  A few issues that I will point out.
a.)  Units taking fire to the front (even in less than 20% cover, take no casualties, whereas fire from the flank causes catastrophic losses).  Sure, I understand that flank fire would cause more damage, but not 10-20x as much.
b.)  Cavalry is useless.  I click charge, the unit literally runs halfway across the map in the other direction.
c.)  Artillery does not unlimber.  It sits there and gets shot at for five minutes while I try to figure out how to get it to unlimber (because there is no button?  why?)
d.)  Same charge issues with infantry...how do unlimbered (ie, pushed) guns run away from my charging troops?  Explain please.
Ultimately, what I have found playing back and forth is that the defender wins 90% of the time.  Units set in defense fire, units attacking are often bugged and do not fire, so they just stand there and get shot at.  Because of the bad charge mechanics, the Confederates advantage in morale and skill (ie, hand to hand) is basically null and void.  Similarly, if trying to push guns forward to support an advance, you lose all of your guns because they bug and won't unlimber for four or five minutes (I timed this, actually).
Because of this, I view this game as being pretty much unplayable.  It's no fun playing a strategy game when your strategy won't work because of bugs or flawed mechanics.  It makes no sense that when I order a bayonet charge, my troops just mill around in a big mass, neither attacking nor retreating.  It also makes no sense that units route in one or two volleys.
If you want a good recreation of Gettysburg, maybe you should have modded Shogun 2 or another Total War game.  At least their units actually charge.  Also, I find the morale mechanics in Total War to actually be more realistic, as opposed to the units that run away when the enemy sneezes at them, or when they are sitting in an open field not even close to the fighting.

I love sniping games. Well, I'll rephrase that by saying I love the power and potential one has with a long-distance killing machine.
That's what this game does. Not only does it show you the value of power and how it feels to wield it, but it also shows you how easy it is for it to be taken away.
This game is meant to be played on its highest difficulty, the 'Sniper Elite' difficulty, as it includes bullet drop, a wind speed factor, as well as miniscule health/ammo. You are given a plethora of tools at your disposal such as dynamite, trap mines, and even the ability to throw rocks with the intention of distracting and leading your enemies elsewhere for a humanitarian purpose. (Most of the time)
And this is that power I was referring to earlier, the ability to manuever and manipulate your foe without them knowing who is leading them on.
However, if they find out...
You have to remember that you are only a sniper, and that the extent of your abilities only ranges from long-distance and is sub-par face-to-face.
But enough with the philosophical♥♥♥♥♥♥ this game is pretty ♥♥♥♥ing badass. (Can I curse on these reviews?)
No really, I'll be whooping and hollering if I get headshot after headshot, the killcam doing the perfect amount of justice in allowing me to witness the damage I internally cause with my one bullet.
You see bones breaking, nuts cracking, and eyeballs bursting, making a mess in the most grueseome yet destructively beautiful manner possible.
And the graphics, scenery, and atmosphere are very breathtaking at points, especially when you have a bird's eye view of your battlefield.
And for those who want to have an idea on how the game runs, my rig consists of a FX-6300 and a EVGA 760 and I can run this game from 45-60 fps Maxed out with 2X SSAA.
If this review doesn't sit tightly with you, then try out the demo which does half as much justice since it includes only a small portion of the game's features; but regardless, it won't hurt to try.
Have fun!

That's not what happened here in technicality, but in functionality, that is 100% what happened.
And yes, it was all good: three whole unique, polished, and memorable campaigns of NES-style platforming, all well-stocked with memorable characters, interesting and fun stages, bonus challenges and secrets, and an extensive, well-crafted OST.
And no, it doesn't rely on le ebin nostalgia- this is probably the only good modern, Mega Man-styled game you'll play in a very long time. Even then, it resembles Mega Man only in structure- the items, combat and level design work entirely different, making Shovel Knight a thing of its own.

I'd like to recommend this game as it was a bit of fun for me, but I think it's too flawed to recommend as a non-free game. Sure it's cheap at $10, and I got it for 50% off, but it was 2.5 hours long for me, and some of the content is stretched out a bit (like a 4+ minute segment of simply driving a car along a hazardless path to the next level). Chongo had a few good moments, but overall the characters aren't funny or memorable while jokes are delivered in quantity but without quality. It feels like a really good rough draft for a game, but that it needs some serious revision.
Poor performance wasn't a big problem overall, but I think that's due to the gameplay being very casual with rather simple requirements and lack of twitch reflexes, as well as the majority of levels being very minimal and bland. The game starts in a fairly detailed town with many structures and moving objects, and there's another level full of traffic and landmarks passing through the scene that's fairly detailed, but other levels are mostly empty rooms and tunnels with textured walls and few objects. I ended up playing through the game on Low graphics attempting to improve performance, but even then FPS was only 30-40 in the nice areas. In other areas I probably could have turned it to high and done fine.
I wouldn't say this game was a waste of time, but it doesn't really have the impact to justify playing regardless of the price. If you are really interested in it, then go for it, as there are much worse ways to spend time and money, but if you're on the fence then just pass. I wouldn't recommend watching a Let's Play, as the minimal entertainment it provides comes from driving the deputy.

The goal of the sniper is to strike from secret. He is not a run-n-gun assault trooper. He creeps into a hidden spot and waits for his victim to enter his line of sight and then, at the appropriate moment, surgically eliminates his target. Far too often, Sniper Elite v2 forgets this and instead throws you into the fray as if you were Rambo.
Oh, on occasion the game remembers that it is a game reputably about sniping. In these moments, the tension is palpable as you try to peg that crucial target without giving away your location. But alas, the game seems far more keen on luring you into narrow, linear death-traps so it can spawn waves of enemies who advance towards you, magically knowing where you are even before you make your presence known to them with high-velocity bullets. Sadly, these too-frequent battles feel unoriginal and dull, and the game has little else with which to redeem itself.

Okay so, this ♥♥♥♥ing game, as you can clearly see, it gets nothing but positive reviews, my review in particualr will get swept away and quickly forgotten or never read, BUT that does not really matter, for one simple reason. This game is so gosh diddly darn fantastic, I feel more dirty not reviewing it.
To begin there was a wonderful little game called shovel knight, if you were playing it on PC the controls were a bit wonkey, but hey, you can change those, said little game felt like a call back, a loving little tribute to all the classic 2D platformers that we loved, yet with its own modern flare that set it above the rest, uniqu character designs, great backround art, each stage feels alive and pops in its own way with beautiful complimentary colors and unique enemies, the story was nice as well, it was heartfelt and not so shockingly had a happy ending, even down to the little stuff like the after credits scenes had a heart felt touch to them. its amazing! Not to mention all the power ups you can both buy and find, it provides insentive to go and replay a stage, just as a stand alone game, shovel knight would have been just fine. But oh no, then out of no where BAM co-op baby! Now I could both shovel AND knight with a buddy? Sign me the ♥♥♥♥ up! Now sadly I have no friends who have the game on the PC as well, so I never experianced co-op, but its a great example of a content creator hearing and listening to a suggestion from thier customers. Think thats it? nope!
Secondly, out of literally no where they came out with an update NOT a DLC, I'll explain that in a moment, the update was titled "Plague of Shadows" and you played as one of the earlier bosses in the game, Plague knight, your entire gameplay strategy was changed, the way plague knight moved, interacted with the enviroment, his attacks, his interations with the "towns people" etc, all was different, but that doesnt mean its worse, now the world is built for your type of movement as plague knight, its all diferent and you need to adapt, its engaging, its interesting, its just a good ♥♥♥♥ing game. Not to mention this came as a free update to the game, not a purchased DLC, which is an amazing surprise, and its not just a litle do it quick side mission, its an entire other game, both shovel knight and plague knights adventures took me about 5 hours each, money well spent, 9/10 would reccomend, if you enjoy two different perspectives and story lines both beautifully animated and having loads of personality, go and buy this game.
...
Wait, whats this? ANOTHER UPDATE, yes folks thats right, they came out with a third update, this one titled "Specter of torment" and much like Plague Knights update, this one was free of charge, added a whole new game, as well as a new and unique way to explore the world. You play as specter knight, which I personally wasnt too stoked about, he's the second boss of the game, and his stage was always a little tricky for me, so I didnt think i was going to like it. But chuck ♥♥♥♥ing testa, I fell in love, everything, EVERYTHING about the specter knight storyline I loved, from how its a prequel, to his shattered memories, to the sheer badassery they game him. Plus you can grind on rails using your scythe. Dope AF. I won't go in to too much detail, because this review is already crazy long, but needless to say, play the Specter of Torment update, you wont regret it.
All that being said, if you've got 30 bucks laying around, and you like a 2D platformer with lovely animations, great pixel art, frog puns and apple fish, and you get 2 bonus stories on top of the title story (maybe with more to come) then please buy this game, you really wont be disappointed. 12/10 would strike random walls looking for wall-chicken again.

So after quite a bit of time playing this game, modded, unmodded, singleplayer, multiplayer, etc. I feel its about time I write a review.
+ Gigantic maps full of scenery and towns and cities
+ Constant dev support and new content releases (free DLC even)
+ Very high quality campaigns with replayability
+ Dozens of guns and vehicles
+ Sandbox type map creation and mission creation
+ Steam workshop
+ Enormous and mostly friendly community
+ Lots of gamemodes (Roleplay, Invade and Annex, Intel Recovery, Hostage Recovery, etc.)
+ Extremely detailed models and guns, replicating real world counter parts
+ Difficult FPS that thankfully pushes away immature and whiny players
+ Teamwork based game (Going lone wolf style will result in failure unless the mission is designed for it)
+ Modding from third party websites in additon to the Workshop (Armaholic for example)
-
- Extremely clunky and buggy engine. It looks nice but its outdated. A 64bit edition was released recently, fixing FPS issues and other problems but the game is still very clunky. (You can vault through objects, flip cars by touching sidewalks, and bullet physics dont always work as they should)
- Unbalanced. You'll find a lot, if not the majority of gamemodes in this game are co-op, PVP gamemodes have heavy restrictions on many weapons and gear as well. This is because between the 3 factions (BLUFOR, OPFOR, and Independant) there are many inconsistencies and balancing problems that make certain weapons and gear so powerful that it renders many others useless. For example: if you own the Apex DLC, you get access to the Special Operations (VIPER) gear. This includes: a bullet resistant helmet with built in thermal and nightvision, a underarmor clothing that is bullet resistant (more so than some vests) and is thermal-proof (this means you will not show up under any thermal scope) and a automatic rifle that switches firemodes from 5.56 rounds to .50 BW rounds based on what mag you have in it. By paying for one DLC you get access to these weapons, while non-dlc owners do not. The AI however, are not DLC locked, and have access to this gear and will use it and the other high tier weapons and armor that you may not have access to.
- The recent DLC: Jets. Now this part is personal preference, but the newest DLC called "Arma 3: Jets" is, to put bluntly, a donation DLC. By this I mean you're buying it, not because of what content it provides, but because you want to support BI. Now this is perfectly ok with me and all to you if that's what you wish to do with your money. Many of the DLC in this game (such as Helicopters) are in that same boat of content vs. price. Now you're probably asking "Why?" and here is why: the steam workshop. I'm a fan of BI and have purchased the entire Arma franchise with all DLC back to Operation Flashpoint, and why? Because it was good quality. The newest DLC releasing however, has not been. The Jets DLC features 3(?) new fighter jets and a static aircraft carrier to be placed in the world using the editor. Along with this came a free platform update, overhauling the flying mechanics, radar system, and more for all players, DLC purchasers and not. The problem with this, is that through the Steam Workshop you can find (in my opinion) better planes and a MUCH better Aircraft Carrier with all the features of the DLC one and more. And the best part is all of these are free. Now as I said, this last point here is entirely personal opinion and I know people who love the new jets and aircraft carrier, however I'm not a fan.

I really like the idea of this game.  It is basically heavily modded minecraft meets factorio.  You are in an open world / sandbox with lots of resources.  You can explore and exploit those resourcs similar in a manner to minecraft.  However, there are enemies which wish to destroy your base, so your resources go to teching up and building defenses.  Id love to see a lot more games like this.  I had a lot of fun, but I didn't finish it.  It does have its problems.
The good:
It is a wonderful minecraft like game and the designer does a lot of nice things that other games can certainly take a hint from.  For example, you can access any object at any distance as long as you can see it.  IE:  To craft things you do not need to walk to your crafting table, you just have to look at it to use it.  To pull stuff out of a storage system, just look at it, even if you are 60 blocks away, and you can access it.   Then you also get a grappling hook that lets you move around very quickly.  This is an invaluable too.   There are lots of technologies and systems to build.
The Bad:
The documenation is terrible.  You have to spend research points and you only have a vague idea of what it is you are getting.  You also can research things early on that you can not build for a long time, due to tech requirments.  Also sometimes there are "packages" of research items where buying just one item is useless because you will need to buy 2 or 3 others to complete the set.  If you spend too many RP points, you may end up stuck (although ultimatly you can get out of this hole, but it can block you for a while).
The tech tree is also just a mess and the organization on the build tab makes little sense.  Often I have to search for the item I want to craft because I have no idea what tab it belongs.
The mechanics of how to progress and how to use things are often mysterious.  There is a wiki, but it is often out of date.  You shouldn't have to use an in-game wiki.
The ugly:
This game is grindy.  The designer just makes things take a rediculous amount of resources in terms of materials, power requirements and crafting time.  A good example of this is some machine that will take animal parts and turn them into some generic part that you can craft items with.  This machine takes a huge amount of power, and takes 5 MINUTES to craft 1 component.  You may need 20 to 80 components to craft some of the items you want.  So for 20, you are looking at 1 hour and 40 minutes.  It gets even worse, it takes 10 raw material to get 1 component.  And gets even worse, that these components will rot unless they are put in yet another setup that is also power hungry that extends their life time.  Its nuts.
That is just one example, there are others, like the 100 MILLION units of power needed to charge a certain object, that you need to do 4x.  With several stacks of turbine generators, it can still take like 4 hours per charge.  This isn't fun, its boring.  Many of the crafting recipies just require rediculous amounts of material for no good reason.
Summary:
For the price, the game is a great deal.  I had a lot of fun with it until the grind killed me.  Maybe Ill check it out again in 6 months to a year.

This game fills a gap in good tactical civil war combat games, and has a very simplified interface that makes it accessible.
Brigades are the smallest unit of command, which I found unfortunate because it left me unable to replicate the involved maneuvering and micromanagement of Sid Meier's Gettysburg.
Perhaps the best feature is the game's branching campaign, with the level of victory the player achieves in any given battle and what objectives were taken setting the stage for the next combat.
A great deal is under the hood and hard to understand- different brigades are between 1 and 3 stars in effectiveness, for example, but certain brigades reload faster than others of the same rank.
If anything the two sides are too asymmetrical- Union infantry's morale is brittle to the point of being near useless on the offensive, while its artillery is much better than the confederates. (Equipment for both sides was largely dimilar, and the engine evidently tracks what artillery is equipped with what piece, but does not make this knowledge public to the player. So it will be a mystery why "Cooper" artillery shells so much more effectively than "Stevens" or so on.)
Maneuvering can be fiddly, units reform after having their morale broken far too easily, and melee devolves into one side fleeing while the other pursues and is shot by adjascent units far too often. This is made most egregious when artillery units flee bayonet charges. Artillery also is suspiciously impervious; an exposed battery can be expected to take a couple of volleys from a brigade before thinking bettery of their situation.
Some sort of tooltip system would have been nice- In larger battles where you find yourself commanding 40,000 men, it is possible for units to stand unresponsive in blistering fire without being noticed, and the game becomes focused on herding rallied units back to the front and making sure no disasters are taking place more so than coordinating interesting maneuvers.
Still, Ultimate General Gettysburg is easy to jump into. Compared to Sid Meiers Gettysburg or the Take Command series, is wanting in period feel. More music would not have been amiss.
All in all a good effort marred by some minor issues. I look forward to the sequel.

Amnesia is more than a game, it's an experiance. A terrifying and disturbing experience that will last with you long before you put the game down.
I'm someone who loves horror and all that is creepy, I'm someone who can calmly play any Resident Evil or Silent Hill game. But with Amnesia, I don't have that option.
See, with other horror games, you're given weapons, a way to defend yourself. In Amnesia, the only weapon you have is your mind. That's right, there's not a single weapon in the game, and this is a great thing. With no way to defend yourself, all you can do is run and hide and hope that monster walks past the room where you're hiding in. This captures nothing but pure terror.
Monsters don't just hear you and see you, they can find you based on your sanity level. Staying too long in the dark or looking at disturbing things will drain your sanity. To regain it, you must progress and stay in well lit areas, which are often hard to come by in Amnesia. It goes without saying that you should do everything in your power to keep your sanity level up, or else everything is harder to do, even to tell whether that noise you heard is a monster, or just a product of your imagination.
In addition to the terror aspect of Amnesia, there is also an interesting story and detailed areas to explore, that capture the dark feel of the game. Also, there are custom stories for this game, that are mods created by users that add to the playability to Amnesia. Even after you beat Amnesia, there is more to play with these custom stories.
So, the question is, should you buy this game? Yes, absolutly. At a sale? If you wanna wait and save a little money, sure, but I recommend getting this game even at full price. Whether you're familiar with horror, or this is your first horror game, it has something to offer you, an unforgettable experience.

This is hesitant negative review, the game does have a lot of potential and has provided nearly a 100 hours of fun game play despite a lot of short comings. And in that sense it's a good purchase. It has fairly unique feel to it and in the beginning the open world mantra of feel your way around to figure out how things work and what your goals are is a lot of fun.
In this phase you can overlook a lot of little things, odd interface for dealing with inventories, an apparent disdain for chests to the point of letting you hold 1000's of bars in your inventory. No RPG like interface to hold upgrades for your character ( which are essentially armor upgrades ) so they just sit in your general inventory. Tons of little visual and animation glitches that don't affect the game play. Some odd sound choices like your power storage ( batteries ) making a lot more noise than your generators, which leads to the odd situation where when you run out of power and your generators power up , it suddenly gets quite.
But at some point all of these little things start to get harder to overlook and the game starts to change from fun to a grind that will have you leaving it running in the background while you do other things.
The big problem is near the end game, the design philosophy suddenly changes from one that provides fun and rewarding game play while designing your automation systems to one of forcing you into massive grinds. You are no longer automating for the joy of designing virtual machines or because you feel rewarded for doing so, but because the game forces a lot of pain on you if you don't.
In the end I don't regret getting the game, I had a lot of fun with it for a good amount of time. I do regret getting the DLC and that's about the only recommendation I can make, make sure you complete the first part of game and are ok with how it plays in the end before committing to the DLC ( although in fairness even with the cost of the DLC it was a good value )

For a game that's been in early access and development for so long you'd think you might buy a product thats worth even the measely $5 it had gone on sale for.
The answer is no, it most definitely is not worth even a fraction of that. It'd be questionable to even play this game if it was F2P as you might as well just chop out your frontal lobe and you'd get the same effect as playing this game but in a much shorter time.
1. Gunplay is awful and inconsistant, the developers probably thought it'd be funny to make every weapon act on more of a RNG then actual predictable spray patterns and recoil, no the bullets literally spray in every direction even when aimming down sight, so the most effective way to play the game is to run and gun simply because the odds are in your favor that the bullets won't go where they're aimmed and that's even harder when the target is literally all over the place. That being said, when it does decide to do something, the game pushes out awkward conflicts, where the 3 AK-47 rounds to the torso while wearing bodyarmor, beats that of 24 into the dome of the other player. Yes, the helmets break chance is also RNG, so you can pepper someone in the face with a SMG and the helmet won't break and they'll effectively take no damage. Yes, rifles have had a much higher chance of it breaking but it's quite odd how an AR-15 to the face at less then 10 feet won't break it but their SMG will break it on first shot. These usually leave you with a bad taste in your mouth as you feel more like you were cheated by the game rather than outplayed which unless is a intentional mechanic of the game. Is just an annoyance. As well as you'll often be shot by people while behind them as it appears as if the hitbox has a delay in following it's player model, as I've been clearly behind someone and they just shoot the air which I last was and I die, more occasions then one, perhaps this is a "Shooter-Advantage" where, wherever I am on their screen, is what they can actually shoot at. So ping-abusing is a functional strategy in this game, maybe, I'm not 100% on that but it's a possibility.
2. The map is flawed in more places then one, On several Solo matches and playing with Duos and Fives, I've just fallen straight through the map with no explaination and then die to toxic gas during my perpetual fall. Also, you might like to try and jump over a fence or run past a car, you're likely to get stopped by exaggerated polygons which will leave you with no where to go but taking a wide turn around said object, unnecessarily. Most solid objects on the map can provide cover while some seem to just outright ignore their purpose on the map. Sitting behind a vehicle as someone just peppers bullets straight through the vehicle as if it's just air has happened more then a couple of times.
3. Hackers, alright I get what you're going to say. "Git gud, there's no hackers just bad players." in this case I find that isn't true. Combat Zone (Basically FFA deathmatch which you will likely also be shot once or twice before you actually see where you are on the screen) I see it more prodominantly as the respawns are constant and I can get plenty of opportunities to enter a gunfight. This leads me to more occasions then one where players will do full rotations into headshots, not just I see them turn and then begin to shoot, while I might be experiencing lag that makes it appear as if they never actually turned to look at me and then suddenly are staring at my face I have a hard time believing that they seem capable of landing every headshot on a target which moves unpredictably, seeing as most games I play in, there's always 3 or 4 players who never die and ONLY land headshots. While, maybe they just have gained that skill over time or have dropped far too many hours into the game, I find it hard to believe especially with the weapon mechanics that it's a likely thing.
If you want to play a battle royale game. I would recommend Fortnite if you have a tight wallet or PUBG, Fortnite is more cartoony and you can build forts and PUBG focuses on a sense of realism, with a wide variety of weapons and attatchments to come across during the action and being far more team-oriented and friendly with the ability to pickup downed teammates (Fortnite has this too.). While it does have it's fair share of glitches and broken mechanics. It plays far better then this game by a long shot. Sure it's expensive, but trust me, it's worth it.

Even after all these years, UT04 not only holds up both in terms of gameplay, but is actually better than most current offerings. There are 2 main reasons for this: Simple but timeless gameplay, and massive amounts of content.
Games like this remind us all of the sad state of the current games industry. This game was released in a era where people expected their games to have content. There was no DLC. If you liked Trials Evolution, then there's plenty to love here.  I've seen some complaints that the game is light on single-player content, and while it does seem pretty lean, you have to remember that Trials Evolution Gold Edition is actually a combination of two games in one, so it should have substantial more content.  Then you have the DLC, which I have yet to play or purchase, and it is disappointing that the content wasn't included in the main game.  I'm sure I'll buy the DLC eventually but I'll wait for it to go on sale.
The gameplay is much the same as its predecessors, but the UI and game progression feels more modernized with the level-up system and the addition of level challenges in the single player career mode.  Of course there's the addition of trick courses added to the arsenal, which are kind of fun but still not as much as the main game.
The environments and feel of the levels are a big change from Evolution, as Fusion sticks with a more futuristic setting.  It's a little more unnatural, but I appreciate them mixing things up, and I have to say that the environments have a ton of detail and are really pleasing to the eye.  The addition of Portal-esque humor between two robot AI characters kind of falls flat, but I still really appreciate the constant slapstick of your character rag-dolling at an end-of-level hazard.
Uplay is still there, but it's a non-issue.  It's never crashed my game, and I haven't had performance issues.  I also can't speak to the user-content or multiplayer as I've yet to touch it.  The core of the game remains intact, though, and there remains little more in all of gaming as satisfying as passing a seemingly impossible level in the Trials series.

Sale edit: Every DLC is on sale right now, this hasn't happened before, so take the very low price into account with my DLC reviews :)
Awesome level MAX Edit: This isn't included in the season pass, and as yet I do not own it. I'll update this section with details on whether the DLC is worth a full price or not when I purchase it for myself. As for the introduced microtransactions, they're purely cosmetic and not required.
This was the first Trials game I ever played, and it's great. Don't let the negative reviews put you off, most of them are negative simply because it uses Uplay, which I shall talk about further down the review.
First off, the environment in this game is stunning. For a game like Trials, in which you just ride your bike across level after level, you wouldn't expect this level of quality, the world looks like it's part of a much larger game. There's also plenty of variety, as you quickly move from the futuristic city to platforms in the sky, ancient ruins, outdoor courses, underwater bases and even the planet's core. There is also some slight hints of story included through a few characters talking throughout the game, which hint at how the world became like this.
It's trials. You drive your bike, tilt your weight and try to make it to the end as fast as possible and with as few failures as possible. Every level also has three challenges that encourage you to play differently, and some even involve minigames entirely different to how the game is usually played. The difficulty as you pass through the levels is done very well. By the time I was met with much harder obstacles, I'd already got a basic idea of how to surpass them, and not once did a death feel cheap.
The DLCs add some nice extra content that also gives you a look at more of the world of Fusion, and provide some decent challenge. I wouldn't recommend buying them seperately, but if you don't want to buy the Deluxe Edition, here's a summary of their content and quality:
The first DLC and the weakest. Featuring only 6 levels, an FMX course and a mediocre minigame. -
Same as above, 6 levels, FMX and a minigame. The levels are a bit better than Rustlands,
Breaks the chain and includes 8 levels instead of 6, as well as the FMX and minigame at the end. This DLC gives an interesting look at an underwater empire that used to live under the ocean. Some story is delivered through another AI who speaks to you at certain points. The levels are of a higher standard than the first two DLCs,
9 levels, FMX and a minigame. In this DLC you are even further down, underneath the planet's core. As you move from level to level you go further underground, giving a nice indication of your progress through the DLC. There are also multiple secret recordings hidden around the levels, which give some extra information about the world, and what went on in the mines.
Personally, I believe this is the best DLC. It drops one level and returns to 8 trials again, but the quality of the levels steps up greatly. This DLC has a focus on technology, much more so than previously shown, with teleporters, anti gravity machines and Mechs featuring. The levels in this DLC are very inventive, including
and
The sixth and final DLC. Same as above, 8 levels with an FMX and Minigame. One of my main disapointments with Trials Fusion was the lack of detail as to what was happening. I understand that this is a game solely based on a random guy riding a bike through obstacle courses, but with such an interesting world, with many deeper story elements hinted at throughout, I really wanted to learn more. After the Incident does so nicely. It's set in the future, when all the world is in ruins after the aforementioned "Incident". The levels all focus on fairly different areas, all destroyed or going through some form of crisis. Similar to Fire in the Deep, you can find secrets in the levels, which give you some backstory as to how all of this started. The way this is done is great, as
If you want to know more about the world behind Fusion, or just want to play even more levels,

As such, I highly recommend you get the Deluxe edition during a sale, I managed to pick it up for £10. Otherwise, if you beat the game and decide you want more, you will be paying a much higher price. Say you got the base game on sale for £6. Now if you got three of the DLCs, that'll cost you an extra £12. Half the DLC total DLC and you've spent £18 already. The Deluxe edition is a much better purchase (During a sale of course. The DLC is good but not worth £30!)
Now, there are three main flaws that have gave this game so many negative reviews. First main point is the multiplayer. I played the game entirely solo and had fun, I can't really comment on it.
Secondly, people seem to be complaining about this being a bad port, and having a many performance issues. For reference, I ran the game on an i5 3570k, 8gb RAM and a GTX 770 with constant 60fps and no issues of any kind. The issue may be related to lower-end machines.
And as for the last point, UPlay. The majority of these reviews are from people starting the game, seeing Uplay, closing it and leaving a bad review. I will say right here that if you avoid this game because of Uplay, you are stupid.
The impact of UPlay is nowhere near as bad as the reviews make it sound. You start the game on Steam, UPlay appears, takes a couple seconds to log in, then minimizes and starts the game. You only need to interact with it once in order to create an account, and after that you don't need to touch the thing, aside from closing it when you are done.
EDIT: UPlay now does not even appear when you start a game through Steam. It minimizes itself. Seriously guys, the impact is so minimal it's not even worth arguing about!
All in all, I recommend Trials Fusion to anyone who is an existing trials fan, or enjoys 2D games with high difficulty. Though the price is a little steep for the content on offer, so I'd suggest waiting for a sale and getting the deluxe edition. As earlier stated, it's much better value as the DLCs never get discounted, and only costed £4 (the price of a single DLC) more than the normal pack in the latest sale. And finally, do not avoid this game because of UPlay, there is no reason to.

This game does so many things right!
The Good:
Runs stable on low-spec systems and on newer OS, no problem.  I have yet to note a bug other than a single instance of pathfinding stupidity.
The tutorial and interface are both very easy to grasp.  This game is very deep, but also very approachable.
Family lines and member traits that give the game a slight RPG feel.  A coherent and interesting tech tree is present and units are well described.  The sprawling map with many factions vying for power promises an incredible amount of replayability.  Strategic and tactical levels of gameplay are both well polished.  Geography and financial management are constant considerations while playing this game.  Good implementation of spies, diplomats and assassins allows strategies that aren't entirely based on having the better army.  The AI is passable but that might be because it only has to simulate barbarians half the time.
The not good.
The AI consistently misses key opportunities both strategically and tactically.  At times the stupidity can ruin immersion.  Tactical naval combat is not present, all naval battles are auto-resolved.  Thankfully, naval action takes a back seat to the land action and I have yet to see a naval battle autoresolve in an unrealistically illogical fashion - it is pretty predictable.  There is no co-op campaign option or hotseat option.  Last, the graphics.  Even over a decade old, the graphics are still passable, but if you need a little more and eye-candy you to enjoy a game, look elsewhere.  Despite these modest negatives, for the price this game is worth a shot for anyone interested in strategy games and definitely one of the best "bang for buck" performers I've seen on Steam.
Summary:
A classic.  I played Medieval II+Kingdoms prior to playing this.  Almost passed it up in fact because the gameplay is so similar to Medieval II and the graphics are older.  Believe it or not, I am enjoying this game's campaign more.  Perhaps it is the idea of Rome.  Perhaps it is the soundtrack.  Perhaps it is the pre-battle speeches that are missing from MedII+Kingdoms or the sense that Rome's units are more differentiated somehow.  In the Kingdoms expansion especially, it seemed like very little effort was put into making native american factions different from one another.  It is hard for me to put my finger on why, but this game has simply been more enjoyable.  If you want a decent engine that offers outstanding mods, MedII+Kingdoms is the way to go.  I highly recommend both, but "out of the box," I personally prefer Rome.  Score: 8.7/10

It is an open-world RPG like Oblivion, except with almost no interesting places, very small and drab dungeons, some of the worse voice acting in history, and tedious quests. It did have a fun inventory and equipment system where you'd upgrade your stuff and you didn't invariably end up with the same equipment at the end of the game, because you could upgrade mid-level stuff to be competent later in the game...
I also finished Two Worlds 2, and the above description kind of fits this game too. A bit tedious, meaningless quests, boring story, cool equipment upgrade system... However it did everything slightly better than Two Worlds 1, so the developers should at least be congratulated on improving their game considerably.
The magic system was probably the most interesting part of the game. I'd urge people to play as a mage if they try the game, but it means your equipment will be rather boring for most of the game and you will end up looking like a ridiculous mage from Harry Potter with a stupid hat.
The magic system uses a card system where you can combine various effects and types of spells and chain the effects too. You could cast a spell that 1) spawns a bunch of anvils and 2) immediately casts a tornado that has them spin around you. One of my favorite spell was a firebolt (1) that had an area effect (2) which spawned a zone of confusion (3). So my enemies would get charred and promptly start attacking each others. The mage is kind of overpowered.
The game looks very good too. The environments are gorgeous... But again mostly emptied of anything interesting. There is even a large disappointment in that a huge part of the world map ends up being unexplorable. You think you still have a huge island to explore (the biggest one on the map) but nope, can't go there.
I can't say I was THAT disappointed when I started to realize that this last island was unexplorable... Mostly because the repetitive quests were getting really boring and I was looking forward for the game to end. I don't remember even Two Worlds 1 being as annoyingly overlong towards the end.
Also it has one of the worst endings of all times. And the final boss is a horrible frustrating gimmick where you can't really use your hard-earned powers to fight.
So in brief, for ameliorating the UI, character builds, equipment system, magic system, graphics, combat handling (combat animations are pretty cool!), and most aspects of the game, the company deserves some praise. But for creating yet another uninteresting story, repetitive quests, and lots of tedious parts... Um, Two Worlds 2 can't get a recommendation from me. A very average game and your time is probably better spent elsewhere.

1. Let's start with animations:
My character's running looks like a japanese schoolgirl running towards senpai (the kneecaps face inwards when running), his attack movements (especially spellcasting) are just off. The horses I guess are okay, but a little clunky in movement.
2. Menus and stuff:
While the developers have tried to add a sense of fantasy into the menues, gold and blue don't go well together, especailly in this game. Their dragon thing surrounding the health bar looks extravagent. They should try a more minimalistic design.
3. Quests:
While the quest system is fine, the objectives and how you get there is often confusing and hard to navigate. Also there's nobody you can ask for clues, or even to repeat the quest dialougue. However, in some situations the quest navagation system is too straightforward, and I literally skipped through half the plot and beat the boss without really knowing the Story while I spent the other half of my time trying to scale mountains and get to the destination before realizing there was a shortcut that can only be opened after completing the quest there. While this might sound intruiging, I assure you it is not after 3 hours of rigorous scaling.
4. Difficulty spikes:
I don't know if this is just me, but there have been huge difficulty level changes ever since the start. The game expects you to grind, and if you don't, you can't progress. When I was in the swamp navigating my way through undeads, it took me ten minutes to kill 7 of them, and that was using summons and heals all the way through. While about ten minutes before, I was tearing through monsters in the last chapter easily. While this may sound like a personal complaint, I think TW2 should at least offer you a decent difficulty slope from chapter to chapter.
5. FInal boss:
I spent the entire game building weird magic spells that held so much potential they could be viewed as cheats, and the final boss turns out to be an FPS.
6. Voice acting:
Don't turn on the sound, just don't
Overall, although I rated it down, this game is worth getting (ONLY ON SALES WHERE THEY ARE 80% OFF)

This is a game that requires investment of time and effort. Most of the time in this game is spent building stuff and setting up elaborate pipelines so you can ... build more stuff. You can avoid the automation but then the game gets grindy, plus it's becoming harder and harder (both because of extra limitations to push people towards automation and because barriers to automation are removed so it's always the easier option).

Sniper Elite V2 is one of those games that's hit-or-miss (pun semi-intended).  I only just got the PC version, but I've had the Xbox 360 version for close to a year now and the only difference I can see is the graphics quality.  In fact, let's start with that, shall we?
The graphics of Sniper Elite V2 are surprisingly excellent.  The game world itself is far from beautiful, but that is to be expected when you're a lone wolf sniper crawling through the rubble of Berlin in the twilight hours of the Second World War.  The amount of detail is extraordinary.  You can see the leathery texture of an SS officer's jacket just as you're about to blow his brains out.  My only concern is, perhaps, optimization.  Could have used a bit more, but nothing too serious.
The storyline is nothing to write home about, but it gets the job done of linking the missions together.
A lot of the time you'll be crawling around in the ruined streets of Berlin, but you do get to see a few other environments.  Each of the levels is quite linear.  To a lot of players, this is what breaks the game, and I can understand that.  However if  you can get past the linearity it is still a very enjoyable experience.
As for the gameplay, well, it's a sniper game.  You get a sniper rifle, a pistol, and an SMG, along with various booby traps.  The star of the show truly is your rifle.  This should be your go-to weapon throughout most of the game.  The sniper mechanics in this game are phenomenal, and highly customizable.  Bad shot?  You can set it so that bullets come right out of CoD and hit where you're aiming.  Just got off of a BF gaming binge?  You can set it so that bullets are effected by gravity.  Really want to challenge yourself?  You can set it so that not only is there bullet drop, but also wind as well.  On top of this, you will always have to watch your heartrate.  If you're running around a lot, your heart rate is going to spike and your scope will sway heavily.  Stay low, move slowly, and take your time and your heart rate will drop and you can focus on the shot or even slow time.
Once you take that shot, it is very likely that you will go into a bullet cam, which will often show an X-ray view of your target as their organs are shredded by your sniper shot.  You can control the frequency of these bullet cams if you're squeamish or just don't like much gore, but I do not believe you can completely turn them off.  It is, however, quite satisfying when you see your round enter through an enemy's skull, exit out the other side, tumble realistically through the air, and proceed to take out his buddy behind him.
That AI themselves are quite varied between the difficulty levels.  Easy AI will have them walking in circles, wondering where the sniper is that just dropped their friend while you proceed to plink away at their ranks.  Hard AI means that one wrong shot will result in your death.  Medium AI is comfortably in between the two.
Finally, the co-op and multiplayer...  I admit that I have not tried to competitive multiplayer yet, but I did take a quick glance at the options and servers.  There are quite a few servers running and the options for a custom match are outrageous.  As for co-op, you can team up with a shooting buddy and take on either a challenge mission or a wave-based survival mode.  I can say that both of these are extremely fun and, in some ways, make up for the singleplayers linearity with open maps that allow you to roost in whatever sniper perch you find suitable.
All-in-all, I'd say that Sniper Elite V2 is not a game that I would pay a full $60 USD for.  At the current price of $30 USD, however, it is a great game, so long as you're interested.  If you're looking for a game that has basic, yet functioning, stealth mechanics, fun cooperative play, and excellent sniping mechanics, then I suggest you pick up Sniper Elite V2.  It's not the end-all-be-all of sniper games, but it's a hell of a lot better than Sniper: Ghost Warrior.  I can tell you that much!

I'd give this game multiple thumbs up if I could! Wish I had heard about this game sooner, I happened across it purely by accident while browsing around steam.
I've played a lot of games and never come across something like this. I'd best describe it as an automation/crafting/logistics simulator, mixed in with a bit of Spider-man of all things!
The "blocky" look initially turned me off as I thought it looked too similar to Minecraft (which I have not played, mainly due to the low rent blockyness). Yes, the world is made up of blocks, but the similarity ends there - the textures are quite detailed, and while everything you craft/place in the world is using the same large block grid, the machines and other items are quite detailed and have excellent animations.
The game's premise is you have crash landed on an inhospitable world and must mine resources, research new technologies, and gain enough power to eventually escape. The open-endedness of this allows you to build up your base and production systems any way you see fit. It doesn't take long at all before you have a fairly complex system bringing in several types of materials from deep underground.
The whole experience can at first seem VERY grindy, but this is where the beauty really lies - in automating everything. Everything can be as automated as much as little as you like, and if you have the right materials over vast distances!
There is just so much to do at every stage it can seem overwhelimg - in a good way! The best games give you consistent challenges to overcome, with multiple ways to approach the problem, and this one has it in spades. The development cycle is very active and new things are being added all the time. If something is too easy or exploitable, its patched! As soon as you think you have a handle on things and start expanding your operations, digging deeper, or upgrading, new mechanics will come in to play to keep you on your toes.
You WILL die quite a bit, especially at the beginning - from falls or exposure to the extreme temperatures. As you buld up you will start to have waves of creatures attack your base, but at this time there is no real "death penalty' or loss when your central base hub is destroyed. The inconvenience of either of these is more than enough of a deterrent however, and the attacks can apparently set back your progress on the end game run. It can seem a bit lonely, as the planet is generally devoid of any wildlife on the surface or anything that attacks you directly without being provoked. But there is multiplayer which I have not tried, but it seems like it could be a blast building up with friends.
If any of this or the screenshots/videos sound remotely interesting, grab this game - you won't regret it!

Rome: Total War is the sequel to the first Medieval: Total War, and despite the game's age it still holds up very well in my opinion. Just something you should take into consideration is that the game with the default configuration often does not launch on Windows 10, there are plenty of tutorials out there that can help you solve this problem. Now the PROS and CONS:
PROS:
+Awesome modding community; There are a lot of awesome mods out there for Rome: Total War, just be wary that the game doesn't have a Steam Workshop though, so you will have to download these mods from other websites.
+The game allows you full freedom over the faction you control, as one of the Roman factions you can choose to do the missions the Senate gives you, which will give you rewards such as troops or money, or ignore these completely (which would ofcourse hurt your standing with the Senate, that in the early game wouldn't be a good decision) and as one of the non-Roman factions you do not have an optional mission given at all (Unlike in Medieval: 2 Total War).
+Due to the freedom of the game, you can play a faction in a campaign multiple times without it becoming repetitive because you can choose to set different goals every campaign. (I have over 500+ hours played, still haven't gotten much into multiplayer yet that the game does still support and has people playing it).
CONS (Things to take into consideration):
-The game runs on 1 CPU core, so on modern systems the game wouldn't run as well.
-The pathfinding in cities can often be odd and sometimes requires micromanagement if you don't want your troops running into different directions, other than this the pathfinding is good however.
If you are considering getting Rome: Total War, get it!

First of all, do I recommend this game? YES!! I've been playing this game for a few days with a friend, so this is a review in progress. Let me start off by saying, this game, even in its current state.. is incredible. There's so much depth to it.. it's very expansive and there's endless possibilities. 9.5/10
Pros
+It takes a very long time to gather resources and alter the terrain whilst building houses, and villages. That's a good thing. It makes it more immersive, realistic, and require teamwork. It also feels so rewarding when you complete a project you've been working on. So far, after 3 days.. me and my friend have managed to build 2 huts, a garden, fence, furnace, and blacksmithing station.. even though this seems extremely miniscule, I feel really proud.. like I accomplished something.. and we're planning on accomplishing much more. The more people you have in your group, the faster you can raise your village from the dirt. As long as everyone is working together of course. You'll never run out of things to do.
+You also cannot specialize in all of the professions.. you can only specialize in 1 or 2.. maybe more depending on how you spend your points. So you will need to communicate with other players on what they are specializing in to fill that gap you need to efficently build your village.
+It takes a LONG time to dig a tunnel
+\- Combat? I'm a bit iffy on this one as I haven't had too many violent encounters. While the combat right now is in fact, buggy and the hitboxes are miles off, the concept is amazing and I think this is going to be improved. I got shot by a crossbow, in which I took off running and eventually collapsed from bleeding and then executed. This gave the combat many positive points in my book. As of right now, it will certainly suffice. But don't take my word for it, I've only beat a moose with a primitive axe and got shot with a bolt. I will update on this once I'm more experienced with the combat.
Here are some of my nitpicks, or rather, suggestions on what it would take to make this game utterly perfect.
-This is a big one. Currently, you need to specialize in certain equipment in order to actually use it. This is disappointing. You should be able to use any equipment, regardless of your expertise in it. Expertise should affect how well you use the equipment though. For example, a low level in Crossbow would make aiming shaky and inaccurate. A low level in Mail Armor would make your stamina drain faster. Ect. To not be able to use it at all is unrealistic.
-When you die, a gravestone appears. This is immersion breaking.
And here are some current alpha problems that are surely going to be smoothed out in time.
-Crashing (a lot)
-Lag
-Bugs (of course)
-Freezing
-Stuttering
These are all to be expected. But don't let them stray you away from this awesome game. For these issues to be present while I simultaneously give the game a 9.5, that means this game is GOOD. I can't explain it. It's just amazing. MANY hours are going to be spent on this game. :)

I've been a fan of survival horror games since the original 1992 Alone in the Dark. I'm totally on board for the idea of a horror game with no combat, I was even a fan of this company's previous horror games, the Penumbra series which were prototypes to Amnesia.
This game is not only not scary, it has no clue about even the theory behind being scary.
The big problem is that the game TELLS you that you should be scared instead of MAKING you scared. The player character breaths heavy when something "scary" happens. The music goes berserk. A ton of blur filters hit you upside the head. The camera starts to blur and throb if you stay in the dark. Enemies might as well be carrying signs that read "Okay you're REALLY scared now!" This is horrible. Monsters should be scary on their own. The PLAYER should be the one screaming, not the player character. Darkness should be unsettling on its own. It's all shoved down your throat via artificial means and it quickl gets too annoying for any chance of scaring you.
Here's the entire game:
-Entrance to the area you need to go to is blocked. You must assemble X items from nearby areas to form Y contraption that will clear the way.
-Walk through an empty area, be constantly interrupted by annoying, pointless flashbacks that convey redundant information you already know.
-Find an X puzzle item on a table and pick it up.
-Monster spawns or structure collapses. The game will take away control for the camera to pan to the monster/collapse to make sure you don't miss it and take you out of the moment.
-Easily run past monster to get back to central hub area before heading to another "X puzzle item area"
-Form Y contraption once all X items collected to proceed.
-Repeat till game is over
Occasionally you'll be thrown into a danger area where you have to survive something instead of forming items. These are generally better than the item areas, but there are only 10 minutes of them for every 1-2 hours of item puzzle areas.
I was really looking forward to this after all the rave reviews and my enjoyment of the earlier Penumbra games. Amnesia however is just clumsy and annoying. Skip this and pick up the Penumbra games instead if you're into these kind of horror games.

Sniper Elite V2 is a third person tactical shooter video game released in 2012 and is a sequel/remake of Rebellion's own 2005 game Sniper Elite that takes place in the same timeframe and location: The Battle of Berlin in April/May 1945 but with an altered narrative. The story follows an American officer who must capture or eliminate the scientists involved in the German V-2 rocket program while the Red Army invades.
Graphics wise, while I of course cannot judge how real this game looks when compared to actual WW2 setting, it does look very much like most of the WW2 movies that portrayed that period of time. Characters have a nice worn out rugged look, and buildings and vehicles feel rather authentic. The graphics, while not top of the line, does its best to portray its setting pretty well.
Sound and music are very well done, with every crack of a sniper rifle, every thundering boom of a German Tank being an aural joy to the ear. Both elements combine to make it an even more realistic feel of a WW2 battleground. I also especially appreciate when German or Russian soldiers actually converse in their appropriate native languages. I like this attention to detail and it definitely helps alot in the immersion factor.
Gameplay wise, it focuses very much on using stealth, and relies heavily upon 3 main factors: Conceal, Plan, Execute. There is even an ingame mechanic which makes use of ambient environmental sound. This means that enemies are less likely to be suspicious when you fire a shot when a church bell rings nearby as compared when you fire a shot with no ambient environmental sounds.
The game even goes so far as to have special Kill-Cams X-Ray scenes which gorily shows the penetration of the bullet and showcases the damage done to the victim if you were to fire an exceptional shot. While it is probably nothing more then a gimmick, it definitely feels really satisfying to score a difficult shot AND seeing how much damage you did to the guy. This kill-cam is even available during multiplayer co-op mode.
The main campaign can also be played co-operatively with 1 other friend, and the whole game becomes that much more tactical, where friends can help each other spot potential threats and encourages communication. If you are planning to get this game, definitely give the Co-op mode a try as it is extremely fun.
Downsides, there is just a minor nitpick that i have. The inventory system feels a little clunky. I wished it was somehow more streamlined that its current design. Perhaps holding down a button could activate an Item Wheel in which we could immediately select the item we wanted instead of slowly checking thru the list.
Overall Rating: 9.0 / 10
Sniper Elite V2 is definitely one of the more enjoyable games I have played in a long while. You really feel badass when landing a difficult shot. The various interesting missions and the co-op experience simply makes this a very special game indeed. Definitely two thumbs up.
