After putting some hours into this game I realised that it is pretty fun although there are some problems in it. It is pretty damn hard for Hack'n Slash games to live up to the expectations of those who ever played God of War. I'm one of those. In comparison, this game has a lot of problems: the atmosphere, the gameplay and the whole story is not that great. But if we look at the HnS games that was released on PC... well, this is one of the best. Here are some cons and pros for the lovers:
PROS:
- The character desing is badass
- The main hero is badass
- Everything looks badass
- The graphics has a unique tone in it, it kinda reminded me of Prototype, which is pretty nice
- The gameplay is a standard HnS, but I've never seen a game responding this quickly for the killing moves. Literally I press the button and it happens so quickly it seems like it's part of the combo. Even God of War can envy this flow.
CONS:
- The story is dumb
- The characters don't really have a personality
- At first, the combos can get very boring because you need time to buy some and until that it's just the some 3-4 moves.
- The mouse controlling is bad, so I decided to use a controller which works fine, but the key bindings are a little complicated to use in a fast paced combat.
- It's a shame this game has no memorable music. I set the volume to the max and there are simply no epic tunes while I  kill the hell out of the enemies
- There aren't many enemy types, should have more
ALL IN ALL
After DmC, this game is the best HnS I tried on a PC. On a sale you can easily give it a try if you are a fan.

Props to Yacht Club games for making a strong female characrer like Shield Knight.
You are given quite the variety of weapons to use throughout the game. There is the traditional shovel that you get to upgrade and swing around, and it's suprisingly fun. Admittedly, when I first picked up the game I thought using a shovel was going to be a dull experience but was pleasantly surprised with different combos and powers it can get. There are also magical items you can buy as the game goes on (which is a shame that no matter if you find them in the dungeon or just get them in town you have to pay either way). Some of the magical items stand out as being vastly superior in clearing levels and boss fights (green orb, fire wand, phase locket), while a few struck me as mostly useless (coin toss, spinny top). If you're able to micromanage your inventory and stay on top of buying magic items, the levels begin to feel a lot more accessable.. If not however, you may find yourself grinding your teeth and asking for a better way to get through the insta-death spikes (losing all the money you could be spending on the items you need to better progress the game).
The level design also employs a very great way for the player to learn all the new aspects of each level, progressively adding things on and giving checkpoints when neccesary.
I cannot review this game without a nod to Yacht Club games. A LOT of games that go on Kickstarter don't make it off the ground, run away with the money, or even just release the game half-baked on Steam in early-access asking for more money, but Yacht Club did so much more than the bare minimum. This amazing studio released a solid game for a solid price and then had the audacity to release TWO MORE FREE CAMPAIGNS for FREE. (!!!!!FREE!!!!!) If you owned the base game. While I have not yet played through the optional two campaigns (!!!!!FREEEEEEEE!!!!!!!), the base game alone is worth the price I paid, and my hat is off to Yacht Club games for the astounding work they've done here.
[9/10]

I don't know what other reviewers were expecting from DNF, but all I wanted was a Duke Nukem game, and I got exactly what I was waiting fourteen years for.  It's not groundbreaking, and the game shows its long development cycle, but the elements that made DN3D groundbreaking are all there.  The humor, the heavily interactive environment (which few games even now bother to have learned from DN3D), the references (something I dearly love), the crazy enemies, the zany weapons, Duke and friends' over-the-top personalities; everything you could ask of Duke Nukem.  The love and care of the developers is obviously present, even if the game shows its age.
Now, if you get terribly upset about the objectification of women or swearing, just walk away now.  There's nothing in Duke Nukem for you.  But for those of us who've kept the faith, who cut our teeth on Roddy Piper and Bruce Campbell, the Duke is back in fine form.
It's not perfect, not even after fourteen years.  But I really like it.

I really should recommend this game. It's 3D Factorio, and I love Factorio and 3D.
Alas, while I kind of like it it's just too grindy and slow. The game gives you all sorts of cool tools for you to play with, but they're so expensive to build (smelters) or power hungry (automatic tools like excavators/belt layers and the like). The early game in particular is awful because of how hard it is to locate basic ores. If you find a new ore and analyize it before you've memorized or marked the location the ore won't show up while pinging unknown anymore, so good luck finding it again. This is but one example of many about how FortressCraft Evolved wastes your time with boring crap.
The developer could learn a lot from Factorio and slash the power and material requirements for everything by quite a lot (like, a factor of 10), then it would be a fun game. Also other stuff like ping colored ore should be the default mode for pinging known ores, and that shouldn't be locked behind research or cost a ton of suit power. I'm not holding my breath for these changes though, the developer has released at least 7 major updates for the game since it left early access and hasn't reduced the grind significantly at all.
Update: I tried this game again with update 10 and casual settings and got to the point where I was minining lithium. It's still just as tedious as it was.

The first Two Worlds is arguably an abomination, surely it had a decent sized open world, a huge range of equipment and online to boot, it was executed badly and i really mean badly, it's one of the glitchiest rpg's...no, games of this generation.
People were horrified to hear that there was a sequel to this foul game, so much that they thought it was laughable that it even got a sequel in the first place as well as the running joke of "two worlds two" but in fact, a sequel was just what this game needed.
Although it was supposed to be an expansion to the first two worlds, reality pump and topware clearly saw that the first game wasn't well received and decided to improve upon it rather than adding on to it. As a result they decided to make a sequal...though it does seem to be a remaster of the original two worlds with the main villian of the first game returning in which you clearly beat him (ganondorf much?), that is if you picked the good choice. It's easy to say that this game is a lot more engaging than the first and you can see that they really worked hard on this game. The graphics for starters are pretty good, something you wouldn't expect to see after the abomination that was the first game, you can clearly see an improvement. Unfortunately this can make the game pretty unstable at times with plenty of lag issues (especially if you're playing a mage character).
The game opens up in Castle Vahkmaar where you have been taken prisoner by the evil emperor, Gandohar (what a step up eh?) and you have to escape the prison where you end up on this small island and meet a prophet as well as a band of orcs, afterwards you are free to explore the open world...well not exactly everywhere. You unlock new areas as you progress through the main quest which may be off putting to some. One of the games strong points is it's questing. Unlike most wrpg's Questing doesn't always feel like a tedious affair, sure there aren't as many quests as most wrpg's such as elder scrolls but there are a lot less "filler" quests, most of the mundane ones being buliten board quests. Quests in Two Worlds 2 feel more interactive than most, though the main game gives you very little options in choice, there are often multiple paths/choices that you can take in side missions and many of them are engaging if only for the bizarre sense of humor in them and their creativity. Some quests may seem plain and simple at first however there are many twists and turns which may take you for surprise or they're just plain funny. Some quests can be pretty mundane but there aren't that many of them, thank god (seriously if you're going to add side quests at least make them interesting).
The main story itself is pretty standard fare for most wrpg's, don't expect anything amazing. Two Worlds 2 can catch some players off guard though as it's storyline does have a few twists and they are well explained. put simply, do not play this game for it's plot. The main story does have some interesting moments and scenes however, just don't think about the plot much and enjoy your time in antaloor, pay the story no attention.
The game play has improved from the first game and is similar to that of Diablo 3 but far superior (expect something Diablo esque with the game play) every element of game play feels reminiscent to Diablo, heck i even made some spells from the original Diablo in two worlds 2 such as immolation and nova as well as mana shield. Expect a lot of potion drinking and keep well stocked. Unlike Diablo however, this game is more open world style and isn't top down, so if you want a more modernized rpg with a Diablo like combat system, you've found it (heck even the health orb is reminiscent to Diablo). There are three different classes, melee archery and magic (Diablo much) and you are able to become a hybrid of these three classes should you choose to. Each class has their own set of skills available which you can learn in any order you please but before you can begin leveling up your character's skills you need to buy skill books to learn the skills initially (formerly learned from trainers in the first game) in order to use them and to level them up.
Melee learn skills which can assist them in staggering the opponent and breaking guards, they can also deal extra damage, one move in particular allows you to deal considerable damage to an enemy but is only useful against an enemy who is left open to attack as is is easily blocked and hard to connect with. Using these skills also allows you to interrupt enemy attacks so you should use them wisely
Ranged learn skills which can alter their elemental attributes and affect the speed and damage, most ranged skills are passive. There is a sniper mode however it is badly implemented which makes it useful only to pick off foes who haven't noticed you yet which is useless in many of the games dungeons due to their lack of space.
There is also a "sneak" class however sneaking isn't effective enough to be considered a class of it's own, sneaking doesn't seem to work well in this game and it is simply easier to not bother with it.
Mages are arguably the most diverse class as Two Worlds 2 allows the player to customize their own spells to create new ones using spell cards which give mages devastating effects. This is one of the games strong points as it allows you to experiment and be creative which is always good. the only problem is that their strength is limited, very much like in Diablo, unlike melee classes which become stronger and deal more damage with strength, mages do not get stronger with willpower as it merely gives you more mana and grants access to higher level mage skills, this is rather disappointing and in the later half of the game you will usually end up using ricochet spells simply because they are the best spells available and deal the most damage just so the mage can keep up with the other classes.
The melee class is arguably the strongest in terms of base damage but they are required to use potions often, however the mage is a lot more versatile and can take out enemies at a greater range and it's spells can hit multiple targets making it somewhat more deadlier than melee. Ranged isn't really much different from melee other than it is long range. On paper ranged are the best choice of class but they most certainly aren't as they lack the complexity of that of mages and they don't have enough skills to balance with the other classes, unless you are best on being a ranged character i would strongly recommend against it as you will find the other two classes far more interesting.
In terms of inventory and equipment, Two Worlds 2 feels a lot less diverse than the original which is disappointing, you will likely be stuck with the same armor you start with for a very long time and will be unable to upgrade until later. However the inventory system has made several improvements, items are a lot more clearer now on the screen and it is easier to organize, one of the few gripes i have about it though is that when you equip an item, it just shows a highlight marker so if you're not careful, you could accidentally sell it to a merchant. There is a new crafting system to replace the combine system from the first game making it far more balanced and you are able to dismantle items and save their parts for later to upgrade other equipment. There are also gems which you can socket into your gear to give them added effects, you can also combine them to make higher level gems using the fusion skill. You can also colour your own equipment using pigments to give your equipment the colour you desire, though not every equipment can be colored.

Shadow Warrior 2 is the sequel to Shadow Warrior (2013) which is an in-direct (i.e. has not much to do with) sequel to the original Shadow Warrior from 1997.
Like the 2013 reboot Shadow Warrior 2 combines the old school fast paced, action packed and incredibly fun (read: statisfying) gameplay of "old school" shooters with the additions to shooters of the modern age.
This translates into great gun play (Sounds could be a bit better though, especially for assault rifles) and melee combat
combined with an leveling and loot system.
However instead of making the leveling/rpg/loot system the main focus of the game, Shadow Warrior 2 instead opts to have it an additional system catering to the core game mechanics.
Hence guns can be modified in a variety of ways, but it isn't quite necessery on the two lower difficulties.
Is it more fun to use weapon mods?
I'm sorry, did you just ask if a remote controlled intoxicating scatter shot rocket launcher is fun?
If that was really your question, then the answer is Wang.
What's important is that skill upgrades, modifications and loot hunting add to the experience rather than being the main point.
The main point of Shadow Warrior 2 remains the same as in the 2013 and 1997 prequels.
There is demon.
Kill demon.
Good, now kill more demons in a bloody, gruesome and motherducking awesome way!
Sure, you'll find the "Destroyer of Realms" rocket launcher and laugh hysterically as your new toy's rockets obliterate hordes of enemies, but there's always the 20 other weapons in your inventory ready to be switched out for a wangfully good time.
From the base shotgun, over the dual wield plasma rifles to the living, toxic breathing grenade launcher.
All the weapons are fun and all of them can be used way into the game's progression, with upgrades pretty much being "better but also different" choices rather than giving the player no options.
I for one will pull out my dual revolvers again for the final battle.
Why?
Wang.
It has to be said though that the game has suffered several issues on the technical level.
Two examples I encountered myself:
1.
While playing with a friend in coop he stated a mission while I was in a menu and this corrupted my save file.
This was annoying at first, but then I just started a new game on the lowest difficulty to get my progress back quickly
and also removed any remorse over the lost save files with demon blood... lots of demon blood.
2.
For some reason while using the quick select menu for my weapons the transparent background for the menu stayed on the screen, this was fixed by restarting the game.
So in the end...
How good is the game?
Waaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaang.
If you like ego shooters that are fast paces, action packed and involve murdering a bunch of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s then Shadow Warrior 2 is a great purchase.
And because Flying Wild Hog is a motherducking flying wild hog the game also only costs 37€ on Steam (15.10.2016),
because being money hungry is for big companies (read: ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ding motherducking ♥♥♥♥faces) like EA.

It's now as bad as The Division (1.2 - 1.3) and every Borderlands game.
Stats are king now on higher difficulties, while they used to be a bonus or incentive to switch
weapons before.
Henceforth I'm revoking my recommendation on this game until further notice.

Short version:  This game re-awakened my childhood love of the entire horror genre.
Long version:  Though I used to love horror and the macabre when I was a child, reading not only every Goosebumps and Christopher Pike book I could get my hands on, but also the classics like Edgar Allan Poe, in my teens, I got sick of watching horror films because most of the time, it was either cheap jump scares or gory torture porn.  There were relatively few things that left much to the imagination.  So for over ten years, I haven't been a fan of horror.
For some reason, I kind of got into watching Let's Plays a few years ago, and about two years ago, I saw the beginning of someone playing Amnesia: the Dark Descent.  The commentary was hilarious, but I watched only a bit of it.  While the story was kind of gripping me, I realised that it'd be best if I played the game myself, but I was a bit too frightened to do so.  This year, a friend sort of inspired me to finally get this game.  It took a while, but I eventually started it.
This game finely trod the balance for me between being intriguing enough to me to want to continue, and scaring me enough to make me not want to continue.  Sometimes, it took a bracer of pickled herring and liquid courage to continue, and occasionally it took a break of a few weeks to get me to feel the need to continue, but I did eventually complete the game.  The individual levels are short enough that you can almost justify playing just one more if you're not too frightened.  This game did punish me for becoming too cocky at one point, however.
At one point, I had been introduced to a monster.  I'd become almost used to hiding from the monsters, and if I heard one spawn, I ran and hid in the corner until I felt it was safe.  So this time, when I heard it spawn, I figured the closed door would be plenty sufficient to muffle any sounds I'd make if I played quietly with some boxes.  As I was stacking them, one fell from roughly knee height--and the abomination started breaking down the door.  After yelping and hiding in a distant corner for a while, I waited what I thought was a sufficient time for it to go away.  I peeked around the corner, and it appeared safe.  I carefully looked out the doorway, and it was safe.  I carefully went into the larger room, and it was safe.  I confidently marched down the hallway, raised my lantern, turned a corner, and ran face-first into an abomination.  That was decidedly less safe.  I shouted and tried to run away, but my hand was tremoring so badly from the fear that I was simply raising and lowering the lantern until in a pure panic I hit alt+f4.
The insanity meter in this game is fantastic from my point-of-view.  Some of the effects from the sanity loss are actually similar to what I see when I'm very frightened.  Figuring out whether it's just the character in the game freaking out or me was a bit fun.  As well, though the game does get quite disturbing later on, for me, enough was left to the imagination that it was truly horrifying.  In fact, the game does require you to use your imagination a lot, or at least question whether what you heard was from the game or you just being panicky.
This game did terrify me, and though it might not be for everyone, it certainly worked well for me.

Harkening back to some of the best old school platformers ever, like Mega Man or Super Mario, Shovel Knight has become one of the most fun game ever created. While it's obviously influenced by those NES/SNES platformers, don't think for a second that this game is a copycat of any of them. Shovel Knight carves out its own niche among great platform/action style games. One of the best things about this game is the sheer variety you can find within it. You can play as the titular Shovel Knight himself, and use your shovel like a pogo stick to bounce off an enemy's head. You may find yourself playing as Plague Knight, frenetically throwing bombs at his foes, and launching himself through the air with timed bomb bursts. Or you may find yourself as Spectre Knight, cutting through enemies with your scythe and defying gravity with it in the process. It's worth noting, however, that while you fight all the same enemies in these three campaigns, they are all very different. They each have a different feel, and the stages are not copy/pasted between characters either. Each DLC included in the game truly is a different game.
I could wax nostalgic for hours about this game and how it brings back the feelings of old platformers, but that would be pointless. Buy the game and play it for yourself. I can guarantee that you will enjoy every minute of it.

It is great to see games like this thriving in 2015.  If you ever played Take Command: 2nd Manassas or other Civil War-themed games, you will enjoy playing Ultimate General: Gettysburg.
Not only you can lead either of the sides in the battle of Gettysburg, but you can also pick the course of action for the next battle - e.g. try to push on the enemy or wait for reinforcements.
The interface is easy to follow, and you will be met with video tutorials on how to move your troops and artillery.
The graphics are simple and light on the eyes.
Among the drawbacks of this game I would add a fairly simple gameplay, given that the game is designed for multi-platform use. Plus it is dedicated to only one episode of the Civil War, giving it a mission-oriented feeling, rather than extensive campaign games like ones made by AGEod or Paradox. Given the fact that many of the civil war-themed games are either too old or too obscure today, Ultimate General: Gettysburg is a fresh take on one of the most favorite canons in historical wargaming.
I definitely recommend this game.

I know it's a little early to post a review for this game (at least in my opinion) as not every feature has been implemented yet. However, I still wish to review the game as it is with the three current campaigns we have. (Plus a pretty cool rename)
First off, I need to go ahead and say this, every campaign plays differently from each other. I'll go more into depth of that later. I
the pixel art of this game. Call me a nostalgia addict, but I
love this game's visuals. Everything is so well animated, and yet so detailed. As for the soundtrack of this game, Jake "Virt" Kaufman strikes again with his excellent compositions! (Seriously, I can't get enough of this guy's work)
The gameplay of Shovel Knight's campaign, Shovel of Hope, can be simplied as a "Mega Man-like Ducktales adventure" by some people. And I can't disagree with 'em. I can't shake off the feeling I'm playing a Mega Man game, yet it isn't Mega Man. The plot is, while not very innovative, still is kinda engaging. However I don't think plot is important, since after all the gameplay is where it's really at.  I ended up caring for
in the story, even the knights you go up against of the Order of No Quarter. The balance is
fair towards beginners, but it becomes more challenging at the end. There's no real penalty of death other than losing gold, which you do have an oppertunity to get back. This penalty mechanic applies to every character, as of now.
Plague of Shadows however, is where things become obvious the game plays
differently between different characters. If you're familiar with Star Fox Zero, the game had a long learning curve with its controls, they were pretty functional and fun once you get used to them. Now, why did I bring this up? Plague Knight actually feels the same way. Instead of using a shovel, you're using potions. I can't really explain how this goes, but there's a lot of customization with how you can create your potions later in the campaign. Once more, the balance is fair, but it expects you to have beaten Shovel of Hope and had a grasp of what to expect out of levels.
Then we get to Spectre of Torment, the most recent campaign as of this review. I don't know where to begin with this. Not only is this a prequel to the stories of Shovel of Hope and Plague of Shadows, but it also has entirely new mechanics to play around with levels and bosses that aren't as familiar as they seem. Also you get to play as what some people call the "edgelord" himself. While it is a new style of gameplay, it's much simpler to grasp over Plague of Shadows in my opinion. As for the difficulty, there isn't much of a difficulty curve at all, except for the last levels of the game (in which it spikes a lot). Unlike the previous two, you're allowed to choose every Order of No Quarter stage right from the beginning. This means there's no world map and you can determine the difficulty by which stages you tackle first.
All n' all, I'm very satisfied with what we got with Shovel Knight. While they could have stopped with the Shovel of Hope campaign, they went far and beyond and are fulfilling every kickstarter milestone that was accomplished, and even making the campaigns feel like different games rather than "copy and paste" everything.
While the price has been increased due to being more than one "game" now, I still think it's worth the price of admission, especially with King Knight's campaign being released sometime in 2018. So what are you waiting for (unless it's a sale), "Steel Thy Shovel"!

) (2016) is a sidescrolling endless runner by JCKSLAP (J西卡被巴) and, sadly, a very boringly designed one at that. There's hardly any gameplay and about five minutes worth of content, which some might suspect is an inherent fault of the genre, but that certainly isn't the case.
Autorunners or endless runner games can be quite enjoyable, if a developer puts enough effort into their execution. For example, there are titles like CHILLINGO's
(2013), where players ride a motorbike and can run over, jump on top of, or shoot at all kinds of zombies. Then there's Robot Invader's
(2013), in which players have to think quickly as this runner turns into a fast-paced puzzle platformer with the protagonist having to block or execute attacks, jump from wall to wall, or roll beneath obstacles; and finally there's games like
(2014) by Lucky Kat Studios, a title that is actually not an autorunner, but an endless auto-scroller. The character controls like one would expect from regular  2D platformers, but the camera keeps on moving right, so players have to keep up to not get crushed by enemies or fall into bottomless pits. Sadly, none of this kind of ingenuity made its way in
.
Upon opening the game for the first time, players will realize that the options menu is comparatively barren and only lets them lower or raise the volume of the music and that of the special effects. There are no graphical options and no means to individualize the control scheme. This means that players can only control the game with their mouse: their left mouse button to be more precise. Upon pressing it, Montaro, the shiba inu, jumps. He has to jump in order to get out of the way of antagonistic poultry, avoid bulky refuse, or collect school girl panties that also happen to replenish his health. However, if he happens to run over a banana peel, he also jumps, which means that players can often simply let go off the mouse without being faced with a game over.
As for the life bar, it consists out of three panties with half a panty being deducted every time Montaro slips on a banana peel. Not having any life doesn't kill him though, but merely prevents the player from pressing the jump button for a couple of frames. In fact, the life meter might as well not even exist in the first place as all obstacles and enemies kill the dog in one hit (save for the banana peel), leaving the panty meter to simply be a rather functionless shōnen (少年, aimed at prepubescent boys) trope.

Unlike other casual titles – e.g.

never truly raises the difficulty as the game progresses, and contrary to
(2013), doesn't incentivize players to improve their reaction times to get ahead. This leaves this adorable little game to be oh so dull and looking like a student project. An overall excellent "single battle, multiple scenario" war game, I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys games of this genre.  See below for Pros/Cons.
Pros:
1. Unit morale (courage) and equipment (condition), combined with health (troop number in a single unit) combine to make individual unit strengths and weaknesses interesting.  (As opposed to a single health and damage option.)
2. 3 types of units, infantry, cavalry, & artillery, along with differing ammo types for artillery, combine with (1) to further increase "simplistic diversity."
3. Map elevation, cover (in the form of trees and buildings), provide for strategic planning of the individual scenarios (days) of the battle.
4. Different scenarios, outside of the historical ones, are available for both sides of the overall "battle" depending on how well you do.
Cons:
1. The bottom of the visible map isn't completely viewable.  As such, especially when playing as the CSA (Confederacy), the AI Union will run troops "underneath" my units when they are cornered.
2. The controls take some getting used to, as they are made for touchscreen compatibility vs. "only mouse/keyboard use."  However, they are quite logical and easy to use once you get the hang of it.
3. Unbalanced multiplayer scenarios, especially when playing the original campaign ones.  (As the historical battle was "unfair" to different sides on different days.)
Overall, the game easily fits my personal rule of "pay a $1, get an enjoyable hour of play from the game" rule.

Many people seem to complain about the game being too grindy or the tutorial being not helpful because it only teaches the basic basics.
Many people are apparently not playing the game in the way that this game should be played: by automating everything.
The early game can be a really bad and boring grind, but only if you are either sitting at your base and waiting for your ore extractors to dig up some ore and then grab it to smelt it at your base or exploring too much too early and as result of either, not having enough automation going on, which results in slowing the game to a crawl.
If you truly feel like the game is far too grindy, my advice would be to look up a tutorial or something that teaches you how to *actually* play.
Oh and the latest patch brought a rather large amount of improvements to early game progression to help starting in a new world.
The game itself can easily called a 3D factorio, although that would be a bit too simple - Fortresscraft has many features that allow it to be similiar and yet different, such as the world being literally infinitely deep and having massive underground caverns (which make the ones in minecraft look like caverns for ants) to explore.
Overall, I can wholeheartedly recommend this game to fans of basebuilding, automation and tower defense. (The upcoming expansion will also add tower defense comparable to the Creeper World series, which is great too!)

When I started playing Two Worlds 2, I was not too enthousiastic about it. In the first few minutes of the game, you start out in a prison (hm, in which RPG have we seen this before?) and you immediately notice that the human models are really ugly, the animations are clunky and the voice acting is even worse. I could not really care for the storyline. Oh, nearly forgot to mention the UI...
The combat system takes some getting used to. Especially in the early game you will die A LOT. The areas in the world do not scale with your level (as far as I've seen), so you will probably die to a one-hit from a Grom a few times on the starter island. I focused on the melee type of combat, switching between two one-handers and a two-handed weapon, depending on the stats. It should be possible to play a hybrid warrior/ranger/mage, but it will probably make you a lot weaker. I should mention that you need to wield a staff in order to cast spells, but you can easily switch between 3 sets of gear.
Character customization is pretty well done. You can upgrade all your gear (if you invest skillpoints into the blacksmithing skills) using raw materials that you gather by breaking down your useless items. You can add gems to your equipment and combine gems to make them stronger. You can even apply some paint to your armor, but I did not really feel the need.
The graphics are fine and the athmosphere in the game is pretty nice, especially dungeons look nice and dark (better than Oblivion imo).
I nearly finished Chapter 1 and I'm not sure what the end-game will look like, but so far the game looks interesting enough to keep playing. Overall, pretty average RPG, well worth sinking a few hours/euros into.

Sale assessment: buy if under $10. Under $20 if you're like me and really love sniper gameplay. $50 is highway robbery.

They may try, but they will never beat Rome: Total War.
Of course, the game is ageing, and with each new Total War iteration struggling to refine the gameplay it was always going to age somewhat badly. The soldiers which at the time seemed technological marvels now look blocky and cartoony, the campaign map looks less vibrant and more modular, the little portraits, banners and such all look unimpressive and much of the interface seems vaguely unresponsibe, low resolution and unattractive.
But they will never beat this game.
What was Rome Total War? Think of cars coming into a world of carts, think of chocolate coming into a world of porridge. People had dreamed of seeing the vast armies portrayed as 2D sprites in the original Shogun: Total War in glorious full 3D, and this game delivered in every way imaginable. The roman cities were sparkling, shining in the sun, the landscapes were the scale of the real world and the armies were, indeed, massive. The formations looked just as good as you always hoped they would, and things like charges had the very, excellent, feeling that we had all imagined.
Not only that, but the game was deep and
, with hours upon hours of varied gameplay promised, with any faction we wiped out in one playthrough being available to control in the next campaign - something that Empire: Total War really should have allowed. The (strangely Australian) tutorial woman left
to chance, and we never felt out of control, rushed, or under any pressure that was not a direct result of our own actions (all faults that would plague later titles in the series, in my eyes)
The characters were great - real world names popping up here and there, generals increasing in effectivness. Money flowed relatively easily if you were but a little thoughtful about it, and developing more advanced troops was intuitive and straightforward.
In short, this game got everything right. It has just the right mix of gameplay imposition and gamer imposition, input from both sources comign together to create a sandbox empire building experience that could suck you in and satisfied you for tens, hundreds of hours.

I would give this game a 6/10.
The story...very enjoyable and entertaining side quests let you meet some very colorful characters.
The Graphics...it is a bit buggy at times, but makes up for that in great scenery and wildlife graphics. I wish they had done as well with the human graphics, they are not horrible but could have been so much better. The water graphics... WOW the best I have seen in a game!
The Fighting system...great balance of attack, parry, and defence that makes you think and time your moves for the best outcome. Very enjoyable!
The Quest system...very in depth with clues along the way and map marks to help get you where you need to go.
The Transportation...boats...horses...teleports...what else does one need? :)
The Magic system...fun but complicated. You can create your own spell combinations using 'cards' that you find while exploring, hunting, and buying from merchants. It makes for some fun effects if you have invested in the skill far enough to cast what you have created.
The Alchemy system...fun to experiment and make your own recipes that you can save and click a scroll to create later with ease. Water walking potion? Squee!
The Crafting system...on the fly and anywhere crafting! Dismantle what you don't need for components and use them to upgrade the stuff you are going to use! And don't forget the dyes...what color do you want to wear? Find dyes at merchants and use them to our hearts delight!
Overall I really enjoyed this game...though it is no Gothic, Dragon Age or Skyrim...it was still fun!
Mods...I would recommend the Two Worlds Merged, mod. It expands the World into one large map with no barriers, adds more dye options, an in depth add on series of quests that are quite fun and add hours of gameplay...and many other features that add to the fun!

Before you read, this is just a friendly notice: Do not buy this game if you haven't got any friends to play it with!!
With that out the way lets talk about the game!
Dead realm is an overall fun game to play with friends, yes it does have glitches and bugs but they aren't that significant and gamechanging which make the game 'unplayable'. The glitches are minor such as having limbs occasionally pop out of hiding spots such as wardrobes when playing the game mode 'hunted' or being able to see outside of the map if you are to stand up in crouching spots, for instance in the 'dead silence' map.
The game has lots of replay value and is always a laugh to play with friends, you can play with 3 or more and have hours of fun; the ghosts have distinct looks and can honestly frighten you when being reaped off guard and you feel tension throughout the experience of each round.
There are so many intricate and clever hiding spots within the game which continue to make the game replayable, still I am finding spots to camp in after 9 hours of playtime which goes to show that developers did take a lot of effort into making this game and its maps and game modes.
There are an abundance of game modes to play:
Seek & Reap -  A hide and seek with the ghost having powers and the humans cameras and motion trackers to detect the ghost. This is my favourite game mode as it is fast paced and very tense, the ghost and humans are both well balanced in this mode.
Hunted - A hide and seek however the humans have weapons and utilities such as guns and flashlights, motion trackers etc whereas the ghost has a single knife and the ability to find players with a glowing mist when still. By itself, Shovel Knight is a great game. I imagine it will appeal more to players who were interested in the 8- and 16-bit eras of games, because nostalgia no doubt plays a part, but there is a fundamentally solid and enjoyable platformer underneath the layers of rose-tinted glasses. It's difficult, sure, but also forgiving, and as the game progresses, special abilities allow to approach problems in multiple ways (well, bosses can be approached in multiple ways, the platforming challenges have more or less one solution). There are so many secrets and unlockables and the fact is that you have to get pretty good at the game to beat it, which makes revisiting earlier levels pretty enjoyable to see how far you've come - it's worth replaying.
If Shovel Knight was all you got, it would be well worth it. However, I have to say that Yacht Club Games has delivered possibly the most well-supported video game ever. The two subsequently delivered game modes (Plague Knight and Spectre Knight) could have easily and justifiably have been released as $10 DLC packs, but they were just given to owners of the game (as far as I know - I don't think Shovel Knight ever had multiple versions, some of which would have locked out future content packs). This is a shining example of how developers can choose to treat their players, and - if I'm being entirely honest - probably a little unfair in the gamer's favor.
Not that I'm complaining.
There are some things that I could mildly complain about. I hated knockback into insta-kill pits on the NES and I still hate it, now. The initial learning curve might be a little high. I feel like I died on Spectre Knight (the third boss) in my first playthrough of the game about 50 times before I figured out the patterns and managed to win. But these complaints probably have more to do with me being bad and / or not always up for the challenge this type of game presents. I can't really blame someone else if they weren't either, but they would be missing out, in the end.

This game used to be fun.  Key is USED TO.  If you played in earlier versions you will understand.  Every new patch he changes things to force players to do things his way.  Things that are(were) fun are being nerfed all in the name of because you are not playing the game in his vision.
He has removed the ability to craft things manually and now force you to make these one-off machines because these are 'new machines'.  So now players need to make a production chain just to make some of these infrequently used intermediate items instead of allow players to craft by hand which many of has only a single purpose.
Not even considering previous nerfs, the current nerfs already announced include the inability(or limited) use of the grapple so they will not work in certain areas as well as the inability to smelt anywhere but on the surface.  AND NO... CC Furnaces does not count as that requires a separate PAID subscription to patreon to access currently.  And the newest nerf announcement of limiting the amount of ores you're allowed to carry so you have to play the game as he sees fit.
The nerfs aren't even the largest issue.  The attitude of the developer is just bad.  Many of his replies on this very forum are just condescending replies.  So instead of discussion he would routinely just reply "You do know there's a machine for that, right?" or the ever helpful "You have read the help files, right?"
Fundamental changes should have been done from the beginning.  The game has been in Steam's Early Access since 2013, but waits til NOW to make some of these changes.  Which brings up the final point.  All these changes are always justified because of 'serious discussions with other players and we feel it's for the better...' type posts.  These are usually the hardcore players who sit on his daily stream and chats.  These evangelical players are not always the best gauge for tuning and balancing and you will see them defending the developer tooth and nail for these changes on these same forums.
I fully expect many of them to vote down once he tells his stream viewers but many things needed to be said.  IMO if you are interested in logistics and think this is factorio in 3D, you would be sad.  If you wanted a sandbox game, this is not it. The game by itself is amazing and the $/hour value is insane with all the content you get from used created content, but there's a slight flaw which is best explained with an example:
1. Decide to play the game.
2. uDontPlay update
3. Launch game - unskippable logos, but that's okay they're short.
4. Preload before the main menu. Okay, could've done that during splash screens, but okay.
5. Connecting to Ubisoft servers.....
6. Still connecting.
7. Failed to connect to Ubisoft servers, hit retry,
8. Finally connected to Ubisoft servers, yay.
9. Browse around the menus checking for new stuff.
10. Random freeze, Ctrl+Alt+Del => End task.
11. Wait for uDontPlay to do some bs before it shuts down.
12. Relaunch game, surprisingly uDontPlay hasn't been updated since then.
13. Splash screen logos, preload, connecting to Ubisoft servers.
14. Failed to connect to Ubisoft servers, hit retry.
15. Go straight for playing this time, let's see the new content.
16. Spend ~2minutes to complete the first medium map in the new pack, loving it!
17. Autosave after the level completion takes about as much time as the level itself.
18. Lost connection to the Ubisoft servers............. That explains it.
19. Hit retry, twice this time, before it actually works.
20. Back, back, back, back, quit game.
That's ~15-20 minutes of Ubisoft bullcrap to play two minutes of an otherwise solid game.
Guess I'll try again in a couple months.... but every time I try to pick this game back up it's the same reason that makes me shelve it and that's uDontPlay.
I'll admit, the freeze could've been a bug from Redlynx's side, but I wouldn't be surprised if Ubisoft DRM is so well integrated that it is the reason why the menus are so slow to swap inbetween to begin with.
Setting up Excitebike on a NES emulator from scratch would probably take less time than each fresh launch of Trials through uPlay after a prolongued absence.

I recommend this game if you're a fan of the Zelda games by Nintendo. This game plays similarly to those ones, segmented into dungeons with bosses and tools that you find in the dungeon to beat the boss. You progress through the game and improve your character by finding treasure rather than by leveling up with experience points, you have a finite magic meter that you can expand, etc. The combat plays like God of War, but it's actually the weakest part of the game. You have three main melee weapons but the game really doesn't do much in the way of involving them in combat. The Scythe looks cool but is weaker than the sword, and the gauntlet is too slow to be of use in combat. Most of the fights are "mash x, dodge, mash x again, press b to kill the guy." Some enemies which could only be hurt by a certain weapon or used different tactics would have been nice.
The story isn't anything special, but I do have to give Vigil Games props for using a setting (loosely) based on Revelation rather than the generic medieval fantasy world. The main character doesn't have much personality beyond smoldering with generic rage, but Mark Hamill's Watcher (the sidekick/Navi-type character) is far more interesting.
On the technical end, this game was not designed for PC and was ported horribly. There are no video options at all besides toggling V-sync on or off, and you have to force anti-aliasing through your graphics card manually. I got the game to run at 75 frames per second normally but I get huge stuttering and frame drops for inexplicable reasons sometimes. Keyboard and mouse controls are unintuitive and you can't rebind the keys. Using a controller isn't just recommended, it's required. Even then, some of the controls are really wonky. You have to hold LT to target and enemy but then have to hold LB to select your magic, meaning you have to deselect a target before casting unless you hold LT with your middle finger, which almost no one does, and block and dash are mapped to the same button for who knows what reason. The game also has numerous bugs. Don't be surprised to see it crash if you alt-tab out of it at all and then lose your achievement progress.
The technical issues don't really ruin the game, and I still recommend it for anyone who likes Zelda. It's a fun diversion despite its lack of originality.

Most fun i've had in long time - hits all the right notes with me. It's an  FPS RPG like Borderlands\Destiny with gameplay tropes taken from Diablo - while the gunplay itself reminds me of the recent doom - hectic. Loot system is very satisfying, most drops are useful and feel balanced, fantastic variety of weapons that are creative and fun - play on hard or higher for a decent challenge so you've gotta keep moving to avoid getting swarmed and play smart with your loadout and ammo. If I had to level a criticism (note I haven't finished the game - but played enough now to gauge core qualities), GFX are mostly great but some of the models (especially facial) are very rough, compared to most other games out there - not enough to be a problem, but you do notice it. By itself, Shovel Knight is a great game. I imagine it will appeal more to players who were interested in the 8- and 16-bit eras of games, because nostalgia no doubt plays a part, but there is a fundamentally solid and enjoyable platformer underneath the layers of rose-tinted glasses. It's difficult, sure, but also forgiving, and as the game progresses, special abilities allow to approach problems in multiple ways (well, bosses can be approached in multiple ways, the platforming challenges have more or less one solution). There are so many secrets and unlockables and the fact is that you have to get pretty good at the game to beat it, which makes revisiting earlier levels pretty enjoyable to see how far you've come - it's worth replaying.
If Shovel Knight was all you got, it would be well worth it. However, I have to say that Yacht Club Games has delivered possibly the most well-supported video game ever. The two subsequently delivered game modes (Plague Knight and Spectre Knight) could have easily and justifiably have been released as $10 DLC packs, but they were just given to owners of the game (as far as I know - I don't think Shovel Knight ever had multiple versions, some of which would have locked out future content packs). This is a shining example of how developers can choose to treat their players, and - if I'm being entirely honest - probably a little unfair in the gamer's favor.
Not that I'm complaining.
There are some things that I could mildly complain about. I hated knockback into insta-kill pits on the NES and I still hate it, now. The initial learning curve might be a little high. I feel like I died on Spectre Knight (the third boss) in my first playthrough of the game about 50 times before I figured out the patterns and managed to win. But these complaints probably have more to do with me being bad and / or not always up for the challenge this type of game presents. I can't really blame someone else if they weren't either, but they would be missing out, in the end.

It has three campaigns: Shovel of Hope, Plague of Shadows, Specter of Torment and a fourth (unnamed) campaign for the King Knight character. Four campaigns 100% guaranteed to give you hours of fun.
If you like the Mega Man, Shantae, Cave Story, Metroid, Castlevania or Duck Tales NES then you're gonna love Shovel Knight!
Alright, dig this jive daddio: Shovel Knight takes the level designs and boss rooms from Mega Man, game mechanics from Metroid, Castlevania & Duck Tales, the map system from Super Mario Bros. 3 and throws it all together in one mindblowingly fun package.
I've had almost
in this game, and it's never been a dull moment. Yacht Club hasn't let me down; I've thoroughly enjoyed Shovel Knight and I would recommend it to absolutely everyone... unless they get frustrated and/or angry easily. It's not that difficult, just be prepared to die a lot at first.
I'm on the edge of my seat waiting for the King Knight campaign, and I can't wait to see what Yacht Club Games has to offer with their next game.

First you look at grass, then trees, then ground that you flatten, then you look at ground you are digging into, then you look at ore you are mining, then the furnace you are smelting it in, then the leather crafting equipment, then the forge, and finally; you look at people running away from you, before you catch up to them and kill them with weapons and armor.
11/10 Would fail to communicate with peasant thief because of Alpha Build, then kill him and take all his rocks, rags and apples.
EDIT - There seems to be a LOT of confusion about combat in this game, rightfully so. People say it is broken because they attempt PVP VERY EARLY INTO THEIR PLAYTHROUGHS, and try to beat each other to death with tools mostly, iron and primitive.
However, that is not true, you take a major penalty when fighting with tools that can be reduced (Although never fully) by leveling a skill called "Militia Service," which attaches to a penalty free weapon, the familiar pitchfork! The pitchfork is effective, as you are unarmored and agile, you can also outmaneuver them with your speed. A peasant not to be trifled with to say the least.
Additionally, "real" combat features a not visually impressive, but still very immersive and fun combat system. You will find yourself strategizing against your opponent, anticipating his moves and stamina, spotting weak points in his armor. You will want to duel your cohorts almost constantly, when facing Hank, the fully armored Zweihander♥♥♥♥♥♥victim in the comments. I found myself circling with him in a defensive posture and thinking, "First, he'll aim to parry, strike, backpedal and swing, then disengage and recover." You will feel A LOT of satisfaction when your opponent executes precisely as you anticipated before you press the attack. It will drive you to almost never want to make things in the game again, only steal and kill from those who do.

you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

The 2013 Shadow Warrior was a mighty fine game, in terms of mechanics, level design and graphics. This game is a step back. In an effort to make the game bigger, the game has been stripped of any personality it has and is filled using randomly generated levels with a set base map. Enemies randomly pour on you from all sides, dying has not much meaning except losing money and XP. Guns do not feel powerful because well, this game now relies on numbers as much as a regular RPG would. So you keep shooting that somewhat big enemy with your shotgun and it just never stops. Even small enemies take more than two shotgun blasts at times to die. The sword, which could slash most regular enemies in one hit in the first game feels like a razor blade. I guess they wanted death by a thousand cuts or something, for the enemies in the game. Like many have said, this game is now a half baked borderlands clone with a garbage shooting system and a garbage upgrade system.
The graphics are nothing to brag about either, frankly. They all look like as if coated with flourescent paint. It all looks like someone put neon lights eveywhere. It is not pleasant at all.
Overall, this a borefest with several filler fetch quests and poor gameplay and graphics. Maybe worth playing for 2-3 hours and that is it. Buy it when it goes to bargain bin, if you really want. Otherwise, stay away.

Summary: While this game is pretending to be everything it fails to become anything in the foreseeable future.
Yes, the game has absolutely no future except being an early access title until its distant demise. Yes, it will be early access for very long time. Take a couple of years.
It is ridiculous how with such large gameplay scope developers fail to design even basic features and mechanics. It's not even interesting to study the design of the game as it is usual with other early access games.
There are several very obvious evidences that the game is designed very poorly. What is bad about design flaws? Design flaw is much worse than even a hudred bugs. You just can't fix it without destroying some part of the game. And one design decision is always connected to the others. Redesign is a chain reaction that involves most part of the game to be reconsidered and recoded.
As it is usual happens with independent developers they pay very little attention to a game design. They jump to start coding and modelling. Well it's good if you're designing another simple puzzle or arcade game - they tend to have very short development cycles. On the other hand - games with such gameplay scope as LiF have very long development cycle - about a year. It means time needed to code a tech demo after design revision.
This development cycle we have now is already wasted. Next development cycle will be wasted too. Not just because developers are bad or something. But because the game system will be so complex that there will be unexpected results.
To prove my point, here's some design flaws.
1. Terraforming.
Terraforming system is purely artificial and is a subject to heavy changes in the future. Right now terraforming consists of too artificially combined systems: landscape terraforming and tunneling. It is very easy to see that tunneling artificially blocks landscape terraforming in its vicinity. That's just because developers have no idea how these two systems should interact.
Terraforming lies in the basis of the game so any changes to that system will result in a redesign of the whole game.
There are so many questions that needs to be addressed here. Will there be a cave-ins? Can you build a house inside a mine? Maybe a farm? Do I need light inside? What if I will dig upward to the surface?
2. Skills.
Right now there are too many skills in the game with very little logic behind them.
Let's say you want to be a hunter. Track animals and kill them to get hides and meat. Not so fast. It seems you have to learn how to plow ground first and grow crops. And only then you will be able to dry a deer's hide. That logic.
Same problem with terraforming, prospecting and mining skills.
There is no obvious way to choose some simple role. Skills are divided and interconnected in some weird and unexpected way. Obviously skill system will be revised very soon. It's just awful.
3. Skill cap.
Well, I bet developers are very proud they have "invented" a such an original way to milk LiF MMO players for money. Of course you will have to buy character slots. Why else this skill cap is even implemented? You won't be able to create anything in the game without 3-4 different characters involved. That's the only reason.
The worst of design flaws are those which was made to make us spend money. Because you can't fix them and they ruin the game the most.
4. Hunger.
It is the best example of a system that haven't even been thought about. It's a typical placeholder. And yet it's the most important system. It is one of the reasons to make players settle in some place. Some place where they have created a food production chain. If you won't be able to make them settle - they will be roaming around freely to kill and destroy. Because it's the natural pastime of human beings.
Right now you don't have to hunt, fish or grow crops. You only need to make weapons and armor to kill someone.
Well, I'll just name few more problematic mechanics which have to be designed yet.
5. Quality migration.
6. Private property.
7. Claiming lands.
8. Criminal acts.
9. Water travel.
10. Howling-transporting goods.
11. Deconstruction.
12. Siege.
13. Off-line characters.
14. Tracking down criminals.
15. Trading.
... and much much more.
It's sad to say that developers doesn't even bothered to study some references. Like Haven & Hearth, for example. It's obvious they have played it. Yet they haven't analyzed it's design decisions and flaws. And they already trying to invent something "new". While they only will end up reinventing the weel.
Edit: Fixed mistake about skinning a deer. It was about drying hides, not skinning.

Amnesia : The Dark Descent is a blend of adventure game elements such as exploration and physic based puzzles in a horror themed environment. They complement each other well, as the places you wander through get gradually more terrifying, the fairly unconvoluted riddles help you ease the tension that can become almost unbearable at times. This is where this game shines, the pace is skillfully mastered, even if you have difficulties persisting in horror games you might very well finish this one. The design is tighly knot around exploration, lightening candles and torches to ward off the darkness, finding the scattered pieces of the story and a death mechanic inconsequential to your progress. The game manages to fill you both with a sense of curiosity as you descent further into the abyss to unravel its mysteries, and a sense of dread to what awaits you in its darkest recesses. You won't be disappointed by its climax.
Amnesia : The Dark Descent is a very enjoyable and rewarding experience, yet a highly unpleasant one, reaching that difficult balance each horror game aims to find. It lasts 7 to 8 hours, and there is the possibility to play custom stories, which I might review here as I go through them.

Downloaded this not knowing what to expect....I am glad i did! Not knowing much about the American Civil War I was not sure how the game would play out. My first game I chose to be the CSA. I felt sure I would lose, however following 4 or 5 engagements I managed to achieve a deadlock result which was slightly disappointing as my tactics and execution seemed spot on. I love the way this game looks and feels. Now the pros and cons bit:
Pros:
1. Easy to use and units respond to my commands straight away (also a con but we will come to that in a bit).
2. Cleaver use of terrain to determine line of sight.
3. AI - i played with a balanced Union foe without the AI boost and still found the battle challenging, defiantly some points during the battle where I had to think on my feet to react to a clever flanking move!
4. Atmospheric and sound effects good.
5. Fog Of War well represented especially during night skirmishes.
6. Great value for money.
Cons:
1.	Would have liked to have zoomed into the action a little more.
2.	Ease of use, maybe too easy to execute commands, I think for a more realistic experience the execution of orders should have a delay from issue to execution. I am sure that I would have had a tougher time if this were the case.
3.	Would like to have seen the effects of powder smoke play a part in adding to the FOW.
Suggestions:
Add some music of the era to play over the action, Battle Hymn of the republic would be great as my troops advanced or if you play as the Union – Yankee Doodle!
Please please introduce more battles or a linked campaign with other battles such as Bull Run or Manassas.
Overall an excellent game, looking forward to playing multiplayer!

I've actually owned this game before random Neo-Confederates decided to make Apple pulling it off their service their casus belli.
So for anyone looking at the game and not interested in Neo-Confederate rhetoric being the driving opinion I would say buy it for the great gameplay regardless of any flag fiasco.
Since objectively the game is very good and somewhat reminiscent of Sid Meier's Gettysburg!
The Union has a slightly easier time due to the game making them better at shooting while the South is better at close combat and general morale.
The UI is very intuitive with a simple click and drag system.
One thing that should be said is that the campaign while existent does not nearly draw you in as much as Sid Meier's Gettysburg!'s use of reactment cutscenes.  Instead there's a sort of barebone summary of orders and a hidden skeleton tree campaign.
Enoyable nonetheless but if the game had a bigger budget and more people working on it, it could be an obvious area of improvement.
On a last note I should also say that the AI is suprisingly good with multiple personality types to match what you choose.
So I highly recommend if you're fan of strategy games in general and have an interest in the Civil War period. I do not recommend it if you just want to buy it to protest a private company's decision over a flag and want the internet to witness your political leanings.

I bought this out of nostlgia for the good ol fraxis classic sid meiers civil war. I will sum up my review (i wont go into too much depth on specific units, locations etc as my civil war jargons a bit rusty) in the one battle i played last night and it lasted simply one hour. Being the cockyish rts gamer experienced in many hardcore strategy games i picked a custom battle, chose devils den as the location and put the ai on the hardest most aggressive difficulty with the ai boost (whichever one was in the bottom right for difficulty selection).
On the first match which lasted all but 15 minutes the csa made me believe that i had won our first engagement, it was a tough 5min firefight and i was still learning the controls but the csa soon retreated. Feeling overconfident in my perceived strategic prowess i sent all my forces in to not only route but ahnillate the csa forces. To my horror i not only had sent my men into the main artillery brigade of the csa forces but was soon enveloped in what i would say was a near perfectambushing maneuveur that surrounded and then routed my forces. Mouth agape, and pride wounded, i went for round two. This time i used every trick i had.
I formed a tight defensive perimeter focusing on holdingwhatever high ground or structured positions and keeping my flanks secured to the point where i was nestled in the upper right hand corner of the map. I slowly advanced with sharpshooters acting as scouts and marking where batteries and battalions etc were. as the first forces of the csa began to engage (quite effectively) with both musket and artillery, whilst my artillery was out of range, I quickly ended the skirmish and fell back to the upper left corner. As the confederates advanced toward the treeline and farm (again i dont remember the exact names) down from there position of the high ground they soon came under range of my artillery. The main bulk of the confederate forces began to sweep down to my right flank and using scattered forces harrassed my main line and left flank. Their artillery effectively pushed my main force back as far as i could allow. all the while I was cycling fresh troops in with those who had been fighting and taking heavy losses. The fight was at a dead heap with losses pilling on both sides.
The csa forces then recieved reinforcements and proceded to attack my left flank which was already slim as I had moved almost half of them to fortify the rigth flank. I sent two artillery batteries within close rang of these attacking forces and with the excelsior and iron brigades as the last defense for the left flank. The csa forces soon went in for an all out charge on the left flank whilst the right flank was still in a dead heap and the main line exchanging light musket fire, with the majority being harrassing from various artillery on both sides. Just in time the V corp (i believe) came in to reinforce the left flank which was now routed. My main line at this point was in danger of being flanked from behind, simultaneously the csa forces engaging my main line went in for an all out charge in an attempt to route my entire III, and II Corp (again i dont know which was which at this point). In a last ditch effort to buy time I put my previous danger close batteries set to canister shot to fire relentlessly at the charging confederates, the csa only mistake at this point was rerouting its troops that were still in a pitched fight with my right flank to join the main attack.
I quickly but at great risk moved my fresh V corp to the right flank (i did have a plan). At this point my left flank was broken my main line was all but enveloped. If it were not for those two batteries that were preventing the confederates from maneuvering completely around im certain 75% of my forces woudve been wiped out or routed. Im hectically recycling routed troops with semi routed ones, units that had 1800 men were down to 600, the iron brigade had all but 200 men left. As i said earlier the csa main mistake was all but abandoning the right flank, with my fresh V corp and semi-battered reminince of the I believe IV corp I swept up in almost a semi circle taking heavy fire from csa batteries and routing the small remaining csa forces guarding the right flank. The bulk of my now IV and V corp swept up and I saw my chance. A chance which im sure the ai saw as well. My IV and V corp formerly the right flank swept up and semi enveloped the now mob consisting of my shattered left flank and near routed main line and the bulk of csa forces who it seems as the victory bar (bar in the upper right corner) were about 75% to my 25%.
However since they maneuvered their right flank to try and brank my left flank, and theire main force was in hand to hand with mine, the only defense their rear had was a couple of batteries (not to be taken lightly) but not within range of canister shot. The ai attempted to secure its now completely open rear but its attempt at routing my left flank earlier in the battle had left their forces too battered and simply too far to defend itself in time. As i began to envelope them one by one they began to route, csa batllte flags began to flash white (except for the texas brigade they didnt give a sh!t that they were completely surrounded) and just as it had begun it was over. I was absolutely ecstatic at seeing that I had procured a hard fought major victory for the union I hadn't felt tht accomplished with a game in years. I lost roughly 10,000 men to their 9,000 losses, though i was outnumbered, in the end though I was not outmaneuvered. I had my ego realigned and reminded myself the reason I had so much confidence in my abilities was simply because of hard fought and as my first game showed me hard lost battles like these. So to end this long story I learned three things.
One this is not sid meiers civil war, it is something, different, it is more chaotic, and like chess you win or lose in the first moves of the match.
Two the Texas brigade has to be wiped out, dont think you can route them, dont waste your time trying to, trust me.
Third if youve stuck around long enough to read this whole thing and if any of this sounds appealing, BUY IT. I know ive only played this game for an hour but ive played enough of these and i consider rts, and simulations to be my bread and butter for gaming and i can tell right away that it is worth the fifteen bucks.
Thank you Game-Labs I look forward to your future projects,

90's video game action hero Duke Nukem is back with more of his over the top machismo as he saves the world and our babes again from the same aliens he humilated last time. Lots of action, alien♥♥♥♥♥kicking, and one liners will keep you entertained both in single and multi player game modes.

Many a day of my life was lost playing this game as an early teen. I returned to it now, 7 years later and it still smokes any non-military (meaning not in the vein of CS, Battlefield etc.) competitive shooter out there.
As AlexOfSpades put it, "before the days of shooters that holds your hand and aim for you, that regenerate your health and show you what to do like a baby, there was this." Yes indeed. I have gotten so accustomed to these games that, when I bought this game and went straight to my old habit of a warm-up Masterful bot DM, I had my♥♥♥♥♥HANDED TO ME. Time. And Time. Again. Until my rusty inner gaming beast finally tossed away the awful crutches that today's games forced upon it and I once again felt the rush of a full-blown UT deathmatch.
This shows what a bunch of wimps today's "fast-paced shooters" are made for. This game requires insane concentration, mental sharpness, quick decision making and finger/fine motorics coordination of a freaking Navy jet pilot. Stand still - dead, wrong weapon for the situation - dead, miss a powerup - dead, let the enemy pick up a health pack - dead, shoddy tactics in team matches - dead. No room for error (providing you have set the difficulty level high enough to actually be challenged). It's a wild ride and there is no better feeling than finally letting go of your poor, burned-out mouse and seeing your username at the top of the scoreboard.
Technically, the game excels at everything. The weapons are perfectly balanced, the powerups are perfectly distributed, the gameplay is smooth and uninterrupted. The graphics are 2004 appropriate, but even today, they are a thing of beauty, the colors are clear and it doesn't have the murky, gray/brown "drape" like UT3. The only thing that kind of bugged me was no native widescreen support, but the fix is super easy, no problems there.
However, as much as I can gush over the "old days" of adrenaline-fuelled arena bloodshed, it's dated. Not the game itself, as I said, it is arena mayhem at its most perfect, but the concept itself has sadly fallen out of fashion. There will always be devout maniacs such as myself and a lot of people who gave this game a thumbs up, but ultimately, I think there's little hope of this kind of action coming back in this form.
Long story short: if you spent days trying to find a tactic to bring down a Power Core in a certain map, or spent days honing your no-scope headshots, get this, and feel the rush. If you're a modern gamer new to this game, get it, take it easy at first, up the difficulty when you feel you have the grasp, and realize that CoD is about as intense as PacMan. If you're expecting to get your mind blown by anything other than a Flak Cannon, don't get this game. This is nothing new. It is something old. And it still kicks gobs of♥♥♥♥♥
