SEv2 isn't a terrible game, but it's not great by any means. The only reason I even tried it is because it combines three of my favorite concepts in games: stealth, playing a sniper and killing Nazis.
Unfortunately, there are a bunch of technical issues with this game.
For starters, you can't save when and where you want. I know that doesn't bother some people (there are even those who prefer it that way, for some weird reason) but I find it extremely annoying.
Fortunately, the game does include a semi-save state. It's not a true save state because that'd mean you'd reappear exactly where you left. Instead, you can quit and appear back at the nearest checkpoint, so you don't have to replay the entire mission over.
The AI is atrocious. Ironically, the enemies don't appear until you move closer to certain areas, so don't plan on sniping everyone from a distance -- you know, the sort of thing a sniper does. In addition, enemies will give up looking for you within a minute, only to step over their dead friend and suddenly act surprised, despite the fact they were just screaming about a sniper moments ago.
Despite this, the game does offer some fun game mechanics. For instance, if you pull of a particularly good shot, the game will show you the bullet, in slow-motion, flying through the air and penetrating your target. Even better, this is done in an x-ray view, so you can see the enemy's internal organs and bone structure. This does get tiring after seeing it a bunch, however, so you can turn it off.
Also, SEv2 models hit detection exceptionally well. If an enemy has a grenade strapped to his belt, you can shoot it and he'll explode. If you time your shots right and aim at the right areas, you can potentially hit multiple targets with one bullet.
There also some nice touches to the game. Enemies speak in their native language, so you'll hear Germans speaking German and Soviets speaking Russian. I think you can turn subtitles on which will translate what they say, but for the most part, you don't need to know German or Russian to get the gist of it.
The DLC doesn't add much except for some extra missions and two rifles. One of the available DLC allows you to kill Hitler, which is never a bad thing.
I haven't tried the multiplayer. It didn't interest me and it's not why I bought the game. From what little I understand, MP really boils down to "dueling snipers." This could either be extremely tense and exciting or about as boring as watching paint dry.
In case anyone's wondering, no, you can't play a German soldier or a Soviet soldier. You're an American behind enemy lines. That's it. If that bothers you -- and it apparently does annoy more than a few people in the SEv2 boards -- then perhaps this game isn't for you. Maybe there are some mods out there that change things.
Look, SEv2 is fun so long as you don't expect a decent story, don't have a problem with AI or game elements, and don't feel bothered by having to replay entire levels over again.  In other words, give it a try if it's on sale (I got it at 75% off the normal price), but otherwise, pass it up.

I didn't expect to have as much fun as i did with this one.
The game starts off pretty weak with the regenerating health system being the main flaw that i could spot instantly.
This coupled with enemy placement in the early stages makes the game feel too easy even on the highest difficulty setting as there is little to no consequnce if you get shot.
In turn this enables you to be pretty reckless using the crosshair or "quickscoping" to take down targets in one shot even from point blank distance, neutralizing the need for a sidearm in CQC engagements.
Later on, however, the pace picks up and the stakes get high as there are more enemies arround and you'll have to plan your shots accordingly lest you want to be dead within seconds.
Another feature that plays an important role later on but is sadly downplayed on the earlier levels due to the reasons mentioned above, is "masking" your shots using ambient noise to avoid being detected by the enemy.
As the game progresses engagements and scenarios become more memorable with a certain fire fight on the rooftops of war-torn and ravaged Berlin being an incredible experience.
The game's trademark feature (or gimmick) is the gruesome killcam that resembles MK9's X-ray moves. Personally i love it but there is the option to reduce its frequency if you want to.
The game's story is forgetable and it's there only as a reason for you to snipe some dudes.
On a technical level the game looks and performs great and there are lots of options in the menu to customize your experience. A benchmark is also included.
What stood out for me though in the technical aspect was, inspite of the levels being pretty big and beautiful, the load times were incredibly short and almost zero on my dated sata2 7200.11 drive.
As far as multiplayer is concerned there is a slew of co-op missions and 3 different modes as well as vs with a server browser. From what i got to play the netcode was good and the vs part was surprisingly active and fast for a sniper game as you could tag opponents for your teammates to see, effectively countering camping to a degree and preventing the game from becoming a total snoozefest.
Recommended.

Just recently finished my run through Darksiders; I must say I was very pleased with the experience.  The game reminded me of a cross between Legend of Zelda and God of War. The plot of the story isn't necessarily anything to write home about, but the actual atmosphere of the game is superb. I found the environments in particular to be highly immersive; each area has its own unique theme. The non-player character models, including their animations, are extraordinary.
The combat isn't particularly evolved and the game itself isn't exactly challenging. I personally played on Apocalyptic and would recommend others do the same. There were a surprising amount of puzzles, invariably utilizing some recently acquired gadget. These items are often necessary for collectibles, but rarely are required in areas beyond which they were designed.
If I had to summarize my experience with this game I would say this: It starts very strong, but begins to struggle in the end. There are enough "awesome" moments that keep you engaged through the ~15 hours but the repetitious challenge/puzzle formula, shallow improvement system, and anticlimactic ending make for a mediocre finish.
I still recommend the game. It was quite an enjoyable adventure and I'm looking forward to seeing more of this stylish world in Darksiders II.

Similar to the Penumbra games, Amnesia: TDD is all about atmosphere and storytelling.  The biggest difference between the two series is that Amnesia does include more of the classic horror induced moments of being chased and hunted.  Not that Penumbra didn't have a bit of that, but I'd say in Amnesia, there were specific moments designed to inject some action.
Overall however, the game is paced similarly.  I could wander about, sip some coffee, read my notes and mementos and take in my surroundings.
This may sound casual but what Amnesia succeeds in doing is creating a sense of dread.  Brennenburg Castle is a miserable place and rarely do you find yourself feeling too comfortable. When an enemy does discover you and then gives chase, it is probably one of the more scary moments I've experienced in a game.  The music, the blurriness of your view, the sound of the monster chasing you...not to mention, when you do finally get behind a closed door and find a hiding spot, you then get to watch as the door is violently brought down into pieces. All you can do is hope you're not spotted as you stare at the wall (there is a "sanity" element if you're new to these games).  IRL, I am guilty of some audible "gasping" during these moments.  During one particular chase I couldn't find an adequate path to get away from my pursuer and let out a frightened yelp that I am ashamed to even admit. Though, it is important to mention that I allowed the game to get under my skin purely because it was better that way.  I could have played it and completely steeled myself from letting it get to me (e.g. left the lights on, lowered the sound, casually approached the objectives), but what's fun about that?  For me, nothing.
As far as the story is concerned, I felt compelled to move forward to find the next clue.  I could feel a bit of excitement (or perhaps it's better described as relief) every time I saw a new note to read or completed a puzzle.  Naturally I won't reveal any spoilers just in case someone does read this review.
I must emphasize that this is not a game full of jump scares and over the top gore.  With that being said, there are some very disturbing scenes that you come across.  I walk away from this game still thinking about some of what I experienced. Not just from the imagery but the story in general. Per the recommendation from the developers when you first start the game, play with the lights off, don't worry about saving and allow the story to drive you forward.

EDITED - AFTER 500 HOURS OF PLAY TIME
This is not an easy game to review.  And I am not a reviewer.
Played a full game on Rapid/Plentifull settings.  Took about 350 hours.  Was awesome.  I'm mid-way in a coop game with a friend and I just started a new world, solo, with slightly less beginner-friendly settings.  Still love it.  Still discovering new strategy.
This is the most addictive+long lasting NON-MMORPG game I've played.   Ever.   Over the course of the last 30 years... !
First, I want to give my 2 cents about the comments from some reviews about "the developper".  It seems that some people have some problems with some aspect of the game, report it to the developper, who refuse to fix it... and then down-vote the game.
4 things about this :
1- This game is pretty "elitist".  It's slow paced, strategic, atmospheric... not easy and not for everyone.  It can be quite punishing at times, but also very rewarding.  Some aspect that do not suit some players are there on purpose because the developper (and the targeted players) love it this way.  It's not lazyness.  (Not the way I see it)  Exemple : there is no ladder to ease vertical movement.   You have to deal with failing hookshot.... or build/manage elevators... or, later on, teleporters are jetpacks.  A ladder would just make it all too easy !
2- The developper (a single guy) actually reaches a new level of customer support/interraction, the way I see it.  Not only does he spends time on Steam forums and comment/answers on many posts, but he develops the game while streaming near-100% of it, while interacting LIVE with the payers.
I actually posted some questions in the forums (for the general public ! I was not targeting the developper at all !) the DJ (the dev) actually answered 3 out of 4 of my questions himself ! Kinda awesome.
3- Some people complain about "core parts of the game are locked to supporters".  That is not true.  Developper gives early access to the patches he is working on to the early supporters so they can TRY (and help debug) the UN-COMPLETE, "IN PROGRESS" patches.  But they get no bonus materials "in game". Except maybe a few more "skins".  Nothing "un-fair".
So yeah, he may take decisions that you do not like.  But..... that's too bad !
4- EXPENSION PACK (FROZEN FACTORY) : Some people complain about "DLC" and its price.  This is not a "DLC" as per now-days definition.  This is an EXPENSION PACK, like in old times.  The game alone will give you 100++++++ hours of game play.  When you're DONE with the base, you can optionally buy the expension pack to reach deeper layers of the game.  It's a full fledged expension pack bringing an additionnal 50+++ hours of gameplay !  And the expension pack content "begins" after the base game "end-game"...  (and obviously it's not "free" since the developper needs to... you know... eat !)
Now, the game.
A cross-over between Minecraft and Factorio.  That's what it triies to be, and that's what itis.  With some features that differ from both games.  It has its own identity.
Part 1 - Compared to Minecraft :
The "surface" of the world is no fun to explore.  You space-ship-crashed on a desolated, icy planet.  The surface is very rough, with huge mountains and huge holes and caves.  But it's a single biome.
The exploration is more vertical.
3rd ore begins to spawn under -180-ish.
4th around -300-ish.
6th around -400-ish.... !
(the max depth is like, -2^64 (or -10 quintillions.... or infinite, basically), but for now I think there's nothing new under -2000)
And you will find HUUUUUUGGE caves to explore.
The games allows some nice little twist to instantly build whole lines of block and such, which can allow you to build a 50x10 plateform in about 15 seconds.  This is nice.
This game is NOT centered on building random, useless strucutres for no reasons.  Materials are ugly and the planet is somewhat dark.  Even during the day, you never get a beautifull sun that will make your structure shine.
It's all about being functionnal and automated.  GEtting your ressources manually won't work.  You need to build machines to automate the ressource gathering and transformation.
Which  brings us to :
Part 2 - Compared to Factorio
Similar yet different.
I LOVE Facotrio.
Factorio is "all about building your base".  No exploration.  No digging.  Just gather ressources, and build.
In 15 hours, in Factorio, you'll have a huge, top-tier base.
Since Fortresscraft has a whole "digging" and "exploroing" part and you have to deal with the 3rd dimension, it'll be much slower.
In 15 hours if played on "casual" settings(default), you'll barelly have time to automate the extraction and transformation of the 1st tier of materials... !
Factorio is somewhat linear and never felt overwhelming (to me).  What you first build will be used to build the next tier, which will be used for the next, and so on.  Your first building are never rendered useless and you always grow from what has already been done.
Fortresscraft allows more freedom on those aspect and can sometime feel overwhelming !  So many possibilities !  And news building CAN make older ones useles.  So spending a lot of ressources on early stuff CAN eventually feel useless...
A bit more hardcore.... not a bad thing : I'm just saying.
Edit - I triied the "faster" mode.  Extractors can hold more ores, power is abundant, receipies requirement are divided by 4... I did in 2 hours what took 20 hours in my other game.  This is good news for people who are in a rush.  The difference in pacing between the various game settings are huge.
So yeah, I give it a huge thumb up.

My first playthrough had these little robots floating around occasionally, but nothing like the threats I have seen here. On a side note, the amount of fun I have had in this game is comparable to the fun i've had in Factorio.

Sniper Elite V2 is a satisfying WW2 shooter taken from the perspective of an awesome sniper. The game is about the sniper stopping the V2 missiles from being launched but really, you probably won't care about the story. This game is all about the satisfying sniping mechanics. When you pull of a long distance shot, the game will follow that bullet in slow motion and show you where you hit the enemy and what bones you shattered. The game is extremely brutal but that is part of the fun. The game offers high difficulties that will make the sniping even more satisfying with more things to take into account such as the wind and how it will affect the destination of the bullet, and general bullet drop based on distance. The game doesn't offer a great amount of weapons for you to choose from but they all feel pretty great to use. The campaign in this game isn't all that long. You can finish it within 6-10 hours depending on the difficulty and how you progress through the stealth sections. One mode I can't really comment on is the coop in this game because unfortunately, I have no friends that wish to play this with me and I couldn't find anyone online. If you wish to get more out of this game, be sure to have a friend that wants to play it as well since the coop is dead. The sound in this game was pretty great and the graphics were good. The challenge maps were pretty good and it was pretty satisfying to shoot Hitler straight in the balls. 75 + 5 for being able to shoot Hitler in the balls and have an awesome bullet cam for it. 80/100

First, let me toss out scores, then explain them.
Story: 9/10
Graphics: 6/10
Soundtrack: 9/10
Gameplay: 7/10
Camera: 3/10
All-in-all, a very compelling game that I played for the story.  Coming from 2015 and playing this 5 year old game, I can say with certainty it is a bit dated and the port from the console is frustrating as hell in many aspects, but I would have been just as frustrated with them on a console as well.
Key annoyances:
*Twice over a two day period I was so annoyed with the camera during battles that I had to walk away from Steam.
*Wall climbing + camera chaos = more "aaaaargh!" moments.
*Map is terrible for referencing where you are and what you want to do, with consolitis written all over it (the controls are facepalm-inducing).
But, when it comes to actual gameplay, whether you are looking for a spectacle fighter (like Gods of War series), hard puzzles, or epic boss fights (Dark Souls series), Darksiders competently handles all of those things. On top of that, the soundtrack does a great job of mood-switching during fights, bosses, puzzles, exploring, etc. to set the tone for your activities.
I can cautiously recommend it, as long as you don't mind setting up your controller or re-key binding to your liking, plus you still have to be patient with a camera that chooses the wrong time to pan around, focuses the wrong enemies in combat, and laughably "smart adjusts" during platforming/leapfrogging puzzles.
Final note (and this is just another case of a hastily tossed together port for Steam) - the achievements are bugged beyond belief. I've completed the game, but it stopped giving achievements somewhere around the spider boss.  It needs a Steam-specific patch, yesterday.  This doesn't detract from the story though, so go play some War and prep for Darksiders II because Death (in 2) is incredibly fun to play and I'm going to do a review of Darksiders II as soon as I beat it. :D

Note, I played the game on Hardcore mode from the get-go here. So these comments are from the perspective of only the hardest difficulty level, on single player scaling.
Pros:
+Runs like a charm, no FPS drops even during intense combat. (This is on a mid-high end rig)
+Funny dialogue that only occasionally falls flat. Kind of like a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
+Diverse array of weapons to use and unlock.
+Great looking levels.
+Fairly diverse array of creatures to mutilate.
+Great viceral feedback from melee weapons.
+Dashing feels good, and helps traverse boring open space quickly.
Cons:
-Awful level design. Tons of backtracking through empty areas, and tons of "open areas" to "explore", that 99% of the time have nothing of interest. Not even enemies to fight. The game wants you to parkour, but gives you almost no tools to do so. Only certain ledges can be grabbed. You find yourself running around a lot looking for ways to move toward the objective. Very UN-ninja like.
-Very little variation in fights. All the monsters behave the same. Ranged dudes kick you away when you get close, and melee dudes try and keep their blades in your wang at all times. No matter what type of creature they're skinned as, this remains true of all enemies.
-The chi system is tedious to manage. You usually only have the option of using and focusing on a single skill. Even with maxed out regen/pool size cards. This will almost exclusively be the heal, since most elite/special enemies have a debuff aura that stacks with each element type, and force you to constantly spam the heal button to remove them since they'll kill you in 3 seconds if you ignore them.
-Ammunition starvation & Bullet Sponge Enemies. Ammunition drops are FAR too scarse in the hardcore difficulty. You mag dump the entire ammo pool of every weapon type into 3 bullet sponge enemies, then have to use the chain saw or katana for the rest of the map until you pick up 10 shotgun shells per every 10 enemies you defeat. Gets tedious very quickly.
-Completely unnecessary Borderlands style stat management / Diablo style gem system. Slows down the action, and forces you to stop and switch mods when certain immune enemies show up. Biggest downside to this though is the ridiculous amount of low level mods you will pick up that clog your inventory. There is no effective way to quick sell mods below a certain level. You need to manually mark every single of of them as "junk" and then sell them to a vendor. It's tedious. The mods also sell for virtually nothing. Even the "legendary" rank mods.
-Loot gathering. I shouldn't need to stop on top of dead dudes and mash "E" to gather book drops. It slows down the action, and makes me have to back track after kiting enemies after long fights that usually take 5-15 mins due to the bullet sponginess of enemies.
-Sprinting. When you're spamming dash constantly, sprinting doesn't really do anything. Either make Wang always run at the sprint speed, or remove it altogether. It's tedious to manage.
-Melee skill charging. Why the hell does it take 5+ seconds to fully charge a melee stab/spin attack? Slows down the action, and makes you need to kite for an unnecessary period of time.
I'm sure some of these things are influenced by having 1-2 more players. However, the bullet sponge enemies that aren't bosses are ridiculous. I shouldn't have to chain saw into a Yakuza's chest for literally 120 seconds with a min/maxed  fire damage warrrsaw on enemies that are weak to fire. Even on the hardest difficulty. Make the AI smarter, or have more abilities/better weapons. Don't just tack on more HP and call it a day.
Steam really needs a "mixed" option for recommending games. This game is perilously close to thumbs down territory. But, it's fun enough if you can look past the more tedious portions of the game mechanics.
If you're looking for a shorter, less open Borderlands with more♥♥♥♥♥♥jokes. This is your game. If you're looking for a non-stop slasher/action shooter - pass on this game, or play it only on the lowest difficulty setting.

In 2010, the Earth is going to be hit by some meteorites. These are not just rocks, but the actual armies of Heaven and Hell, ready to fight each other in an epic battle. Mid in the fight, another man falls from the sky: The Apocalyptic Horseman War. He does not fight for any side in the battle, he is just there to keep the balance, but there is one problem. The Horsemen are only allowed to interfere when the 7 seals are broken. And nobody broke them. War gets teleported to the fiery council, who go into court with him because he broke this rule.
He tells them that he has gone to earth because he thought the seals were broken. The fiery council gives him another chance to get rid of his guilt, by killing The Destroyer, the one who started the battle between heaven and hell. So War gets sent back to earth, 100 years after the apocalypse.
The gameplay is a typical Hack'n'Slay. War is badassily strong and gets to fight against a lot of enemies at once.
His sword swings hit many enemies at once, and there are other weapons to be aquired with other abilities. The battles feel good and fluid, the finisher moves are brutal and the blocking/evading works great.
But there is more than just fighting. The game provides levels and riddles that make it feel like the result of hot sex between God of War and The Legend of Zelda. The riddles can get really hard at times, but not frustratingly hard, so the game does not get boring.
There are a lot of collectibles in the open world, and they also help War, like the Abyssal Armor. There are 10 pieces to find, that are pretty well hidden. If you find all pieces, you get one badass armor.
Sadly, the programming is weak at times and lets the game crash from time to time. There are also some bugs, like falling through the ground (happened to me 4 times). Good thing that there are enough checkpoints to make up for such annoying bugs.
The grafics like a bit comic-like. The characters look extremely packed with muscles,
blood squirts en masse, the bosses are huge and monstrous. The environment is very variable, from the destroyed remains of New York over a forest to a huge desert. The light effects look great and the textures are detailed.
Huge, aggressive sounds of orchestral rage are violating your ears in this game. The music fits extremely good with a game where you play as The Apocalyptic Horseman War himself.

I've been following Fernbus Simulator for a number of months and have been very much looking forward to its release but I am mortified at how dreadful this product is in its current state. It is painfully clear this game is completely unfinished and should either be listed as an early access game or pulled from Steam altogether until its completed. The devs have simply jumped the gun and the supportive community who have invested in the game day one have been completely let down.
Firstly; the user interface looks something I would have designed at school in the mid 90's - it is an absolute embarrassment and this is made infuriating for users when trying to understand the very basics of the game as there is no tutorial in place. The controls are an utter shambles too, and instead of plugging in an alleged fully supported Xbox controller and playing right off the bat; you have to faff around the shambolic manual configuration menus. It was only until the game was released did the developers then drop the bombshell that this game has no full controller or wheel support at this time which is absolutely outrageous for a simulator.
When and if you finally do get started; you'll find that there is no career mode or anything interesting to become engrossed in - just create a journey, do it and that's it. The AI is absolutely woeful and many other realism aspects need a lot more work to reflect the quality and detail of the cities and landscapes. This being the only redeeming feature of the game so far. You will only see the game in all its glory if you can actually apply the correct graphical settings as this is yet another broken aspect.
This game also had a long beta phase but instead of the devs collecting critical technical and gameplay feedback from YouTuber's like Squirrel who were handed access on a plate; they instead just used the opportunity to freely advertise the game and the community have been left to deal with this catastrophic mess at release. The beta should have been issued to people who not only care about the development, but have a certain level of technical expertise whilst offering crucial input rather than ones that just want to make milk ad revenue from videos and offer nothing but free advertisement for the product.
It's games like this that make me appreciate how well SCS Software have done with their Truck Simulator titles in terms of general polish and execution. I thought Fernbus would be a major competitor in the driving sim genre but this game is still stuck in the bus depot despite being 'fully released'. I also advise users to not waste too much time stuck in the menus fiddling as you will lapse over the two hour refund limit. If the developers fail to address the most basic of problems within the next few days; this is the unfortunate route I will have to take. When you buy a finished game; you expect it to be finished and Fernbus is still missing a string of fundamental features as well as the expected polish that a completed game delivers.

Want to play God of War, but don't have a PlayStation?  This is your chance.  There are some differences between GoW and Darksiders, but it feels like much the same game.  Definitely pick up a good gamepad to have the best experience.  Overall, the game is pretty satisfying.  The combat is largely just a matter of mashing the attack (X) button until the enemy falls, but every once in a while you'll encounter a boss that requires something different.  Still, boss fights are fairly straight forward affairs where, once you've discovered the successful attack pattern, you simply repeat it three times to win.  There are plenty of collectibles to keep you coming back to earlier areas.  There are 'puzzles' throughout which are fun to solve.  The dialogue is your typical, over the top growling, and the story is barely relevant.
Be aware that there are some technical issues with the game.  It will sometimes crash as you transition areas or screens.  I also ran into some graphics glitches from time to time.  Thankfully the autosave feature is active often, so when you do experience one of these crashes you will not have lost much progress.
Overall, I would recommend giving Darksiders a try.

The only thing scary about this game is the camera filters, and once you turn that crap off in the options after 10 minutes because its making you nauseous, all that's left is Gatherer's and Old Crumbling Building Syndrome.
When you first start off the game, it gives you a bit of text saying something about how this game is all about immersion and that you shouldn't treat it as a game and you should just be immersed in the atmosphere automatically. What this game is trying to do is put you into a state of mind to psych your own self out into believing that the game is actually immersive and scary without actually putting any work into making it scary and immersive at all, which is what I assume happened to everyone that played this game. When you take away the stupid camera filters that make you want to puke from motion sickness, the only immersive thing about this game is the music.
This game prides itself in the fact that you have nothing to defend yourself with, so every time you encounter a threat, you should run and hide. The reality is, there wasn't any threat to begin with. Why? Because the game actually REWARDS you for dying by spawning you in a better location that’s void of Gatherer's, or spawning you exactly where you needed to be anyway, while still letting you keep all the items you've collected after the last save point. So instead of being scared and intimidated every time I encounter a Gatherer, I just end up running straight at it and dying intentionally in order to further progress through the game. Not to mention the fact that sometimes the AI just completely breaks and a Gatherer will block an exit and just stand there until you come at it no matter how many rocks and bottles you throw to distract it, so you have no choice but to die. That is the complete opposite of immersion.
The game's levels in a nutshell are: Scary zone, safe zone, solve puzzle zone(s), rinse/repeat until boss fight. Except I don't think I can even call them puzzles, since it really just boils down to "fetch X amount of Y in order to use on Z machine" So it sends you on a scavenger hunt, which is like trying to find your car keys when there's no power in your house and you keep stubbing your toe on every piece of furniture. This wouldn't be such a big deal if this wasn't 75% of the damn game. It feels like you only get 15-30 minutes in a scary zone and then you're stuck in the "puzzle" zones for 1-2 hours just looking for♥♥♥♥♥♥without any real threat occurring. Am I playing a horror game or am I playing Sherlock Holmes?
The only redeeming quality about this game is the story. Which really isn't enough to save this game since this was marketed as a horror game. The first 30 minutes of Outlast was more terrifying than this entire game. So if you're looking for a horror game, get Outlast. If you're looking for an adventure/mystery game with a semi-interesting story, and good music, then give this game a whirl.
Maybe this game was just incredibly hyped and I had such unreasonably-high expectations for it, but in all honesty, the only scary part in this game was the water lurker part, which only lasted like 15 minutes.

Arma 3
Ah, yes. So you must be interested in buying Arma 3? Well, I can assure you, the game is enjoyable. Can I say this for everyone? No. No I can't. So, I will try to explain what EXACTLY it is, and who might enjoy it more.
Arma 3 is a Military Sandbox Simulation. What that means is: It's a game, where you are in the military, you yell locations and callsigns at other people to reveal enemies, make battles, and shoot people. Also you can kill your teammates but that's a stupid desicion.
So, you think CoD is the stuff? Yes?!? Well then, this game is probably NOT for you. This game is more realistic than CoD, and I don't mean graphics wise. It's a game that expresses real military actions and callsigns. Callsigns like: "Enemy infantry, 200 metres Northwest!". If that's not your thing, then I do not reccomend Arma 3 to you. Id you want more out of a military shooter, be my guest.
If you do not like giving out enemy locations precisely, or real life military sims, this is not for you. If you want that stuff in a game, and you want to see more realism in present-day military sims, buy this game! KEEP IN MIND: you need a really good graphics card for this game, since it is not optimized. 20-60 FPS is still playable, but BOHEMIA NEEDS TO OPTIMIZE THEIR GAMES!!!
In my opinion, I ADORE this game. I love it! It's just like real war. When they say "This is war" they mean it. At times, it can be confusing, but it won't stand in your way(at least, it shouldn't).
"It's hard to find a server" I call ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t on that. I can find a server in SECONDS.
"It's mostly just fooling around" Again, it's bullcrap. ALL the servers i've ever been on are more serious than messing around.
"The community is toxic" Ok, if anyone has said this, I'm quoting trump here. WRONG. The community welcomes new players. They take the game seriously, but not TOO seriously. I.E. the CSGO community.
"The tutorial is a bit bad" I agree a little. The tutorial was a bit bad. It tells you how to play and what controls do what, but it needs to be a bit more extentive.
"The campaign sucks" Who plays campaign anymore?
The setting(s) are on the islands of Altis, Malden, and if you get the DLC, Apex. The year is 2035, but it's not super future minded, it's more modern day minded. You can customize your character, the weapons, and even what you wear. If you find a helm you want, you can add it to your character w/o restriction. Same goes for body armour, bags, shirts and pants, glasses, night vision, and a bit more. You have a vast collection of weapons, grenades, and even vehicles. As well as drones. Those too.
In conclusion, If you like milsim, airsoft, or want to experience the military once more, or want more realism from CoD, or just want some fun, buy it. If you do not want to look at a compass, or do simple math at times, don't waste your money! Save it for a DLC or for the new CoD. Or something.
I forgot the sandbox. OH THE SANDBOX!! You can play different scenarios, or situations of combat. The AI is smarter in Arma 3 than CS or CoD's AI. I submitted a scenario, and it's much easier to make one that you might think. It's simple to place enemy AI and friendlies.

TL;DWTR:
It has a steep learning curve.
It is a challenge.
It is a factory game.
You get attacked.
You try to endgame.
You try to endgame again.
If you love slow paced 'crafting/automation' games (like Factorio, but not 1 hour and you're done), with a sense of acheivement when you build that massive (3 dimensional) factory that does exactly what you ask, while you are being attacked, and trying to grow your factory, so you can be attacked more while you try to endgame, then you will very much love this game.
It starts slow, and has a steep learning curve, but players who can bear to not have their hands held, will love it.
NTL;WTR:
I love the Battlefield series of games.
I love getting into a fresh round of fast paced action.
I love killing those 4 blokes who all came up the elevator at Siege of Shanghai C.
And most of all, I hate the fact that players who have all played the game a long time and acquired knowledge and experience in the game think it is their right to "Always be on the winning team". Where is the challenge in fighting a bunch of noobies that don't know what they are doing? Where is the fun without a challenge?
FortressCraft Evolved is nothing like Battlefield, thank goodness.
There is no teamstacking. There is no "How the f did he get me". But it is a challenge. And it is fun.
I've only owned it for a little bit. And when I first started playing it, I wasn't sure what I was doing, and not much has changed for newbies. Spend a week on making a proper tutorial for new players, and the player base may just grow.
The primary developer does listen to community feedback. Heck, he even ASKS for it. Sometimes he downright ignores it. But few times has the primary developer's actions been detrimental to the enjoyment of the game.

A fun little team based shooter that never seemed to catch on, Lead and Gold did a lot of things right: diverse classes, passive buffs encouraging teamwork, good map variety, attractive visual design, and satisfying gunslinging firefights. However, its matchmaking always left a lot ot be desired, lag was a consistent problem, and on some maps and servers, there was serious imbalance between the classes, leading to everyone toting shotguns and chucking dynamite.
Overall, it's a shame the player base has been gradually dying off since release, and I hesitate a recommendation if you are buying alone. If you have a few friends interested, I recommend picking up a 4-pack; it's a great deal, and you only need six to eight players for a really solid match.

Critics are strange guys.
They're all amused and happy when 10000000000th CoD-like game is released, because this is what medium audience want to hear, and they have also a good word when the 1000000000th "tech-demo-and-nothing-else-new FPS" hits the scene (yeah, i'm really thinking about Crysis 1, 2 and Warhead and similars) arguing that "there is nothing really new in this game, but LOOK THE GRAPHIC ENGINE!".

So they beat it 'til death, just because yeah, it's just fun, but it's non-conform to modern standards (i.e. it's not the 10000000001st Cod-like fps) and tech is out of date.
Don't trust them.

Definitely a must have game. Gameplay is about... sniping, what else? Featuring a bullet cam and realistic mechanic, this is as close as you can have for sniping simulation.  Single Player campaign is pretty expansive although AI can be below expectation sometimes. Mission is generally straightforward and simple, so you don't have too much choice here.
Cooperative missions are based on single player maps, but they offer different feeling when done together with friend for example. I'd recommend doing it on highest difficulty once you are familiar with the maps/missions.
Multiplayer is where this game really shines though. Combat is incredible. Kill your opponents from distance based on skill - see who is the best at aiming and calculating the gravity and wind to compensate the bullet path. Make sure you have good mouse here.
Verdict: Worth every penny.

Don't get me wrong, by itself Trials Fusion is a decent game - Great graphics, great scenery and keeps the elements of its predecessors without changing too much. However, as a person who has dedicated over 120 hours into Trials Evolution Gold Edition, I must say that Fusion is pretty underwhelming compared to it.
First of all, there are significantly fewer levels in this game than there are in TEGE - it took me at least 20 hours to get the medal tally required to unlock the platinum medals, but in Fusion it only took me 4 hours. It definitely felt like a step backwards in content.
This leads to the next point - Ubisoft decided that in order for us to get more levels, we'd have to fork out money for a season pass. That's right, they took our beloved Trials franchise and decided to include DLC in it. It definitely feels like a dog move against us.
Lastly, they decided to leave out the most essential feature when they released this game - online multiplayer! And only this year they decide they're finally going to release it? Pretty crap if you ask me.
Final verdict - If you have played Trials Evolution Gold Edition for a while and feel like playing some new, different levels, buy this game when it's on sale, as if you ignore all of its flaws it's a pretty good game.
If you have never played a trials game before, buy Trials Evolution Gold Edition as it is a lot more fun to play than this game.

This game in a nutshell: super ♥♥♥♥ing fun.
The action is fast-paced, but you can pause at any time to get a little more control over frantic situations; the scenarios are well-managed, and your mistakes in a single battle can and will haunt you for the rest of the campaign. The challenge is real, but highly customizable thanks to the game's fantastic tunable AI.
The AI -- oh, man, the AI. It feels like you're playing against a human. I can't make a single mistake, leave a single gap in my lines, leave a single high ground unoccupied without the AI punishing me for it. It takes advantage of opportunities, cuts its losses when it's outmatched, reinforces its weaknesses as soon as it's pressed. It hides its units behind hills and ambushes you when you advance. It's murderous.
The game isn't without flaws; unless you tell your units to hold, they have a tendency to wander (and even just telling your units to ROTATE loses their hold order). Unit selection is finicky, and a single click often selects three or four units (if they're closely bunched together). Sometimes, enemy units walk right through my lines in a heated battle (!) and start attacking my artillery (!!), then rout into my rear (!!!), reactivate, and run around capturing territory (!!!!!). I even once had a group of Confederates become invincible, so that no amount of my men could even hurt them. Thankfully, all those flaws are rarely game-ending, though it'd be nice if they were fixed.
Most importantly, though, this game FEELS like Gettysburg. I remember playing Sid Meier's Gettysburg all the time when I was a kid. It's what got me into Civil War history. As many Americans suffered and died on the fields of this little Pennsylvanian town as did in the Vietnam war, all in the space of three summer days. Capturing that feeling -- a desperate, hard-fought struggle, rivers of blood running across idyllic pastures, the nation's fate resting on the outcome -- is difficult for anyone to achieve. This game totally gets it.

"And when he had opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature, saying: Come, and see. And there went out another horse that was red: and to him that sat thereon, it was given that he should take peace from the earth, and that they should kill one another, and a great sword was given to him."
Forget post-apocalyptic survirog games, here, you ARE the apocalypse. But something went wrong, the Seventh seal is not broken, the call to the Four horsmen was apparently never given and only one of them rode - War (a.k.a.you). The war between Heaven and Hell started too early, mankind was wiped out and everybody and their mother blames you. You must find the Destroyer and find out why you've been framed.
There's nothing here in any way new or surprising. Demons with big teeth and bigger horns, demons that look like bats and spiders and bulls, angels that look like people with some sort of steampunk wing contraption on their backs (love this part). Even humans (what's left of them) - pitiful zombies that look like Iron maiden's Eddie. As you progress, you unlock new equipment, so you can smash certain barriers, swing on a chain from certains anchor point ar slow down time. The last hope for originality dies at your feet when you get a portal gun.
But it works. Combat is fun, with unlockable sword moves and special abilities; enemies are varied enough to keep things interesting; boss battles are of the "figure out how to do this" variety and you have a bunch of nice puzzles thrown in. Controls are pretty decent, considering it's a console port. You'll want to use a gaming mouse with 5-6 buttons, though, makes things easier. Being a third-person-perspective game, it has surprisigly few instances of camera screwups.
There are a few moments that make you want to rage quit and smash your PC into tiny little bits, but none of them are game-breaking. You'll come back and finish. The game is worth it.

(Skip to bottom for review)
STORY
I found out about this game a week before it came out, and my excitement was crazy! I cringed at the price, but knew that i was not only getting this game, but getting a slot in the MMO RPG version as well: which made me feel less nervous about  the price. Finally it downloaded, and i jumped right in with a few friends.
It was hard in the beginning because we had absolutely no idea how to play. But we got along nicely. We found a very nice European server where we joined up with the locals in making a town. I was incredibly surprised to find that i had no lag though my ping was 200. Once we got the rhythem of things, we began to enjoy it alot more.
We set up a little village in a valley where it would be easy to make a living. Farms surrounded our village, mines were started on the outskirts, and the village flourished...kinda. I will point out that it is very hard to start a village, let alone maintain it. But we did!
At this moment our village still sits in that little valley, where we live in peace and hope to one day become a flourishing city...
REVIEW
This game is a very ambitious one: the amount of things you can do is outstanding!
Everything from mining and crafting to cooking and farming: this game offers a spot for every person's interest.
There are bugs of course, but they are being resolved quickly, The developers have proven to me that they are dedicated, and show that through the patches that are put into the game, however small they may be.
The bugs i've noticed are more server side and game crashes than actual in-game bugs. In all honesty, the game as Early Access is coming along quite nicely.
However good the game may be, people still get turned off by the price.
So my advice to people thinking about buying the game is this: If you are interested in the game, by all means get it. But be warned that you may have some troubles along the way. But in the end you get two games out of it: Life is Feudal: Your Own edition, and the MMO RPG version when it comes out.
My advice to the developers is this: Please tone down the price. 40 dollars is not something you would expect from something labelled as Early Access, however far a long the development of the game may be. I understand that you are trying to fund the MMO RPG, but more people will buy it if the price is around 20 dollars. You will still make the same profit you are now because more people will buy it.

I cannot stress how much I love this game. I bought it in July on Steam, and absolutely adored it. I felt no shame in buying it again for my Nintendo Switch, as it is just such a replayable and quality platformer.
I'll start by gushing about Shovel Knight's campaign. The main feature in this-Shovel Knight's trusty shovel blade and its various abilities-is fleshed out extremely well and feels amazing to control. The levels were fun and never cheap or too difficult. Every one of my deaths was my fault...well, most of the time. This game does have knockback, which can get annoying, and only gets more annoying in Plague of Shadows, but the knockback is understandable, as this is a platformer. The levels do drag on sometimes, but that is due to the comparitive lack of stages compared to platformers such as Mario. The game also looks gorgeous. I fell that 8-bit visuals are used way too much in indie games such as this, but Shovel Knight takes the 8-bit art style and improves on it to make the game very visually pleasong.
Then there is the second campaign, Plague of Shadows. I am...much more mixed about this one. While the game still looks marvelous, the controls are not very good. There are very minimal changes made to the stages, and that just does not work considering how radically different Plague Knight controls compared to Shovel Knight. He is much more floaty and has a ranged bomb attack, but the stages are designed around tight platforming and melee combat, not that. This is especially apparent in a section of the final area where, in Shovel Knight's campaign, you are expected to hit a statue forward to create a pathway. They keep this exactly the same in this campaign, where you...float over the obstacles. Intentional or not, that is just lazy. Now, I do like some things about the campaign. The upgrade system is great and the special items are creative, and the whole "parallel to Shovel Knight's campaign" thing is cool. I just feel that this campaign has less heart than the original, and I had much less fun playing it.
With my mixed feelings of Plague of Shadows, I was worried about how Specter Knight's campaign, Specter of Torment, would turn out. I am relieved to say I love this campaign. The controls are great, and Specter Knight's main features- wall climbing, wall jumping, and using a mid-air scythe slash to propell you into the air-work extremely well. The stages were also given a redesgin, which I am very thankful for, as they now fit Specter Knight well. There's not much to say about this otherwise. Everything is good in this.
It may seem as if I skipped over some aspects, namely the music and story, but that is because I tend not to pay attention to those things. Sorry if that was what you were looking for. From what I can tell, the music is pretty excellent and the story, while bare, is enjoyable and sets up the stages well.
There is still one more campaign, King Kinight's, and a battle mode coming soon, and I'll edit my review when they do release. But, for now, Shovel Knight is an amazing game packed with content, love, and fun, and I definitely reccommend it.

I became addicted to this game in the oddest way. There were probably three or four minutes in the entire day of total playtime that I actually enjoyed myself. But the more I invested myself in the game, the more I felt determined to get something out of it, and the more time I shoved into it. I spent almost all of yesterday (5/16/2016) playing, desperately trying to make progress.
There are several problems with making progress.
First off, this is not a single player game. It may have the ability to be played single player, but it's not single player. There just isn't enough progress for it to be single player. In order to make a reasonable amount of progress on my own, I edited files in order to vastly speed up my gameplay. Somehow, that made it go from very boring to incredibly boring.
Nothing happens quickly on your own. Even with the game settings set all the way to the quickest, easiest, fastest settings. You need 32 bars of something to build x. Well, settle in, that'll take a while unless you've already got five or six systems running. And it's not like setting those up is quick. Or cheap.
And don't get me started on how long it takes to research pretty much anything once you've got the laboratory. The projects take ages to complete, and enough resources that after a day of highly sped-up gameplay, I was barely able to make some of it.
But that's not the worst part about this game.
This game is NOT finished. This game was early-access, and still should be! It's nowhere near complete. I find bugs everywhere I go. I come back to my base and all my turrets are facing firmly in one direction, a giant laser firing out. The ship I crashed in is on fire (it's only been two months in-game since I landed, I'm sure that's normal). The CPH is projecting some kind of field that is making it awfully hard to see. Various other things are making all sorts of very bright frames of animation that make it practically impossible for me to see what the hell is happening in my base.
My laser turrets are still working fine. It's just impossible to tell that.
I place another laser turret on top of another block I've placed, and all the bugs disappear in an instant.
Before I do that, the ship hurts me if I get too close.
Now? No worries, I can walk straight through it.
I assure you, this is one of many, many bugs that I've encountered. The list got so long I didn't bother remembering them.
Then, there's the simple fact that some things are either badly implemented, have missing icons, mismatched icons, or maybe their help file doesn't exist.
Make some iron pipe if you can. Or find something that requires iron pipe and look at the picture. As of this moment, the picture is a big red x and the words "NO ICON". Go grab some cave flora from the cold or toxic caverns. One of each. Then, place them. Place them against a wall, and turn them twice, so they're actually right-side-up. Don't ask why. Now, compare the flora you just placed to the icon. They're mismatched. A is B, B is A, C is D, etc.
How about auto-excavators? Place one on a wall, and you'll probably think it can dig a 3x3 hole horizontally. Maybe if you place it on the ceiling, it can dig down, instead of up! Why would you think that? Because the column of light indicating where it can dig shows that!
You'd be wrong. Once you power it up, no matter where you're trying to 'aim' it, it shoots up.
The list goes on. There are things that are just plain problematic. Things that are useless. Things that make no sense. Things that are poorly implemented, buggy, unfinished, and more. It is, quite frankly, awful, and if you look at the pictures saying "Oh, I want that!", then either join a server with a dozen other players or be prepared to keep playing for WEEKS (Actual time played, not number of days you played for a little while) in order to get there.

I have put a lot of time in the last few months into this game and keep coming back to it almost daily to try new strategies and to see what dev has added to the game (which is done almost daily).   I have never personally experienced a game that had such an open forum for the development of a game.  As a long time game player from games back to Everquest, WoW, Minecraft, etc (and even back to the days of Zork and before) I can't remember ever having the opportunity to give feedback on something and have it actually become a part of the game.   (Don't expect every idea you come up with to be implemented, but if you have a well reasoned and thought out idea you stand a shot).
Fortresscraft takes some work.  If you are looking for a game you just start up and have it hold your hand all day while you mindlessly hit a few keys, then this might not be the game for you.   But if you like a challenge and are looking for a game that is constantly evolving and growing, a communitity of players who will help you if you have questions, and a game where you can go online and watch the developer streaming as he builds new game content then you may want to consider this.
I am addicted to the game and although I have a lot of hours of play time I am nowhere near completing it.   Like the old saying goes, "it isn't about the destination, it is about the journey".   The journey of playing Fortresscraft Evolved for me has been a blast.   I only wish every game I had ever purchased had given me so many hours of fun and enjoyment.

After hearing how horrible this was in all the years since its release, I have to say that I was pleasantly surprised by this game. The voice acting is terrible, the combat is weird at times, and the context sensitive keys seem like a useless relic from console porting, but this game feels like the first Witcher, but without timed button press combat. so far much of what I have been doing is following a tiny main quest thread and running around killing monsters for people.
I'm a total sucker for games with a crafting system, and even though this one is kind of bare bones(only item improvements; no actual item creation) it is still fairly rewarding. Another huge bonus somewhat related to this is that your armor actually changes when you equip new pieces. It isn't just 8 reskinned versions of the same armor ala Dragon Age: Origins. Every set so far feels like a unique and interesting enough looking piece of armor. Cloaks abound, with decent cloth physics, though I have seen one scene where the cloak was draped across a character's body the wrong way, clipping through his chest and draping over his front.
I'm playing this game with the Worldmerge mod, since I have the DLC and it is reportedly more immersive this way. The game looks amazing with DX10. Whenever I launch it with DX9 it just looks fuzzy in comparison. There is a huge amount of realistic plantlife dotting the landscape. It makes grassy fields in skyrim look like child's play.
After putting it off for such a long time, I feel absolutely blown away by this game.
Edit: the ending is a little confusing and kind of a let down. Just...be prepared for nearly nothing to be explained.

Starting out can be rough, depending on your world. I tried a couple before I found one I was happy with. At first, you will have to babysit things. You simply don't have the resources to get things rolling on their own for the first hour, maybe two. Watch a couple of videos on it. You'll see how others do things, you'll get a good understanding of the basics, and you'll have some ideas as to how to set your own system up. It takes a lot of time to really get a lot going on, but if building up to that isn't your cup of tea, then I might advise a different game type. There are several more mechanics at play here than in MineCraft, and pretty much any other game in this vein. It takes a lot of the concepts explored in Space Engineers, removes space, and instead focuses on mining materials and setting them up to work for you.

Still has a disproportionate amount of issues for a release. Should have been early access IMO.
- AI is horrible. Drivers ignore traffic lights most of the time, slow down for no reason or keep going well under the speed limit even if the road is clear.
- Traffic lights are not consistent. One intersection with two traffic lights, one for "straight ahead" (red) and the other "straight ahead or right" (green).
- The left lane of the autobahn sometimes is marked off for 100m for no apparent reason. You can ignore it though.
- Cars keep spawning and despawning in  your field-of-view.
- Speed limits seem to change arbitrarily and don't always match the signs. Once there even was a 100kph sign about 100m in front of traffic lights. Good luck braking in time..
- The sim tries to judge your driving behaviour, however it is difficult to understand sometimes what exactly the criteria are. All you get is usually "steering misbehaviour".
- Traffic jams on highway on-ramps, even if the left lane is clear.
- Controller setup is a bit finicky. I wanted to invert the vertical view axis. Instead of a button or checkbox to invert the axis you get to edit the input mapping curve. By default it's a linear function going from (0,0) to (1,1) AFAIR and you need to chagne the slope to -1 in order to invert it. So you need to adjust the sliders so it goes from (0,0) to (-1,-1).
Also the sterring sensitivity was a bit high. You can edit the nonlinearity coefficient though. In my case setting it from 3 to 1.5 helped but it's not great.
- Translation is a bit off sometimes, e.g. "Could we make a break?" seems to be literally translated from the german "Pause machen". The same trigger however also causes the more correct message "You need to take a break".
In summary: The idea might be nice but in the end it's too buggy, runs poorly and is certainly not worth 30 euro. I've played early access alpha games of far superior quality than that.

I cannot stress how much I love this game. I bought it in July on Steam, and absolutely adored it. I felt no shame in buying it again for my Nintendo Switch, as it is just such a replayable and quality platformer.
I'll start by gushing about Shovel Knight's campaign. The main feature in this-Shovel Knight's trusty shovel blade and its various abilities-is fleshed out extremely well and feels amazing to control. The levels were fun and never cheap or too difficult. Every one of my deaths was my fault...well, most of the time. This game does have knockback, which can get annoying, and only gets more annoying in Plague of Shadows, but the knockback is understandable, as this is a platformer. The levels do drag on sometimes, but that is due to the comparitive lack of stages compared to platformers such as Mario. The game also looks gorgeous. I fell that 8-bit visuals are used way too much in indie games such as this, but Shovel Knight takes the 8-bit art style and improves on it to make the game very visually pleasong.
Then there is the second campaign, Plague of Shadows. I am...much more mixed about this one. While the game still looks marvelous, the controls are not very good. There are very minimal changes made to the stages, and that just does not work considering how radically different Plague Knight controls compared to Shovel Knight. He is much more floaty and has a ranged bomb attack, but the stages are designed around tight platforming and melee combat, not that. This is especially apparent in a section of the final area where, in Shovel Knight's campaign, you are expected to hit a statue forward to create a pathway. They keep this exactly the same in this campaign, where you...float over the obstacles. Intentional or not, that is just lazy. Now, I do like some things about the campaign. The upgrade system is great and the special items are creative, and the whole "parallel to Shovel Knight's campaign" thing is cool. I just feel that this campaign has less heart than the original, and I had much less fun playing it.
With my mixed feelings of Plague of Shadows, I was worried about how Specter Knight's campaign, Specter of Torment, would turn out. I am relieved to say I love this campaign. The controls are great, and Specter Knight's main features- wall climbing, wall jumping, and using a mid-air scythe slash to propell you into the air-work extremely well. The stages were also given a redesgin, which I am very thankful for, as they now fit Specter Knight well. There's not much to say about this otherwise. Everything is good in this.
It may seem as if I skipped over some aspects, namely the music and story, but that is because I tend not to pay attention to those things. Sorry if that was what you were looking for. From what I can tell, the music is pretty excellent and the story, while bare, is enjoyable and sets up the stages well.
There is still one more campaign, King Kinight's, and a battle mode coming soon, and I'll edit my review when they do release. But, for now, Shovel Knight is an amazing game packed with content, love, and fun, and I definitely reccommend it.

It saddens me to write this review, because it was one that I was excited about. However, that excitement has died quicker than it existed.
I originally played the game and thought quite highly of it; however, I only got roughly an hour in, and wished to wait for them to fix a few things in the next update. Fast forward to a few days ago -- I had been involved in some development projects, work, life, etc. My girlfriend and I were sitting here talking about games to play for Halloween, and I had remembered Dead Realm. I actually got her all hyped about it, and then came on here to purchase it for her.
When I got to the store page,  I quickly noticed the bad reviews, the lack of news, and people mentioning that the servers were dead. I re-downloaded it, and went online to try it for myself, and sure enough, within a 30 minute time-frame, I had seen ONE person. Him and I actually played a few rounds together and discussed what the game had been up to -- which was nothing.
I decided to hold off on purchasing it for my girlfriend, out of fear for us only getting an hour in, with the same bugs, and no one to play with. However, I did try to contact the company themselves, explaining that I did not want to see the game die off because I thought it had great potential, and that I'd offer my services to them on a developmental level completely free for now (should we ever discuss compensation later). The next day, I had seen that they read my message, but no response.
Later on, I had spoke to another person within this community who had said he offered the same thing to them. Simply to help out with the game, so that we could get it going again. And he received the same result -- nothing.
It's safe to say with almost absolute certainty that the game has died off.  There is zero communication from the developers/publishing company. No announcements, not a glimmer of hope. Again, it saddens me to write this review, because I had some huge hopes for this game, even to the point of assisting them free of charge if it was just a team that they were lacking. The support pages for the company seem to be offline as well, no activity on their Facebook page, and numerous others have mentioned they tried with no luck as well.
Save your money, and hopefully one day they will return to finish what they started. Should that happen, and the game picks back up, I will change my review. For now, don't purchase it. The servers have ZERO people on them, and it has issues at the moment which can cause it to be unplayable.

Every game comes with its positives and negatives. That being said, I think this game is one of the greatest games made to date! I absolutely love it! Epic Games and their engine really did create what I'd consider a masterpiece that is UT2k4. Originally, I got introduced to the Unreal series through the predecessor UT2k3 when I was just a little kid and I almost instantly fell in love with the game. My family was fairly poor at the time, so they could never afford to buy me the game, so I had to get a pirated copy to play. Once 2k4 came out, I loved the even greater variety of game modes that it had to offer as well as the old game modes that were only offered in UT99 at the time. As soon as I started working and made a steam account, I bought Unreal Tournament 2004 because I really do think it's well worth its price. Heck, I even bought it for a few of my close friends for them to play too just because the Unreal series NEEDS to be known, or at least I think it should be. I'll start out with the positives and the things I love about this game.
Positives:
- Multiple multiplayer game modes
- Very different difficulty levels of AI's that do test your skill well, or can help you learn easily
- Generally strong, polite, dedicated community (I've met moderators of maps that still hang around ever since the game launched!)
- Immersive and very well balanced gameplay
- Fast paced
- Challenging (In all honesty, I think this game truly tests your weapon handling skills in terms of shooter games)
- Fun community game mods and a very well done game editing kit
- Competitive
- Satisfying gameplay
- Many gaming and option features
- Character design is fresh and different, many maps to play on, and large gun variety (as well as some sweet vehicles too!)
Negatives:
- Arena shooters aren't as popular as they used to be
- Graphics are outdated (Who cares?)
- The rare but occasional hacker
Honestly, for me, the negatives don't even hold a candle to the overall game and my rating for it is an easy 10/10
That being said, if you want to test your shooting, dodging, reaction time and/or any other skills I highly recommend this game!

One of the best games i've ever played, and it's nice to see it on Steam. Most reviews are right about this release being bugged (freezes after the opening cutscene), but it is not completely impossible to play and enjoy.
Altough the game is bugged, there are a few tricks to make it possible to play in Windows 7 and 8/8.1 (32/64 bits), even without compatibility mode.
The easiest workaround to make the game playable is to use a different WAIL32.dll, and, as so, use it to substitute the one that comes shipped trough this Steam release (which may be illegal).
If you've managed to do this, the game will actualy load to the point that you will be able to start a new game. Do this and after the map loads up you must disable the sound effects (you may let the music on if you want to, but the sound effects are the real issue). If you don't, the game may crash after sometime.
Of course I know this not the best solution, but it may save you some time and frustration if you already enjoyed this game in the past and was happy to see it on Steam.
A few crashes may happen even if you've managed to do all these steps, so be prepared to have autosave as your allie (or save by yourself from time to time).
One of the things that I missed so much in this release is the lack of network gameplay. Which is not impossible if you use the old CD version.
The best possible (and legal) solution to play this game in Win7/8/8.1 would be running Steam inside a virtual machine with Win XP.
If the crashes are something you are considering to workaround with, and have hopes that Retroism/Night Dive Studios (or who else may have the power to) do any proper fix in the future, buy this game.
If you have patience, and don't want to have headaches because of the possible crashes, don't buy this release yet and wait for a proper solution.

FortressCraft Evolved is definitely a game that can absorb a lot of your time because of how expansive and intricate it is.  And that's a good thing!  I find myself constantly experimenting, changing, and iterating my systems to take advantage of new tech or just to maximize efficiency.  As of this writing, I have 200+ hours in game and I plan to at least tripple that.
At first glance, it might look like Minecraft or Factorio.  But this game is much more than that and really isn't comparable.  This game rewards efficient, scalable design, not one-off systems.  You can do many things by hand, but eventually, everything must become automated.  And that is a good way to understand the game.  You must automate everything.

-1 point for bad mouse control (read con below)
-0.5 point for buggy steam achievement (read con below)
Bought this game really cheap, so I was not expecting much from it, but it turned out to be a really pleasant surprise.
Game reminds me of Onimusha i used to play years ago, the hack and slash action and especially the counter move.
Pro:
- very good animations. slahsing demons is fun ok
- some VERY good puzzles. this is where it surprised me. I was thinking this is a straight forward hack 'n' slash game but nope. Some puzzles took me quite a while to figure out and so you feel really satisfied when you solve them. You might feel annoyed sometimes when you get stuck on a puzzle somewhere and you just wanna get on with the game, but when you do solve it (without looking at guides that is) you will feel very good about it lol
- nice music
Con:
- biggest con is this is a console port and it's obvious from the EXTREMELY badly done mouse control. Aiming is jerky and not smooth and it makes gameplay really frustrating sometimes
- also sometimes keys do not register properly. I died many times when I pressed jump but didn't work for some reason so i just fall off the map and die
- very frequent tearing if you don't have vsync turned on
-
this is widely known by now. A lot of times your acheveiment will not unlock on steam. In order to get all achievement, you have to shutdown steam, and only launch the game from its exe file. Also never use Steam overlay, especially the browser.
- you get to have 3 weapons, and after you level them all to max, you realize it's all for nothing because at the final boss fight you get ANOTHER SWORD and it's the only weapon that will do damage to the final boss.  This was disappointing.
overall:
I would recommend this game for its great Hack n' Slash action and VERY SATISFYING puzzles. Can't stress the puzzle part enough, it is REALLY fun. However due to its badly done mouse control and the buggy Steam achievements, it is recommended you only buy this at a discounted prize.

No guff, just sweet, hyper-refined animation and (seriously) gorgeous artwork, accompanied by similarly jacked action. I enjoy(ed) my time with the original campaign, but it felt a bit flat in its slower pace. Plague sped things up a bit, but personally I still felt a bit vulnerable and not in total control. The Specter campaign, however, manages to be both fast-paced, while giving a sense of control I didn't get from the first two. Albeit, it's probably 'easier' in a sense as you have far more recoverability and movement options, but damn if it isn't an absolute pleasure to play. I paid $15 for the original when it was released, and have steadily been suprised to see full, free campaigns popping up since, which is to say nothing of the unbelievable polish and care gushing from every possible orifice. Would've -gladly- paid for the campaign updated, and DLC is something I pass on almost 100% of the time save the rare cases where the developer / publisher have proven that their content is actually worth having, and even then it's a begrudging purchase. Looking at you, Unkindled One.

A few people have asked for my opinions on this game, so here they are.
1. The visuals of the game are really nice. The whole thing looks atmospheric, deep forests, rich villages and nice vistas give the player a nice experience from just walking around. 8/10
2. The Ideas that the game portrays are very good. There's a very in-depth crafting system and a good building placement system which have little floors but there could be a bit more done to liven them up a bit. 7/10
3. The general gameplay is very nice. Being able to enjoy it with your friends is great and the contact currently in the game is brilliant! There's a lot of fun to be had here!
1. Performance. I run this game with a 3.4GHz i5 processor and a GTX780 NVIDIA graphics card. If I bump the settings up a bit from the defaults, maybe I increase the tree/terrain detail a bit, my FPS drops a large amount, heading down towards 20FPS. But the game is ENTIRELY playable on the default settings and still looks really good, I'm just not sure how it will run on lower processors/cards.
2. Terrain interaction. The way that you interact with terrain/rocks/trees in this game is very bulky. You look at a tree/terrain segment and are faced with about a dozen options, which for a new player is quite overwhelming. Everything is based on: "Look down at terrain" -> "Click" -> "Select option" -> "Animation plays" -> "You get things". There is currently no real player interaction with the environment around you.
1. The UI. Some elements of the UI, mainly linked with the terrain interaction above don't look or feel very nice. But this is an Alpha and that can change VERY easily.
I will certainly be playing more of this game with a few friends of mine. If you think this game has a bright future like I do then grab a copy, test the bejeebus out of it and send those bug reports flying in!

This is THE game that got me into gaming, I was 9 when I started playing it in 2004 and I still come back every now and then to play some good 'ol Unreal.
Almost every game-mode is fun and well designed, they range from regular old Deathmatch to Capture the Flag with Ion-Canon tanks and Jeeps with blades on them, invasion was always my favorite, it was so well designed in fact that games like Killing Floor were born from it.
The weapons are also a blast to use, PC Gamer even crowned Unreal's 'Flak Cannon' the best gun in PC gaming, but it doesn't end there, the are plasma and laser guns to mess around with, but you also have your trusty old rocket launcher and even a steerable mini-nuke. If you don't like messing around with such a huge arsenal you can play with an Instagib instead, which is a slow-firing weapon with 100% accuracy that instantly kills (and gibs, as the name suggests) anything you hit with it.
Another thing that made it so vastly different from all the boring arena shooters we have nowadays was the crazy mobility, you could do double jumps or jump against a wall and then jump from there again, leading to some pretty hectic but awesome gameplay, you could enable a handy little device called the Translocator that allowed you to shoot a disc and teleport to it with a simple click, making camping virtually impossible.
The game has tons of maps from itself, but Unreal has a very lively modding community and thus hunderds of maps for every game-mode are available for download, you can also download costum skins and even entirely new weapons, just a shame that the game has no steam-workshop.
Even though the game is pretty old by now, there's still a reasonable amount of people playing this gem, if you want to play one of the best sci-fi shooters on the market I'd suggest giving this one a go (And not Unreal Tournament 2007, it didn't live up to the standard of the Unreal franchise in my opinion).

Slow, tedious, not worth your time.
Does the idea of taking 6+ hours to achive even basic automation which you could accomplish in Factorio or modded Minecraft in under 30 minutes appeal to you? How about 2 hours to be able to safely explore away from your base for more than 5 minutes at a time? And that's in what this game calls easy mode - "Casual" mode it literally say is for people with jobs and families. (Who is the target audience, then?)
Every upgrade and machine will cost more resources than it should, and perform below expectations. The game's basic generator can only function in the shallowest biomes (not enough oxygen deeper apparently), and even then it will decline to near 0% efficiency before you reach the next layer. Said layer will freeze you to death in under a minute until you build a suit upgrade... using ore from the layer below it. Everything about the gameplay feels like it's punishing the player.
Apart from the mindbogglingly slow gameplay: The graphics are generally unappealing - it tries 'realistic' textures which don't look good in voxel games in my opinion, but I will acknowledge that's subjective. The surface is ugly as sin - you will never go exploring looking for a pretty place to build an outpost, because none exist. The 3d models are passable for an indie game. Animation is barebones.
The sound design is decent, the effects get the job done, some of the (brief and intermittent) background music is nice.
I didn't notice any bugs whatsoever, so good job on that.
Much of the flavor text in item descriptions includes the author's attempts at forced humor, which I found grating.
I actively played this game for about 15 hours, with several more afk idling while waiting for automation to process materials. I did my best to give this game a chance, I kept waiting for it to become fun, and it just never did.
If you're one of those GregTech-type masochists out there, you might enjoy this. (I don't understand that either, but to each their own.) Anyone else, avoid.
