"The Heaven hunts you. The Hell hates you."
Darksiders is a brutal Hack'n'Slay Adventure.
___________________________________________________
++Story++
In 2010, the Earth is going to be hit by some meteorites. These are not just rocks, but the actual armies of Heaven and Hell, ready to fight each other in an epic battle. Mid in the fight, another man falls from the sky: The Apocalyptic Horseman War. He does not fight for any side in the battle, he is just there to keep the balance, but there is one problem. The Horsemen are only allowed to interfere when the 7 seals are broken. And nobody broke them. War gets teleported to the fiery council, who go into court with him because he broke this rule. He tells them that he has gone to earth because he thought the seals were broken. The fiery council gives him another chance to get rid of his guilt, by killing The Destroyer, the one who started the battle between heaven and hell. So War gets sent back to earth, 100 years after the apocalypse.
++Gameplay++
The gameplay is a typical Hack'n'Slay. War is badassily strong and gets to fight against a lot of enemies at once. His sword swings hit many enemies at once, and there are other weapons to be aquired with other abilities. The battles feel good and fluid, the finisher moves are brutal and the blocking/evading works great.
But there is more than just fighting. The game provides levels and riddles that make it feel like the result of hot sex between God of War and The Legend of Zelda. The riddles can get really hard at times, but not frustratingly hard, so the game does not get boring.
There are a lot of collectibles in the open world, and they also help War, like the Abyssal Armor. There are 10 pieces to find, that are pretty well hidden. If you find all pieces, you get one badass armor.
Sadly, the programming is weak at times and lets the game crash from time to time. There are also some bugs, like falling through the ground (happened to me 4 times). Good thing that there are enough checkpoints to make up for such annoying bugs.
++Grafics++
The grafics like a bit comic-like. The characters look extremely packed with muscles, blood squirts en masse, the bosses are huge and monstrous. The environment is very variable, from the destroyed remains of New York over a forest to a huge desert. The light effects look great and the textures are detailed.
++Music++
Huge, aggressive sounds of orchestral rage are violating your ears in this game. The music fits extremely good with a game where you play as The Apocalyptic Horseman War himself.
++Features++
Given that Darksiders has a little bit of a comic style, there is also an actual official comic that helps the players understand the lore and get more information about the 4 Apocalyptic Horsemen. Search it on google, it is worth it.
___________________________________________________

This is a fun game that's seemingly a bit underrated. It's a 2012 remake of the 2005 original Sniper Elite.
As the name implies, the main focus of the game is playing as a sniper, and this is where the game really shines. Most missions offer plenty of options for careful and considerate tactical planning, with the conclusion being most satisfactory if pulled off properly.
CQC (close quarters combat) can be a bit tedious at times, however, as the interface for machineguns and pistols tends to be a bit clunky and unwieldy. Because of this, manoeuvring in tight places for prolonged periods of time can be a bit of a frustration.
The ballistics are rather realistic, and the X-Ray vision kill-cam is also of particular, if somewhat gruesome interest.
The story and plot are fairly straightforward, taking place during the "final days" of the Third Reich. The "feel" of the sniper rifles and the "atmosphere" of the various missions is great. A small nitpick I have in this regard concerns some of the German voice acting. Sometimes adversaries will drone off things like 'Ich werde dich finden' (I will find you) in the most monotonous tone imaginable, as if it's completely trivial or a mere banality - think as if someone was addressing no-one in particular and says "I'm going to pour myself a cup of tea".
This comes across as slightly absurd if they've just seen someone killed right in front of their eyes. "Oh, look, Gunther's brain has been splattered all over the wall next to me. Seems like there's a sniper out there. Well, I'm going to pour myself a cup of tea - I mean, I'm going to find you." In the grand scheme of things, this nitpick is relatively minor, though.
My main gripe with this game pertains to the way the levels are scripted - it's a bit too much of a pop-up shooting gallery sometimes. On higher difficulties you will find you're often relying somewhat less on your skill with a rifle and rather more on your ability to remember where the enemies spawn and how many of them there are. At times, this can be a frustrating exercise.
Co-op is where this game really shines - whether you play the campaign together or one of the various one-off missions, it's tremendous fun.
In the end, this game is probably not for everyone, which might help explain the relative underrating. This is not your average a dime a dozen shooter. Here, mindlessly running around, "running and gunning" are sure-fire ways to get yourself killed. Every mission requires a modicum of tactical planning and manoeuvring. Especially on higher difficulty levels, even the slightest mistake can easily get you killed and/or cost you the objective.
The emphasis here really lies on the role of the sniper and/or spotter, and if that's not your cup of tea, you might want to pass on this one. The game, unsurprisingly, revolves around sniping. If you do enjoy the role of the sniper, covert operations, sneaking around and planning things out, then this is definately a game worth checking out.

This is hands down, the very best (U.S.) Civil War-based game since Civil War Generals 2. The controls are easy learn and the "drawn path" for troops to march is much easier to use than - for example- Total War's waypoint system. The gameplay is far better than I ever expected. Of course there are some nit-picks though. In my humble opinion the artillery needs some work: It seems to be designed to affect the enemy's unit morale more than anything (which was more the case in the 14th- early/mid 19th centuries.) But artilley of the mid-late 19th century was much more accurate and damaging than it is in this game. Even canister at close range from a battery of 10 or so guns causes very few casualties. But that's a small quirk and it's not a major problem. (I just happen to be a major proponent of the "Grande Baterie" so not-so-effective artillery breaks my poor little heart.) Speaking of centuries, the graphics are very much Windows 95'esque. But I'd much rather sprites that work well than polygonal characters that are buggy and unresponsive. And other than having to run it in "Alternative Rendering" mode I have yet to really find any bugs or snags. I run it on Windows 7 64 bit so I have no idea how it would work on Windows 8. But for me it seems to be very stable. I hope they can get more battles soon. Maybe less celebrated ones such as Mobile or maybe Alatoona Pass. Cold Harbor would be nice as well.

Two Worlds II: Pirates of the Flying Fortress Expansion
Just to reconfirm the following covers my six hours invested in the Two Worlds II (Reality Pump should've been drug out into the street and shot for that title) expansion pack “Pirates of the Flying Fortress” and not the base game itself.
I am nowhere near the end of the expansion but after the amount of time invested I felt compelled to race in with good word before this game is lost to Steam's dungeon archives and forgotten all together.
Forget what you know about the first game in the series (Two Worlds). Although it wasn't entirely a bad entry in sandbox action/adventure games it mostly certainly left a lot of room for improvement which I feel was successfully implemented in the sequel (or at least its expansion).
Now, I must warn to not to do what I did – Which was skip to the expansion immediately without playing the base game first. I warn simply for the fact that your character's achievements and equipment are meant to carry over into the expansion from the base game. If you begin Flying Fortress not carrying over anything from TW2's base; Flying Fortress will start your character with far more than your character needs greatly reducing the challenge that Flying Fortress may have otherwise offered.
Not only did I find myself starting off with the best of the best there has been very little acquired during my six hours of play (Armour or Weapons) that improved on what I had.
And this game is Loot-Heavy! The looting element in Flying Fortress is on par with the obnoxious pack-ratting found in games like Torchlight so my mistake of starting the expansion first has pretty much killed a lot of the game's excitement during exploration.
I feel the best approach continuing onwards is to relay my experience in contrast to The Elder Scrolls games which you more than likely would've asked first and foremost. To summarize: Flying Fortress has sacrificed the massive scope of TES landscapes for a grand improvement of visuals. Reality Pump appears to have aimed for enclosing more relevant and interesting material into a smaller sandbox area. Teamed with very good optimization (modern day developers please look this word up it will help your efforts tremendously!) Flying Fortress plays like a much more aesthetically appealing Skyrim that cuts to the chase.
So if I could choose either Two Worlds II or Skyrim? Skyrim simply for the fact of hosting much more content and therefor longevity. Being able to afford both, however, it would be hypocrisy for TES fans to turn their noses up to Reality Pump's entry in sandbox action/adventure genre.
Price Recommended: $20 w/ Expansion

Similar to minecraft, in that it is a block based, 1m x 1m x 1m type game. The similarities disappear shortly after that. The build gun is an amazing tool for building or removing blocks at long range and is capable of building large platforms or walls very quickly. Most of the game is based on automation of resources or manufacturing, similar to Factorio. The game play in single player seems to flow through 3 distinct types of gameplay: you start off in a survival game, fighting the elements and trying to just manage; mid-game is filled with automation of all sorts, from power generation and transport, to quarrying, refining materials you obtain, and auto-crafting items; end-game is similar to a tower defense game, fighting hordes of enemies, trying to keep them from destroying your Central Power Hub and resetting the charge on your end-game structure. I thoroughly enjoy it, and can easily say that it's worth the full price.

This game is a part of the world-famous and highly ambitious and beloved series Teddy Floppy Ear. It was made by the AAA game studio Forever Entertainment, which is located in Poland, one of the greatest countries for games in general.
The game looks and feels great. It supports all kinds of system and graphics card configurations. It can run at an incredible framerate of 144 frames per second! The game is beautiful, and it's artstyle is very nice. It has a very lovely and calming atmosphere to it. It also features some of the latest and greatest advancements in graphics technology, such as fullscreen mode.
The gameplay in this game is very enjoyable and well-crafted. It is both calming, relaxing and fun to play through this game, and it will both challenge and reward the play with clever puzzles and mysteries. It is an open-world point-and-click adventure, and the world is also very unique and well made. The player will need to explore and think to make it through. The game is reasonably lengthy, and it can both be played casually or all in one sitting.
This game follows the story of young Teddy Floppy Ear, who is going on a trip to the mountains to visit his uncle. Teddy Floppy Ear will meet several unique and lovely characters, who all are very unique and have something interesting to say. The story is family friendly, altough some parts might be a bit too violent for children. Teddy Floppy Ear is not very intelligent, so you will have to help him, and he will solve several mysteries and problems while on his adventure. The only complaint i have about the story is the fact that the most interesting and funny character, the bear, does not appear alot in the game.
The game controls smoothly and logically. It features mouse controls, and the cursor will change when you hold over a relevant object, so that you can know when something is interactable. There is also a button in the top-left corner, which makes Teddy talk for a few seconds while you can't do anything at all, which is great.
The game is very well optimized, but it will still require a heafty graphics card to run smoothly. This is mainly because of the intense graphical effects and the realistic fur rendering on the bear i mentioned earlier. It is possibly one of the best looking titles released in recent years, and i personally believe it will be a hallmark for what humans can accomplish. The game still works well on alot of different system configurations, and it supports both Windows, OSX, and Linux. Wow, where to begin with this game. Let me first start with my opinion. I love this game. However, I can not recomend it as of yet. I spent 24 hours of game time as of the time I've written this, and I still don't really have a clue what's going on. It's advertised as a tower defense mincraft clone, but I've never played minecraft, so I'm not really sure if it is. I really like the idea of having to dig to find minerals, the blocks you can remove, the things you can research, but I don't like having to search outside the game or go through a million other steps to get a general idea of what I should be doing.
Let's start off with the 10 second tutorial. It sucks so bad, after the first time I booted the game up and watched the unskippable (in this day and age, really?!) opening scene, I had no real idea of what to do or how. Sure, there is a help menu that gradually fills up with more information as you need it, but isn't the point of the tutorial to teach you what you need to know? There's no real explination of day or night, no real explination of what you can craft, and nothing tells you what you're research unlocks until you've already researched it.
Now the community is great, and all the answers can be found someplace, but to me, that takes time away from the game. It's advertised as a tower defense, but it's more like a base defense, eventually. I'm not going to get into the nitty gritty, but this game needs a ton of polish before I can actually recommend it to anyone. The learning curve is HUGE in this game, and I'm still finding things out the more I play, but if that's your thing, feel free.
Update: With the new patch that came out, I truly do love this game more. I still can't recommend it though until it does some serious polishing. No game ever should keep basic things away from the player, and that level of transparency is exactly what this games lacks. It's also unbelievably slow. I've been playing for days and there are still things that are hidden from me and I have no idea what they do until I actually spend the 5-6 hours unlocking it. As a player, it's truly the only reason I keep this game thumbs down.
Update 2: Got back into the game and tried some new things. Things ran smoother since I now know more, but the game still has so much information withheld from the player, even after 100+ hours I still haven't tried everything. It's simply too time consuming to be fun anymore and with the recent patch, there seems to be even more steps and buildings to build to do what you were able to do before without those steps and buildings. I haven't ever had the chance to charge the beacon and win the game even once. This game is dead to me, and I will not change my stance on it.

I'm normaly too lazy to bother to write a review for a game... But I'll make an exception.
Shovel Knight is easily one of the best games I've ever played, and no doubt, my favorite platformer. It manages to make a perfect mix of engaging, fun mechanics, challenging difficulty that values actual skill above anything else, a nostalgic, but at the same time modern look, an amazing soundtrack and a sprinkle of simple, good humor.
I bought this game when only the Shovel Knight story was out, and it was easily worth its full price. Even if short, the game was very engaging, and just a real joy to play.
Then Plague Knight's story came out. When I saw it, I thought 'Oh, cool! I might buy this some time, maybe.' Then I realized that it was free, and thought that maybe it was just a reskin of the base game... I was very wrong.
Plague of Shadows was an absolute rework of the game. It kept the same world, with a story that, while not breaking the main one, was still very engaging and a joy to follow; most importantly, though, it brought a whole new set of mechanics, changing gameplay to something not just different to the main game, but also just as original as Shovel Knight itself had been before. I had paid for 1 good quality game, and received 2 games I dare call masterpieces.
And now Specter of Torment came out, and with just what I have played of it so far, I'll have to correct my previous statement. I received not 2, but 3 masterful games, with a fourth one on the way!
This isn't a game that you'll just play, have some fun with, and then just forget about. This is a game you can, and will, thoroughly enjoy.
Yacht Club Games, just for the ammount of care and quality that can be found in simply this game, are just a cut above most other developers.

I would strongly advise anyone against buying this game for dozens of reasons. The game has many shortcomings and is missing features that have been industry standard for decades. Throughout the game there is a severe lack of quality or attention to detail. Contrary to how the game advertises itself, it is not very realistic nor is it very flexible. These issues range from small to large, and mods have been unable to fix them over the last decade (ArmA 1, 2, 3 and various expansions). ArmA 3 continues this trend. As it can take hours to write down each any every point of low quality, I will mention some of the big offenders:
-          Incomplete weapon animations. Not a single weapon has both sets of animations done, and mods cannot fix this. What is present in the game is of meddling quality, often with hands and uniforms clipping into weapons, sounds not fully synced, and more.
-          AI gets lost, stuck, runs each other over, shoots each other in the back and more very frequently. They can also walk through many objects and props on the map which is very immersion breaking.
-          Mission editor buries the most common and frequently used functions. What should have a graphical user interface (GUI) often does not, requiring you to memorize many complex scripts. For example, making a mission end by killing certain enemies will require a script to be written. Other games such as DCS, Jane’s USAF (1999) all do this via a GUI.
-          Poor squad AI command interface. It is slow and cumbersome.
-          Inaccurate squad movement commands. If you want to accurately position your team members like other tactical shooters you will be out of luck.
-          Unrealistic weapon sway, to the point aiming and hitting someone 50 meters in front of you with iron sights will be a chore.
-          AI has difficulty following roads, even when you place highly detailed waypoints. AI has severe difficulty crossing bridges, even with well placed waypoints. Now way to make a waypoint automatically follow a road, which is common in other games with mission editors (DCS, a flight simulator, does this).
-          AI is fairly inconsistent; inconsistency increases the larger your mission is.
-          Almost every remedial task in the editor will require some form of scripting, either in game or via an external file. Scripts which should be simple, such assigning artillery to more than one player, may require a full page paragraph script to be written.
-          Player loadout editing  is fairly limiting. You cannot carry two rifles as an example, which is common for many real world snipers.
-          Vehicle damage modelling is very sub par, and mostly relies on a hit point based system with some damage.
-          Enemy AI often unfairly cheats. While your player is abnormally weak and can’t hold a rifle steady, enemies can spin around in the prone position, spot you laying prone in the grass 500 meters away, and get a head shot on you within 3-4 shots. You can tweak their accuracy, but in general it ranges from Terminator to a blind man.
-          AI has severe difficulty navigating indoors, which includes frequent clipping and walking through walls. Likewise, AI often gets lost in cities or cluttered areas. The player will often have to stop walking and take a 1-2 minute rest every 3-4 minutes to  wait for team members to find you.
-          Poor control layout and UI. The same function to open a door also switches to your pistol, or ammo type, or any number of things. Often times you may be trying to close a door, only for option to disappear from the scroll menu and your player will instead swap to their pistol.
-          Many seemingly simple things are not possible. Exiting a boat and walking onto a pier is not possible. Instead, you will fall into the water, and will clumsily swim around to find a ladder if present. This is also true for AI.
-          Making AI surrender and other mid level type of mission editing will require many scripts.
-          Different grenade types are present via mods, but the quality of their effects are very low end. Don’t expect flash bangs to work like flash bangs.
-          Placing a plane on a runway and making it take off requires a lot more effort than should be necessary. Flight sims can do this automatically with a few clicks, yet ArmA 3 requires much more.
There are many other shortcomings, but these are just a few which come to mind. To summarize, ArmA 3 is very limited and frustrating. Mods and scripts can occasionally offer patch jobs for shortcomings, but few can fix the experience. The game lacks the detailed micro management found in games such as SWAT or older Rainbow 6 titles, and also lacks the attention to detail the flight sim genre has made common for simulators. In many instances, such as movement and weapon handling, mainstream games such as Battlefield 4 top ArmA 3.
ArmA 3 could have been so much better, but ultimately falls flat for anyone who values quality and realism. Inconsistency, immersion breaking actions, awkward workarounds and AI limitations will prevent anything but the most basic missions from playing out convincingly. Eventually placing a bunch of units which do little more than walk and shoot each other will get old, and you will be very disappointed in the limitations holding back your mission designs.
I would not recommend ArmA 3 or ArmA 3 Apex or any of the piece meal DLCs.

They're like a far reaching side jump, so when your about to get hit you can quickly move off to side into safety (or impending danger) faster than you would have jumping. Since you are unable to rocket jump, shield guns are used as a subsitute. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥where do I start.
This game is doing something that's never been done before. Sure, you could bring up Xsyon or Wurm Online, but those games are nothing like Life is Feudal. This game is limitless in what it can achieve and is easily one of top games with the most potential on the market right now. This is the kind of game that you couldn't get tired of because there is ALWAYS something to do due to the fact that player interaction is key to playing. Being a lone wolf won't cut it, you'll HAVE TO team up with someone, and the more the better which makes the game that much better.
Life is Feudal brings the whole survival genre to a new level. In Rust or DayZ, it's just a bunch of trolls/bandits running around killing people and causing mayhem just because they can. Life is Feudal has systems in place to combat this...the alignment system. Stealing/Robbing/Killing lowers your alignment, and after a certain point, there's no going back. If you die, you loose a big chunk of your skills and items whereas players with high alignment don't. It makes people think twice if it's really worth it to kill that poor farmer whom isn't bothering anyone and has nothing.
As I stated before, the potential this game has far surpasses any game I've ever played before. They were always limited by the game engine or just the way the game was built. DayZ is doomed to be ♥♥♥♥ed with all the bandits and hackers, Rust is doomed with all the trolls running around killing people for no reason, but Life is Feudal stands a chance. The possibilities in this game are ENDLESS. Once you finished doing something, you are always tasked with doing another thing to keep you going and going so you don't bore yourself like in DayZ...or should I say walking simulator? With over 3000 different alchemy combinations, dozens of different things to construct, and making alliances with other towns, you'll always be doing something.
Now you may be asking yourself, "What about the PvP?" Life is Feudal has that in check. They are implementing a system so that when you go to war against a town/guild, you don't take any hits to your alignment which allows full scale wars city vs city. It will easily satisfy your blood thirsty hunger.
Now, I know this may very well be the game that could revolutionize the way we see the survival, but it doesn't come without it's flaws.
The game is very poorly optimized even though I have a GTX 780 Ti. I've noticed that turning down the quality of trees in the settings dramatically improves frames. Even then, the game still occasionally dips below 30 FPS. It also crashes quite frequently which can be very annoying.
Even with the games flaws, those can be easily fixed and it isn't something that we will be stuck with forever.
Thinking of buying the game? Well, at 40$ it's quite expensive and I would only recommending spending that much as long as you are ok with the flaws the game presents
Remember, Life-is-feudal.

As a professional Bush and Tree tender, I feel as though this game meets, and easily exceeds, the expectations for a realistic gardening simulation. I feel that the livelike, vivid and realistic graphics and physics of each branch and leaf add a certain life into the game, that is certainly lacking in other tree simulator games. This, however, is no simple simulator game. This is an in-depth, fully simulated bonsai tree simulator.
The realism behind this game is definitely one of it's strong points, as each and every branch, root and dirt particle is realistically simulated, utilising the advanced Unity engine to give each particle a life of it's own. This allows for incredible experiences, as it feels as though the bonsai that you spend so much time creating and obsessing over really comes to life, and the entire experience is one of the most rewarding activites available on Steam, or perhaps in life.
The only downside to this game, however, is that it does not currently have VR support. If the developers add VR support, I feel that the entire experience would be improved, as I would no longer have to simply "imagine" being next to my tree, and caring for it, but rather, I could actually interact with my bonsai tree.
Overall, the developers have cared significantly for this game, and deliver constant update patches, along with new features, so I don't see VR support being very far away, and I am sure it is already in the works.
In essence, this game is a must buy for any gardening simulator fans, or even someone who might just want a relaxing experience, especially with the tailor-made soundtrack for the game.

Like Tetrix, some game excels because of its simplicity. It is so true for the Trials series. The goal of the game is simple, to get your bike from point A to point B as fast as possible without crashing, and all the controls you have is accelerate, break, leaning forward and back. However, the game gets challenging very fast and you always want to try again just to chip a few millisecond or to manage that difficult jump.
Compares to its predecessors, Fusion offer a cleaner, more futuristic setting. Some players will miss the more gritty setting of Trials Evolution. The game offers nicer lighting, some neat bloom effects, and nice post-processing effects. Overall the graphic is very beautiful and crashes are spectacular.
The game add a few new twists like being able to pull tricks with your right thumbstick. I find it a shame they add this feature and yet removed the ability to share replays on Youtube. What is the point of pulling spectacular stunts yet unable to show off to others?
Likewise, there is no longer online multiplayer, which is promised again and again by the developer but no ETA is in sight. Given there are already 2 DLCs released you can tell the developer is focusing their efforts on making money instead of finishing the multiplayer feature of the game. There is local multiplayer you can play with your buddy on the same sceen.
You can also make your own tracks, and at the writing of this review there are already over two thousands user generated tracks online, and many of them are top quality and add to the longitivity of the game. Which is necessary because there are much fewer tracks than Trial Evolution Gold. Again, I feel the developers are holding off the initial release of tracks to sell them as future DLCs, which BTW at 4.99$ for 10 tracks is quite pricy.
Gameplay wise the official tracks are well designed but most of them are shorter than TEG. I find there are some twicks to the physics and overall a bit more forgiving than TEG. You can also make 1 or 2 faults and still get Gold on some tracks which I like because it is less frustrating, but I can see hard-core player won't like the change.
Overall, I'd still recommand the game just because the overall concept is awesome. However, I don't like the business practice of the developer and would recommand you to get the game when on sale, where you can get the main game and the season pass as one package within reasonable price.

"You are War, Rider of the Red Horse! Not some puppet on this pathetic creature's strings!"
Darksiders, the Wrath of War is a third person hack and slash game in which you play as War, one of the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse. You are wrongly acused of breaking the pact between Heaven and Hell and bringing destruction to the Kingdom of Man. You must now singlehandedly take on the Destroyer's armies and restore the balance to the universe.
Gameplay:
+Flashy combos and moves.
+Very fluent feel to it, but not the best (Arkham City does miles better on fluency).
+Many a demon lost their heads that day (lots of gore).
+Awesome finishing moves.
+Weapon upgrades and other items bought from merchants work very well.
+Fun to reap the rewards of exploration.
+Good amount of length, 14 hours and counting on my Apocalyptic (hard) mode difficulty.
+A lot of people like to call this game "Zelda with gore" (I wouldn't know however, I never played  Zelda).
+/-Good enough parkour (not AC good, but decent).
+/-Relatively easy when you're fighting normal minions (half your moves result in a stun lock).
-Combo system is kind of weird, having a 40x combo and a 2x combo doesn't seem to make a difference and the combo is sometimes lost for no explicable reason.
-Block and dash are bound to the same key.
-Those awesome finishers get old after the fourth time. They can always be used on a minion when it's at a certain health level, and each minion only has one or two finishers.
-Only three hot key spots for items, and only four for spells/potions (this could be a design choice, but I get the feeling it's because this game was made for consoles).
Level Design and World:
+Not entirely open world design, you have to have this item to go here, but you can return to areas and farm some loot.
+Very grand design on many places.
+You get a good feel of "This was New York, but that was before the appocalypse hit".
+Unique system with fast travel where you have to run a short distance in the "Serpant Hole". This can include jumping puzzles.
+Very atmospheric.
+/-Puzzles. I find the puzzles that are really just glorified Lego Star Wars puzzles to be irritating. They just a way to drag out time inbetween big fights, but I know some people enjoy them. They aren't particularily hard however (unless you turn off game hints like I did so you have no idea what anything does).
Characters and Story:
+Very unique approach to some characters and the biblical stories.
+The characters all have their own personality.
+The Watcher is a nice comic relief at times.
+Interesting story that is slightly mystery, and mostly bloody fantasy epic.
+/-Lots of names to memorize and try to pronounce (I personally love names like "Azreal" and "The Stygian" but I know some people will just be annoyed).
-War suffers from the "Batman" personality syndrome (mopey badass whose personality is about as deep as a puddle of water).
Graphics:
+Great design and art style.
+Very fantasy feel.
+Angels and demons feel very angelic and demonic.
+/-Very flashy and cool, but repetitive animations.
-Low resolution.
Sound:
+Great music.
+Great voice acting (you even get a Mark Hamill character)
-Sometimes a little glitchy.
Overall:
This game is one of my favorites of all time, along with the sequel, but it's not for everyone. If you're a graphics stickler, you're going to have a bad time. If you don't like gore, you're done. If you don't like Hack and Slash games, why are you here in the first place? But if you like hack and slash games, if you like an interesting story, if you like great art and environmental design, you're in for a damn good time.
EDIT:
Because the characters and story are heavily based on biblical stories, if you're sensitive about religion, this might be a game to avoid. I personally did not have any issues with this part of the game; from what I could tell, they deviated greatly from the original biblical stories, so I just took it as a fantasy story, nothing more, however I get the feeling some people will be turned off by this.

Still my favourite of all the multitudinous Total War games. Having played the Total War series since CA first came out with Shogun, I have to say Rome was the one that really turned me into a Total War fan through and through. The factions all have their own unique personalities - Rome's heavy focus on infantry; Egypt's swift chariots and devastating archers; the powerful hoplite infantry of the Greek states or the freewheeling Parthian horse archers. The game itself is easy enough for a rank beginner to learn the basics, but challenging enough for even the most grizzled of Total War veterans to take a beating. And even the strongest of factions, when stomping across the map, can suddenly find their full-stack armies reduced to nothing by a well-placed ambush, the point of an assassin's blade, or the treacherous bribes of a high-ranking diplomat...
Overall, Rome Total War immerses you in the Mediterranean world of the last few centuries BCE, lets you take charge of many of antiquity's most celebrated nations, and conquer the known world through a combination of sly negotiation, swift backstabbing and - most importantly - the iron-shod feet of your mighty legions. And that's just the campaign map.
Rome Total War, as all the games in the series are, is a game of two halves. The campaign map is probably the more in-depth and fascinating part of it for me, but there are also the impeccably tuned real-time battles. Your units face off against those of your enemies using a fairly basic rock-paper-scissors arrangement: infantry fight cavalry; cavalry crush archers; archers blitz infantry. Upsetting the balance somewhat are the fearsome Egyptian chariot archers with the speed of cavalry and an even longer range than foot archers; the same can be said of Parthian horse archers, while the Roman legionaries can Testudo in the classical formation, protecting them from archers. The battles are well balanced, enough so that you can pull a victory out of your own personal Thermopylae one turn, while the next your vastly numerically superior army can be utterly crushed by a much smaller force with superior weapons. (Pro tip: don't take a 3000-man-strong army of cavalry into a fight with 200 Spartan hoplites...)
Rome Total War does have some technical issues on Windows 7 and later. These can be worked around with certain resolution tweaks and a launch option, although it's unfortunate that these issues persist despite many other older games being updated for Steam and newer OSes. I have yet to notice any of the old Crash to Desktop issues RTW used to have, but I'd like to see a compatibility update at some point.

My favourite iteration of the UT series.
Vanilla UT2004 has more than enough game mods and maps to swallow up huge amounts of your time. The bots cater for every skill level and do a good job of making offline matches fun in their own right. It also has a campaign mode that lets you buy and sell players, challening other clans to matches as you head on up the league table. It was very enjoyable back in the day and I was sad When UT3 didn't have the same sort of campaign.
The game will run smoothly on all but the most basic of computers and has been a staple of LAN parties ever since its launch. It has aged brilliantly and was well supported by its community back in the day, making it worth getting for mods like 'Air Buccaneers' alone!
Before UT2004 there was a 2003 edition which was very similar. There was outcry when this version was announced, with people accusing it of becoming an annual series, much like EA sport titles. I'm almost sad that that wasn't the case, since this 2004 version contains everything that came with the 2003 edition, doubled the number of maps, added new game modes (including a very popular vehicle mode which is better balanced than I had ever expected it to be) and generally rendered the previous version of the game obsolete.
I still haven't scratched the surface of what this game contains. It's big enough that even if you only like a small fraction of what it has to offer, you'll still have more to play with than most entire games have to offer. An odd little side-note, but both girls I've shown this game to have loved it, even though they're not generally fans of aggressive, adrenaline-based frag fests. Odd.
It's a thumbs up from me. The only irritating thing about it is that occasionally matches reach a frustrating stalemate, or you begin to lose through no fault of your own which is an incredibly frustrating experience. You'd expect that in online modes but offline, when you're outperforming the bots by a considerable margin, can get very frustrating. I've hardly touched the online part of this game, it's never appealed to me. Call me a noob, but the fact this game still holds my attention should pay adequate testament to the quality of this title. UT2004: 10 games rolled into one. Fun for all the family. 'cept children, probably not suitable for them.

SUMMARY
Excellent strategy game.  Definitely worth purchasing.  Very challenging and realistic within each 6 hour time period, but Southern forces are moved back from taken objectives after each 6 hour time period change.  If you can live with that frustration, it is a great game.
PROS
Very accessible, intuitive controls, adequate graphics, realistic movement, tactics, morale, cover and elevation advantages.
AI is fully adjustable from very cautious to risk taking.
The individual time period slices are great fun to replay to try different moves etc.
I saw no glaring bugs or performance issues, it ran very smoothly and glitch free.
It is fun to play as the South and try for a different from history outcome.
CONS
There is one glaring problem.  Southern units are moved back from taken objectives every time the 6 hour time portion changes.
The 3 day battle is chopped up into 6 hour portions.  During each portion you have complete freedom to implement your tactics and try various what if approaches to how the South Attacked.  This yields a great deal of re-playability.
The problem is that when the game changes to the next 6 hour period, it completely repositions the South's forces far back from the objectives they previously had achieved.  Hundreds of yards, not just a few feet.  Example:  By 6pm the first day my rebels were able to capture Culps hill.  When the time period runs out and jumps to the next one,  Souther forces are moved north about a mile and the Union again is in control of Culps Hill.
The only thing that remains constant between time slices is each sides casualties and troop count.  Heavy losses are carried over to the next time slice.
In a nutshell the South can kill more Northern units than historical, but it is very difficult to take objectives since the time slices forfeits them over and over.

In fairness, even though I myself would like some more advanced options for units and leading, I think this game actually is a very good blend that suits new players and more veteran players to this genre alike. As a new player you won't have a hard time understanding this game, as a more veteran player of this type of games you will have your work cut out for you as well.
For anyone interested in this period and this battle, this is a very good pick, but it does lack some replayability once you've played each side and won. It will give you alot of fun hours up until that point though.

As it is now, I can't reccomend this game. It's hard even on the 'easy' settings to do anything really. With the combonation of heat/cold, energy storage of your suit only one begginer smelter and a whole lot of things early game take way too long! It is a time sink that is in my opinion far worse than other 'builder' games. I will compare to one that most everyone should know: Minecraft.
Comparing Minecraft to Fortresscraft
*You can easily build multiple smelters right from the start really/ Fortresscraft you may finally unlock a basic smelter after a few hours play.
*Ores are generally spawned with more of a pattern/ Fortresscraft is more luck based. Meaning it may take a few hours to even build the basics.
*You already know all crafting, you just need the proper tool/ Fortresscraft you need to scan almost everything, and research it. Use the researcher to gain building rights. Making the beginning game so long and tedious.
These are just a few issues I have.
One could argue: Recode the recipes in the data files. I shouldn't have to. One could say use creative mode. Then I lose out on needing anything and lose on battling enemies. Plus you don't get all the energy stuff or anything. Or none that I could see.
I wish there was a kind of hybrid creative/ survival mode. Kind of like how you can switch between the modes in Minecraft with commands. And the creative mode in Fortresscraft had ALL the blocks plus being able to battle enemies should you choose to.
So unless you have hours to sit down and figure this game out, don't expect anything to be built quickly. As it is, I can't reccomend it. Maybe it's not for me since I don't have hours and hours to sink into it to find everything and such. Which is why I like Minecraft better. If you want something that does similar to this but qucker, Try Factorio. You can even cheat if you wish, and I don't feel cheating ruined the game for me on that as I still do a lot.
It has potential. I love the idea of having a factory with belts/ transporters, and building a defensive base and all that. So I WILL check in on this game from time to time as I do like the ideas. It just needs to be a little more open I guess you could say. Allow us to do what we want, if we wish to speed things up some allow commands to do so or something. I'll keep watching it for updates and such and may update my review at a later date.

Very basic game for a 4x RTS. Way too basic.
The User interface is clunky at best. Theres no way to build units from a base structure except by zooming in to said structure and building it. Takes precious time, and is difficult to do if the building is surrounded by swarms of your own ships. No shortcut to select it, no empire tree or similar manager.
No hotkeys whatsoever and no settings for controls.
This is in space. SPACE. Despite that, unit maneuver are severely limited since there seem to be only two levels they can fly in. They cannot really fly over each other. Yes, this means that in a space game, you're restricted to x-y movement. No z-axis movement. It is odd to see that cruiser class ships are able to turn around on a dime in a short span of time... then not be able to move becuase of his two wingmen. Then all three of them try to figure out how to move for the next 30 seconds straight.
Ship models are basically bricks with different lengths and very low detail. From what I've seen so far, most ships do not even have more than one weapon system (ie all the firepower from a destroyer comes from a SINGLE cannon).
Everything in the game screams overly simplistic. From the combat mechanics to the resource mechanics, to the user interface and the graphics (I'm usually not too concerned about graphics if the game is good, but on max graphics, weapon projectiles are VERY low resolution TEXTURES. COME ON. Homeworld 1 in 1998 had better projectiles with higher resolutions. For the Homeworld fans: One of the projectiles looks exactly like an energy weapon projectile from Homeworld Cataclysm, but lower resolution. This is 2012, not 1998).
As a long time fan of Homeworld, Sins of a Solar Empire and the space RTS genre in general, I cannot really recommend this game unless you enter with rock bottom expectations. Anything higher and you will be dissappointed. I didn't even have any expectations and then it disappointed me.
Risk it only if its on sale. Thats luckily how I got it, so it wasn't too much of a waste.
PS: The metacritic score for this game is 53. There's a reason for that, too bad I didn't listen.

Coming into FortressCraft my only survival building game experience has been minecraft. So I'd like to say my expectations were high. I had read FC Evolved was similar to Tekkit modded minecraft and I was getting excited.
Firstly I dislike space themed anything - and this is definitely space themed - but I've found it to be fine.
My first 10mins of gameplay I was confused AF. It's fun to learn and work out what you have to do - which could be avoided by watching a gameplay of FC Evolved on YT, but I wanted to throw myself into the deep end. I'm at 20+hrs in, 17hrs of which in this one world, where I like to pretend I know what I'm doing. And I feel I've barely scratched the surface.  Once you figure out a methodology and approach, and are fast acting on it, I think you could have a world up and running a LOT faster than what I've done in this first attempt - and that's one of the selling points, become efficient.
+ Loads of gameplay
+Looks pretty [I run at good, and occasionally stutters - my gfx card runs Farcry 4 at decent settings]
+I love the mobility [compared to MC]
+I love the grappling hook mechanic
+I love ctrl+clicking to build 30blocks in a straight line
+I love seeing a base grow and become automated
+I love pressing K to find where I placed that ore extractor, because I totally forgot where I put it
+Addicting gameplay
+Always something to do/alter/change/move/collect/kill/mine/ping
+You can leave it in the background/ALTTab and even on single player, the world continues to simulate - so if you have automated mining set up, you can do other things away from your PC and come back to collect smelted ores.
-I wish there was lights - early on. Throwing a bright green torch is ugly and hurts my eyes :')
-I wish conveyor belts could be placed with ctrl+click, as that would save me time
-I wish the music was better? A lot of annoying sounds. I find it actually nicer to play with sound off becaues of this.
- Confusing progression.
Overall, I paid ~$15.00 for it[?], and it has been worth it. I plan to put a lot more hours in.

"Meh" pretty much defines this game. it's fun, but nothing to run home about. combat system is great for a while then you discover that you can just equip a melee wepon hold the block button down and beat everthing without magic or poison into the ground.
i'm a huge rpg fan, and i have i think around 40 hours or so in the game, but i don't know what everyone talks about when they call this game huge. the campaign takes about 9-10 hours if you do a smattering of sidequests along the way. which is miniscule for an rpg. the story starts poorly and doesn't really go above mildly interesting right untill the end. even then the big twist involves characters that haven't been developed through more than about 3 cutscenes. over all it lacks vastness in either story(circa dragon age or mass effect) or in just size (oblivion for example) though there are sizeable maps one you get a horse (and you can get one as soon as you leave the tutorial island) you can cross most of them the long way in 5-6 minutes.
action wise it remids me of the first witcher game, you go in guns a blazing against a shriveled corpse weilding a stick with your big two handed sword, and get your *** kicked because of the strict "don't go here" leveling system. if you are like me however and say "suck it i'm going in anyway you programmer!" this game becomes intesly fun. combat is very hit and miss, sometimes hitting something 33 times with a stick will kill it, sometimes hiting something 300,000,000 times without being hit back get's about half it's health down, and you're instantly killed, by a monster 2 levels higher than you that you've killed 30 of in the last area. unfortunately it falls in the camp of blocking as a method of damage reduction rather than deflection. so you always take damage from every attack. which sounds like a realistic idea, but actually leads to simply pouring out damage as fast as possible and trusting to your hero's glut of health to soak up hits.
TW2 feels small, and while it boasts a meaty crafting system, a nice potion system and a great magic system, you'll never come across enough materials in game to take great advantage of these. (and i depopulated an entire island in order to play with the potion system). i've sunk lots of time into this game trying to make it into the epic game reviewers seem to think it is... but ultimately my 40 hours on this game are due solely to the fact that it's one of the few RPG's that worked on my mac. after i got bootcamp(moved to windows) i've shelved it and never looked back. it's fun, but i'll not recomend it, purely because there are many other more deserving titles out there for this price.

Let me start by saying that this game IS FUN.  I have played for many hours(although a lot of that time was spent afk... I tend to forget I have games running) The basic concept of the game is great, gather resources, build massive assembly lines, defend against attacks, all to save yourself when you crashed on a freezing planet.  So then why the negative review?
The game appears to be a released title but upon deeper investigation (after I had bought the game, stupid me) I realized that it was still in Alpha/Beta but the developer wanted to make more money so he "released" it on steam.  The game has missing icons/textures, wonky AI, and is still has a MASSIVE list of features to be added, bugs to fix, and balance issues to address.  I havn't encountered the game breaking crashes/bugs others have reported.  IF I WANTED TO PLAY EARLY ACCESS I WOULD BE HAPPY.  The game is being updated and features are being added.  The negative review stems from the fact that it is not a complete game even though it appears that way at first.
Oh, also the dev has stated that he is breaking the game into several expansion packs.  So you only get part of the content for your initial purchase.  However he only recently decided this(or made it clear).  I can understand wanting to get paid but it is sneaky and dishonest to publish an unfinished game and then charge people more money if they want the finished product.  If all this were clear on the store page I wouldn't be writing this review(and would probably be fine with it... although i would have waited until the game was complete before considering purchase).  The sneaky way it is handled is what bothers me.
So FOR NOW I do not reccomend purchasing this game.  When it is finished (provided it get's there, i've had baaad luck with early access titles, I will rewrite this review.

Explosions, one-hit kills, and anyone able to pop up anywhere (there are no choke points in any map) can make for a very random, hectic, and skill-less battle at times.
But if you can put up with it's unforgiving, crazy nature, it's rewarding. Unfortunately there are just a lot of games that do this style way better. The most unique thing it has going for it is the Wild West. 4/10

This game presents itself as a relaxing tree growing game, however the achievements make it into a grindy clicker game, and both are pretty bad. Watching the trees grow initially is actually decently relaxing, however the lack of control, limited options, and poor visuals are very uncompelling. I honestly wouldn't have a problem with this game not holding my interest for more than 5 minutes with this price tag, had
not been able to make a hell of a relaxing plant growing game for free.
For a causal game with a concept so pure and relaxing, this game is frustrating as hell. You have no influence on how your tree grows besides clicking it to make it grow a bit faster. You don't even get to decide what tree to grow, it's all randomly generated. All you can do is remove branches you didn't like where they grew and hope they are nice next time.
This game doesn't have a goal, but if you're one who plans on 100% the achievements for it, cutting branches is what you will be doing  for way too ♥♥♥♥ing long. There are two extremely grindy achievements for no reason that just gives you time to examine all the flaws in this game.
Grinding is nothing new, but it's usually rewarding. You gain things and feel progress throughout to remain intrigued, however this challenge is only external, there is no reason or demand for you to do them in game.
The design of this game is also awful.
The music is super annoying, which for a game that is supposed to be relaxing, and one that you will spend a lot of time idling in grinding, is a huge problem. At least you can turn it off.
The "level" is minimalistic, but also rough and janky which contrast each other really horribly.
The leaves are revolving 2d sprites and float around the branch instead of on it which look horrible as the tree gets bigger.
It also crashed and glitched a few times, but it was infrequent enough that I will state it's "buggy."
In conclusion, don't buy this, play
instead.

Not too shabby. Lead and Gold's an addictive multiplayer focused third person shooter that is very immediate, visually impressive, besides being remarkably cheap. I like that the class balancing is spot on for the most part, being fairly flexible moving between play styles aswell, unlike Monday Night Combat in contrast. Lead and Gold's trump card is solid tactical play and teamwork, game modes rotate largely between Attack and Defend playsets which are not to be played in a straightforward manner like in any other multiplayer game. Yet on the downside, Lead and Gold is overshadowed by a poor lobby system and community. Inviting friends into a match, any match, is hard work and there is no clear way of balancing or switching teams without calling for a democratic vote in scrambling teams. Not many players on Lead and Gold will admittedly play fair either, with spawn camping and noob hunting being common sport in matches. Keep this in mind if you consider buying the game.

Very interesting take on a hardcore survival sandbox style game, in a good way. Unlike all the other developers hopping on this quickly developing genre, LIF takes the emphasis out of PVP and places it instead upon cooperation and survival instead.
Upon my first few hours of gameplay, i encountered my first player,
I equipped my knife to the best of my ability(I was still learning the controls, so it was sketchy) and ran at my target. I struck him twice out of the three swings I got in before he became aware of the attack. He was on the run, and I figured I could finish him off within the next few swings, seeing as one might imagine that knife-wounds would be fatal. I couldn't have been any more off-track. Upon checking my combat log i discovered my knife lunge had done a whopping .80 damage, to the head nontheless. One well-aimed surprise knife attack was not capable of depleting even 1/100 oh my opponents health.
I waited until my opponent was a safe distance away(he was still fleeing despite my pathetic damage output) and then made my retreat, as winning this fight would inevitably prove to be more trouble than it was worth.
I realize now that this is because it's not meant to be a sort medieval rust/dayz with better crafting, this game truly strives to break free of this generic PVP sandbox archetype that has somehow become the standard of this genre.
That's not to say that PVP Isn't important, it's just not designed to be a game in which you hop in and have the (realistic) capacity to kill people. Which is good! it helps to change the direction of these games, instead of just mindlessly bashing someone with a rock to get their belongings, you have to cooperate with people to establish the means to build those weapons in the first place. Which adds a layer of depth and establishes the foundation for group combat and politics among other villages.
It strives to be something that truly deviates from what we know now as a pvp sandbox title, and does so succesfully.

fair price.
You have a double jump, and a quick dash that you can do in any direction, on the ground or mid-jump. You can easily flit in and out of the fray, chopping up enemies with melee weapons before quickly ducking out to rip into them with gunfire. You also have a few spells (healing, force wave, invisibility, etc) that draw from a mana meter.
Shooting and slicing both feel good. The animation on the melee weapons is fast and weighty, and enemies will come apart differently depending on what direction you slice them. The guns are worse; sound effects are OK at best, and the animations lack the snappy punch that the melee weapons have. Shooting stuff is still pretty satisfying despite that, thanks to the way enemies react to being shot: a scream or grunt, a meaty sound effect, a gratuitous bloody particle effect, and maybe some dismemberment.
Enemies seem to go down with a reasonable amount of punishment. So far I've been playing single-player on normal difficulty and I haven't felt like the combat was getting tedious.
Like others have said the game is pretty Borderlands-y, except it isn't terrible with how it handles loot and progression. Instead of throwing out obselete guns every twenty minutes, you amass a collection of weapons over the course of the game which you never get rid of. You upgrade your character and weapons with progressively better trinkets and doodads which you find in chests and enemies. If you decide you want to use the starting pistol in a later mission you just equip it with the latest and greatest upgrades, and viola, it's up to date.
You find new upgrades all the time, maybe even too often. If you stop to inspect and equip everything you find, you'll probably drive yourself to madness. I finally decided to go through my upgrades between missions. They don't make a ton of difference by themselves. Plus 5% movement speed, +8% fire damage, -10% reload time, stuff like that, though some of them make more drastic changes, like dual-weilding or exploding ammo. They were pretty generous with the drop rate for rare items (unlike ♥♥♥♥ing Borderlands), and higher difficulties apparently increase the drop rate further.
The levels are randomly generated, but the hand-crafted parts they're built from seem pretty large. Levels are sprawling and non-linear, with plenty of space to go off the mission path and explore.
The character models are pretty ugly for the most part, and textures are kinda average, but the game is gorgeous in motion. Striking color pallete and indulgent use of particle effects really make it. I'm running the game maxed out on a GTX 970 + Intel i5 4690k, and I get about 90-100 fps. I've seen a couple minor issues, like flickering shadows and small objects, and I climbed up a ledge into a wall once, but I haven't experienced any major bugs or frame drops.

If you cut down a 80Ft tree you will only get one Log to split into boards. The current way skills go up is entirely angering as if I didn't turn up the multiplier after 4 hours of play I would of spent the 12 hours just being able to have the skillset in order to cut boards out of logs by slowly taking bark from trees one pain-staking piece at a time.

I ran out of cookies and so far after 12 tries on each skill I can neither gather any wild plants nor gather any berries. I have also tried my luck at fishing and after 18 tries caught nothing. An entire wood billet burns in the campfire in about 20 seconds, so in order to have one constant fire you will need a forest to supply it.

A few items/weapons add some spice to gameplay but collectibles for the most part are just items for steady strength building. I was really hoping for some "secret" or amazing things to find, but there really isn't.
Boss fights are fun and actually reminiscent of the later 3D Zelda games where you find a weakness, exploit, attack, repeat -- but the design for each is varied and keeps things fresh.

The first Darksiders game has got to be one of my most favorite games of all time...
I enjoyed the game so much- that originally I had it on my Xbox- but decided to buy it again for PC since converting. I had 100% achievements on my Xbox version- and during the time of writing this, am nearing 100% achievements once more for my PC. However, the game does have some faults to it.
Firstly- keyboard controls were rather annoying. I tried to play the game with mouse/keyboard, but (and perhaps this is me personally since I was used to the Xbox controls prior to the PC port anyway) I just had to hook my Xbox controller onto my PC just to play this game. The PC port is good, I have not once dealt with any crashing- sometimes there will be a light flickering texture and shadows are poor quality- but nothing too crazy and certainly no framerate drops. Not a whole lot of options either when it comes to changing the graphics quality- Darksiders 2 offered more options regarding that and even then, the sequel still lacked a lot of graphic options. Overall- decent PC port. They could have improved on it, added more options- but the game is playable and fully functional.
If you couldn't tell from my first paragraph above- I absolutely love this game. Between the story, gameplay, functionality, etc.- this game has had me come back for a fifth playthrough and I still want more. The second Darksiders was rather disappointing for me and never did drag me in quite like it's predecessor did (still trying to force my way through a second playthrough with that one...). As I said before though- despite my clear obession with this game, it does have problems:
A lot of people felt this was a combination of many games. For instance, God of War-like art and violence, Legend of Zelda puzzle elements, and small things such as that. The combat can get dull at times, you have your sword which you are practically button-mashing up until you get a secondary weapon (Scythe or Gauntlet-depends)... and even then you still are button-mashing with a little more varity added to it since there are no "weak" or "strong" attacks.
And there are puzzles in this game- some you will be able to solve without losing a sweat, and others you may just want to pull your hair out on. By no means though- does this compare to Legend of Zelda nor Portal (and similar) puzzle games.... In all honesty, think of it as the watered down puzzle mechanics of those said games. If you play a lot of puzzle games, you are going to fly by with these dungeons. As for those of you who are like me and despise solving things, even you can solve these on your own without looking up the walkthrough videos!
As for the story- it's a revenge quest type of story. You play as War, one of the four horsemen of the Apocalypse. You were tricked by someone/something to start the Apocalypse early... and because you were framed- it's up to you to clear your name and restore your honor through any means necessary. As lame as my summary of the story may sound- it's actually a lot better and more indepth in the game itself. You aren't going to be faced with too many cutscenes in Darksiders, but  the few cutscenes that you do get tell the story well.
Boss battles will keep you on your toes depending on the difficulty you are on though they use the same attack animations constantly. Only a few boss battles make you use your head instead of just going up and hitting them as many times as you can. The bosses while not challenging, can really take a number on your health if you aren't avoiding their attacks.
As for enemies... look I'll be honest with you, they reskin enemies a lot. I noticed even from my very first playthrough years ago- that they were same attack animations and same take down animations, just different skins. Later on, the enemies depsite being reskinned- will block more and it takes more hits to kill them while their attacks are also more powerful. But overall- a skeleton warrior's animation from the very beginning of the game will be the same animations used in a ghost warrior's (Don't know the proper names of these enemies, sorry :/) animation towards the end of the game. I think they could have done a lot better with enemies and they should have added more variety- but regardless, combat is fun- but will get boring after awhile.
There are a ton of collectables in this game: Runes, Life Shards, Wrath Cores, Abyssal Armor pieces, and Fallen Legion Artifactions. Collecting them all while tough- can be very beneficial to you towards the end (and if you care for achievements, that as well!), especially on hard difficulty. Abyssal Armor and Life Shards/cores will give you more hit points, Wrath Cores will allow you to use your powers more often (which can be a major life savor), Runes can power up your weapons (Such as one rune will provide you with more damage, while the other will allow you to detect objects on a map, and so forth), and Fallen Legion Artifacts can give you a ton of souls/currency to buy health, wrath, or combat moves with.
I personally enjoy this game much more than the sequel. It does have it's flaws, but somehow- this game has made me come back for more where other games are lucky if I even look at them again after beating them. I would recommend this game if you enjoy the RPG genre, and don't mind a bit of button-mashing. This combat in this game isn't the best, but it's not awful either- it does feel like it drags on at times but regardless, this game is overall very well made. The PC port lacks a bunch of options, but no frame rate issues and no crashing I have experienced (I have ran this both on an Intel and AMD PC).

Fantastic game. Fast-paced, fun, requires skill, accuracy, a bit of thought, quick reflexes, and the ability to actually move around properly.
Dodge, wall-jump, and double-jump mechanics allow you to combine these in any order. They allow you to move quickly and be all over the place, making yourself hard to hit, and allow you to get across the map faster.
There are a multitude of weapons to be picked up off of the map, all of which are unique and have their own special functions, and alternate firing modes.
Hundreds of maps, most with great art-style, environments, geographical design, and music.
Being a game from 2004, the game still looks fantastic (better than many games today, unsurprisingly), and has a multitude of great bonus features.
-Press F11 and the game opens a built-in in-game music player that allows you to play any of your own, or in-game songs, instead of what the current map is playing.
-In the audio options, there is a feature that enables built-in text-to-speech for the chat and IRC areas of the game, that way you don't miss a word as your head spins on a swivel, while you are caught up in the fast-paced shooting and battles, with no time to read.
There's a ton of game modes, Deathmatch, Bombing Run, Double Domination, Assault, Team Deathmatch, Capture the Flag, Vehicle Capture the Flag, Onslaught, and many others.
Get the game, play against bots (start off on just below masterful, trust me. Just BELOW Masfterful), and have some fun. Instant action and campaign, once you find a decent community, play some online. Do NOT play sniper camping, zark (especially), or ballistic weapons mods exclusively (24/7, or primarily). Also do NOT play DM-Rankin all the time.
SUPPORT the servers that don't suck balls and have ACTUAL map rotation!

I'm reluctantly recommending this game to Civil War fans. The overall experience is a phenomenal one, with remarkable immersion via strategy and AI tactics but I feel it's all weighed down by the price tag and lack of future content.
I should preface this review by saying that it will be mostly negative as it pertains to the business model and future of the series, rather than the gameplay itself. I feel the gameplay speaks for itself and you'll see that when/if you partake.
That said, I cannot comment on multiplayer as I have zero interest in it. I've invested thousands of hours into Civil War Generals 2 over the years and the content just hasn't dried up. For Ultimate General: Gettysburg, the current content becomes redundant, predictable and stale in a matter of weeks; at least it did for me. The game encompasses a three day battle but there are only so many ways to battle it out on the fields of Gettysburg. Either you're cautious or you're not. Either you're a Union commander or you choose the Confederacy.
At $15, the price tag is ridiculous. By comparison, I purchased The Witcher 2 a few days ago for a few dollars and the amount of content I still have to dig through is staggering. A $15 price tag is better suited for an MMO subscription, not for a one-off title with no clearly defined future. Disappointingly enough, any rumored content releases (or DLC) will have a price tag as well and likely be sold as an individual title. To me, I find this disrespectful to those who purchased this game in hopes of a bright future in a niche market. UGG has never cracked the top-99 most played games on Steam and it's not likely to. Whether that speaks to the price or the content, I can't say but I'd wager it's likely a combination of the two.
If you have the $15 to spend whimsically and want a bit of nostalgia, ala Sid Meier's Gettysburg (this engine is quite derivative), then I can confidently recommend this game. Just don't expect the same level of excitement a few weeks from now unless participating in multiplayer battles that are frequently rendered moot after adjustments to mechanics are made in the never-ending battle to balance the game for a war that was never balanced to begin with.
If you're looking to buy a game with meaningful content that will last you a few months with no desire to purchase a new game, then I strongly recommend that you steer clear of this and just go nab yourself a copy of Civil War Generals 2 (which still manages just fine on Windows 8.1).

Sniper Elite V2 (SEV2) follows very closely in its older brother's steps and then one-ups him by doing a fancy dance at the end. This is a francise that is very good at conveying bullet physics to glorify the art of sniping which is the bread and butter of this game. From the controlled breathing to the bullet-time kills with faithfully simulated WW2 rifles, SEV2 could be mistaken as simply a graphical upgrade to its predecessor. Even the AI seems to have migrated over intact and flawed in a very "Nothing else matters YOU WILL DIE" Terminator kind of way.
But just as you get comfortable with the old ways, Rebellion steps it up a notch: a cohesive (if sparsely scripted) narrative, an x-ray mode that further baits the kill-fetishists in a manner similar to the latest Mortal Kombat outing (exploding testicles anyone?), the opportunity to assassinate Hitler, Steam achievements, and...
...multiplayer which is where SEV2 really shines: Deathmatch? Wham. Horde mode with co-op? Bam. Single player campaign adjusted for co-op with more enemies for you and a Steam friend to annihilate together? Thank you ma'am! The co-op mode together with voice-comms really creates the tension of working together whilst creating fun sense of light competition for higher kill tallies. I particularly love Overwatch mode which is a fantastic combination of teamwork and a division of specialised labour which more co-op games need.
It's just a darned sight shame that the AI, which is a core dependancy for this game to work, is "simplistic", to put it politely! This is a great game that just misses the mark by lacking some necessary polish and punch to make this a bullseye title. SEV2 is still a worthy game to catch in the next Steam sale.

A very tentative "Would recommend", but with caveats!
I debated whether to buy this game during a recent Steam promotion and the deciding factor was a recommendation with the comment "If you loved Sid Meir's Gettysbury, you'll love this" - well being as I was actually having a quick look on Steam to see if Sid Meir's version was here I dived in, only to be disappointed.
Pros:
* Beautiful map
* Easy to use control system, I like the click and drag for route selection
Cons:
* Lack of ability to provide granular enough commands, (need company level)
* Lack of ability to control formation, (line, Double line, Skirmish, Column)
* Graphic image of the troops doesn't appear to be entirely in sync with their actual location, line can be facing one  direction but when you try to reposition the controls imply its facing the direction you wanted in the first place.
* Artillery can't be instructed to concentrate on other artillery / troops.
Also in the time I played the much trumpeted AI wasn't apparent, the enemy did some odd things that made my victory so much easier, it never once surprised me.
Based on the patch notes I'm under the impression that they are still working on this game, so I still have hopes that the problems will be rectified in later version, I'll keep my eye on it and any future titles.
On the whole I would say, if you are looking for a simple and quick strategy game then jump in, the price is right with this one. But if you are looking for an updated version of Sid Meir's Gettysburg then this is not for you.
Heading back to Sid Meir's version on my Win 98 virtual machine, I would honestly recommend that the developers do the same and then update this with the features we have in a game 20 years older.

So after more than 100 hours in game, I can finally make my review:
This game is very unique (in my opinion) to the other games. This game MAY be blocky as minecraft, but the textures are detailed, and pretty, with out them being blocks. They do have blocky hit box, but hitboxes aren't that important ;). So beck to the topic. You can build BIG mining operations, and factories, and what not, on pretty much anything. Because of the worlds size that is 200 LIGHT YEARS (or 1892146155423912000 meters !) long in every direction from spawn, you can build what ever. It's kind of hard and challenging to start up, but when you get a bit automated, you are all good (and challenges are fun, right?).
Now lets talk about mining. You get an ore extractor, that mines ore veins. Each ore vein is different in size. Some can be up to 32 mil. ore!. That is going to last a very long while. But to do that you need to send power down, and then with conveyors, pipes, ore matter movers, up to the surface and smelt it.
Goal in this game (right now) is to kill 4 overminds, with orbital strike. Now there is at least 100h of gameplay. But this is not like factorio (I still love Factorio tho), that you win, and not play anymore. If you win here, you can still do stuff! But if you kill them, nothing will attack you (for now)
Now about updates and performance. Well, updates are often, and also you have different "betas" to play on, like Bleeding Edge. That is game where is new stuff, that will be put into mainline. But this comes at the risk. You can crash, your world can get corrupted, and bugs. Well, that is why its called "Bleeding" edge ;). Preformance is pretty decent. Give this guy your money. It's like a cross between Factorio and Minecraft like others have said, a couple key features that really stand out though. First is the fact I'm pretty sure there's no limit to how deep you can dig. Gameplay zones right now go as deep as what, 1000 blocks or something? A minecraft map is 128 blocks from the tip top of the ceiling to the very bottom of bedrock, with only around 60-80 of those being actual land blocks and not empty space. In Fortresscraft, you keep digging down to progress further in the game, and right now I think the last zone is around 1000 blocks or so with plans to develop layers even deeper than that.
Second is the uh, the holoview or whatever, where you hit a button and you can see all your constructions through walls. So when you're digging around and trying to get all your power lines to match up underground, you don't have to count blocks. You just hit a button and bam, everything is visible. It's truly amazing. Also yes, there's elevators.
If you have any interest in this kind of thing whatsoever, give this man your money. Even in its current state you'll have a blast messing around with stuff, and future plans to develop it into a full PVP base-versus-base type game have already been stated, so seriously, give this guy your money. If development ever makes it that far, this will be one of the greatest games ever made. It's already extremely well optimized and well put together as-is. Absolutely worth the asking price.

Pros:

Cons:
(-) "Game" started with extremely loud music, but settings have no audio controls whatsoever
(-) Wasn't able to run it without fullscreen.
(-) Can not choose type of tree to start with
(-) No tutorial, no background information, nothing - not even credits.
(-) Horrendous user interface. Why do you need two buttons which only toggle each other ? Clicked on the "water" icon while it was already selected, therefore the "scissord" button was automatically selected, and instead of growing the tree. I cut it at its base irrevocably.
