While still in the development stage, FC Evolved still provides a plethora of things to keep you occupied while build and advancing your way through the technology tree.
I would like to see some more in the way of building materials but with the games heavy focus on the tech and the logistics of collecting resources, I am not sure we will see much improvement on that front.  That is not to say that building is a wasted effort.  With a little bit of creativity and ingenuity you can create some pretty impressing structures and fortresses.
The method of researching new tech through discovery and a later stage Research Laboratory was a welcome change to other methods I have seen leveraged.  I cannot wait to see what awaits for Tier 4 and beyond.
The survival mode GUI is still a bit rudimentary but it has been promised by the developers that it will see improvement by the time the game is finished.  A hopper GUI is a much anticipated addition.
All said and done, FC Evolved is an immensely immersive game that will provide hours of frustration and enjoyment as you work to gain new tech and build the most epic of fortresses all while trying to fend of the attacks of the local population.
I will continue to play and look forward to the further development of the game and happily purchase any and all DLC and Expansion packs to support the amazing work done by the developers.

Could pretty much be the one game I've been waiting for my whole life. It's got everything you'd want from a cooperative mmo.. Although there's one BIG downside: The singleplayer has the same restrictions as multiplayer. Now I will cut them some slack, as they are working on fixing this issue.
What exactly am I talking about? Well, the game focus heavily on teamwork and each individual focusing on one major task, and to fulfill tasks by working together. The whole concept is brilliant, and it works! But for the single player, you're supposed to be able to lift this "skill cap" that only lets you focus on one major skill at a time, to allow you to play the game freely (since you're all alone, hence -single-player).
The game ruleset has a skill cap at 600 for multiplayer, and in singleplayer you're supposed to have full freedom (3000), but at the moment this feature is -NOT- working. But as I said, it's in the works and hopefully released sooner than later.
Other than that, I can only say this game has soooo much potential.. I don't envy the dev's having full control over this "baby", because a lot of people are relying on them not f'ing it up :P I just hope they make the right calls, and don't screw it up... Cause this pearl of a game could be something immensely huge!
Pro's:
-Pretty good graphics and atmosphere
-Extreme depth of skills and crafting
-Feels very down to earth and realisticly themed
-Condones teamwork and condemns kill-on-sight mentality (and executes it well)
-Gives long stretch goals which feel rewarding
-Quality of items which have an impact on crafts and stats
-Amazing music!
Con's:
-At times, can feel very gray and depressing (fog etc). Add some more colors!! :D
-Very laggy and non-responsive server list that critically needs work - FIXED
-Clunky animations both on players and animal interactions (most likely placeholders)
-Crashes at times, especially when using the push-to-talk in-game feature
-When leaving a server, you actually leave the whole game (add a log-out feature to menu?!)
-Depending on server ruleset (skill multiplier) tasks can get very repetative and drawn out
-Lack of explanation (F1 has some info). Would like more tool-tips when mouse-over
-Inventory is pretty nice, but can get frustrating when trying to stack items (Add white border on items when mouse-over them perhaps?)
-Quite a few bugs
Overall feels very early alpha'ish, BUT this does not ruin my experience of the game. It can only get better. Easily a 10/10 if the skillcap-lift was working as intended.. Til then, it's a 7/10.

The Realm may be Dead but the fun lives on.

Dead Realm is esentially gang-up Hide and Seek. One player plays as the Ghost and has to catch and "Reap" the survivors. When reaped, the survivors become spirits and join the ghost's team. The Ghosts must eliminate all the survivors before the time runs out.
Positives:

This game takes good parts the previous Shadow Warrior, and mixes it with the semi-open world highly similar to Borderlands. It does have 70 different weapons, all the weapons are unique, there are no reskins or same stat weapons. Unlike Shadow Warrior 1, this game changes the weapon upgrade system so that enemies drop stat boosting items and you can equip up to three onto each weapon. There are a few damage types (like Borderlands), like Fire (damage over time), Cold/Ice (slow effect also freeze), Toxic (less damage, but there's a chance when poisoned foe dies that their corpse explodes; spreading the poison), and Shock (does less damage than fire, but can eletrocute: paralysed). There are your common enemies, the superior enemies, which are bigger than their common counterparts and tend to have significant stat boosts, and your elite enemies, which have elemental affiliations, are huge compaired to the common variants, and are very good at getting up close and tearing up your s***.
Devs are looking very good right now. Within 9 days they released a patch even touching on rebalance amongst the slew of bug fixes. They are also talking about free updates, and are fairly interative with the community.
It looks really damn good. I run all setting on high on a 1920x1080 monitor using a gtx760. It's damn fine.
The combat is much faster paced, especially when you're on the higher difficulties. You can double jump, dash, and sprint, without it affecting you at all. You have 2(eventually3) main bars, Health and Chi. Chi allows you to heal and use things like knock enemies back or turn invisible temporarily (do note that there is no real stealth in this game). You'll find yourself dashing around, trying to avoid the elites that heep getting in your face, and double jumping to search for the huge amounts of secrets and loot that litters the maps. This game has secret passageways, sneakily hidden doors, and things hidden in plain sight. There's a whole new batch of fortune cookies with great satire written on them, and enemies drop journal entries which provide a big amount of backstory and side information about the game's characters.
The game used randomly generated maps for the levels. It is not perfect random generation by any means. Some sublocations that are generated are guaranteed to have secret located there. You'll start to recognise locations that were in one mission that manage to appear in your current location. By the time you get to this point, you'll be close to the end of the game, so it isn't something to worry about.
You get to be a scitzophrenic again. It's somewhat similar dialogue to that of Hoji from the last game.
The game is also littered with easter eggs and references to other things. For example, the double barrel shotgun " The Stick of Doom" is held on the middle of the screen, just like the super shotgun from the old Dooms.In Smith's display room, there's a very phallic sword on one of the stands...
TL:DR it's pretty good, Devs are good, Shadow Warrior meets Borderlands with high paced combat.

As a series, Total War has almost carved out its own sub-genre within the RTS genre. Each game effectively combines the depth of a grand strategy game, with the more direct strategic warfare of a real-time strategy game.
The original Medieval and Shogun games were well received and popular, but Rome took the series to another level. The visuals saw a significant upgrade from the previous title, and in my opinion they still hold up pretty well even today.
Perhaps the most revolutionary change in Rome: Total war is the era it is set in. Set during the expansion of the Roman Republic, there is a fantastic amount of variety in terms of factions. You start with the ability to play as one of three different Roman factions based on powerful patrician families, and you unlock new factions to play as by defeating them completely and removing them from the map. Personally, I don't like the separation of Rome into three different factions and would have preferred one faction, it feels like you are forced to expand into a particular direction; however this can be fixed by simply playing one of the mods that have a single Roman faction. As I said though, the variety provided by the factions is great. For example: the Romans focus on organisation and their poweful heavy infantry, but have to keep the senate and the other Roman families in mind; the Greeks have excellent phalanx infantry and skirmishers, but are vulnerable due to being spread out across the map; and the Parthians have their deadly combination of horse archers and cataphracts, but have limited expansion options due to being positioned at the eastern edge of the map. To contrast, Medieval II for example doesn't have this level of diversity simply because the fighting styles during that era were much more similar across the continent.
The battles are extremely satisfying; as has come to be expected of the Total War series, though balancing between units is definitely an issue that seems to be persistent in the series. The campaign map gameplay has fantastic depth, so much so that you can often play for hours without having a battle and still be satisfied. The game's soundtrack is excellent; possibly the best in the series, and it really adds to the intensity of the battles.
Though the vanilla game is amazing, the wealth of mods available to this game make it even better in various ways. There are a number of large scale total conversion mods but I have found that if you want the ultimate Rome: Total War experience you have two choices: Europa Barbarorum, or Roma Sur♥♥♥♥♥♥ II. Europa Barbarorum focuses on making sure everything is as authentic and historically accurate as possible,especially the barbarian factions that are somewhat neglected in the vanilla game. The campaign map is considerably larger, going as far south as southern Arabia, and as far east as India, and the roster of factions is extensive. However, the insane level of depth can be intimidating for some players. On the other hand, Roma Sur♥♥♥♥♥♥ II occupies the middle ground between the vanilla game and Europa Barbarorum. Whereas Europa Barbarorum pays particular attention to the barbarians, Roma Sur♥♥♥♥♥♥ focuses on fleshing out Rome itself. The mod adds a new system that adds a variety of Roman legions that each have a unique look and feel to them, and this really adds to the authenticity of the mod. There are plenty of new factions, and all the factions look and feel very unique. Roma Sur♥♥♥♥♥♥ II also looks much, much nicer, as the graphics have been improved a great deal on both the campaign map and battle maps; it looks about as good as Medieval II: Total War. Roma Sur♥♥♥♥♥♥ is only silghtly more complex than the vanilla game too, so it shouldn't be as intimidating as Europa Barbarorum. I wouldn't normally talk too much about mods in a review, but I honestly think that the optimal way to play this game is through one of these mods, as they improve almost everything.
Even without modifications, Rome: Total War is a phenomenal game. If you enjoy real-time strategies but want a bit more depth to the strategy then this game should be just what you are looking for.

Excellent mini-wargame made by the creator of DarthMod. I've only completed a single campaign against the Balanced AI, but I enjoyed it immensely. It reminds me of the old Close Combat games, in all the best ways, only more grand scale.
I love that the campaign follows different engagements throughout the entire battle, forming a narrative that teaches the player about the actual battle. The US Civil War was one of the last wars where line battles were still the order of battle, and this game represents them very well, with fluid battle lines and artillery breaking formations up.
The AI is very good, able to respond to your movement and fire, all while finding ways to exploit weaknesses in your line. The rules of the game (reload times, morale, stamina) are basic and make sense.
I like the simple, but effective art style. It has lots of personality and detail, while having very low system requirements. The units perhaps could use a few more frames of animation, but that's unimportant in the end as it's only eye candy.
My main complaint would be the difficulty of determining terrain height, which is helped by using the elevation toggle button. I only learned about it after I had already completed the campaign. I suppose it's a necessary feature with any 2D engine, so I don't see it being a big drawback.
Overall, I highly recommend UG:Gettysburg to all wargame fans, and to anyone who is tired of the terrible AI Total War games have gotten over the past few releases. This is the work of the Nick "DarthMod" Thomadis after all, who fixed so many of CA's  broken releases. I'm glad to see his game is as great as it is. I'm looking forward to the Antietam sequel!

It's fantastic. Plain and simple. It's like someone played MineCraft and thought, "Well, this is pretty fun. What else can it do?" So they dug through mods and found Technic. Then they played that for a bit and thought, "This, too, is pretty fun. But it wasn't really made for this...I bet I could make something like this, but better." And so they did.
Starting out can be rough, depending on your world. I tried a couple before I found one I was happy with. It will take time.The game is heavily based around automation, so you can continue to dig deeper and find new things, then automate those new things to get it all back to your base. At first, you will have to babysit things. You simply don't have the resources to get things rolling on their own for the first hour, maybe two. Watch a couple of videos on it. You'll see how others do things, you'll get a good understanding of the basics, and you'll have some ideas as to how to set your own system up. It takes a lot of time to really get a lot going on, but if building up to that isn't your cup of tea, then I might advise a different game type. There are several more mechanics at play here than in MineCraft, and pretty much any other game in this vein. It takes a lot of the concepts explored in Space Engineers, removes space, and instead focuses on mining materials and setting them up to work for you.
Never played anything else quite like it. As of this writing, the devs have moved to a new engine and made several quality of life improvements. There are more updates coming, and the community that I've interacted with is outstanding. This is a prime example of an early access game taking full advantage of what gamers can bring to a development cycle.

Trials Fusion is the latest installment in what has generally been a game that offers a simple premise but provides a lot of gameplay punch.  While there aspects of Fusion that I am greatly impressed with, there are a few things that I am unhappy with.
For those unfamiliar, the Trials games are a very simple premise. You're riding a motorbike (along with other vehicles in Fusion) across a large variety of tracks with physics being the ultimate gameplay component. You have to control the bike properly or you will wipe out.....A LOT!
I've broken this into a simple pros/cons list for anyone that has tl;dr issues :-)
Pros:
+ Looks fantastic. The colors are rich and have real pop to them. If you can play this in Ultra at the highest resolution you're in for a treat, even at lower resolutions it still is great eye candy
+ Base game course design is interesting for the most part and the futuristic setting adds more than I thought it would.
+ Trick/FX gameplay styles really add to the depth and encourage playing tracks multiple times with both fastest times and trick scores being seperate goals.
+ A ton of community made tracks at your fingertips.
Cons:
- Pricey DLC with the season pass costing the same price as the base game making MSRP for both base and season pass (a.k.a. Deluxe Edition) just $20 less than a AAA title. There have been two DLC packs released thus far with more to come.
- Some base game courses are much shorter than you'd expect.
- Lacks the challenge at the lower levels that earlier Trials titles brought. Seems watered down for casuals/newcomers in respects. The physics are still brutal depending on course, but definitely easier to get the hang of. ATVs are disgustingly easy.
-  Four months after release and online multiplayer is still not in the game, yet is promised by the developer. This is UNACCEPTABLE when being advertised as having multiplayer especially at the cost of the full package. Local multiplayer only at the moment (8/23/14 is the date of this review).
- Tedious unlocking system.
- There seems to be some measure of a "story" mode to the single player game where you're regularly spoken to by a female AI similar to GlaDOS of the Portal games, except the Trials AI lady lacks the wit of that classic character and is generally just grating.
Let me be clear, while my cons are glaring, I do not regret my purchase of this game. I have a real soft spot for this series and have gotten a lot of mileage out of the earlier titles and am going to continue to play this one as it plays well and I can't overstate how great it looks. I was first introduced to Trials when it came out on Xbox 360 Arcade and I put well over 100 hours into that iteration of the game. I hesitated on this new one until I upgraded my hardware and now that I have, I am very glad I waited at least until then.  That being said, unless you are like me and a fan of the Trials series and know what you're getting into, do yourself a favor and hold off until this is on sale.
I recommend this with a caveat. Definitely pick it up when on sale, but unless you're really into the series/gameplay style, you're fine waiting.

Well... This will be complicated.
First off, full disclosure: I recieved this game from the Dev after expressing my doubts and disbelief on the forums. The topic can be found here:
And on to the review itself...
Fortresscraft is something I have difficulty playing objectively. I snagged the original back when I was a gamer on the Xbox 360 before switching to PC, and I was not impressed. It was a 'Minecraft clone', in the sense that it was blocky and HD and there was not much value in it other than blowing up the water and watching the broken physics for it cause it to spread across the entire world, but only after you had reloaded the level.
Upon seeing this title on Steam, I was, understandably, not impressed. So, after downloading the Dev-given game and booting it up, I found a few things out.
First, the game has some derps and issues. The tutorial can be confusing and derped at times, leaving you with little idea of what to do. I have heard there's a wiki up at this point, but there was not one when I started.
You enter with little idea of how to do things, which can honestly be great. I've played Dwarf Fortress with less. Still, however, it's not a great introduction.
Further on, I can see hints that this is something that I might enjoy and thrive in if I could only
, for lack of a better word. It's not that the game is complex, it's that I just can't figure out where to go, after a bit. So many things that would really improve things for me are either missing, or I am not finding them.
I know, and I can see, that this is really a good game, especially where it came from. I did have a bit of fun, and the mechanics are mostly solid, but I just couldn't get very far.
Overall, the reason this is 'recommended' is because, in the end, I know it's a good game. It just isn't my type of game. I'll stick with my complex RTS addiction for my fix.
In numbers: 6/10. Above average, at least. Steam really needs a 'mixed' review setting.

Life Is Feudal is a hardcore sandbox MMO('ish) game with great potential. You'll be able to build villages, farms, castles, craft armor and weapons. And not to mention - kill people with those crafted weapons. There's an arsenal of weapons waiting to be crafted, both ranged and melee, but not all of them are implemented yet.
The game is still in alpha but you can already get a feeling of what the released game will become. It can sort of be described as a mix between Wurm Online in gameplay, and Rust with it's graphics. There's a couple crucial bugs at this point (for example the server browser freeze) and the servers go down alot, but once you get on a server and start playing there's hardly any bugs bothering you - which is pretty impressive for a alpha build these days.
One thing that's important to mention though, is that this is not really a singleplayer/solo game, you would want to gather your friends or join someone else in-game when you set out to build those small, big and gigantic settlements. And you and your friends will need alot of patience in the process of building your land and skills. The world is available for you to shape and form as you like, but like the real world it's going to take lots of time to shape it.
I would definetly recommend buying the game for the sandbox fans out there, but there's no rush in doing so. I would guess the most crucial bugs are getting fixed pretty soon though, and when they do Life Is Feudal will bring you tons of hours of fun even in it's alpha stage.

I want to start off with the good parts of this game. I played the previous Trials games on the console and I was hoping that I could continue the series on PC. To an extent, I did. The gameplay was as I remember, i.e., incredibly addicting and rewarding. If you were to compare stills of this game to the previous games, you could tell it looks incredibly better. But after I got past the introductory phase, I started realising how annoying logging into Uplay was. I also ran into frame rate problems. I'm not implying that I'm running a powerful system (my graphics card being a Radeon HD 7870), but compared to the smooth 60 fps I can maintain on medium settings in Metro: Last Light and Bioshock Infinity, I found the 40 fps and often 20 fps on low settings to be COMPLETELY absurd. I'm quite offended that the developers put less care to the PC version but I suppose it's my fault for assuming otherwise from Ubisoft. Although I do enjoy playing the game on occasion, I cannot recommend it to anyone without a more powerful system. The low fps is more than nauseating as usual but actually disruptive in the gameplay. Please play the demo, which I'm very grateful is provided, before thinking of purchasing it; something I was too anxious to do.

Old Review:
I'm giving this game a "thumbs up" for now, based on what the game *could be*, not on what it currently *is*.
This is my game.  And by this, I don't mean that this is a game made for me, or a game I "like".  I mean this is literally a game that I designed from the ground up.
Let me explain.
I'm a wanna-be game developer that's had a game design formulating in my head since Ultima Online came out.  The basic premise of my game would be heavily influenced by Ultima Online (such as it's skill systems, resource systems, even the inventory system, and the ability to loot people you kill).  However, it would also be a game completely "built" by the players.  You'd basically drop them into a world that was empty, and it would be up to the players to build their houses, communities, cities, etc.  To that end, it would also need a robust resource collection and mining system (not unlike minecraft).
So this was my game.
Well, someone beat me to it.  My wife and I just stared slack-jawed at this game, at how precisely it was exactly the game I had always talked about making.  I'm not accusing the developers of "stealing" my idea at all.  It's just that clearly great minds think a lot alike.  So clearly, this is a game I want very, very, very much to play, and enjoy.
Unfortunately, the game is still currently in an early alpha state.  The fighting mechanics are fairly broken, and you can crash a server by doing some simple in-game tasks, such as using a sling.  But I say again, it's in early alpha.
This game has the potential to be THE game I've always wanted to make/play, so for that reason I'll give it the tentative "recommended" with the assumption that the developers will get all of these quirks worked out as the development continues.

ROME TOTAL WAR AND ROME BARBARIAN INVASION ARE NOT THE SAME THING!!!
That being said. RTW is one of the best strategy games ever. I loved it for many reasons. Large armies, good, fun battles, espionage aspect, and finally at some point all there is left is other big civs that you have to fight. It makes for a great time.
I would like to add that i am a big total war fan. I know how to run the economy, use agents, win battles, plainly, I know how to manage my faction.
Now we come to BARBARIAN INVASION.
This is a great game in its own right. Personally I do not consider it an expansion because it is so different. It is similar but not the same as vanilla rome. Different time period factions, units, but also a different play style is needed. It was not designed as a conquer the world type like vanilla Rome was.
Keep in mind that I know how to play total war. My opinion is not that it is bad, it's just that it is not for me. Vanilla Rome had a long campaign setting for 50 provinces need for victory. In B.I. most have an 18 province requirement.
The odds are stacked against you. It is not too hard to beat I just found that it was too much a chore to enjoy. I play games for fun which is different for everyone. I tried many factions. My last on was the Saxons. I tried to see it through thinking that once I got enough cities I could have those big armies  I wanted. I had 10 provinces. I clawed my way up to this point. I still could not......
get a lot of money,
get massive armies,
stop having to gruel my way through the campaign.
In short BI is a good game with a good challenge. I m just saying if you like vanilla Rome then I suggest you get  Barbarian Invasion demo before making your decision.

15 years. One and a half long decades. That is how long the world waited for a true sequel to Duke Nukem 3D. Stuck in the longest ever known development hell, switching engines multiple times, and winning a crapton of vaporware awards, Duke Nukem Forever seemed destined to never see the light of day. But see the light of day it did, thanks to the combined efforts of Triptych Games and Gearbox Software!
Triptych Games was founded when 3DRealms closed it's doors back in 2009, and they worked out of their own homes for no pay to make DNF what it is today. Then in 2010, Gearbox Software bought the franchise, hired on Triptych, and helped them polish their work, resulting in the badass beast we know today.
The Duke Nukem series has always been known for it's balls-out irreverent sense of humor, and DNF continues that fine tradition of debauchery with gusto. The traditional Duke charm is firmly imbedded in the game's design, managing to give fans a good laugh along the way and in the process completely offending those who don't get Duke's particularly awesome brand of humor.
The gameplay is a melting pot of what's best about classic FPS games, and the best of their contemporary counterparts. Gone are random medkits and stimpacks, now we have a regenerating EGO bar that represents Duke's Dukeness. Let it drop to nothing, and he might not be able to shrug off that next bullet. Dive behind cover and rest a moment and you'll be back in action in quick order. Or you can take the manly route and use an execution move on an enemy, this instantly refills Duke's ego bar.
The signature interaction introduced by Duke Nukem 3D is back in force, with pool tables, pinball machines, weight benches, arcade games, air hockey, and more ready to entertain those who want to take a break from the carnage and just mess around.
Most items give you a permanent EGO boost the first time you use them, to try and mess around with anything and everything. You can even recreate the infamous microwave scene from Maniac Mansion.
Dukes signature arsenal is back in former glory, and this is where the Xbox 360 version takes a bit of a sidestep from the PC counterpart, on PC they patched in the ability to carry four weapons at once, but on the console as of this writing you can still only carry two. Still, the game is amazingly balanced, with plenty of guns lying around to take your pick from. During boss fights you can usually find an ammo crate to keep the rockets flying, so don't be afraid to use your firepower.
Multiplayer returns big time in DNF, with Dukematch, Team Dukematch, Capture the Babe (capture the flag, but easier on the eyes) and Hail to The King. A diverse array of maps are included, based on locations seen in the campaign. My personal favorite is Duke Burger, which sees the players shrink down to action-figure size, and let loose in the kitchen of the iconic fast-food joint. Earning EXP in multiplayer earns you new items to decorate your personal penthouse, and completing challenges gives you new shirts and hats to customize your Duke.
Duke Nukem Forever may not be the greatest game of all time, but despite some long loading times on the Xbox 360 version it stands tall and proud in representation of the Duke franchise, and in my humble opinion it should be played by fans and newcomers to the series alike, as it finally brings closure to the most epically insane development saga in the history of gaming. Modern shooter design has evolved such that the headshot is the most desired action. Game after game, we are conditioned to aim for the head  thanks to the unique animations and sounds that result. But in this game, headshots are just the beginning.
On the surface, Sniper Elite V2 seems like yet another brown WW2 shooter. Every level is "bombed out European city" and you're America's answer to Golgo 13, casually blowing up tanks, trucks, and rockets with well-placed rifle fire. But the kill cam makes all the difference. With most killshots, you get a dramatic slow motion shot of the bullet traveling and killing its target. An X-Ray shot lets you see exactly which bones and vital organs are obliterated. Now, you've incentive to aim not just for the brain, but the heart. The lungs. The testes.
THIS NEVER GETS OLD. EVER.
You can adjust enemy AI and ballistic modeling to suit your tastes. Don't want the videogame-y HUD assistance? Turn it off. Want to have to adjust aim for distance? How about wind? The option's there. You can sneak if you want too, being mindful of sound and enemy line of sight as you hide bodies, cause distractions, and use a crappy silenced pistol. But there is zero penalty for neglecting to use stealth, and eventually you HAVE to fight. By all means, go...ballistic. This isn't Hitman. You have to get spotted. That's why you can and should set traps for when the Nazis and the Reds come a-runnin'. You can't set off your own mines, but you can get hurt when they do explode.
The fact that you're given points for each kill encourages you to just shoot everybody you see. Incapacitate a guy in the open to draw his friends out to save him. Then put one shot through both of them. BONUS POINTS. You actually get the fewest points for sneaking up behind someone and melee killing them. Co-op play is supported through the entire campaign (albeit with fewer X-Ray shots), and there's special co-op multiplayer as well. Versus multiplayer...eh, it's a game about camping and sniping. Don't bother with that.
The Metacritic score is wrong. The reviewers are wrong. This game is a goddamned TRIUMPH, and every level is highly replayable. The DLC's pretty good too, especially its infamous "Kill Hitler" mission. No co-op on those, sadly.

If you love FPS games and want to try something different than CoD, Battlefields etc, Arma is probably something you'll want to check out.
Yes, it has a steep learning curve.
Yes, there's a lot of bindings.
Yes, your mad CS:GO headshot skills will be useful & recognized, but won't be enough.
Yes, arma physic can be wonky af at times and standing on a rock might kill you.
Yes, you might encounter hackers, trolls, angry kids & baked russian players.
Yes, spacing IS important.
And oh yes, you'll die a lot without seeing anything.
At first.
Then you learn. Then the fun begins.
Then you know your whereabouts, and know how to communicate efficiently with your teammates.
Then you become able to locate and identify a threat. Just with the sound of a gunshot in the distance.
Then you know how to use terrain to your advantage efficiently.
Then you learn why each stance is useful, why roles are important in a squad, how each weapon, each scope, each piece of equipment can be used.
Then you start playing with vehicles too. All kinds of awesome vehicles (you'll probably die a lot again in the process)
Then you discover the endless possibilities offered by a glorious modding community. Or become part of it.
Then... you're close to 800h in the game, and still can't get enough of it.

The game conists primarily of talking to an NPC which gives you a problem which you have to go back two screens and talk to someone else to solve.

The shepherd tells you that you can get a cable car a bit further on which will bring you back to town, basically going around the goat. En route you run into a marmot who asks you to help tidy up the rubbish in the area, which results in a minigame. So you have to go back a few screens talk to the maramot to get the glasses to give to the eagle so you can finally ride the cablecar down and get a picture...
A better game in the genre would have had your uncle give you the painting for helping him, and the maramot give you the glasses for helping her.

Further on in the game you have to collect carabiners. Whilst there is a picture of them, so the task is completable for those who don't know, an explanation as to what they are isn't given until after the task is completed...

Highly, Highly recommended game especially if you enjoyed modded minecraft and/or Factorio.  Why?  Becauase this takes the best of both of them and puts it into a really nice game. Since my last review on march, 2015 it would take too long to list all the items that were added.  Even since the first paid expansion, Frozen Factory, was released it would take too long to list all the things that were added to the base game for NO ADDITIONAL CHARGE.   This is free content that doesn't even require the DLC that was released after the DLC.  The entire tutorial system has been changed, a new robotics system is being worked on, induction chargers ect.  Just to give a little idea of how much the game has changed, there has been 14 content patches since my review(16 since exiting early access) each giving new quality of life features, new machines, new mechanics along with a major expansion.  Each patch has a public beta that updates every day or every few days with balance changes, bug fixes, ect.
It is a game that can take as little or as long as you like.  On the easiest settings a 50 hour game is possible.  on the hardest settings alone, you are probably looking more to 200-400 hours even more with the expansion.
It's a game where you can design things as simply or as complex as you like.  You can for the most part play it however you like.  Don't want to setup complex automation, it's possible to do everything without using some of the advanced stuff.  Might not be as efficient but still possible.
Without a doubt if you like automating stuff, if you like to add some base defense to that automation, and if you like the thrill of going up a 400m mineshaft using a grappling hook at high speeds this is the game for you.  It's a game where in the 50-200h of playing you can always find something to do!

Let's start by saying that this game is still being heavily developed despite being out of early access.   Some of the newer stuff doesn't have icons but besides that the game is basically 100% completable in what constitutes a pretty decent end-game that can take 50-100+ hours to get to, with additional difficulty settings for pretty good replayability.
The game does a good job of combining a minecraft style sandbox with tower defense.  It takes some of the slow and annoying parts of minecraft and removes it and gives the player a lot of tools to assist them with common tasks such as building.  building 50 blocks in a straight line in survival mode is very convienent, not to mention no wait on breaking a block and protection mode from breaking multiblocks.  The grappling hook is quite fun to use and makes grappling up a verticle mining tunnel a lot of fun.  On my 4 year old computer the game runs smoothly even with a lot of stuff going on.
Overall when buying this game remember some developers wait until they have everything that they can possibly do to the game done with before exiting early access, this allows them to make excuses for whatever bugs are in the game.  This developer has done a great job at leaving early access and releasing a very stable main build along with a constantly updated bleeding edge build.  The game might not be as complete as some other games that have exited early access, but it is stable, there is a lot of fun things to do, and my biggest complaint about the game is that $12 is just way too cheap.  I would of gladly paid $20-$30 for it possibly $40

Bonsai is a simple tree growing and pruning branches simulator. Like Viridi it's also a longtime investing idle game with not many options. But what does it have to do with bonsai? AFAIK no Bonsai master has ever used a chainsaw to prune armthick branches. This unrealistic game works like growing your tree to the max with intense watering and then prune endlessy regrowing branches. After 100 GCs the stem and branches got thicker than you can cut off with any scissors. So to speak a logical disappointment. Though the fractal branch generation and the typical tree characteristics look quite neat you wonder why this game is not educating you more about the Japanese philosophy. What about perfection through reduction? Cutting down growlings and leaves to force a tree into a bonsai shape. It could be more fascinating to generate miniature trees than normal trees. And to cutoff 6k branches as a master goal wouldn't be neccessary anymore. Pity what a missed chance ...

This little gem caught my eye about a year ago, when it was in early access. I decided back then to let it mature before buying it. As such I was excited to see it was out of early access and the full release was out.
As another voxel based survival game this one seperates itself from the pack by focusing more or automation and refinement, matched really only by Factorio (but in 3D!!!). It looks great, at first glance, until I bought the game and played it...
It played smooth. REAL smooth, in that it was between 150 and 200 FPS. There is an option in the Settings menu to change that, but it didn't do anything. No change whatsoever. So you try restarting the game, and there is still no difference. Now that is a pretty basic thing to set up, so why it doesn't function is beyond me (again, in a full title out of early access). It hogged all my computers resources to keep up with that rediculous update speed. But ow well, let's play on!
So you start in a tutorial setting, protected from outside influences by a forcefield, which lifts when the tutorial is done. Awesome! The tutorial is short but informative, so even after restarting hundreds of games I can't see much of a speedbump there, and it's practical...Until the shield lifts and a giant spider robot walks over your base, its feet several blocks away from its legs (assuming said legs aren't jerking over it's head).
At this point I noticed the text at the bottom right of the screen saying Development Build...Okay, probably started a Beta through Steam???...uhm...no...the game is still in beta...and the spider is supposed to be some kind of boss enemy to be encountered later in the game, which was left at the players spawn probably to debug / test.
Why do I have a Development Build for a game that has been out for 5 / 6 months and without running a Beta?
This game is not done, and it is out of early access. I concider that seriously disrespectfull towards the customer and a violation of my consumer rights. I don't mind buying a product that isn't finished, as long as you're honest about that and don't play morally and legally questionable games.
In 10 years of Steam patronage I have never ask for a refund, and to be honest I thought Age Of Survival warranted it, but at least they are honest about the game not being done yet...
EDIT: People don't seem to understand, so to make a bit more clear: I liked this game, I really did, but there is no excuse for selling a game that isn't finished, that is still a 'Developer Build'. The moment we as consumers accept that as 'okay' we collectively accept blatant disregard for our consumer rights and those rights will disappear.
Steam has agreed with my complaint by refunding my payment, so at least I know I'm not entirely wrong by fighting this...

Apparently I'm in the minority by saying that I honestly enjoyed this game. Bonsai, contrary to what many people think, is the Japanese art form of cultivating and pruning miniature trees grown within small containers; it is NOT a specific type of tree. And this game is exactly that.
You start out with a tiny sapling on a square of grass, and either a day or night sky background depending on the time you play. You can water your sapling to speed up its growth and it will steadily grow into one of five types of tree: each with its own species appropriate bark, leaf shapes, and leaf colour. As it grows branches and twigs, you use the scissors to trim it into whatever shapes you wish. Trimming and shaping the tree's growth is supposed to be calming and contemplative. I found it to be rather relaxing.

The spell system is very creative.  You can combine different modifiers that custom alter your spells, but many times applying the alterations creates completely different spells altogether.
The game allows you to quickly switch between three different outfits with the touch of a button.  I didn't think I would like this at first, but it allows me to play warrior, mage, and archer/sneak as the situation allows.  I have specialized gear for all three roles and it actually works.
It has really creative quests without being the go and fetch variety.  When the rare occasion of running errands arises, the story line has a compelling reason and makes you want to do it.
If you like old-school, dark, un-mapping (as in you need graph paper) dungeons, there is  a unique challenge in chapter one that lets you try your hand at it.  It is not necessary for the story line, so that is optional.
I'm a huge fan of Morrowind, Oblivion, and Skyrim.  It's no Elder Scrolls, but I would give it a 90/100.
Whatever bugs existed at release have been smoothed out for the Steam version and the game hasn't given me a single problem for over 70 hours of play.
And it is huge!  I am in the middle of the second chapter with much left to go.  I am a person that does every little quest, so I figure I have about 100 hours left in this thing.
I have no idea why I never heard of this game and don't hear people talking about it.

I went out on a limb getting this game and do not regret it at all. It's as if minecraft and Skyrim were mushed in to one incredible sandbox experience. I could take quite a while extolling the virtues of the game but I'll break it down to pro's vs cons.
Pros:
-Totally sandbox. You can do practically anything given the proper skills.
-No "levelling" in the traditional sense. Your skills accrue as you use them, just like Elder Scrolls or Mount and Blade.
-(opinion) Mounta and blade style combat system. If you don't know what I'm talking about, check it out, it's really cool.
-Friendly community. With few exceptions I have not seen nor experienced greifing by other players, and everybody if pretty helpful when possible (not any "experienced" players yet, since the game is in development still)
-The crafting and building system is very intuitive, but there are some guidelines built in so you know what you need to get to make stuff.
-There's a huge variety of things to do and make in the game, despite it being in early stages, you won't get bored.
Con's
-The server screen is fairly buggy, and takes a while to get situated, so be patient with it.
-It can be hard on graphics, but with a game like this that is par for the course.
-(this can go the other way for some) The learning curve can get pretty crazy, and there aren't many guides out there. But doesn't that just make getting things right more rewarding? Once you get the hang of things it will go much more smoothly
-Fairly regular crashes. Just today I had three crashes and a few server time-outs, that's going to happen a bit as many servers are privately run. Of course, my internet is not the most stable, either.
-No single player. This game is larger than one person is supposed to deal with, anyway. If you want to be on your own, you're gonna have some problems. but you can try if you want.
Overall, this game has 10/10 potential but currently rests around an 8.

NOTE: This is a long, detailed review. Longness may occur past this point.
I had never played a Trials game before, but was familiar with the series, so I bought Fusion before the Summer Sale ended. I figured I'd be playing it a lot over the summer and as a general timewaster, so I bought the Season Pass with it, for a total of $30.
Honestly, I feel like I've wasted my money buying this game.
Having never played any other Trials games, I have nothing to compare the gameplay of Fusion against. I do know that it has no online multiplayer, which is a major disappointment. Looking through other reviews, I can see that the game is apparently lacking in other places (lack of tracks, buggy trick system, etc.), but again, I have nothing to compare it against, so I can't verify these claims. In my 2 hours of playing, the core gameplay has been solid. However, it's been mostly unenjoyable, which brings me to my first major quip with this game:
I started up my game to my rider rising up an elevator in the first tutorial level. It was going pretty slowly, maybe for dramatic effect. And then the slowness carried on through the level. and the next one after that. What was the problem behind this?
The result? If you run it at 40 FPS, every 3 real-life seconds becomes 2 seconds in-game. 30 FPS? Your game runs at half-speed. 20 FPS? A minute-long tracks now takes 3 minutes to complete.
And don't you worry, they thought of that one supercomputer that can run the game at 90 FPS, so the game caps at 60 FPS so it doesn't run away.
All in all, after crippling the resolution, video settings, and everything else, the game ran at an average of 45 FPS for me, where it started off at 15. My GPU may not be the greatest in the world (AMD Radeon HD 7640G), but it gets the job done for every other game I've played at decently high settings. Trials Fusion at its lowest possible settings
brings my GPU to its knees.
A little backstory here. I bought Burnout Paradise during the 2013 Summer Sale. Upon launching, EA promted me to make on Origin account, which I did. They didn't bug me any further, and from then on, Burnout launched through Steam and my Origin log-in was confirmed after launching.
So why is it that Trials Fusion requires you to install uPlay, and that launching Trials from Steam
If I only had to make a uPlay account to play (like with Burnout!), it would be fine. But why do I need a
game-launcher just to accomplish the task of launching my game, Ubisoft? So launching Trials Fusion is clumsy and weird because it requires installing uPlay, which seems bad enough. For me, however, it was the start of my problems.
A couple of days after installing TF, Flash videos stopped working, which required me to disable hardware acceleration to fix. Whatever, Flash is buggy anyway. And then weird black bars appeared near the top of the window when I was watching a Twitch stream. OK, maybe something is wrong here, so I'll run an antivirus scan. My computer crashed mid-scan, and then I got my first blue screen the next day. The day after that the most ominous thing of all happened. I was watching a video when it flipped to another screen that said, "You can activate your operating system under the Settings tab." I went back to the video, and minimized my screen to reveal that I could now see my OS and build in the lower-right hand corner of my desktop. At that point, I went to System Restore and got uPlay the hell out of my computer. It's been about a month since the restore, and to date, nothing nearly as spooky as the aforementioned things has happened again.
You may notice next to the thumbs-down that I have 2 hours logged playing this game. This is due to a combination of the problems mentioned above. In my short time playing Trials Fusion, the gameplay wasn't that good for me, because it didn't run at full-speed. I can imagine it would be a great game if the damn thing would run correctly and stop being so picky. Ubisoft has done a decent job patching their errors, adding things like "better" optimization and custom Supercross tracks. Until they fix the bigger things though, I can't say anything good about this game. In conclusion...
-Only get this game if you're absolutely confident in your computer's specs, ESPECIALLY GPU
-Don't expect online play anytime soon (because the poor slow-motion guy would be left behind...)
-uPlay is a piece of crap
-If your computer fights back after installing uPlay, you should listen to it

I've seen the praise this game got, and I've read through many of the glowing reviews it received here on Steam. I bought it when it went on sale, and tried it out. After testing out its gameplay, I had to stop and think, "Did I buy a different game than what others played?"
If you remember Sid Meier's Gettysburg or Antietam, this is basically the same system: moving units around and engaging in pitched battles against the enemy. The similarities made me laugh at the professional reviews that called this game unique and creative - it's basically those two past games, but with updated graphics and a slightly different combat system. As is obvious by the title, this takes place at the Battle of Gettysburg, and like the Sid Meier's Gettysburg game, you play various stages of the battle, depending on how well (or poorly) you do. However, unlike the Sid Meier games, which used to suck up my entire day due to awesome gameplay, my frustrations with this game led me several times to rage quit to the menu after a few minutes of gameplay, and eventually just uninstall it from my computer.
One thing that annoyed me was just how quickly your men will retreat. Seriously. I think a few minutes of a firefight and even the Iron Brigade are crapping their pants and running. What's even more annoying is how your artillery will automatically retreat if the enemy gets too close - and I mean like still close enough that the cannister fire would be effective. I tried everything to get my artillery to at least wait a little longer, but they would just up and run, even with their morale still pretty decent. Remember how Mercer fired at the French cavalry until the last minute at the Battle of Waterloo? Apparently if there's an Ultimate General: Waterloo, Mercer will see the French at 800 yards and think, "Well, boys, that's it. Let's go home."
I also am not certain how the casualty system works. While I know artillery at this time had become really advanced and was one reason for the consistently high casualties in Civil War battles, artillery seems a tad overpowered in this game. Sometimes my men will be taking from artillery fire at a non-stop rate - it literally looks like their number is decreasing like a New Year's Eve countdown. Movement is likewise annoying: walking seems to be taking your sweet time, while running is take your sweet time with a slightly faster footstep. It doesn't help that sometimes when you tell your artillery to move, they'll seemingly waddle around aimlessly at a location, or will set up their artillery JUST BEFORE the spot you told them to go (this is especially annoying when you try to work with their line of sight). Another game mechanic that was annoying was the "Auto" function for artillery. It seemed to just stay on solid no matter how close an enemy unit was - after a while I just gave up on "Auto" and manually controlled all my artillery.
Overall, this game was just a disappointment. I tried playing the Union and the Confederates, I tried looking up the manual to see how to better play the game better. I tried playing different styles. The same frustrations came up over and over again, and finally I just gave up. It's rare that I quit this early on a game, but this was one of the rare cases.
Total War at its best. Such a beautiful memories.

At the time of this review I have put about six hours into the game.
When I picked my first server I started facing the beach, the sea was beautiful and the land surrounding me felt realistic and rugged. As I turned around a man was standing before me holding an axe. I backed off him and he spoke to me, he asked me to leave his camp as he did not trust strangers near his territory. I kindly agreed to give him distance and moved about my way.
Not long after I met up with two other strangers who were looking for a place to settle. They were kind and friendly and we scoured the land for the perfect place to build our home. Once we found our ideal location we shaped the earth for hours, sowed the lands with crops and build our homes togeather. Three people, with no history of knowing each other dividing the labor of the land equally. It was a beautiful and magical friendship that was formed.
As night approached we built a campfire and lit it. We all stood around in envy of the beautiful flames and as we stared at eachother in awe of our accomplishments thats when the server crashed and kicked all of us off the game. I was never able to find these players again and honestly I am really dissapointed to lose such great companions.
Do I think this game is worth $40? Yes, as long as you realize that this game is VERY buggy. The crashes happen often and it takes forever to load. I also found that pushing buttons in certain combinations will result in a crash.
Despite all this, this game has amazing potential. It nothing like DayZ where you will get PK on sight. While I ran into a few sticky situations with other playesr I managed to fend them off or successful run away from my attackers. I found that a majority of players are willing to work with you rather than just kill you for all of your loot.
I really cant wait until this game works out its glitches. Because when it finially does, I feel that it would be the perfect middle age simulator for anyone to enjoy.

Rome: Total War is certainly one of my favourite games of all time. Don't let my small hour count fool you, I had this game on disc for years, I'd estimate around 400-500 hours all up.

Learning to balance and manage economy, diplomacy and military all those years ago was both challenging and rewarding, from the tentative first steps expanding an empire to later rapid expansionism all while trying to keep the populace under control. There is a lot of content and detail, but not too much to feel oversaturated. The core concept is simple, become the dominant empire and rule the world!
You start the game with just the three Roman factions unlocked. In order to unlock more factions you had to either defeat that faction in a campaign or by completing a campaign you would unlock all the playable factions. This added a massive amount of replayability tot he game, as many of the factions of different cultures function quite differently, especially the barbarian factions when compared to the more 'advanced' factions like the Romans or Greeks. One of the few features to actually annoy me was the small total number of factions, for example all of the Greek cities (Sparta, Athens etc) are all lumped together an one faction, but I imagine there would have been limitations in the engine back then. It was a decade ago after all.
There is so much content and I haven't even mentioned the Barbarian Invasion (BI) expansion yet, which is included within this game. BI is set towards the fall of the Roman world, at the time when the Empire is split into East and West. BI introduced religion, adding further depth to campaign play, as well as more advanced barbarian factions, hordes, the mighty Sassanids and Huns, and the ultra hard mode which is playing as the Western Roman Empire.
Summary:
Pros:
- Hit the sweet spot for detail
-Rewarding gameplay
-Replayability
-Diverse factions
-Barbarian Invasion
-Nostalgia!!!!
Cons:
-Limited number of factions
-Visuals are dated now in 2016 (still great back in '06)
Final Verdict:
9/10

+ Setting is great (Who doesn't love Rome?)

Cons:
- Burden of knowledge is huge. Expect to be confused if you're new to the genre, but stick with it
- Consequently, the tutorial is also very long. Be prepared to set aside an hour or so to get through it
- Can sometimes be difficult to find information on the game's mechanics (e.g. "How does the culture penalty work?")
- I have had a few instances where the game will crash after I end a turn. Disabling the AI via console commands (disable_ai and run_ai) fixes this temporarily, but it means the armies on the map do not move or attack, taking all the fun out of the game.
Altogether a very solid purchase, good entry title into strategy games. Would definitely recommend.

Not a bad game really.  Some of the voice work sounds like it was phoned in, or like they approached the actor and said "just try to sound huge and scary".  Much of the story actually feels tangled up in itself until the end.  This is usually okay if a game gives it to you in a way that makes you sort of guess or deduct what is going to happen and be surprised or pleased when you find out, but this game just sort of splashes it around in random cutscenes with short lived characters and you end up just waiting for someone to tell you what the heck is going on instead.  My last real complaint is that the game is especially easy.  If you play hack'n'slash to any degree, go ahead and crank this one up a notch or you will just breeze on through most anything that it puts in your way.  Even the last boss.
All that being said, the combat is fun when you get the hang of it, which doesn't take long.  It has a sort of zelda quality to it in the form of: getting to a dungeon, getting a new item to help you get through said dungeon, then use the item to beat the boss and go collect treasure from the rest of the world that you couldn't get to before.  I like this style of game if it gives you good stuff to look forward to, and this game did.  While the story was not peiced together well, it was still interesting all the same.  And even though the game was simple, it was fun and was just long enough to not outstay it's welcome.  Heck, I might even go back and get some of the cool stuff that I missed before just to see how OP you can really get!
All in all, I liked it.   It was easy, and at times generic, but it maintained a status of "I want to see this through to the end" for it's entire playthrough.  Give it a shot on a sale price, and when you are in a bit of a gaming lull and I think you will find something to like about it.

Shadow Warrior 2 is exactly the sequel that the 2013 game deserved. I was a big fan of it and hopped on board the hype train and soon as I saw the trailer.
Combat feels fluid, fast-paced, and brutal with both swords and guns. The addition of various types of guns allows for a lot of experimentation to find what kind of combinations of upgrades you like for each gun (charge-up shotgun and dual revolvers for me). Right now I'm playing on hard difficulty and it feels like a great challenge that rewards you for playing well. The sword combat has changed some from the prequel with regular swings no longer being directional based on movement and the removal of the stronger hit with right clicking. However right clicking with one of the asdf keys now uses one of your moves (stab, vortex, etc) and feels just as good to pull of in combination with your other moves.
The procedural generation of missions makes the level feel different and more fun to explore each time you revisit it. After a while you'll begin to notice certain landmarks, but the overall layout varies pretty dramatically in my experience.
The game runs great so far and I've had little trouble in terms of frames or game-breaking bugs. However I have experienced some bugs where the character's dialogue keeps repeating the first word of their lines and a cutscene or two where a character doesn't appear.
I'm about at about 50% completion and this game is worth so much more than the pricetag. Definitely recommend for the Wang.

This is not a terrible game by any means, but it feels like a definite step back from the previous installment and, by comparison especially, a lousy value proposition.
The tracks are significantly fewer and blander, and that's not balanced out by the new mechanisms.
Doing tricks seems to be based on your angle and the input on the right stick, but it feels pretty sketchy/inconsistent. The stages built around doing those tricks for points are too unforgiving: the checkpointing means you only get one shot at each jump trick, so any failed attempt means you've lost a potential 20% or so points for that stage. Maybe losing your multiplier would have been enough of a deterrent; as it stands, falling is too easy and too costly, so it makes sense to play it safe -- and that's boring, especially for a mode that's supposed to be a bit more crazy than the precision driving at the core of the franchise. Uniracers did it first and better, basically.
'Challenges' are either Easter eggs hard to figure out without a guide, or require feats like finishing with zero fault while doing 10 tricks or never letting go of the gas pedal. That's one way to stretch playtime over a small number of tracks...
Tournaments are one thing that's improved, though: they're time-limited and renewed every few hours, which is a good encouragement to participate and try to rank high.
Now that the first piece of DLC (out of a planned 6) is out, it's obvious that we can't count on them to fix the fundamental problem of there not being enough content: each will be the size of a world, so 6 regular tracks and 2 gimmicky ones (and the first pack is boring like the rest, too).
Are RedLynx / Ubi counting on player-created content to pick up the slack? Trying to find really good content is still a crapshoot though -- you can only rely on the 'featured' categories, very basic filters, or a percentage of positive reviews. There's quite a few enjoyable enough tracks, some with clever moments, but few if any are comparable in quality to the dev-made tracks from Trials Evolution, and you have to be in the mood to rummage around for them.
It pains me to say it, but this is a disappointment. Just get Trials Evolution, and don't get Fusion until you've played so much Evo you're sick of it. And even then, be aware it's not great value at full price.

A long time ago, a game called Sid Meier's Gettysburg! did much of what this game offered. Simple controls, flexible AI and multiplayer ability to relieve (or change) the multi-day battle of the American Civil War. This game has a very similar feel to it, and all the better, as the map looks very nice and the battles/scenarios play pretty well.
My favorite part of the game is, should you decide to fight the entire battle, the game keeps track of you and your enemies casualties, allowing the battle to progress differently depending on how well or poorly you did. You may be getting all the key objective initially as the Confederates the first few days, but if you took a lot of casualties, you'll find yourself struggling to finish off the Union when their entire army gets there. Likewise, giving up too much space as the Union will make it harder for you to hold off the deadly rebel charges. It adds to the replayability of the game. The standalone scenarios also allow for more randomization, and the varying AIs will provide whatever challenge you'd like.
The only negatives I can think of is that you might not be interested in just playing this battle in spite of the different factors. But for its current price, it's an excellent Civil War game, and a pretty decent entry in the strategy genre.

I have played this game as it has been continuously updated, and each time I am blown away by the amount of work that the developers put into Shovel Knight.
The core game with Shovel Knight is a blast, with challenge that is tempered by checkpoints that you can use, OR you can destroy them for currency. You get to choose how punishing death is. The level design, the hidden areas, the quick pace, it all adds up to a great game.
Months later, they release a new character, which is practically a new GAME. The mechanics, items, and story takes the core game and forces you to play it in a much different (but still fun) way. Plague Knight trades a short-range shovel for bombs that have an excellent span of usefulness and custimization. THIS game is also a blast.
Today I see that my game updated. What I am greeted with is YET ANOTHER GAME. I have a new character available that (again) has new mechanics, new items, and a new story. The opening was brilliantly designed to teach the new mechanics, and it's not long before you're deep into a save file because you're having too much fun.
Kudos to the game developers, and thanks for continuing to support this game with fresh content!

We have an expression in Australia that means the same thing as the ‘F’ word. It’s called to root. Therefore to have been f***ed is to have been rooted. After playing Rooted Concepts’ Bonsai for  a short period of time (an entire 82 minutes) that’s exactly how I and my poor computer (which was an upper echelon computer when purchased new back in July) feel. The game is a complete resource hog for absolutely no excusable reason and what is present isn’t much of a game whatsoever. This, my dear readers, makes Bonsai the plant version of the infamous Bad Rats and a game that will be given as a prank gift for years to come.
It’s as much a game as watching grass growing is a spectator sport. Seriously. In order for your plant to grow you wait extended periods of time – you’re best alt-tabbing out during that time and doing something else – and then when it’s grown enough you can then snip the parts that you don’t want. But it’s the waiting that is annoying and the fact that every time it grows it takes up yet more resources. If your tree grows enough the amount of resources that are consumed becomes ridiculous and will slow your game down to a grinding halt. It’s a very bizarre combination of poor design and programming choices.
If I were to find two things that are redeeming and positive about the game then the first are the cheap achievements. Start a new game and if you get a type of plant that you haven’t grown before you receive an achievement. The other is that the game does have the potential to be a soothing experience. That is if you have China’s supercomputer to run the program on due to the game being a resource hog.
Unfortunately, I cannot recommend Bonsai to anyone due to the problems with the programming. It’s just a poorly programmed and designed game that shouldn’t have been released in its current state. Had the title been released in the Early Access programs the issues may have been overlooked because it is clear that they need a lot of work and that’s what that program in part signifies. However, it’s not and I can’t see the problems with the coding or the design choices changing nearly as much as is necessary for the game to reach recommended status.

I purchased this game primarily to play with my son as he's a big Minecraft fan and it was appealing to him.
Multiplayer, at least "out of the box" did not work for us.  Computers would not connect and always generated a "connection timed out" and UPNP needs to be enabled or port 27012 forwarded statement within the game.  Sadly, there is no option of just clicking on your steam friends name and sending an invite.
I ended up spending over 3 hours troubleshooting this error to finally give up in frustration and decided to refund this.   UPNP was enabled on both PC's.  Port 27012 was forwarded in the router and added to the firewall exemptions. I even went as far as to drop all the firewalls and see if that would allow the games to communicate. It did not.
In this day and age UPNP enabled on both PC's should just work. It doesn't with this game, or at least, doesn't with me.
Throw me in the "computers for dummies crowd" or whatever, but I can say with complete confidence that many titles on Steam and elsewhere have a very smooth multiplayer connection system that works with a few clicks of the mouse. This does not.
When I spend more time troubleshooting a games systems than playing the game, it's time for me to move on.
In summary, right now the multiplayer connection system for this title  is archaic at best. It feels and looks like something I'd play in a Early Access game.
I suppose it could be a good game, and I'd love to revisit this title once they clean up their attempt at multiplayer connectivity.

put factorio and starforge in minecraft, and you get this game. Obnoxiously large world, vast, HUGE expances of caves, like Hang Son Doong big. Think it's just night because you can't see the cieling big. Recreate Dwarven cities big. This game revitalized that sence of wonder, being overwhelmed, and exploration that the first time I played minecraft did. Those that like Minecraft, and are a little done playing modpack after modpack and geeting burned out on it should DEFINENTLY play this game. and come on, it's only $13 (on 2/15/2016), why WOULDN'T you get this game?
I must say though, that if your computer is a toaster, it'll get frustrating with the game turning into a slide-show. This game isn't exactly friendly on your ram or proccessing capabilities, but you can drop the detail and graphics WAY down and still have a good time, it'll just look like it was done on the N64. But, normally this game is gorgeous, provided you have the computer to handle it.
For those of you who are experienced in minecraft (particularly tech mods) you'll discover that you will be making LOTS of controll based mistakes. Also, you'll have a decent understanding of tech progression, however, it is dificult to know ahead of time what you need to do. I would recomend that you play a few worlds to better understand what to do, and what way you prefer the most to do it. Your first few worlds are likely to fail in your eyes, this is fine, and fixable at just about any time, but you can always start fresh.
I would like to see a more comprehensive creative mode, as it does not lend to helping you actually mess around with logistical ideas, and what not, which I would like to see. currently, if you have an idea to use a system, you have to just try it out, which makes experimentation a potentially costly endeavour.
The short version is that this game is amazing, and any fan of starforge, minecraft, and/or factorio should most deffinently fork over the cash and get this game. it's not even all that much cash in the first place.

It's Trials.
In spite of requiring Uplay to run, and regardless of what you think of Ubisoft as a publisher, it's still Trials. That alone is enough for me to recommend it.
Aside from the future motif, what's new from previous games is a trick system with some freestyle events to go along with it. I found the system to be really finicky, and most of the time I just skipped the FMX events in favor of the standard trials events. Also, they added a quadbike along with its own separate tier of events, which I enjoyed riding. It's 4WD and heavier than the RWD bikes we're used to.
Also, apart from the usual replayability from the medals and leaderboards, there are also different challenges for each trials track. Some of them are skill-based (e.g. flipping, riding without leaning, etc.), some involve manipulating the environment, and some are just funny or gimmicky. However, many of them are quite difficult to figure out, and the squirrels from Evolution return as well. Also making a return is the track editor, which allows you to create, share, and ride user-made tracks.
And then if you feel like enough of a badass, there are the ninja stages, which just make me want to cry...

This game started out rather fun, despite having little content. The developers slowly updated to include more maps and characters as well as game types. It seemed like it would be a great investment to make if you have a small group of friends to play with, or if you don't mind playing online (as it did have a voice chat feature).
Unfortunately, several months back the game was updated and wound up breaking the game in various ways. Servers slowly emptied out since nobody was having an enjoyable experience. The developers posted 3 months ago saying they would have "significant updates... very soon" due to player feedback.
They have done absolutely nothing and the servers are a wasteland now. This game became another cautionary story of why Early Access is such a risk. Yes, you pay for the product with an understanding that the game is unfinished. However, you also pay for it with a general understanding that the game will eventually be polished and be ready for a full release.
Dead Realm should serve as a good reminder to anyone who considers investing in Early Access games.
That's not to say all Early Access titles are bad (Killing Floor 2 has done an amazing job of updating and maintaining transparancy. Dead by Daylight is working on the same thing, though at a slower pace. The Forest was a great title right from launch, etc etc).
Just don't bother investing in this until you see an update from the devs and responses fom those of us unforunate enough to have invested in it already.

The single player is rather fun though, even if it does show how dated it already is. If you are to pick this game up, you really need to pretend that it came out back in 2009, or maybe even earlier if you want to give the game considerable leeway.
Try this game when it becomes a bargain bin title, as some concepts like the shrunken Duke sections are really neato, but in reality, the game becomes rather defunct once you've beaten the game.
Don't even bother with the multiplayer as dedicated servers haven't even been working since launch, which shows enough how much they cared about it.

I just bought this game during the flash sale for the sole reason of recommending it. Unfortunately, I have the 2004 original DVD version added to my account so I couldn't write a recommendation.
This is the game that shaped my initial PC multiplayer gaming experience. I've logged about 4000-5000 hours (just an estimate) in the last decade. If it wasn't for this game, I probably would have discovered PC gaming much later than I initially did.
Moving on to the official recommendation: the single player is very simple, but holds an interesting enough story for its time. The graphics are dated, yes, but honestly I think the game still looks very aesthetically pleasing. There is a general play mode called "Instant Action" where you can choose your gamemode, and play! This includes classics like deathmatch, capture-the-flag, and newer gametypes such as Bombing Run, vCTF and more. All of which are very, very fun.
The multiplayer community was thriving from between the initial release of this game all the way up to about 1-2 years ago. The community is still somewhat active and there is a good 20 active servers out there with different gametypes to play. There are also several mods that you can download. The modding community within this game is still somewhat active, too. The UDK is also a great tool for learning to map.
I still play this game everyday, and have done since 2004 when I was only 11 years old. It is very cheap right now (and offers trading cards, so badge collectors, it's worth the buy alone for that).
This is my all-time favourite game, and if you decide to purchase it, I'll introduce you to what's left of the very tight-knit community.

A technically complete game that is still being worked on, it's easy to dismiss this as a "Minecraft Clone" due to the voxel based game world. But there are aspects of FortressCraft Evolved that blow Minecraft right out of the water (and I really like Minecraft).
For one, the world size. It's massive. I have found cave systems that could contain the build height limit of Minecraft, and then some. I have tunneled straight down and have so far gone well past 7,000 meters below the surface level, while Minecraft goes from 0 to a comparatively limited 255.
As for the gameplay itself, it can be very technical. You have to build a logistics and mining network to defend your base from attacks, generate power, and be very careful not to feed any near by hive minds.
In terms of how long you are playing? Well... I'll admit I'm probably not the best player, but so far I've put in 112 hours and haven't reached the "End Game" as of yet.
