'Bonsai' is a good idea in theory, but it's developer (and publisher) Rooted Concepts has put very little effort into it, not to mention doesn't quite know what the concept of a "bonsai plant" is or what one looks like. This title immediately comes off like the most basic of Unity clicker assets, the kind you see accompanying 'Clicker Heroes' knock-offs on various mobile stores, crossed with 'Viridi' except with a price tag and none of that free title's charm. What's worse is the Steam community voted for this dreck to be on the Steam marketplace.
Yes, ninety-nine cents US doesn't seem like much until you start playing what you just bought, or what someone gave you as a gag gift because "You like♥♥♥♥♥♥ make a let's play out of this!" and you'll feel bad if you don't. A small patch of land with a sometimes ribbed-for-her-pleasure♥♥♥♥♥♥♥looking tree that only grows, leans and throbs when the game is running is all you get. The options are sparse as well, and all you can do to the tree is prune it. After two hours I found my mighty Oak finally bloomed, and upon pruning nipped the tip and had to start from scratch. When I did this, however, I was eventually greeted with magical floating leaves with no branches to prune, as shown in the above video.
This title's also a surprising resource hog that needs a sturdy computer to run. An i7 is required, but for what exactly? The branches! Yes, whenever they show, there's so many you can choose from to trim and rid yourself of the obvious clip art leaves that seem to grow in at all the wrong angles need strength to go from one highlighted spot to the net. Of course they have an obvious base background color around them, leading me to suspect yet more google images copy and paste tactics like 'The Slaughtering Grounds' was guilty of. The music is also severely out of place and sounds like a cheap knock-off of Train's "Hey, Soul Sister" at time, but done with a ukulele and xylophone instead. It made me want to smoke up and chill at a beach barbecue more than relax and trim my "bonsai" tree. A simple Youtube audio library search and I found a royalty free classical piece that better suits the whole purpose of the game, and didn't cleash with the obvious 'Vivardi' knock-off visuals and core concept, so you can't say finding a similar piece out there on the internet was impossible given the power of Google these days.
Further more, there's three save spots, and (feel free to correct me if I'm wrong) no way to choose which tree to grow. It just happens. Again, nothing grows when the game is running, so you either need a good rig like I do to play something else while it grows (I put another hour into 'Victor Vran', personally), or just walk away for a bit and hope the appendages of the tree don't cause your computer to crash or go up in smoke. Seriously, 'My Name is Mayo' probably could run on an old 486, but this sit-back-and-do-nothing-but-watch-a-digital-tree-grow simulation game, the Steam equivilent of the USB Pet Rock, needs a core-i7 and NVIDIA GeForce GTX 660 card minimum? It all just seems like bad programing to me, really. Perhaps the looped audio made the developer snap before loading it to Steam in the firstplace.
'Bonsai' honestly just looks and feels like bad/lazy programming on every level. There's room to make this a fairly zen experience, or offer elements to make it seem like you're actually nurturing your tree such as weather augmentation controls, laying down mulch or dirt, pulling weeds to make your tiny patch of floating-in-eternal-purgatory land look nice. Hell, even simple customizations like adding a bird house after a certain point would help make it more of an experience, all of which Rooted Concepts completely ignored for what looks like nothing but a quick buck at the expense of the fools who green lit this title, and those looking for a gag gift. Unless you absolutely hate someone or yourself, 'Bonsai' is well worth passing on, especially if you're eyeing this up solely for achievements (they're not worth it, trust me on this).

An incredible magic and item management system, a beautiful, open world, and a roster of interesting characters that inspire empathy are marred to unplayability by bugs, broken DRM, extremely unbalanced mechanics, bad voice acting for the main character and about a third of the interactions, and a blase storyline.
Pros:
--The magic and inventory management is hands-down the best I've seen in an RPG in decades. This alone has kept me investing my hours in this game. Do-it-yourself spells and every item in the game upgradeable and able to be dismantled into the components needed to upgrade anything makes character building a treat.
--Though the character models and textures look like something from 2003, the post-processing is very good, and the world is vast and full of surprises.
--Between dice, grinding, pickpocketing, vendors that buy and sell at different prices, and a DDR-like musical minigame, there's plenty of ways to make money.
--horses, boats, and fast travel - you can get to where you need to go quickly. It's almost too easy...
Cons:
--extra DRM! The Steam release of TW2 did not have the original CD DRM stripped, and the activation server is almost constantly down or unreachable. You will have to call a German number and manually activate it, or find the developer forum and email the head developer to have him manually activate it. This game came out in 2011, not 2001 - this is outright unacceptable, and if not for Steam's no-refunds policy, I would be screaming for a refund. (Glares menacingly at Ubisoft and EA for the same sin)
--Yo Dawg, I heard you like DRM... Used one of the patches before the end of Chapter 1? Uh-oh, you have to re-activate at the end of Chapter 1!
--But not in the
version. Seriously.
--Bugs. Do not upgrade before Chapter 2, every patch breaks locked doors that require using cheats to unlock in Chapter 1. Some quests get bugged horribly, and some vendors never open up after dawn ever again. Save often, you never know what will screw up. Getting bugged through walls and off cliff edges, items skyrocketing because collision detection went insane, items that don't deposit into inventory correctly...ugh.
--Butt-ugly inventory management system. It really is one of the most innovative ever, but damn is it ugly. can't move anything in stacks, have to click an "are you sure" dialogue, meaning selling 30 of something is 60 clicks, what is equipped on a different build is not highlighted in any one build, so accidently dismantling or selling another build's items happens. And Equipped items are not moved to the top or a special area, they stay scattered in inventory.
--Unbalanced gameplay. Sword and board? You can take out most enemies anyways. Fast hits interrupt attacks, meaning slashing quickly disables an opponent. I've taken out things 20 levels higher than me. There's a mod to fix this, but seeing as the enemies and spells are stupendously unbalanced and grinding to meet an opponent between every quest gets tedious, it feels pointless.
--The magic system is utterly broken. The magic system is innovative beyond belief - and that's its downfall. Random objects like anvils, stones, and barrells can be summoned, thrown around by force spells, and the like. But spells that concentrate stones toward a single enemy can one-shot everything. Meanwhile using missile splitting consumes almost the entire mana pool for a tiny fraction of the damage. Hypnotize doesn't work, altars are titanic and can easily wall off the innumerable small hallways in the game (but luckily don't summon for much longer than a minute). A lot of enemies are strong against or immune to most of the weapons and magic you can garner. Just use a mace and fire, because everything else does little to most enemies in the game, there's only a handful resistant to fire, and they fall quickly to a mace. And on top of all of this, until about halfway through the game, just because the player is commonly in the 5 digit money category, magic is expensive as hell. Invest at least enough in strength to use a good club as a mage, because you sure as hell aren't casting or making more than a few dopey spells until the second continent opens up.
--Censorship. Plenty of swearing and violence, but no blood, no nudity, and even though there's a "sex scene", there isn't one - you just see her butt, she and the lead almost kiss, cut to black, wake up the next morning and never see the character again. Anticlimactic (pun intended). Armors can be recolered, so there's a decal system, but no blood. This feels like something from 2003. With The Witcher coming from Europe, I mistakenly thought a German game would be as no-holds-barred. Nope. Those Germans got it rough.
If you want this game, and it does have a few things going for it, get it from GoG - that version has the independent DRM stripped out, and works better to boot. We all learn from mistakes; TopWare and Reality Pump have made some beautiful trees in this game into an ugly forest - let's hope they learned from this walking mistake.

As the only person I know who finished the original Two Worlds game (a notroriously awful game which truly was a chore to get through) I was sceptical about playing Two Worlds 2.  I managed to pick it up cheaply as part of a bundle however and decided I had nothing to lose by giving it a go.
TW2 is not a perfect game by any means but it is a vast improvement upon the first one.  The graphics are absolutely stunning, the dialogue is much better (althought still a bit cringey), the storyline is much easier to follow and the mechanics have really been cleaned up.  I would say the game's environments are one of it's stongest suit, something which even the first game did particularly well with.  With sprawling savannahs, treacherous tropical rainforests, gorgeous beaches and insidious marshes TW2 has one of the most diverse maps I've ever seen in a game.
Other Strong Points
- Crafting system (Being able to constantly upgrade your weapon is something I loved about the first game).
- Range of weaponry (I really do love a game where I can go from a cutlass to a katana to a halberd to a polearm!)
A Few Negatives
- Controls can feel a bit awkward, but still much better than the first game!
- Dialogue is a bit cringey.
- Menus are slightly difficult to navigate, especially the quest log.
Don't feel deterred from playing this if you haven't played the original (I played it and I couldn't tell you what the heck it was about) and it is a solid RPG that is definately worth a go.
In short; not perfect but better than the first one by far.

After two playthroughs as a warrior first and mage second I can say it is MUCH more rewarding to play this game as a mage. The spell system is first class, with the card system allowing you to make your own spells, with almost limitless potential. Add more cards to make it more powerful but cost more mana, add modifier cards that effect the way the spell works, such as a firebolt homing in on the target, splitting into more than one bolt (add more cards get more splits!), add a card that makes it ricochet off the target etc. The feeling you get when you finally get that spell to work that fires a frostbolt that splits, and summons a creature where every split hits. or that heals you when it hits is great. You feel like a mage testing his own spells and crafting exactly what works for you.
Pros to the game for me included: Graphics are still amazing even being almosted 3 years old, the lock picking mini game is enjoyable and requires some skill, and you get a lot of bang for your buck in that the main story is relatively long (1 1/2 playthroughs netted me over 60 hours, mainly just doing the main questline and whatever side quests I happened to bump into). As the game progresses I found all the creatures still gave decent challenges, there was no level of gear or skills I obtained that made me one shot all the mobs. I am sure though, that there is some derivative spell I missed that can do this if you can find it :)
Minor cons for me included the amount of cut scenes and dialogue. You will spend a lot of your time listening to the charactors talk. At higher levels you can also summon a lot of creatures that your charactor doesn't clip through, and when you are not in combat, they crowd around you. I found far to often that I had to stand and wait the 60 secs for them to despawn before I could move as they had boxed me in. I also had a lot of random crashes, mainly during cut scenes, the game would hang and would need to be shut down and restarted.
The major con I have with this game is the final boss fight. Most RPG's, and this one is no different, require you to level, increase skills to take on harder challenges as the game progresses. Imagine my surprise when I discovered all those spells that gave me fuzzy feelings when I finally got them to work were absolutely useless, as you do not fire one spell at the boss. All the potions I had crafted were useless, resistance potions had no effect on the damage I took, damage potions had no effect on the damage I dealt (as you don't cast spells at the boss). Reflect and shield spells I had crafted had no impact on damage taken either. Only the health pots were usable (and I went through a few of them). All the time finding the best gear, upgrading it, adding crystals useless as well. I found this out as I decided to respec to add a lot more health at the expense of damage, but the damage I took was the same, as it appears to be a % of your health.
All in all apart from this, Two Worlds II provides an enjoyable experience, fun spell system, and deep, though not very original story. As it seems to come on sale a fair bit, paying $15, or $7.50 for it is well worth it, but I also think it is worth the time full price.

*Edited review at bottom due to new 1.6 patch*
At first I wasn't sure what to expect.  I've grown up playing various games depicting this era of warfare, ranging from old Comadore 64 games, Amiga 500 games, etc etc.  Most of which focused purely on body count over tactics used, or went more of a goofy style (IE North and South).
This game has quite a bit of focus on 'good ground', something you hear alot if you watch movies/read books on warfare from this era.  While moral/endurance/cover severely effects combat, both ranged and melee... ammo/supply is strangely not an issue.
Battles are in stages, each step is based on a part of each day of the overall engagement.  You get to choose initial combat style (For instance if you are doing well on first day as union, you can decide to try to push rebels away vs hunker down), but the AI likes to severely change the flow of combat.
There are 9 different types of computer AI, each having different types of combat styles, as well as a random option to basically give it a completely unexpected battle.  The AI feels alive, but makes mistakes much like a player would, something I enjoy greatly.
While I would have loved to see supply/ammo be an issue, the game feels like a nice hybrid between a Total War game and something from the History Channel, making for a fun game.
Iron Brigade, how I love thee.
*New review:*
Before the patch I found the confederates quite weak, and while I could win (the AI had it's weaknesses and didn't really push the way it should have) as that side it was obvious which side had the advantage.
But now...
I started up a new match, picked hardest difficulty and ran as the union.  I pulled back and consolidated my forces as usual, expecting the good old boys in grey to uselessly charge my lines.  But yet... they didn't.  I was flanked hard to the north, they took the ridge and put imediate pressure on me. I was both horrified and amazed that suddenly what was an easily predictable opponent now was finding all kinds of holes in my lines.  It was able to counter my army's movements, each step I found myself behind it's plans, making me losing the first battle where usually I won hands down.
I applaud the devs for making a FAR stronger AI, almost so that I found myself horribly unable to fight effectively.  I took severe losses in that first fight, really pressing upon me what that first day must have felt like to the officers in charge, the utter hopelessness in the fight.
Bravo, sirs/madams, bravo.  This is now by far my favorite strategy game.

Let me preface this by stating that I got this game as one of three free games from a thin selection of Radeon rewards after getting a new R9 290. Even considering that, it still feels like a waste.
On their site it was miscategorized as an "action RPG" which in my opinion it is not. It lacks any real RPG elements, and there is no customization to speak of. I also felt deceived by the vast majority of the reviews for this game being so positive. Hence why I felt compelled to write a rather negative review.
The premise is thin, the characters shallow and ill-conceived, and the story feels like something a teenager wrote thinking it sounded really "cool". As such I found it hard to play, and impossible to get into. I just couldn't take this game seriously, even though it seems to insist on it.
The controls are a bit off, it's probably a console port. Parts like climbing/hanging feel particularly clumsy. Other than that, the hack n' slash action is okay, but definitely sub-par compared to games like DMC.
I'm usually quite patient with games, and I am a fan of this genre/style of games. That being said, In my opinion this is just plain a bad game. It really didn't have any redeeming qualities for me. I won't be playing it again.

There are not enough words to describe how good this game is. The developers have certainly revolutionised some key elements of strategic games, most importantly the way you can command and position your units to make use of strategic advantages provided by terrain (cover, elevation, line of sight, ...). Other aspects such as unit condition and unit morale, which have also been implemented, play a key role in planning your moves as well. If you order a brigade to stay in combat for too long, its condition will slowly diminish, giving you a severe disadvantage in prolonged engagements. If morale gets too low, your units will be easily routed through cavalry attacks and bayonet charges, causing them to retreat in disarray, disobeying your commands. So you need to really take care of your units as you go, especially since they will reappear in later stages of the battle.
As you go and make your decisions, lose or win single engagements, the Battle of Gettysburg will always take different courses. So even though the battle itself lasts a maximum of five days in the game, the gaming experience will never be entirely the same.
The AI of your opponent is pretty good. You can select different types of AI commanders when you start the battle based on difficulty and aggressiveness. A defensive computer player will try to position itself on the high ground, pounding your positions with artillery barrages until the arrival of fresh reinforcements encourages him to attack your weakened positions. An aggressive opponent, on the other hand, will try to spot weaknesses in your formation, attacking these positions vigorously and without fear.
All in all, this is a must for any person who loves strategy games, in particular those who are interested in the American Civil War.

I hadn't played any Total War games until I bought this one. After downloading and running it I went through a tutorial that taught me how to push buttons, and then I began the campaign. I started as the great Roman house of Julli, and began my great campaign.
After pushing north to the alps, driving out the Gauls, I made peace with the nearby empires. The Gauls had been raiding me on occasion, and I had always beaten them back. Things seemed to be going well, until I asked to buy a city the Gauls owned. Now, of course, I offered a fair price. It was an incredible price, in fact, but they denied it. I offered again, with even more money and goods, and again they denied. This was the last straw. How DARE they deny me?! Don't they know who WON all those wars? I then decided that I had had enough of these ancient Frenchmen who dared to think they are equal to us great Romans. I not only wanted to teach them a lesson; I wanted them gone. So thus, the Great Gaul Genocide began.
It was a truly incredible campaign. Several new armies were raised. All traces of Gaul in the east were annihilated first, and a great push into the west began. Whenever I captured a city I was given the option to either occupy it as it was, enslave half the people and disperse them among my empire, or slaughter 3/4 of the people in the settlement. Naturally, I chose the latter. My goal was elimination. Death to all those barbarians who dared to have national pride.
I pushed into the Gaul empire, taking city after city. The enemy had a bigger empire, perhaps, but mine was far stronger. Our great Roman soldiers killed all in their path. Despite a stumbling point where one Gaul army managed to defeat mine and save their city, two new armies took its place. The massive campaign wore on until, at last, the final Gaul stronghold fell. The people were slaughtered, and nothing remained of the once great empire.
I had kept a running body count as the genocide wore on. The final results were:
Gaul Soldiers killed: 3,659
Gaul Civilians killed: 33,689
Total Barbarian Gauls killed (citizens and soldiers): 37,339
Brave Roman soldiers lost: 1,258
Final body count: 38,597 people dead.
It was only after the genocide was over that I realized I'd forgotten why I was mad at them in the first place.

Temos aqui o terceiro (em ordem cronológica) título da série Unreal lançado no Steam. Lançado em 2004 e que teve o Unreal Engine 2.5 como base. Um FPS frenético onde tiros de metralhadoras, foguetes, plasma e ogivas nucleares vão garantir que você não saia vivo. Agora temos a presença de veículos, mais classes e novos modos de jogo para garantir a diversão por muitas e muitas horas.
Temos poucas opções de customização de personagens, nada além de opções de rosto e cor das vestimentas, porém porém isso é mais que suficiente pois na maioria das vezes os corpos simplesmente explodem no meio da partida. Apesar disso, temos cerca de 11 raças para escolher. Não faz muita diferença, pois o importante é destruir o adversário antes que ele te destrua.
Unreal Tournament 2004 traz diversos modos de jogo. Muitas horas garantidas e muita variedade para todos os gostos. Estes são alguns dos modos de jogo disponíveis:
-
: Neste modo de jogo a grande jogada é o uso de veículos, e você precisa destruir todas as bases inimigas para capturá-las em
, todas elas espalhadas em um mapa enorme. Capture todas as bases para ter acesso ao
da equipe inimiga, e destruí-lo. Há grandes conflitos concentrados em bases-chave.
-
: Uma espécie de futebol assassino. Você tem que pegar a bola que está no meio do mapa e atirá-la no arco (gol) inimigo. Arremessando a bola você faz 3 pontos, pulando junto com ela você faz 7 pontos. A bola pode ser passada aos aliados, e é derrubada se você for morto.
-
: Este clássico ainda está presente. Faça pontos capturando a bandeira inimiga e levando-a até a sua.
-
: Seu time faz pontos ao capturar os 2 pontos de controle e mantê-los por 10 segundos. Cada ponto fica em um lado do mapa.
-
: Uma partida Deathmatch comum, e o primeiro a morrer se torna o "mutant". Este jogador recebe munição ilimitada, camuflagem e super-velocidade, mas perde saúde com o tempo. Quando o "mutant" é morto, os poderes dele passam para quem o matou.
A trilha sonora do jogo é interessante, se diferencia um pouco do estilo das músicas de seu antecessor, mas continua sendo bem "animada". Ideal para um jogo frenético como este.
Belos gráficos, muito melhorados se comparados ao Unreal Tournament anterior, agora temos mapas em vastas florestas, cavernas subterrâneas, naves espaciais, mapas submersos e até mesmo do lado de fora de naves no espaço!
Os mesmos controles de um FPS comum. Algo que pode ser difícil no começo é o sistema de esquiva (apertar duas vezes rapidamente para alguma direção faz seu personagem "desviar" para aquele lado. O que também pode fazer um novo jogador se confundir são os atalhos para as armas, pois temos um total de 19 armas!
Ah, o arsenal de UT2004 continua sendo letal e variado. Dentre as mais interessantes temos:
O Translocador, que te permite atirar um disco em qualquer lugar do mapa e se teletransportar para o local onde o disco está;
O Bio Rifle, que atira placas de lixo tóxico que grudam nas paredes e na superfície da água;
A Link Gun, um rifle que atira rajadas de plasma quente ou uma rajada contínua do mesmo;
O Flak Cannon, uma arma que atira estilhaços quente de metal nos inimigos, que ricocheteiam nas paredes;
O Rocket Launcher, dispensa comentários, lançador de foguetes que também pode lançá-los em forma de granadas temporizadas. É possível soltar até 3 foguetes ao mesmo tempo;
Redeemer, a arma mais poderosa do jogo. Lança uma ogiva nuclear com imensa área de impacto, o que garante diversos Multi-Kills. No tiro secundário, é possível controlar a ogiva com uma câmera. Apesar do poder de fogo, a Redeemer só pode carregar 1 ogiva por vez.
Temos diversos servidores com a grande maioria dos modos de jogo disponíveis ao redor do mundo, sendo assim o lag pode ser algo a atrapalhar, ainda mais num jogo com ritmo frenético como este. Apesar disso, o Single Player ainda pode ser um grande desafio nos modos de dificuldade mais avançados.
A série Unreal Tournament foi (e ainda é) um dos grandes pilares dos FPS, ao lado de jogos como Quake e Counter-Strike. É um FPS especialmente interessante para se jogar, pois proporciona uma experiência bem diferente da que outros jogos de tiro podem te dar. Vale muito a pena.

This one surprised me.  It's prequel was a solid shooter for its time, but it handled in a rough fashion and its environments were pretty sterile.  You had corridor shoots and overly-aggressive enemies.  They took a shot, flopped over, and invited other opponents to investigate.
V2 is not only far more detailed, its weapons feel meaty, and its shooting mechanics are deliciously balanced.  There is a trapping mechanics with explosives and lures, so that your foes pay heavily for coming your way.
But the killshots? Oh, the sweet killshots.  A Mortal Kombat-esque xray mechanic lets you drink in every impressive shot.  If your machine can render the shadows, lights and effects (mine sort of can), you will grin every time you land a sickening deathblow.  Variety in arms is a little light, but every one that's there has a distinct personality.  Definitely worth checking out - look for a bundle sale.

UT2k4 is a legendary multiplayer FPS that made Epic more then a studio that made the engine Deus Ex ran on. It featured fast paced deathmatch and amazing balance with it's weapons. Note: I have played this game for embrassingly numerous hours outside Steam, certainly many thousands.
The Total War series revolutionized a strategy genre that was stagnating. After years of the same things over and over again, strategy games with only campaigns and no war, sitting and waiting for this mechanic or that to play itself out, games that made the GUI a bit messier and called it depth, features that just made the same stuff a bit more Heath Robinson and called it progress and innovation, battles where you watched columns of numbers, or 7-8 little RTS guys bip and bop for 30 seconds until the game told you who won... Total War brought in a tactical scope with depth to it, actual battlefields where real time decision-making and some sensible tactical considerations played roles, and where the clash was a grand spectacle. In one fell swoop, this series revitalized the genre, indeed carved out its own genre - strategy games where real time wargaming is actually a thing.
Then, some time into the series, this game - this beautiful, beautiful game came along. Not content with what they'd achieved already, they made a game so good it broke the mould. Not content with creating their own groundbreaking genre, they then pushed further.
It might have aged now, and it isn't such a surprising, groundbreaking thing now as it was back then, and it has its warts and annoyances (like all of the games in the series) but I still have to say that for me, this is possibly the best computer game ever made. Certainly one of the best.
Also, it is a great family game, as long as the subject matter is ok for your tribe, we have had many years of fun out of these games. It is not bloody and gratuitous at all, although obviously war is violent in itself.
There is nothing else that does computer wargaming like the Total War series, and this is the glorious pinnacle of it. 100/10

The latest updates have had some issues IMHO. The game is still a lot of fun, but the Frozen Factory expansion is very grindy. The only reason I've kept playing is because I can fire it up at work for 6 hours and leave it alone.

If some of the more heavy-handed tweaks are able to be turned off in the future, I'll update the review, but that doesn't seem likely. I still recommend the game, but not as wholeheartedly as before.

That's one of the few old school platformers that I have played, and it's probably the most frustrating one, and not in a good way. I don't know how good controls are compared to the older platformers but it feels slightly clunky. Sometimes you can't dodge an attack, sometimes you have to leave a frame because the brown mice didn't move as they should have. Sometimes you fall 3 frames down because the developper thought it would be funny to make floorless frames. But the most annoying part is the loss of gold when you die. It's not a problem in Dark Souls or Hollow Knight since you can easily get back what you've lost as long as you don't die again. But in Shovel Knight if you fall down in a pit there is no way you're getting it back unless you fall down again hoping the bags will appear higher (because it was too hard for them to place the bags on the floor). The only way to get the money back is to restart the level. I've done it  dozens of time. Guess what : it's not fun. Another issue : half of the items you will earn during the playthrough are totally useless outside their own level. I think this is a lazy deisgn and the last levels could have been way more interesting.
Overall : good bosses but bad level design and useless items
Edit : Tried Plague Knight and Specter Knight. Plague Knight is even more clunky, and spending time in the menu to change bombs while fighting breaks the flow. HOWEVER, Specter Knight is way smoother gameplaywise and I had a blast playing him. Sadly the gold loss issue remains the same and Specter's hitbox doesn't match the visual, making some jumps very hard .That can't be acceptable in 2017.

Update - I wanted to update my review to note that the vast majority of multiplayer issues have been remedied: I am now able to play the game with my kids without constantly restarting or replacing someone's suit upgrades because of sync issues.  Hooray!
This game's been out of early access for a couple months now, but it gets more content in its free monthly patches than a fully supported Blizzard game.  There is an upcoming, 8 dollar expansion pack that I'd gladly pay for (Dev's cat's gotta eat) based on what I've seen thus far.  To anyone confused about the patreon bit: A patreon sub enables a very small handful of cosmetic, VIP "bling" blocks if you will, and early access to the expansion.  It's a donation with a tiny thank you; not a sales' offer.
My original review, less my comment on multiplayer:
Factorio meets Minecraft, kind of like playing feed the beast/Industrial craft mods but with the cohesion of a single dev behind it rather than 100 separate mods in a package that never works or updates quite right.
If all of that's greek to you, the game consists of finding raw materials, and constructing the logistics to extract, move, and process them, either into more logistics, research pods, or defenses against attacking wasp things.
The GOOD:
Engaging base building game
Lots of recipes to craft across several tiers of stuff.
Good visual feedback on logistics letting you know what's working or not
Still being actively developed (IE more's coming)
The BAD:
Currently there's very little variety in the enemies that attack you, or your defenses to deploy against them.
Gameplay between the last available research and charging the OET (winning) is currently just a huge grind for more power generation.  I expect this gap will later be filled with more interesting content, but were the dev to win the lottery and stop making the game, it'd be poorly balanced in its present state.
Overall, I could recommend this game: it's less than the cost of minecraft and basically takes the most interesting parts of minecraft to me and expands them.  WIth the mulitplayer issues fixed I expect this will be a fantastic game to play on LANs or with a small group of friends.

This is often described as "Dark Zelda" or "Evil Zelda".
Well, it kinda is. Character action game with some puzzle and platforming elements.
The artstyle and overall look of the game is very stylish and colorful, which is nice.
The world has a nice gothic apocalypse feel to it, though a tad repetitive. You'll often find yourself doing the same task three times to get keys or release an ally or something like that.
Combat is very nice looking with funky (but rather useless) finishing moves and a nice feel to hits. Bashing a group of demons into a bottomless pit with that baseball-bat-swing is AWESOME.
Buuuut since blocking is almost useless you
to dodge attacks... only many of the enemies have so much reach that they hit you regardless. Great.
The puzzle elements involve a lot of the usual "find Object A and bring it to Object B" but some time-bending and portals (yep, actual portals, they even glow orange and blue!) lead to some welcome variation.
Only the jumping puzzles are held down by the sometimes very clunky controls. Platforming tends to be imprecise, not only in the movement where War tends not to jump for some reason and then fall to his death, but also in that you often can't properly see which ledges he can grab onto, again resulting in a needless fall into a bottomless pit.
Especially bad is the aiming with guns and stuff, the reticule tends to jump between "way too fast" and "way too slow" making precise and fast hits almost impossible.
Also the Port is
: no options to speak of, no AA at all, and the cutscenes are pre-rendered in low resolution. Also the game is
unstable.
But you can put up with clunky controls and the occasional crash, somewhere in there beneath the instability and control issues is a very good Action Adventure / Character Action game.
But definetely not for full price.
So overall recommendation is "Yes, but only for fans of the genre or on a sale."

It's not that it's too difficult or too buggy or anything like that, it's just too... samey.

The Watcher likes to annoyingly shout hints during the most simple of puzzles (like where the door right in front of my face is) yet needs to be manually summoned during some boss fights if you want to confirm that what you THINK is the correct way of doing something actually is, and when you DO summon him during those times you'll often find him less than useful.
The biggest bore comes from the personality of War, who approaches setting the Apocalypse right like a moody 17 year old approaches a family function. He didn't want to go, he's going to grumble and refuse to emote and above all else he'll refuse to acknowledge he's having any fun no matter what.
A lot of the puzzles are no brainers that seem there just to pad the gameplay length, which is why I'm assuming the fish monsters are there as well as they offer no challenge and just serve to make swimming take longer.
If you're looking for a mindless hack-n-slash sort of game that has some of the play-style of the God of War series but without the jaw-dropping set pieces this one works. It gets a recommendation but just barely, and a hearty eye-roll for introducing a half-dozen "puzzle solvers" that seem like they could have just as easily been omitted rather than stolen from other more popular games to (again) pad out the length and add some "variety" in the dullest way.
TL;DR 6/10 worth playing to kill some time but best purchased on sale.

Fortresscraft Evolved is a very orginal game indeed. Looking for a minecraft clone? Then you're not going to find one here. After many years of running modded minecraft servers, I was quite sick to the back teeth of the game. That being said, I did get this game thinking there would be some similarities and expected to get bored very quickly. This game, quite simply put, is amazing. The developer is nothing short of a genius!
The game has you start with afew supplies, after crash landing on an Alien planet. You are given a small tutorial, and then thrown into the deep end. At this point, I went and watched a few episodes of Direwolf20's lets plays. After being educated a little.. I jumped back into the game.
You begin by scanning for various ores, and setting up mining equipment. While this is happening you will be also scanning new blocks and plantlife. This accumulates research points which you can use to unlock new research projects and equipment.
It's not long past this point, you realise that 5 hours of game time has passed, and you've simply got lost in this enormous game! By this point I had found my first 4 ore types, and had begun building a system of convayors that could fill my smelters on the surface. Research seemed very simple at first.. but another few hours in and I was now constructing a lab and researching new projects was taking several hours at a time. This was ok though because I had so much other stuff to do while this was happening.
However.. the bigger your base becomes, the more power you use.. the higher your base threat becomes.. and it's not long before you threat analyser is telling you.. "Attack immanent!". Now for those like me who love the tech, and the factory side of the game.. the invading alien swarms will only attack your central hub.. and once it's health is 0, it just reboots. That is unless you're playing hardcore.. and then its game over.
So as I went deeper into the ground, I realised just how big this game was. Some of the caves, from top to bottom, were bigger than minecraft, bedrock to sky... I would liturally hold my breathe incase I fell off a ledge, as death meant I would drop all my equipment. So far i've been 1,187 blocks deep.. and everytime I go exploring, I just can't explain the feeling of being so small, in caves so large..
This game is great for those wanting some survival, some tower defence, and some tech. I love all the machines that automate the ore collecting and the minecarts that collect the ores.. the way the power system works, and the defending of my base. It really is very well balanced... and it has just the right difficulty level to keep most playing, and not getting bored.

STOP!  Please STOP... BEFORE you buy this game!!
Please READ this CAREFULLY.... BEFORE you spend your hard earned money on this game!!
I remember watching the video before this game launched on early access, and thinking it looked EPIC AS HELL.
So then, the game came out, and almost every review was positive and full of great praise, and the game was a new #1 TOP SELLER on Steam!  WOW!
So I  worked hard to earn some money.  I sold a bunch of toys and my old bike at my folks yard sale that weekend.  I HAD to have this game!!
And then Sunday evening, I finally convinced my father to buy it for me, even though I was still about $10 short.
And as I played the game, my heart full of super expectations began to break slowly but surely.
See, I had been worried before the game launched that the game might not be complete enough or be a bug-infested mess.  That's not the problem at all actually.  In fact, the game feels solid, way more complete then so many other early access survival games of it's sort.
...So, why was I disappointed?
Well, watching the video ads for the game, and reading all the great reviews set me up to be disappointed.  This is NOT a survival game anything like Rust or DAYZ but just better because you can do more stuff and farm and make cooler houses.  I mean, I'm sure you can.  IF you have a group of friends all playing together and all agreeing not to pull your hair out in the insanely steep skill curve of the game.
To give you an idea, I spend three hours in the game.  I traversed a large path through the map, looking for anything or anybody on an existing server with players.  I found not a single animal to run from, attack, fight or even just watch run off.  I saw no other players either.  But I did start trying to harvest and learn the crafting system some.  And OMG.  Let's just be honest and agree that in a game like Rust, most players don't have the patience to harvest wood, ore, and other materials themselves, and instead just try to kill other players to collect their loot.  Okay, now that we understand that, imagine a resource collecting game that is about 1/100th of the speed of collecting reosurces in Rust.  Actually 1/100th might be too fast, it might be closer to 1/500th of the speed of collecting resoruces in Rust.  I mean everything just goes soooooo slow here.  It takes 20 seconds to snap a single branch off of a tree.  Then you need to spend 20 seconds to collect some plant fiber from a plant.  Then find some rock terrain and spend another 20 seconds searching for flint.  Now you can craft maybe a primitive shovel.  Another 20 seconds, and bam!  So you're thinking cool!  That's not so bad, right?  Uhhh yeah, but now this shovel and your skill at using are crappy as hell.  So even if you set your terraforming skill to max at the character creation screen, terraforming even a small square of land is going to take HOURS.  And then you repeat the process to make an primitive axe, and you start hacking some of the smaller trees down.  More time, for every single little log.  And you move slow as hell to move that log where you want it.  And seeing as how it looks to take about 1,000 logs to even make the most basic of houses, you're talking about a time sink of hours and hours and hours and hours just to make anything even half way decent.  Compare this to a game like Rust where you can find a single woodpile, harvest it in 20 seconds, and make a complete shelter three minutes into the game.  or collect a few woodpiles and you can make a nice 4x4 2 story house in 20 or 30 minutes tops.  And remember that in Rust, 90% of the players are too lazy to even do that, and instead just look for other players to killl and rob.
So sure, this game might be great when you get to the point of the videos on the store page, but after playing this game for a few hours, that it obviously so far away that it's honestly just not worth it.  I'm not going to spend 10,000 hours of grinding away in the game to get there.  And yes, I could get friends to buy the game and help me, and yay, then all of us only need to spend $40 each on the game, and spend only 2,500 hours of game time skilling up and getting to that point.  Ugh.  I hope you see my point.
Before you even think about responding yelling at how bad my review is, instead go to youtube and watch some random game play videos.  And in all of them, you'll see people doing the exact same thing I did in my first few hours.  Collecting twigs, and plant fiber and looking desperately for fun, but saying something about needing to find friends and learn more about the game.  What I mean is, people are going to be boring crap.  You're not gonna see people with awesome houses and cities and advanced armor and weapons and epic fights.  No, you'll see this same super grind of skills, collecting the most basics of resources and the videos will honestly be pretty boring to watch. Now, if all of the videos now for this game are boring to watch, imagine being in their shoes playing the game and advancing at such a super crawl in the game.  Oh boy!
The game is pretty solid, the graphics look plenty nice.  But honestly, I see about 98% of players being wayyyyyy too bored to continue to invest the time required to 'get to the good stuff' in this game.  I am a patient gamer, but playing this game made me want to break my arm to go play with the hackers in Rust instead.
Buy it if you know what you are getting people.  This is not Rust.  The game might be deeper and better yes, but realize that you are going to be the most patient of all patient people to even get anywhere.  I mean in the upper like 1% of gamers.  For over 90% of gamers, even thouigh they might like the 'idea' of this game at first, they will soon find something with a much quicker speed of game play and advencement.  Not many people will want to spend 30 hours just searching for flint and twigs and plant fiber and then realize that OMG now they need to spend 90 more hours at the next most basic stage of character skill development.
Most people complain of GRIND in mmorpg games.
Magnify that grind by about 1,000 and you have 'Life is Feudal'.
You've been warned.  Buy at your own risk now.  (I wish I had seen a review like mine here BEFORE I bought it)

Overall, a very good sequel to the reboot, though it has some flaws that make it not as good as the brilliant reboot.  I'd still heartily recommend this one, but just be aware that it's not quite the same kind of game that the first reboot was anymore.
Pros:
-The noment to moment gameplay loop is still top notch.  Melee combat is still great, and the weapons are interesting and feel good to use.  Combat is still super fun and fast paced.
-The story is interesting, with decent voice acting
-The humor from the first game is still very present here
-Sidequests add some extra fun things to do, though it makes the game feel a bit more meandering.
-The game looks beautiful.  Graphics are top notch.
Cons:
-The borderlands-style loot system is too complex for what this game is meant to be, in my opinion.  I'm here to chop up a bunch of demons, not stop very 10 seconds to vacuum up all this loot and then try to figure out whether this new "+4.5 damage, -1.5 movement speed" socket is better than the one I already have.  It breaks up the action and makes the whole game feel less tight.
-On a related note, the random level generator they touted is a nice idea, but in practice it made the levels feel empty sometimes, without even any enemies to fight.  Entire buildings were just completely barren, with maybe only a chest sitting in the middle.  It really is jarring when you compare it to the great art design of the one-of-a-kind sets they made, both in parts of this game and the last one.  I honestly think I'd prefer fewer but custom designed areas, rather than this huge number of samey, empty feeling areas.

I'll preface this review by admitting that I'm not in the target demographic for this game. I played many of the NES and Master System platformers when those systems were still new, and had hoped to see a new contender in the oldschool platforming subgenre. I thoroughly enjoyed Super Meat Boy, even though I never did get good enough at it to beat the hardest unlockable levels. I find 20XX delightful, and have had a great time with Terraria. Shovel Knight is something else. It's a game that describes 8-bit platformers in meticulous detail for the people who didn't get to play them in the old days.
Shovel Knight takes great care to look like an 8-bit platformer, character model sizes notwithstanding, and succeeds admirably at that effort. Everything from the chiptune sound to the clunky menus are preserved in a historically accurate manner. The animations don't have many frames and the things that are and aren't platforms aren't always easy to discern at first glance. If it had been released on the NES in the early 1990s, it would've been regarded as a technological marvel and a pretty good platformer. Not as good as Super Mario Bros 2 and 3, but better than Street Fighter 2010 or Wrath Of The Black Manta. A solid 7/10.
So why don't I recommend it? If you've been frustrated by the likes of the Adventure Island series, Duck Tales, Jacky Chan's Action Kung Fu, Master Blaster, or Mega Man 4, you know what to expect when Shovel Knight gets frustrating. It simulates that sensation flawlessly. What it doesn't provide is the fun of the aforementioned games, or enough of its own fun to make up the difference. If you're an old gamer who's played a lot of platformers, there's virtually no chance that you haven't already played a better game. If given the choice between Shovel Knight and any of the classics from the old days, Shovel Knight simply doesn't stand a chance. And the best modern 2d platformers (see 20XX, Super Meat Boy, Terraria, etc.) are much better, too. It's not a bad game. In fact, it's actually pretty good, but it's hopelessly outclassed by both the old and the new classics. At just over 2 hours with Shovel Knight, I'm already far too sick and tired of it to finish it, and so I'm giving it the tumbs down.

At this point of the game (1.3 upgrade) I think I can say it's some the best in the strategy part of the pc games world.
The game is about the famous Gettysburg battle of the American civil war. The batlle is played in a row of small parts in 3 days. That's something like 4 or 6 battles for a complete campaign (or complete Gettysburg battle).
Every decision that you have made in a battle counts for the next one. Units losses, the ennemies that you have killed, the important spots in the battlefield that you have captured (they are represented by victory points). Sometimes thanks to your bad or good results in the previous encounter you may be presented by three options for the next phase, sometimes you have no choices at all.
The battle management is at the same time extremely easy (brigades/small skirmishers and cavalry units/gun batteries and corps commanders) and complete (arrows for units movement, orders, the terrain really counts for something)...so it's a game easy to deal with and with a lot or replay value (stand alone scenarios, multiplayer).
The devs are still interested to improve the game, even months after the release.

This review is for the vanilla version of Amnesia. I did not play any expansion(s).
My first horror-game was the DOS-classic "Alone in the Dark," which was rebooted years later as a horrible game and even-worse movie spinoff. The game scared me as a child, and since then, no game has ever been truly frightening for me. That is, until I played Amnesia. Rather than relying on "pop out" scares, Amnesia manages to pull of something that was almost impossible: scaring people out of atmosphere and suspense alone. A few major horror games have come and gone since Amnesia, and none have scared me like this one. Disclaimer: I only went about 3-4 hours in before writing this review.
* Incredibly creepy atmosphere. The graphics are not the best, but they get the job done remarkably.The sounds are all 100% original (gamers, you know we have an ear for sounds that get reused across different media) and make every creek of the floor, gust of wind, and dampening of a candle 10x more frightening.
* The game uses sanity/insanity effects with great accomplishment. Although the idea is not entirely original, they are similar and work just well as those in "Eternal Darkness", although they are perhaps less varied and surprising. They do manage to turn a casual stroll through a castle's basement into a horror masterpiece.
* NO WEAPONS. When Amnesia was released, this was almost unheard of in a first-person-"shooter." As a player, you rely only on your lantern and hiding ability to stay safe (and sane).
* The game uses a light/dark system. If you remember when Super Mario Sunshine was announced with very few details, many gamers squeeled over the possibility that standing in shadows/sun has different effects. Without going into too much detail, Amnesia takes this idea and perfects it. I am not sure if other games have done this before (it seems like something that should have been done by  now), but I was VERY pleased at the originality here.
* In relation to the light/dark system mentioned above, the inventory system is truly awesome. Similar to the ammo-conservation system in early Resident Evil games, Amnesia forces you to decide whether lighting a torch or using your lantern is worth the last tinderbox or bit of oil in your inventory (or attracting enemies). The payoff for going through some places "in the dark" may be worth it, or in many cases, not...
* The game also has a great narrative. Although the "title character has amnesia" gimmick is ultra-cliche, I was captivated by the story of Daniel (your character) and his relationship to the castle.
* There was one element of the game that interrupted my suspension of disbelief: why did someone hide supplies in the fireplace? For that matter, why are so many supplies inconveniently hidden behind stacks of boxes? When I found a "tinder" hidden behind some boxes within the first five minutes of play, I compulsively checked behind EVERY box in the game (there are several hundred) for hidden supplies. I understand the developers' sentiment, but I think it is time for atmospheric gaming to move beyond the "check every corner" gameplay first introduced in early 90s adventure games.

So I've been able to get a little bit over 4 hours of game play in Shadow Warrior 2 during the past couple of days, and I have to say I love it! Now a lot of people are making the comparison between Borderland and Diablo, mixed with Doom in mind. I would agree, though Flying Hogs took a gamble on keeping the old fighting mechanics from the reboot in 2013. And who could blame them? They rocked then like they rock now. There is something spectacular about cutting limbs off a demon with your katana, then swiftly pulling out your pump action shot gun to finish the job with  buckshot to the face. Now let's take what is good and make it better by adding a variety of cool melee weapons and guns like Futuristic (a plasma blade katanna), Demonic (a flesh-made rocket launcher), and more common weapons (like the pump action shot gun). Gems are also available like in Diablo that you put into weapons to make them stronger or give a faster reload time. I also found a bullet mod that gave explosive rounds to my pistol, which was a nice touch. Some people, I'm sure, will knock the gems because most of them do very little change, and what can end up in the menu longer then one should assigning gem slots to weapons instead of slicing up deamons.
Now skills: I've found that, after completing missions, not only do you get new wapons but you also get new skills. The starting skills are broken up into 4 different categorie, 2 of which are passive abilities, 1 is a set of melee moves (such as a Zelda-like sword spin), and the final is mystic skills (like healing yourself, or turning invisible). Much like guns and gems, you can find skills in chests, completing missions, and even from vendors.
Finally, the actual story. If you're a loot lover, then SW2 is for you, But if you want story I do recommend playing the first game or else you may be confused with the plot. The remake is more like Doom in that it has a set of weapons and the "wang-to-the-wall" feeling of tight corridors and a linear map layout. While this game is still linear (mission based), there are more opportunites to explore for chests filled with all sorts of loot. The games humor is very tongue and cheek, which some people may enjoy while others might find annoying whenever Wang shoots off a quip.
Overall, Shadow Warrior 2 is worth the price and is great fun!

Hey guys,
this is my first review ever. Really like this game. I find it hard to remain interested in games after a day of smashing them, but im still playing this one. So that says something pretty big. Also my mrs is starting to hate this game as im on it too much.
Pros
-Exceptionally fast load time. once you double click the games shortcut, you are in world within a 15-20 seconds. great for those of us impatient or busy people. I really really hate bull**** loadtimes. I want to play a game not make a cup of coffee and come back while waiting for the main menu.
-Good game progression.  for once a game that doesnt bog you down waiting for research, construction, or resource gathering/grinding. It has a nice balance of automation to the point where all that stuff can be done while you are off exploring. Ive often been off exploring a cavern and come back only to find that the slowest part of the system is myself and it is easy to get to the point of automation that most things become trivial (Wtf do i do with 5k copper now?)
-enemies and death. you can make the game as hard as you like, and the consequences of death as permanent or trivial as you like in world gen. Which is really nice when you are still learning how to grapple around a massive cavern or falling down a really big hole.
- The world. OMFG it is huge. The underground caverns are enormous, like really really really big and the terrain changes with depth, always serving up something different.
-in game help. it is incredibly intuitive. It could be a little more indepth with some items but still very well thought out and just a blessing.
-holobase function. you can track realtime how your network is functioning and where any bottlenecks are
-good steam community who have most answers for you.
-developer that is active on forums and takes interest in our feedback.
cons
-there is no way to pause the game as yet. you can camp out next to a torch or leave and come back (which is not that big of a deal due to fast load times) but pause would be awesome when you have the mrs trying to talk to you or a baby screaming at you. I understand the dev has said that it is a survival game but it could be a deal breaker for some gamers.
-controls take a while to get used to. now and again im still trying to access hoppers with e.
-the options could be a little more in depth with the sounds and music. took  google to find out how to turn off music (ctrl -m)
-a coordinate system would make digging holes to your mining operations soo much easier.
all in all a great early access game. very well thought out and designed. a clear development roadmap and it gives you what it promises. anyway back to the mrs tasks

When I saw many reviews both good and bad point out the similarities between this game and Borderlands, I immediately purchased this game to try out.
I am huge fan of Borderlands game.
I also like this developer's previous game "Shadow Warrior", "Hard Reset".
Also, a part of initial members of this developer were from People Can Fly which created legendary FPS Pain Killer.
Probably a good developers who can create a real game since People Can Fly, after aquired by Epic Games, created a complete mess known as Bulletstorm.
But enough history, Let's talk about the game. Shadow Warrior 2.
The previous game, Shadow Warrior(2013), was a linear FPS game. A ridiculously overpowered melee focused combat with useless toy guns.
This game retains the much of combat mechanics from the previous game. But the guns becomes useful.
The combat strategy is simple. You randomly mush your buttons until all enemies die.
Other game mechanics are indeed Borderlands-like.
You accept missions from hub location, then, you teleport to the procedurally generated map to complete the mission objectives(most missions are fetch missions. you collect items scattering around the map)
You loot the Weapons and upgrades with variable generated specs, but under normal difficulty and so far, the initial weapons are too powerful to bother with these minor differences.
So yeah, It's much like Borderlands.
Unlike Borderlands, most missions are generic item fetch misions with not much interesting background stories.
(You can say that to Borderlands too, But Borderlands 2 has much better story telling missions)
Unlike Borderlands, combat is faster, no point to spend your time on grinding or farming.
So this is it.
I recommend this game but it's not for everyone's taste.
If you like Borderlands(looting, missions) and DOOM(running around with guns blazing), you probably like this game.

You play as a Knight with a shovel who is looking for/trying to save his love Shield Knight. Along the way you meet quirky but loveable characters that breathe life into the towns and game, I found the dialogue quite funny. The graphics in this game are amazing (for this style), the music is even better. Some of the level tracks are some of the best retro tracks I have ever heard. To top it all off the gameplay somehow manages to be perfect. Tight controls, alot of ways to play differently with relics plus an entirely different playable character that feels nothing like playing the original with his own unique power-ups.
In my opinion if you are looking for oldschool nostalgia, a great platformer, a funny game, or just something new to fall in love with I recommend this game. Codex of Victory is really I a game I saw by accident This seemed to be an IO build. The game universe sees humanity colonize the stars as the imaginatively named Kingdom, the stellar feudalism being born from early corporate expansion efforts. It came across to me to be a medevil knights game to the stars. The campaign is centered around an XCOM-base, which gathers resources, produces disposable combat units, stores them and conducts research with everything centered in battle around Action Points. Seems like a capture and hold type turn base than a mission sends your soldiers to minimized sizes. Some good pros and cons
PROS
•	A; Reminds me a lot of the early Warhammer 40,000, Endless Space, X-com and Supreme Commander games but with different simplistic actions.
•	B: Everything is easy on the eye, simple, and the cartoony vehicles are pleasing to see.
•	C: Stats are quite simplistic and the navigation of the game easy and non-confusing.
•	D: It’s a game that get’s more complex in the amount of battles and vehicles. What you build is what you use.
•	E: The Campaign has some plusses and minuses. It will keep you in the game or may not. It is a plus that it is trying to do something different than copy X-com, but it does not offer you enough.
CONS
1.	Its Campaign which is simple is also it’s weakness. It is too simple and though the game will make you hold ground in three areas. I am not sure your will care what happens in game. WIth X-com there is an invested storyline, here not so much.
2.	Graphics are ok, and effects are ok, and the interface is ok…but is OK enough for you. To expert complex players not so much.
3.	There is no real sound to this game, effects yes, but the lack of flash narration, passionate story telling hurt the over all concept.
4.	There could have more puzzle and complexity to the missions to avoid redundancy and the lack of story is probably why. Like bad dialog in a movie this left the developer just making missions of capture and hold than each being complex and even multiple task oriented. Instead of A + B = C in the mission story task. It becomes turn based number unit battles stuck in the early chess development stages than complex gameplay.
OVERALL: Codex of Victory is an OK game. It is fun to see that it is trying something different than the norm, but as any game progresses in it’s chess base strategy. You want to have reason to continue. The story is very weak and terrible, that your really don’t care, and that is its fatal flaw. This is a nice game to get super cheap, but not a must to get. I am giving it a marginal thumb up, but there are better turn based games out there. I would see the VIDEO play in the discussion section, watch and then decide. This isn't bad, but you should know what you're getting into when you pick this one up.
It is *not* a plot-driven mech-drama done in the Battletech/Mechwarrior style. Nor is it a smooth, clever, deterministic Advance Wars clone.
Codex of Victory feels like a last-minute conversion of a wait-timer-driven tactics MMO into something a bit more Advance Wars-y. It has timed resource-harvesting, item icons that look exactly like something you'd see on Kongregate, and an overall structure that emphasizes waiting for upgrades, waiting for buildings, waiting for resources, etc.
Still, if it's a rushed conversion, it's a fairly good one. Codex might be a little bland, but it has a good gameflow to it, and the strategic and tactical elements actually have some bite to them.
In Codex, you build units in your X-Com base, then travel to combat sites and spend them in skirmishes. Everything you do from deploying to moving to shooting in combat requires Action Points, which are generated by taking and holding strategic sites. Strategic sites also allow you to deploy new units from them, so combat tends to revolve around taking and holding key territories and chokepoints.
All of that is very Advance-Wars-y, but here is where Codex differs. First, it lets you move and attack with units the turn you deploy them, which means you can take a territory, spawn a unit from it, take a territory, spawn a unit from it, etc until you run out of AP. It also makes attacking a fortified position more perilous, as failing to take it in a single turn means the enemy gets to start warping in reinforcements, all of which can fire on your units as they come in.
Codex is also heavily upgrade based. Every unit can have ten upgrades, which must all be slowly researched and paid for, and there are a *lot* of units in this game. You're not going to be able to afford to max out everything or even most things. This gives units and armies a high degree of customizability, even if the fruits of that customization don't really start to show until mid to late in the game.
Codex's campaign is fairly beefy, but unfortunately the flat dialog and uninteresting world mean that it kinds of outstays its welcome as anything other than a tactical exercise.
On sale, this is a reasonable pickup if you liked Advance Wars and want to try a slightly different take on the genre.
However, if you're looking for lore, world-building, and engaging writing, it's probably best to wait for Harebrained's Battletech to release.

The people who made this game, 1C, made one of my all time favorites series called kings bounty. That is the better turn based strategy game, codex of victory is an unfortunate step down. In summary:
The Good:
- good graphics
- Fast load times
- mechs and tanks
- module system lets you tweak your units
The bad:
- Inconsistent pacing in a relatively short game: Game starts giving you unlimited time to 'cheat' and get credits, then the region defense timers get more and more frequent until it is not possible to keep up
- None of the units matter but your hero characters. By the end of the game most maps can be completed with just one or a few heroes, including the final levels, because they are so powerful
- Because of the broken power levels of heros vs units, by mid game you end up with unrealistic/cringey broken full storage. I had 260+ units in my hangar that only stored 100 units by the end of game. My uranium and iron was also maxed out above the limits. The ONLY resource I was short of was credits that slowly drip out of your command center. The only thing you need money for is upgrading your heroes.
- Very very repetitive. You will play the same 10 maps over and over and over and over, and they will take you all of one to three turns
- Sir Lionheart can one shot enemy bases. So OP it's game breaking
- The chancellor can fly anywhere on the map and two shot an enemy base. So OP it's game breaking
- So short, and ending is underwhelming
Final Thought:
Buy on sale if you like the genre.

I was lucky enough to be able to test this game throughout it's alpha and beta stages, only to see it finally launch a few weeks ago. I would have written a review earlier if I had the free time, but obviously with it getting this close to December, people that are still in school know that it finals are coming up quick. Anyways, seeing this game progress through its development has been eye opening in how games can be designed. The developer takes comments and suggestions to heart, and will even possibly show up in future updates.
This game is essentially BroForce turned competitive along with different game modes and the ability to use the propulsion of your weapon to your advantage. As you have seen in the trailer, it can be quite useful to propel yourself using your gun, similar to advanced techniques in Duck Game actually, in order to cross gaps or even get the "drop" on your opponent(s). You can use everything from flamethrowers and grenades to miniguns and smoke grenades to take out your enemies. There are even modes like capture the flag and turkey hunt to add variety.
Jump Gunners is the most fun for 2-4 players, but still has fun challenges similar to Duck Game for single player. Unfortunately, I would not currently recommend this game to players that do not have friends locally available to play with them, but the single player content supplements the local multiplayer content. Hopefully one day we can see online multiplayer be implemented so that these players, as well as the players that do have local friends available to play with, can enjoy this game!
Another thing: If you are looking for a game that is extremely fun with friends, this game is for you. If you are looking for a game that is balanced and competitive, this may not be for you in its current state. Updates have been making it better, but there are items that are definitely more powerful than others. With the randomly generated items, it makes it quite hard to rely on these weapons compared to the likes of Duck Game that have set weapon spawns or Towerfall that have set chest spawns.
In terms of a local multiplayer game, I give this an 8/10 for how much fun it is with friends, but unfortunately I cannot see this forming a competitive scene like Duck Game and Towerfall have semi-developed. The good parts include the weapon, stage and mode varities, unique gameplay that this game offers compared to others in its genre, fun and stressful single player challenges, well-developed soundtrack and great pixelated graphics. This game can only get better and I cannot wait to see the updates that future holds for this game.

After a long time of wanting to play this game, I've finally been able to play it and holy cow it's more terrifying when you are actually the one controlling Daniel's movements and such. Still, it's absolutely amazing. The story is interesting and unique, with elements you wouldn't quite expect when playing this game. You start the game with what seems to be a flashback of a sort, though really it's just Daniel (you), disoriented and constantly reminding himself of who he is and ends up collapsing in a dark and rainy hall (the name of the hall you wake up in is actually called Rainy Hall xD). If you're a first timer playing this, you will be very much on edge by the very beginning because of the sounds and effects (even though you won't be in any real danger until an hour or two in the game). You find a letter you have written to yourself, explaining you had taken an amnesia tonic and that you must kill an old man named Alexander. You are also told that something is on your trail, so you have to be on your toes the whole time. Despite having no explanation of why you need to kill Alexander or where the hell you are, you move on, going deeper and deeper in Castle Brennenburg,
The game just gets worse and more horrifying the more you play, which is the best part of it all. As someone who has been a fan of this game for a couple of years, I definitely reccomend getting this game. It's pure horror combined with an interesting plot.

So last night....I stayed up until midnight, preparing to attack Rome, three full stack armies, two of them coming from the North, full of Urban Cohorts and the most elite troops I could get. One coming from the sea to the west, a fodder army of lesser troops. The turn before I plan on attack, SPQR denounces mine and the other three houses. Instant Civil War, four or five of my settlements beseiged by the other two houses, but I press on. First, my fodder army lands, 2-3k of my troops against two full stacks of SPQR elite troops, some 5-6k. I manage 681 kills to their complete annihlation of my army. SPQR forces have HUGE buffs. But it works, one of their armies is too far away from their capital to provide back up, so I lay siege. As soon as my towers are built, I assault the city. Walls so large they fill the entire screen, my onagers unable to penetrate them. The SPQR has less than a thousand men garrisoned in the city, but my reinforcements are delayed, they may not make it to the battle. With the enemies army marching at us from the other side of the city I quickly charge the walls. Sending my top units up the towers, I lose a thousand men, just trying to take the walls that less than four hundred defended. I rush a company of men to the other gate, to prevent enemy reinforcements from entering the city, they get there just in time. Now they must use my siege towers, I turn my onagers against them, destroying my own siege towers. But I haven't the ammo, one remains. With my battered and half killed army, I march to the city center, leaving only one unit back to defend the walls, along with my archers positioned along the enemy's approach. Half of my forces retreat from the city center as soon as combat ensues. The other half fighting bravely, but slowly losing. The enemy army reaching my tower, and then, reinforcements, my own. Finally arrived, striking the enemy in the back as they try to clamber up their own walls. I send the calvary and some infantry around to the side gate, attacking the city center from behind. I lose near on a thousand more men fighting the contingent of several hundred in the center, but I take it. Now I must hold it. With the enemy army at my back, attacking the walls my men so valiantly took. My second army charging at them, forcing them up against the walls, ballista's and arrows raining down on them. They begin to break, but so do my men. The might of the SPQR is undeniable, their armor thicker, weapons sharper. Sending the calvary out of the side gate, hitting them in their flank, finally the break. And the city is mine. The SPQR is destroyed, but the war has just begun, now the house Julii must reign supreme over the other two houses, they must be dealt with and swiftly. And with the Britons to my north, I know my victory of Rome will be a spec in comparison to the battles that I must fight to be declared ruler of the Roman Empire, and the world!

I bought this game early access because Darth did a great job with the Total War mods. I played it a few times, and was pretty pleased. I let it sight for a while and picked it back up a few days ago and was so impressed I was moved to write this review.
UG:G is a breath of fresh air in wargaming. It presents the complete battle of Gettysburg in flowing smooth (pausable) real time. The game has a number of scenarios, that reflect your performance on the battlefield. If Buford's cav gets really shot up on the first day, their strength will reflect that and they may not be available at a critical moment later.
The AI is very good overall, but I think the game is easy (still some good fights), and it is something Darth updates regularly.
The game is a joy to play, whether you are trying to scouting the map to find a unit to plug a hole in your line, or just watching as your offensive develops, the battles are faced well enough that you can keep a grip on the battle, but also that there are no lull periods.
Overall, I strongly recommend this game if you like wargames, and Gettysburg in particular.

And if you're not that big a fan of RTS, and so on, then this could still be a good start. It's a simple game, has a nice artstyle, and is quite unique. Since the game is simple, you can quickly learn the controls, and get right to it.
9/10, considering the size of the game, genre, etc., in my opinion.
