Solid hex based TBS. Core TBS combat is cookie-cutter affair, few surprises and fewer outright innovative mechanisms (that I've seen yet). However, that's not to say it's bad - it's very familiar and easy to grasp even for casuals of the genre.
Pros:
Familiar and polished, but simplified TBS
Has all the regular features - zone of control, movement costs, LoS targeting, special attacks, special abilities.
AP points system offers a fresh strategic take on the genre
Well integrated real time base building
Cons:
TBS combat lacks depth - terrain only offers movement bonus/penalities and no other features
Scenarios esp. early on are a little small in scale - lots of small fast skirmishes rather than prolonged battles (personal opinion)
Real time base building feels like a freemium game (a sentimental criticism rather than a gameplay one)
Real time base management offers a fresh between combat fun on its own. Plays like all the freemium time-based base builders out there. Construction queues, unit production & management, resouce management (cash, common & rare resources) with a player controlled time acceleration feature (that stops at points of interest) plus research & customization (unit modules).
Abosolute masterpiece, forget Rome 2 this is much better, Better gameplay and strategy and good Diplomacy. This is the Total War game that you want!!!!!

From what I could gather, I believe we assume the role of Amelia Ash. She is 15 years old and loves to record herself while she laughs. She loves her life. She loves her friends. She felt that she deserved a better birthday so now she can’t enjoy her life anymore. Her number one dilemma is to fend off several haunted dolls that roam her house. They got a bit unruly and found a way to transform into a “human.”
Yeah…I think that’s what it’s about…
---
The player must survive until 5 am. The game starts at 1 am and the dolls wake up around 1:30 am. During the course of the 5 in-game hours, you must avoid the dolls, things, whatever they are and try to survive. You can press the space bar to listen “closely” but I never found any use for it. Quite frankly, it’s useless because no matter what you do, the enemy will always get you. There’s the standard light source, in the form of a flashlight (pre-patch), or matches (post-patch). An exclamation mark will appear on the lower right corner of the screen if someone is nearby.
There was a patch that “changed” the game mechanics but in my opinion, it worsens an already terrible game. I actually waited for this patch to happen before I wrote this review but it didn’t change my impression of the game.
So pre-patch, I found an exploit that if you go to the highest floor of the house, and stand on a certain spot, the “dolls” will not be able to kill you. That’s how I was able to beat the game, by just standing there. Now, post-patch, they added this PaPa character to spice up your day. PaPa corrected the exploit I found while adding new problems in the process. PaPa needs to be taken care of so the player needs to search for a music box and wind it. Wait for an exclamation mark on the screen to appear and calm him down. Perhaps I have the timing wrong but this doesn’t work even when I walk towards him while winding the music box. He still jumps on you and ends the game. (Really, that’s the best part of Dark Night)
There is a certain amount of cheapness in how PaPa kills you. I don’t mind games being difficult games. I even don’t mind PaPa but he needs some kind of cooldown or he needs to gradually introduce himself throughout the night so that the player can learn his pattern. This is what the other dolls do…well kind of. Their patterns are pretty basic but they have a pattern.
PaPa’s cheapness becomes apparent during the bonus challenge after the credits. It’s still 1:00 and I’m rushing to get the music box. I figured I have some time. Can you guess what happens? PaPa comes rushing in. Then, I thought to myself, “Maybe, I should memorize the route to the music box.” Okay, that’s should be good. NOPE…he still gets you. I repeated the action several times with improvements here and there but he still gets me. Death after death, I am reminded of my inadequacy. I’m just not good enough. Thanks PaPa.
Lastly, I did mention briefly that there are light sources. The flashlight is there during pre-patch (v1.09) and v1.12 patch replaces the flashlight with the matches. I thought the flashlight was terrible. The battery drained too fast but at least I can see what’s in front of me and conserving the battery is manageable. However, with the matches, it goes out too fast, and the throw of light is nonexistent (Might as well not have the bloody thing!) I know. It’s not fair to the matches. It is a match versus a flashlight. Of course the flashlight will win the day so why remove it?
*clears throat*
Ending rant. Thank you.

+Great controls
+Colorful sprite graphics
+Awesome platforming and some well designed levels
+Relics (aka secondary weapons/items) are fun to use and find.
-I like Jake Kaufman and he did some great work on Contra 4 and Double Dragon Neon, but this game doesnt seem to have as nearly as much memorable music. Dont get me wrong some of it is good, but a lot of the music uses what i call the "tinny" high-pitched whiny instrument on later NES games (like Mega Man 6).
-I was hoping each "zone" would have a set amount of levels and then a boss level. I wasnt expecting just about every stage to be a boss stage like the Mega Man games. The world map made me think it was going to be like SMB3 with some levels, then maybe a midpoint boss (like the little castles from SMB3) and then the final boss for the area.
-The upgrades arent that great to me. Some armor choices dont really make them worth purchasing as well as the shovel attacks. The relics are ok but in this way it tries to be too Castlevania-ish and kinda slows down the game slightly having to cycle through which one i want to use, (but certain ones are fun to use for the plarforming bits).
-I quickly discovered that New Game+ scales up the damage done to me but not the bosses, and also replaces the health bonuses in many (maybe all?) secret areas (and some mini-mini boss fights) with bombs. Its annoying to know that there is a wall i can destroy but oh no!, theres a bomb! I really like this game so far!  I have only played for two hours or so.  I have done five battles, and built my base up quite a bit.  The base building is very similar to XCOM, and that's ok in my book.  It works well in this game.  There appear to be lots of upgrades to your building modules, e.g. you build a command center that gives you money.  Then later you can upgrade that command center to improve its output (I think, I haven't upgraded it yet).  There are a good amount of buildings, foundries, workshops, hangars, factories, and I'm still very early in the build tree.
The combat is standard hexagon map with turn-based combat.  The very unique part of this is the action point mechanic.  Basically, you have so many action points (AP) per turn, and you can use them to move and attack, or deploy more units to the map (based on how many units you built back at your base).  So, there are always tough decisions whether or not to deploy another unit, or move your units and press an attack.  It's very unique and I love it.  One reviewer said it got pretty difficult later on, as the AI always seemed to have more APs than you, but we'll see.
So far so good.  It's a fun game, the combat is enjoyable, and the base-building is quick and easy and has enough variety to keep me interested.  I hope the game continues as well as it started, as I'm having a blast!
So, my early review is a big old fat thumbs up!

From Advanced Wars, Command & Conquer, XCOM,  to Starcraft, I am familiar and love all types of strategy games. So when Codex of Victory was assigned to me I was rather excited about the big turn based battles and hopefully big robots. Developed by the team behind Majesty 2, Warlock and Elven Legacy; Ino-Co Plus, this is in very familiar territory when it comes to the genre.
For the most part Codex of Victory does meet all of the needs and desires one could want in a strategy game. Despite still being in Early Access the game feels rather well put together and feels like a complete game. All I want is more giant robots, but that's a personal thing.
Now everybody has different takes on what makes a good strategy game. Some people crave troop customization, high difficulty, expansive twitch based strategy, or, my favorite, putting huge giant armies against each other and watching the chaos unfold. My point is, that the strategy genre comes in many forms and flavours. Codex of Victory borrows from other great games and blends them into a deceptively simple title that is easy to approach and play.
Let's talk story. Some royalty in the future gets in trouble and you save them. They make you a "Lord" which is basically the equivalent of XCOM's "Commander" and voila! You now have a base and an army. I will be honest, the story isn't the games strongest point right now. There is some nicely designed character illustrations and small attempts at a story but I didn't find it all that memorable. Basically, you have to conquer the planet in the first act and then move on to conquering other planets in the sector in the next.
Moving on to the good stuff, we have base building up first. Anyone familiar with XCOM is going to be instantly at home with this mechanic. You start with a basic set of rooms that generate resources, build troops, modify modules, research upgrades, etc. You dig for rooms and expand more and more as you progress. The base building part while enjoyable does seem to lack any tactical value beyond just getting you ready for the next fight and altering troop composition. One thing I did enjoy was the modules system in the game, which enables customization to a degree. You can add hit points at the cost of damage, add a range boost but deployment cost more or baseline upgrades like a plus to crit chance.
Sadly, these little customization items are only found after completing levels and are type based. Meaning that it effects all units of that kind instead individually. It could be argued, that individual level of micromanagement isn't the games style. Codex of Victory is more Advanced Wars in nature, where everything has a set value, damage, defense, health, etc. Don't get me wrong, I enjoyed the amount I could alter my troops, I just wanted more ways to make them my own.
Speaking of unit types, this is where I do have a bit of gripe. Codex has more of the run of mill type of troops then I would've liked. I wanted and expected more Mecha-style combat, but  instead got futuristic themed versions of tanks, artillery, and attack choppers. There are some cool Mecha in the game, but not enough for my taste. So, while the design of the units themselves is rather well done, it rarely caught my attention, and by the time the enemy units start to get interesting, that's quite a way into the game -- so, it was a little underwhelming.
Like I said before though, the game graphics are good. One thing I will give kudos to the developer for is the ability to zoom in more than most games allow. You can zoom in on the base building, combat, and units themselves and they look rather detailed. The carnage itself is also visually pleasing, as things explode, energy sizzles, and missiles zoom. An area that could use improvement is the maps themselves. The level design itself is rather simple, and the map textures aren't really anything extraordinary -- it's not a big requirement in strategy games, as you mostly just focus on where your troops are but it could've been more pleasant on the eyes.
The nitty gritty of combat is hexagonal movement using the AP system. The AP system is the be-all-and-end-all of the way battles work. When you first start a level you are handed a limited number of AP points to use in summoning units into the field. Usually you can bring either five light units, two mediums, or one heavy unit. It's rather limiting but it also depends on the mission itself. Once you pick a couple of starting units the AP act as a means to bring more units onto the field, move units, and attack as well. You gain more AP per turn by capturing control points that add to your total.
The AP system for me was a bit of hit and a miss. I loved the idea of having to balance all three aspects of troop deployment, movement, and attack but it become increasingly frustrating as I got deeper into the game. The enemy usually starts out with a cadre of troops already on the level and can summon even more once the combat starts. There are some levels that suggest avoiding enemies but this is nigh impossible due to the way movement works and the enemy is extremely aggressive. Difficulty spikes happen on occasion and it just feels more like a slug fest than tactical combat. This is fine by me, and there were some levels that were chaotic as hell but rather enjoyable as everybody exploded.
Simply put, because the way the AP system works it feels like your enemy always has the advantage. Add on the fact they also can add enemies to the field and are a couple of tech levels above you, and things can become frustrating. Just don't get attached to your troops. There is some variance in mission goals that I did enjoy, and the troubles with the AP system are alleviated. On occasion you might find the enemy just sits there and is happy to let you stack AP, which is nice. Ultimately, balance is all that is required here and that is what Early Access is meant to do. All the issues with AP system are manageable with a couple of tweaks here and there.
Campaign aside, there is also PVP in the game. This area seems rife with opportunity as this lets you create your own custom set of troops without all the confines of the base upgrades, resources, and such. Same idea is applied here. You are given a hundred points to divide among a number of troops, upgrades, etc. Then you take them into battle and see the better army win. While I didn't get to experience the PVP aspect too deeply, I did like what I saw here and look forward to what the developer adds to it.
There is more here to discuss such as music, amount of content/innovation, and replay value but as the game still isn't quite finished yet, time will tell on some of those.
Like I mentioned, Codex of Victory brings good ideas together and makes them its own in unique ways. The game has plenty of potential and will definitely please strategy fans. As of this writing the game is sitting at $9.99/£6.99 and currently features Steam cards.
Until next time, ready up and good luck Commander!

Before continuing into the meat of this review there is something you need to be aware of, while this game is aesthetically similar to minecraft it needs to be made clear that it is not a clone. The world made of cubes and mining had already been around before minecraft, and moreover its an aesthetic that is not something minecraft owns. If you can't get past the "all cube based games are minecraft copies" then stop reading here, onto the meat.
Pros:
1. This is a common one yet still important, the option to play with high or low difficulty in finding ore, the strength of hostiles, and even obtaining the energy you will so dearly need throughout the game. This is important as being able to enjoy the game from both a higher level and casual standpoint is a must.
2. The hostiles, they are exactly what should be in a game like this, instead of only straight forward hit you and the face type ememies you have an enemy that will attach itself to your conveyor belts and such and devour all your ores making its nest ( the hivemind ) larger, and a little stealth cube thing that will drain power from your mining set up underground. Better yet, they still include a straight forward hit you in the face mob, and a little or dropping resource mob to boot for your tin needs.
3. Instead of making you dig out a staircase, one of the most tedious  hardships one usually faces in "cube games", this game offers a high powered grappling hook, you can dig straight down and then grapple back up, this may seem overpowered however it will already take you quite some time to acquire resources and set up your automated mining and power system, if getting back to the surface were to take forever each time this game would be rendered unplayable by those of us who just dont have enough time.
4. The automation that can be achieved in this game is satisfying, when you go from having to run back in forth to your copper mine set up to watching the copper roll in on a conveyor into your hopper then into your smelter, and at the moment you are looking at the 200+ stack of copper, you will feel a level of satisfaction on par with properly heating a plate of pizza rolls and not burning your tongue and throat.
Cons:
1. Despite what I said earlier about the hostiles, the game could probably use a bit more in this area, if you know what you are doing they are pretty easy to handle as is, there doesnt need to be too much more of this but some for sure.
2. The learning curve, if you dont watch some videos, you are likely to flounder about having no idea what you are doing, this does hurt the game quite a bit. If you are against checking out some videos to figure things out this might be the deciding factor for you.
3. Being a little to intense with the autmation, if you arent a fan creating (sometimes) complex systems to acquire, smelt, and convert your ore into useful objects then this game just isnt for you.
4. The name, if you have played the old fortresscraft, then you go in expecting something quite different from what you will get, it is misleading and could be the leave a sour impression depending on whether you did your research or not.
Conclusion:

Epic game.  Quite feature-rich and playable, while still being in active (and community engaged) development, yet designed with the innate desire (I would say promise, if this wasn't the world of software with its ever-emergent unknowable bugs) that its development will never force a world reset.  The dev is on the forums almost daily, actively engaging with users re: feature tweak/addition suggestions, bug reports, balancing issues... rather than buying a buggy in-development game and getting cryptic or dismissive responses to your suggestions/issues from the obvious PR arm of things (as opposed to the techies who know what the bleep you're talking about), you're buying Minecraft-esque access to a living, /thriving/ beta version, with much less endemic issues than Minecraft, ALONG WITH front-row tickets to real-life large-scale game development unfolding in front of your eyes.
And, it is incredibly well-optimized when it comes to visual/computing-resource playability.  My favorite feature of the game, far and away, is found not in the gameplay, but in the settings menu: click a checkbox, set your target framerate, and the game will take ahold of the quality and render distance settings in order to keep you achieving that.  In a frenetic base with umpteen-gazillion things going on, it'll automatically turn down shadows and maybe kill the render distance - just like our IRL brains would tend to focus on a small subset of the goings-on in a real hectic factory - while during landscape exploration, you can get the voxel equivalent of Skyrim's brilliant vistas.  (Hint to DJ: World-gen structures of awesomeness maybe?)
Geeky stuff aside, the gameplay... wait, never mind about "geeky stuff aside."  If you just want another alien shoot-em-up with resource management and base-building mechanics in the tactical background, then this game isn't for you.  If you want a tower-defense game where mobsKilled is proportional to resourcesAvailable through some arcana, this isn't the game for you.  If you want another (Modded) Minecraft, where you have the option that the base can be there just for aesthetics, or for helping you The Player become the Great Lone Warrior and Loot-Collector of Your Infinite Domain (not that many take this option, but from some of the forum posts, quite a few do), this isn't the game for you.
BUT, if you want a game that blends ALL these elements, plus ever-present environmental factors, automation systems that would appeal to Rube Goldberg and Henry Ford alike, and a strong requirement to Go Forth and Explore... then as long as you can handle the irreducible complexities of such a system, this IS the game for you.  This is the game for the MacGyvers of Minecraft, the Fords of Factorio, the Kings of Kerbal, who want to apply their problem-solving, epic-failing, and grand-constructing skills to an infinite-yet-efficient landscape and a stable-yet-expanding game mechanics platform (with official modding support much closer than with Minecraft).  If you're geeky, 10/10 would recommend.

Pros:

+successfully mixes elements of lite puzzling, action RPG, and hack 'n' slash
+it's a pretty long campaign
Cons:
-the controls can be clumsy (using 360 controller)
-the worlds are realtively uninspired and poorly detailed
-it gets lonely in many levels because there just isn't much there
-often very repetitive: spammed by the same enemies, bosses require wash-rinse-repeat playstyle
-it's like a bullet hell of hack 'n slash. Bosses and harder enemies can seem unaffected by endless attacks
I recommend it on sale. How long walking down the same corrodors, fighting the same enemies, or seeing bland backgrounds can keep your attention, however, will depend.

Rome: Total War is a great game. You know this game came out in 2004 and twelve years later this game managed to heavily impress me. From the small part of diplomatic relations to the absolute massive battle scenes, the game just immediately sucked me in. Now the Total War games had never really been a big thing to me up until this moment so I was just a bit dubious about how much this game would appeal to me, but I am a history buff and I was trying to find a way to spend the summer so I picked it up during the sale. What I found was an actually really good game that managed to combine the turn base parts with the real time strategy.
The game as said is split into two types of strategy. The first part is map screen. From here you manage your settlements and your armies. You can upgrade your towns and recruit new units. From here you can also send out your diplomats to other factions in order to institute trade agreements and forge alliances for wars. The diplomats have actually quite a bit that they can discuss with the other factions. You can make demands such has making them hand over a territory or you can create a trade agreement that can help your income or just allow them military access to other parts of the world. Another thing that impressed me is that they can reject your offer and make counter offers. This really does feel like an actual negotiation rather than just a basic “I declare peace or war thing.” One thing I’m going to say though is that there is a severe problem with the lack of anything to really during peace time. In the end though the map screen is fantastic turn based strategy.
Now as for the actual battle screens it is one the greatest parts of the game. The sieges and the battles are just so massive that it is impossible to be swept away by it. The fights aren’t too complicated. It doesn’t take long to figure the strengths and weaknesses and of each unit. Just know when to charge and how to flank the enemy and that’s rather easy to pick up. What makes it really work though is just the basic ability to pause the game and figure out your positions and where each unit should go. This takes a lot the panicking and stress out of other strategies that usually takes me out of most strategy games. The units are widely varied and it is rather cool to see the progress of your units to much more powerful troops.
In the end what really sells the game is just the absolute scale it has. The game just feels massive and every advancement you do makes you feel more powerful. If you haven't played a Total War, game before, and even if you have, olden but golden Rome: Total War is no let down.
Based during the age when ancient empires were being built, RTW is both a RTS and TBS in one game.
The Campaign mode(TBS) allows you to take control of a historical civilization and take its humble roots and create an empire. Improve and manage your economy, infastructure, military, taxes, and more. Quell uprisings and keep your people happy. Lash out upon the world: wage war and wield clever diplomacy to accomplish your goals. Take on the world all at once or one piece at a time: create your empire as you feel fit!
When engaging enemy forces for battle in Campaign and when playing Multiplayer(RTS), utilize a variety of faction-unique units to dominate your opponents! There are many, many playstyles to fit your taste; no one strategy is going to be your all-time winner, though some playstyles may be more comfortable for you. These battles can range from petty skirmishes to all-out conflict. No one battle is ever the same.
The graphics are decently good, the gameplay is superb, all in a single package. The only downsides lay in occasional multiplayer trolls and that the RTS combat can be a bit overwhelming/arcade-like since it can be very fast-paced at times. Get used to that, and you have yourself a wonderful game.

My first playthrough of (the imaginatively titled) Dark Night:  A whole lot of black with the words "press Space to skip" on-screen, and a highly meandering and poorly recorded female voice going on about...something or other.  After about thirty seconds or more of said all-but-black screen and the♥♥♥♥♥♥poor audio "atmos", I wonder if I'm just meant to press Space anyway, and...oh no, wait, the title of the game has come up.  Right.  I WAS supposed to wait then...good thing I didn't just skip ahead, and miss any of that all-important exposition.
Righty-o, then:  It's a dark night, some girl with a distant, echoey voice is, er, taunting me or flirting with me or something, and...oh, the game has started!  I appear to be in a sparsely-furnished room, and...well, let's have a look around, shall we?  Oh, another sparsely-furnished room and, apart from the odd bed or table with absolutely nothing on top of them, the ONLY decorations around here appear to be...CREEPY DOLLS!  Gee, between the title and the scenery, I wonder what kind of game this is going to be?  It's certainly not heavily influenced by, say, the writings of Stephen King...in which♥♥♥♥♥♥boring folk with INCREDIBLY normal lives - and INCREDIBLY NORMAL HOMES - are most unexpectedly terrorized by the supernatural.  No, the character you play in this game clearly WANTS to be terrorized by spooky things, or else he WOULDN'T LIVE IN SUCH A RIDICULOUS ♥♥♥♥ING HOUSE.  Anyway, back to the game...
First playthrough proceeds for a short while, a couple more otherwise-empty rooms with spooky dolls and...oh!  Appears I have a creepy Nosferatu-type dude who's decided to HANG HIMSELF in one of my many empty rooms!  Isn't that quaint of him?  Oh, the game seems to be warning me that I'm coming up on 1.30am, and I do recall it telling me something about things getting hairy right about th -
Oh.  My screen appears to have frozen.  Wait ten seconds, move mouse a bit...no, game has definitely crashed.  Ahem.  Does happen, even to the best of games, I suppose.  Excuse me while I just restart this again...
Second playthrough.  My expectations are, needless to say, EXTREMELY high by this stage.  Start off much the same, spartan rooms, creepy dolls, guy who's hung himself in my house...find a key, open some doors...oh, look, a hole in the floor, presumably to a basement or something...was that a message which just came up on the screen super-quickly and I neglected to read it and hey, it must be pretty close to 1.30am now and...AAAARRRRGHHH!!  HIGHLY EFFECTIVE JUMP-SCARE, I MUST SAY!!!!  But, er...I was supposed to avoid this...HOW, exactly?!
Third playthrough.  Decide to head straight down the hole this time.  Get jump-scared by same (completely un-scary, come to think of it) guy again, even though it's definitely NOT 1.30am yet.
Fourth playthrough.  Don't get far before game crashes again.  Nearly taking my WHOLE COMPUTER with it, this time.  Cheers for that.
Fifth playthrough.  Not gonna let this game beat me!  Find some stairs leading up which are INCREDIBLY well-hidden, considering that it DOESN'T appear to be an attic, and assuming there ever was any PRACTICABLE intent behind whoever designed this place, architecturally-speaking.  And I'll be buggered if I can see any good "hiding places", like I'm allegedly supposed to look for, especially when I can't CLOSE ANY DOORS BEHIND ME, or even CROUCH DOWN...eek, nearly 1.30am...oops, crashed again.
Sixth playthrough.  Find a hiding place, behind a cupboard, and manage to get to 1.30am without the game crashing.  I think the game is warning me to find another hiding place, but I’m really not sure, ‘cause it’s the same warning which sometimes seems to flash up, like, ten seconds after I ENTER A ROOM, irrespective of whether I've found a hiding place or not.  So I'll be ♥♥♥♥ed if I have any idea what this game even CALLS a hiding spot, much less how you're supposed to effectively creep around from one to the next and...oh, jump-scared again!  By the same actually-very-ordinary-looking guy.
Seventh playthrough...actually, I lie, there isn't one.  I concede defeat.  This game has officially beaten me, and my limited patience.  This game can honestly EAT MY BROWN, STEAMING♥♥♥♥♥♥NUGGETS, along with all the smart♥♥♥♥♥♥♥who are bound to come along and ask me how I can possibly write a review for a game with so little "time" up.  You know how I can write a review with so little time up?  I'll tell you how I can write a review with so little time up.  BECAUSE ANY ♥♥♥♥ING FOOL CAN TELL WITHIN TEN ♥♥♥♥ING SECONDS OF STARTING THE GAME UP THAT IT'S GOING TO BE A STINKING PILE OF BLITHERING MONKEY♥♥♥♥♥♥♥  Good thing that you people have masochists like myself who just CAN'T ♥♥♥♥ING HELP OURSELVES, isn't it now?!
Having said that, I'm definitely looking forward to the sequel:  Bright Night.  Or perhaps they should save that one for third, and just do Medium-Lit Night in-between?  And hopefully the devs will learn how to bring the rest of the game up to the level of their admittedly well-done jump-scares by then, 'cause ♥♥♥♥ knows, THERE IS ABSOLUTELY NOTHING ELSE WHICH WORKS IN THIS GAME.  Not the scenery, not the "enemy" models, not the "stealth" mechanics...NOTHING.
Man, I tell you, these cheap, quickly-made, cynically-minded "horror" game cash-ins make me SO ♥♥♥♥ING MAD.  Can't wait for the next one.

The main part of the game is a string of tactical battles tied together into a campaign. The core of the battle system is the action points. You spend them to move units, to attack enemies, and to deploy new units on the battlefield. More powerful units take more APs to deploy (for example, you have to spend 1 AP to deploy a jeep, but a tank or an artillery piece needs 4 APs). Occupying neutral bases increases the number of APs you can spend per turn. Occupying enemies' bases also robs them of this crucial resource.
Between battles you upgrade the base, research unit upgrades, and build more units to replace losses and to prepare for the next challenge. You also get unit components as loot. You can attach the components to unit types, making them even more powerful. Some of the components have trade-offs, for example, you can get regeneration at the price of the incleased AP cost to deploy the unit or increase attack while decreasing defense. The mechanics are not overly complicated but still leave ample room for interesting decisions.

Bits and pieces of CoV are like other games I've played, but taken as a whole, this is something unique.  It combines elements of base and army building with its core focus, tactical battlefield strategy.
There are two phases to the game: (1) base/unit building; (2) tactical battlefield strategy.
Base/unit building takes place between the tactical missions as your spaceship flies from one region to the next. The travel time of your spaceship (shown in hours/days) determines how much time you have to build up your base and army. You can go over that time limit by refusing to begin the mission when your spaceship lands, but (I believe) that leads to penalties at the start of the mission.
This is where strategic planning really shines. What should you build? How should you upgrade your units for this particular mission?
The number and type of units available to deploy on the battlefiled is largely dependent upon what you choose to focus on prior to the mission, and that has real consequences on how successful (or unsuccsessful) your attempt will be.
Should you fail a mission, you can pick up at the start of the build phase so you can choose to make and upgrade different units for your second attempt.
Tactical battlefield strategy is based on an "Action Points" resource system. It requires a certain number of action points to deploy each unit, 1 AP to move a unit, and 1 AP to attack with a unit. Juggling these points is a large part of the stratgy. You also need to be tactical about where you place your units and how you use them during your turn. You can bank action points or use them, and as the mission progresses and you capture map locations, you'll gain more AP each turn.
You also have access to a hero unit on each mission, which is powerful but not overpowered (a good thing).
From what I have seen so far, there is very little luck involved in gameplay. You're dealing with pure numbers rather than a damage range. Critical strikes are the lone exception, and a unit's crit chance is always visible. This makes the tactical play feel more like chess than other games where numbers can wildly fluctuate. Pure strategists will love it.
The story feels more like a generic backdrop to the rest of the game. So while there is a story being told, it's not what's going to attract most folks.
At this time (in early access), the game shows a tremendous amount of potential, and it's already quite good.

There is PvP arena with army builder too. Hope, the matchmaking will now be faster with more people joining the game.

Definitely has got some promise for multiplayer.

It's... Incredibly intricate, interesting, and promising at the current state of it.  But that doesn't mean that it's something that everyone will find enjoyment in.  Taking survival elements that're comparable to DayZ and Rust with mechanics for needing food or proper medical attention, crafting elements that put Minecraft to shame, terraforming elements and potential building mechanics that seem almost obscenely intricate... Time consuming would be an understatement of the year though; in a few hours in a single-player game with the skills-gain set to a hundred times the base, it still took me the better part of three hours to get merely the most primative toolset.
It seems like one of the best potential games for creating, influencing, and enjoying the fruits of your and you friend's labor I've seen in a long time.  That feeling of actually getting together an actual township, of raising together against a common enemy to defend the little you've scrapped together seems like it will be absolutely incredible.
I'll need to wait for some stability updates and some of the other promised features before I find myself playing it too terribly often, with two or three hourly disconnects from servers, but I'm certainly looking forwards to them.

I've logged over 200 hours on R:TW off Steam over the past few years, and it's one of my favorite Total War titles to date. Great micromanagement, great immersion, and caters to many playstyles.
Extremely well thought-out and put together and with a very approachable learning curve, ROME puts you in the shoes of the head of a Roman Great House. Take on the Barbarians in the North as the Julii, wage war with the Greeks in the east as the Brutii, or dominate the deserts of Africa as the Scipii. As you expand a facet of the great Roman Republic, you eventually must take on your neighboring Romans as time passes. With either popular support within the Senate or with the Plebs, or by whitlling down your alliance with the other Houes, civil war breaks out and you can take Rome itself for yourself, and crush your past Roman allies. After completing a campaign as a Roman house, you unlock a new package of factions to play, all quite a bit more difficult than your Roman campaign.
In the expansion Barbarian Invasion, you face a lot more challenges this go around, the Roman Empire is suffering, plagued with Rebels on each side, and taking on enemies on all side. You can choose to repair Rome to it's former glory as the Western/Eastern Empire, or watch Rome crumble as a barbarian faction. From the Saxons in the North, to the Hunnic horde in the east, you have the same template ROME provided, but add hordes, changed regions, religious conversion and new units/buildings.

Fun fun fun fun FUN. Slick, fluid, fast gameplay reminescent of doom (original) or demonsteele, interesting customization, silly but great dialogues, high difficulty that doesn't feel too bullet spongy.
Some notes on the gameplay:
- Unlike in the 2013 game, weapon switching is almost instantaneous.
- The quick melee button has been very cleverly replaced with weapon switch to melee.
To clarify, when you change to a melee weapon in combat you do a slash while unsheathing. It looks great and plays even better.
- Dashing is infinite, but many enemies can keep up with you in terms of speed and you'll be forced to dodge in particular directions.
- Enemies will follow you even through rough terrain. Some can get stuck sometimes though.
- There is a skill that allows all your weapons to be reloaded every 5 seconds. Finally a FPS where I don't have to reload stuff. Just switch out and it's magically reloaded like I'm doomguy.
Particularly of note, one shining gameplay mechanic is that your weapons usually force staggers/knockdowns on enemies if they pack enough of a punch, and this compensates very well for the additional health the enemies have in higher difficulties.
Without this mechanic, you end up with some atrocity like doom4 in which any difficulty beyond games journalist will give you peashooters instead of real weapons.
It's a bit short on content variety and the story is weak, but it's still great fun.
The game is an absolute blast and probably one of the best fps of all time. Highly recommanded.

Take it from someone who has put way more hours in this game than is even remotely neccessary: this game is the pinnacle of horror games to date. Frictional Games nailed the formula with Penumbra: Black Plague, but it wasn't until Amnesia: TDD that they got it out to the mainstream public. They effectively showed that a good atmosphere will absolutely sell the game, that its not just the jumpscares that make the game terrifying, its the way the player reacts to the enviroment, the way the sounds, the music, the level design, all come together to actually make the player terrified. At the same time, with Amnesia: MFP, they showed that too much atmosphere, and not enough jump scares, can make the game lacking.
Amnesia: TDD has the perfect amounts of both atmosphere and jump scares. The atmosphere is foreboding, it makes you fear the oncoming jumpscare that you know is happening, and the jump scares are actually there for you to learn that the game isn't just messing around. Its incredibly well paced.
The puzzles are fairly intuitive too, they tend to be challenging, but not too difficult. As long as you search all the areas, you're bound to find the solution.
The engine too is also quite remarkable. Having played around in the editor myself, they allow for a lot of interesting things to be done. While, strictly horror focused, anyone with enough drive and modeling/texturing software could make their own fully fledged game in the engine.
The only downside that I will offer: the plot. At the start, it feels nice and fresh, interesting even. Yet, the eventual twist was predictable, and the ending felt rushed and was largely unsatisfying.

An interesting concept, being a blend between minecraft and factorio
It's decent enough, however I personally found that the early game suffers from "many paths, only one that is any good"
The tutorial teaches you about power automation, which is good.
The tutorial does not teach you that you can put multiple ores into the same hopper, and the game obscures that fact by only showing you the most recent item.  It seems you 100% need to do this to get your smelter operating with any sort of efficiency.  It should be part of the tutorial.
It feels like giving players access to the research path before they have _built_ the smelter upgrades and the suit & robot power upgrades is a mistake.  It consumes a ton of resources and takes focus away from the income engine.
There's lots of other odds and ends you can waste resources on early game, research is just the one that got me.
So the early game is not as broken as I thought, however I suspect it's been optimised for someone who already knows how to play.  New comers without existing knowledge are likely to get harshly punished for sub-optimal play.
This is something that both minecraft and factorio seem to handle quite well but this game drops the ball on

The Two Worlds II Game is a great RPG game that has a lot of adventure game like elements in it, I think it will appeal most to PC game players that likes to use character to run around and explore and do a lot of battles along the way. The game has good support for gamepad for full enjoyment of the the game I must recommend using a gamepad such as the Logitech F510/F710 or similar. The game offers large maps to explore and if one prefers one can simply roam the maps and gather loot and ressources taken fromn enemies, animals, plants or found in maze like caves, chests or if skill good enough from places in buildings entered by picking locks or getting money from gambling or pickpocketing (both difficult unless high skill or great luck) - of course one can also get new objects both through quest and trade and one can trade objects/loot away also. High Lock picking skill is a must in this game. Also don't overlook that you can also scroll on teleportation maps so that you can travel to previous locations.
A prominent feature is also the ability to, after breaking down loot into elemental components, being able to combine components and to upgrade items (both demanding aquired and spent skill points for abilities). Though the player have a map of locations then in some cases in can be difficult to find a few of the locations (or to get there).
The game is to large extend non-linear but as it is story driven one ofcourse must perform some tasks to unlock other tasks or possibility of access to places...

Two Worlds II is a kinda fun rpg whit alot of unused potential.
The game is obvious a port and the mechanics are a bit clunky and not as smooth and responsive as it could be. The Story is a bit unrealistic and kinda shallow, Some might even guess how its gona end before geting halfway through the story!
When it comes to the Story it's linearly and seems to try cover alot of diffrent cultures (European, Asian and Arabian-African) and most of the time you need to help others with random tedious quest in order to progress. The dialogue in most conversations are boring and uninteresting and even cuts itself off or doesent fit the mouth animation on evry charachter, but the most unsatisfying is the main characters bland voice which more or less kill the mood of evry conversation whit the npc's.
One thing where Two Worlds II stands out from most rpg's is the skill tree or development, you are not forced to go down one specific route but have the option to mix magic with stealth and/or other abilitys, for example you could become a two handed water mage (might not be the optimal route but it exist) but sadly the strength lies in the mage class where you can create and customise extremly powerful spells which makes the other classes/abilitys inferior to the mage class/abilitys.
one thing alsoe worth noting is that the monster level does not scale well and most of the time the enemys are way to easy or kills you in one hit but the Ai isnt that good which make surviving kinda easy regardless.
One thing that realy bothers me is the potential of exploring the game could have had. There are boats you could use to explore the sea but there isnt alot to se in the sea and the boats are not a fast method of travling even the horses arent that great of travling becouse your character has a pretty got pace to his speed and horses can be a bother to find and they cant fast travel with you.
in the end the game is still kinda fun its just sad that it have hidden potential and the story that isn't interesting enough. for an rpg i would give it 5,0/10 becouse there are some elements to it that makes the game somewhat diffrent from other rpg's and works well in the rpg genre!

Original Review: Two Worlds Two has a dumb name, as a consequence of being a sequel to a game with "Two" in the title, and is generally pretty weird. It's huge, the magic system is crazy, the world is beautiful, and there's a few interesting quests and plot elements, but even still it's not for everyone. There's some really terrible voice acting, which is a bigger knock than you might expect as the worst character in that regard is the main character. Each world area you get to is deceptively smaller than the previous, also, slowly constricting you and forcing you down a main quest path that stalls in the final third of the game. The combat isn't 100% great, either.
Even so, I feel it was unfairly maligned thanks to its predecessor's reputation and an overly-long tutorial. If you can get ahold of it on the cheap, I'd say it's worth trying out if you're a fan of open-world fantasy. There's a chance you might fall in love with at least one element of this weirdly disparate game.
It's original but some puzzles are unclear and the game is really too short, so it's not worth the price.

At the request of the community manager I gave the game another shot today, 2015-06-09.  Two hours of gameplay, 0 fun was had.  None.  So here's a few observations from my time playing, and a brief summary at the end.  Feel free to make your own decision.
PROS:
- Players seemed pretty cool, showed me some stuff, let me try out combat before I gave up on it.  I got the impression if I'd decided to really dig into the game they'd have happily been right there to help me get into it.
CONS:
- I couldn't come up with any pros about the game itself.  Just not a fun game for me at all, but I feel like I gave it a solid shot.  After a total of three hours of gameplay (one hour at launch, two recently) I did not enjoy a single second, a solitary aspect of the game.  I cannot think of one single other game I've ever played that was just singularly without enjoyment.  Maybe it's just not for me.
- MMO-lite.  Ever want to play an MMO, with all the ability cooldowns, HUD clutter, various chat windows and whatnot but didn't feel connected to the people in the community?  Did you ever go, man, I wish I could MMO but with a small collection of people I could know like a close friend because we play together day in and day out rather than these large groups most MMOs are for?  Yes?  Well maybe try LiF because that's it.  It's all the fun and engagement of a generic bland MMO, and with all the community and simultaneous players of your average online FPS.  It's like they took the two most lackluster aspects of two things and crammed them together.  I -really- don't like MMOs though, so this might be far more of an issue for me personally than you.  YMMV.
- Grind.  Dear GOD the grind.  Everything, and I mean everything seems to be: 1) initiate action.  2) grab a drink, browse the web, whatever while this bar fills up.  3) repeat.  There's no engagement with what you're doing, no immersion with the animation or the activity, and it's like it was done to just forcibly pad out the time it takes to do literally anything in game.  I got the direct impression as I watched this little bar fill up time and time again someone felt loading screens were the best thing ever, so designed an entire gameworld filled with miniature versions of them.  Based on what I'd seen while playing, accomplishing anything in game is akin to a second job.
- Combat.  "Think mount and blade" was what one of the players told me, and it was somewhat true.  The controls for swinging melee weapons was very similar with the 'shift mouse and left click to control direction' but the combat was slow and sluggish, moreso than mount and blade even.  The words "Think mount and blade" kept coming up in my head too, as I watched my axe pass through my enemy again and again without doing anything, and randomly to strike for seemingly no reason.  I didn't feel like I was in any sort of control.  I'm sure some blind stat / skill combo in the background was to blame but that hardly makes me enjoy the game anymore.  Also, related to combat...
- Popups.  RELIVE THE GLORY DAYS OF AOL, modem screeching in the background as your screen is suddenly flooded with popups!  Click here to receive no more alerts in your face that your attempt to get a stick off of a tree was unsuccessful.  Then, immediately afterwards, an alert that you found no flint when searching the ground!  Oh-ho, but click here for no more alerts about flint on the ground.  Now you get an alert that you took damage in combat, which, by the way, also takes you out of the ability to attack back until you reactivate mouse control.  Why is this default?  Why is there no clear option to make all popups show up in the system window and why do popups have to rip me out of the gameworld and into the interface mode?  Also, protip, you start the game in interface mode.  Push tab to control the game.  It's in the help file, but it's still frustrating to deal with.

A lot of people have been asking my opinion on LiF- so I figured I'd go ahead and write a lengthy review on this game and lay down (what I think) you should consider if you're going to drop the $40 for this game in its current alpha state.
First off, if you are someone who expects to be slaying dragons, fighting other people fully decked out in plate armor with a war horse and a golden lance within 30 minutes, and destorying them in 8 seconds with Mount and Blade style combat- do not even remotely consider this game.
At the exact time of this review I have sunk about 7 hours into this game (and of course plan on playing much more) and have managed to JUST NOW build myself a small shack and obtain a little iron to POSSIBLY create into tools. Mind you this was done with the help of around 6-7 other people who were working in extreme cooperation with one another. Just to give you a little sense of how "hardcore" this game really is when it comes to progression. (I was also playing on a server with hardly any skill multiplier, there are servers where you can level things much faster and thus progress with greater speed if you're looking for a more solo experience)
Now down to picking out the major aspects of the game people wish to know about:
1. Combat: Being someone who loves the fighting aspects of games, I will admit that Life is Feudal's alpha combat is nothing to write home about. 3/4s of your swings WILL miss until you get the range of your weapon (which is different for each weapon) and once you've actually got the combat down you will still have difficulty hitting. It is /not/ Mount and Blade combat. Is it close? Yes- but it is not M&B. Trust me. However, there is only alpha and it will likely get MUCH better and I can certainly see a fantastic combat system coming out of this. All in all, the combat at the moment is basically an unpolished combat of what can make a great system. 6/10
2. Crafting: Crafting is definetly one of the stronger aspects of this game. It is rich and complex, certainly has massive potenial to be added onto. Even in its current state there is quite a lot to do. However I have been met with some pretty strange bugs that cause me to crash (which is totally to be expected in the alpha testing phase, but I am after all reviewing the alpha) and some recipes are implemented but do not even work, for example the bow and torch. Overall, crafting is going to be very good when it is refined and expanded on, and even in its current state it is very useable. 7/10
3. UI: I am bunching UI and Mechanics together due to the fact that there isn't much to talk about regarding them. The User interface is clearly in an early stage, but much like the crafting, very useable. There is a bit of a learning curve when you first get into the game (trying to figure out how the hell to do anything basically) but once you over come this, you should be able to experiment and figure out everything else on your own. Don't expect this game to spoon feed you, and honestly after 7 hours, I'm sure there is stuff that even I haven't figured out yet. 6/10
4. Skills and Mechanics: The skills system is still very much a work in progress, I'd say about 1/4(?) of the skills have still yet to be implemented. However, that doesn't detract from the complexity and potential that the skill system has. From plant gathering to cutting down trees, to using a sickle effectively as a weapon under "milita service", the skill system is impressive. One of the coolest in my opinion is the formation skills when in a unit, I'd write more about it but it is something easier looked up. As of right now I have only encountered one bug with the skills and that is when you pray it actually respawns you (for some odd reason). The skills system is definetly going to be something to enjoy once it is fully completed. 8/10
Now my final thoughts on whether you should drop the $40 or not: As you can see in a lot of what I said, these systems will be great "once they're complete" and take that exactly how it's said. This is without a doubt an alpha, and if you can't get past the crashes, bugs, and imperfect systems- do not spend your money. If this was around... $20 I would say you should still give it a go, but this price tage is a bit steep. However- if you wish to support the development process and you can get past the grime thats covering the shine, you're going to enjoy the living hell out of this game and I would highly recommend it.
Hopefully this helps some people make their decisions.

Two Worlds II is a rather enjoyable experience. While it doesn't certainly have the quality BioWare or Bethesda RPGs tend to have, it has some unique features that make it worth looking into, at least.
One of these is the combat. The combat in this game is very fluid and diverse. You can choose to play as a warrior, an archer or a mage. There are no preset classes, you gradually become better at your chosen role through leveling up the needed attributes and skills. Sort of like Oblivion in that regard. However you have a set of active combat skills as well, and these vary greatly, from breaking someone's block to countering someone's attack while you're doing the blocking yourself. Even when switching from blunt to slash weapons. Archery is usually done via auto aiming, but the active combat skills that an archer can use will require you to use manual aiming, something which is very welcome. The cream of the crop though, is magic. If you've ever played Magicka, you know how crazy you can get by combining spells to make something truly unique. Two Worlds II? It's the same way. You can customize and build your spells thoroughly, and it never gets old, providing a really rewarding way to play.
However, if you're a completionist, and upgrade your equipment well, which is done by destroying unused weapons and armor to gather raw materials to reforge them as upgrades to your current set, (very neat feature) this game will be really easy save for the final battle, thankfully, which is actually challenging.
Having at least two different forms of combat is important at any given time for the enemies in this game are plenty and each have their own specific weaknesses. While some will die anyway by just button mashing, it'll take a lot longer if you use the wrong weapon.
The plot is.... to say the least, confusing. The pacing is all over the place and I was disappointed with the abrupt and sudden ending, though you can choose to play after the game ends, thankfully, either to tie loose ends or to experience the pirate expansion. (i've not played it so no opinion on it) You do get to understand it fully by the time you're done, but I do wonder if one would have needed to play the first Two Worlds to know everything.
The world is quite large and varied with several continents and remote islands with loot ready to explore. You can actually buy a boat and be able to sail it in this game at your own will, something I really got into, except the content for this was sorely lacking. And while I did mention the world is large, which it is, some of it are just smoke and mirrors as 70% of the largest continent isn't even accessible, all you'll get is a "Can't go this way" message and you get teleported out. -_-
There are horse races and several faction quests, complete with a gladiatorial arena series of battles. This game took a LOT from Oblivion, but it's different enough to not come off as a ripoff.
The graphics in this game are quite pleasing to the eye, and yes, it has a LOT of options to customize it perfectly should you choose to do so. Nothing but thumbs up from me in this regard.
The music was okay. Nothing special about it. It did its job but sometimes it could get quite repetitive.
The voice acting was not that great. No performances came off as fantastic to me, while some other few cases were completely crap. Your main character loved to sound tough, and he NEVER, NEVER shuts up. Whether he finds or kills an enemy, opens a chest and goes swimming, he'll say one of 5 lines every single time. Get ready to hear him repeat them hundreds of times before the game's finished, which by the way is a bit long, though I seriously expected it to be a lot longer given the game world.
If you've went through all the greats in the RPG genre and need a fix for some more, you could do a lot worse than picking up Two Worlds II. While it certainly doesn't feel like a polished game, it's got its heart in the right place.

I rarely have bad opinions about games and I really wanted to give this a positive review, but I just can't.
I usually never stumble across game breaking bugs or even common ones, and when I checked what others said about it I really didn't think I would encounter literally all of them.
To start with pros, the only real ones are the fact that the idea of the game is quite okay for a clicker/idling game, the layout is unique (or at least less common as far as I know), and the soundtrack for some reason fits with the overall vibe of the game and its art style.
The problem is that the game is really, really grindy in the beginning until you are allowed to get walkers (basically auto-clickers), so you'll end up getting tired of the soundtrack too. As far as the rest of the game.. I don't know, because I came across a bug which was the final straw for me.
I finally managed to get one of those auto-clickers and left the game on while I had something else to do away from my pc, and when I came back, I saw it had crashed my steam client completly. Sure, annoying, but it wouldn't have stopped me. What stopped me was that when I started it up again, all my progress was wiped out. Almost 2 hours of manual clicking in the hopes of getting to a better part of the game, just gone.
In my ~2 hours of actual gameplay (the rest being idling before actually playing the game), the game crashed three times, two of those times causing my steam client to close completly.
The other bugs that I personally found were "bonuses" that appear every once in a while, which give you a bonus of nothing basically, just a text box that spells "BONUS" and sometimes fails to go away for much longer than intended. Also, as far as I played, every upgrade that you can make has a value that increases, but for some reason resets when it reaches a certain one, which in long term would make the game unnecesarily easy. I didn't even know what upgrades did in the beginning, or how to properly place things, because the only "tutorial" you get is basically "make money", with no further hints, neither in the beginning nor as your progress in game.
I'm not the only one who's encountered these bugs, I'm almost 100% sure no one has ever been able to actually finish the game (as in get all the achievements properly, if it doesn't have an actual ending). Someone suggested that maybe you could do it if you'd play the whole game in one sitting, but it might not even be possible considering it crashes randomly. You can look through reviews of lots of other unimpressed players or even just through the community hub, you'll see the exact same complaints, if not even more.
I'm really disappointed, because this had a lot of potential and I was really looking forward to playing it. Overall, this game is a good idea, but with a very, very bad execution.
PS: Just because a game costs only $1 it doesn't mean it's allowed to be completly unplayable.

Amnesia is a masterpiece, bringing together all aspects of the horror genera. It is clear to me that this game has a team that clearly has mastered practically every aspect of a consumer-quality, Grade A PC gaming experience. They convinced me into playing again and again every time. The story is ABOVE AND BEYOND what anyone could have hoped for, and it is in the sense of revelation, as a good horror game plays the scene. It works the player as it should, slowly, and then all at once. It emerses you into the world from start to finish, keeping you emotionally bound to the game's protagonist, Daniel. Not only does the game look to involve you Mentally, Psychologically, and Emotionally, but the game has mastered the ability to emerse the player into the story Morally as well, which is a factor that has to be earned by a high quality character plot. The game forces you to, at times, make quick, rash decisions that ultimately affect the game's path, and ensure the further survival of our friend, Daniel. The game is a touching experience put aside the violence and gruesome horror, and truly feel what the main character is enduring. It is as described, and other-worldly experience to step into Daniel's shoes. The way it brings you into the game affects each new player individually, and this is how the moral aspect into play. Will you seek out hateful revenge bound in blind rage, or will you seek to understand Alexander and the others and to realize your fate? You can either keep running or accept destiny... the game forces you to realize the unavoidable.
So will you avoid the truth, or embrace it? All is revealed in the end...

Seven years since the release of Unreal Tournament 2004, and it still stands as a paragon of the FPS genre.  Gameplay is fast and furious, but death is seldom instant, a feat rarely accomplished in today's world of a-bullet-scratched-me-take-cover health regen games.  Health and shields are static, restored only by pickups.  Ammo and weapons must be picked up and are not granted with perks.  Everything from vehicles to weapons to ammo is out in the field and just waiting to be grabbed.  And there is a great variety.
UT2004 features instant-hit weapons, slow moving projectiles with fierce power, inaccurate but fierce automatic weapons, continuous-stream energy weapons, sniper rifles, sticky grenade launchers, and even moving, intelligent mines that can be redirected by the player with a laser.
It's colorful, enjoyeable, open to modding, and perhaps the single best shooter of the last decade, even if it wasn't the most influential.

Lume is a pretty simple point-and-click puzzler. I feel like this works to the game's detriment. I have about 4 hours on record, and honestly, most of that was spent recording a video walkthrough. This game is short enough that it feels like a demo, as opposed to an actual game. For $5.99, I'm glad I picked this up in a bundle--I'd have felt cheated otherwise.
That said, this game is breathtaking in presentation. The graphics are simply gorgeous, and the music lends to the atmophere that ties presentation up with a beautiful bow. The puzzles are fairly unique, but I wouldn't call them challenging. Overall, this is something that could easily kill an hour or so, but there's simply not enough content to justify purchasing the game in any form other than a bundle. I'd like to see a sequel, expansion or update with significantly more content. I might change my tune if that were to happen.
UPDATE: I was unaware of the sequel. Given that the sequel is $20 and adds a mere four hours of content to the game (based on the reviews), I feel as though the sequel should have no bearing on my feelings toward Lume in general.

I been a big civil war buff since I was very young. I read any books or movies I could get on it and I played most of the video games. The first being Robert E. Lee Civil War General the hex game back in 1996, and some time later Sid Meier's Gettysburg, I even played Gettysburg mod for Starcraft because of its awesomeness. So of course I have ridiculous standards, I won't deny that, I will not say this is a bad game, for me it makes me want to go back and play my old favorites. I will just say for a game on this subject I cared about so much to get the thumbs up from me, it would need to give me something more. I feel the developer wanted to take an approach for realism, but this for me has been done, with games like Sid Meires, and better. I loved the unit progression in some of the older titles, where you actually got to upgrade your guns between battles, maybe even some stats for generals.
Pros
+ Progression - after every engagment your casualties carry over to the next one
+ Progression - again the game focuses on one battle, but its not just the lineral historical route of the battle, you get to make choices after every engagment, many strategies were never implemented in the actual battle, but here if you for example win you can chose to hold the hills on the outskirts of town instead of falling back the ridge behind it.
Mix
-+ Multiplayer - There is a multiplayer, can't complain about that, its balanced in ways FPS are, its skill based; can't complain about that either! Its just nothing like the predecesors, its 1v1.. When I think of civil war I think of multiplayer, before there were 'clans' in video games there were very well organized armies in games like Sid Meires that put almost any form on online groups to shame these days. We do not get the 3v3's we use to have back in the day, not much community here.
-+ Realism - I always loved realism in games, In this game the units will do what they want, and the choice to have them unpredictable was a choice by the developer to add realism or in his words: frustration (since thats what actually happend in the civil war, your subordinates didnt always listen to you) I sort of think a better choice would be the ability to give your leaders overall stance orders, like aggressive, or defensive. This would let them do what they want, yet not do something ridiculous like a rouge brigade charging down a hill you wanted them to defend.
Con
- Graphics - They are functional and look good, but the terrain is 2D, the units are sprites,
- Line of Sight - I think this needs some work, its very difficult to figure out where your artillary can actually fire, since half the time if you actually check their LOS they wont actually be firing at units within its range, the best thing to do is to find 1 arty unit that is firing, then put all your artillery on that spot, which is a bit crazy in terms of historical strategy.
I am basically giving it the thumbs up for if its on sale, its not a bad buy at all.

Title:
"Amnesia: The Dark Descent"
Developer(s)/producer(s):
Frictional Games
THQ (retail)
Writer(s):
Mikael Hedberg
Genre(s):
Horror, Survival
Mode(s):
Single-player
General info:
The game was critically well received, earning two awards from the Independent Games Festival and numerous positive reviews.
Originally released independently as a download, the game has since been published in retail by 1C Company in Russia and Eastern Europe as well as THQ in North America. A collection of five short stories set in the world of Amnesia, written by Mikael Hedberg and illustrated by the game's concept artists, was also made available.
In addition, the game's soundtrack is available for purchase and a free content expansion called "Justine" has been released as well as many fan-made expansions and stories.
Gameplay:
In a similar vein to the developer's previous games, Amnesia is an adventure game played from a first-person perspective. The game retains the physical object interaction used in the Penumbra series, allowing for physics-based puzzles and interactions such as opening doors and fixing machinery.
Few in-game objects are operated by toggle; to open a door, for instance, the player must hold down a mouse button and then push (or pull) the mouse. This gives the player stealth, allowing them to peek out a barely-opened door or open it slowly to sneak away, but also adds to the player's sense of helplessness, as it is now entirely possible to attempt to push open a "pull" door whilst danger approaches from behind.
In addition to a health indicator, the player's sanity must be managed.
Being in darkness too long, witnessing unsettling events, or staring at monsters will reduce their sanity, causing visual and auditory hallucinations and drawing the attention of monsters. Light sources help restore sanity, and if none are available the player may use tinderboxes to ignite candles in wall sconces and candelabra, or deploy an oil-burning lantern found near the beginning of the game.
However, the number of tinderboxes and the amount of oil available are both limited, and standing in a light source also makes the player more noticeable to monsters. The player must balance the amount of time they spends in light and shadow. Sanity is fully restored once the player completes an objective or progresses the game's story.
If a monster spots the player, it will chase it until it's out of sight. If spotted, the player must flee, as Amnesia does not give the player access to weapons. The player must then find hiding places or barricade doors with rocks, chairs and other obstacles; however, monsters are capable of tearing down doors in their path and kicking obstacles out of the way, and move extremely fast once they have spotted their prey.
Monsters who lose sight of the player will search for them for a time, but will eventually leave and vanish.Players can also choose to hide in the shadows, at cost of sanity, since the main character ironically enough suffers from Nyctophobia (severe fear of the dark).
Story:
In late August 1839, Daniel, a young man from London, awakens in the dark halls of the Prussian Brennenburg Castle with little to no memory about himself or his past.
All he can remember is his name, that he lives in Mayfair and that something is hunting him. Shortly after awakening, Daniel discovers a note written to himself, from which he learns that he has deliberately erased his own memory, and that he needs to descend into the Inner Sanctum of the castle. There he must kill the baron, a man named Alexander.
The exploration of the dark depths of the castle (following a trail of pink liquid that he seems to have left for himself) is also a journey into his own erased past, as he discovers not only notes and his own journal entries, but experiences visions of past events that took place within the castle's countless chambers - including memories that are not his own.
While Daniel unravels the mysteries of Brennenburg Castle, he also finds himself hunted by a dangerous unearthly presence that manifests itself as a corruption that is slowly covering the castle in fleshy, acidic growths.
As if this was not enough, baron Alexander has sent out his minions to find Daniel - bizarre, zombie-like monsters that are relentlessly hunting him.
Daniel's only hope is to as quickly as possible reach the Sanctum, before he succumbs to either the monstrosities or his own damaged mind...
My opinions:
I was first introduced to this game a couple of years ago, by a classmate who had downloaded it.
He was passing the time by playing it on a break in school and I was watching.
At the time I didn't think much of it and had not yet been introduced properly to the genre of horror-games.
What I do remember, however, is that Amnesia: The Dark Descent was scary to play even whilst sitting in a fully lit room.
My friend - who was a bit of a coward - even hightened the gamma setting in the game, making it lighter (something I would not recommend unless you're a cheater). But even though he had hightened the lighting, we still got scared off our arses when the first jump-scares started to show up.
Besides "Outlast" - which is another brilliant game available here on Steam - Amnesia: The Dark Descent remains in my top five of all horror-games I have ever played. Sure, it was developed with a much smaller budget and by an indie-studio, but that doesn't make it any less of a horrifying experience.
I don't really have that much more to say about this game, except these simple guidelines:
1. Buy it and download it.
2. Play at night, preferably alone and using headphones.
3. Turn off all lights and get ready to get scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥...

I've played a fair number of "D platfirmers. Rayman, Mario, Sonic, super meat boy, donkey kong country, Braid, VVVVVV, LittleBig Planet, and many others.
I can honestly say that out of the many 2D platofrmers that have been revolutionary, aged like a fine wine, introduced the genre's most defining ascepts and created the genre as a whole, Shovel Knight and its currently released dlc campaign (specter of torment coming in April of this year), Shovel Knight feels like what the genre has been climbing up to for 30 damn years now, and Shovel Knight is the summit. Whilst there are stand out titles on the genre like Super Mario Bros & Super Mario World which made it as popular as it was back in the late 80s early 90s, Super Meat Boy made it ball crushingly hard, Braid gave it a compelling story that weaved its way into the gameplay and actually posed the player a question that few games ever ask (see Spec ops: The Line as another example of that, sorry but no spoilers here), and VVVVVV traded in a genre staple for a carefully crafted and meticulously made gameplay mechanic that never felt like a burden or a gimmick.
Shovel Knight stands out for simply being incredile. It's taken the gameplay elements from games like early Mega Man, Duck Tales, Zelda 2, various Super Mario games, etc. and polished them to an outstandingly mirror shine. Its controls are an absolute dream, jumping and the consequential descent feel just right, its ice physics for Polar Knight's stage are easily controllable, it made a ♥♥♥♥ing water level not a ballcrushing nightmare, it has enough story to keep you engaged, but the story is but on the backburner for the gameplay at all times, and it is testing of the player's abilities at all times, but it does something that every game, not just platformer, should do to some degree: teach the player a specific level's twist in a safe environment. Take the Ice level for example. It has snow that floats in mid-air, and when its touched it falls to the grounds and covers the spikes beneath it in snow, meaning you can walk on it. How does it teach you this, you ask? You fall from the previous screen onto some, which save you. You fall onto the snow, which then immeidately covers the spikes and saves your life. Then you think, " maybe the other bits of snow will stop me from dying on spikes too", so you try it and it works! Then you can take on some platforming chalenges and enemies while on the snow covered spikes, and eventually fight polar knight with the snow on the ground.

Rich world-building environment with emotional characters, and interesting NPCs; harkening back to the depth of feel of older classics like Final Fantasy 6. They even patched in an epilogue to offer a glimpse into the future of the characters' lives after the events of the story, which does a good job in finalizing the chapter of Ara Fell.
Pros:
- Rich Story
- Character development
- Ability to control stat level-ups is cool
- Controls
- The soundtrack is amazing!
Cons:
- Very easy, with no hard mode option (more below)
- Character development (yes, both pro and con)
- Replayability is non-existent. One and done, no reason to revisit.
--Character development
On one hand, the characters have great detail and a clearly developed personality. This is wonderful and helps to engage in the story, because the characters actually care about the world and its inhabitants. Some even have growth as they endure the story's hardships/uptimes, and character arcs that unfold as the story progresses.
On the other hand, some characters seem devoid of character growth
or end with a real left-field head scratcher
- which is sad because they are so cool and they deserve more growth/reasoning.
-- About it being easy
I found the game super easy, to the point I nearly felt it impossible to lose a battle. Granted; I'm good at these types of games. Just to try to keep the battles somewhat entertaining, I purposefully NEVER equipped top-tier equipment on my characters and left old armor on them instead of upgrading -- or used the armor that provided No Stats (but half MP bonus is crazy). For that purpose; you can mitigate this issue by NOT equipping strong gear(which you can acquire very fast), then the battles can be somewhat more entertaining.
I wouldn't have said anything about this if there were a "Hard mode" option available for us veterans/fans. It would offer a form of replayability.
Overall? I would say this game is worth a play, even at the full $10. I have heard the author is working on a sequel, and do intend on purchasing it when it is released.
