Alright, let's talk a little bit about Lume. To give a short answer: do I recommend that you purchase it? No - go pick up Lumino City instead. It's the fully fleshed-out version of what the developers were more-or-less experimenting with here. It's absolutely beautiful, and I would recommend it in a heartbeat. For most people, that's probably all you need to know. So go check out Lumino City.
If you're still reading, here's some slightly more in-depth thoughts. Lume is effectively an early experiment for what would become Lumino City. Here, State of Play got a good sense for how this "animating on top of a paper world" idea could work for a fully-fledged game. That being said, this is not that game. It is very short, there isn't much of a story developed, and some of the puzzles are not presented in a way that gives the player any clues as to how to find the solution. It is very much the little brother of Lumino City. It's clear that the team had dreams of larger environments and a bigger story, and some of the puzzles (the wiring and the music lock) were improved upon and included in the larger game. And of course, they used Lume to experiment with this fantastic art style. Basically, Lume serves as a historical artifact of how Lumino City evolved from an idea into the amazing game it is. So here's my recommendation: Go play Lumino City. If you enjoy it (and I think you will) and are interested in seeing how it came to be, pick up Lume when it's on sale for $1-2. But you have to come at it knowing that this isn't some astounding game, but a stepping stone towards one.

This brilliant strategy game simulates the escalation of battle from a small initial skirmish up to the final showdown of forces. Every battle has reinforcements and these reinforcements usually have to move quite a bit to reach a conflict zone. This makes this game quite unique.
Here, for example, a commander can ambush and stall such reinforements by infiltrating a small force behind the enemy lines. To do that, You can use a terrain features that break the line of sight of enemy. Forests, hills, riverbeds will provide such cover.
I wish we could have a similar "battle simulator" for WW2 era battles.
The only downside of this game is that sometimes battle outcome is evaluated in a very strage way. I had once a whole union army encircled and broken, and it was only a matter of time for them to be completely annihilated - they had no place to retreat and regain strength and cohesion. But the game decided that battle is over and it is a "tie".
Anyway - this is a Yes from me, and every strategist will enjoy this game.

This game is pretty badass. It plays like a mixture of Zelda and God of War/Devil May Cry/Bayone- Look, you do puzzles and crazy combo attacks, and sometimes you press a button/key to rip some poor soul's limbs off. It is, for the most part, mindless entertainment (other than the puzzles and the brief strategy involved in the combat).
The story is based on the Judeo-Christian Apocalypse and one member of its heralds, War of the Four Horsemen, accidentally starting the end of the world too soon. It quickly becomes a story of revenge, justice, and answers as War travels across a destroyed earth (or, more accurately and area that could easily be just what/where New York City and some part of New Jersey used to be. It's not the full planet) taking down other biblical beasts and monsters of both Heaven's and Hell's host. If I am not mistaken, War is actually described as, "Hunted by Heaven, and Hated by Hell."
While its fun, it is a bit straight forward up until the end, in which you're thrown a few twists and turns.
Speaking of being straight forward, the game is fairly linear, but in a more Zelda-y or Halo: CE sense than a Call of Duty and FINAL FANTASY XIII way. You're given many areas (Forgive me for not remembering the exact number, it's actually been months since I played the game) to explore in a pseudo-open world sense, with at least one dungeon per area. In the dungeons, you go back and forth between combat and solving puzzles to progress, and like in Zelda, acquiring a new skill or tool to complete the dungeon and open up old paths for exploration in the other areas.
I know I keep referencing Zelda, and while some might consider that to be a bad thing, I certainly don't. I love that franchise, and the only reason I keep alluding to it is because it's a forerunner in its field (kinda), and it really is the best comparison I can make with this game. I'm sure there are a bunch of other puzzle-y, platform-y, RPG-ish games out there that have the same feel as Darksiders, but I just don't know them.
Anyway, the sound design is pretty damn spot on. Things squish, crunch, rip and smash in brutally good sounding ways, and War sounds like the embodiment of destruction should. Oh, and Mark Hamil has a voice in this game, and he's always welcome because, well, hell, it's Luke GOSHDANG Skywalker and The Joker (and Skips). The demons sound demonic, the angels sound pious and righteous, and the music... Um. The music didn't stand out to me, at least not like the sequel's does. It was adequate. Enough for a post-apocalyptic action game.
The art design is definitely one of my favorite aspects of this game, and the sequel too. It's all comic book-y, and I love it. There's plenty of realism in the environment and some of the characters, but not enough that it looks like it's trying too hard, and not too little to the point that it feels like I'm defintely looking at a cartoon.
Now, there is leveling and a small degree of customization involved in the game, but I quickly found a weapon I wanted (which do not present themselves too often) and loaded it with the skill I liked the most (health absorption and DoT, mainly), so I didn't really delve too deeply into the game's RPG elements. Oops (look, this is my first big review, and like I said, it's been a while. Please don't kill me).
So I think I covered everything I needed to regarding this game: setting, story, sound, visuals, gameplay. I'm sure I'm missing some stuff, but I don't think I'd be able to say much on it in that case. Anyway, I'd definitely recommend this game. At its worst, the game feels like a 6.5/10 (which it really only hits when trying to solve awkward puzzles), and at its best it's about an 8.5/10 (which it hits quite frequently in my book). Solid game. Solid entry to the genre of Action RPGs. Solid start to a series that I still hope continues on with good development like the first two.

Whether an American Civil War buff or just a strategy gamer, you will find this game challenging and fun.  You take command of brigades from either the Army of the Potomac or Army of Northern Virginia in this mostly tactics base  combat game.
The Battle of Gettysburg was a chance meeting of two large armies in Pennsyvania and everything was up for grabs.  If the Confederates destroy the Army of the Potomac, the road is open to Washington and indpendance.  If the Union destroys or al least repulses the enemy here, they can secure Pennsylvania and take the war back to Virginia.
You are in command of brigades in this battle and you will face a lot of the challenges the leaders really did face.  Will you be conservative, taking and holding good ground that offers cover yet surrendering the initiative?  Or will you be daring by attacking and forcing the other side to match your moves, possibly making a mistake?
Your brigades are affected by a number of things.  Their morale is based on real examples but is affected by whether a general is placed nearby, whether they are in the open, how many men have been killed, how many men
have killed, and how bad they are being pummelled by enemy artillery.
The gameplay is simplisitic with easy to use controls.  Simply clicking a unit and dragging where you want it to go is all you have to do.  To change alignment, simply click the middle mouse button and rotate.  There are other commands but those are the basics.
The graphics are simple yet detailed.  The map itself is simply beautiful, showing real locations of hills, ridges, farms, and roads.  The farms even have the names labeled and I have used that to research those buildings.  By hitting the M button you can bring up a topographical map that will help you place your infantry and artillery in the most advantageous positon.
The campiagn can be played as either side and the effects of one phase of the battle effects the next.  If you get your Iron Brigade slaughtered in the morning they will not be as affective later that day if they are needed.  You are also given options that are not historically accurate to change the way the battle of fought based on your decisions.  For example, do you want your Union forces to fall back midday on the 1st day to Cemetery Hill or do you want to hold Seminary ridge?
The sound is decent but I wouldnt say I ever marveled at how great it is.  The sounds of artillery and rifled musket fire are distinct, as well as the bugles and yelling when troops charge.  What I would like to hear is the rebel yell when the Confederates attack.  It was a shrill yelping/screaming sound that is said to give you a feeling of dread as you await attack.
Overall, I love this game.  There is the campaign and invidual scenerios you can take part in, as well as multiplayer.  I haven't tried multiplayer so I cannot comment on it.  The game to me is very stable and I have had no issues running it at 60FPS at 1920x1080.  I also have never had a freeze or crash.  I saw crashes talked about but I think those are older versions.
9/10 Buy this game!  Hopefully they will contemplate an Ultimate General:Shiloh, Chickamauga, Antietam, Vicksburg, Chattanooga, Mobile, Petersburg, Chancellorsville, Second Manasses, Atlanta, or Charleston!

A beautiful little gem of an RPG that brought me right back to the older Final Fantasy titles and time spent with lots of turn-based RPGs on my GameBoy Advance. I didn't know what to expect at all when I bought Ara Fell; I noticed that someone on my friend list had it and the premise seemed interesting enough and the art, like I mentioned above, made me super nostalgic. I figured there would be no harm in trying it out!
But wow. After completing Chapter 1 of the game my feelings went from vaguely interested to actually invested. And it is so rare for me to get so emotionally invested in a game's story and characters so quickly, but Ara Fell did it. What I thought would have been a cliché story actually ended up surprising and shocking me on many occasions. (I also may or may not have teared up once or twice.)
This game shines in its ability to do so much with dialogue and pacing (Lita can be downright hilarious), in the way it is grounded in its lore and world-building (without spoiling, the plot reveals, revelations, and raising of the stakes were all really well done), while not falling* too heavily on combat or exposition, and in creating memorable characters that I ended up truly caring for and looked forward to seeing again (Seri Kesu may just be one of my favorite video game characters of all time).
All of these elements, combined with a touching, engaging soundtrack and surprisingly powerful atmosphere, make Ara Fell one of the best RPGs I've played this year. So happy that I didn't let this game pass me by. Also, as I saw that the epilogue was added on a bit after the game's initial release - I have to say that for me, personally, it was greatly appreciated. It gave me a much-needed sense of closure after completing the main story of Ara Fell that I would have been otherwise searching for had I been left with the pre-epilogue ending.
*Can I get a +1 for my first time ever using a pun in a review?

Ara Fell has a classic feel, charming spritework, little environmental touches to help with verisimilitude, and clever ways of getting you invested in the characters inhabiting this world. While I had some issues with the game, ultimately I found it to have a lot of heart, and it won me over. I can't wait to see the sophomore effort from these developers.
I found many of the game's emotional moments impactful. The characters emote in a number of ways that help them come alive - unique sprites come up during the most important parts of the story, the heroine has a generous amount of portrait art to depict her various emotional states, and parts of key dialogue text are manually timed to mimic the cadences of human speech, instead of just printing a flow of characters. These choices of presentation pulled me into the characters and their plight, and the game's sparing use of blood and death helped heighten the stakes.
The battle systems and stat progression could have done with some rebalancing. The plethora of gear and stat combinations you can come up with seems to invite experimentation, but all the skills/spells scale heavily on Intelligence - even the physical attack skills. Around the midpoint, this led to a dominant strategy of giving all of your party members high Intelligence, and using multitarget attacks to win. Once you get the sorceress character, the game seems to encourage doubling down on this tactic. A freeform level up system was a cool idea, and I was into it, but in practice it didn't quite work out. That said, I still loved seeing that my characters levelled up, and giving them more stat points. Certain rewards seem to never get old.
Some of the music could have used a few more compositional ideas, but I enjoyed the texture and contemplative feel of the soundtrack. The song that plays during the prologue adventure, as you explore mysterious ruins at the break of dawn, lent it an attractive air of mystery, and it made me want to learn more about the story and game world.
For the next title from Stegosoft Games, I feel that a more flexible game engine would suit them better than RPG Maker and its limitations. I suspect not being able to move the menu cursor during a battle animation was one such limitation. I would love to see a choice of engine that allows their vision to flourish, as I so enjoyed their storytelling and characters. The RPG Maker stock sound effects are serviceable, but I hope to hear assets of a bit higher quality in their next title.
Despite my complaints, I think this game will stick with me. I am glad I played it.

This game stands as a savior for Indie Games everywhere. It's a retro game almost done right, with great music, graphics, game design, etc.
However, it's obvious that the developers are not as experienced as the makers of your favorite retro games were. Unlike the Megaman games, Shovel Knight is filled with moments where it feels as if the game got you killed out of nowhere. Megaman teaches you about gamplay elements before throwing you into the danger; Shovel Knight just has you killed. But hey, unlimited lives, you just lose money, so what's the problem? There are switch mechanisms that form blocks that disappear after awhile. Cool, disappearing blocks just like Megaman. But right when you take the last jump between blocks, going as fast as possible as to not run out of time, a cheap enemy jumps from off screen and knocks you into the pit. Great.
Perhaps these cheap deaths and lack in the level/enemy design are offset by the unlimited lives, but it's all the same a frustrating experience. Nobody likes cheap deaths, which is unfortunately a major flaw on an otherwise amazing game. They took all the greatness about Megaman and other classic games, but unfortunately go a little extreme on the cheap deaths. Funnily enough, the same thing was true about the NES-styled Megaman 9.

I thought i would re-play and re-review this before i start the sequel to this game "Lumino City".
This is a nice little point and click adventure game with a beautiful visual style and interesting puzzles. Although, with that said, it's very important to mention that this is almost an introduction/demo into the world and the style of the game. This would definitely not pass as a full length game.

I first played this a while ago and i can say that it was definitely a disappointment as a game at the time. I was very impressed with aspects of the game but it's barely an hours worth of gameplay, it has no real story and as pretty as it is, it isn't worth the price. I would only recommend buying this if you can get it really cheap or even just free.
The only reason i have come back to it was to remind me of the world, style and the setting before i started on the sequel. As a stand alone game It's definitely not something i would recommend.
However, as a "taster" of sorts for the next game, my short time in this game did definitely manage to grab my interest once i found out a full length game was being released as a sequel.
The art style of the game is wonderful. A hand-made, miniature model, stop-motion and animation mix of a game. I love the extra care and attention that are put into these sorts of games. It does really manage to make them unique. The game is made to feel very homely and cozy with this kind of technique and creates a warm and relaxing feeling.
The puzzles were fun and quite interesting. There was one that was kind of hard to find the logic behind without resorting to a guide, but that was the only one I had trouble with. The others were interesting but do-able. I hope to see more puzzles like these in the next one.
As it goes, i think i will have to down-vote this game on the basis of it being a stand alone game.
But with that said, i am looking forward to writing a very positive (hopefully) review of it's sequel.
All in all, It's decent for a demo or taster, but not as a game. Play it if you can get it free or just really cheap. Otherwise, just take a look at the sequel instead.
TL;DR : Just buy Lumino City.

It's surprising that some oversized pixels, a bit of text and a simple emotive melody can evoke such shivers across your skin or lumps in your throat.  But they can, and this game does. This is a game for those of us who love the story-centric RPGs of old (Final Fantasy 4 & 6, Chrono Trigger). However, it may disappoint those in it for the tactical combat (Final Fantasy 5 & Tactics).
While Ara Fell doesn't nail every aspect, none of its flaws are enough to hamstring an otherwise great game. A few examples include combat that is rewarding for a while but some oversimplification of mechanics leads to many fights playing out the same way. The story and level design leading up to the end feel a little rushed. Puzzles are another weak point.
But you won't care because you'll want to see how these characters will grow and reveal more of themselves to you over time. You'll wonder what's beyond this bridge choked with fearsome trolls. You'll thirst for that next big equipment upgrade and a challenging boss to use it against.
I should note that this is a shorter game than those that inspired it. It took me 18.8 hours to fully explore, do side quests and complete the game. In that time it tells a complete and satisfying story. It may be on a smaller scale, but it feels a little bit more intimate.
I really enjoyed the writing in Ara Fell. There is no voice acting but each character still has a distinct voice because of the way they are written. They all have their own flaws, quirks, mysteries and struggles. Character portraits depicting different emotions fill in nicely for voice tone and body language. Frequent light hearted moments and a few running gags keep the mood light. I did notice a few typos and spot genre tropes at times, but nothing near enough to ruin the experience.
It's not just the heroes that are well written but the villains as well. Not all of them are as fleshed out as I would have liked, but those that are display motivations deeper than the raw evil you often see. While their actions are still wrong, they do become more understandable once you've seen their perspective. Their past is integral to the lore of this magical land in the sky. I like how distant history is poorly kept in Ara Fell because it forces you to constantly question whether the information you come across is myth or reality.
Non-story related NPC dialogue is competent but could have used more depth and variety to truly shine. It is better earlier on in the game but thins out later on. There is enough change in what they have to say after major events in the story to make this world seem reasonably alive.
The recently added epilogue is a very welcome addition. I can see how the original ending was too abrupt right after the climax. Now we get closure while still leaving the door open to a sequel.
Battles follow a familiar turn based system where each party member has their own specialization. It's main unique feature is that MP pools are small but quickly recharge, allowing you to make liberal use of special skills. There is an unfortunate lack of variety and progression in skills though. Once you gain access to a character they'll either already have all their skills or will quickly learn the rest of them.  Having a single, full party buff spell on the healer means you'll start every boss battle by using that spell, without question. Seemingly in an attempt to streamline, the developers forgot that having options is more fun. Thankfully, frequent bosses do a decent job of shaking things up with their own gimmicks.
If there is a sequel I hope to see puzzles removed or vastly improved. I'd say that this is Ara Fell's weakest feature. Some are so simple as to be merely busy work. Dragging a brazier onto a glowing spot of the floor presents zero challenge when you can both push and pull. It's impossible to get stuck yet they have a floating orb nearby that allows you to reset the puzzle. There was really only one puzzle that I thought was good and it was a central element to the dungeon it was in, so you'd expect it would be.
The game is technically open world, however that doesn't make much difference in practice. Story events must follow a specific path and there's little incentive to venture into areas far above your level. There are some gated areas too. They do a good job of marking when a new area is significantly harder than the zone it connects to. I also like the save reminders before important events. I used these as turn back points when I knew there were still side paths I hadn't explored.
It's worth delving into the nooks and crannies since money is relatively scarce. Most of my gear upgrades came from chests or crafting rather than shops. I've seen other reviews complain about this, but I think it was fine. I was constantly striving to get to the next upgrade until the very end of the game when I was able to max out every equipment slot. Leveling up is less impactful than most new gear, but it does allow you to customize your stats if you want to specialize more.
Visuals are impressively done in a retro SNES style that will appeal to any who fondly remember that era. The colors are vibrant and the land is richly detailed. Plants are numerous and diverse; harmless wildlife flutters overhead and scurries underfoot; and the creations of people display signs of life from both present and past.
As you might expect, the soundtrack is also a prominent part of the game. It adds impact to cutscenes and flavor to the world. It may not be very complex but the melodies are pleasant and memorable. I'm glad the soundtrack is included for free in the game files folder.

I do not normally go out of my way to write a review after finishing a game, but after finishing it a few minutes ago I was too delighted with Ara Fell to not say something. I'm a child of the triple hits - Secret of Mana, Final Fantasy 6, and Chrono Trigger - and occasionally pick up an RPG Maker game here on Steam to feed my inner 10 year old something 16-bit. It didn't take long into my seventeen hours of play to appreciate the extra layers of development that had been put into Ara Fell's creation, compared to the other RPG Maker games I'd played. My favorite of these extras is the amount of fauna roaming the landside. From rabbits, to birds and butterflies, Ara Fell is never a lonely place. I was reminded of another mid-90's game, Tales of Phantasia, in this regard.
For a game with much less hours under its belt than the ones listed above, I thought the main characters were well rounded, interesting, and consistent with unique voices. Even most of the important NPC's packed a developed character in their small fraction of an appearance.
My biggest complaint is that many of the game play elements I appreciated in the early hours of the game gradually took a back seat as the story entered into the last half of the chapters. Free exploration, the crafting system, and any real need to fight battles on the map all lost their touch. The latter half of the game doesn't have much useful off the beaten path discoveries, I'd often have better gear by the time I could craft a useful item (due to the great gear that can be found during the free exploration of the first half), and it was easy to over level from intentionally fighting every monster group at least once.
I'd say this was all forgivable due to the story structure being able to hold itself up the whole way. I'm glad I played after the introduction of the epilogue, because it gave me just the right balance of both wanting a sequel and feeling like the story was done.
All in all, Ara Fell has a way of raising the bar on the RPG Maker genre, while being disappointing only in that it doesn't give you more of itself. I’ll be keeping an eye out for more from Stegosoft Games, whether or not they choose to make a direct sequel (yes, please!)

Basically Sid Meier's Gettysburg remade with modern UI and graphics.  Nothing revolutionary or very ambitious, just a nice simple quick addictively fun game.  Scenarios are like short segments of the battle, usually only like 1/4 of the army is in any one mission, and the full battle is played as a branching campaign of these short scenarios.  Unit losses are preserved (and even positions, sometimes) between scenarios, which is a nice effect that gives a sese that you really are using the same brigades in each engagement.
The AI isn't horrible, but I don't see much evidence of it's awesomeness or intelligence... it seems to understand "attack" and "don't attack", and maybe its positioning troops defensively (or maybe that's just the default destination reinforcements are sent to?) but it doesn't seem to know how to flank or anything more complicated than a mass rush attack.  The gameplay is basic enough that there isn't really much it can do wrong, though, so it's decently competitive anyway.

Sure, we are treated with a very creative and fun visual style during that time, but in the end Lume feels like a very pricy demo version of the incredibly superior sequel,

I've played a lot of strategy games, and being an avid history nerd, mostly historical ones. From Rome: Total War to Civ 5 to everything inbetween by every developer to every time peroid. From Paradox Interactive to Relic games, from World War 2 to the Antiquity. I've also had the pleasure of playing Darthmod's amazing mods for the Total war series, my particular favourite being the Empire and Shogun II Varient. In short, I have no life.
After announcing he was going solo on his own project a while back, I was surprised when I saw this pop up in my recommened list, as it had sort of gone under the rader for me. I picked it up in the Christmas sales, and gave it a whirl.
I have only a faint intrest in the ACW, but I knew enough about Gettysburg and the scale + importance of the battle to be interested.
What a shock I was in for.
Firstly, I was struck by something that CA and others have dragged it's feet on for so long now, and that's proper AI difficulty. You can choose to face AI who is Risky, Defenesive, Caustious or Aggresive to name just a few, and it also gives you the option to face a Random AI charateristic, as well as the option to boost the AI. Something as simple as this can add a lot for replay value, not to mention be incredibly fun.
Upon loading in the game (Confedrate naturally, because nothing beats shouting "YEEE-HAAAA!" at the top of your lungs in a Mississippi accent charging into canister shot), I was presented with a nice clear tutorial, and thrown into it. It took me three tries to beat the first day of the battle, but it was the most fun I've had with an RTS ever. The controls were so fluid, giving orders was simple, the terrain  and line of sight mechanic were so easy to understand due to simple lighting effects, the combat was brutal, and by using a simple casulty ratio to dead sprites, you could fit the realistic amount of men without feeling the map was cramped,  and the continuation from day to day with yesterdays resources was a really nice touch. I emerged with a minor victory and a beard Grant would envy after 3 days of bloody mayhem , but I was proud as punch.
The Map in the game is a piece of art, with the terrain and hills being prominent features that look and feel important. Historical POI's  and landmarks are all labelled (everything is labelled in fact) , so for the history nut it's really a great insight into what sort of conditions the battle was fought in. The noise the battles produce feel real, with rifles peeling and cannons booming. Projectiles and impacts fly around the place like rain, with thousands of men firing volley after volleys into each other. It feels and looks epic.
There are a few drawbacks. The game is still realtively new (not ALPHA new, but new new) and bugs exist, sometimes controls can glitchy (especially with cavalry), Multiplayer can be cruel, and considering your playing nearly 10 euro for the 3 days of Gettysburg, I feel it's a little much to ask for. However, I'm happy to give it over beacuse the game is being patched all the time, and for the first time since the bitter dissapointment of Rome II, I'm really looking forward to seeing forward what comes after this.
So, in conclusion, buy this game because not only is it the most realistic ACW battle simulator I have ever seen, it's also breaking ground in a rather stagnant strategy genre, and it's beautiful to watch.
TL;DR
Buy this game, so you too can know the joy of being a Southern Gentlemen (the
kind of gentlemen) whilst losing your entire army beacuse you risked Pettigrew's brigade charging up a hill and forgot you had cannon reserves somewhere to the rear. But God Damn, it looked spectacular didn't it?

This is the game you pick up when playing Skyrim no longer holds your attention. It is a solid sequel to a solid game. It has all the basic RPG elements that it needs to be great, an easily understood levelling system with variety, a well thought out story, plenty of different enemies, an interesting villain, and enough quests to fill the wee hours of the morning as you lose track of time. Two Worlds II has a classless, fluid gameplay that allows you to be what you want to be and couples itself with a combat system that allows for economy of combat without mass confusion. It is interesting and engaging throughout the main storyline while giving you enough digressions to make you feel like a human instead of a mindless automaton set on Cleanse Evil Mode. Apart from combat, great writing and voice acting staple a great experience together and leave you with a thoroughly enjoyable Action RPG that will by no means equal the greats like Skyrim but will fool your clock into thinking it has.

What happens if you take a healthy chunk of Rust, add sprinkles of Wurm Online, flavour it with bits of Mount & Blade and top it all off with a mixture of Ultima, Darkfall and EVE Online? Whether your answer is "A flavourless, chunky paste" or "A gourmet masterpiece", both have relevance when it comes to BitBox Ltd.'s first major project Life is Feudal (LiF). Yet still, while combining the well-known aspects of games like those mentioned above, the devlopers claim that LiF is absolutely unique and are working on some features to set it apart from its main competitors.
In essence, LiF is a medieval themed sandbox online RPG, including all the survival and crafting mechanics the industry is so crazed about as of late. Familiarly, you are thrown into an immense world with nothing but some dirty clothes, provisions to last you a few days and your bare hands to help you survive. The now well honed instincts of a survival game expert should kick in immediately and drive you to forage for food, look for some basic resources to craft primitive tools with - you know the drill all too well. Where LiF differs is its skill system. Every character has a set of attributes and skills which will determine his ability to pretty much do anything, from a "Nature Lore" skill that will help you find more edibles on the ground to an array of crafting skills such as Carpentry, Masonry or Smelting. LiF is not intended to be played all by yourself and you will quickly find out why, as there is a skillcap in place, preventing you from being perfect at everything. Not long into the game you will have to decide which paths to go down and which ones to leave to other players. Eventually, your quaint community will should consist of a number of specialists working together. Building said community is one of the key features of LiF, as it offers every player total control over his environment. You can terraform the landscape, flatten out areas or dig up moats for your improvised stronghold, mine for minerals in underground tunnels (the world is voxel-based, much like Minecraft but with smooth edged) or build structures - watchtowers, shacks or entire castle towns, provided you have the resources for it and architects skilled enough to build something more complex than an axe made of a stick, plantfibre and flintstone. Another important skill-tree offers various combat skills, increasing your efficiency with certain weapons, armour or even horses and mounted combat (not yet implemented). This will help you fend off agressive animals or indeed other players, as LiF features full PvP and looting. While there are some penalties to going on a murder spree, it is an option and you will surely see more foe than friend. To help bring structure into this potentially chaotic environment, an upcoming feature will include land claims for individual players and for player-owned factions. These lands will be completely safe, but can be contested and captured in PvP faction vs faction wars. Three faction types are planned to exist: Bands/Orders, Fiefs and Kingdoms, the difference being size, influence over other factions and the amount of claimable land. This feature, however, will NOT be part of the game you see linked to this very review. LiF will effectively be released in two different versions: LiF: Your Own (reviewed, current build) and LiF: MMO. The latter will, according to the developers, feature a true massively multiplayer online persistent world with more than 10.000 players, a much bigger world and many features not available in LIF: Your Own, but is still well beyond our reach. LiF: Your Own meanwhile features dedicated serverplay with a maximum of 64 players playing on a 3x3km map.
"Life is Feudal is a Unique Sandbox MMORPG." is the claim made by the developers. Does LiF live up to it? While the current Early Access release build is actually still in early alpha, it is plain to see the effort behind the project, as well as the sheer amount of features available now and the even bigger number of things "not yet implemented", but already planned (horses, deeper combat, even more crafting). "Life is Feudal" is furthermore not just the title of this game, but one of its main directives. Survival is hard, especially when you're on your own. Learning skills takes time and dedication. Death is best avoided. If all of this sounds appealing to you, giving this game a chance would definitely be recommended. Be warned, though, because the current build (20/9/14) is pretty much as early as Early Access gets, so you will run into bugs, balancing issues and many buttons with the "Not yet implemented"-stamp on them. Buying the game now means you are willing to help fund the further development of this title and be eligible to offer your own feedback.

I got this game excited to play a procedurally generated twin-stick horde-based dungeon crawler.  I could only get near the end of the second zone before I quit, because I was bored out of my mind.
It's procedurally generated, but in a way that's actually really bland.  It's just an array of rooms that look the same.  Just square rooms.  The only variation in them are the rocks and the doorways to other rooms.  That's it.  And the enemies, though it looked like they would increase in difficulty over each wave, are always the same.  The timer essentially just refreshes the enemies in the room.  Even more unfortunate is that you have a chance of enemies spawning on top of you, with no indication of where they will spawn.  The only way to avoid this is to step out of the room when the timer gets close.  But wait, there is an item that you can get out of the shop which makes you invulnerable for a few seconds when enemies spawn.  You get to Spend 1000 Blood (about 5 minutes of grinding, in my experience) to fix a fundamental flaw in the game.  That's just bad game design.
Remember how I said I was excited for a twin-stick game?  It's single-stick, though that's not inherently bad.  The way that gameplay works is you run around and you shoot left or right, depending on which direction you were facing last.  It's really simple, and that's okay, but there's two glaring issues with this:  You shoot automatically and you can only shoot left or right.  If there's a wall of enemies above or below you, you have to sacrifice your health just so you can get through.  And before it's said that this is "just a part of the difficulty", well, you're not wrong.  But bad controls are not a good way to make a game difficult.
Then there's the items.  You start off the game with a choice of weapon.  But it doesn't matter much, because as soon as you bump into a chest, even by accident, you lose your weapon for one that's likely inferior.  You have no confirmation.  You have no choice.  You cannot get your weapon back.  It's instant, and it's irreversible.  And they're never anything good.  Just the same three barely-useful weapons every time.  I'm not sure if I was just really unlucky with that, but I spent a fair amount of my gameplay time grinding enemies just so I could get a half-decent weapon out of the shop.
If they add a way to shoot vertically and a confirmation of some sort (even just standing around the chest and/or weapon for a few seconds), this could be a pretty good game, even with the monotonous level generation.  It would be even better if the rooms were reworked and difficulty was added for each new wave, but the fundamental issues should be taken care of first.

So Much Blood is.. severely disappointing. I was pretty excited for this game, but then I played it.
The game is inherently flawed in design. You can move in eight directions, but you can only shoot left and right. This makes traversing and dodging enemies really difficult for no reason. The enemies themselves are practically useless, but some of the game's "mechanics" make them worse than Hell to deal with. This wouldn't be so bad if you could either shoot in multiple directions, or if the game was horizontally based. In that there was no vertical room generation, you just move left or right. But then that would make the room generation even more bland. So with that said, the easiest way to fix the broken mechanics would be to completely change them.
On top of the two-directional shooting, you cannot control when you fire, or even lock direction. If you want to move left but fire right, that's too bad. You are constantly firing, and turning around automatically makes your direction of firing flip, as well as the bullets that have already been fired flipping. (Which is completely nonsensical and allows the player to kill things that are literally in another room, through a wall)
And for my biggest grievance with the game, enemy spawning. When I played the game, I must have had enemies spawn on top of me at least a dozen times. It is absolutely
to take damage from something you cannot prevent, especially when it is a third of your health, and when the only way to recover health is to navigate the horrid maze of a level and spend your hard-earned grinding points at a shop.
I have given feedback and advice to the developer multiple times, but he always seems to discard my criticism and try to explain to me why it works for the game, and how the whole game is designed around the poorly executed mechanics. "You can get armor that prevents damage for a few seconds when an enemy spawns" is not a proper workaround for enemies
That should not be a thing. If anything, have two or three seconds of invulnerability base, and add a few more seconds with the armor. Or at the very least, give a spawning icon, akin to Enter the Gungeon, so you can see exactly where enemies are spawning before they telefrag you.
This armor that makes it unable for enemies to harm you when they spawn costs 1000 points. That might not sound like a lot, but it's at least ten minutes of grinding the same boring enemies over and over again.
From what I've heard from the game, there is only one track. One really generic, repetitive track that got old really fast. I found myself disabling the audio within 20 minutes. There may be more music later on, but the game is so boring and grindy that I couldn't bare to get far enough to hear a difference. (I played up until Zone 2.)
The dev added gamepad support, but it doesn't really seem like it was tested that much. Turning around with the joystick makes you stop firing for ~0.5 seconds. It doesn't seem like much, but when you can only fire in two directions (and you're constantly firing anyway,) you definitely should not stop firing when
This game has many, many flaws that could easily be fixed if the developer would just listen to criticism and understand that it's not antagonizing, it's feedback. And this doesn't even scratch the surface, the GUI is really ugly, you cannot skip the unreasonably long introduction cutscene, the bosses are giant, overhyped sponges, the game uses at least four fonts, and some of the art looks placeholder, namely the shopkeeper.
If I could get a refund, I would. But it's been too long, and thus, I cannot. I whole-heartedly discourage you from purchasing this game, at least until the flaws are dealt with. But seeing how the updates have been going, it doesn't seem like that will be happening any time soon... I really hope the developer reads this, takes the feedback seriously, and at least tries to change things. I want to like this game, I really do. But in this state, I cannot bring myself to enjoy it.

I thought to myself "It's a clicker game for only a dollar." but I was wrong.
It starts you out with a minimalistic UI that is not only unintuitive, but open to interpretation, as there is nothing to say what is and what isn't a button or what said buttons do other than a cryptic one word description like 'material' and pricetag--much like being thrown into a job that you know nothing about, but have accepted out of desperation.
Once you grasp the basic concept through trial and error and discover that half of the screen scrolls with your mouse wheel, while the other you have to click and drag, still confused by 'max 5/10' which means seemingly nothing, you ever so slowly inch your way up to 20 workers and begin furiously clicking away. With the imitation of success, you look at your funds, but find that your income doesn't seem to actually increase any faster than when you had one worker. In fact, it might be increasing slower. This accurately reflects the hourly job model where more work does not equal more pay.
"This game makes snails look turbocharged," I joked to my wife who had aged 20 years in the time it took me to purchase sewing machines for 10 of my workers. I wanted to see this game through to the end so I could write a fuller, more complete review, but I just couldn't bring myself to do it. I may have encompassed the entirety of it though. Tell me if I'm wrong.
I was wrong, this isn't a game, it's an ironic satire on the idea of running a sweatshop wherein you slowly realize that *you're* the underpaid sweatshop worker, and that you are now minus one dollar, and 8 hours. Just like when you spend more on food in a day than you make at your job.

Same old Trials, New Maps.  I fell in love with this series years ago on console, and for the most part this installment hasn't dissappointed me yet.  It's addictive. It's frustrating, but the feeling of satisfaction when you finally gold medal makes it worth the anger. The new FMX mode and 4-wheel drive vehicles add some slight variation to the old formula. The Community Track Creation has huge potential and some pretty good tracks have already been created, but sometimes the direction changes are clunky and completely throw off the feel of the tracks.
If your framerate drops below 60 the game goes into slow motion mode, which can get really annoying, but with a decent pc and nothing running in the background that won't usually be a problem. Every other review has taken care of complaining about Uplay for me so I won't bother.  No Online MP, Local only (Something tells me we can expect to have to buy a "Online Multiplayer DLC Pack" in the near future).  "Season Pass" seems awful pricey (it costs as much as the base game) so the devs better be planning some massive DLC packs to justify that price, otherwise I'm passing on that for now.   The Commentator Audio gets VERY repetitive if you get stuck on a track.
Overall, It's enjoyable with a few small flaws that can be easily looked past. If you liked any previous Trials games, or if it's on sale, you should definately buy it.

Advertising may not always be accurate, but "the most fun you can have online" really is an accurate description of TF2. The game is without a doubt the most fun PC/multiplayer game ever made - it's simply something you have to play to believe.
In the event that you're scrolling through comments looking for downsides to the game, I recommend you quit searching and begin playing.
True, the game may not be as great as it once was. Indeed, the Meet Your Match update, as an example, removed one of the last unique features of TF2 by making the game matchmaking-based (which in the process caused community servers to fall by the wayside). Many long, negative reviews can easily be based on this fact, and no doubt those reviews are correct that the game isn't as great as it once was.
However, the game still has likely the best community you'll ever find in a big game - the fact that so much of the community was against MYM helps prove how dedicated, devoted, and friendly this group of players really is. As long as you're with us, of course - if you're a particularly edgy player, you'll find this game is definitely not for you. (And the community will ensure that you never hear the end of that fact, unless you're willing to learn to become a Team Fortress 2 player.)
If you're willing to join the community (large tip: don't shoot Heavies who aren't fighting anyone, they're Friendlies and should be defended as a proper TF2 species), then TF2 will be a great community to join.
TL,DR; Team Fortress is easily the most fun game ever made. The colors, weapons, and characters (and their associated Valve-made animations) will never cease to bring joy, as long as one uses them right and remembers to keep having fun. Try not to worry about stats, and just be the best teammate you can - if you're good with that, then by all means, join TF2 today.

I don't tend to write reviews, but I feel like this game deserves it. I'll try to keep this short since I tend to ramble.
Overall, I really enjoyed the game. The plot is pretty standard RPG fare, but the character design is quite a bit more interesting. I really did feel like the characters were more believable, and because of that I definitely got more attached to them. As others have likely said in their reviews, even the villians are written well - they have their own reasonings for doing what they're doing, and you can feel somewhat sympathetic towards them. Somewhat, anyway.
Controls/UI wise, the game played well. I found it odd that ending a battle with a character selected and ready to attack caused parts of the UI to overlap, but I suspect that's a problem with RPG Maker itself. I am VERY glad that there is controller support now, the game picked up my Wii U pro controller without issue. Although, I expect the game would play just as well on keyboard.
I will say that I found the inventory somewhat hard to manage when it came to buying new equipment and comparing stats sometimes, but again, guessing that's a restriction of RPG Maker.
Graphics and sound, I think is somewhat subjective. I know some people LOVE this sort of retro/pixel theme (I'm one of them), but I understand others may not. I will say that I loved the music in this game as well, but I also am a fan of this style of music anyway.
Now for my only real issue with the game, at least in some ways... difficulty. Overall, the game wasn't terribly hard, but I also went out of my way to explore absolutely everything, do all of the sidequests, etc. I only really had to grind once, and that was before I got my full party. After that, I felt like just doing sidequests and occasionally clearing out monsters as I traveled to new areas sustained my leveling. I feel like random encounters are a bit unbalanced in terms of the difficulty/exp given ratio. Maybe I'm incorrect, but there's one specific location with easier enemies early on that was just far easier to grind at than anywhere else available at that time, and it was because those enemies didn't get upgraded after getting my full party together like everything else did.
As for coins, I felt like random encounters were a bit stingy, but at the same time I also didn't have any issues funding my potion uses throughout the game. This may be because of all of the sidequesting, or it may be because all of the smaller amounts from each random encounter added up.
And for a couple random points before I end this... random encounters. There aren't any. You can clearly see where monsters are, and you can just... avoid them if you prefer. This made this game FAR more enjoyable, since I tend to hate random encounters in video games. Another random point is poison/other status effects - I NEVER found any sort of item or spell that could cure status effects, and that irked me a little. I do understand they contribute to the difficulty, but I wish I had some sort of ability to counter it. It didn't seem like the heal spells did anything against them, at least in my experience.
I think that's everything, and this ended up being ridiculously long as I expected it would be. Oh well... to summarize - I loved my time playing this game, and I feel like you would too, if you enjoy RPGs with interesting and believable characters and a good story. While it does have a few flaws here and there with the difficulty and a couple of (purely visual) UI issues, it's overall a well put together game. To give a number of hours, my second attempt at playing it was around 15-16 hours, and that's with me attempting to find most of the secrets this game had to offer (and likely still missing things). Not an extremely long game, but well worth the price, in my opinion. Thanks for reading (suffering through?) my rather rambly review.

Story and characters: I like how Lita's hero(ine)'s journey was portrayed and how instead of instantly getting used to her role, she struggles with the pressure of being responsible for Ara Fell's safety, as well as how she struggles to control her new power. I also like how the major vampires (save Baramon) aren't flat villains and have their own sympathetic reasons for wanting the Sunstone. However, Doren's love life seems like it could be written better,
Additionally, I think some characters' backstories should have had flashbacks, especially in the case of Baramon, Nash, and Doren, to flesh them out.
Gameplay:
The good news is that the bosses are balanced so that lone bosses have much higher speed than a properly leveled (or even overleveled) party, making it so that the player's headcount advantage isn't enough to curbstomp the enemy. In contrast, group bosses are more evenly matched with the player in speed, though they should probably be given a bit more HP so that they can't be cheesed with AOE skills.
Like many players might have stated, the strategy for all bosses after Nash's first encounter is pretty much the same, due to how overpowered Doren's buff song is. It's pretty much a "do everything" buff that requires very little thought. Additionally, there's little incentive to use any of Seri's spells other than her Elemental Burst spells, since most random enemies will die before status effects become useful on them. And bosses tend to resist most status effects, making it pointless to use any element other than maybe ice to lower their defense. I guess players can challenge themselves by not using Elven Song or Elemental Burst.
The crafting system makes it easy to get some good equipment early, but I find that crafting potions is pretty pointless. The total sell amount of all the ingredients for a potion exceeds their price in a shop, meaning players are better off selling the ingredients to buy items. This could be remedied by making the crafting system generate multiple items so that crafting is more efficient than using the shop.
Personally, I think the EXP rate should be lowered and the money drops should be increased. Even though I found a specific area (south of the Springs) where the EXP was low compared to the money and sellable item drops, I still felt like I leveled too quickly before I could afford to buy what I wanted.
The touch encounters are a nice feature and are implemented in a way where the monsters don't chase you too quickly and there's still some room to move around them, making it possible to avoid them if the player is skilled enough. Many other games implement this in a way where the enemies may as well elite security guards who are nearly as wide as the hallways that they're guarding.
The stat building system is designed in a way where every stat is useful while making it inexpensive to reset one's choices, making it a more fun and less anxiety inducing than if all stat decisions are final. This allows the player to freely experiment with different builds while getting used to the game's balance.

Ara Fell is a competent little RPG that did quite a lot with RPG Maker 2003. The combat system is good, though lacking some variety desipte the unique mechanics that several of the bosses introduce, the music is really good, and the maps are gorgeous with lots of little secrets to find.
The game also respects your time. There are tons of prompts to save before cutscenes and bosses (since afaik this engine doesn't support autosaves), and nearly every cutscene can be skipped outright. There's also a story mode that gives you an option to just autowin any combat if you don't want to engage with it.

It's a solid 12-15 hour RPG with some cool ideas, and a plot that is mildly generic but has some high points. My only real complaint is the character portraits could use some updating to match better with the official art and maybe dump the default RPGMaker font for something prettier.
I think it was worth the ten bucks I spent on it and look forward to the next game Stegosoft puts out, as it should be a competent followup.

Yes or No?  Yes, but with a caveat.
I paid 1,49USD.  Was it worth that?  Sure.  I like puzzle games and point-and-click adventures, so it hit the spot for my appetite.  I played it with my wife, and it was worth playing.
If I had purchased it for 5,99, would I have felt satisfied?  No.  The game has two big faults: brevity and obtuse puzzles.  We fully completed the game in about 1,5 hours.  The game takes place in one location, really, and with only one real task to accomplish.  So any length has more to do with puzzles that have solutions that are rather obscure.  Not only that, but actually several moments brought intense frustration as we found that the correct click boxes for specific objects can be only a few pixels in size, while the rest of the object brings no success.  So you click on one object to see what it does and find the task fruitless, only to click somewhere NEAR to where you originally clicked after exhausting all other options for 15 minutes and find that it now works.  That is infuriating, and better designed objects could have made this game a much shorter experience.
I don't know what else to say.  If you're okay with a snack of a game for $1,49 (or your regional equivalent) then it's good enough for that.  But for $5,99 you should look elsewhere.

Hello everybody, Shaun Meyers (Kyo Akiara) here to bring you a short overview of our review for FortressCraft Evolved. If you'd like to read our full, in-depth review, you can find it here:
I've been watching FortressCraft Evolved evolve over the course of its development ever since we first previewed the game quite a long time ago and it's become an incredibly impressive and fun survival based game.
I'm normally the type of person to avoid survival based games in truth but out of the many that we've previewed so far FortressCraft remains one of my favorites, with it's incrediblly massive world to explore, tons of craftable equipment and excellent gameplay, it's a joy to play.
I will also say that the game requires an immense amount of time and patience to really get anywhere and since I lack the patience to create vast mining cities I found myself a bit bored after a while. This doesn't mean the game is bad however, it's just that I can't play a game for that long haha.

I'm kind of torn on this one. The reason I bought and finished this game, was because it reminded me of Final Fantasy VI, which is my favourite oldschool RPG of all time. However, the more I progressed in Ara Fell, the more I noticed on what could've been done better. In the next bits, I will take Ara Fell and Final Fantasy VI at face value and outline the differences between these two games.
1. First of all, I want to focus on the gameplay. I usually like turn-based combat, if it is accompanied by some feeling of progression, inventive (boss-/enemy-) mechanics and consequently, adequate difficulty spikes. I can't deny that Ara Fell's combat gets the progression-part down, still, there is a lot to be desired on the latter aspects.
If you ever encounter a boss with a new mechanic, these won't affect you much (Debuff every round, kill everything around the boss first, etc.).
In Final Fantasy VI, I remember encountering a boss that would randomly possess one of your characters without any indication of who the possessed one might be. While the boss stays invulnerable, you have to find out who the possessed character may be, by killing them yourself one by one.
To me this is one of many examples of how to make turn-based combat infinitely more interesting, engaging and tactical.
2. Now to the plot. Ara Fell has a very passable plot, although it is a little generic imo. Essentially, it's all about saving the world from the bad guys with a little help of some artifacts and so on.
It would be unfair to compare this plot to FF VI, as Ara Fell is a 15 hour game at most.
3. And finally the music. I'm usually not a fan of video game music, but I happened to like the first track at the start of the game a lot. The rest of the soundtrack is pretty solid, though these songs didn't surprise me like the first one.
It's mostly the same concerning the music of Final Fantasy VI. The soundtrack is solid all in all, though I wouldn't listen to any of that given the opportunity.
There's a lot I wanted to point out like e.g. animated facial expressions, but I feel like cutting it short here.
In conclusion, Ara Fell feels like a mini-RPG, content- and plotwise. It doesn't drag on to long, everything is clearly explained, the characters are okay, the plot is okay and the visuals are neat. All in all, this game may be good for people who haven't ever played any RPG and want to try something new.
I personally appreciate and understand the effort of the one person who made this game by himself, which despite its shortcomings warrants a thumbs up.

I don't use Steam. I use 2 other websites for my gaming, but I specifically got steam just so I could buy this. This game is sincerely the real deal; a JRPG, that (SUCCESSFULLY) brought together so many things to love - making it so much more than a conventional JRPG. I cannot express how disapointing it is that I keep seeing "great for RPG Maker" or "can't even tell it's RPG Maker", even though they are compliments. Long review short; I played all the great JRPGs from back in the day. All of them. Ara Fell is a love letter to those with many updated features. The combat is relatively standard (no random encounters), but perfectly balanced; albeit maybe a bit too easy (for me). The story is the best to come from a jRPG in a LONG time. The world is open and beautiful with wonderful music to suit. Characters are loveable and engaging; customization of characters comes down to equipment, skills, and stats. :lita:
Those are simply the footnotes (I don't want to give too much). This game REALLY has SO much more to offer. If you like RPGs, Japanese or any other, you should get this. It's as close as you can come to a perfect 2d jRPG.

Oh, no! The power is out, so gramps is off to take care of things, Actually, gramps is off doing who knows what, and it's up to Lume to break into his carefully safeguarded home by solving his puzzle-based home security system. To make this, and the eventual destruction of his bicycle, up to him, Lume and the player decide to restore the electricity, thus emasculating grandpa and taking away his sense of personal validation.
*ahem*
A breathtakingly gorgeous puzzle game, Lume is brought down by a few technical problems and its incredibly short length.
What technical problems could a game like this have? Well, the resolution is (according to the Steam details page) 800x600. If that's not correct, the fact remains that even at fullscreen, it takes up a tiny portion of my screen. Very tiny. Laughably tiny. It was so small, it affected my ability to appreciate its aesthetics and, at times, solve the puzzles. Yes, puzzles -- did you think those last few lines referred to something else?!
*ahem*
Furthermore, and this is a choice made by the developers, the Myst-like screen transitions have got to go.
Finally, the game was built in Flash and is clunky. I wish they had... well, done anything else, to be frank.
All but one puzzle -- perhaps I'm forgetting another -- were quite easy. The other wasn't difficult so much as it required careful observation and recollection as to what we had investigated thus far. Expect to spend most of your playtime wondering what the heck the game wants you to do on this one, or perhaps another. Oh, and by investigated, I mean clicked anything that switched the cursor icon to a hand.
Honestly, there really isn't much else to the game. That's because Lume is a demo for a larger title, Lumino City -- a fact I did not realize until moments before beginning this review. I'm disappointed, and while I really want to recommend this, I don't think I can. Maybe watch the trailer, and if it strikes your fancy, and you don't mind shelling out $1 for a charming one-hour puzzler, pick this up. If you want something with more meat on its bones, check out Lumino City. I have not played it, and... hm. I may not. As of writing, I'm undecided.
Too long, didn't read: Lume is beautiful, and has some decent puzzles, but the mobile-spawned graphic settings will irritate anyone playing on anything other than an old laptop, and the fact that it's essentially a tech demo is a turnoff.

Ultimate General: Gettysburg is one of my favorite strategy games right now. Although this game is all based around a single battle (meaning the battlefield does not technically change), it is still absolute fun to play!
With astounding historical accuracy - and, for the good, inaccuracy - UG:G takes on a real-time strategy viewpoint of a war and battle that do not get talked about very often. The Civil War was one of the wars in our nation's history that clearly defined the way our country was headed. And for military history enthusiasts like myself, you will find that the Battle of Gettysburg's recreated accuracy is astounding. For those who could not care less about historical accuracy, you will enjoy this title as well. Minute by minute, relive the battle that changed the course of and ultimately defined the Civil War. Play as the Confederacy or the Union and play for historical accuracy and conquer Gettysburg as the Union or rewrite history as the Confederate Army and destroy the Army of the Potomac and decimate their infantry and artillery. There's not much to this game as far as technical opportunities, it is a simple game to play: click a unit, draw a path for them to walk, shift their facing direction, order them to attack, hold, charge, or fallback, or barrage a unit (artillery). The goal is to overpower and outflank your enemy in order to gain control of key sectors of the battlefield. The incredible thing about this game is that, because it is all entirely one battle yet not one single level, the key areas of the batttlefield you posses - not to mention the number of men per unit (loss or gained) at the end of the level - will carry into the subsequent level. This continues until the Battle of Gettysburg ends. And trust me, if you lose the whole battle, it could very well be because of a mistake you made in one of the first  levels of the game!
I highly, highly, HIGHLY, recommend this game to anyone who likes miltiary real-time strategy games, and board-game style combat commanding.

From what I've played so far, Darksiders is a fairly fun game from a gameplay perspective, though I will concede that its character and monster design, storyline, and voice acting are a bit bland and overdone.
Basically, you're one of the four horsemen of the Apocalypse, and you're sent to Earth some 100 years after humankind's destruction to cut a bloody swath of destruction amidst demon and angel alike in a quest to restore the balance between the sides. In doing so, you'll fight through a slew of miscellaneous enemies, solve puzzles, conquer dungeons, and slay mighty bosses. It's sort of a God of War meets Legend of Zelda sort of thing, but without much of the originality of either of those franchises.
I will say, however, that the level of violence and gore in this game borders on the silly. In fact, in some cases, it completely crosses that border and delves into full-on Cannibal Corpse Album Cover territory. The over-the-top blood spilling out of everything at all times could be either a positive or a negative, depending on how you look at it. Personally, I find it kind of amusing.
Anyway, overall, this game is a pretty solid 7/10. Several years old at this point, it isn't going to rock your socks off, but it isn't going to bore you to tears, either.
Slight addendum: I've only played this game using a controller, specifically the X-Box 360 controller for Windows. I have a hard time imagining how this game would even be playable without a controller.

As a reenactor and amateur historian, I was very dubious when I saw the early version of this game, which would have been around mid-2014, I think. That Christmas, it was on sale, and it had been overhauled so successfully that I didn't even realize that I was looking at the same game. If you are into American Civil War (ACW) RTSs, this is a good game for you. There are, IMO, a few small kinks to be worked out, but I was very pleasently surprised by how much I enjoyed the game. Once again, Darth Vader (aka Nick Thomadis) impresses. Keep up the great work!
- Tangentially, I hope that versions of this game (DLC?) come out for other battles of the ACW. There are so many good ones! You could go in the direction I've been urging NorbSoftDev to go with Scourge of War; there's Chancellorsville, The Wilderness, the Manassases, Shiloh, Chickamauga, the list goes on. These battles would all make great games. Fluid battles should be the ones concentrated on, certainly not assaults on fortified positions (e.g. Cold Harbor), as fluid battles would be more engaging for the players. Aside from the Civil War, this engine would be great for moddeling battles of the Revolution, War of 1812, the Napoleonic Wars, the Mexican-American War, and the various wars contributing to the rise of the German Empire.
- Constructive Criticism and Suggestions (c. Jan 2015):
1) "Hold ground". It seems that units holding their ground either lose range on their weapons or are unresponsive to enemy threats; I have to manually tell units to attack a target, taking them out of Hold Gound stance (does it even do anything?). Corollarily, Sid Meier's Gettysburg/Antietam had a similar feature that, when used, units would actually use nearby resources to build fences and makeshift breastworks, but could not change their facing.
2) Altitude perception. The topo map is an invaluable feature in this game. However, if it were not for that, and my own knowledge of the ground at Gettysburg, I would have a very hard time judging the battlefield's topography. Perhaps something can be done to make altitude more easily distinguishable?
3) Unit formations and relative space. While the current formations are acceptable, it would be better if each unit took up a relative amount of space based on it's numbers and, possibly, a formation which the player tells it to assume (see 4). Additionally, it would be great if the soldiers in the brigade were split into smaller formations representing the actual number of battalions present in that brigade at the battle. It would not even be necesary to divide the number of soldiers in the brigade proportionally into battalions; even division would be fine. This effect could be purely aesthetic yet add more realism to the game. As it is, each brigade is portrayed, effectively, as a single battalion.
4) Formations. It would be really cool if the player could choose from more than one formation for their brigades to assume. Column could allow faster movement at the expense of lacking firepower; Single Line would take up more space and be vulnerable to melee engagement, but allow an individual brigade to bring all of its guns to bear; Double Line would take up less space and allow the player an easy way to make a defense in depth, at the expense of the firepower of the rear-line battalions; and Assult Column could limit a brigade's firepower to the front regiment and be extremely vulnerable to rifle and artillery fire, but allow it to act as a battering ram of bayonets. These are just some basic formations that probably wouldn't be too difficult to work in and would add a new tactical element to the game.
5) Uniform variation. It would be great if there was more than just a generic blue/grey unit model for each side. For instance, some Zouave uniforms would be nice, green uniforms for the US sharpshooters, and more butternut for the Confederates.
6) Hording (?) There is a term for what I mean when I say that; when units stack on top of one another and fire over/though one another. A pretty classic RTS problem from which UGG does not appear to be exempt.
7) Weapons and unit characteristics. To simply say that Confederate troops have better morale and officers, but Union troops have better equipment and training, is extremely generic and over generalized. I did not even see how these factors contributed to the game except in that it seems, when playing Union, most brigades will retreat at the first Confederate volley. Those kinds of factors should really be considered on a per-unit basis, not national. But now we're talking about an excrutiating level of detail which may be outside of the scope of this game. Still, it never hurts to hope.

This is the most intuitive strategy game I've ever played. Instead of trying to match unit types against each other- sending cavalry against archers, axemen against spearmen, etc- the key to winning is to control the high ground and preserve units' morale and conditioning.
The two sides have different strengths. The Confederates have high morale, which means they can charge harder and stand longer before running. The Union has superior firepower, so they can butcher anything that stands in front of them for too long. Different overall strategies are required for each, with the Confederates trying to headbutt and flank their way through Union lines while the Union cuts them down and tries to repel them.
I can't wait to see more from this developer.

4.9/10 - Not Enough To Make Sweat Shops Cool Again...
I received a discount so I decided to check this one out! I wasn't totally disappointed. I don't know why, but I'm embarrassed...I played at least 7 active hours all yesterday. I completed the game the first time in 6 hours, at this time you can 'reset' or ascend to the next factory; which is the exact same except you earn coins faster. I was disappointed in this for sure!
You are responsible for the effective management of a small upstart business. (Sweat shop). You will have to purchase desks, platforms, sewing machines, cloth and workers; this stuff doesn't come cheap either! Aside from adding new equipment and workers your only job is to collect the clothes once the worker is ready. If you wait too long your worker will fall asleep and wait until you collect the clothes.
This game really had some potential for a monotonous clicker but let me down in a couple of areas:
1) When I ascended there wasn't anything new or different; just a coin bonus. I worked extremely hard for 6 hours waiting on a payout that didn't come.
2) Some of the achievements don't work. I maxed out everything in the first ascension so I should have received at least a few more achievements. This immediately made me want to quit playing.
3) The "collectors" bug out and vanish without a trace. These units are so important because they collect cloth automatically. Unfortunately, they start to disappear once you hire more collectors than you have rows of workers. This really sucks when you are trying to auto and take a break from actively clicking.
Overall, I would give thumbs up if these 3 issues were fixed. At this current state I don't recommend, but I did have some fun with it!

Alright I started playing this game in early acces around patch 4. We are know on patch 10, beginning work on 11 soon. The game is fantastic. I found this game on the featured part of steam one day and thought, "Hey I like modded minecraft, this might be fun." I had never heard of games like factorio, but This game introduced me to that as well. Both of these games are similar and while  Voxel Games tend to be considered a minecraft copyright just due to popularity,  these are not that similar in gameplay. I consider this game to be much more mentally challenging than simple despite using a cube world generation (which actually makes the game much more enjoyable when compared to non-voxel games like Space engineers which does share some similarity to a vague extent with this game).
The game starts you off with a nice tutorial introducing basic concepts. An ingame help entry is available for every block, machine, and item you see in the game. The game tests the players' ability to create well balanced logistics systems, mining operations using automated technology, and tower defense skills.
I never understood what big meant in a voxel game till playing this one. Minecraft worlds are 256 blocks tall. This game's first cave systems is found at -256. World's currently include content that is fully implemented all the way to -2000 meters down. 10x the depth of minecraft and 100x the content. There are around 11 different resources that need to be automated and all of them come with unique challenges involving their logistical transport. some are so far down that cargo lift elevators are needed to move 1000s of items at a time from deep underground to the surface for smelting. The game takes the logistics fo factorio, the easy to grasp gameplay of minecraft, combines them into a 3d world, adds unique challenges and mobs, throws in a bit of towerdefense early game, and a VERY UNIQUE enemy later with the first DLC that adds literally the same amount of content as the base game alone. These all combine to create what has been one my favorite games of all time. It's still updated almost daily on the beta branches and a new patch adding tons of content comes to the stable mainline every month.
The 800 hour reviews that don't recommend the game simply have salt with the developer who I have never had an issue with and I've given him proably 50 ideas that have been shot down with logical reasoning as to why they shouldn't or can't be implented. Love the game, love the devs, and love the cost.
I honestly don't see any downsides, and the game comes with over 12 different difficulty combinations that you can use to fine-tune the challenge to your liking. 200 hours seems like a lot for a full playthrough? drop it to Casual mode and you can speed run the thing in around 40. It's not nearly as hard, but it's still extremely fun. And upon completion of the survival mode, alternative game modes are unlocked offering new challenges. There is so much content in this game and even if a few things here and there aren't everyones cup of tea, $13 is not something that anyone can complain about. Call of Duty and other AAA games offer less content for their respecitve genres, less community interaction, and most of all, MUCH less balancing of implemented features based on player feedback.
Buy it. Just do it. Thank Me later. And if you honestly don't enjoy the game as much as everyone else does, then refund it and say "I tried something new and didn't give it an awful review on YELP" No harm, no foul.
