I am rewriting my review from scratch. This may be a pretty long one because I would try to go in depth here. MAY CONTAIN SPOILERS!
I wrote this review when I spent 5 hours in the game and I was telling myself "It is not bad but if  it did get so overwhelmingly possitive reviews your game will surely do so too!" I was almost sure about that as the game started as a an usual jRPG - a very unique idea in the center and a lot of cliched tropes filling the rest of the game.
The main plot line was likeable but the side quest were there just for the sake of having some side quests. I guess most of you are already tired of killing N amount of monsters to help someone "clear the infested area" or to "control the population". Did any of you feel the urgency to capture the Rangers' Guild bounties? I doubt it. These supposed criminals seemed to not be related to the rest of the world at all. Hell, the supposedly horrible bandits even refused to kill a party of warriors that kept attacking them.
Also, the character's roles and powers were debateable. Adrian was a heavily armored peasant boy and Seri Kesu was a great mage who happened to get her♥♥♥♥♥handled to her by some bandits and by most  of the monsters wandering around aimlessly.
As the game continued on though I started seeing better and better why this game was so successful. It has characters you start to care for. Despite the world being very unrecogniseable amongst the most of the other fantasy worlds the game had a cast of characters that you need to see winning, overcoming all the obstacles and saving the day. I can bet that the world build was not the premise but was done mostly to serve the characters and the conflict between them. The author knew the story he would tell long before he knew how Silvara fed itself and most probably even before he knew how a half of the world is super cold and the other is cosy warm.
Having said that I need to address the few issues I had with the plot. I would skip the cliches like the arrow splitting the previous one in half, the unlikely hero, the prophecy, the traitor who becomes the main villain etc. Tropes became tropes because they were successful but still I dislike it. I disliked the most of deus ex machina moments we had, especially the Talani one. I never really used Talani and I ignored her all the way. Her saving the day had no impact on me and deus ex machina having no impact is a failure by definition (at least for me). The moment with the dwarves saving the day in the grove was okay and I guess that the army coming to Lita's aid at the end was okay but a little overdone by having even her little brother come to fight Baramon (WTF?! What were they thinking?!) Also, the Asari one was pretty out of place IMO. The destruction of the Sunstone was anticlimactic. Also, I was kicking Kefk...uh, Baramon's butt until he pulled off a 9999 attack out of his sleeve which I tend to despise. And I could not agree with how things turned out for Nash or to be more precise what Nash did until the end. I think that he should've joined forces with Lita. These and even more moments pulled me out of the game and its world.
However, even if there were 10-20-30 such moments it is not too much as I tend to be more critical usually and this happens with each and every game I play. For example I liked the variety of movement - jumping and swimming but I felt that it got overused at some point (especially the swimming). Also, there were a lot of places with an open area at the end of the map. I get that it looks better but it is not a good thing. You create a rule ("The map ends in an open spot = you can go to another map") and you do not break it. At least that is what I value more than the otherwise very good mapping.
Overall the game held well and I liked the most of it except for the battle system. I tend to prefer the turns before the timer based and the hybrid ones. I disliked it not only because of that though. It just felt non-responsive most of the time. It felt super unpredictable in terms of who comes first and if I would be able to just click faster and heal/attack before I receive an enemy attack or not.
Overall I think that this game suffered from it being started by a developer who grew up and started understanding what makes a fantasy world better but did not want to drop his project. The game starts slow and rather usual but as the plot continues forward it is becoming more and more interesting and better overall.
I listed pros and cons below. They turned out to be an equal amount but IMO the pros overweight the cons by a signifcant margin. I liked the game a lot and although I have been super critical here I really see what it did right and it even inspired me to keep on working on my own project and finish it some day.
Pros, Could've-been-betters and Cons:
+ Easily the best mapping I have ever seen from an RPGM game
+ Heroes were well fleshed out and likeable
+ Customizable stats
+ No random encounters
+ Interesting plot
+ Good music
* Crafting is not bad but had more potential than that
* Skills had more potential than that
* The world build is okay but I think that more could've been done here
- A lot of clichés
- A few bad deus ex machina moments
- Very slow, non-coordinated and sometimes frustrating combat
- Mostly ininteresting level design with the exception of the flying circles but they get old fast
- Uninteresting side quests
- Somewhat uninteresting weapon/armor system
Overall:
I loved the game. It came at the right moment and gave me the spark I needed to restart work on my own projects and assured me that I am on the right track. However, I would prefer that we stop reusing Tolkien's ideas and start seeing more unique fantasy content. I guess a sequel or a game that takes place in the Abbyss somewhere would be a nice place to start.

Before I go into depth I want to specify that I did use a gamepad for this game - I strongly recommend using one and would go so far as to say to skip this title if you don't have one. It's a console port, guys.
Darksiders is a game that wears its inspirations on its sleeve famously, and to a ridiculous degree. When you're traveling through a Legend of Zelda-style dungeon solving puzzles with a Portal Device, you know you're not playing a game that's focusing on being particularly innovative.
That's fine, it doesn't do it does particularly well though.
The dungeons, level design wise, are all threadbare. Puzzles never get more complicated than "get past the obstruction using the item you got in that dungeon", platforming reaches its maximum amount of complexity 20 minutes into the game, and exploration is limited because despite the expansive levels, there's very few optional areas. You're taken in a very roundabout, but ultimately linear, path and led by the nose from start to finish.
Combat doesn't fair any better - it has all the tools to play well, but the way it's executed is an absolute mess. Even the Counter, the quintessential "up yours" high-risk high-reward move that's been a staple of decent hack n slash games for over a decade, will often be cancelled and interrupted because it doesn't interrupt a good deal of enemy attacks - seemingly at random.
The moveset cops a lot of flak for its simplicity, but once you unlock the full movesets for each weapon and supplement each weapon's combos with another weapon (you can even switch out your sidearm and combo them into each other) you can get a nice amount of combat variation going on.
Design doesn't support that, though, since the game has the a conceptually moronic weapon leveling system that strongly discourages using more than one weapon - the difference between weapon levels is more than just palpable. Add to that that combos have no impact on anything whatsoever.
At its best, it plays like a more forgiving Devil May Cry, but mostly it plays like a more brainless God of War and it suffers for that heavily.
The whole lack of finesse seeps into every corner of the game. They're terrified you'll play it wrong, or will look in the wrong direction for more than a second - puzzles will constantly be interrupted by those infuriating drawn-out mini-cutscenes which point out what you're meant to do, the Watcher is used as a device to call your attention to something that's already flashing, and many more examples. One particularly egregious example has you explore a small environment for four challenge portals, that as well as having icons on the map and having giant beams shoot up into the sky, even have Eye of Sauron-like icons on top of the beams just to be extra sure that you don't actually have to explore.
Darksiders has all the tools and capability to play well, but it adamantly refuses to.
On a more positive note, the environments are absolutely fantastic, I was personally fond of the character design  - despite my usual complete distaste for giant pauldrons - due to just how well done it is, and it has some of the best flashy particle use I've ever seen.
War as a lead is bland, but he isn't antagonizing or unlikeable. The supporting cast is similarly lacking in character but inoffensive (with the exception of Samael and the Watcher, who were both pretty enjoyable). The story isn't particularly interesting, but isn't grating.
It's an incredibly pretty game (despite the very noticeable lack of anti-aliasing in a game with so many sharp edges), and if you're looking for a stylish hack n slash and are willing to overlook a few design issues that drag it down, then check it out.
I wouldn't outright recommend it to anybody that isn't looking for that particular type of game, though.

Having played every Trials game since 2, i've seen the series go from warehouses to the great outdoors and now to the future and with every iteration, it gets better and better. Trials Fusion pretty much kept what made Evolution great and added a few things to keep it from being just another Trials game. Here's my verdict.
The GOOD.
-"WELCOME TO THE FUTURE....MAN, MACHINE, THE FUTURE!"...yeah MUCH better intro than "VROOM VROOM, im ready to go, time for the muh muh muh muh muh muhnday nitro!"
-Trials and Tribulations: The easy to learn, hard to master gameplay is still here and still as good as its ever been.
-HOLY EPIC PC PORT BATMAN!: Redlynx learned from their mistakes, a much better port than Evo was. No texture pop in, no long load times, no FPS studdering all while adding a lot of graphics options to cater to many different setups. Nothing but good, clean, beautiful visuals at 60fps.(up to 120 would've been great though)
-Challenging: The new challenge system adds ALOT of replay value to each track, although after beating Inferno IV, i don't wanna ever do that again. But its nice to go back and do 15 backflips on a track or finding that secret entrance or play tennis with a penguin to get XP for that fancy body kit you want.
Here's my Inferno IV results if you don't believe me:
The MEH.
-Tricky: The FMX system is nice...but finicky, i've used keyboard(my main setup) and a PS4 controller and no matter what i do, i can never get it to do the trick i want to do during FMX events(Especially the ones that ask you to do specific tricks), i can only do coffins...EVERY TIME! Frustrating at times but a neat little addition nonetheless.
-From an easy stroll to a trip to hell: As a long time player, i've gained a bit of skill over the years. I can gold(and above) every track up to the Rainforest bit, with ease(minus challenges). But after that, man does it go from easy to hard in an instant, i feel like newcomers are gonna have more problems adjusting to the difficulty curve than i did. At first its all about high speed and looking cool, after the ATV section...its all about control and balance, ESPECIALLY after unlocking the Pit Viper.
-Do i look pretty?: Customization options are here, but a bit lacking, you can't operate on individual bike parts anymore(in favor of body kits) the rider customization is Tiered and in different themes and you can only change out the helmet, the shirt and the legs. Which kinda sucks, but there's alot to unlock and each tier is better than the last.
The BAAAAAD.
-Aside from the FMX, there really isn't anything new.
Conclusion: Its Trials, if you've never played one, do yourself a favor and pick this up, this is by far one of the best arcade series out there. If you're a fan and you needed more Trials, click that buy button.

TLDR: Worth it.
Some people hear the word puzzle game and think that it's a pain in the neck that you pay for and that's fair because most of them are. A few puzzle games are on a higher level than that, though. Engare is one of them.
Two reasons you should buy this:
This is an exercise in artistic concept.  The more you understand that concept, the more entertaining it becomes as you get better and better, firing the neurons in your brain that are required for this charming endeavour.
The music is enthralling. I'll let you know now that it is repetitive but, so is the complex, pattern-based essence of the game.
Two reasons you should not buy this game:
You have already mastered the form. You're such a pro that this is just a banal tool for the masses to enjoy and are not at all challenged by timing the beginning of the pattern.
Nearly inconsequential and very infrequent button detection bugs throw you into a severe rage, destroying your ability to relax and take in any form of beauty.
I should say that Engare may not have taught me a single fact but, I feel like a useful lesson has been imparted on me every time climb to the next difficulty.  That's what a puzzle game should feel like - that epiphanic, 'Ah Ha' moment. I have always understood the basic idea behind geomatric art, having been one of those kids who received an apathetically purchased spin-art set on more than one occasion. Now, when i see this medium in everyday life, I have a greater, more informed appreciation for it. Good job, Mahdi Barami, and thanks.

I don't normally write reviews, but this game deserves a review. I absolutly adore this game and has tons of wonderfull ideas and features with literally constant updates. So lets get into the game. What is it? You could say its minecraft but in all honestly...it kind of isnt. It is its own unique game with tons of unique blocks and features that I would love to have in minecraft, that not even modded minecraft can offer. So lets get the good and the bad in the game listed in a nice little list. This is a little lengthy so if you dont want to read all of this and want to know the short version
SHORT Version: Its a good game lots of features and updates, little bugs, if there are it gets fixed pretty quickly, dev streams and listens to his watchers. Also they look at feedback and love to get feedback on the game.
LONG: If you want more depth here you go.
PROS:
-It is constantly updated on a daily baises. There are new features almost weekly and when they did a poll on their twitter, literallythe next day there was a solution and was implemented within a pretty short amount of time. A day or two before it was in the game.
-Bugs are quickly addressed when reported and usually will have a patch in a decent amount of time, depending on how game breaking it is of course.
-Multiple tiers that you work your way through as you go deeper into the world.
-Researching those tiers. The deeper you get the more Research points you get (RP) The more blocks and flora you scan the more you unlock.
-Replayability. Theres a lot of replayability in this game and with constant updates and a lot of features being planned it is always a new experience. (Especially if they add the planned features like space)
-ARTHER. An amazing little robot that you can dress in a top hat, eye monocle and an good looking moustache. Love it! Though hes really useful ingame with status updates and back up power if you run low.
-Much more to list that would just make this ungodly long.
-Multiple game modes that are pretty fun ranging from hardcore and rush mode one or two others that I cant think of atm.
CONS
-Not everything is implemented yet. Some stuff is in there but it hasnt been properly fleshed out. (Though this isnt in early access, it still technically is because of a lot of reasons that you need to game developers point of view to understand. (Which the dev actually explained to us in a stream in depth which gives you a big understanding of the gaming industry. Like the top games make 90% of the money. Even though fortress craft is in the top 500 for steam games they still struggle, so even though this is the con section, I highly suggest if you buy the game you buy the DLC with it to help support them))
-Things can be a little difficult to piece together, even with the handbook, so it may take a little bit of time to figure things out or do a little research (Again its being fleshed out and the handbook is still unfinished so its understable)
-Your kind of stuck in spot defending the same area. Now Im sure they have plans to change that especially when they plan to implement space, so for right now your kind of defending your castle.
Honestly Im just prying cons out of anything I can just to make this seem fair, but there really arent to many cons. If you cant launch the game then talk to the dev. They'll try to help you. Trust me, they want to help you and expand their player base. You can listen into one of their streams and their ideas and viewpoints are really nice to listen into and really put time into their game. It is a bit of a tedious game so it takes time to make things but once you get the hang of it you will surely have fun. This is truly a fantastic game and you should give it a chance. I would honestly even say that this game should be valued way more then 10-15$ for the amount of work they put in, so its a pretty good deal for a game like this.

I don't do many reviews but this quirky gem of a game has grabbed my attention.
A great voxel builder. Lots of interesting systems to figure out and problem solve with.
At only 30 hours in I can't speak much about the end game tower defense game.
The fact that it even exists adds spice to the early game...
The early game tower defense game is only required if you choose to
pay attention to it.  You can play hardest core where it is absolutely required
to win every battle.  Or you can play easy ignore it and let the mobs "kill" you
central core - which reboots in about 2 minutes and your are back
to another hours of building...
Unlike some voxel/pixel builder games, this one is about setting up a system to do the work,
not grinding through the building process yourself.
We build new structures, we explore, while we explore - the machines mine, refine, shape and build parts from the ore.
PRO: Big world, Interesting systems, Interesting tech tree
Tech growth comes from an interesting combination of exploring and crafting.
CON: Small team, very active development (which are pros) means that
community resources like wiki's stuggle to keep up.
While there is in-game help, you can only find out about topics as
you run into them, and the explanations are not complete.
If you like to plan ahead you will need to scour forum posts
and the guide seciton. The FAQ in the guide section is essential to understanding
some key concepts.  Other steam forum posts contain key tidbits.
The lack of documentation combined with all the things you can get the
system to do make for a steep learning curve (at 36 hours I am just getting
out of the "early" game.)  But puzzling out how to get what you want to happen
with all the games systems is a LOT of fun.  You have to work for your tech
upgrades, but they are all the more enjoyable that way.

You know, usually I try to stay away from RPGMaker games. While I love the concept of having this open software that anyone can make games on, in my experience the RPGMaker games that I've played in the past have been low effort, low quality works that just aren't fun to play.
Luckily, Ara Fell is not one of those.
Ara Fell has a coherent, enjoyable story to follow. It's not the most original concept, I guess, but it's not cheesy, it's not forced, and it's just kinda.. good. It's a good story, and it was fun to experience it.
The path through the story is complex enough to be challenging, but not overly convoluted to make you lose your way and wander. At the same time, you /can/ wander around if you want to. It's not entirely open world, but it lets you off the rails enough to explore and have fun in the world. Maybe try to find some secrets.
Gameplay is pretty standard for an RPGMaker game. Turn-based, which I personally enjoy, and a reasonable system of skills to work with.
It's just good. No, it's not a mind-blowing masterpiece, but I can say it's probably the best experience that I've ever had playing an RPGMaker game, and I enjoyed it enough that I e-mailed the company to ask if they're making more. (Good news, more games!)
Absolutely worth the money, which is more than I can say for a lot of these types of games.

I was poking around the steam store, and found this fantastic gem.
I've been following Darth since he modded Rome: Total War (the first one) with his Darthmod. It was one of the best games I've ever played. (I defy any general to play Rome: Total War BI with Darthmod and emerge victorious). His AI work was incredible, and it was a damn shame that he ended up pulling back a bit because the community was vicious to him.
Anyway, the man is a genius. (and of course I must acknowledge the help from everyone else that has gone into this game and his mods. All the playtesting, etc). This game is amazing. Simply amazing. (You know what sucks? I remember when he applied to work at CA....and they turned him down. They could have really used his help...see any tw game and you will see a lot of patchy AI).
About this game though. It is the best civil war game I've ever played. Even better than Sid Miers Gettysburg, which was not bad. This game though....the controls are simple, the map is gorgeous, and the way it plays...it is super easy to learn, but hard to master. A lot of playability comes with the new scenarios that come up in the course of your playing.
You order around units on a real-time map, and deal with morale, org, cover, etc, but all in a very easy UI. The game is super-easy to play and learn.
The real star here is the AI. Simply put, the AI is amazing. You can pick between several different AI's, and you can watch the computer employ strategy that will astound and challenge you. I have lost a battle because I wanted to watch the computer respond to what I did. Being fooled by a computer is amazing after playing Total War. My God, I just got flanked and hit from behind? DId you just take a hill I thought was protected? Damn losing was never this much fun.
I cannot recommend this game enough. If you have any interest in civil war, strategy, or anything of that ilk, then this is the game for you. Support this team, and this developer; they are doing amazing things.

This is a tiny strategy game, and when I say tiny I mean the overall content of the game. There is a short campaign that takes you through the battle at Gettysburg and you may do so by either playing the Union or Federate side, changing history while you're at it.
But the game is NOT tiny when it comes to the amount of fun you can have with it. You can switch up the AI's playstyle and difficulty for every playthrough and you also change your own way of trying to beat it. If you're a RTS player that enjoy the fighting part of the Total War games you will probably enjoy this game as well. It does not have THAT much of depth yet, there are not a ton of different manouvers you can do for each unit but the overall gameplay feels amazing.
Drawing lines over the battlefield to move your units feels and works great. It takes a second to get used to, but as soon as you get the controls in to your head you're gonna focus on putting your units in the best strategic positions and doing brave charges in to the enemy lines.
There are however some issues if you play on a lower difficulty, you can actually be to agressive and push the AI army in to a corner of the map making them unable to move. But then again... there is also a multiplayer mode!
Great game overall. Recommended!

The puzzles are rather difficult for a game whose looks seem to be children-oriented and the game gives you almost no-clues. The lenght of the game is, to be honest, too short.
The studio behind Lume (State of Play) is working on a longer and more complex sequel to this game, but unless you catch Lume on a bundle or at a great low price, I would recommend you to buy this first game on the series only if you really love to contribute to small indie teams or if you hate long games (Lume really, really feels too short).

For us gamers that have played SM: Gettysburg, this game is a refreshing take on the battle we spent so many hours on in the past. While you do not have as much control as you did in SM: Gettysburg, the controls are a lot easier. Instead of having to move every regiment individually, you now control brigades. You can select a certain part of the battle to play through or play through the entire Battle of Gettysburg day by day.  Here are the pros and cons I think of when I play this game as a SM: Gettysburg veteran (even though I know this isn't SM)
Pros
-Easy controls make moving units simple
-Game does not throw too much information at the player
-Being able to choose how you want to advance in the battle (Defend Cemetary Hill, or try and counterattack the Confederates and such)
-Historical Units
-Cool graphics and animations, line of sight is generally easy to see
-Topographical map
-Units keep their strength after a battle(If the Iron Brigade losses 800 men defending oak hill well...it'll be a lot weaker in the next battle)
-Lots of diffrent types of AI difficulties(More aggressive/More tactical)
Negatives
-Control brigades instead of regiments
-No flanking bonus(I might be wrong)
-Units rout or panic a little too easy sometimes
-No option to toggle between skirmish and line formation
-No option to limber/unlimber artillery
Overall, I give this game a 8,8/10, I really enjoy this game and I think that you will too!

I am quite late to review this game, but I got it on the Halloween sale and buckled down to beat it.
The game gets a lot right but it also gets a lot wrong. Starting off with the good, it has a cool plot, and an interesting setting. It takes a twist down "Apocalypse Lane" as it were, but with a biblical/fantasy twist.
The game is a mish mash of every action adventure game out there, heavily influenced by games like Zelda, God of War, Prince of Persia etc. In typical THQ fashion there is nothing original about the gameplay but I do not hold that against the game.
The one inexcusable, frustrating, made-me-brake-my-spacebar-fault is the controls! They are abysmal and unintuitive which really hurts a game like this. I played on this highest difficulty, and the controls caused me to die more than the game itself. And I am not whining about hard to pull off combos, even basic things like aiming/locking on to targets is unecessarily complex and annoying. Having to press and hold five different buttons to ride and shoot simultaneously is just stupid. I also looked at review for the consoles and apparently they are no better.
One good thing about the game is that the challenge is there, the hardest difficulty available to me at the start is what I chose and I did have my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me many times. The character design is also very well done, and the game has its own style. Kudoes for that.
All in all this game is a pit stop amidst the ongoing journey of a action adventure game fan, and is nothing to write home about. It has a lot of issues but manages to be enjoyable despite that.
TL,DR: A mediocre title, worth buying if you get it on a sale else don't bother.

TL;DR: Played this game a while ago when it came out for Xbox 360.  I enjoyed it greatly until the game had some very poor performance and became unplayable.  The PC version works a lot better and is well worth the sale price.
Rest of review:
This game is poorly optimized, similar to The Witcher 2, with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ framerates in environments that look rather simple.  The performance issues aside, the game isn't gorgeous and offers little visual stimulation in return for your hours of progression.  The said, if you have a decent enough computer to run the game at a smooth 60fps, I imagine it'll be a fun game to toy with.
The magic system is interesting.  You collect and combine cards to create magical skills to be used in the open world.  Don't misunderstand: this isn't a card game.  You simply use the cards to make stuff.  It's done fairly well and offers a lot of customization to your magical arsenal.
The open world is fairly big but not as freely roamed as Skyrim or Fallout New Vegas.   There are a lot of linear, story-driven missions which get in the way of your exploratory experience.  However, you can explore a lot of areas in this game, and often, you are rewarded with both loot and side quests.
Update - Dec. 2014: This game is now only $1.99, so get it.  Yes, it was in a few bundles recently, and that's probably part of why the game became so cheap on Steam.  The game is open world and offers a lot of exploration, but the game's performance is rather cumbersome to say the least.  If you have a decent enough machine for it, it's a decent enough experience to be worth the two dollars at least.

Darksiders seems like a safe bet.  Just take the overall game design of The Legend of Zelda, then give it a God of War combat system, and the art style from World of Warcraft.
Unfortunately, this paint-by-numbers approach misses the subtleties.  Zelda's charm, God of War's finesse, and Warcraft's humour are all notably absent, and this results in a game that suffers from a serious identity crisis.  It's really hard to take the games post-apocalyptic setting seriously when the visuals are just so... colourful.  It's hard to take the combat seriously when your combo library is so limited, upgrades and new attacks are so expensive, and your characters moves so slowly.  It's hard to find any charm when every character you meet is doing their best to be completely unlikeable.
The plot is stupid beyond belief.  You can tell that they're aiming to establish some deep and interesting lore here, but more often than not it just seems like they're making up the rules that govern the world as they go along.  I had trouble following certain elements, not because it was confusing, but because it was so uninteresting.  There are characters characters and concepts that are introduced in the early hours, but never revisited in the later game.
That's enough ripping on the game.  The truth of the matter is that Darksiders practically defines the 6/10.  Some good ideas, most of which are implemented well enough to make them seem interesting, but not enough to save the game from complete mediocrity.
The game's dungeons are truly Zelda-esque.  They manage good pacing between combat rooms and puzzle rooms, and the brainteasers manage to hit the sweet spot of 'not too easy, not too difficult' more often than not.  The one exception is the games final dungeon, which sees you scaling three massive towers with the help of a simplified 'Portal Gun'.  It's creative, but after clearing the first tower, it'll start to seem like pointless and tedious length-padding.  Oh, and each tower ends with the exact same mini-boss fight.  Not only that, but each of the paths towards the first two dungeons requires you to beat a series of combat challenges, some of which introduce some very immersion wrecking conditions.
The visuals are incredible.  In spite of it's grim-dark attitudes, the ruins of our civilization has some incredibly colourful locations.  Barren wastelands quickly give way to green vistas very early in the game, and the various locations each manage to maintain a different visual identity.  The levels are packed with plenty of detail, but it never gets in the way of communicating what you're supposed to interact with.
Overall, the game does deserve a qualified recommendation.  If you're genuinely curious to see what a mediocre Legend of Zelda game could look like, this is it.  Dull and repetitive combat, unlikeable characters, and a moronic plot bog down what was a generally enjoyable experience.  Darksiders is at it's best when your solving puzzles in any one of it's unique dungeons, and there's just enough of that to make the entire experience worthwhile...

"My name is..............my name is...........Daniel" and that's the start to this dark and totally engrossing horror game that grab's you by the scruff of the neck and refuse's to let go of you until you have finished it and seen all the horror's that it has to offer.
This is one game i had on my radar for a long time and one i had heard a lot about,either written or from friend's who have played it and the word's "CLASSIC" and "GENRE DEFINING" have been mentioned on more than one occasion.
But i allways take this with a pinch of salt and allways make up my own mind,but trust me when i say that the two phrase's that i just mentioned dont do this game justice as it is both of these and so much more.
Amnesia: The Dark Descent - Trailer - YouTube
You start to play not knowing much other than your name and that for some reason you are here to do something that will affect not only your life but that of other's as well,and as the game progress'es you will come to learn not only the nature for your being here but that of the scream's that haunt the castle you find yourself stuck in.
And that's all i will say on the story of the game as you should find the secret's this game hold's and the many twist's it take's on your own as nothing is more horrifying or scary as not only hearing but witnessing these thing's for yourself first hand instead of after the fact.
The graphic's may look a little dated but trust me when i say they do their job perfectly when it comes to the scare factor and the things you will see not only make you jump (some jump scares in game) but also repulse you as well.
The sound and music in game is top notch and really help's in setting that "OH MY GOD" type atmosphere that a lot of games like this seem to lack,this is down to the work of the composer Mikko Tarmia without who's music the game would (to be honest) not have the impact it does.
He is currently working on Frictional Game's next project SOMA which i for one am waiting for with eager anticipation!!!!
Amnesia The Dark Descent - Soundtrack - (Mikko Termia) - 04
All the spoken dialogue in game is delivered to perfection as well by the voice cast and some of it just has to be heard to be believed as to how good it actually is (and for a game like this that's all about delivering a powerfull story that's what was needed,not some half baked ham handed attempt-"HAMMER HORROR" movie's anyone).
The gameplay range's from puzzle solving (finding items that are laying around in the castle) which can be quite frustrating as some puzzle's can be quite offbeat to running and hiding from the monstrositie's that pervade in this dark and forboding castle from hade's (a lot has been said lately about game's using this mechanic but here it suits the game and makes it more nerve wracking to play).
Amnesia The Dark Descent: Closet Hiding! - YouTube

So would you like this game and the answer is yes if you are looking for a classic and one of the best game's the horror genre of games has ever had to offer but if you are not one for this type of game and want something a little more action packed instead of full of story and an interesting and horrific tale then i would look elswhere.

Engare is a game about mathemoatical drawings and repeating motions, sounds interresting right?
Well I played through the entire game, and here are my thoughts on it!
Positive:
+ great introduction, which made me excited to get in and start playing and seeing all the cool complex shapes I'd be seeing
+ The music is great, and so is the artstyle, kudos to that
+ the first few levels are great and show you a bunch of complex and beautiful shapes (for the most part at least)
+ the drawing tools are absolutely amazing
Negative:
- past the first 2 areas, it feels like the dev had already shown you all the cool complex shapes too eartly on and ran out of ideas for shapes so he just started giving you a bunch of basic/uninterresting shapes to make with more complex puzzles, meaning that the payoff for the harder puzzles became more and more dissapointing as it went on
- the last 2 puzzles of the game are just levels where you make the shape that you want to move on, no idea why those are main levels and not just one mode avaiable in the area of the game that let's you play around with shapes (screenshot 3 and 6 from the store page are form that zone of the game)
- the first few areas had all those interresting setups, with grids of squares moving in odd patterns and blocks colliding with each other and swapping blocks with one another making finding where to draw the sahpe quickly, except that those went away after that and the last areas became 80% nothing but rotating sticks attached to one another (the ramining 20% being circles in circles)
- the drawing tools are locked behind those main game levels, which is a shame
So all in all, the drawing tools are amazing and I have nothing bad to say about them, however I do feel inccredibly underwhelmed by the main game itself, and the drawing tools being locked behind those means that you'll have to get through them all to unlock all of the tools.
Final Score: 5/10

Out of all the 'Metroidvania' games I've played, Shovel Knight is one of few that I'd recommend even to someone who doesn't play modern Metroidvanias. And let me tell you why. Shovel Knight is the best use of modern gaming technology to refresh an old medium without attempting to update it. Many modern sidescrolling platformers either utilize 3D models and environments in a 2D experience (something I just personally find off-putting) or attempt for a "retro" look of 8-bit graphics by giving you a series of various rectangle enemies and rectangle levels to be beaten by your rectangle hero. Shovel Knight's pixel art graphics pay homage to the love and care that went into gamemakers who did their best to create art and a setting within their limited medium. It's one of the few pixel art games I've been able to use resources from as a background without it looking and feeling tacky. Beyond the visual art is the music, which, while not my favorite platformer soundtrack, does an excellent job enhancing the setting without being either distracting or lackluster.
The unlockables and upgrades feel satisfying and well spread out. You're constantly able to experiment with and revist abilities without feeling like there's a learning curve or needing to take time away from actually playing the game. Bounce physics from the down attack feel satisfying, as does the knockback from side attacks. The game makes you feel powerful while also retaining its challenge, especially punctuated during its boss fights. NPC interactions range from adorable to hilarious to legitimately emotional. It's an extremely polished experience that I'd describe as a classic metroidvania experience that only utilizes modern system techology to make itself as authentic as possible. Yacht Club really came out of nowhere to produce this absolute gem of a game.
And then they released Plague of Shadows for free.
Crazy respect to the devs, I'd have gladly paid $4.99 for the experience Plague gives, and they gave it to us for free. Shovel Knight is obviously a labor of love for them.
TL;DR:
Great art, great game, great devs. 9.5/10 if not 10/10. I'd recommend it even at full price, but if you see a good sale I'd say that it goes into must-buy territory.

Alright... where to start? Well, I suppose I should start off by saying I can tell this game takes inspiration from "industrial"-themed Minecraft mods, in that you're setting up production chains and transporting items and mining and all that stuff. The problem is it's only taken inspiration, and pretty much fails in every other regard.
Fortresscraft is initially simple and you might have fun for the first hour, but the fun soon stops as the game becomes a parade of
, either due to bad game design, intentional grinding, and a slew of other bullcrap that keeps you from that carrot on a stick; progression.
Now, you may be wondering, "Higgs, what's so annoying and bad about the game? Look at all the positive reviews!" To that I say; everyone is stupid except me, and you... if you listen to my gripes about this game.
Starting off, the graphics. Now, I might be playing this on an ancient GTX630 graphics card, but that's still no excuse for a game with these sorts of graphics to not be hitting 60FPS, at the very least on low settings. The models are simple and bland, they look like they're out of a PS2 game (a bargain-bin one at that), and the blocky terrain clashes with this. The textures are muddy, dull and needlessly high-res, and have parallax for the most mundane things. The developer seems to have slapped on as many special rendering effects on top of the game to cover up the mediocrity of the art style, to the point that it can be difficult to see when some of the bloom effects or screen overlays do their best to blind you. As a result, the game tends to chug despite the low poly-count.
The gameplay itself is, to a point, what you'd expect from a Minecraft ripoff. Break and place blocks. Simple enough, if the UIs weren't a goddamn nightmare to navigate. Every single screen seems to run on a different set of rules, and despite what might seem like a solid framerate your clicking and dragging will be laggy as hell. The focus of the game, the machines, are obnoxiously unexplained; even with the in-game help it either seemed to gloss over the function or rules of things lioke hoppers, which never EVER behaved in the way you wanted them to. I'd be fine with that if I could mine by hand, but you CAN'T. Ore blocks aren't supposed to be broken apparently, and yield junk when you turn your laser onto them. You have to place a grinder thing beside an ore vein, then wait for it to chew through it sluggishly. It's obnoxious and it just doesn't make sense. Even breaking normal blocks manages to be awkward and clunky, they break far too fast and the range for the laser is too far, making digging stairwells a chore when you accidentally dig at more or less than a 45* angle, meaning you have to dig out the ceiling or place blocks to make the stairs smooth again. With the way blocks break in Minecraft, you have far better control over what you're digging, to the point that I find mining to actually be one of the more enjoyable activities even after at least 5 years of playing the game, Fortresscraft's awkwardness just vomits all over that sense of zen that I get.
It's worth mentioning again that almost nothing is actually given context in the game. Despite dismantling a tree with my laser I can't make planks to make a crate to store all this garbage in my inventory. What do all these over-detailed glowing plants do? Slimes everywehere? Are they bad guys? Sometimes when I'm underground a block decides it hates me and kills me (dying has no consequences outside of respawning, yet another annoyance). Are THOSE bad guys? How do I fight them? I had to go down to -150 meters to find lithium ore, yet the device that beams power underground requires that I already have piles of lithium? Why do I have to nrun back and forth between my power station because there's little option for providing power to underground drills? How many times am I going to get HYPOTHERMIA?
Also, no pickaxes in the game apart from the logo. That really miffs me for some reason, maybe because I can't mine myself and the machines are frustrating to deal with. Placing conveyor belts is an exasperating chore; they never go the way you want them to the first time, and you'll often need to dig a hole to stand in to get at the right angle to place them up a wall (that doesn't even make SENSE).
Did I mention this game is ugly? Holy hell is it ugly. Again, I have to reitterate that the flat, blocky terrain clashes with the semi-detailed models; Minecraft might be ugly too but at least it's a consistent sort of ugly. Every texture is far more detailed than it needs to be, to the point that it looks less like a texture and more like a grey blob at every distance apart from directly in front of your eyes, in which case it's got so much detail it looks almost uncanny valley in a way. The lighting SUCKS, it hurts my eyes. I hate looking at this game.
In conclusion, if you really, absolutely must play a voxel-based mining game with machines, buy Minecraft and install Technic launcher, there's dozens of well-made and POLISHED mods for you to play, with far more content and without the graphics drain and constant frustrations.

There is lots to love here for fans of the sandboxy-RPG realm, I suppose. I'm no authority on the genre, but the combat and magic system, for example, actually offers a superior level of fun in some ways than that of titans like Skyrim, IMHO.
The musical 'mini-game' deserves a paragraph unto itself. It's Medieval Guitar Hero, with song arrangements that are actually quite inspired and a surprising joy to dabble in with the various bards-at-large in the realm.
But at the end of the day, TWII seems kind of hamstrung by flat voice acting, repetitive sound design, and a maddeningly middle-of-the-road stance on how seriously it wants to be taken.
At times this tongue-in-cheek, knowing stance works in the game's — and the gamer's — favour, giving it a disarmingly approachable feel for an 'epic' RPG. At other moments, however, you may find yourself desperately wishing it could make up its mind to stop pulling punches and fully embrace one way or the other.

Picked this up on sale the other day, and wow, is it fun.  The controls are absolutely intuitive and address most of the problems I've had with similar grand strategy games (namely, pathfinding is not an issue in Ultimate General: Gettysburg).  I was surprised by how competent the AI was, and how differently you have to play in order to beat each one--so far I've played three different iterations of the battle against three different AI opponents, and it resulted in radically different outcomes each time.  The historical detail is also astonishing.
That said, the game isn't perfect.  My main criticism is in the way different kinds of units are handled.  You'll primarily be using infantry--which is to be expected, since it is the Civil War--but I haven't gotten much mileage out of the artillery or videttes (mounted cavalry) you have access to in this game.  Soldier for soldier, infantry is much more effective and everything else seems kind of useless.  Some of the battles end pretty quickly, too; I had one end before the reinforcements I got halfway through could make it to my line.
Still, this is a very good tactical strategy game, and as a bonus will definitely satisfy Civil War buffs who have gone without a good representation of the period since the Sid Meier games or the Civil War Generals series.

I am the House of Julii.
I am to the North of Italy. I am part of the Glorious Roman Republic, sharing with three other factions; the blue Scorpios (I think) who have decided to take a couple of islands and then the big parts of Africa. The green Brutii, who decided that looking ridiculous would best show the Greeks what's what. And I, wearing fantastically imperial red, who was tasked with sorting out the dirty Gauls.
I quickly began a conquest that would put the Black Templars to shame, sending out army after army, conquering town after town. They tried to resist, but my men were worth two of theirs, and my men outnumbered their three to one. As we came, we took most of them slaves, built up my core towns, built as many temples to convince more people to shag as possible, and continued on our merry murdering way.
Occasionally, the Guals or Brittony or Germans would manage to scrape together an entire army of 2000 people. These were the battles I, and my family, were born for. We smashed together, blood and sword and sinew, as my Velites threw their spears overhead, and cavalry quickly hit them from behind. Few enemies died facing us in the north, many ran and most died with sword wounds in their backs rather than face us.
We tried peace once, and we paid the price with roman lives. When they begged for our mercy, they found only our gladius. We heard the lamentations of their women as they were taken back to mighty Arretium, our capital city. And how it had grown; on the back of slaves and the glory of our men, we raised great arenas and temples to show our glory! We raised great barracks to train our men! We grew the greatest of men to enforce our will! And the north of Europe was stained red with blood; the map of Europe was stained red with our flags.
We found that land ran out quickly; Europa gave way before our bloodlust did, and we turned to look back. We were disgusted with what we saw. Corruption. Weakness. Our supposed equals made peace with the savages, our supposed superiors hide behind the walls of Rome. They whispered of treachery, but we knew weakness and corruption when we saw it. The spineless Scorpios had no trouble gaining the favour of the Senate; spending more time on their knees in glorious Rome than sword in hand over Carthage. The Brutii failed to live up to their brutish name; content with a paltry pile of sand, growing fat and lazy as we had grown lean and numerous in both flesh and glory.
We recalled our armies to home, to the swell of the crowds. They chanted our name, and spat at the mentions of the Senate. All had been united under our banner; did not the Celts and Gauls and Germans and Thrycians alike not bend the knee to the glorious Romans, all beneath the bloody red banner of the Julii? Mars had made his favour clear; he doesn't favour cowards, and Jupiter didn't let the weak rule. We built temples in His Name, and spread his name further than even the diplomats know. All that was left was to follow the glory given to us, under the gaze of the gods and cheers of the people, we marched the final path.
All roads lead to Rome.

TL;DR: This game is an upgrade from the previous Shadow Warrior in almost every way. It has great gameplay, visuals, and voice acting, with a stellar soundtrack. It does, however, fall far short of it's predecessor in terms of story. I'd give this a solid 7.5/10
Ok, now on to the super long and more personal review.
Shadow Warrior 2 is the sequel I wanted, with the preperation and delivery that every other video game developer should aspire to. It's gameplay is, in terms of mechanics and gunplay, a dramatic improvement upon the first game in this remade series. The soundtrack is somehow better than that of the first game, which I absolutely adored. The voice acting is on point, which a slew of new and returning characters. And the new loot system is implemented incredibly well, for this to be the first iteration of it in this series.
The main issue I've had with this game so far is the story. This might be more of a personal issue for me (being a fan of the first game's story), and won't affect the majority of new players, but I don't really like the fact that they (being the devs) felt the need to kind of rewrite the lore/history and characaters of the first game, especially considering it took until bascially the end of Shadow Warrior 1 to finally understand what was happening in this universe we were thrust into.
To be perfectly honest, I thought the first game was painfully average. The only redeeming qualities to Shadow Warrior 1 were the sword play, soundtrack, and story. That last one was super important to me. Flying Wild Hog had done an amazing job of delievering a story more based on eastern culture, one of revenge and hate, rather than the normal western story of a good guy saving the world and coming out unscathed.
Shadow Warrior 1 made you feel a slew of emotions, from the tounge and cheek humor of Lo Wang, to the sad ending of seeing him lose basically the only person he ever called a friend. This game, however, drops the ball on that aspect. There is honestly just far too much humor in this game. So much so that I sometimes just want to skip the cutscenes so I don't have to hear Lo Wang talk anymore (which surprised even me, seeing as I LOVED Lo Wang's humor in the first game).
Remember that awesome backstory of why Hoji (who hasn't even been mentioned once 8 hours in) was banished to the mortal realm? Those really interesting, hand drawn cutscenes that showed a more serious side of the Shadow Warrior story, and laid down some lore for the (apparent) franchise? Or maybe the flashbacks of the bosses that explained their motives of siding with Enra? Nope, all gone. Now those super interesing and kickass bosses and NPC's from the first game are replaced with shells of their former selves, who insist on keeping the♥♥♥♥♥♥jokes and mindless banter going. And your hilarious, if not mysterious/dangerous, companion is replaced with a whiny girl who calls you an idiot every 5 seconds.
I don't know, maybe I was expecting too much from this sequel, but I'm quite sad (and angry) to see any sincerity that Lo Wang, and this story, might have had stripped, and replaced with a constant slew of♥♥♥♥♥♥jokes, and remarks of how "unintelligent" and "moronic" you are (from literally everyone, including the girl you rescued) for saving the planet...AGAIN! But, I digress.
Shadow Warrior 2 does, even after all the issues I have with it, deserve a purchase. The absolutely astounding gameplay, soundtrack, and visuals are worth the $40 alone. But do NOT come into this game expecting the story to be meaningful, or to even pick up where the first game left off, becuase it certinaly does not.

I feel like I'm going to hell for this, but honestly this is not a good game, and I'm both surprised and disappointed. I was hyped for it ever since this April 2016 preview from Killscreen. So many ticked boxes: A video game (Check!) about the mathematical (Check!) beauty (Check!) of Islamic Art (Check!). How could this not be absolutely awesome in an awesomely original way?
So I was very excited when I saw it in the new releases on Steam. But awesome it is not.
Instead, it is a small collection of "puzzles" that are easily solved within an hour. Calling them puzzles is generous because you solve them with a single click, plus maybe a few clicks of trial-and-error if you don't get it right the first attempt. What do they consist of? Typically, you are confronted with a few geometrical shapes that rotate in intricate ways, and a small drawing/pattern that is your target. You have to click on the part of one of the shapes where you want to place a virtual pencil. The shapes continue their movements, carrying the pencil with them (think spirograph) and if the resulting pattern sufficiently resembles the target, you win. it's all very simple and also very easy, except in some puzzles that inexplicably require millimeter-to-millimeter reproduction of the goal pattern (most levels are somewhat lenient with this, as it should be). The very last levels have sliders to adjust the size of the geometric objects and/or the speed of their rotation, but it doesn't make the puzzles more challenging or much more interesting.
What the game does well, is exposing the simple geometry behind some typical islamic decorative patterns. As a limited educational tool, it's not bad. But it completely fails as a game, never offering any enjoyable challenge. The content is almost laughably thin: don't expect to spend much more than a single hour with it. As you progress, you'll unlock a few drawing tools to use in a kind of sandbox mode, but again, this is very limited in what it allows (you can't customize the colors, for example) and in the time you'll want to fiddle with it.
There is so little content that one can only wonder what happened during the 18 months separating the preview with the game's release.
Add a few annoying but non game-breaking bugs, and it's really impossible to recommend. I am convinced there is a good game to be made on the subject of Islamic art. But Engare is not that game. It does have nice music, and that allows me to conclude on a positive note.

I think the concept of "drawing tool + puzzle game" is brilliant, but i also think the price is currently high in relation to what it currently offers. A few ideas to improve future versions, which i hope are planned (i would like to see a linux version too):
right click should control the "play/stop" state of the needles.
imo the option to change background color of puzzles or use simple textures would be appreciated.
I would like it to have world-maps like angry birds and similar games, and also that the game was offered for free with a litlle more content than current version; additional levels and a level creation tool to allow players to share new puzzles could be part of dlc. i think that could help make the game more popular and visible, and also improve sales: new levels and game mechanics as extras.
a "vs mode" could be interesting for those who buy the game; could work as a race to see who solves more puzzles within a time limit, or also by forcing the other player to start playing a different puzzle each time a puzzle is solved. More songs, music player in the start menu, and a gallery for 3d and 2d models of actual architecture and rl art should be offered as rewards imo, and also and psychedelic animations with fractal patterns for the ending of each level rather tha the minimalistic ones it currently has (which should be optional to play at the end of each sublevel). this would help the game to be taken more seriously as both a cultural and educational tool.
All options related to the drawing tool should be open from the beginning, and choosing to start the game or the tool should be included in the start menu. an option to change volume in the middle of the game, and even background themes (like in tetris games) should also be present. the drawing tool should export to svg and png too, and be able to export and import text files with settings to generate different patterns.
also 3d models and more options should be available, like the option to use color in designs made with the drawing tool, and mix patterns with transparency and bevel effects; in general, more options to experiment more seriously and make it more useful so it feels lees like a toy; could have a "switch mode": "simple (toy) mode" and "pro (designer/entusiast) mode".
i visited the website of the dev, and imo the other game about 3d illusions could easily be ixed with the concept of this "game+tool" if the concept of art+educational (puzzle) game was expanded.

The land of Ara Fell is a special place, groups of Islands floating in the sky for untold ages, families living in caves made into homes, nature and magic living in peace side by side. Of course such a lovely utopia can't go unspoiled forever and even though this is a review, I'm not spoiling the story, as this is the reason you are buying this game.
The Story is amazing, and for those who wish to experience it, the developer has included a "story mode" attack. It will, in essence, end any battles you encounter, and I would highly recommedn you choose to have it, not because the game is hard persay, in fact I find it pretty well balanced in terms of enemy strength vs player strength, but because there are times you want to get to the next story bit and it will make things much easier. The characters, not just the main cast but any npc who gets more then 2 boxes of dialogue feel very fleshed out and you'll fnd yourself agreeing with them many times. A lot of User Friendly features have been put in to help you get aquainted to the game world and how the game itelf works, and while some of them may feel a little hand holdy (The game will flat out warn you that your hitting a Point of No Return and offer to save, then offer to let you back out of continuing, but to its credit, it also lets you skip long cutscenes should you have died to a boss and are going back)
It's not perfect, as there are a few clear polish issues that I discovered, like difficulty in figuring out what was a decoration on the ground and what would actually heed my progress moving forward, towards the end of the game my character seemed to acquire the ability to jump when going horizontally (though there was a "reset jumping" option that may have fixed that that I never tried) and a large one in that I completed a side quest involving a old necklace and while the game informed me I'd gotten a new item, I had to stop playing shortly after and when I came back, I still had the old necklace and the quest giver was gone (i.e. quest completed)
Regardless of the few bugs mentioned above, if you are or ever were a fan of JRPG's that didn't rely on shoving a world big enough to qualify as a GTA game, wish for a showing of how Narrative can be a bigger draw then combat, or just want to relive the days of old, Ara Fell will certainly scratch that itch.

Out of all the 'Metroidvania' games I've played, Shovel Knight is one of few that I'd recommend even to someone who doesn't play modern Metroidvanias. And let me tell you why. Shovel Knight is the best use of modern gaming technology to refresh an old medium without attempting to update it. Many modern sidescrolling platformers either utilize 3D models and environments in a 2D experience (something I just personally find off-putting) or attempt for a "retro" look of 8-bit graphics by giving you a series of various rectangle enemies and rectangle levels to be beaten by your rectangle hero. Shovel Knight's pixel art graphics pay homage to the love and care that went into gamemakers who did their best to create art and a setting within their limited medium. It's one of the few pixel art games I've been able to use resources from as a background without it looking and feeling tacky. Beyond the visual art is the music, which, while not my favorite platformer soundtrack, does an excellent job enhancing the setting without being either distracting or lackluster.
The unlockables and upgrades feel satisfying and well spread out. You're constantly able to experiment with and revist abilities without feeling like there's a learning curve or needing to take time away from actually playing the game. Bounce physics from the down attack feel satisfying, as does the knockback from side attacks. The game makes you feel powerful while also retaining its challenge, especially punctuated during its boss fights. NPC interactions range from adorable to hilarious to legitimately emotional. It's an extremely polished experience that I'd describe as a classic metroidvania experience that only utilizes modern system techology to make itself as authentic as possible. Yacht Club really came out of nowhere to produce this absolute gem of a game.
And then they released Plague of Shadows for free.
Crazy respect to the devs, I'd have gladly paid $4.99 for the experience Plague gives, and they gave it to us for free. Shovel Knight is obviously a labor of love for them.
TL;DR:
Great art, great game, great devs. 9.5/10 if not 10/10. I'd recommend it even at full price, but if you see a good sale I'd say that it goes into must-buy territory.

Still, definitely recommended.

Quick Review:
Look, this game doesn’t have “Call of Duty” kind of cash to market it; so that means something caught your eye while you were looking for a new FPS post-DOOM ’16. Great news, you found one of the BEST Loot n’ Shoot titles of all time, if not the best Loot n’ Shoot game on the market. Shadow Warrior 2 is DOOM ’16 meets Borderlands 2; chaotically fun, hilarious, gory, and 5x better with friends.
Review:
Shadow Warrior 2 is easily one of the best games you will ever pick up for $40 bucks. The game has a lot of replay value; there are secrets everywhere, no 3 Play Sessions will ever be the same, there is 4 Player Co-op, your main character is ACTUALLY funny and interesting, and it is a chaotically fun game that brings a New Standard for the Loot n’ Shoot genre.
Pro:
01)  The Loot n’ Shoot System has changed so that “Modifiers” are collected, sold, or exchanged. You always keep your favorite gun, and you can modify it to be the best damn gun ever.
02)  The Levels are randomized, not Procedurally Generated. The Dev Team boasts that they have created 10’s upon 10’s of levels that swap out each play through, which has turned out to be true. Meaning you can play through the game 3x and still have a unique experience original maps.
03)  The Combat is fast, precise, gory, and glorious. You cannot execute the Oni like the Demons in DOOM ’16, but you are 2x Faster than DOOM Guy; plus, you’ve got more mobility and guns to use then you will ever know what to do with them.
04)  Lo Wang is a character who is genuinely a sarcastic, comical, 80’s hustler thrown into a world run by Demons and Pretentious/Humorous Jackasses. Lo Wang is portrayed organically, his lines and personality brings character to the FPS Genre and everyone within his game is written perfectly for his character to shine as a “Deadpool” kind of Anti-Hero.
There are technical problems. The game can get buggy for no reason at times or even crash. But this is a Must Buy $40-dollar game. I have no reason to think anyone interested in this game would walk away disappointed.

You win two things when you buy this game? 1) a short and swift game puzzle game experience and 2) a tool for artistic/geometric expression and discovery.
The first one is rather small, but nonetheless managed to provide a kind of puzzle that I've never seen before. Usually, with puzzle games, you face a system that feels difficult and strange at first (think Braid or sokoban games), but you progressively feel more confortable and start to think and feel like the system wants you to. This process usually takes a couple of hours, but with Engare it is very much faster: within the first few levels you go from not understanding how to solve the puzzles to think in terms of movement rather than static forms. Of course, you can just brute-force your way through the challenges. But the real experience is the change of perspective this game offers: you start to see movement in static images and static images coming out of mathematical patterns of motion.
Which brings you to the second part: experimenting with these patterns to create your own images, rather than copying what the levels want. This is probably the main experience of the game, and what really makes it worth the (very small) price. It is an incredible and potent tool, and at the same time very intuitive and simple.

The characters were surprisingly charming and had a fun dynamic with each other. The music was good, the environments were nice. Definitely a good experience for money.

Still, definitely a good find and a good experience. Thoroughly recommend.

I remember playing a demo for this in the early 2000s when I was really into the RPG Maker scene. It's pretty nice to see the complete game on Steam more than a decade later.
What really impressed me when I played this originally were the graphics and atmosphere. Everyone who's tinkered with RPG Maker 2003 will recognize the famous REFMAP tilesets, and they're used extremely well here, with a lot of birds, butterflies and critters moving around the maps, which really gives this game an atmosphere which stands out among other RPG Maker projects. It's not the first RPG to use floating islands as a setting, but a lot of Ara Fell's quirks (people living in caves, vampire / elven designs in ruins...) contribute to making it more original.
The music is absolutely amazing. The theme that plays in the quarry caves (and some other places as well, but I heard it there first) is up there with all those SNES and PS1 classics.
The scenario is a bit different from what I remembered from the demo, but It's probably better now (although it still is about a chosen one fighting vampires, it's no longer rife with Buffy references, which is a good thing since it clashed a lot with the setting, on top of being very fanficsey). The writing is good and the characters likeable, even though the main antagonist feels a bit underdeveloped - I liked Vampire Lord Nash better.
Gameplay-wise it uses RPG Maker 2003's default battle system, which I pretty much despise (it tries to emulate Final Fantasy's ATB, but sadly it's extremely slow and clunky, it often interrupts you mid-action and the targeting is awful), although the dev tried to balance the stats / equipment (which is actually pretty rare in RPG Maker games) and make complex boss battles with a lot of special moves and scripted events, so that sweetens the pill. Thankfully, at the beginning of the game, you can also activate a special mode to give you a skill that rains 9999s on the battlefield, which helps with the grinding (I remember adding something like that to my characters whenever I tested RM2003 games, glad the dev thought ahead of me this time).
+ Great visuals and atmosphere
+ Excellent music
+ Interesting boss battles
+ "Story mode" which cuts on grinding
- RM2003 default battle system (I
don't like it)
- Ending felt a bit rushed
7/10 Despite engine-related woes, it's still leagues ahead of most other RPG Maker games that try to emulate SNES RPGs, and I recommend it if you're into that kind of thing.

I love this game!
It is NOT just another minecraft.

Your grandfather has gone missing and you need to solve fiendish puzzles with cryptic clues left behind by a madman. The only hope you have of seeing your grandfather again is to solve these puzzles and get the power working again. Lume is a point and click puzzle game. Each puzzle is masterfully done, adding layer upon layer. Its not just typical puzzles, but these are puzzles are off kilter. A is E, a triangle is 3, north is north east sort of off kilter. There are cryptic clues are everywhere. You'll get an inventory of parts to create a power generator and see your grandfather alive.
The truth is that you play as a child and your grandfather has gone to go investigate something. So he left clues for you to get his power up and running again. He's the madman. There is no threat, danger or game over. There is a variety of puzzles. Everything from lock combinations, to spinning wired tiles to connect all circuits. The clues for the most part will be in select pages of books and following instructions meant to get you lost with irrelevance. It is all a brain teaser's dream.
The game itself looks unique, because it looks as if someone made it with construction paper. Then filmed transitions between environments. The real downfall about the art is the resolution is stuck low so its a small screen with a giant dark frame. With such a unique art style, it should be a higher resolution to bask in its glory.  There aren't many environments. Just a three interiors, two closets and an exterior consisting of two screens.
The controls are simple, just click things. Since it is a Flash game, just hover your mouse over something and the cursor will change to a pointer. Your inventory is easy to get to at the top of the screen instead of completely switching to an inventory.
At the end of the hour or two game, you find out this is just Episode 1. These were some difficult puzzles, but without the unique art style it would have gotten lost in the shuffle.

This game is OK. The civil war game is really an abandoned genre unfortunately.  This game is what I would consider a "hack and slash" RTS with no real strategy.  You basically just line your troops up and out flank the enemy.  No real emphasis on position or cover just sliding armies over and out flanking.  Strategy beyond the immediate battle field, you get like two choices "defend this flank" or "attack this hill" which is really just their way of asking if you want 1 of three different battlefield maps they have available.

Radiant Defense is a tower defense game.  Its missions are played on a grid.  Enemies get one or more starting points, and they have to make their way to the ending point.  Towers have to be placed on modules, and while there are fixed modules for each mission, you're also allowed to put some down yourself, which means you're allowed to change the route of the enemies.
There are about a dozen different towers, including machine guns, laser guns, sniper rifles, and tesla towers.  There are also super weapons, which are more expensive than regular towers but have much better attacks.  Regular towers can be upgraded four times during missions.  There isn't any upgrading outside the missions.
There are also a dozen or more types of enemies.  They can be fast; they can be shielded; they can spawn more enemies; they can be resistant to some of your towers; and more.  The in-game information isn't great, so you have to learn by playing and trying things out.
The missions in the game tend to be long.  Most have over 30 waves, and the peak is somewhere around 70.  Luckily, you get a save before each wave, so if one goes badly then you can load and try again.  This is friendly but also necessary because your score for each mission depends on how much money you have unused at the end of each wave.  So your goal is to kill everything while spending as little money as possible, which adds a little extra strategy.
Overall, Radiant Defense is a pretty vanilla, but it works well enough, especially for the price.  It doesn't do anything new or innovative, but it's colorful and humorous, and it took me over 30 hours to beat the 15-mission campaign plus earn all of the achievements.  The campaign starts out very easy but then gets tough at the end, so don't give up on it after only an hour or two.

I am so confused by the reviews on this game. I've played it and it reminds me so much of what I hated about the archaic Close Combat games from Microsoft. Dumb player controller unit AI. You move your units and select for them to take an action and nope, they decide to do something completely different which inevitably ends in their death always.

TL;DR: No raw stats for anything and towers select random targets instead of the most threatening. These two aspects alone are a deal-breaker for ANY tower defence game!
---------
Artistically, this game is fine. Programmtically, this game has no major technical issues. However, I cannot recommend this game because it has serious design flaws.
I only played for 10 minutes and ran into several design issues:
* UI is not as straightforward to use as it looks
* Enemies do not path in ways which make sense
* One hit death: You take ONE POINT of damage, you lose and have to do the wave over
* Towers select RANDOM targets, not targets closest to the end of their run, meaning luck plays a huge factor in how well you do rather than skill
* NO RAW STATS FOR ANYTHING (Not damage numbers, not firing rates, NOTHING!)
Also, I should point out the game heavily borrows design concepts from other better TD games. For instance, the first, third and fourth towers here are COPIES of the first, third and fourth towers from Defense Grid. Not graphically but in terms of function.

From the brief time I have played this game thus far it is a great game!
It has a great concept and hopefully continues to evolve over the next few years as the developer hopes!

The hope of mankind lies within your hands as you take command to keep thousend of aliens from invading your world. As military commander your only help comes from a scientist providing you with new technology and weapons.
'Radiant Defense' is a tower defence game in space. Its colourful, glowing look is beautiful and the comic style can be deceiving. That's because 'Radiant Defense' is not a simple game. Some players even claim it's too hard altogether. But in my opinion that's not really the case. Yes, the game becomes difficult in the higher levels but it's a clever difficulty. While difficult sometimes leads to frustration in 'Radiant Defense' difficult is challenging and inspires to keep trying again and again until you finally win victory.
Pros:
- nice graphics
- good music
- clever game design
- very good selection of weapons and enemies
- freedom to build your own route in most levels
- more than 300 waves of aliens across 14 missions
- pauses between waves allow you to arrange your weapons
- you can repeat any wave without loosing money if you do not upgrade towers before starting the wave. This allows you to experiment.
- the game automatically saves progress for each level. You can simply stop playing and return right to were you stopped any time later.
- nice tactical component for money. Dead aliens fill your purse but you can increase the money earned by placing money boosters. Additionally you collect further money depending on your funds at the end of each wave. This adds to very interesting tactical twists.
- high number of waves
- nine upgradable weapons
- three super-weapons for mass defence
Cons:
- online hall of fame seems to contain cheaters and you can't find your own position
- one achievement seems bugged (Endangered Species)

I bought Arma 3 in early May, if I recall correctly. At the time, I was very much interested in the ins and outs of military operation. I still am. Arma 3 is an excellent game for those with time on their hands. You see, it is a game that takes a lot of skill and effort to get used to and is unlike any shooter I have played in more ways than one. I would not reccomend this game if you are a casual gamer (casual, as I define, meaning that you play for under 17 hours a week) but, if you have the time, patience and dedication, you can have a lot of fun with this game.
Be that as it may, the pros of the game are as follows:
- The graphics are superb
- The gameplay never ceases to be fun
- The game has a wide variety of weapons to choose from
- The in-game EDEN editor is one of the best in-game editors I have ever used.
- The mechanics of the game, be it air, land or sea, are very polished
And the cons:
- It is poorly optimised
- The gameplay is clunky*
- Every key does something and there is no way to centralise the controls you most frequently use without macro buttons/keys
- The command system for AI is atrocious. There is literally no way to access some controls that are vital to commanding AI and issuing commands takes far too much time.
*The gameplay is clunky on purpose as the developers wanted to create a more realistic setting and this fit that concept. Although I understand that, I don't think it fit the game, rather that it hindered gameplay.
TL:DR - There is a lot to love in this game and I would highly recommend playing it if you have the time, patience and dedication. The flaws in the game are mostly minor if you have a half decent build. I would recommend tinkering with the advanced preferences in the launcher to get it just right. The only major issue is the AI command system but, you can get used to that. I, personally, am not too irritated by it but you might be. Be sure to test it in the editor, to find out whether you like it or not.
