A wonderful and intelligent little tactical RTS. I say 'little' because the core game is the Battle for Gettysburg (of course) drawn out over 5 or 6 different scenarios. But, this is an indie game, and a great one at that, and if this doesn't sound like much, the devil is in the details.
Content-wise, UG:G is quality over quantity. This may annoy some people, but for those that appreciate variation on a theme, the game offers a lot of replayability and it's clear that the developers have done as much as they can to offer as much replayability as possible within the constraints of the game. Firstly, you can play as either the Union or Confederates. Secondly, you can choose 9 or so different enemy AI types which all change the decision making process for the enemy on the field. Lastly, your actions and achievements in each scenario affect the way the game plays out, allowing you to choose from a number of concurrent scenarios that change depending on whether or not you managed to fulfill the goals of the mission before. Multiply all these options together, and for the price you get a decent amount of gameplay.
The control scheme is ingenious and the method with which you relay orders to your units allows for a great deal of finesse and control on the battlefield. Instead of clicking on each point you want your units to walk in a straight line to, you draw the path you want them to take, and the units follow said path. You can flank, withdraw, shift focus, push forward, and more all with one smooth swipe of the mouse, and it allows for a great deal of tactical control without you having to monitor every individual step the units take. I've seen some complaints about orders not working or unit AI performing incorrectly, but I've never had any such experience.
The topography of the map is fantastic - Gettysburg is accurately represented, and the cover-rating for your units changes dynamically as they move from open grass, to forest, to hedges, to homesteads. This cover rating is essential to survival (as in real life), and it all makes sense - when you move into an area that you think should give you cover, it does, and vice versa. You'll find the enemy responds to your attempts to flank them, and you'll want to watch you don't overextend yourself, or the enemy will exploit your failures. Your frontline will ebb and flow as the balance of power changes in particular areas, and you're rewarded realistically for pressing your advantages, and punished with a stalemate, or worse, if you fail to take the opportunities you get.
I feel that this game would have benefitted from covering a larger part of the civil war, and one criticism I could level at it is that it's indeed constrained by its focus on one single battle. In saying that, I only want more because it's so enjoyable, and I think that in focussing their attention, the development team have managed to perfect their game mechanics, which makes for a much more solid and refined product, so perhaps it's not really a criticism after all?
The other point I'd make is that whilst the mechanics that are in place all work well and feel very fresh, there isn't a whole lot of tactical depth in terms of the commands you can issue to the units. Your command extends as far as telling them where to go, who to attack, when to charge, and when to stop. While this all works well and provides a fun experience, there isn't a lot of variation amongst the commands, that again might have led to the game feeling fuller. But, all that said, I don't feel shortchanged, only like I want to play more and more and more. I haven't played multiplayer as of yet, so I'm dying to try the game out against a human opponent.
UG:G is one of the most innovative and entertaining tactical RTS games I've ever played, and I highly recommend it to any strategy fan.

Ultimate General: Gettysburg is an excellent strategy game, you get to take command of either Union or Confederate forces during the battle of Gettysburg. The controls are unusually easy and simple for a strategy game, after your first battle you should have them down pretty good. The art style is unique and fits the game perfectly. Developers give a great deal of support for the game. Bugs/crashes in the game are a rarity (only have suffered one crash in my 28 hours of playing)
If you're a Civil War buff, or just want a game where you can line up hundreds of men and let them fire guns at eachother with no cover (LIKE ME :D!) then this is the game for you!
Overall, great game and I hope the developers add into the Ultimate General franchise.

Classic PC strategy game that still is amazing. The hours I have on this are off because I used to own this on disc, where I played numerous hours. I bought the Steam version due to the fact that GameSpy shut down. Now to the actual review.
Whether you're a history buff, a Risk player, and/or a real time stategy game person, this game is for you. You can play historical battles, either online or offline. You can play the single player campaign very similar to Risk. However, the main attaction of this game are the real time battles, where you command armies in a battle to create your own fights, or to recreate/simulate real fights. It does require very good internet, especially considering the age of this game, which I would say is the only downside. Regardless, this game is a classic game that anyone should pick up to enjoy.

Engare is a really unique puzzle game about art and motion. The game features many levels, some of them really accessible, others particularly challenging. The progression is linear and you unlock one new level at the time. This might sound harsh in case you get stuck, but this actually makes you focus on the specific level until you really comprehend the motion you are asked to reproduce.
It is possible to complete all levels between 1.5-2 hours, but the game features an amazing sandbox mode (actually, 6 sandbox modes!) where you can explore how motion can create shapes. The game even allows you to export the pattern you create and even apply to a dome (and export it as a 3d object). You can really get lost in this mode, and the results are often truly spectacular.
Engare is a truly beautiful and unique game.

I went into Shovel Knight two years late to the party and skeptical if the mass praise was rightfully earned; I exited out after having beat it and its (as of now) free
expansion thoroughly convinced it was and am eagerly waiting for more. A definite recommendation for fans of platformers and games alike.
At Shovel Knight's core is an essential smorgasbord of bits borrowed from a myriad of celebrated NES classics (DuckTales, Zelda II, Megaman and the Castlevanias to name a few) combined with intuitive, reactive controls. And, much like how the eponymous character averts the trope of a heroic knight wielding a sword, the game itself bypasses a common stumbling point that a good many new-age retro games find themselves tripping over time and time again - the difficulty.                                                                                                                               From beginning to end Shovel Knight does an excellent job in remaining a thoroughly enjoyable experience that never felt frustrating (certain feats and challenges notwithstanding) nor too much of an absolute cakewalk. The phrase “just right” does well in describing how the difficulty flows with the level design, the boss fights and how the player is expected to come to master the game’s inherent platforming + relic swapping mechanics over the course of a playthrough. On a more personal basis I think it was definitely on the easier side when compared to the games it drew inspiration from but considering it never set out to be brutally difficult to begin with it’s really not much of a detractor unless you happen to be a masochist.
Then there’s the story. It’s not anything particularly unique (standard journey to save lost cohort/beloved) but the interactions between characters and the occasional regret-fueled dream intermission really made it something else and breathed some much appreciated life into the pixels. It’s not often a simple game with simple NES aesthetics gets such a satisfying and moving little ending to a charming journey but this one does it
to a glorious soundtrack.
So I’ll reiterate; the praise this game has received is well earned and
(alongside, presumably, the future expansions) is extensive and really changes things up with how you play the game and experience everything within. I’d go so far as to say the expansion even outdid the base game in a good many ways, especially in regards to giving the player more options, despite the two covering the same set of levels and as such I’d probably give it...
for the base game and
for the expansion

When talking about Lume it’s impossible not to bring up its length, so I might as well start with that. Lume is very short, especially considering its price. It took me an hour to complete, and that’s including stopping to admire the visuals, and I honestly can’t see it taking much longer than that. You might draw it out to 90 minutes, but that’s about it.
But if you look beyond that you’ll find an absolutely charming and adorable game. There, I said it. I’m supposed to be cynical goddamit, but here I am calling a game ‘adorable’. But it is, it absolutely ♥♥♥♥ing is. It’s made out of cardboard for god’s sake. CARDBOARD!
Yes, this game didn’t take very long to win me over. Look at it though, it’s gorgeous. Sure, there isn’t much to see, but what you do see is incredible. I still can’t get over the fact the game’s made out of cardboard. Man, this game made me grin like a ♥♥♥♥ing child, and I hate it for it.
It is a puzzle game, though the puzzles are rather generic and simple. Still, some fun brainteasers, but I feel resentful towards them because they aren’t made out of cardboard. In fact there isn’t much that is made of cardboard because the area is very small and can be explored in a few minutes, meaning you backtrack a lot and most of the length is spent solving puzzles.
The fact that you don’t get much of the game’s best feature in a very short game is a bit of a problem, so it’s hard to recommend at full price. I got it in a bundle which was perfect, but for a considerable discount I’d say it’s worth experiencing. Then again, I’m all set for getting the sequel Lumino City (get it?), discounted or not, so maybe the price isn’t so bad after all...
It’s made of cardboard though, and that’s got to count for something, right? Besides, this game will charm the pants off even the most cynical of people, even if it’s only for an hour.

After 150+ hours I think I can say : this is a great game! I am a veteran of Minecraft, FTB, MITE and various other custom maps and challenges particularly in survival mode. FCE is similar, but different, to all of these and is centered around your base. You get most of the tools you need from the beginning, and from there it is up to you to build your base around the ore you find, and to automate it. Automation is really cool - you can do things the hard way, yourself, or build a conveyer belt and laser power and it does it all for you! You can just stand there and watch it go, and I often do! After a while you will have to deal with mobs too, so base defences come into play. There is a tech-tree for you to discover which unlocks a lot more of the game, and the "limits" are not what you are used to - there is no bedrock, you can just keep going and going. Super-dig and build-to-me features are "wow" as is the x-ray vision mode, grappling hook and jetpack.
You might think that after all those hours I have done everything there is to do in this game. Well, I have played out a few worlds but no, I still have plenty of things I want to try.
Even though there is Witcher III and Fallout 4 (coming), I'm already calling this my "game of the year". Stick with it and you will find it great fun. Sure, it is still in "early access" but this is already better than a lot of fully released games. What are you waiting for? get it now!
ps. I am in no way affiliated with the devs, I am purely a player.

You start at your home base, with nothing. (As standard.) You wander around, dig stuff up, look for stuff with your scanner. Go back to base. Check out what you've found, discover a few new things to build.
Dig up more stuff, build more stuff, research more stuff. That's the basics.
You can sculpt vast areas, build huge supply chains to feed the machines you build, build bigger machines, set up defenses against the evil natives.
And the more you do, the more you are thinking, ' Just need to do that, then I can do this, and that let's me do that, and then.....' and so it goes. This is a damn big game, and very addictive. Like I said, a lot of games in this genre, but this is the ace in the pack.

Amnesia is not just a game, it is an experience. It truly is something else when you turn off all the lights in your house, put headphones on, and just play the game, the only light coming from your monitor. This is the aproach I took to play this game, as twith most horror games.
So there I am, sitting at my computer around midnight, and I begin to play the game. The first thing I notice about the game is how great the atmosphere is. Depending on the setting of the area you are in, the will hear all kinds of creepy ambience. In some areas you might hear footsteps, in some places you might hear the wind howl, and in some places you might hear sobs and screams.
But all I've touched upon so far is the sound, and building the experience. The story is interesting, and I found myself actually eager to press on. You play as Daniel, who has lost his memory. You find out that Daniel actually drank an amnesia potion on purpose, so you have to piece together what happened from the bits of Daniel's journal you find lying around. That's all I can say about the strory without spoiling anything, but it really does hook your interest.
The gameplay is a good mix of exploring, hiding from monsters, and solving puzzles. The monsters are well planned out, and the game leads you into the idea of them, first only by scaring you by letting you see them, second by having you hide from them, and finally by either having to escape them, or sneak past. The puzzles ranged from easy to hard. They were never too difficult for me to figure out on my own, although a few had me scratching my head for a while. Most of them were just difficult enough that it didn't take a long time to figure them out, but when you did, it was still very satisfying. In terms of control, it may seem awkward at first, but I had no problems, even in the platforming sections.
The game mechanics of losing sanity in the light coupled with a limited amounted of lamp oil and tinder boxes really stuck out to me as genius. While having light isn't exactly necessary, I found myself trying to complete puzzles more quickly, while trying to conserve my lamp oil, and only use tinder boxes in useful places. I failed a couple times, and it really sucks to have no lamp oil in a dark area. I really thought it was a smart way to be able to get the player to keep moving.
The graphics aren't super fancy or anything, which is okay, since they still look good. The graphics are fitting, and the balance between darkness and light was handled perfectly. For instance, whenever you step out of light into a dark area, it takes a second before you are adjusted, and are able to see anything.
To conclude, Amnesia has a story interesting enough to keep you playing, gameplay unique enough to not get boring, and great atmosphere. The game does get a bit stale after the first playthrough, but there are lots of custom stories out there, some of which I've heard very good things about. So, that gives this game a boost to its replay value, something it wouldn't have if it weren't for the custom game option.
Anyway, this game is definitely worth the price, especially if you're into horror. This is a great entry game for those looking to get into the genre, and can be bought for cheap.

Ultimate General: Gettysburg is not exactly a great game. But it's a good enough - and cheap enough - game to warrant picking it up and learning it, getting a play out of it here and there.
Ultimate General: Gettysburg reminds me of Unity of Command in terms of price, variety of content, and quality of CPU opponents. The games themselves are an RTS and a Turn-Based, respectively, and play quite differently, yet share the same strengths.
Overall, for the price, Ultimate General: Gettysburg is a good game, and is worth a look if you like RTS-style games that utilize some of the same mechanics of Total War games (the developer for this game modded Total War extensively).

Rainbow Six Siege is a game that I would recommend to anyone. With over 700 hours played since Season 2 of Year 1, I think I'm qualified to say that Siege is a realistic, enjoyable, fun and ever-changing game with a community that interacts with the developers.
While it's a biased opinion, I consider Siege to be above CS:GO for a lot of reasons. Each and every match played online feels unique and special and can present its own challenges thanks to the plethora of operators available on both the attacking and defending side. Each one has their own unique ability that brings advantages to the team. It's also thanks to the Battlefield: Bad Company 2 style destruction and mayhem that can be caused on Siege, creating opportunities for players to develop strategies and making the game more interesting as a whole.
Unlocking operators is done through earning the in-game currency called 'renown' and buying them. Playing matches, whether they are won or lost earns you good amounts of renown on its own without the challenges, special events and renown boosters available to you on top of this. Renown can also be used to purchase in-game cosmetics for your operators and their weapons, but never once do you feel like you're in an endless grind to get the most impressive headgear or weapon skin. It requires work and time to earn the renown to purchase operators but it's never repetitive thanks to the unique style of enjoyable gameplay that Siege has.
Recently, backlash from the community has been caused by Operation Health. This was a planned 3-month season that was initally meant to be for the Polish Operator group but was instead moved to focus on the future of the game, including fixing bugs and glitches, improving matchmaking, retexturing maps and operators, and fixing the lighting and other aesthetics such as the user interface. With these patches however, the community has come to embrace some of the improvements and they have certainly improved the game's health and longevity.
Siege has a relatively small but close-knit community that regularly interacts with the developers on issues and ideas they would like for the game that are acknowledged. The game's support is strong and the community has spread to sites like Reddit and YouTube where hundreds of thousands of players enjoy funny in-game moments and discuss the pros and cons of the game. Siege's very own Pro League and yearly Six Invitational is incredibly exciting and the energy of the players and live stream viewers is tangible.
Rainbow Six Siege is my most played game for a very clear reason, the game started to little fanfare but has grown incredibly large since its release. It's visually pleasing, ever-changing and definitely one of the best realistic shooters ever to present on the market. No match on Siege is ever the same and that has fuelled its longevity and why so many players love to play it. It never feels like a grind with no incentive.
I 100% recommend this game to anyone who's looking to dive into an exciting game with a great community and immense support. It's most definitely worth your money.

Ara Fell is the best RPG Maker RPG I can imagine being made. I'm not done with it yet but I'm (I think) probably 70% done and will finish it with relish. I'm 32 years old and grew up playing the likes of Final Fantasy VI and Chrono Trigger and while Ara Fell isn't in the same scope as multi-million dollar projects of that kind it absolutely deserves to stand with them in terms of simple craft. I get ticked off extremely easily at JRPG writing, design, and gameplay, and Ara Fell not only avoids all of the ordinary pitfalls of workman-level attempts at this problematic genre, it transcends them to achieve something quite unlike anything I've played before; a synthesis of Zelda-like exploration and tight, miniamlistic, refined JRPG combat with a free-form leveling system and a crafting system that give just enough player choice to be enjoyable without being overbearing. The game isn't hard for an old master like me, I got ahead of the difficulty curve early on and stayed there, but for players less experienced with the genre it should provide just the right level of challenge, and the joy and excitement of finding hidden items and defeating increasingly difficult encounters shines through as well as it does in the genre's classics. This game has my highest possible recommendation and it deserves the support of everyone who ever enjoyed a JRPG.
A special commendation goes to the game's writer(s), who are unquestionably the most talented JRPG writers working in the genre today; the dialogue manages to stay short and punchy while simultaneously achieving emotional depth and avoiding the worst of the genre's tropes, and the plot and setting will be comfortable and homelike to any fan of fantasy without quite falling into a strict formula. The pacing helps a great deal.

Such a clever game, get if you want to try something very different. About 1.5-2 hours worth of puzzles (if you were just playing to beat them) + a creative sandbox mode. Puzzles are not designed to be super challenging, but each one is designed to teach something unique that you haven't realised before about motion and trajectory. Each puzzle itself you could spend a lot of time exploring 'what happens if you do this..' and realise interesting theories that you might not have considered before about simple moving shapes. It's not a multiple-solution kind of game like Spacechem. Puzzles are designed very deliberately to give you a moment of epiphany when you solve it.
These puzzles are not sliding object puzzles (like Snakebird / Stephen's Sausage Roll) or puzzle platforming or time manipulation (Induction), or even any puzzle where you're controlling a character (Linelight), or something that could work on paper. It's not a riff off any existing puzzle game mechanic - there really hasn't been anything even remotely similar before in games that I've seen. Wouldn't be surprised if it will spawn a new group of puzzle games that riff off this one. If you like your games different and unique this is one for you.

Absolutely beautiful, with some highly enjoyable and unique puzzles, this still left me disappointed. My two complaints:
1. The game ended after what felt like an introduction. I am aware that this is the first part of a story that is to be continued, but I think too much effort was made to cram a full complement of puzzles into a small setting without enough actual story to go with them.
2. The justification and structure of some of the puzzles seemed overly contrived. Why store innocuous and highly useful items in an undersink cabinet with an incredibly complex lock? That goes beyond the character justification of Grandpa loving puzzles.
It's not inherently a flaw, but this game also has one of my personal least favorite puzzle structures- a seemingly-unrelated document that you must figure out the significance of and how to use its contents to solve an unspecified other puzzle. In this case, exacerbated by the stretch of my suspension of disbelief that the protagonist somehow picks this one document out of an entire bookshelf. Doesn't bother some people, bugs me badly.
I really wanted to love this game, and I will probably get the next installment, despite the flaws, but given the sense of dissatisfaction I felt at the end, I am glad I got this as part of a bundle. I would be very displeased if I had paid full price. I would have been happier with a bit more room to move, and either a bit more story, or less hinting that there was going to be more; if I had known from the beginning that literally _all_ I was going to do was turn on the lights, I might have been okay with that.

The key to good horror is immersion as it's only really frightening if you feel it's happening to you. Amnesia accomplishes this sort of immersion quite neatly through the use of simple light mechanics. There is nearly constant darkness, so it's impossible to guess what's around the corner. You're never allowed a real rest or relief as there's no certainty to what comes next. The player himself can't really see through the darkness either which left me with my nose an inch or two away from the screen, straining to see. Even in the middle of night with all the lights out, I couldn't see well. This is both a blessing and a curse as it does add to the overall experience, perhaps even makes the experience, but it really is a strain to play and that does limit each session. Amnesia doesn't rely on jump scares, just an ever-present physical threat. There is no combat mechanic, no way of fighting back, and anything that catches you will kill you quickly. This has the player entering a mad dash anytime an enemy is spotted with the knowledge that they'll be dead if they stop or hit a dead end before losing it. The player ends up, unintentionally of course, recreating the classic Blair Witch-esque visual as they sprint through similar looking tunnels with almost no light at all. Amnesia continues to build atmosphere through the slowly unraveling story which can only be pieced together by meager bits of information found throughout the house. The player must uncover what would make a man erase his memory and why he would be so desperate to kill a man that seems to want to help him before being killed himself by whatever it is that makes this house so dangerous. There is a mystery to solve and no telling what's lurking in the distance. The lamp's oil will run out shortly, and with it the ability to see the path ahead, can you afford to stand around and wait?

I'm a big fan of the Portal series, and I was a little disappointed when I heard that the "new" game was just a bridge construction game but now that I've played it, it's really fun and worth it in my opinion.
It's nothing different as in terms of goals from the original Bridge Constructor game, but adding Portal's physics and its features spiced the game up and made it interesting. Not only portals were implemented, but even propulsion&repulsion gel, cubes, heavy duty super buttons, turrets, emancipation grills and lasers.
Giving Bridge constructor Portal's elements turned it into a puzzle, but the goal is always to get from point A to point B
The game has 6 sections, with 10 levels each(making it a total of 60 levels). Initially I was disappointed because I wish they'd have been 100 levels at this point, but the levels aren't exactly easy, in fact, from the second section things start getting harder and to succeed you need to keep... testing basically.
Although one thing I have to point out is that so far I haven't seen anything like Budget limit, the game keeps telling you how much you spent to build your bridge but it feels pointless fo far as of level 20.
The design is basically identical to Portal 2, in fact, it doesn't even feel like it's a different game. It gives that vibe that you get when you're in the workshop area of Portal 2 with all custom test chambers and stuff.
The backgrounds of the test chambers are really cool too.
The music is awesome if you ask me, it's really Portal-like and sometimes it really feels like you're back into Aperture Science's test chambers
In my opinion, this game is actually worth those 10€. You have to keep in mind that they skinned this game with a very well known title plus they had to put music and adapt Portal's elements into the game. It's worth playing since it can be really fun!

When I first bought this game in early 2017 I have to say I was let down. The game saw little to no support, D-Sync and lag spikes were almost a constant, hitboxes and weapons felt extremely inaccurate and the game was clunky as all hell. I wanted to give the game the benefit of the doubt, so I powered through and kept playing it and gave it another chance. After months of devolpers updating the game and addressing the issues that we had with this game (Maybe not as fast the community would like but eventually they did) the game became fun and actually enjoyable.
My girlfriend and I actually won our first duo's game today and we were craving more and more and thats a very rewarding feeling when you do win let me tell you.  After sinking 145 hours into the game I can honestly say this game is a fun, fast paced, arcade like battle royal and I do recommend it to people looking for such a game, but do expect some problems with the game as it is still in early access.
Also the game offers and progression system and a skill ranking system. The more you play, get kills, win games and finish higher up then the more xp and score you will get. You can level up just by playing the game as well as doing things so you can climb for levels 1-80 (The max level maybe higher or lower). Also you can place in skill tiers such as bronze, silver, gold, platinum, diamond, and royality. This offers players a reason to hop on everyday and grind this game.
Verdict: H1Z1 has some kinks and bugs that need to be worked out but at the end of the day offers replay value and a game to play with friends. I can recomend this game to anyone looking for a casual, arcade like battle royal. 7.5/10

Not only as a masterful achievement with RPGMaker, but as an engrossing experience in general, Ara Fell truly thrives despite its small development scale. In fact, it conjures what even many million-dollar projects can't seem to get down - a sense of intimacy and real character.
There's something about 16-bit RPGs that feels inherently nostalgic, no matter how modern or updated in style. And in that vein, Ara Fell definitely feels "modern" (despite originating more than ten years ago) compared with those SNES classics, with its increased emphasis on atmosphere and an "open world" sensibility.
The story is adorable - but it's the exploration, and sheer sense of atmosphere - the birds and creatures fluttering about, the ambient sound effects, the attention-to-detail on every map - that make this experience great (and distinct from many retro games).
I'm probably among the minority of jRPG fans that doesn't love the number-crunching grinding fair, which is also why I appreciate Ara Fell. The character-writing feels sharp and believable, even with the game's NPCs. Lita is a sarcastic, excitable anime archetype, without ever becoming too obnoxious or contrived. The art design feels truly "floating" and vividly otherworldly, despite the occasionally generic map tiles. The soundtrack is completely original, and likewise adds to the majestic/fantasy aesthetic.
I discovered this game many years ago now; and I've always been inspired by it. Having tried my hand in RPGMaker personally, I know the incredible patience and time-commitment it requires to deliver even a halfway-competent experience. This game is far more than competent, though - it's quirky, cute, enthralling and even magnificent in some moments. Definitely would recommend for anyone who even remotely enjoys RPGs or retro projects.

Shadow Warrior 2 so far delivers a great shooter experience with everything you could ask for. Whacky guns like the classic FPS days? Check that up with Nail guns, Gauss rifles, claws and Skull Machine Guns. Want to go fast? This game will make you go fast you won't be able to ♥♥♥♥ing aim anymore. Want to focus solely on melee combat? Well, grab your favorite melee weapon (There's like a dozen, with different move sets and abilities) and go to town ripping demons to shred.
However, the Procedural generation hurts the game a fair bit. Already 6 hours in and I've seen several similar "Assets" (That is repeated map segments) which means you don't see a LOT of new stuff in terms of level design, which is a damn disappointment, seeing that old FPS games always had a point of pride in making level that were unique and memorable. You won't find that in SW2 I'm afraid.
Another down point is the game balance. Due to the procedural generation of the game, some fights will be really really easy, and other times they will be incredibly rough, with no real steady sense of progression. Yeah sure, enemies will get tougher and hit harder with times, but that's beyond the point when some fights will take 30 seconds to end while others take 2-3 minutes. That's not counting the amount of times in these Randomly Generated Levels where you have no enemies to fight against, because they were placed randomly over the map and not in a wave format like the original Remake. While you move very fast, it makes these levels feels incredibly secondary and often empty, which is definitively something you don't want when building a fast-paced action shooter.
I would prefer the game return to its more "Locked room with a wave of enemy" format, much like Painkiller, or DOOM, than the current state it is in where there's a blob of enemies stranded around on the map.
It remains a great game mechanically speaking, but some decisions were a powerful hit, and some were a dreadful miss. Hopefully, we can turn this game or the next Shadow Warrior iteration into a bullseye.
Afterall, the Wang's way is long and hard. But it is ribbed for her pleasure.
EDIT: GAME FINISHED
Honestly, I've never been so underwhelmed after the middle point of the game. While the first half of Shadow Warrior 2 is quite exciting, even with its shortcomings, when you enter the second half, it gets even worse. Everything is so repetitive, boring and unexciting. You unlock weapons who are just so much better than the rest that your arsenal of useful weapons that was already short to begin with, and the same maps and same enemies repeated over and over and over again until you just can't be excited anymore.
The progression system is a mess. There's no progression tree, nothing to look forward to, no super powerful upgrades that changes the game for yourself, like the much better loot shooter like Borderlands or Destiny. From the start to end, you're given cards that only acts as number boosts for your already unlocked skills, and you can just grab everything, and never have to really make a hard decision when it comes to your character. This means you can't make an unique "Wang", you're just making Ultimate Wang every time. That would be fine if the game ever became hard...
The thing with SW2 and difficulty is that the players have so much mobility (Unlimited dash, jumps, runs, and speed movement bonus) that enemies can hardly ever hit you to begin with. There are very very few enemies that shoot projectiles, and almost none that have hitscan weapons. This means that if you constantly dash and shoot, you will almost never ever get cornered or hit, while you can still shoot freely and kill everything in your way. Worst on this are the bosses, who while some (SOME) of them are big and impressive, they're so slow that they're never a threat. No monster is ever as fast and as dangerous as the player, so you won't ever be challenged.
All in all, while I found this game great on the first half, the second half really made its flaws shine. If they ever make a third Shadow Warrior, please focus on making great level design like in the first game instead of this fake RNG maps that are obviously the same chunks paired together awkwardly. Make enemies that have strategies to them rather than just give them elemental resistances that doesn't matter, and that actually can deal with player mobility. And Lastly, make the loot more interesting than thousands and thousands of mods that you have to burn through.

The Quest for the lost JRPG of old is what lead me to Game Development through RPG Maker. I am nothing but an amateur to the likes of Badluck and the people that helped with Ara Fell. This game has blown me away with how engaging it is. I don't have much time to even play video games, but I have clocked almost 7 hours into this game. That is quite a lot for me... Every game that I have brought recently I have less than 45 minutes (except for one PS4 game). I am not sure how far I am into the game, but I want to continue to go back to it every time I think of sitting down to play something. There are just to many games coming at me all the time... the ADHD doesn't help but once I am in front of Ara Fell I don't put it down until I am ready to leave or sleep.
The storyline is top notch with simple dialogue that really makes you feel for the characters. There is enough additions to catch a glimpse of the intrigue that is happening in Ara Fell... and every time I see an elf on the screen I feel like they are hiding something from me!
Now let me tell you something... the fact that this game was made in RM2k... blows me away. I feel like we lost some art in the newer RPGMakers that was there in the olden days. Everything I look at this game from the standpoint of a game development my impression of the game grows exponentially. The usage of the sprites to the beautiful mapping and the combat system... all of it shows a skill in the RM Engine that is getting rarer by the year. I tip my hat to Badluck and hope to see what they have in development for the future!

Greetings dear reader, and thanks for taking the time to read my input.  Before I proceed, I have a suggestion; Do the following:
On the Store page for this game, where it tells you whether the reviews are Positive, Mixed, or Negative, click on that (It says mixed for me right now, but there's no telling what it says for you).
You should see a Heading that says "Helpful customer reviews".  Observe the filter.  I suggest you click on "Negative".
Read a few of the negative reviews.  I read about 6 of them and noticed a trend.  See if you notice something as well.
Now, keeping everything you've read in mind, go back to the main store page and scroll down until you find the link on the right that says "View Update History".  Compare the content of all those negative comments with what you see now on the update history.
Now we may proceed.
Did you notice a pattern?  A trend?  My observation was that it appears that the bulk of the negative comments on this game consist of individuals who do not comprehend the meaning of "Early Access".  I say this because, before writing this, I did those above steps.  I read what they had to say, and compared it to what the game is now, as of this writing.
I found all of their arguments invalid, because they failed to understand that what they were playing was a work in progress.  Their complaints are/were all worded in such a way as if they were reviewing a finished product.
All too often, we see detractors whine and complain saying that "Early Access" is an "excuse" for their poor quality.  I suggest that people who make this argument are either trolling, or lack the intelligence to comprehend what it is they are saying.
The entire purpose of Early Access is to allow the community to support and be involved in the direction and development of the game.  If you expect a game to simply spring forth, fully developed with all features intact and no bugs to speak of, then you aren't looking for an early access game at all, but an ordinary full release product like any other of an endless list of games elsewhere.  You cannot influence a game that is already finished.
This game was very rudimentry when it was first made available to the public.  Some basic block placement and a creative mode.  That was IT.  Early reviews claimed it was a "Minecraft Knock-off" and "Boring".  This is why I asked you to read through all the negative reviews.  Because if those people were to say those things about the game now,  any reasonable person would wonder if those people were even playing the same game.  Remember this when someone says that saying "Early Access is a cheap excuse".  Because those people obviously lack the reasoning to understand how this system works.
There are few games on Steam that I have seen with the level of developer interaction and update frequency observed on this game.  Look at the discussion threads.  You will find that the developers actually engage in conversation with, and consider the input of the players.   That interaction is the POINT of early access.  We as players get to influence how the end-product turns out.  You can't do that with a finished game (barring MODs of course).
I have no way of knowing what your experience with survival sandbox games consist of, but if you're reading this review, there's a strong chance that you are not new to it.  If you are new to it, then you are fortunate to arrive on the scene when you have.  The genre has evolved quickly, and it is continuing to do so.
This game is still early access as I write this, and that's why I wanted you to follow the steps above before reading what I have to say.  I hope that ultimately, if you do decide to purchase this game regardless of it's state of development, that you will be pleased with the outcome.
I myself enjoy this game.  I have watched as new features are added, changed and removed, tweaked, or radically altered.  Ultimately, only you can decide if you like it or not.  But I hope that you'll be able to make a more informed decision whether you want to invest in it's development.  Or if it's done by the time you've read this, only you can decide
if it's worth your money.
My humble opinion is that it is/will be.
FortressCraft Evolved takes the basic block-based voxel genre and adds automation, tech trees to research, and ever increasing risks and rewards for exploration.  Furthermore (depending on the difficulty setting) you'll find complacency to be ill advised.  There are threats looming on the horizon and you
lose.
Some of the more rewarding technologies require exloration into hard to reach areas, requiring you to upgrade your survival suit in order to acquire them.  Some of these areas require an investment in infrastructure and defenses.  Whether you are playing single or multiplayer, you'll find the whole thing challenging and rewarding.
Again, this is just my experience having played the game from very early development until Early Access 1.20.
I have no regrets.

Trials Fusion is just a mindless blast of fun and mayhem. Get some friends together and it only multiplies it, but it's solid even by itself.
Here's a video showcasing my shenanigans in this game for those who are curious. If not, just read the rest of the review below.
I'll start by saying the gameplay is pretty simple, but challenging at the same time. The only thing you're doing is balancing your rider and your bike along a path while pounding the gas. However, the balancing part is the main problem and where all the challenge lies. The courses have you flying and leaping over all sorts of nonsensical obstacles, and landing it perfectly just doesn't happen sometimes. Even more so when you're trying to show off in front of your friends and botch the trick. But in my personal opinion, it's more fun failing than it actually is succeeding. It's hilarious watching my rider flop around because I was being a dope and got overzealous in my flips, which is a huge boon to the game because you're having a blast whether you're succeeding or failing miserably like I do sometimes.
The game also doesn't feel cheap, nor feel like it cheats you out of anything. It's easy enough to get a silver medal on most tracks, but getting a gold is never too out of reach. It saddens me a little that doing tricks doesn't net you anything special besides cool points for yourself, but at the same time, it's one less thing I have to worry about if all I'm trying to do is unlock things. It allows you to play the game the way you want to, and having more options of playing the game is always better.
And even when you run out of tracks to do in the game, there is a track creation tool that can make more and be shared with the comminity, so you don't have to worry about stuff to do. The game is even getting DLC in the future with more tracks if community stuff isn't your thing, so there's an option for you there as well.
As far as negatives go, my complaints are very minor. While the stages themselves look amazing, all the stuff that's happening sometimes can be a little distracting from what you're doing. Or sometimes even the reverse is true, that you're so focused on your bike, you don't notice all the stuff happening around you when you want to see it. Another thing is that all of the stuff happeing in the background doesn't really effect what you're doing in the foreground. It's just fluff. I think it would've added a bit more diversity and dynamics if the stage interacted with the rider more.
There's also still a few bugs in the game or poor optimization. When I went to the create tool, it locked up my comp, which is a beast and shouldn't have any trouble loading anything. The same goes with how long it takes to select a ride at the beginning of the stages. I just stare at a black screen for a good while before something eventually pops up. But thankfully you can just press A to go to the course regardless, so it isn't that big of a deal.
So to sum it up, for 20 dollars, you're gonna have a blast with this title. It looks good, feels good, has a great sense of humor (the endings and the announcer make me laugh quite a bit), has potential to grow, and is fun with friends. Definitely pick this up, even more so when it goes on sale.

Ara Fell is spectecular. For a long time, the game was abondoned. It had a remake in progress which never got finished. However, in 2016, the project was back and completed. And oh boy was it worth it.
Ara Fell is definetly what it promises to be, a throwback to older rpgs. Of course, as a 16 year old who hasn't played that many games before the playstation era, I wouldn't know that too well and I can't exactly call it ''nostalgia''. But one thing is for sure; if this came out back then, it would probably be revolutionary. Anyway, I'm just mumbling. Let's get onto the actual review.
Ara Fell's most outstanding aspect is the graphics. It uses a free stock asset pack, and it uses it well (Ps: Do keep in mind that there are customs in there, but made to match the style of the pack. Some examples would be the blue crystals or the battlers.) Mapping is where it really stands out, as Ara Fell's world feels detailed and large while also being a good enough size to leave you time to explore as you play along. It honestly feels like an island in the sky, and can crete atmosphere just using maps. The rpg maker 2003 engine (which is what the game is made in, fyi) has a lot of limits, and Ara Fell cleverly pushes those limits to their limits with fully animated battle skills, a crafting system and a level up mechanic that lets you increase whatever stats you wish to increase.
The story is not the best thing out there. It's fairly cliche, but the really well written, humorous dialogue definetly makes up for it. Usually, what causes me to drop most long games is that I'll get stuck or end up in a situation where I have to backtrack a lot. Ara Fell makes sure that doesn't happen with quick travels (which should probably be a thing in every rpg tbh) and its length of 15 hours is just about perfect.
The game's music is pretty neat. It doesn't have a lot of tracks, but the few it does have are quite good. There's one battle theme that I found great. It is titled ''Ara Fell Final Boss'' in the files, though in the game it's not actually used for the final boss (A shame, because it's actually much better than the final boss theme we get.)
The game has few flaws, but none that make the game ''not worth playing''. The most minor thing is a few graphical glitches here and there. There's a few scenes where the character gets cut-off by tiles that should be below her, but are above instead. The more major flaw of Ara Fell is the battles. At first, the battles start out difficult, but once you're done with the first chapter or so it becomes much more easier. In a game, the battles should go from easy to hard, not from hard to easy. There's one quest where you have to defeat a bunch of enemies in the area, and without using the easy insta kill option (The game asks you if you want it at the beginning if you want the insta kill option if you just wanna get on with the story instead of spending time on battles, though you can just choose not to use it during battle) it's quite a pain. I really appreciated how quick the game was in healing you though. If you walk a few steps you'll recover hp, and I really liked that.
This has been kind of a short one, but Ara Fell has very few bad sides and is overall a game that's really worth buying. The price is just about perfect, if not a little too cheap. You should really give it a try if you enjoy rpgs.
PS: If you come across a shop that lets you upgrade your skills, get Elemental Burst ALL. It's a beast.

This game is a fun sandbox game with a mainly mechanical focus. You'll certainly feel the grind early on, as you work to gather resources. Getting to know the controls is a must; mining ores using only the automatic things is slow, so make sure to read through the controls to get to know all the stuff you can do to save time (Superdig is invaluable). I never really got to any of the advanced machinery, as the grind just got a tad boring. Also, the creative mode's fun, I guess. All the block textures are highly situational, which is my main gripe with the game. Other than that, it's a fine game.
I'd recommend this game to anybody with some time to burn (this game is great for passing time; one moment it'll be 8PM and the next it's 2AM) and a bit of money to spare. It's nothing outstanding, but it is certainly the sort of game you can use as a filler between games.
EDIT: After some of the more recent updates, I've found that the game can be a fair bit more fun. I found the combat (while flawed in some areas, like the lack of a crosshair and the charged shot doing nothing more than the regular shot) to be rather fun.
Also, after messing around in creative (I was exclusively playing survival to this point) I found that the detail blocks have been MASSIVELY improved since Chapter 1. The ability to have the block textures as either scaled or not is a brilliant addition, because that was one of my main issues with the original. The detail blocks can actually be used for seamless detailing, which is brilliant.
It certainly is an improvement on Chapter 1 in near enough every way, and (in some ways) is better than Minecraft for building larger creations. With the addition of texture pack support, I should hopefully be able to customise the game to the way I would like, which is a brilliant feature.
Overall, I'm changing my rating from "time waster" to "generally good game". It's a good game in pretty much all aspects (if a little buggy at times. I'm looking at you, spiderbot on hills. But that's just hilarious) and great in others.

The game is well worth the money, and I would place it amongst the best of rpg-maker games.
The story is very good and captivating. For me the story is the most important thing I care about such games, and I was not disappointed.
However, imo, the battle system wasn't optimal. Firstly, the INTEL stat is much more superior than the ATTACK stat, for all classes (excluding the fist part of the game when you haven't got much MP). It is rarely worth wasting a turn to simply "attack". Spells do much more damage (even for the figher and archer) and scale 2 times more with INTEL. With enough MP you will rarely ever run out of MP to cast. And of course, INTEL also gives magic resist.
My suggestion would be to simply remove/reduce the INTEL scaling of these classes.
Also, the "Elemental burst" spell is too powerfull, and if u raise the MP of the mage, and craft the armor that halves the MP cost, then you can annihilate everything with ease at the mid-end phase of the game, with just the two elemental burst spells (the ALL and ONE). That makes the mage too monotonus, and the other elemental spells are rarely ever used. All the other classes have a good diversity, with various useful spells.
Lastly, the battles at the mid-late game were all very easy (possibly because of these elemental bust spells). Also, I didn't like the increasing "reset level" cost, because it made me nervous when i was thinking to use it.
But despite these flaws, this game is a gem amongst rpg-maker games. I hope this Stegosoft Games studio will make more such games, and maybe make improvements at future games.

I enjoyed it. As someone who has loved  RPG games since Final Fantasy 1 (would have liked ultima and wizardry too if I had a computer back then but I was just a poor single parent kid), I have played many over the years, and this one is clearly a homage to the SNES type.
First off, while I wouldn't call the music to be like Seiken Densetsu 3, it has some elements of it and instrumentation (sometimes)...something NO other game I've played really has (at least not the same elements this one has). Which is great because I really like the bgm in that game, even more than some of the cult faves like chrono trigger.
The map design detail is frankly better than any of the commercial snes games I recall. The whole floating sky thing with snow lightly drifting melting into rivers that drift off the floating island virtually everywhere you go is really sweet. You know that feeling you get when you enter shevat for the first time in xenogears or whtaever? The whole game is like that kinda, and the whole thing looks good, it doesn't taper off after the first chapter or whatever, or have noticeably less effort.
The characters are enjoyable. Lita is something like Estelle from Trails in the sky, Seri-...uhh. I suck with names. Seri-whats her face feels like a real person. I mean...she basically says the things you think ought to be said that never get said in rpg games, and then she says it and you're like THANK YOU. I particularly liked it when she interrogates someone on their romantic escapades because I was thinking just earlier on 'gee that guy really gets around, I'm surprised someone doesn't call him out'.. welp he does.
The combat system is passable, nothing to write home about imo, but I'm pretty hard to please in that catagory. for example I never really thought chrono trigger had a great combat system either. I would say this one is pretty similar (the whole position th ing in chrono trigger is really fluff imo, line/circle attacks play little role past early game imo, and you can't position your characters anyway so blah). But I imagine people disagree because while I think CT was a good game, I'd say it's a bit over-rated... I think it's due to being one of the earliest rpg games many people have played along with ff7, cuz it came out at around the same time, so there are nostalgia sunglasses going on there.
The length of this game is prob about 10-15 hours (I clocked 15 but I had to afk for a couple no doubt, I was taking my time but wasn't trying to grind, and I avoided a lot of fights later on.. like pretty much as many as I could), which isn't bad given the price, but I have to say the introduction video really makes the game look like an epic 60+ hour thing like trails in the sky... it's not... I mean I know the devs never said it was, but that video really makes it look like one. Great intro video btw.
I feel like the ending was a bit rushed though.. I can't really elaborate without spoiling anything. i mean the final dungeon is well detailed and long, but the enemy variety in it gets tiresome pretty quick, and the final boss is pretty tank and spank which is strange since like the first 3 had special mechanics somewhat. Plus there is a huge opportunity to have meaningful dialogue between many new faces near the end and they're gone as soon as you meet them and it feels kinda like you get cheated.
I feel like the end also sets the world up for a bigger sequel, which I would welcome, I would certainly buy and play it.

Aslo, in the game you can purchase items, upgrades and gear switching between them in the midst of combat and exploration!
From a gameplay standpoint, it's a very solid game. The story is as in depth as you'd expect it to be and the level deisgn and enemy types provide a challenge but not one I found to be difficult. It isn't easy, but it isn't hard either.

Now, let me say this...the base game is solid but I really loved the Plague of Shadows DLC. It opened up a whole new way to play the game. New mechanics, new weapons, access to areas not seen before, hilarious minor characters, a behind the scenes look on what is going on while Shovel Knight is traveling/battling, a character that I found to be endearing and most importantly a rather interesting, if predictable, story.
The ending was wonderful. It's simple but was one of the few endings in any form of media (written/watched/played) to make me "daaaaaw". So Again, on it's own Shovel Knight is worth it but when you add in the Plague of Shadows story line? It's well worth full price.

Great Action-Game with some healthy mix of fighting, riddle-solving and adventuring. [82/100, 20-25 Hours Gameplay]
The story and setting feel pretty unique: Some worthy-to-call apocalypse, raging angels and nasty demons - and you right in the middle being held responsible for the disaster! Comicstyle graphics and absurdly gory and dark scenes and atmosphere work together to give the game an authentic setting. So does the atmospheric sounddesign - weaponsounds, speech, moans, environment perfectly fit. The dark humor finishes if off.
The combat is dynamic: Several combos, dodge and block with counterstrike are available, making fights challenging in matter of good timing and right selection. From time to time one could critize that simple autohitting or the eversame combo might be little to strong though - regarding some of your attempts to do complexe combos simply get interrupted: pretty frustrating.
Out of combat you climb, swim, jump, swing, bomb, drag and eventually port through surface and dungeon - even "Portal" level designers would raise hat!
There are gamecrashes and bugs from time to time. Achievement-hunters also need to consider that one has to restart steam and immediatly start Darksiders in order to get the achievements unlocked - also frustrating to figure after finishing half the game.
I also feel there is some lack of charakter progress - not in story, but in rpg sense. If you don't claim Darksiders to have role play elements, you will be perfectly fine though. And if you do so, Darksiders II should be your choice anyways!
Had I had this on Steam from the start, my play time would be in the thousands. Enough said.

This game, Ultimate General: Gettysburg seems to take advantage of that.
The game is easy to get into, with the AI controlling not only the opponent in single player, but your unattended units as well.  Commands, either by keyboard keys, or mouse clicks are easy to remember and not complicated at all.  Objectives are clearly presented before each battle, so there's an opportunity to plan your attack before entering the battle.  And with over 160 battles (Union and Conferderates combined, including the difficulty levels), there's plenty of "play" in this title, making if well worth the $15 (USD).
What would make this title even more interesting is if the developer were to inclued a "sandbox" mode in SP, where one could create their own order of battles.  None the less, this title is versatile, and fun to play.

Vigil Games surprised me with Darksiders. When I first saw gameplay all I could think was, "Oh look! God of War got a retexture!" After having actually played the game, I was simply amazed by its immersive gameplay, storyline, graphics, and its length.
Immersive Gameplay: Very few games can actually make me scream during intense battles, but Darksiders manages to keep me on the edge of my chair (I fell out of my chair a couple times!) and even yell at the computer screen during intense battles. Darksiders gets your heart racing at speeds that should be illegal. I can't stop expressing that Darksiders makes you part of the game, and you feel every blow your character recieves and get the satisfaction of every blow he deals.
Storyline: This games background story is actually rather lacking; however, I was absolutley astonished at the story that unfolds throughout the game. This is what defines a game: not knowing the history behind the story, but making the history throughout the game. The story in tandem with the beautifully crafted soundtrack, almost brought me to tears at times.
Graphics: For a game released in 2010, the graphics are very mediocre. It is how the developers used them that made this game so beautiful. With intense ambient occlusion and gorgeous models, this game (despite its many dark surroundings) could not be more bright.
Length: This game took me about a year to complete. Its massive boss chain is a big tree. There are tons of mini bosses that lead up to semi-bosses that lead up to big bosses that lead up to the Destroyer! This game is so big! It takes hours upon hours to finally complete, and when it is finished, you feel purposless. If there were any cons to this game it would be that you have no idea hat to do next once you have completed this game.
All in all this is one of, if not the, best game/s I have ever played and I would recommend it to anybody that wants a game that truly stands up for itself. Way better than God of War!!!

Tl;dr: Short low res flash point and click adventure game which could do well with more guides to help you along. Good artistic quality and music.
You play as Lumi who visits her grandfather's place only to find him missing and the house without power. You then go about clicking various items to find clues and puzzles to advance forward in the quest of restoring powering back to the house.
There are about 7 puzzles, of varying difficulty, from matching patterns and numbers, a map with a grid, a puzzle board, to one with a musical sequence. I got stumped at the last puzzle and found it too vague, with minimal instructions and clues. Frustrated and without any further hints in game to move forward I resorted to an online guide. The last puzzle I thought could do with more clearer instructions and/or hints and likewise for the plot device of assembling a contraption which required some items that were not clearly stated. Puzzles and exploring things through clicking around were fine, but it got to a stage where it felt like a wild goose chase, except you are not quite sure what you are supposed to find in the first place.
After the struggles and expecting to progress forward, the game came to an abrupt end with a promise of a continuation. That was about under an hour of gameplay.
The second instalment called Lumino City was scheduled to be released Spring'13 but seems to be delayed, though there are updates on their facebook page as at Jan'14. The sequel seems to involve a larger world for exploration and more puzzles.
Commendable is the artistic quality that was put into the building of the detailed sets and the pleasing music fitted the atmosphere well.
The flash game ran at a small 800 x 535 resolution so it sat in a black rectangular box in the middle of the screen. Overall, the lack of hints or signposts to point you in the right direction along with the short duration and lack of replay value for the game, I find it hard to justify the value of the game, even for a quick one off experience.

This game has a lot of problems I am not going to deny it. However if you manage to get this game running even for an hour you would get a good impression of what this game is about. It can get tedious to get the first levels of your character but after that you'll be rewarded with a large open world map that has a lot of content. The creators of this game have had a lot of great ideas for this game that they have not bothered to think through. You can for example pump the inquisitors clustering maelstorm to a level that it kills NPCs and even your own (or your ally's) mount that shouldn't be possible to kill.

For a 3 USD game i am completely blown away at how much fun i am having with this game compared to the other games in my library that are 15 to 20 times more expensive especially since this game is still in early access. I really believe that the dev could charge quite a bit more for this game and it would be completely justified. You cannot find a better game for this price point at all.
Its a rpg that has a series of colosseum battles called leagues that get harder and more varied with mechanics as you go up in the ladder. You will collect experience points, money, crafting materials, items, weapons, armor, friendship points, skill points, and fans as you battle your way to the top. You will also find secrets hidden around every corner in this game and it will let you know exactly when you found one. If you like collecting things it does have quite a bit to offer on that aspect.
You can build your characters to be a melee fighter, magic user or a battle mage that does both melee and magic quite well. Some characters are better suited for one roll over the other and you can tell by looking at their stat allocation and skills when you get that character which role suites them the best. You use either BP for melee type skills or MP for magic based skills. Each time you land an action you will gain more BP up to the max of 100 BP. It will carry over to the next fight so that you can save and store up your BP for the bosses. Each character has a special skill that they can use for 100 BP and it fills pretty decently to where you don't feel that your character is too op and you don't feel that it doesn't come around enough. Its a pretty well balanced system i think.
The story isn't the strongest i have seen and it isn't the weakest i have read either. Its about par, but you can tell that the dev's 1st language is not english so expect some of the grammar to be just a little off. I don't find it that bothersome at all but it is noticeable so people who are pretty big sticklers you could have issues with that. Do i think that it would ruin your experience in the game, i don't think that it will but it might be bothersome to you
As a rpg maker game the graphics are actually done pretty nicely. The game looks pretty good as you play it. The animations are clean and crisp, the sprites have good detail to them, and the environments are pretty decent as well. Never once as i played did i look at the screen and think that what i was seeing was badly done or not good to look at. I think the art is definitely nicely done
I don't remember much about the music so it neither bothered me nor was it memorable enough to stand out. It fits well enough within the game. With a game like this though you could just find your best epic battle music and let that play instead while you decimate all the foes one after another as you battle in league after league.
Overall i just flat out enjoy this game and i am really looking forward to where this little gem goes. For 3 USD you cannot find a better rpg to waste away your free time. It already has quite a bit to do now and by the time it is done i foresee it having a lot of content that you could waste a lot of hours into. To me this is an easy buy if you like rpgs because the price point is just to hard to pass up for what you are getting now and for what will hopefully come in the future.
The dev is active in the forums as well and you can tell that they listen and take into consideration what you have to say. You can see the passion and the want to create a game that people will love and enjoy as much as they do in creating the game.
Keeps pulling me back to play despite owning all the newer titles.

RPG Fighter League is an RPG Maker game with a very interesting twist. It is also a Fight Management Game where you recruit a team of fighters, and then go up the ranking in a series of tournament style fighting leagues. As you progress you also gather an increasing fan base, which then allows you to buy better gears and items.
There is also crafting in this game. Each fight drops crafting materials, which then allow you to craft useful stuffs. Another interesting aspect of this game is "secrets". There are many hidden details in this game that are not visible and you have to uncover them to gain "secrets". There will be rewards based on the number of secrets that you find.
Another interesting aspect of this game is the vendors (weapons, armor, items, accessories, etc). Many of the vendors are absent at the beginning of the game, and there are interesting quests that are needed to find them and bring them back to the fighting guild.
There are about 10+ different fighting leagues in the game, and most of them have unique features as well.  Some fighting leagues require you to activate switches, some are in ice-covered terrain where you slide along the surface, etc. It is these interesting features that make the different fights enjoyable and unique.
The best part of this game is that the developer is extremely helpful, and that the game is still in Early Access.  The developer is open to feedback and constantly put out patches to fix problems and improve on the game experience. He is still adding enhancement to the game and will doing so, based on consumers suggestions and requests.
I highly recommend this game and feel that it is definitely worth the low price. It will give you many hours of enjoyment.

I was on the fence about recommending this.  I played it for a long time on the Ps3, and just recently wanted to try it for the PC.
It's a great open world rpg, it has a cool blend of modern ARPG and old isometric rpg mechanics.  The world is huge, and beautiful, you never know what easter eggs (or entire new countries) you're going to find.  Some people say the size is a bad thing, that it makes it boring.  I love the size of the landscape, you just have to be the kind of person who likes wandering and exploring in an RPG.  The graphics hold up surprisingly well after all this time.  (try to get the elite texture pack online, Ascaron wants everyone to have it, they just went bankrupt before they could distribute it properly)  The game isn't photorealistic or anything, but the art style and world is gorgeous anyway.  Even after years of playing graphically high end games like Battlefield 4, Witcher 3, etc, I still have to stop and admire Sacred 2 when a flurry of phys-x leaves flows dynamically through a forest.  And it's a lootfest.  Enemies split open like pinatas and shower you with new gear.  You can even co-op with your friends through LAN, just like I used to do with my brother in the old days.
I'm praising this game highly, so why was I on the fence about recommending it?  Crashes.
The game barely worked on Windows 7, and it works even less on 10.  Additionally, it seems the more RAM you have, the faster the game exceeds its 1.5 gb limit and freezes.  I have 32 gb of RAM and a Pascal Titan X, and TBH the game was crashing every 10 minutes.  It was unplayable on PC.  It sucked, because I really loved this game.  I wouldn't have been able to recommend it.
However, THERE IS A FIX.  Install the phys-x drivers the game provides, and once you've done that, hunt down community patch 1.50, and 1.60, and install them in order and follow their directions.  1.50 doesn't fix the crashing, but its a requirement for patch 1.60, and 1.60 has numerous memory handling improvements and code fixes that completely solved my crashing like magic.   Don't listen to the people who tell you to run it in different compatibility modes or do LAA patches or download different .dlls or turn down your graphics.  Sometimes those things help, but none of them fixed my crashing entirely.  Get the community patches.  They're awesome, they saved this game for me.

I've been playing this game on the Wii U, and have decided to get the PC version, so... here's my review
Pros:
- Excellent Level Design, with well-made soundtrack
- Very subtle throwbacks to retro games, like Ducktales, Zelda 2, and Super Mario Bros 3
- Nice, tight controls, with a lack of bs game mechanics
- Platforming is surprisingly well-made
Cons:
- Limited replayability
- Relic system is a bit on the gimmicky side, especially as only one is universally useful.
Shovel Knight is an excellent game with clever retro callbacks, with the more obvious references going to the likes of Ducktales. It's very easy to get accustomed to the game mechanics, and recognize patterns, and the levels kept me coming back. A Super Mario Bros 3-style map, filled with treasure levels, and roaming boss battles, helps to fill the retro vibe.
The level design is very uniform, and the level is consisted of several checkpoints that you can break to get more treasure, at the expense of that checkpoint. I tended to break the middle checkpoints, and completely ignore the checkpoints that pop up right before a boss battle. Each level has a mix of variations of enemies, and level-unique enemies as well, so no complaints there. I also found that the soundtrack is very suiting for each level, giving each level a ice musical theme, further supplemented by the boss theme.
Playing first with my keyboard, and then with a custom NES controller helped me understand that the controls are tight, a callback to Castlevania, which means fhat precision does in fact play a role in the game. There never really was a time where I felt the game cheated me out of a death, but rather, my error in understanding enemy patterns and mistakes in movement were the cause of my demise.
One of my only gripes is that replayability is limited in this game. Sure, there's a New Game+ mode, and a DLC gamemode called Plague of Shadows, as well as a challenge mode, but overall, the replayability is limited in this game. The other gripe is the relic mechanic. In the game, you can access a room with a blue chest in each level, where you can spend a certain amount on a relic that can aid you in the game. I found that each level allowed for use with the accompanying relic, but one relic seemed to be too advantageous, and that was the phase locket, which grants brief invincibility to it's user.
Overall, I really like this game. Sure, the replayability is limited, and some relics can be bs, but all in all, this is a game that bears little flaw, and those flaws are quickly outshone by the good parts of the game. 8/10

This game is good. So good that the creator had to remind me 10 times or so to leave a review (but that's because I'm terrible at remembering this kind of thing, not any aspersion against the game.)
I've followed the game since it's conception, way back in the early 'noughties', and the charm it exudes has been present from day 1. The characters, the world, the atmosphere... all come together very well in order to create a cohesive picture.
The graphics are a combination of the ever-beloved REFMAP (aka Mack and/or Looseleaf) graphics and edits/custom tiles. They are bright, beautiful and work well together to present the land of Ara Fell to the player. Many lighting effects are in use (some a little non-sensical... really BL, you should know better! ;p ) but it's easy to lose yourself in the game due to the atmosphere and setting.
Sound is great from what I did hear, though nothing stuck in my mind that much (I'm terrible at noticing music unless it's earwormy. Sorry!)
The cast is endearing - Lita is handled especially well and is a firebomb of emotion who steals the show. She's bright, sarcastic, independent, childish and is treated well by her creator. She is strong, but isn't afraid to show her emotions - fear and uncertainty, determination and sadness, joy and condescension. She's multi-faceted and her struggle is shown off quite well. The other characters move to her beat, but are not drowned out by it, finding a good balance of time spent on each.
Gameplay involves a lot of exploration and battling. There are on-map skills that are needed to find all the treasure in the game, as well as optional bosses and side-quests aplenty. Enough optional content exists to enjoy for those who prefer that kind of thing (like me!) Battles start off a bit slow, but as your characters grow stronger, they get faster, however they never become a complete cake-walk despite that.
Character growth is determined by weapons, skills and personalisation. You can choose on each level up where stat points are placed, customising your team to how you like, taking advantage of the different spell components required for better abilities. Skills rely on your stats to be more or less useful, so choosing spells that coincide with your build is necessary. There are enough skills to allow for various build types (I personally turned who should have been the main magic user into a one-hit slayer with the use of a particular optional weapon and increasing only strength and defense skills. Fun times were had by me~)
Frankly, this is some of the best that RPG Maker has to offer, so if you'd like to look at what the engine can do, check it out.

(This is a long description, skip to the pros and cons below if you don't want to spend much time on my review)
My initial impression of the game wasn't great, which was largely thanks to the greatest difference between stable and beta branches in a game I've ever seen.   Once I opted into the beta, and selected some easier difficulty options, I found a game that was somewhat similar to some of the tech mods for minecraft, but with far more depth and coherence.   But this game, unlike minecraft, or most other mining games for that matter, requires you to build infrastructure that mines and processes for you, rather than you mining yourself.   The early mining process requires you to locate a sutible ore vein, plop down a ore extracter on it, stick a storage hopper on it, and dump a bunch of power into it, and leave it for about 10 minuites before coming back, recharging it, and taking the ore to refine.
However, every step of that process is automatable, from the very start of the game.   Progression gives you faster, more efficient ways to mine, and automate the mining devices, while encouraging you to dig deeper to get access to more valuable ores, to research and build more advanced and effective machines.
Pros
-Advancing tech keeps you building and modifying structures
-Tower defense aspect adds mid and end game goals
-Scanning and visual tools lets you quickly plan out the most efficent way to set up and debug structures
-All the information needed to progress can be found in game, no immersion breaking forum trips needed
-Large difficulty range
-Multiplayer (Still buggy, will likely be improving with time)
-EXPLOSIVES that you can make as powerful as you have power for (maybe not so great in multiplayer)
Cons
-Not much in the way of a wiki to look up information for optimizing setups, particularly base defense
