As you can see based on my playtime, this game is great fun, though I do have a few qualms with it, it's still pretty worth it even for the $60 pricetag it once held.
Pros:
- Well made gameplay that mixes the more tactical styles of games like Insurgency and CS:GO and mixes it with a faster pace to make a fun and unique experience.
- A bountiful group of operators / CTUs that keeps growing and makes each game a little bit more unique, as each match you can play as a new character with new weapons and abilities.
- Over 15+ different maps that each give their own setting and playstyle. (Well, sort of)
- New updates every 3 months each with 2 new characters and 1 new map, adding more and more to the game each season.
Cons:
- A VERY steep learning curve that will make any new player to try the multiplayer can push them to never play again with instant kill via headshot and how difficult it is to see the enemies sometimes.
- The cost of the DLC operators (i.e. the Characters that came out after the base game, the ones who come out via seasons) is ridiculous, the amount of Renown (the in-game currency that you can get for free, however there is a non-free in game currency called R6 credits, but it costs around $5 for 600, which is the amount you need for one DLC operators) you need for ONE DLC OPERATOR is the same as EVERY SINGLE VANILLA / BASE GAME OPERATOR.
- The amount of time it takes to get renown is ridiculous.
Now in the end this might sound like it isn't that great, but there is one more things to consider. Most of my personal time in this game is on the terrorist hunt mode, which is personally my favorite part of the game, though it also probably just because I love horde modes.
So take this how you want, personally I think this game is worth the $60 dollars it cost when it first came out, and getting it for the $40 price tag it is currently at is a pretty good bargain, and the extra 20 dollars you can spend on the DLC operators, because you're not gonna get many without money, or a LARGE amount of grinding.

This game is a platformer but it has pretty bad platforming controls and movement. Most of the time you will be fighting the movement more than anything else. I played with a wireless xbox360 controller and the d-pad on those are really bad so I had to use the analog stick. I do wonder if the game would have been a lot better control-wise if I had a better controller with a good d-pad (like an snes controller). If that would have fixed my issues with this games platforming (or even partially fixed it) then I would recommend this game easily.
I have a sneaking suspicion they purposely choose level themes that people typically don't like in platforming games. Such as ice, complete blackness, water levels, and relying on an NPC to even be able to deal damage to a boss or survive a boss' attacks.
Is there such a thing as movement acceleration (similar to mouse acceleration)? If so then this game might have it and it's pretty weird and results in lots of hits/falls.
Getting knockbacked even when hitting an enemy (like you got hit) is very uninituitive and can very easily result in extra deaths.
I'd say there isn't quiiiite enough checkpoints on most levels. You will die a lot and have to replay large sections of levels more than I think would be best. Not the end of the world but could be a bit better.
Bosses often felt like trial and error (or level memorization if you prefer) till you figured out the one little way to dodge their attacks.
Relics are fine I suppose but I felt pretty limited in magic power so I didn't use them or experiment with them as much as I would have liked. The game was odd with giving you MP back, sometimes you would be flooded with little blue pots and other times you will go half a level not finding any.
The free updates/DLC with new campaigns as the different knights is a VERY neat idea and I REALLY like that. Playing as a different knight (only plague knight is currently out with spectre knight soon) really changed the way the game feels and plays even though you are playing the same levels again. Fair warning: you will get hit or die a bit more than normal until you lose your muscle memory for how you moved around or dealt with enemies compared to the previous knight you played as (constantly trying to jump on top of enemies as plague knight as if I had a shovel).
The game overall had lots of potential to be really great. Good music, graphics/colors are nice, etc. But man those platforming controls just make the game really frustrating to play causing you to die a lot of times that isn't going to feel like it was your mistake. So many times where I would try to move a little in one direction to hit an enemy but it moves you next to nothing (movement acceleration thing) so you end up missing your attack and getting hit instead which sends you flying into a pit. So you try to damage enemies with jumping on them but sometimes it just seems to not register you are pushing down so you get hit and fall in a pit/spikes.

Nice Opening, Great sound effects and music, as well as a decent title graphic.

The Storyline is written good and the gameplay mechanics are most certainly fun, I'd def put this up in my top 20 RPGs of all time and i've played probably 100 or more easily.

I initially clicked on this game's page not because the banner showed some Anime chick with a bow, but the name really caught me as strange. I looked at the screenshots and it reminisced me of the good times I had playing JRPG games like Chrono Trigger and Final Fantasy, and it was on sale so I said "why the hell not?" I was not disappointed with my purchase. It has an amazing story, fun characters, good gameplay and a really nice set of developers who are there with you every step of the way. Though the game has some bugs, I see the devs constantly scouring the forums to fix bugs, and that's what I love to see about developers after a game release.
This is my first time really loving a game and its community, so I decided to give a full review on my part to show my support for the devs and their game!
Story: 9/10
I love the story, how I get to piece the information I slowly build to formulate my own opinions while the game throws a twist at me and makes me rethink the whole situation. It's fresh, and it was a great experience to see the game escalate in tone towards the climax.
Gameplay: 7/10
At first, gameplay was very fun, leveling up your characters and finding gear to hit for bigger and bigger numbers, achieving new spells to cast and new foes to beat up. However, as you progress towards the end of the game, you unlock all your skills and pretty much find the best gear (or craft it) and it becomes a game of doing your character skills in the correct order. Gameplay got very repetitive and lackluster for the regular mobs, and I rekindle my love for the fights in each unique boss with their own special minigames.
Entertainment: 12/10
Having my mind blown by the story's twists was really a fun experience, and the little humor and dynamic character portraits really helped maintain my immersion in the game's story, which flows really well. Besides having a weird map to navigate, the game flows extremely well and really gets you on the edge of your seat. You don't really expect what will happen next most of the time, as anything goes!
Overall, I really enjoyed my time spent in this game. I hope to see a sequel that will take me back to this fantastic land.

I was a bit hesitant to put my trust in the developers and pre-order the game after the whole NMS scandal, but I am extremely glad I did. Shadow Warrior 2 improves on the 2013 game in almost every single way, adding tons of new weapons, procedurally generated areas, free roaming, side missions, and loads of other content. The game advertises itself as having over 70 weapons, but in reality the number is much higher, thanks to the unique firing mode upgrades that can completely transform the way your weapon works. The game's advanced gore system makes every kill feel unique, as you can actually see enemies fall apart based on where you hit them rather than predertermined "cutting points." The game is extremely well optimized; I am able to run it on Ultra with just the occasional stutter, and the various locations you visit are absolutely stunning. Overall, Shadow Warrior 2 is a bold upgrade from its predecessor that succeeds with flying colors.
Highly Recommended!

EDIT: On a widescreen monitor, you may need to change DOSbox settings (edit RAPTOR.CONF in Notepad to change "aspect=false" to "aspect=true") to fix the aspect ratio. You may also need to disable Steam Overlay then, since the pop-up will get stuck in the margin.
This is a classic top-scrolling shooter from 1994, with an upgrade shop system being the main selling point. That is, your score is measured in credits which you can use to buy upgrades for your ship between levels. The graphics are pretty detailed for the time, similar to an Amiga or Atari ST game, especially the scrolling terrain. Sound effects are crunchy and satisfying, and the cheerful MIDI music is simple but effective. Keyboard, joystick, and mouse control schemes are available.
The Steam version runs in DOSbox, since this is an old MS-DOS game. It was very stable on my Windows XP system.
I used the mouse for this, and it worked out OK. Left button fires your weapons, right button cycles selectable weapons, middle button releases a Megabomb. You need to choose mouse or joystick control schemes from the setup program, and you may need to do some tweaking to get the setup program to run if you have an operating system after Windows XP. (There are workarounds for these issues in a post in this game's Steam forum if you need help with that.)
You can pick one of four face icons and a name and callsign for your pilot, although these are purely cosmetic, and are used mostly to identify the save file. There are four difficulty levels available, the highest is challenging for experienced shmup players. Then you enter a hangar where you can browse the upgrade shop, start a new mission, save your progress, or exit.
There are buttons for each of the three episodes (Bravo Sector, Tango Sector, and Outer Regions) and the "Auto Pilot" button starts the next mission you haven't finished yet. It's possible to play missions from each of the three episodes out of order, or replay a set you've finished to farm for more credits if you're not ready to take on the next episode yet.
The ship you start with has paired machineguns as a starting weapon, but by the end of the first level you've picked up an air-to-air missile launcher, and your arsenal builds from there. A few types of missile weapons can be found throughout the episodes as pickups, but for the most part you're eventually going to want to sell them, and use the cash to buy something more powerful. There are also non-weapon upgrades worth getting, like a boss shield meter and extra shield layers.
It's also possible to find Megabomb pickups in some levels. Middle button releases a Megabomb, which floats toward the center of the screen and detonates, cancelling enemy shots and delivering a powerful punch to all targets on the screen, usually wiping out anything short of boss ships. How long they take to go off depends on how far you are from the center, so it's best to use them before you get backed into a corner. You can carry up to five at once, and buy more in the shop.
You can also buy extra Phase Shields to protect your ship, up to five at once, effectively giving you five extra shield bars.
There are two types of weapons available, marked "Always Equipped" or "Selectable" in the shop menu. The left button fires all of your installed Always Equipped weapons together with your current Selectable weapon, which can be cycled with the right button or selected with the number keys. Your Machineguns are Always Equipped, and you can buy Micro-Missiles and a Plasma Cannon to help them out later, these function much like extra machinegun barrels. Everything else falls into the Selectable category, of which you can carry several but use only one at a time, switching between them in flight as needed. (You can lose these permanently if your shields get severely damaged, but by then you're about to get shot down anyway.)
A quirk of the combat system is that not all weapons can hit all types of targets. There are aircraft, vehicles, and structures. Some weapons can hit all three, some only flying aircraft, some only ground vehicles, and others can hit air and ground targets but bypass inanimate structures like buildings. This can work for or against you in different situations, so knowing your weapon capabilities is important. Usually you'll switch to a ground attack weapon briefly to shoot a tank or anti-aircraft turret, then switch back to your air combat weapons to hit the next formation of planes and drones, and so on.
Getting hit by bullets or missiles chips away at your shields, getting rammed by anything takes a huge chunk out of your shield bar. Some enemies and bosses in later levels have plasma or laser weapons that can strip your shields in an instant, mine-layers are also a serious threat. Getting shot down ends the game and sends you back to the main menu. There is only one save slot per pilot, which is overwritten every time you save, so be careful.
Each mission ends with a massive boss ship to destroy before you can proceed, and some missions have an extra boss ship appear in the middle of the level. These will follow you to the end if you don't destroy them, so get rid of them quickly.
There are a few gripes I have with the weapon balance. The Auto-Track Minigun and Laser Turret easily overshadow most of the other weapons in their price range, and The Bomb (not to be confused with the Megabomb item) would have been useful as an Always Equipped weapon but is basically useless as a Selectable weapon. There's a Power Disruptor which briefly jams the weapons of any ships it hits, but of course to keep it from being too useful they made most ships immune to the jamming effect. And it's priced directly between the Minigun and Turret, so you're not likely to bother with it anyway. Once you get the ultimate weapon late in the game, the Twin Laser, almost everything else you've acquired becomes obsolete except for rare situations, and enemy toughness really requires you to use this weapon by the endgame.
Ship variety and level design are impressive for a game from this period; they do a good job of keeping the pressure on. There is also a huge amount of detailed destructible terrain to tear down.
Overall, this is pretty satisfying for those of us who remember old school arcade games. Kind of cheesy, but still lots of fun.

Never played this game but Steam said that I actually did so instead of judging the game here's a cool way to make skinny guacamoles with homemade baked tortilla chips :
Skinny Guacamole:
2 medium green sweet peppers
2 medium fresh poblano chile peppers
1 bulb garlic
1/2 teaspoon olive oil
2 roma tomatoes, seeded and chopped
1 serrano pepper, minced
2 medium ripe avocados, halved, seeded, peeled, and diced
1 teaspoon lime zest
2 tablespoons lime juice
1/2 teaspoon salt
Baked Tortilla Chips:
Corn tortillas
Olive oil spray
Salt
For the guacamole:
Preheat oven to 425° F. Line a 15 x 10 x 1-inch baking pan with foil; set aside. Quarter, stem, and seed the peppers. Place pepper quarters, cut sides down, in the prepared pan. Cut off the top half inch of the garlic bulb to expose ends of individual cloves. Leaving garlic bulb whole, remove any loose, papery outer layers. Place bulb, cut end up, on a double thickness of foil. Drizzle with the oil. Bring foil up around bulb and fold edges together to loosely enclose. Place foil packet on the pan with the peppers.
Roast peppers and garlic for 20 to 30 minutes or until pepper skins are charred and garlic cloves feel soft. Allow to cool about 15 minutes. When garlic head is cool enough to handle, squeeze garlic paste out of the individual cloves.
In a food processor combine roasted pepper quarters and the garlic paste. Cover and pulse until combined, but still slightly chunky.
In a large bowl, combine tomatoes and serrano pepper. Add roasted pepper and garlic combination and stir to combine. Add diced avocado, lime zest, lime juice, and salt. Gently toss to combine.
Serve immediately or cover the surface with plastic wrap and chill for up to 1 hour.
For the chips:
Cut corn tortillas into wedges and place on a foil-lined baking sheet. Spray lightly with olive oil spray and season with salt, to taste.

Shovel Knight is exceedingly execellent.
+ It looks magnificent. The style is charming, and the pixel art is impressive.
+ Jake Kaufman's soundtrack is superb as always.
+ The levels are deftly designed. Every stage introduces at least a few new mechanics and plays around with them, making you learn on the spot and filling the game with variety. Enemies, platforms and obstacles are placed thoughtfully and behave in interesting ways.
+ The way Shovel Knight controls is fluid and once you're accustomed to his digging animation and the awesome bounching technique it feels very tight and is a pleasure to handle. The way the physics feel is somewhat reminiscent of classic Mega Man, with the slow initial movement that lets you inch forward if you want, and the very high aerial mobility, except that your attack is short range.
+ The boss fights are plentiful, feel thrilling (the rad music helps), and once again feel well-thought-out and full of interesting mechanics. The bosses are memorable and brimming with personality.
+ The overworld and town areas are charming and allow you to buy items and upgrades and spend the mountains of treasure that you'll feel compelled to accumulate in levels.
+ The difficulty is just about right. I died 150 times in 7 hours.
+ The ending is awesome.
+ There's a free extra campaign after you finish the game, with a different playable character who controls nothing like Shovel Knight. A third one is on its way, also for free.

I've tried a few rpgmaker games over the years and I don't think I ever completed one.  I usually got bored with them due to boring stories and repetitive combat.  This was the first one I've ever completed and the only one I'd recommend.
8/10
Overall, I found the story to be pretty good.  All of the characters had backstories and motivations independent of "just group together to save the world!"  The game also didn't boil down to just good vs evil, as there were multiple factions with goals and allegiences that might coincide for part of the game or put them at odds for other parts.  I was interested in a lot of characters - not just the main party and the story was interesting enough to get me through to the end.  I wanted to see how it would all end and the closure and ending were satisfying.
Ultimately it was sort of a "beat the bad guy to save the world" kind of story, but it was an inspired take at that old rpg story archetype and given how much of a love letter the game was to rpgs of the past, I'd say it was intentional and well-executed.
8/10
The level design was impeccable not just for an rpgmaker game, but for rpgs in general.  For most of the game, you are put in the larger world of Ara Fell - an open world.  You have a map to show you the entire continent and where everything is, and you can navigate the world map to go almost everywhere.  Generally, the main story has you going to dungeons on the main map, with a few smaller side areas to explore as part of side quests or extra encounters.
The dungeons themselves were very well designed.  The puzzles are not so complex that seasoned puzzle game players will be challenged, but they were difficult enough to satisfy the typical rpg player.  Dungeons themselves would require the solving of multiple puzzles to progress, sometimes in a non-linear fashion through the dungeon.  I thought the dungeon design was one of the strongest points of the game and figuring out exactly where to go next in the dungeon was something I enjoyed doing.
The one complaint I have is there wasn't quite enough "meaty" side-content.  In the old rpgs of yore there were often larger end-game dungeons hidden in the game with an "ultimate boss" sort of enemy at the end, often stronger than the final boss.  There was no side-content that large in scale in this game, and I would have enjoyed it if there were more dungeons overall.
9/10
The combat and encounter design were the strongest points of this game for me.  Usually, the combat was the weakpoint of rpgmaker games I tried in the past, where it was so reptitive I would get bored and stop.  In poorly designed rpg combat, the player quickly discovers a "dominant strategy" - a way of playing out combat that can be used to win any combat, against any enemy in the game.  Limit break spam in Final Fantasy 8 would be an example of that.  That ruins combat by making it really boring.  This game did not have that weakness.
There are no random encounters in this game - you have to walk into an enemy on the map in order to get into a turn-based rpg battle.  For these encounters against non-boss enemies there generally are dominant strategies to just easily win in 1-2 turns every single time [multishot spam + elemental burst deal with trash very quickly].  If combat against "trash" mobs was more interesting I would have probably given the game a 10 in this category.
Where the game truly stands out is the "boss" battles.  The dominant strategies generally do not work in these, and they are sufficiently difficult.  I wiped several times this game on bosses, learning the mechanics.  Not only that, but the attacks of bosses varied enough that your defensive strategy [when to heal, when to use items, etc.] will differ based on boss encounter.  Also, there were a
of boss battles in this game and it was obvious thought went into each of them.
I'd also like to note that it is definitely possible to grind in this game, though I never had to.
I really enjoyed my time with this game.  It took me about 16 hours to clear, the game had strong level design and combat.  It also had an interesting-enough cast of characters and story to keep me engaged and wanting to know what came next.  The game also had lots of clever quality-of-life additions that all rpgs should have: saving at any time, asking you to save before boss fights, asking if you'd like to skip cutscenes before a boss, auto-combat, an option to play the game without any combat [story mode], and an option to check what the next step in the main quest is and where to go to do it.
I did encounter a few bugs throughout my playthrough that would require me to reload an old save once, and others that prevented completion of a couple sidequests.  I also encountered a bug that prevented completion of the main quest.  I made a thread on the discussion thread about the main story bug and the developer responded within minutes and a few minutes after that a patch was out that fixed it.
I hope the developer creates another rpg, I really enjoyed this one.

I really enjoyed Ara fell! I started this game without knowing what it was about, only have seen the trailer for a little bit, but I enjoyed the ride! Overall it is a great game and I definitely recommend other people to play this. If you want to hear my opinion about the game (spoiler free) Continue reading.
Story:
So in short, the story is about a floating island that is doomed to fall out of the sky and the girl needs to stop it. It's a pretty good story and enjoyable. When I started the game, the story was well introduced. It explained itself pretty well, so I didn't feel like I jumped without knowing anything. You could read all the stories about the island on the bookshelf's pretty soon in the game. There weren't any plot holes that I could find.
Art/design:
The art is really good in this game. It is a japanese style kind of game. Everything was designed pretty well and you really felt like you were exploring (This is why I bought this game, because it looked really good). Everything looked finished and done.
Sound:
The sound is really good, the ost's were really rememberable! Would love to buy the soundtrack and all.
Characters:
This was probably the major turndown for me which I can call annoying for some people. The humour need's to be your cup of tea. How the characters react to certain kind of things in the game was in my opinion a bit mehh. I see where they were trying to do with the humour, but that made it seem like the characters were not real at all. I never got a emotionally attached to the characters, because they seemed fake. From time to time the girl was serious about things and the other time she was completely joking about it, she didn't even seem bothered by all the dead bodies in the game which they also joked about. This was part of the humour though, which again you have to like.
Pve:
I don't play alot of turn based games, but I enjoyed this one! It could have been a bit more difficult, because I actually didn't have a hard time killing things. I never died on my run, only a few times when I tried to kill stuff that was waaay above my lvl. The mechanics were decent, it could have been a bit more various. Overall it was great though and I haven't really encountered anything, which I can call bad. Although I loved the lvling up system you could really have a big impact on your characters, if you wanted to have more defense you could choose that, or if you wanted more damage. Mana actually gave every character a purpose, everyone had to use it and everyone had different abilities. You could even lvl up spells which I think is a great mechanic.
Bug's/things:
There are some slight bugs here and there that you are going to encounter, but it's thankfully not game-breaking. One more thing I would like to mention that some mechanic later in the game can be a bit annoying, not the pve but for the main quest which I hated alot. Ofcourse I can't say what, because that would be a spoiler;)
Overall thoughts:
I did enjoy this game really much, because the gameplay was amazing, loved the exploring, doing all the sidequests. Prepare yourself in no-lifing these 26 hours of playtime like I did, because it gets addicting. The ending was pretty satisfying and again the art was amazing and certainly well done. So I definitely recommend this game to anyone ;)

You know games that are made so well, somehow all of it looks and sounds and feels so effortless? You can just open it up, load your save, and drop so convincingly, so painlessly back into the world and characters. The whole time you're playing, you're not paying attention to the game itself or how it was made - the graphics, script, character designs, etc. You're simply absorbed into the plot like you do when reading a good book, because that's what you've found: a good story.
Few games, whether made by indie developers or big console companies, have been able to succeed at this, but Ara Fell is one of the exceptions - and it's made with RPG Maker 2003, no less! The developers of Ara Fell make creating a JRPG seem like a piece of cake, but only when you look closer, do you realize that a phenomenal amount of skill, time, and creative energy was put into making something valuable. And it IS valuable. Besides the story, there's just the right amount of challenge, puzzles, exploration, tactics, and side-objectives to make a nearly perfect JRPG.
My only 2 qualms are that 1) the map can be confusing and a little frustrating when you're trying to reach a quest point, but I've eventually been able to figure the paths out given enough time, and 2) I wish there were time stamps on your saves so you could load from the correct save slot easier. But once again, these are minor problems, especially when the game as a whole is just amazing. I can't even begin to describe how impressed I am.

When I read about this game I bought it immediately because I'm a big fan of this genre and fascinated by the Civil War. Also, I was exited to see the game these devs would come up with. Unfortunatly, it's my opinion that this game is extremely unsatisfying and also difficult to master. The closest comparison to UG: Gettysburg is probably Empire: Total War although this game lacks meny of the features that made Empire a great game. Here's a couple:
1. The controls don't give you much of a toolbox to lead the battle. Because of these bad controls (and the fast pace of the battles) you won't have time (or the tools) to form proper defensive/offensive lines because you have to control each unit individually.
2. Because of the morale feature and the controls being like they are, I've spent most of the battle time repeatingly dragging each unit towards the front as they pull back every chance they get (you have to command them to "HOLD" after they arrive at each location, but no player (or real commander) can be everywhere at once. This just takes away every satisfaction I would normally get when playing a game of this sort becaus I have to spend all my time doing things a general shouldn't have to do.
3. The terrain is hard to read as everything looks flat. Being about the battle of Gettysburg, everything should really be about defense/attack on high ground. In a way it is, because the ridges are victory point, but there doesn't seem to be any difference between fighting in the open or on top of a hill. I can't say whether or not the terrain gives any kind of bonus/penalty like getting a bonus when on high ground. What I can say, is that it sure doesn't feel like it. The things I thought would be important in a game like this (like digging in and defending a hilltop or setting up defences along rivers and other obstacles) doesn't seem to have any effect at all.
In short, I just don't see the point of playing this game and I'm quite disappointed in the results. Can't recommend it... :-(

Hello beautiful person who is reading this review. If you're interested on buying this game and need help, you might find this review a little bit useful.
ArmA 3 is a game that sends you to war. But it's not like any arcade games, you can't just stand out there in the open and kill every enemy you see. Just like in every military, shooter ect. games, the golden rule is to take cover in a gunfight. Dude, use your mind a little here. You even have a chance of getting shot behind cover, what if you stand out in the open? So, there are many things you will need to do in a gunfight anyways. Keep the cover in mind though, it's important. Why is it important? Why can't you just stay out there in the open, close to an enemy and spray and pray and get them? Because it's realism, you will have %90 of chance getting shot at close range against an AI. %50 against a player. You can actually stay out in the open, but you will still have a percentage of 75 about getting shot. The cover might just take that down to 40. In close range the percentage will surely change about the AI, and even against a player. So, now that you read a bit about this crappy review, let's move onto: "Why not getting shot is important." You can just think about this yourself. You get shot in the head once, you're dead. If you have a helmet, even though if it's armor level is 5(Max), there are still bullets that will penetrate and kill you. You still take 1 bullet to the face if the helmet doesn't provide face cover. You take 1 bullet to the chest unless you have a vest. The vests in this game doesn't stop a bullet, they reduce the damage of a bullet. The higher bullet protection(5), lower the damage the bullets will cause. Oh and you might survive a mine or an explosion in front of you if you have an explosion protection of maximum. Don't expect much from vests though, you still have to be careful during a war you know. Well, if you want to move to cons and pros of the game. Then let's go, shall we!? Oh before we go there, the damage against AI might come to you a little bit unfair. You might take 6 bullets to kill an AI but you still take a single shot and die. That's because you hit the weapon, arms, legs of the AI. You will not take down an enemy in 5-6 shots from the armor. But it will change when you are using different calibers of guns. You should expect the enemy to die with a mag of 9mm while you take down an enemy that has an armor of 5 with a 12.9mm(.50).
Pros
+Realistic gameplay
+Graphics are good.
+Everything looks real. ( Unless you look too close )

Cons

Line of Sight or "LoS" is a huge part of this game. If your units have no line of sight, they won't fire on an enemy even if they are in range. The higher your ground, the better your LoS, so this game is all about capturing the high ground and ridges. Unfortunately, it's not intuitive as to which areas will give you good LoS. I'll fight for the highest ground on the map for half an hour, move my cannons to the top (they are epically slow), ready to blow up evrything in sight and once they get there, for some reason have worse LoS then when they were in their original position. So that can become annoying. I do wish there was a way of "scouting" out a position before sending your entire army up a hill and realizing it has no LoS advantage whatsoever. I can't tell if this system is slightly broken or if it's just mastery of incredibly minute movements that get you good LoS once on top of a hill.

If you enjoy games that crash to desktop constantly, look no further.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Edit: I originally wrote this review back when Steam reviews were a new feature and only people on my friends list would have been able to see it. This was more of an in-joke for my friends. So here's a proper review:
Guardians of Graxia is a single player turn-based deck combat game undone by three things: (1) clunkiness, (2) a lack of polish or support (last patch was in 2010), and (3) you don't get to build or edit the decks. Which means you have no control over the decks.
As you can see by my hours played, I was getting pretty into this. It's sort of like Magic: The Gathering but you can actually see representations of the units and terrain on a tactical board! That's a cool idea, right? It's a decent reason to buy the game, and at first it was enough despite the overral generic-ness and low-res models and textures.
The campaign is simple: Fight a scenario with the deck the designers have given you. There's no option to peek at the deck the designers gave you ahead of time. Instead, as you play you will find out what is in the deck (hope you like surprises). You will also find out your opponent has (opponent generally has a stronger deck and will smash your face in). Most likely, you will fail the scenario the first 3 or so times. After you beat it, you will get moved to a tougher and more elaborate scenario. Repeat, presumably, until the end of the game. I was mainly enjoying the challenge because the scenarios are hard. The AI isn't necessarily smart, but it starts with a board position advantage, a better deck, and more units in play. That was what kept me playing. I like hard games and was enjoying the challenge. It didn't feel too unfair to me to be unenjoyable.
However, things started to get *too* complicated, and this is where the clunkiness and lack of polish start to become problems. By, I think, the third level (forgive me, it's been years) it was apparent that most animations are stilted and take a long time to finish, and you can't skip them or speed them up. There are a lot of animations, and you will be watching them over and over. (Remember, unless you are a gaming demigod expect most levels to take multiple attempts while you learn the deck and wait for a lucky starting draw.) The camera is equally to blame for gameplay being interrupted with slow, unskippable moments. It slowly pans over to whatever unit the AI is currently moving, then you wait for it to move the unit (and maybe the unit casts some spells... which also have slow animations), then the camera pans back, then it pans to the next unit, repeat. Once you start talking upwards of 20 enemy units, each enemy turn takes a while.
The next level added even more enemy units. Now we're talking 40 or so at the start. And it had an intro sequence with those same slow animations that took over a minute to finish. If you lose the level, which you probably will, you'll have to watch it again. And it also introduced another feature: Random crashes to desktop.
I did eventually beat that level to be rewarded with more of the same: A longer, even more elaborate intro sequence (at least 2+ minutes), even more enemy units, new equally slow animations, an increasing number of random crashes to desktop, and a new guaranteed crash to desktop. The latter was a game killing bug for me, and I was unable to beat the level because of it. It's a repeatable sequence which the AI will always do sooner or later, that will always crash the game. It's possibly related to Nvidia graphics drivers or a corrupted install. I don't think it's related to my graphics card because I've tried it with the 3 cards I've had since then and it's the same problem--those cards being an 8800 GT, a GTX 460, and a GTX 670). The game has received no patches in the 4-5 years since I last played it in 2011, and still crashes for me at that spot. I literally cannot progress. Note that the final v1.5 patch from 2010 claims it fixes this problem. It's still an issue for me, sadly, but you may have better luck.
Other thoughts:
Guardians of Graxia appears to be made by a small studio in Eastern Europe, and I feel bad for not being able to recommend it more unreservedly. With a little more bug testing and polish, this could have been a fine game. As it is, I can only give a "buyer beware" recommendation. If you really like turn-based fantasy games, like CCG experiences sort of like Magic but don't care about deck building, have a lot of time and patience to burn, and are willing to take a chance on a game killing bug stopping your progression, this is the game for you.
Also, there's a lot of DLC. So be aware.
Suggestions for alternative games:
* If you want the turn-based fantasy battle part but not the deck part, I recommend the Age of Wonders series, the Disciples series, Heroes of Might and Magic II, Heroes of Might and Magic III, or Solium Infernum (not currently on Steam). Unlike Graxia, they all have a much less generic fantasy "feel" because they have actual world building their own unique voice. They also have world maps, which Graxia does not.
* If you want a similar fantasy feel but don't mind RTS, try the Warlords Battlecry series. They're all great.
* If you want a CCG deck building game where you can see your units, try PoxNora. It's F2P, so do your research first.
* If you don't care about seeing your units, try Magic the Gathering online (not on Steam). It has old graphics, is clunky and a money sink, but has better balance than Graxia. Most importantly, it works, and there are plenty of online opponents.

Given the amount of janky♥♥♥♥♥ports of old games floating around on Steam these days, it's refreshing to discover that Raptor: Call of the Shadows seems plagued with none of the usual complications. No window-sizing issues, no compatibility problems, not even the slightest  hint of input lag (I'm looking at you, Age of Empires II) - I've read of some people having a harder time with the 2015 Edition, but from my experience, the Classic Edition is flawless from a functionality standpoint.
As for the game itself - well, video games have come a long way in 22 years, and you won't find a much better barometer for exactly how far than Raptor. The levels are ugly - they can get incredibily cluttered to the point where it's hard to tell what is even happening, the colour palette gets very dark and murky in places, sometimes to the point where enemies are difficult to distinguish from the background scenery, and both of these things combined with some pretty poor colour contrast means that the inclusion of the occasional night time mission was a very, very bad idea.
The upgrade system is fairly extensive, but ultimately pointless. You can afford arguably the best gun in the game (which costs less than two-tenths of the most expensive gun available), the Auto-Track Mini-Gun, before the end of the first sector, which is to the games difficulty curve what Ivan Milat was to European backpackers.
But ultimately, nitpicking a 20 year old game aside, if you enjoyed the game way back when and are the nostalgic type, there is enough here to recommend, especially for 5 bucks.

I initially purchased Shovel Knight to play on my 3DS. I instantly loved it--enough to buy it again for my ps4. Shovel Knight is a simple game that derives its primary mechanics from classics like Duck Tales and Castlevania. Where it outshines all of its inpirations, however, is in how efficient it plays while lending itself to backtracking and exploration. What you end up with in Shovel Knight is a metroidvania-esque game, with the rhythmn of a 2D platformer that offers an addicting collect-a-thon experience.
Level design is the backbone of platformers, and in Shovel Knight, the levels are crafted with tremendous care. Every nook and enemy placement is deliberate. If you see a skeleton on a strange platform far from the traditional path, there is a high chance that it is leading your eyes somewhere. The way the game goes about teaching you its fundamentals also indicates how much love the devs have for the older classics. There are no written tutorials, but you quickly learn each new mechanic as they come from the brilliant obstacles that quickly follow. The last level in the game is a culmination of everything Shovel Knight has to offer and is worth paying for alone.
The bosses in this game are spectacular. They gave me a Dark Souls vibe when I first experienced Shovel Knight on my 3DS. Their sprites were unique, attractive, while at the same time disturbing. Even the mini bosses are loveable. It's hard to play through Shovel Knight without having a handful or two handfuls of favorite encounters. Beyond their aesthetics, their pattern design is also top notch. There are no fair encounters, and deaths are usually the result of a lack of knowledge or timely reaction.
You will see yourself playing levels over and over for gems,  achievements, and missed relics that are used to traverse new locales so the OST plays a big role in keeping the momentum going. Fortunately Shovel Knight is jammed with mysterious tunes that amplify the lighthearted, yet dark fantasy atmosphere that it is going for.
Perfection does not exist, but if you are itching for a platformer that is close to it, then this game is your answer. Shovel Knight is oozing with years of love for a genre that has taken a backseat amongst the mainstream where graphic giants, FPS, and action games now rule. Shovel Knight is a love letter and a reminder that 2D platformers are still relevant and hide enjoyment wrapped up in simplicity.

If you like good old fashioned board game strategy (and don't mind sussing out how to play without in-depth tutorials to help you) you'll enjoy it, if you want a quick action-fix game you can jump straight into and win you probably won't. Maybe more appealing to the older gamers from the generation that played this type of game out of a box rather than the young 'uns.
Some bad reviews have been posted about this game criticising it's lack of deck building and difficulty. This is a bit unfair as it's not a deck building game it's a board game. It may not be perfect and, to be honest, it is quite difficult to get the hang of it and win but that's not to say it's a bad game though especially for the £1.50 sale price. Gameplay does feel agonisingly slow if you haven't got a good deal of patience and maps can take a while to get through. The odds always seem to favour the other side with their seemingly huge mana pools but once you figure out how to play it I found there was fun to be had there and actualy enjoy it.
A lack of tutorials is one cause for complaint but if you take the time to look at the unit cards, terrain bonus stats/penalty modifiers and battle stats it soon makes more sense. Almost (if not) all the icons can be moused over to get a description of what they mean. Adjacent units give you a support bonus, mana is generated by the squares you control (some generate more than others) and this pays for your spells and units. Difficulty arises because mana is generated at the end of your turn and if you blow it all countering battles in your opponents turn you have none left for your own fights or to activate some unit's special abilities. Sometimes it's worth taking a bit of pain so you've got the resources to dish it out on your turn.
The biggest missed opportunity is the lack of multiplayer. This game is crying out for a head to head mode which would've made it a more balanced and fun experience as well as adding to it's replay value.
All in all it may be an aquired taste appealing to a certain type of gamer but it's not as bad as a lot of the negative reviews would have you believe.

Ara Fell is a love letter to classic console rpgs.
I'm not often compelled to write reviews, and generally when I do it is because the game is simply so bad I cannot understand why steam would have greenlit it, but in this case I'm pleasantly surprised.
Ara Fell has a charming art style reminiscent of Secret of Mana while retaining enough individuality to stand out.  Likewise, the animations have enough frames for most actions to appear smooth, which is something I tend to find lacking in many rpgs these days.  As a pixel artist who works on games, I definitely approve.
The story is amusing, cute, and interesting enough to keep me playing.  In all honesty I keep expecting the game to be over for the small price point I paid, and yet there's still more for me to do.  Lita is a sweet, if stereotypical, female protagonist and her companions all prove to round out the gameplay.  Speaking of gameplay...
It's just fun to play.  The fights have this weird mix of Lufia and Final Fantasy going and I like it.  There's active time combat, characters pop around the screen to do their attacks, and the enemies array themselves in different patterns.  Overall it's enjoyable and I rarely feel like I'm grinding because most of the encounters can be avoided if you wish.
I do think the game is a bit too hand-holdy even with the tutorials disabled, but other than that it is an extremely fun and worthwhile addition to my library -- and hopefully -- yours.

I beta tested Ara Fell in recent months, and have been following it over the years at
, and first of all, I can't express how cool it is seeing an RPG Maker 2003 game for sale on Steam! This is an excellent game with a well thought out story (although a little bumpy in places), and some interesting dungeons/areas filled with puzzles to figure out and things to find.
One big thing I loved about Ara Fell is the aestetics, and the continuous world. This game took the floating island concept to the extreme. Every part of the world feels lived-in and has its own subtly different identity. Instead of using an overworld, it's more open-worldy in that you there's a lot of maps, sidequests and things to check out between objective A and objective B, and as you traverse around Ara Fell, you see those subtlies take shape. Thankfully, there's also fast-travel to quickly get from one place to another, if that's the way you'd rather play.
Anyway, give it a gander! I hope people enjoy this game as much as I did, and that it inspires others to finish their RPG Maker 2003 projects and take them to the edge! I hope more turn up on steam!

Shun not the Makers of RPGs. True, the lazy hobbyists have oversaturated Steam with their rough-draft attempts (a certain prolific publisher will come to the minds of Makers and Maker-players), but the men and women behind Ara Fell are on the righteous path: the try-hard path.

A couple of hours later, I noticed that the game had an update. Curious, I played again from the start, trying to recreate the bug, but found it had been fixed. Whether or not this resulted from my message doesn't matter; this is proof that the developer cares. To you, the prospective consumer, I give this anecdote as a reassurance that you'd be buying a product that comes from loving hands. To Stephen Anthony, thank you very much.

Since I bought the game, I've been playing it non-stop. At its core, it's a bridge constructor with Portal's gimmicks and mechanics.
The premise is simple: construct a bridge that's stable enough to allow vehicles to cross and reach the exit. But there are countless, creative, and ingenious ways to construct these bridges, all while paying attention to the unique layout of each level. You'll encounter acid pits, insecure turrets, your old pal the companion cube, and "Aperture Science quantum tunnels", of course. And if you're worried Portal's dry and witty narrative is absent from the game, you're in luck! It's definitely there, and it definitely made me LOL several times.
It's fun. It's deceptively simple. And truly a blast to play.
My only gripe is it's only 60 levels long, and I'm already half-way through. But aside from that, if you want a good puzzle game to pass the time or just want more Portal, Bridge Constructor Portal is worth the purchase.

Also unfortunately, the game does not support the Steam Overlay, so you won't be able to capture some of the beautiful graphics without some other third party solution.  Overall, I would recommend Lume to players who are looking for a very unique presentation, but don't mind fairly uninspired pixel hunt and puzzle gameplay.

I'm not usually inclined to review on games but it was the support that made me get this and I'd like to add my own to this pile.
The AI makes this game. Rather than simply saying "Easy, Normal or Hard" The AI can be set to aggressive, passive, intelligent or bumbling and makes mistakes that feel so human. Defeat feels natural considering the battle enters "phases" of reformation. Playing with different styles makes it feel original without just giving the army unfair boons to make it more difficult. (I'm looking at you, Rome Total War 2.) The ebb and flow of battle really helps you understand how Gettysburg actually played out.
Not convinced on buying this game yet? I'll run you through one of my scenarios. I'm running a pretty standard defensive set, sliding back, getting the high ground and letting the confederates smash their faces into my cannons. Feels good. On July 2nd I'm given an option to hold tight or extend the right flank to Benner's Hill. I'm winning pretty well on the right, so I go for it and win resoundingly. Reform the lines, and suddenly a confederate cavalry swings around and absolutely destroys my right. I overextended and bad, lost thousands and the retreat was sloppy. Had night not fallen I may have lost Cemetary Hill and the whole battle. For an hour and a half I blamed myself (not the game) and had to focus on getting beat, falling back, getting beat, falling back until we reformed completely. In the end it was a win for me but that battle lasted two more days because of my own mistake.
It still felt great, but that isn't a feeling I've gotten from Rome Total War battles or Europa Universallis. Its always "Well that guy is bigger. I'll wait until I'm bigger and then beat him." Here, not so much. When do we get more games like this?!

FortressCraft could have been a really great game, but I cannot recommend it in good faith. I say "could have been" because development has all but stopped, even though it's still in Early Access. There are currently game-breaking bugs, such as segment loading/saving errors that result in lost items/constructions, invisible walls, unloaded blocks, etc. Sometimes half the world just doesn't load and everything you've built gets deleted.
There are two modes: Creative and Survival. Creative is the same as any other generic Minecraft clone. Survival is a bit more interesting, and it's where I spent most of my hours in-game. The premise of the Survival mode is a mix between Factorio and Minecraft, where your mission is to basically collect resources and build infrastructure with the end goal of...automating the collection of resources to let you build more stuff. There are "plans" to include enemies/combat to give a bit more of a challenge for players who don't just want to mine. Right now exploration isn't that fun. It's a fairly bleak surface world with repetitive caverns below.
*Note: Some of these issues have been fixed by a third-party mod, called LazyMod.

Always been a fan of the Civil War era and there's not a lot of contendors in the genre these days. So it's nice to be able to dive into a fairly decent Civil War game again and bring the Rebs another win over the Union.
Pro's:
- Solid infantry battles and line movement, important to keep your troops connected, you really feel the heat if you
don't keep your army in formation or a section of your line breaks
- Solid sound effects help bring home the ambiance of the battlefield without overdoing it and the graphics are just right
- Smooth game-pace which is fluid and engaging throughout the battle, you will be paying attention and having to make efforts to either take the offense or "hold the line", you control how much territory you want to hold or defend, or advance on
- Variety of AI settings (although I have not tried them all) which help you create the kind of game dynamic you're looking for on the battlefield (some people like a defensive AI where others prefer to attack)...I believe there are 9 different options to choose from
Con's:
- Finding the range, elevation and line-of-sight of your troops can be frustrating, once you figure it out it's not as bad and although there is a tool to help you, it still feels quite non-user-friendly, so you will spend time fussing with this
- Infantry units seem to break at odd times and have a strange pathing when they do, it's a bit unpredictable how they'll react at times, it should be easier to take a quick glance at moral without having to look at each unit or making them hold
- It's not a full-game in the sense of a large drawn out campaign, but for the money it's well-done and the system works well with the style..after all it's called Gettysburg, it's not just the name of the game but honestly you may not even notice as it feels like a series of different battles based on your performance
It's not a AAA title, but if you enjoy Civil War strategy games, I doubt you'll be disappointed. There's not a lot of bells and whistles here, with options and imaginative or breath-taking graphics, but it's what you expect from a Civil War game and it's a good buy if you're just looking to spend a few hours or more on the Civil War battlefield.

Wow, I remember this being a neat game back in the day. But man, today, it plays like aaass.
The ship movement feels really floaty. It accelerates fast, and it keeps moving a bit more when you let go of the movement key. So you can either do large but imprecise sweeping movements, or small twitchy movements, which are not helpful.
The screen area is too small for the kinds of jittery moves the enemies do - there's little room to dodge, so you'll take damage no matter what once the tanks with homing shots start coming in.
The player's collision box does not match the shape of the plane, and is about 50% larger - very misleading to someone used to playing bullet hell shooters. The fact that your hitbox is so big means that any sort of fine maneuvering, like squeezing between streams of bullets, is just not worth it.
The ship health is directly tied to player money. The worse you do, the more you'll have to spend to refill your health, and the less you'll have to buy weapons. The stages get more and more unforgiving, and there's no way to go back and farm up some extra money. So if you don't perform really well, might as well just reload and try again.
And as a final F* you: if you take too much damage, you lose all your weapons. Of course it doesn't tell you in any way. There is literally no point continuing the game when this happens, and if you accidentally save, your game is ruined.

There's a lot to love about this game: Intuitive controls, fun and challenging levels, interesting story and gameplay. There's one thing that falls short on the PC version though: the co-op isn't here.
I first played this game as a co-op adventure with my friend on the Wii-U and enjoyed it so much that I bought the PC version to play with my girlfriend. After a few minutes and a few google searches, I found out that the PC version doesn't have the co-op ability which, it seems to me, is a huge issue. Had I never played the co-op, I could definitely say that this game is fantastic and I probably wouldn't miss it but I have played it and I do miss it.
Every other facet of this game shines brightly and far surpasses what I expected from this game. I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys platformers, or bright, funny, and engaging games. There are many different weapons and abilities to be found and used throughout the game to both solve puzzling rooms and to better defeat enemies. There are also a ton of secret rooms and hidden items all over the game so keep an eye out for hidden goodies!
If you enjoy these types of games then you'll like Shovel Knight. If you think you might want to play with a friend locally, then look into the Wii-U version because the co-op is absolutely a blast to play as you get into each other's way, accidentally hit yourself into a pit and lots of other funny scenarios where you'll both end up laughing quite a bit (as long as you don't take it too seriously).
Overall, I highly recommend it despite missing the feature I liked most about it - it's just that good.

After 17 hours I completed my playthrough of Ara Fell. I could have rounded it out to 20 but I skipped some side quests towards the end because I was so into the story I needed to know how it ended.
Ara Fell is a solid classic jRPG with good characters, good combat, a good story, and a great world. I'm not going to go in depth in this review, but I'll highlight my favorite parts of this game:
1) Some of the boss fights in this game are very interesting. I can't say I expected actual boss mechanics from this game but man were they sick. Nothing super crazy but it definetly required some thought and planning to take some of them down.
2) The world is really fun to explore. You'll be exploring caverns, jumping, climbing, swimming, etc. When you're exploring the towns and larger buildings there are extra rooms and NPCs that are seemingly useless. While they have no function they add to the world to make it seem more complete and real. Add gorgeous pixel graphics and we got a nice package.
3) The story is interesting. Its a big gray area almost the entire time, twists around every corner, and things aren't really that predictable. Even within the last hour of the game I wasn't sure how it was going to end.
If you are interested in just the story there is a 'story mode' where monsters die in one hit. A useful feature for maybe younger players or..well if you just care about the story. I wish there was a hard mode for some extra challenge, but I can't knock it for that.

I'm really excited to see this game finally released!
In my brief review, I'm going to cover a few points: aesthetics, story, mechanics
AESTHETICS - Ara Fell is goooorgeous. Even though a lot of the chipsets are the default, the game looks great. The maps have so much detail and there's so much to explore. There's tons of wildlife running around, people are walking around the villages. Especially compared to other RPGMaker games, Ara Fell just feels so much more vibrant and alive. And the soundtrack is so good. I hope they release a soundtrack eventually! I have bad sense of direction, and sometimes I find myself getting lost though and have to reference the map. One time I wandered into a den of wasps and got killed, which wasn't super fun.
STORY - You play a young heroine who has to save the world, though more out of dumb luck than destiny. Not super innovative, but it definitely tells the story it wants to tell, and it's very well-written. You root for the heroes. The bad guys are compelling and multi-dimensional, and there's way more going on than at first glance.
MECHANICS - As a RPG, your main mechanics are combat and levelling up. Normally I don't like turn-based combat systems, but Arafell does some stuff that makes it fun. Your magic regens during combat, so you can keep using your skills rather than saving them, and HP regens out of combat. I really like that system. Also the bosses are pretty cool and require some thought to beat, which I liked. Levelling up is cool too because you get to make decisions where to put attribute points, though I'm still figuring out if I'm making a solid build or not for each hero. The dungeons aren't just fighting. Since the enemies are persistent, you can avoid them if you want (though you might be underleveled for a boss battle), and you also have to solve puzzles to progress. Ara Fell has a crafting system which I like but haven't played around too much with (I mostly make healing potions), and a quest-tracking system which is really helpful for keeping on track!
Overall, I like Ara Fell a lot! It has beautiful visuals, music, and writing. It tells a compelling story, and the game mechanics don't get in the way of that and are actually pretty fun! For an RPG, that's definitely what I want to get out of it. <3

This was the part I bought the game for and put full day of play in. The name „Fortresscraft“ evoked in me that I will face enemies and build fortress to repel them… well, no. Enemies are not implemented yet and so this part of game does not exist.
The survival in current game is about energy - how you prevent to lose it and how you handle when you on zero not to freeze/burn/die from falling damage, nothing more and nothing less. So far I play my first play and have not died once because I am cautious (although I twice did mistake nearly costing me life).
On start you have few pages to read – and frankly, who wants to read so much text? Afterwards, although there is nice feature of research of everything, it is not used to serve information in nice small relevant packets. What a shame.
I fear that this part was heavily underestimated with regards of „early access“ – and by that discouraging many new players not able to absorb the game system.
Game gives player very powerful tool – grappling hook. It seems to me that easiness of movement around is dependent on mastery of this helpful companion. It allows quick ascending, but also horizontal movement.
And for moving down there is falling… 20 blocks of fall being ok was something I had trouble with in the beginning, but then I got used to it and started to make my digging to use this as advantage.
Summary: if you will make ways minecraft way, you will spend a lot of time makong stairs where they are not needed and simple shaft-mining is more rewarding.
Game has two types of resources – blocks and ores- Blocks are rapidly mined by hand. There are many types of blocks but sadly with nearly no difference – why is there hewn stone, stone and deep stone is quite a question for me (it is not even to mark depth, as for that you have your HUD. And why only hewn stone can be used as item for crafting is again very questionable.
Ores are mined through mining devices – and are probably intended for core concept of automation (so you build way to provide them with fuel or raw energy and to bring what they dug back). But that is simply not working for me and is demotivating by fact that the ore vein is depletable so what I build will stop to work sooner or later. Also smelting the ore in smelter is example of punishing mechanism – if you do not set it right and provide not enough energy, all will be wasted on failed attempt to heat it up with no real smelting in the end.
Although my comments are showing mainly negative aspects of current state of the game, I believe it has potential and as it is in early access, I give it positive result. Still, there is much to do and I believe that some of core concepts will need revision, especially when enemies will be added – they can change the game to be addictive… or not. I hope for the first.

This one doesn't use mana however, the skills you have are based on a a cooldown, and managing that cooldown, choosing the skills to lower it and planning when to upgrade your skills is a big part of the game. Once you get the hang of it, it's pretty rewarding. Furthermore, skills can be chained in combos and blah, blah, i'm not here to explain the system in detail. It just works in a different fun way than most other ARPGs.
There are TONS of sidequests in the game and the world map is huge. It's not randomised, but it really doesn't need to be for how big it is. Discovering every corner of the map and finishing all the quests will take a very long time. Sidequests are not needed beyond leveling a bit for the next main quest (if it proves to be too difficult), but if you want a lot to do in a game, you'll have it. They're a bit repetitive though, but only if you plan on doing all of them (which is not really the point).
There are a lot of classes, most of which can choose a light or dark campaign (some are locked to either light or dark), and each class has 3 aspects of combat arts to specialise in, not to mention skills  and stats. If you like exploring builds you'll find a lot to do here, but it can be a bit overwhelming at first and take a bit of time to see what you like until you get all the combat arts and try them out.
There's metric tons of loot to get here and some builds are designed to maximise the chance of getting good loot. Which you can then share with your other characters or other players in co-op.
Co-op works over LAN only (older game so no more online servers), but you can get past that with some virtual LAN programs like Hamachi or the like.
The graphics are vibrant and still beautiful, dynamic day-night cycles, weather effects and, if you have a Nvidia card, Physix effects. The graphics still hold up today, and while it isn't included in this version, search the internet a bit and there's an official high resolution texture pack. It's a minor difference, but if you want that, it's an option.
The downsides are there too though. It's poorly programmed and while the fan patch rectifies a lot of the game's programs, you still need to fiddle a bit to get it running and it takes a lot of resources (for an older game) to get it to run smoothly. Running it as administrator and setting it to compatibility mode for Windows XP (SP3) is a must, and it has some weird regional settings that cause problems when running the game if everything doesn't match, but you can get around that by adding a registry key to the game's registry entry. The answers are easy to find just by googling, and any problems are pretty easy to fix. Still, the game won't run "out of the box" in most cases, so prepare to do some googling on how to get it to run.
So, despite some issues at the start, when you do get it to run, what's not to like? It's an ARPG that's very self aware and almost a parody of itself and other games of this genre so don't expect the game to be too serious. The characters break the fourth wall with their idle cahtter ("I need increased attack and defense values" says one character when casting a buff), and it's very entertaining. It's not over the top, but the details reveal the lighthearted nature of the game, and while it can get a bit repetitive and sometimes slow to level up, it's always fun to run through the world killing stuff in an ARPG that doesn't take itself too serious.

I really wish Steam would allow for neutral reviews of games instead of either yes or no but here goes. I have followed Darthmod through the Total War series and I have always been a fan of his work.  Therefore, I was excited extremely excited to learn about his upcoming game and bought it within the first few days of its' release.  That being said, I am not a fanboy and do have gripes about the game.  I am sure he did not have a large budget and did the best he could but I still see a lot of room for improvement.
PROS
-Feels like Sid Meir's Gettysburg
-Stunning graphics, they work well for the genre and time, nothing really to complain about
-Stunning map design.  I could tell alot of work went into the detail and accuracy
CONS
-Artillary needs a rework.  It is sort of hard to get guns in place and the Line of Sight is broken.  They units don't respond very well, if at all sometimes when you choose ammo type, even with enemy within range.  Rate of fire is fine though.  I know some of this was done to prevent artillary from panzering in games but come on.  You could even include limber and unlimber like Sid M. did
-Need more details on how morale and cover actually work.  Fences and rock walls seem to offer little if no cover.
-Too simple gameplay in my opinion, it felt like I was just making battle lines and hooking units around theirs on the flanks.  Somehow try to figure out a way to add more depth and emmersion into the game.  Play around with making your men volley, fixing bayonets, being able to stretch unit formations into longer lines, something like that.
Final Thoughts
The game is worth the money you pay for it and would be fun on a roadtrip using a tablet or laptop.  But overall it is shallow gameplay in my opinion for a PC game. Darksiders was a year in the making of finishing for me. I played about 14 hours into it, got frustrated with the controls (more on that later) and never looked back until I saw one of my Steam friends going for 100% on it. So I decided I should come back to it as well. Darksiders is the story of War, one of the Four Horseman of the Apocalypse, who is tricked into bringing the end of the world. That was a little bit of a problem so it's up to you to help him clear his name. Darksiders is in a genre which is one of my least favorite as I am absolutely terrible at them. The puzzle platformer. My struggles are compounded by the fact I play these games on KB/M. Yikes. Make no mistake, there IS combat in Darksiders and it's very well done. Very visceral but the majority of the time you will be tripping levers, making jumps and solving lots and lots of puzzles. If it wasn't for Youtube, I would never have finished this game (thanks you Kuddlesnot). While I disliked the sheer amount of puzzles there is a lot to like here. The aforementioned combat is well done and gory. The level design is excellent. The story and voice acting are very nice. The bosses are large and the fights are epic. The game is VERY lengthy. If you think you're to blast through this game in eight hours, well you are the best gamer in history because you're looking at least in the 20 hour range. Overall Darksiders gets a minor recommendation from me. Lots of stuff here to like but it's overwhelmed by the puzzle solving, which led to a whole lot of frustration. 7/10 from me.

Had I never played the co-op, I could definitely say that this game is fantastic and I probably wouldn't miss it but I have played it and I do miss it.
Every other facet of this game shines brightly and far surpasses what I expected from this game. I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys platformers, or bright, funny, and engaging games. There are many different weapons and abilities to be found and used throughout the game to both solve puzzling rooms and to better defeat enemies. There are also a ton of secret rooms and hidden items all over the game so keep an eye out for hidden goodies!
If you enjoy these types of games then you'll like Shovel Knight. If you think you might want to play with a friend locally, then look into the Wii-U version because the co-op is absolutely a blast to play as you get into each other's way, accidentally hit yourself into a pit and lots of other funny scenarios where you'll both end up laughing quite a bit (as long as you don't take it too seriously).
Overall, I highly recommend it despite missing the feature I liked most about it - it's just that good.

It's you against the world. Thousands of planes, helicopters, tanks, boats, and stationary guns, and nothing standing between them and you except an arsenal of ridiculous weapons and your own twitch skill. Elite mode is basically suicide, and your keyboard will not survive. It's played with arrow keys + ctrl-alt-space, which is a little clunky but you get used to it.
Raptor survives the test of time, released more than 20 years ago, and the polish that Apogee put into it really shows. The pixellated graphics are skilfully-rendered and it's very clear what's happening, which is definitely a good thing since the game is basically a bullet hell. Skillfully using the situational weapons you buy and find is critical to keeping down the flood of enemies so that you aren't overwhelmed. Every enemy and building destroyed yields money at the end of the mission that can be used to fix up your top-of-the-line fighter with shields, radar, conventional missiles, auto-tracking miniguns, experimental EMP waves, and eventually my favorite weapon, the laser that fires twin beams of azure fire.
The levels initially follow a simple progression: Fight off a few enemies, pick up a weapon, use it to maul your way past the rest of the level while trying to avoid damage and make your end-of-level repair bill as low as you can. Eventually you'll fight a boss (Known to the devs as a "Battle Cow," strangely), which is usually an immense airship bristling with weapons. If things get too hectic, there's a pricey but room-clearing Megabomb just a tap of the spacebar away. It destroys everything onscreen (Dealing heavy damage to bosses) but takes a few seconds to go off (As it floats to the middle of the screen) adding a bit of strategic depth on timing and being able to expect yourself to get shitcanned a few seconds before it actually happens. A bit later in the game, some of the original bosses make appearances as mini-bosses which always calls for a hectic all-out DPS-dump. Take too long and you'll be fighting off the mini-boss at the same time as the level's standard enemies. Later, the bosses will manifest as humungous, multi-turreted ground-based fortresses, which have immense health bars and require a good amount of timing to cut down.
A lot of the weapons are designed to be worthless in certain situations, picking the right one is always the key to survival. A couple of the weapons are total duds, but the small handful of "always active" weapons are always a safe bet. Save up for the auto-tracking minigun and prepare for a ♥♥♥♥ing good time because its DPS is huge and it shreds stuff to your sides, which most weapons can't do, quite useful if you've only got a pinprick of health left and a giant boss is obliteraing the airspace directly in front of it.
It's not nostalgia, it's just damn good: Raptor is tough as nails and the harder difficulties will probably beat your♥♥♥♥♥ Do yourself a favor and pick this up.

While I recommend Deus Ex: Breach because it feels like playing Deus Ex in the Tron universe, and it is a lot of fun when everything works, both Eidos and Square Enix should be ashamed of having their names on this title. It is a minimal effort money-grab, plain and simple, and the weakest title in their lineup. While completing the game without spending a dime is entirely possible, it requires playing stealth (ammo costs money), a bit of luck in crate drops (one trick is to send challenges to other players, which drops crates when they fail), or a lot of time (read: grinding). I prefer stealth, and I might have gotten lucky, so I was able to beat all of the servers and the story missions with tons of credits to spare, but to 100% all of the challenges would definitely require real-money for power-ups or a lot of luck and grinding to get them through random drops. The game continuously gets harder any time the player attempts to hack a server (even just to try and get a better score on an already completed server), which further encourages spending on power-ups and makes boss fights, which inherit all of the worst features from Deus Ex: Human Revolution, needlessly tedious. The story and the writing are basic, and some dialogues are outright cringe-worthy, with only the most superficial ties to the Deus Ex narrative, and could be dropped entirely without anything being lost (beating the game does not produce any sort of ending, so there is no real point to completing all of the servers anyway). All in all, Breach has a great Tron feel to it and a lot of free content to enjoy for a couple dozen hours if you prefer playing stealth, but it is definitely not worth taking too seriously or spending any money on.
