Guys, i personally think this is much better than Mankind Divided. It has its own art style, creative features, and has a better gameplay focus than the full game. Mankind Divided focuses way too much on moral choices and the stealth, which are always repetitive and feel extremely unengaging with bad dialogue and awkward voice-acting, and the balls-out action it has is its best feature, and it is what it does least. Breach feels a lot better for giving us a better feeling of what we can focus on. The art style and overall concept feels much more creative than Deus Ex Mankind Divided, and it really feels somewhat innovative. It sure has Pay To Win elements, but it's all worth the grind after such visually fantastic moments that the gameplay gives you, and intense overall value, it's fun and feels at times like survival horror even. Its pay to win elements are well made, while other games get defended on their even worse aspects. It just feels overall exactly what kind of gameplay focus Mankind Divided should have had, and the rest of the series does everything right, and how Mankind Divided ♥♥♥♥s it all up. The gameplay has a design of the "Running against time" feeling, in a rush, but unlike XCOM 2, this feels much more at home and better than any other timed mission XCOM 2 gives you. The shooting feels satisfying, and using these guns always feels very unique despite knowing that these guns aren't that different from what was shown in the main game. The story still has some awkward dialogue, but it feels a lot more believable, and the main game suffers from what other even worse games like Horizon Zero Dawn does. It's free to play, and overall the soundtrack, composed by Edward Harrison, master of gaming soundtracks as he composed NEOTOKYO's soundtrack, made an astounding soundtrack with another composer. It is absolutely gorgeous and sets the tone and atmosphere for this creative experience. It provides creativity on the visual representation of hacking into systems and virtual reality, with a unique art style that i don't think other games would have catched so well. It feels awesome infiltrating into these virtual places, and it really does feel like a good visual representation. The stealth feels much more intense due to the large amount of consequences you're given, as of the time limit, and it feels more of a decision that's got to be made fast. The pay to win elements didn't annoy me at all. The gameplay is basically the same from Mankind Divided, but it feels somewhat less repetitive since it has more things that holds it up from its flaws. Mankind Divided has something that makes its stealth feel utterly repetitive, and just less challenging and with much lower stakes, which makes it much less repetitive and even less rewarding. Overall, i don't have much to say or can't explain my feelings that well, but i just prefer this way more than Mankind Divided, but it did sure lack a lot of things, such as a little more branching storyline and more gameplay features to make it feel somewhat more unique than it is already, and some enemies don't feel all that good and sometimes it feels just a bit odd in the way to win guns, and the way you have to replay levels isn't quite well executed, and some levels are the same with different placements, and hacking into some plataforms doesn't feel like a good idea, mixed in with the rush you have, but i can tell why the choice was made. It could have had more things, but overall it just feels about right and an enjoyable experience to pass time through. Deus Ex Breach is the most unique in the series, and is a large spin off, with cash grabbing pay to win things, that aren't really all that attractive as the grind overall feels like something that is really worth it in the end, and a utterly unique atmosphere, soundtrack, concept and art style that separates it from other free to play versions of paid games, and dialogue that doesn't feel as involving as it should given the situation's seriousness, but it still feels believable in its own fair way, and the content could have more into it, and less of the supply drop-ish systems it has, but overall it just feels about right and very enjoyable as an experience that feels like something that is usually always fun. It gets creative each time you play more, and the biggest issue has to be the animations. As it uses the content from the main game, some animations end up glitchy. But that's honestly about it of a large issue, it's nothing game breaking. One bug happens when the screen goes black out of nowhere when i try taking down one enemy while in cover. Happened once but only that time. The game also has a really good way of pleasing people intrested in both story and action. Investigating certain Darknet files can either be done by just passing through or actually reading it and focusing on its outcomes, or just like i said, get it passed through and get to the next mission, making it a lot more satisfying in both ends, than the main game, which you have to get quite some attention to its story. Overall, this is a great game so far.

Note: This is an Early Access review and may not reflect the finished product.
After spending aproximately 170 hours in FC:E I feel that I am able to give a fairly accurate review of the current state of the game.
FC:E basically has two modes to play in; Creative and Survival.
The game looks and feels very similar to many other voxel based games out there - notably Minecraft. However, FC:E stands out from the crowd due to the rather powerful tools that are available to the player. The various tools that you are able to use allow you to make very large and very intricate creations. Copy/Pasting sections of the world can be done very quickly and the ability to create your own blocks using the ingame workshop function allow a level of creativity that has not really been seen in such voxel games previously. I myself have not spent a huge amount of time in creative, however from the limited hours I have put in it became clear rather quick that those who enjoy the freedom of making anything they want will really benefit from these tools and this level of freedom.
Here's the mode that has stolen a huge amount of my time. In basic terms the survival aspect draws many of the gameplay aspects of those in Minecraft - mining, resource management etc. but here's where FC:E does it differently. A huge focus of FC:E's survival mode is based upon automation and logistics, creating large transport, mining and power networks to build a base and gather resources.
The blocks that exist in the game all have useful functions and although can be a bit daunting at first, are quite easy to use and options for creativity open up once you get the hang of things. If you've played anything like the Feed the Beast modpacks for Minecraft or Factorio then this is the game for you.
As far as I am aware the engine for this game was built by the developers themselves, allowing them to tailor it to suit the needs of a game like this. It's definately not perfectly optimised, but I have certainly seen worse and the development team are constantly working to improve on this as well as fix bugs, this is to be expected in an Early Access game.
There's a decent amount of content in the game to allow you to spend quite a few hours building and creating what you want. The development cycle is quite fluid and the creators are quite active on the forums, responding to questions, asking for feedback, addressing issues etc.
Mobs and combat are the next big thing to come, which will add quite a bit in terms of gameplay as you will need to defend your base and resources.
Multiplayer in Creative is complete and as far as I'm aware pretty free of bugs. Survival Multiplayer is currently in a working condition although there are some bugs still to be ironed out, but as mentioned previously the devs are quite open and transparent about this and work on this is constant.
Overall I believe this game is a steal at it's current price. Judging from what is already in the game and what has been discussed as the future of FC:E on the forums I really think this game sets itself apart from all the Minecraft clones on the market.

Very clever game about building a character and strategy around a coin bag. When you loot chests, you choose a certain number of coins from a selection with different powers and values to add to your bag. In battle, you get a set of coins randomly drawn from your bag each turn, and have to choose to use them, redraw, or simply wait. There's very little to gameplay beyond your battles with enemies and looting chests; the game makes it interesting with a wide variety of coins and enemies. It's a roguelike, so you have to enjoy some grinding while you work out some broader strategy. Absolutely playable without the DLC, but the DLC is also one of the few game additions I've never had second thoughts about purchasing.

I really wish Steam would allow for neutral reviews of games instead of either yes or no but here goes. I have followed Darthmod through the Total War series and I have always been a fan of his work.  Therefore, I was excited extremely excited to learn about his upcoming game and bought it within the first few days of its' release.  That being said, I am not a fanboy and do have gripes about the game.  I am sure he did not have a large budget and did the best he could but I still see a lot of room for improvement.
PROS
-Feels like Sid Meir's Gettysburg
-Stunning graphics, they work well for the genre and time, nothing really to complain about
-Stunning map design.  I could tell alot of work went into the detail and accuracy
CONS
-Artillary needs a rework.  It is sort of hard to get guns in place and the Line of Sight is broken.  They units don't respond very well, if at all sometimes when you choose ammo type, even with enemy within range.  Rate of fire is fine though.  I know some of this was done to prevent artillary from panzering in games but come on.  You could even include limber and unlimber like Sid M. did
-Need more details on how morale and cover actually work.  Fences and rock walls seem to offer little if no cover.
-Too simple gameplay in my opinion, it felt like I was just making battle lines and hooking units around theirs on the flanks.  Somehow try to figure out a way to add more depth and emmersion into the game.  Play around with making your men volley, fixing bayonets, being able to stretch unit formations into longer lines, something like that.
Final Thoughts
The game is worth the money you pay for it and would be fun on a roadtrip using a tablet or laptop.  But overall it is shallow gameplay in my opinion for a PC game.  I am sorry but I expected a bit more.  Some of things I said may be attributed to my "not understanding the game or being bad at RTS" as some people might think but I have been playing RTS for over 15 years and also renacted, am a history buff  (MA in history) and love the Civil War and war games in general having served in the army, and visited many historical battle sites.  Get the game if you want but I think updates and add ons will really add to the depth of the game.  I hope Darthmod performs his magic like he did for fans of TW.

Ultimate General: Gettysburg is one of the best American Civil War games out on the market now in my humble opinion.
Pros:
The map is extremely well done, with much attention to detail.
Each unit has been created with precision and with close observance of historical facts.
The game engine is remarkably well rounded.
The AI is the most challenging AI in any real-time game I have ever played, and it does not cheat to be difficult. In other games like this *Cough*Total War*Chough* when one attempts to make the game more difficult, the computer simply gains ridiculous advantages over the human as the difficulty goes up, for instance, militia units who normally run at the first sign of the enemy, miraculously turn into the Cold Stream Guards in terms of resilience and fighting ability. In Ultimate General: Gettysburg, the computer gets no advantages, it simply out plays you. It notices weaknesses that you have not seen, it flanks, it charges, it hammers you with ungodly amounts of artillery. Simply put, this AI should be able to give any skill level player a run for their money.
And the final Pro is that the game makers actually listen to the community. As someone who has had early access since the open beta, I can tell you that they have made many changes to the game based off of the testers comments.
Cons:
As of right now there is not a thriving multiplayer community, so most if not all of my games occur against the AI. Now, that should change as it has just been released to the Steam store so as more people buy it, it should be much easier to get a multiplayer matchup.
You may encounter a rare glitch in the game where troops move the wrong way or you take losses without being fired upon, however, these are quite rare as most if not 99.99% of such glitches having been removed and fixed already. If it does happen, report it through the in-game bug reporter tool or on the forums and it will get fixed quickly.
Overall:
This is one outstanding game. Neither side is overpowered, both having their own advantages and disadvantages. This is a great game for any strategy lover!

If you have played Sid Meier's Gettysburg! you must play this game. The basic idea of the game is you either control the Union or Confederate army during the Battle of Gettysburg. The campaign lets you make choices before each battle which can greatly change how the campaign plays out as the "maps" you play on and the unit layout will change. (i.e. Attack their flank or stay back and defend a ridge will lead to different battles). The controls may be simplified but because of this, it makes the game greatly enjoyable. To move units, you select them and trace their movement path with your mouse. There is no unit formation selection or anything like that which lets you focus on your overall tactics. The game is very easy to get into but difficult to master since you must learn to use the terrain to your advantage. In terms of difficulty, you have a great way of selecting the AI as you select your difficulty on a graph chart. You can select an AI that is careful but smart, an aggressive idiot, or some form of combo (you have 9 different choices). There has been many times where the AI has surprised me with it's tactics and pushed me across the map after I thought I had won. For anyone who likes rts games or history (especially if you played Sid Meier's Gettysburg!) I would highly recommend this game.

Darksiders was a welcome surprise when I tried it out a few years back. I’m a big fan of the game’s art design and concept, and the gameplay is deceptively simple despite looking really cool. You can watch the game’s opening cinematic on Youtube for a pretty good idea of what to expect in terms of story and style. It’s awesome.
First off, it’s an older title so most of you folks should be able to run it with no problem. The game is a 3d “hack & slash” played in third person perspective, but not “over the shoulder.” The game plays well with a controller, but I went through it with keyboard+mouse with no problems.  There’s no “loot” system so you’re fixed in the weapons you can use, but by unlocking different “moves” you can build combos. I’ve heard that the game is really similar to the God of War series in terms of combat, but I’ve never played those so I can’t say for sure. Not only is there a large variety in the enemies you can fight, but there are a bunch of boss battles too. Be warned though that there are puzzle elements to some of the levels which can get very annoying. I had to look online for puzzle solutions a few times.
In the story, you play as War, one of the mythical 4 Horsemen who are tasked with preserving “The Balance” between Heaven and Hell.  When the “End War” starts and Hell invades the Earth, it’s time for you to step in kick some♥♥♥♥♥ both demon and angel. After you’re done with the game you might scratch your head a bit trying to figure out what happened (why did this character do that?) but when you’re actually playing it doesn’t pull you out of the game. Also, the ending cinematic really revs you up for the sequel.
Overall, the game a definite must play. It’s been in Humble bundles a few times so you might have it without even realizing it. It’s definitely worth your time to play through. A piece of advice though. If you’re playing the game for the first time with the help of an online walkthrough, DON’T collect the Abyssal armor for your first play through. It makes the game too easy.

I have played many tactical or strategic Civil War games, each of which has a focus on different aspects of the period and different pros and cons. In Ultimate General, I would argue, you get amongst the best all-round experience of warfare in the period. The AI is really tough. The unit combat 'feels' authentic with reasonable casualty numbers resulting from the different sorts of fire. The scenario-to-scenario system owrks really well and allows for lots of different 'what if' scenarios to emerge from your gameplay. Finally, the control system is FAR more intuitive than just about any other game for this period. You can pick up the controls within a handful of minutes. All in all a fantastic experience.

Civ IV will always hold the top spot for the Civilization franchise in my mind. Civ III's unbearable graphics and having to press the button to move every time you wanted to move was annoying. You couldn't just right-click like you can in 4. In IV, telling your city to produce anything in a row that was not the same(IE, telling it build a swordsman, then a granary) was a bit of headache, and barbarians provided a healthy challenge and a way for my unit to earn promotions without crushing city walls and skulls alike. Civ V's 1 unit per tile was annoying, and personally, I always preferred the squares over the hexes. If you ask me, in V it should have a limit, as 1 unit per several dozen quare miles was annoying. It should be 5-10 units. Another thing that made sense in IV was that if nobody was in your city, the enemy could march right in. In V, you had to put other cities "Under Siege"(That's not what it was called, but Under Siege sums it all up). It would make sense having to do that to cities in some eras, but in real life would somebody rain artillery fire on New York before marching in and taking it? Probably not, unless there were enemy fortifications there that needed destroying. I also feel that the cottages could have recieved more attention, possibly having themselves a small list of things it could build, like things to increase it's growth speed or gold output. It also would have been interesting if they could eventually become cities. I don't have much to say about 6, since my computer only runs it at about 15-20 fps, if I can even boot it up. But from what I have seen of it, I think I liked Civ IV's graphics the best. Civ V was a world that looked quite real, and while I don't necessarily have a problem with it, I feel that it lacked something. Civ VI looks much too cartoonish, with the map looking like what you'd expect from a 1600s era map. But Civ IV was the perfect balance of real and cartoonish, enjoyable but just a little light hearted. Until it consumes your life and you find yourself locked in M.A.D. with some other civ. However, let's hope civ VII draws inspiration from IV more than 5 and 6 did.
For you TL;DR people, 1) don't be lazy, read more often. 2) Civ IV was the best civ, little room to improve upon. 9.5 out of 10. Do reccomend. Especially a good deal if you got it on sale.

All I can say for this game is, it's a real treat for the Portal fans out there. I've only played about 12 levels so far and I can say I'm loving it. It's good to have a bridge constructing game but it's a whole other level when it's Portal themed especially if you're a fan of Portal. The game mechanics are easy to use and are tidy so it doesn't look bad and creates a nice feel for the user.
-Features Portals which makes the bridge building really feel like you're trying to solve those lovable Portal chambers once again.
-Turrets make an evil but cute return to act as a bridge puzzle mechanic (they act as an obstacle to prevent the passage of vehicles.).
-Features the Aperture Science Heavy Duty Super-Colliding Super Button as well as another puzzle mechanics such as the Aperture Science Vital Apparatus Vent, Aperture Science Weighted Companion Cube, Aperture Science Material Emanscipation Grill and more from Portal & Portal 2.
I recommend this game especially to the Portal fans out there as it's a nice treat to get since the release of Portal 2.

I came, I saw, I conquered. Those words mean a lot in this game. When i saw this game in my local MVC shop before it closed down nearly 11 years ago. I wasn't sure if i would enjoy it. I loved games which involve empire building and controlling large armies on the battlefield like the good old AOE series. Although this game doesn't lead on the same path as AOE, it brings a lot more entertainment with empire building and controlling vast armies on battle map. This game, like a few others are the types of games that i could play for ages. They are my golden games to which i will never sell or never forget. Each faction has a strength or weakness, but it also depends on which units and buildings you create. It is up to you and you alone to survive. Its not a simple hit and run game where you can do anything you want and get away with it. Each choice, move and final act you make will to a certain point have an impact on your empire and your armies. You will never know who will betray you, attack you or ask for an alliance. The battlefields are more or less the same, once the battle begins, its fate, skill and intelligence that helps you win and leads you to world domination.
Although the game will have its moments be it bugs, crashes or simple copy and paste. If you ever play the game on the hardest difficulty, the feeling of victory after an hour+ long battle is beyond satisfying. The battle music is perfect, the power and awesomeness before battle and the clash between your army and the computer AI is just as good. Many factions do have the same units and it can be rather annoying when facing the Roman's, but it can also be a wonderful challenge, but again, that all depends on the choices you make because one wrong more and that's it, everything could come to an end.

This game was a classic, yet if you do not already own it, it is now more trouble than it is worth.  As someone who has put many hours into this game (owning it on CD long before I bought it again for steam) I have to say its many bugs combined with its age mean it no longer the game it once was.
You may boot it up and find yourself enjoying it, only to discover any one of many game breaking bugs.  These bugs are older than many small children and most have no known solution.  I myself have had trouble with CTDs upon ending my turn, graphical glitches, freezes deep into epic battles and others. I am a terrible general !
And for once a game is actually not afraid to show me how terrible i am.
The game doesn't hold your hand, there's a short tutorial that mainly explains your keybinds and some commands you can give to your troops.
Other than that, you'll have to find your own way.
And i'm ok with that, because the game doesn't require you to memorize build orders, or min-max with statistics or whatever you can think of that usually involves RTstrategy.
The way you play is all very straight forward.
You have your troops, you have the briefing and you choose your course of action, usually involving either staying on defense or going for an attack.
Once on the battlefield it's all up to how good of a strategist you are. You move your regiments in an elegant way, allowing you to make swinging flanking manuevers or try a blitz attacks on the center or create choke points that limits the enemy's movement or whatever crazy idea you can come up with.
Due to the slower pace of the game, your mistakes won't be immediatly noticable. You might be running your regiments into a death trap and you'll only find out 5 mins later, when it's too late to still salvage the situation, or is it? If you're a genius, maybe you can still turn things in your favour (i have yet to find out :p).
In terms of content the game is somewhat limited.
You only get to fight gettysburg, but it is split up into multiple battles spanning 3 to 4 days, with a few battles per day. So one campaign usually involves around 10 battles, but it varies.
While this is limited, it does have a lot of replayability. Your success or failure on the battlefield will affect the next battles, so not one campaign will have the same outcome.
On top of that there are 9 AI settings which can give you a different kind of opponent to fight which in turn can affect the way your campaign goes.
And offcourse you can fight with either the Union or the Confederates giving you 2 different campaigns.
Anyway, i think i've typed more than enough already.
If you're a strategy fan then this is a must buy.
Maybe you will like it, maybe you wont, but at 12€ you can't really go wrong.
Even if you don't really like the game, i'm sure as a strategy fan you will appreciate what these developers have created.
I eagerly await to see which campaign will be featured in the next ultimate general game.

This is still the best first person horror game I have ever played, and it still surpasses it's sequel in every way.
The music, the atmosphere, the voice acting, the gameplay, everything comes together to create an outstanding gaming experience that everyone must play at least once (before they chicken out).
The game itself is beautifully detailed, and I would suggest you stop and look around at some of the level design (when you aren't being chased by some of the most terrifyingly designed monsters ever). The controls are perfect too, and the the fact you have to actually use your mouse to pull open doors/cupboards/drawers really adds to the immersive experience.
If I had to nitpick, the game isn't as long as I would like it to be, the final "boss" is the easiest I have ever beaten and some of the puzzles aren't very challenging (for someone who has grown up solving puzzles in horror games), but this doesn't detract from the experience at all.
Mix it up with a superbly Lovecraftian story and *the* most disturbing and unsettling sound design ever, and you get this gem of a game. Even now I'm a bit scared to play through it again due a lot of sleep I lost from playing it originally.

Counter-Strike: Global Offensive is a strategic, and competitive game, with an insane marketplace, and in-game economy that builds from it's players. It requires the team to work together in-order to get the win, and of course, knowledge of the maps, and properly developed strategies in order to go against the enemy team and secure the win.

To be able to control recoil to perfection, to knowing smokes, and grenade spots for each of its types. Making manouvers in order to outsmart enemies, or maybe just trick them, and decieve them. Of course - you can get help for all of this online, YouTube and such, or learn it yourself as you gain hours progressively.
A huge issue with CS:GO, is the cheaters and smurfs that overrule the game, in large quantites. The cheaters, of which claim smurf, or the smurfs, or so claimed to be, which are cheating. Let's discuss.
Smurfs:
Commonly, ranked above DMG, wishing to purchase a secondary account, to play in lower ranked games. Usually unable to play their own ranks, so they play the lower ranks to feel like they're better at the game than they actually are. Whilst in those lower ranks, accused of cheating a lot due to hours, and rank. "I'm a smurf" doesn't cut it anymore, I suppose. These people, when played against make it even harder to rank up after ValvE updated the lovely ranking system, making it a hell to understand, and/or rank up at a decent rate, despite if you're good or bad at the game. Playing against an actual smurf, whom of which is above DMG, whilst you're in Gold Nova, or Silver, is going to be one hell of a time for you, as they will likely have a better understanding than you would at Silver / Gold Nova.
Cheaters:
Many people mock, and curse the VAC system we currently all know and love. It doesn't work as well as it should, and everybody can admit that, with the amount of people cheating. The only issue is, that people now legit hack. This means, they do cheat, put have configurations/settings of which make it look like they're playing as if without cheats. Maybe, using walls, but playing as if they weren't. This can easily bypass VAC, and leave it to Overwatch to predict their fate, but the majority are very good at hiding such a thing, making Overwatch, a joke like VAC. The thing being, with these cheats, is that they're so well known, and easy to gain access to for a small sum of cash. Commonly cheap, as well. This is an issue ValvE is doing nothing about.
The race against cheaters will never end, as programmers and modders will always be out there finding ways to gain the advantage in online games. Cheating, is something that can never end, as it will always be possible, even if it were to be completely illegal to use said cheats. ValvE is implementing a system of which their 'bots' will have a further-developed cheat detecting AI, which learns from cheaters how they operate, and move, and detect inhuman moves, that could not be done. They've currentely got Version 1 of these bots released in CS, of which only detect spinbotters, which is good progress as the processing power required for such a thing, is a large demand. The thing that can go wrong with this; are the shots some people hit, mainly deemed as 'lucky' could be detected as 'inhuman' and therefore, that player being banned. I think the bots submit the player to Overwatch though, which invalidates my point.
ValvE are doing something against the issues with CS, but not as much as they could be doing.
Don't get me wrong though, this game is a wonderful game, if I'm quite honest, as it truly offers actual thinking as you progress through the ranks, and offers a sense of achievement within the ranking system when you rank up - the community on the other hand, being no better. I wasn't sure about Breach, but to my surprise it turned out to be an incredibly fun and challenging arcade game which is also free!
The following review contains some tips to beat Breach without any problems.
Pros:
1) Fun puzzles with Deus-Ex vibe
2) No microtransactions necessary, I've completed all levels without needing them! Besides, the microtransactions can hardly help you as most of them seem to be purely cosmetic, and all the weapons or ammo you may need (actually, more than you'll need) can be obtained with in-game credits or as rewards.
3) Good non-linear quests (darknet files), which require thinking and true decision making (Imagine Deus Ex where every choice you make is non-replayable and linked to your account forever. Hardcore!)
4) Hardcore gameplay (you'll have to plan your actions carefully and fail multiple times until win).
Cons:
1) Absolutely terrible optimization. The graphics is very simple and minimalistic, but the game hardly can show 30-35 fps on GTX 750 TI 2 GB!
2) Many levels are created via templates and therefore feel repeatable sometimes (though they still have significant changes).
3) Having some augmentations are 100% necessary to complete the game. I don't see any way to beat the bosses without Focus aug and to complete many of the stealth levels without Cloaking aug.
4) After some time you can't have all you augs at the same time (memory pool "feature").
5) Hardcore gameplay and high demand to the player's patience and strategy thinking may scare the weak and make them whining about "necessary microtransactions" with no real reasons. :)
Key to success in this game is simple -  take your time exploring the levels before using expendables like "cheats" and ammo. You WILL fail the first time almost always, and in many cases you'll need multiple attempts to complete a level. Be patient, conserve ammo and cheats items unless you're sure that they can provide necessary boost to complete a level. It's useful to fill all your empty inventory with different guns, because default ammo in them is always replenished for free, so having multiple guns can help you to have enough firepower without spending money on ammo. Upgrade B-grade guns over C-grade (B-grade have more starting damage), buy ammo for AP-ammo guns only to beat the bosses or hard elimination levels. Use Stun rifle + manual takedown to easily destroy the heavy units. Be sure to have Focus aug for the bosses and Cloaking for the stealth levels.

At any given point the game can crash and you have to undergo the entire enemy turn again. So even if you have defeated 3 invasions and are working on your fourth, you win it and just as you are supposed to return to the turn based space view, it crashes and you are back to the start of the enemy turn and have to repeat all the fights. Really makes it unplayable. Other than the obvious problems of this games programming, there are other options which are clearly lacking.
Many of the standard options you would come across in games these days like easy to control rally points or grab all military units commands are not readily available. First impression:
- Cool. It uses gamepad.
- Hey, some people over there!
- Awesome! There are multiple characters I could use!
- Except they require an expansion I don't have...
- Okay! Walking through a forest!
- There's an enemy!
- I guess this is the attack button?
- Am I meant to memorise these icons?
- Is combat turn-based? There's a Slowing coin, but would I be just better off selecting actions faster?
- There's a wall over there.
- I can't see any keys.
- (a bit later after fighting a bunch of enemies and wondering if I'll run out of attack coins) Oh, apparently I have a key.
- There's a chest here, which has a key.
- Why can't I grab the key?
- I'll just come back for it, I guess?
- I only grabbed 1 of 2 coins, but now the chest appears empty? Does that mean I missed out on the key entirely?
(I then died to what I think was a fake chest, and didn't get a chance to go back and try to get that second key.)
Maybe the game would grow on me if I played it more. It's probably great once you get into it.
But when the first thing I see is something forbidden to me unless I spend money, and there doesn't appear to be any sort of tutorial - or at least, none that I encountered - it doesn't make for the beginnings of an immersive game experience.
If I get back into the game and it's fun, I'll certainly change this review. But my first death happened 7 minutes in, and I still hadn't figured out the basics.
Even something like having coins tend to show up in certain positions on the gamepad would have been helpful. Make it so that Attacks (red) are more likely to be on B, make it so Healing abilities (blue) are more likely to be on X, make it so Shields/Armor abilities (green) are more likely to be on A. That way I'm not constantly having to stop and double-check that I'm using the correct ability each and every turn, as the +4dmg Attack ability constantly bounces around between buttons each time I would get to use it.
At the end, I had an opportunity to spend coins towards unlocking 3 characters. I'm not sure if those were the same characters I saw at the start which required the expansion or not, but pressing A (and expecting to be sent to the next screen) started funnelling coins into one of them. A pity I was more interested in unlocking one of the other characters that showed up on-screen, and there didn't appear to be any way to undo the effects of that button press.
The game has potential, but I'm just not given enough information - and I shouldn't have to go and quickly Google a new player's guide in order to figure out wtf I'm meant to be doing in a game. The game should be able to explain that for itself.

This is an amazing little game.
The game starts out very simply, with just a few planes to control. As you guide them successfully to their destinations, the number of planes in your space increases, and so does your mental load.
A simple and effective interface lets you put your air traffic plan into action almost as quickly as you can think it (via any combination of keyboard, mouse, and touch).
Before long, you must be completely focused on managing the traffic to keep everything running smoothly and your score increasing.
Eventually, you slip up, and your score drops a bit, and the number of planes in the air drops with it.
You catch your breath, refocus, and try to push your score up again.
I guarantee that you will find it a challenge to get a score of 30 (the final acheivement in the game).
For me to get it, I had to think quite a bit about the traffic strategy I was using, and find more efficient ways of solving particular congestion scenarios.
You can also cap the number of planes and play it as a relaxing game of solitaire.
If you like to get lost for a while in games that require mental focus, give this game a shot.

When Rome: Total War first came out, I remember ordering it off Amazon and being so disappointed when it didn't turn up in it's little box on the scheduled date. Having played both Shogun and Medieval Total War, the originals, I was chomping at the bit to see what this next generation of strategy was going to be like.  This time you wouldn't move armies like a chess piece. This time they'd move like proper people across a living map. Betterx than that... the armies would actually seem to have three dimensions and not the old paper cut-out effect of the previous games.
Over the next year and long before Steam existed, I probably clocked in some disgusting triple digit number of hours in gameplay. It was beautiful to look at, ground-breaking in every way and completely sucked in my life. Everything that I wanted from a classical strategy game was right there. And it still is.
Some time later Medieval 2 came out, which once again I diligently spent too much of my time playing. Now we have Rome 2 and Attila. Are the later games (with patches) better? In my opinion: strategy map yes, battles no. It all really boils down to the person and their attitude towards graphics.
The other day I downloaded Rome 1 due to a nostalgic hangover, and have spent even more of my time ruining the afternoon of various Gaulish villages. I would never say 'don't download Rome 2' because it's also great fun, but Rome 1 is solid entertainment throughout.
If you haven't experienced Rome 1 and are a fan of the TW series, or even a newcomer looking for a strategy game... I strongly suggest you give it a chance.

This is a really neat little wargame.  It's essentially an RTS, but with a more relaxed pace than most.  Mechanically, the battles are much like those in the Total War series.  Since it's just covering one three-day battle at Gettysburg, you might think that there's only one map, but it's more like 30 overlapping maps, and each scenario uses one.  You have a limited amount of time to take certain victory points, and are often required to hold other points you already occupy.  When time's up, the game lets you know that everyone is out of ammo and needs to take a break, and you're provided with an assessment based on casualty statistics and victory objectives.  Although you will receive reinforcements at scripted intervals, casualties carry over from one scenario to the next, lending weight to each risky decision you make.
You can play as either the Union or the Confederacy.  The Union has weaker officers (poor soldier morale) but much more disciplined troops (better rate of fire) and better artillery pieces.  The Confederate troops are enthusiastic but not well trained, and as such, they fare much better in the visceral immediacy of melee combat than in the smoke-choked dread of a sustained engagement at range.  If you're Confederates, charge the enemy.  If you're the Union, skirmish, bombard, and ambush.
The AI seems to really earn its victories rather than cheat for them.  There are nine to choose from, arranged in a 3x3 grid with difficulty on one axis, and aggressiveness on the other.  "Determined" is in the upper right, and is formidable.  "Cautious" is on the lower left, and it mostly turtles to defend, and attacks in massed formations under artillery support, flanking when possible.  That's actually not a bad approach, generally speaking, but the Cautious AI panics easily when taking casualties, and that can be exploited with a vicious counterattack.
When playing, don't be afraid to pause the game and click through your units to check on them.  You only see stats for the currently-selected unit, and it's vital to ensure that their degree of cover is roughly what you expect it to be, that they're not physically exhausted, and that their morale is holding.  Unaware of their poor condition, I sent a group of soldiers on a surprise downhill bayonet charge that would have been wildly successful if they'd been up to it, but they ended up routing so badly that I lost the whole unit permanently.  If I’d kept them hidden, they could have rested safely and charged the next threat.
Some general tips: Don’t force the men to run too much.  Move mounted officers near demoralized troops.  Press M to turn on relief lines, to get a better sense of the elevation of the terrain, and seize high ground.  Check a unit’s line of sight to see who threatens it; this game does not allow indirect fire, so if you can’t see it, it can’t hurt you.  Place units at the top of the downslope of hills, not the peak, to ensure line of sight.  Don’t micromanage the artillery ammo type unless you’re really going to watch it; you want those guys switching to canister shot if they get charged.
Just prior to writing this review, I was playing a scenario where I was a little bogged down.  There was a fairly long but ragged battle line, broken up by hills and forest.  The Union had some artillery on a hill, and most of my men were reloading in cover and firing at the approaching Union forces opportunistically.  Much as I wanted to charge my men right at them, it would mean crossing open terrain and taking losses from the artillery.  To the north of this, I had a fairly strong infantry brigade and a unit of skirmishers holding a victory location against a rather pathetic Union attack.  Just then, my artillery finished moving into range of those weaklings and opened fire, causing them to scatter.  Precariously leaving that artillery piece to fend for itself, I abandoned the northern victory point.  I sent the skirmishers straight south, recklessly charging the Union artillery pinning my southern forces, while the strong infantry brigade moved around to flank.  When they turned to face my skirmishers, my southern forces broke out of cover, shattering the Union advance and routing their troops.  My skirmishers and strong infantry brigade annihilated the Union artillery and fell upon the fleeing bluecoats.  The battle had been pretty even up to that point, but it ended with 3500 union casualties, while I lost less than 2000 men.  The way the whole thing turned on one quick maneuver was immensely rewarding, and I look forward to pulling it off on a harder AI.

There's a gamble that comes with attempting new mechanics in a game. We've all been around long enough that we expect certain things to work certain ways, and cutting against that grain can really turn people off. But nobody wants to fight the same monsters and gain the same levels forever, and so we must give games like Coin Crypt their dues. Easily one of the most unique roguelikes I've ever played, Coin Crypt not only forges forth with a bold new concept, but constructs some brilliant strategy around it.
You are a lootmancer, unraveling the secrets of a mysterious island in the Pacific in the search for more loot. And you're going to find plenty of it in the form of coins, dozens upon dozens of different kinds of coins. The thing is, these coins are how you do EVERYTHING in the game. Attack coins do damage to your enemies, healing coins heal you, shield coins protect you, stealing coins take your foe's coins, key coins unlock things, and so on. Run out of life OR coins and it's game over, so you need to be just as careful about spending yourself into oblivion as you are fighting monsters.
If that sounds daunting, then let me assure you it is, at least at first. You start the game with a basic set of coins and find more in chests liberally scattered throughout the levels. Coins can also be nicked off your enemies or collected when they perish, but must be spent to defeat them. Combat is far more complex than just attacking or healing, though. Enemies can also be beaten by running them out of coins, and there are a wealth of coins that can steal coins, drop coins, clone coins, switch coins, and more. You'll always need to size up your foe before launching a strategy, because armored enemies might be easier to take down by running them dry, or low-health enemies might be better handled through status effects.
I really cannot stress enough how deep the combat system is. It's real-time as well, with each coin having a cast time to consider. That means you can launch quick steals to stop a heavy incoming attack, or fill a swift enemy's pockets with self-damaging coins, or just wait for a basic attacker to waste their coins against your shields. Your available coins are drawn randomly as three options so you won't always have your chosen strategy up, but you can re-draw or find items or buffs that affect the coins you tend to draw.
This brilliant combat system is the heart of Coin Crypt, particularly because there's a pretty simple game built around it. Levels tend to be short and contain few features outside enemies and chests. There are shrines to loot deities, wishing wells, and shops to spend your coins on, but with all of these you'll need some experience to know when to spend and when to save. Your coins all have value, of course, and so their worth as actual currency may also color your strategy. You'll even find a few secrets and shortcuts, assuming you take the time to explore a little.
There's a daily challenge mode on top of the regular adventure, and a whole gaggle of characters to unlock, each with their own unique playstyle. It's all wrapped up in an adorable blocky presentation of bold lines, primary colors, and bouncing rectangular people. The sound design is fine as well, though I can't say I remember much outside of the pleasing jingle of coins. But really, that's all you need when the core experience is so good. Coin Crypt does a lot with a fresh concept, making it something worth digging into and spending hours mastering.

First of all, I am an early backer and have been testing and playing this game since it was released on Steam Greenlight/early access.
Graphics:
the graphical style of the game is fantastic. It gives an impression of a large battlefield, while still showing enough detail. Everything is clear and crisp, with the smoke and explosions looking great, and the battlefield getting littered with dead bodies. The landscape is a beautiful rendition of the land around Gettysburg, and you will easily pick out all the historical spots, like the Cemetery, The Peach Orchard, Devil's Den, The Round Tops, The Angle, etc.
Gameplay:
The battles are fluid and smooth. You can either play individual battles, or play the full 3-4 day Battle of Gettysburg campaign. Factors like morale and casualties carry over to the next battles, so managing your soldiers is important, and fresh reserves are valuable. The game is relatively balanced between the two sides, with each side having its own advantages. The battles give fairly realistic casualty results, and the battle lines ebb and flow as soldiers push forward or fall back. The AI is probably the best I've ever seen in an RTS game like this, and on the hardest difficulties provides a formidable challenge most of the time. The AI will fall back, use its reserves, launch assaults and flanking maneuvers, etc. The game is very replayable, with the campaign having many different branching outcomes based on your decisions and performance in battles, and you can play against different AI personalities who have very different playstyles, giving a different experience every time.
Sound:
good. The cannons and muskets and rifles sound great, and give a good ambiance to the battles. You hear the men shouting, guns firing, trumpets sounding, and it gives a great feeling of the intensity of the fighting going on.
The music in the game is decent. Not outstanding, but it is acceptable.
Realism:
Overall, the game is a fairly realistic representation of the Battle of Gettysburg, with three large exceptions:
1) the performance of cavalry. Cavalry in the game are way more powerful and influential than they ever were during the American Civil War. In the early battles, the fictional "Vidette" units are capable of wiping out artillery batteries and are more resilient to getting shot than they should be. In the later battles, when the Union and Confederate Cavalry divisions arrive, they are able to cause massive casualties in melee. The cavalry are simply not historically accurate in the game.
2) artillery. In the game, artillery units show men rolling around cannons. They move very slowly, and are quite resilient against gunfire, leading to the possibility of using artillery units like tanks to push forward into the enemy. They also tend to inflict more casualties than they did historically. Historically, ACW artillery had horses and limbers that allowed them to limber and move around the battlefield quickly, even faster than infantry marching. This prominent feature is notably missing from the game. In short, artillery should be more mobile, but also more vulnerable to casualties.
3) entrenchments and breastworks: historically, infantry entrenchments and breastworks were a pivotal part of the American Civil War, particularly at Gettysburg. While cover (like forests, fences, rocks, etc) do give a sizable cover bonus to infantry, there is no feature simulating how infantry holding a position for an extended time would dig in and fortify it, making it very hard for the enemy to push them off (see Culp's Hill).
Controls:
Controls are very easy and fast. Extremely intuitive. The way you can give movement orders by dragging a path is perfect.
OVERALL:
This is a great game, and I would definitely recommend it. It is very fun, sports top-notch AI, and is a very unique game. While it has some serious historical inaccuracies, it is still a good game. I personally hope that the devs introduce some modding support eventually, so that players can fix those inaccuracies themselves. I am looking forward to future sequels and expansions, as well as future patches to the game.
Oh, and I wish they would work on an Android version, and not just one for iPad.

I'm seeing a lot of folks refer to God of War when talking about this and how it borrows a lot from that game.  Thankfully (I guess?) I've never played a God of War epic, so this game is all fine and dandy to me.  I am, however, a major Zelda fan, and it was actually those comparisons that caused me to give this bad boy a go.
I'm not always a fan of hack and slash games, but when they are fun enough, I can dig 'em.  There's enough variety between murdering your way through demons and having to use your brain for environmental puzzles to keep you going.  Just when you think you've hit your daily limit on beheading yet another insignificant hell spawn, a dungeon full of Zelda-lite elements come at you to switch it up.  It equals a very satisfying experience.
In short, I think I kind of love this game.
Except the controls are obviously meant for controllers and to use a keyboard/mouse combo means some pretty acrobatic finger gymnastics that could possibly very well lead me to carpal tunnel surgery.  Not nearly bad enough to ruin the game, of course, but annoying enough to add unneeded challenge to boss fights and some otherwise simple platforming.  Maybe it's just me, and perhaps other players have more dexterous fingers.
That, however, hasn't stopped me from firing this game up whenever I get a chance.  It's pretty addictive with some great voice work and a cool enough storyline to keep me charging through.  Definitely will be checking out the sequel at some point.

Darksiders gives off a very strong Legend of Zelda vibe with explorable enviroments, various different weapons (used to solve puzzles) and a strong storyline. I'll talk about each of these briefly in this review.
The graphics in Darksiders are surely not top notch, but they have a style i personally enjoyed greatly. The enviroments are beautiful, the characters (while horribly over the top) are memorable and the soundtrack is decent. Not top notch, but good enough.
The gameplay is pretty straightforward. See creature -> swing sword at creature -> creature dies. However, in its simplicity lies its greatest weakness. Fighting enemies quickly loses its appeal, since you don't have to think about it too much. Just swing, dodge attacks from some of the stronger enemies, and you're good to go. You unlock a wealth of alternative and upgradeable weapons throughout the game, but to be honest, all of them fail to improve on what your sword already does. They are, in general, so weak that there's no point using them outside of puzzle solving. Especially once you get certain unlockables, the sword vastly outdoes anything else you'll find, adding to the tedium.
Now, the story... The story actually delivers. You are War, arriving on earth to witness to apocalypse in progress, only to be called back in the middle of combat to answer for starting the apocalypse too early. What follows is an entertaining tale of betrayal and redemption (though admittedly, it does not nearly have the substance that Darksiders 2's story had, and the pacing is fairly slow until you start nearing the end).
In short, if you're looking for a game that will entertain for a week or so, Darksiders may be worth picking up. While it certainly has its appeal, it won't do more than that.

I like both sacred for their somehow very satisfying way of slaughtering tons of mobs and gettin rad loot. The combat mechanics work flawless for close combat. Ranged combat has some slight issues with terrain sometimes. shots getting blocked by hills, props whatever and some mobs have such a huge movement in their attack animation that they evade shots. Those are little flaws that dont matter too much since sacred is so smooth and fluent in its combat that it doesnt matter if a few shots miss or you misscast your spell out of bounds by accident.
I dont say its impossible to put a good story into a hack and slay game, I am saying that a hack and slay game can be fun and entertaining even without any story.

Now a list of issues other user describe and my thoughts:
- game is too easy / outleveling quest areas: If you are seeking the challenge the game has to offer skip all guides and start your character in silver difficulty. Even if you do every sidequest there is its nearly impossible to outlevel silver before you have done every quest there is. If you happen to stumble upon really broken stuff like the BeeEffGee build just dont do it.
- buggy quests: yes, there are some quests that dont function well or at all but so what ? there are hundreds of quests and for the density of actual content its impressive how few quests are actually bugged. Also quests do give exciting rewards like set items. In fact with the Bargaining skill at 75 quests are well worth your time in higher difficulties IMO.
- boring story / lore: yep, lets be honest nobody plays this game for its quality story. If you are interested in a good told story go read a book or play some games that are actually made for that. If you dig deep and actually read the books that drop every now and then you see the effort of immersion or lore and sometimes its even slightly interesting to read. Just because Sacred isnt based on a 100 bands thick story like Warcraft it isnt automatically bad.
- it doesnt bring the same charm as Sacred (the first one): well nostalgia can be a real pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ I personally like both games. They are similar and I feel like Sacred 2 is in fact the better game concept wise. You have more diversion in your class. And I feel its not so punishing as the first for going trololo and skilling whatever. I however feel the Sacred genes.
- hard to controll camera: yes the camera can be a nightmare but by fiddeling with the options you can live with it quite easily. Just disable follow camera and collision and you are good to go. Just use the rotation keys to keep the boss centric bossfights so that the boss is north of you and you wont have problems with movement or attacking.
- progress loss by crashes / corruption: I dont see the problem here. The game has the option to bind save game. Just put it somewhere comfy and hit it every now and then. Never lost more than maybe 10 minutes. I always save after finding an item id like to keep, saveing the game doesnt interrupt the game at all. Atleast for me with the game on a SSD might be different on HDDs. It never ever happened to me to corrupt a savefile. Even if you fear corruption its easy to create a backup every now and then.
TL:DR Sacred 2 is a good arpg with alot weighting on hack n slash. The story would be better off missing completely than this sorry attempt. Its still a good Sacred and its fun to build and play diverse characters. I can definitively recommend it to somewhat openminded Sacred fans. If you want it to be a Sacred clone with better graphics you are bound to be dissappointed.

Shovel Knight is a shining example of retro-style games done right. It does something that a lot of these pixel art "hey remember the NES?" indie games fail to do - balances nostalgia with new. Shovel Knight goes beyond replicating the past and instead keeps the parts of those games that were fun and throws away anything that wasn't.
When it comes to platformers, there are three things that totally made sense back in the day that have become obsolete: lives, time limits and high scores. All of these things were nessesary back in acarde days, because even console games usually had an acarde version. In order to keep you putting coins in, they had to make sure you could only try so many times before putting in another quater. This is why we have lives. But what's to stop you from putting a quater in and messing around, never winning but never dying, and hogging the machine? That's where time limits come in. And to top it all off, high scores would give the game a competitive edge, so even when you "beat" the game you;d have a motivation to keep playing, and by extention keeping pumping your allowence into the acarde machine. In an acarde, these things not only make sense, but are nearly crucial to having a functioning and sucsessful acarde game.
Skip to the modern day, where many indie desingers are trying to recreate the clasic 8-bit platformer experience, but often times don't see around these inherit flaws. Those things that made acarde games work now only hinder a fun game experience, but for the sake of nostalgia they often tims make their way into games anyway.
Shovel Knight is different. This game focuses on what made those games so great - tricky platforming, exciting combat, challenging bosses, and just enough story to justify everything - and does away with naything that doesn't add to that core experience. Instead of a life system, this game uses a checkpoint system similar to that of Dark Souls. If you die, you go back to your last checkpoint, but lose some money - but if you can get back to that spot and pick it up without dying again, you can get that lost money back. It's a very clever system that isn't too punishing but does have consequences. No time limits or high scrore, either.
This understanding of what isn't nessesary anymore is just the first of many reasons Shovel Knight is a fantastic game. It has incredible pixel art, tight controls, fun and challenges levels complete with awesome bosses, a few hidden collectables to find (not too many that it becomes overwhelming, but enough that secrets are plentful and fun to discover), unlockable abilities/buyable upgrades, lovable characters and a simple story that is compelling but doesn't take too much screen time. This game has no filler content. Its 100% fun platforming action. This game is so solid you'll forget it's a "retro game" because this game is so much more than a nostalgia trip. This is a game that loves retro but understands times have changed, keeping only what still works and ditching the rest, making for an extremly tight, no time wasted, focused action platforming adventure like no other. Highly recomended to all gamers.

Well now here's a lovely indie gem we dug up from the ground.
Right, pack the puns in. Game's better than one of the lowest forms of wit. Essentially, we've got us here a cute mixture of old NES classics as a game. Little bit of Castlevania, little bit of Metroid, a bunch of Zelda II, and a smattering of well written story and humour.
Storywise, the game has you play as the titular Shovel Knight, an honourable and great warrior who, with his love/companion Shield Knight, defeated many enemies and brought peace to the land. Then, Shield Knight gets captured by what is essentially darkness itself. Oh buggery. So Shovel Knight's gotta go rescue her.
Which brings us to gameplay; bit of a high octane platformer, the player controls Shovel Knight through Metroid-style levels, requiring the use of simplistic and excellently designed smooth movement as well as an armoury of tools, toys and trinkets to get you through the level. Each item you find has specific purposes, and all are necessary for victory, giving the player slow growth through the game along with a natural progression for both exploration and action.
Combat's very Zelda II: you can slash left and right, smack stuff with shovel bouncing by aiming downwards, so on and so forth. Controls are simple and well done; wasd to move, J to attack, K to jump. E opens your inventory, which lets you change your items and usage thereof even mid boss fight, extremely enjoyable.
The game is harsh but fair, and has a rather fun Dark Souls-like mechanic where when you die, you can recollect lost gold if you pick it up before dying again. Which yes, the game has gold/money, and yes it matters very much. Items are expensive, and upgrades can be quite difficult to acquire if you die often.
A simple game, excellently designed and presented, beautifully programmed, surprisingly inventive music and art, and a game that I've replayed several times through just to enjoy it again. Worth the purchase, get it full price.

Valve's flat organization has made it so that the TF2's team is tiny, and it honestly feels like they have lost their passion. Valve is like that depressed kid with zero motivation that's sitting on a gold nest.
Scout's scattergun can't hit for♥♥♥♥♥♥ If your aim isn't 100% perfect, you're not going to hit. The Scout's mobility is great, but when a Sniper can headshot you after you triple jumped with the Atomizer from halfway across the map, it's pointless.
Soldier's just slow, doesn't deal enough damage, his projectiles can easily be deflected by Pyros, and everything just falls apart. Rocket jumping is a skill that isn't worth it when it takes health off you, making you even easier to kill. Equipping the Liberty Launcher and the Gunboats makes rocket jumping actually viable, but then you consider the fact that fall damage is a thing too, so that's out of the window.
Pyro is just too OP. The fact that the Phlog's afterburn can build up its own charge is the epitome of bad design. Its lack of airblast is almost not a downside when the airblast is so hard to get down in the first place. The very fact that ranges aren't very clear when you're playing as Pyro just makes it so much worse. Why can't the flames also be colour-coded so you know which team the Pyro is on at all times? But no, that'd require effort, and Valve doesn't know what that means anymore.
There is no class I hate more than the Demoman. I hate playing as him, I hate playing against him. Sticky spamming is the worst thing and is absurdly overpowered. The pills deal 100 damage on direct hit, which would be fine if there were fewer of them. There are never fewer of them. The fact that they deal an absurd amount of splash damage just makes it worse.
The Heavy is the class I played the most, and literally the only reason I like playing as him so much is because there is no reloading. The reloading in the game takes ages, and while I understand that you have to get the rhythm down, it's still a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ The fact that he can't hold down a button while running to spin up the minigun is absurd, but I understand why. However, when you have 300 health, have the Fists of Steel out, and can still die to a Tomislav Heavy in less than 2 seconds, you know health doesn't matter in the game, and you might as well just always have 1 health for all the fat load of good that does you.
The Engineer is both a good class and a bad class. His buildings are absurdly easy to destroy. Do you like dying to good spies - which every spy on the enemy team is? Then pick Engineer. Do you like your buildings being constantly sapped and shot at and destroyed and die all the time? Then play Engineer.
As the Medic, you die all the time. All the time. Taking cover doesn't matter when Scouts with the Back Scatter come up to you and with one pull of the trigger kill you. Staying behind the Heavy doesn't matter when he goes left and you go right for only a couple of pixels and your head gets popped by a Sniper. Doesn't matter even if you stay behind your heal target perfectly, a Demoman will still get you with his grenades and/or sticky spam.
Do you like missing? Do you like dying? Do you like being useless to the team? Pick Sniper. I have no other words left for him. He's useless to me because the hitboxes are so specific. Your aim can't be anything but one hundred percent accurate, otherwise you're dead. Not because you're actually seeing the respawn time, but because you're useless.
Do you like dying? Do you like not being able to backstab because the hitboxes are horribly specific? Do you like Razorback Snipers and Jag Engineers that are sitting on their dispensers? Do you like perfectly perceptive enemy teams? Pick the Spy and go to hell.
It doesn't help that so few maps are actually good, and even the ones that are good become terrible when your team is just bad. Dustbowl is likely infamous, but I enjoy it well enough. However, there is one exception, one singular thing that ruins it for me, and that's the first part of the third stage of Dustbowl. It's nothing but RED Übered Phlogistinator Pyros. And it would be so easy to fix by just having a no-entry sign in those three entrances in the bunker. But no, that requires a smidgen of effort, and Valve doesn't give a flying ♥♥♥♥ anymore.
Am I being salty from losing so much? Undoubtedly. Are my criticisms invalid because of it? Maybe. Is what I'm saying what I really feel? Absolutely.
Dying is the same as failing. If you lost, that means you shouldn't have even tried.
Bonus points, at least disconnecting in Casual carries no penalties.

I'm not sure I'd want to pay full price, but I got this on sale, and I'm really enjoying it. I got it more because I liked Naruto than because I particularly love fighting games, but I find the game mechanics engaging and fun. It seems to me that, with the recharge mechanics for various actions, combat has a light tactical feel. For me, this is a plus; I don't especially enjoy games that value twitch reflexes over all else. (...My favorite games ever were Medieval Totar War and Heroes 3).
I find the game very nice looking, the colors and designs more vibrant and interesting than in the anime itself. In ~13 hours I've had two crashes, both in a row, and no other stability problems. In a few cut scenes I've noticed visual stutters, but that's about it for technical complaints.
I do have two larger gripes:
(1) The variety of characters is undercut by the fact that some of them are very similar. E.g. There are at least four different narutos -- not Naruto costumes, but Naruto characters, and I think a comparable number of Gaaras. It's really not that I find the variety of characters bad, just that the claim to 100 playable characters doesn't mean as much as it might seem. That said, I do enjoy that it's not super complicated unlocking new characters; you can get most by playing any mode.
(2) I wish there were a tutorial and/or a more detailed game manual. There are some modes/mechanics that I still haven't managed to figure out by playing, and I wish there were a text searchable pdf where I could read about them.

1st July, 1863. 9:48 am. Having encountered forward elements of Lee's Confederate Army, my Colonel deployed his skirmishing units to blunt the forward movement of the enemy thus giving the "Iron Brigade" and the other line units of I Corp time to come up. The enemy countered with a sledgehammer style assault on the weak points in the skirmishing line driving back Devin's and Gamble's units to McPherson Ridge. I ordered my cannon to fall farther back to give them time to set up again. We can hear the pipers of the "Iron Brigade" and are well aware of their stature on the battlefield. The enemy is surely aware of this as well, and I think they can expect a hot welcome of fire and shot when they arrive.  My Colonel has trained his cavalry well but has reservations about the quality of the commanders he has been given. However our Detached infantry units have performed admirably in their mission of delaying the enemy's advance.
10:13 am. Davis' brigade has suffered terribly as they tried to cross the valley floor and the enemy center is considerably weakened. Our line held at McPherson's Ridge only because Pettigrew and Heth's Skirmishers elected to take the comparatively  minor Oak Hill. The "Iron Brigade" has arrived and is busy in the south pushing Brockenbrough back towards the Confederates gun positions. As General Buford seems to have things in hand in the north, especially with the arrival of the remainder of I Corp the General has decided to push the right end of the line north, in an effort to accurately gauge the strength of Pettigrews brigade. Our cavalry has done some very good scouting and we are fairly confident of the locations of the artillery and hope to move on them soon. Orders from the Colonel are to leave our guns on Oak Ridge as a deterrent to Pettigrew and the light forces with him. We should be getting artillery reinforcements at any time now, and several more Brigades.
10:38 The Rebs have regrouped and have forced the light units off McPherson Ridge. The General has pulled all the units back to Oak Ridge, there to wait until Cutler and the others are able to come up. There was bloody and savage fighting by the light units in the valley as they screened the other Brigades repositioning, but they have taken minimal losses and are still a bright beacon of Valour for the rest of the Army. The General plans to visit those men tonight.
11:00 am. Our enemy has nothing more to throw into this fight and we are slowly but surely pushing him back. The Iron Brigade has done the impossible and taken Herr Ridge from the weakened and demoralised Rebs. The damned cannon continue to harass us though as it was deemed more important to take the strong point at Herr Ridge and deny the enemy a vital point of contact with the main body.
11:45 am The fighting has been horrendous at the bridge near Spanglers farm but Baxter and Paul have inflicted a serious bloodletting on the enemies III Corp, driving them back and killing them mercilessly. The "Iron Brigade'" occupation of  Herr Ridge seems to have thrown the enemy into confusion and forced Heth, and Pettigrew to move off Oak Hill, which now has our scouts on it, observing the enemies movements. The General has begun telling his subordinates to push the Rebs hard and give them no respite. If we can trap them in the valley we can inflict awful casualties on them in that dead ground.
Would I recommend this game? HELLZ YA! A good replacement for Meyer's Gettysburg. However, it is not that game, so try to give it a shot on its own merits. There are some things wrong with it. For example. Why on the next phase of the battle does the computer move my units from where they were on the previous map? After I had carefully positoned them for maximum effect. AND in some undesirable locations.  The map is hard to get used to but with patience it can be read. I thoroughly enjoyed my first couple of tries. I  still like the random General selector button. Haven't used anything else really. Got my @SS handed to me a few times before I got the hang of it. I like that you can save at any time. SAVE OFTEN!!! The controls are easy to use after you get the hang of them, and the tutorial video set up is a great initial learning tool.  Nice Work DarthMod and Team. RECOMMENDED for gamers. But gonna downgrade this from a 8.0/10 to a 7.5/10

So far this game is pretty great considering it is still early access.
I haven't personally had any bugs or game crashes.  Game loads very quickly as well as the world generation or world loading as you move around.
At the time of writing this I'm 14 hours in and still haven't reached mid game.  I would guess even at the early access level of development there is at least 60 hours of entertainment to be found.
If you're a fan of minecraft you might like this game, if you're a fan of factorio or crafting / automating style of games you'll really enjoy it.
The only negatives at the moment I have is that there is no real threat in surivial mode death just spawns you back to your base, and mobs have not been added yet, but again, still in development and the games current status works well.  Also the progression to being able to do anything efficiently besides manual filling/unloading miners, hoppers, etc. is a little much.  I ended my last game session to finally being able to build my 2nd smelter, which is a bottle neck that limits progression more so then having a consistant progression of acomplishments.  But as i've said several times it is in beta so I'm sure as more mid game and end game things are added smelters will be more available early on.

Overall the game is great and quite entertaining.  $9 bucks for what I expect to be 30+ hours minimium of enjoyment is better then any cost to entertainment ratio I expect from most AAA games.  And once they start doing more patches I'm sure I'll get even more enjoyment out of it.

I loved parts of this game. The parts that were good were extremely good. The parts that were bad stuck out like a sore thumb. The story was amazing, characters were interesting, and the environment was ridiculously beautiful (as beautiful as a post apocolyptic world can be). This game had everything going for it. Weapon upgrades evenly spaced out giving you enough time to play around with them all without getting bored. I loved the sidequest that had me gather tokens from every zone, giving me rewards for each one i collected. This was the first game I used every single power up because they were ALL useful and beneficial. This is by far one of my personal favorite games I own.
Onto the bad. One thing that frustrated me most is that the Achievements for this game can and will glitch out. I cant even remember how many times i would find all the collectables and realize the game FORGOT to award the achievement and thus result in me having to RESTART THE GAME in order to get it all over again. This is only an issue if you care about achievements, this does not hinder gameplay in any way. The second thing I can complain about is the lack of replayability value to this game. Once you defeat the bosses and aquire the collectables, there is no reason to go back, and the enemies get replaced with weaker ones, making the zone a joke to clear. If this game let me restart with my currencies after i beat it, that would make it much more fun and give me that reason to play it again. But as it stands, once you obtain the collectables and beat the bosses, there isnt much of a reason to continue playing.
In conclusion, this game offered me a great experience while progressing through the story. Problems arose as you start entering your last quarter of the game where there becomes less and less to do. It's great that you aquired all 10 pieces of your abyssal armor set, to bad there isnt much to do in the game by the time you get it other than defeat the final boss with it or use it while obtaining the last few collectables.
8/10 if i were to rate this game. It's great but could've been better with just a few additions.
EDIT: apparently you can create a new game after you beat the last boss and start with the abyssal armor if you collected all the pieces in your first playthrough. This is vary nice and does add some replayability.
