Wow, this game really challenged me.  I love the Total War series to death, but there are some things that I get out of this game that those could never really achieve.  First off, one of the things I love the most/the bane of my existence, complex moral.  Once a unit is broken, you can almost guarantee it will come back, which really makes it more viable to move your army around, take advantage of situations and also it keeps some units really tied up keeping an eye on the routers.  It’s really interesting to see the men slowly start trickling back and then everyone run for it.  It adds quite the element to the battle.
Secondly, I like that the battle is broken down into phases, or days, and that unit sizes and locations (to an extent) carry over day to day.  It’s good to have the map move around like that and between fights I like balancing my options of what my next step should be.  Press my advantage now?  Or wait until tomorrow when I am re-supplied and re-enforced?  It can turn the tide of the battle.
I enjoy the fact that both sides are not equal and have their own strengths and weaknesses as well, and that this even works its way down into single units having differences as well.  It makes planning your strategy and setup much more interesting.  This combined with being able to set the AI's difficulty and tendencies is a killer combination.
Unit placement can be tricky however, and I would like to be able to see the space my regiment will be occupying with perhaps a hotkey of some kind, and a more cohesive grouping ability would be nice as well.  Sometimes I noticed some units move about on their own, even if they aren’t routing, and I understand this to an extent, but it could be dialed back a tad, it creates more micro-management and can leave holes in your line when a regiment gets excited and charges around for no reason.  Also, I get that high ground provides an advantage, but some more environmental effects would be nice as well.    Aside from unit placement, I think I’m just nit-picking.
Overall, I really like the game, I’ve had some intense fights, like the Union holding cemetery in the last quarter of the battle, and me desperately charging them where you could almost hear “I wish I was in Dixie” playing in the background as I captured the hill.  Keeping in mind the game is early access I give it 7.5/10, but I expect on full release this will get bumped up by 1/1.5 points or so.  To anyone who enjoys strategy, this is a fun, cheap game that has already given me hours of fun.  I recommend it strongly.

I went in with moderate expectations due to the number of good reviews for this game, but left extremely disappointed. No, I did not complete the game, but I played for a lot longer than I would have if it weren't for the reviews. A game shouldn't have to take an hour to get good. If you are only 10-15 mins in, and you've already noticed several issues, and are already frustrated, the game is bad and needs fixed. I stopped playing after the game got stuck in the shop menu, and I wasn't able to back out, sell, or buy.
I can't speak to the concept much because I quit only so far into the game. The tiling was better than some titles, but was also very lacking and just downright confusing in places. Some female NPCs appeared to be glowing, and I am guessing that was not the intention. Plus, given the inability to sprint anywhere in-game, the tightly packed spaces become very tedious to move through. The music is rather bland, and was poorly trimmed, so when it loops back to the start it is very noticable.
The combat system seems fresh, at least comparitively, at first, but then I noticed all the issues with it. Enemies get priority, and can move even if you haven't and are able. When it is your turn to attack, the battle continues while you select your move; enemies can hack away at you while you consider your attack, or fumble around the slow battle menus. The speed system would be nice if it made a difference, but it doesn't and only leads to you wanting to spam enter. Damage dealt is on a very low-luck roll system, where using skills you often do less damage than a normal attack. Enemy battlers all look like they are from different projects and scaled differently; I would think goblins would be at least noticably larger than mushrooms and slimes. In battle, you can accidentally choose to do nothing by either canceling when your move comes up, or by selecting the actor's name. Why is this a thing? Not to mention the obscenely high encounter rate, if you want to leave the forest, beach, or whatever area you're battling in, buckle up you've got a good number of fights you have to get through.

Darksiders is, without exception, the longest linear game I have completed. Without mucking about trying to 100% the secret items (including what I understand to be an entirely overpowered suit of armor), I completed the game in 20 hours. With no substantial exception, that twenty hours was spent navigating a series of single-branched corridors and single-solution puzzles that felt simultaneously inorganic and unfulfilling to navigate.
War is a hulking, grumpy nephilim who fancies oversized armor and weapons, action-film dialogue, and violence as the answer to every problem. Which is all of it perfectly fine- the game has an aesthetic which kept me playing along despite its derth of challenge or mechanical variety (not to mention the unfortunate amount of retreading that must be done as part of normal gameplay).
But if you are not sustained by the aesthetic- and I only completed the game out of a combined masochistic streak and desire to learn more about bad video game design- Darksiders will quickly lose your attention, as War's repetoire of attack skills is limited to attacking, countering, dodging, and little else, with the vast majority consisting of mashing the X button until the enemy has either died from damage or can be executed by a special move that never varies and often takes substantially longer to perform than a death by damage would.
The puzzles are generally straightforward and are less jigsaws and more mazes with a handful of steps that must be completed in a precise order before the player can proceed. Very rarely do these prove taxing intellectually, but they are often taxing of one's patience, as the solution generally becomes obvious long before the player can realize it through a series of platforming obstacles and stiffly targetted bomb-throwing or shooting tasks.
The very BEST that Darksiders has to offer is in its boss fights, several of which force the player to quickly analyze the arena and boss itself to determine the method by which the boss can be defeated (there is generally only one method). Some of these drag on with the shear number of blows that the bosses sustain before being defeated, with no change in difficulty during the repetition of the fight mechanics. The first and final bosses proved to be the most challenging and satisfying.
In sum, I can't recommend this game. There are a large number of superior games of this genre, mechanically and in terms of story, and $20 will go much farther with them.

Cons:
This game randomly hard-locks my computer. This happens with no other program and I have throughly tested my memory.
The menu does not pause the game, so you can die from adjusting settings (especially in the first 5 hours in a world).
You're in constant peril of death for the first several hours of the game and after patiently strategeicly attempting for almost 12 gameplay hours in a world, I just got to the point of crafting the first 2nd tier item. Survival is frustratingly slow.
You start with a single device to smelt ores, and to build another is a 3rd teir build and reportedly among the community takes roughly 30 hours of gameplay to get to. I have more than 20 hours and can still not yet survive going deep enough to *find* T3 resources.
Can very easily jump into a block and see through the level. There is even a four-click method to see through the world reliably at any time you want. Major game breaker.
Pros:
The mining is automated for the most part as you grow. Then the smelting becomes automated. Then the building.
Cool system, allows for huge top-end growth.
Really nice voxel graphics.
Summary:
The ore mining/energy/processing is a really cool idea, but this game has screwball glitches, partial graphics failures regularly, inventory failures often, and total system lockups on a healthy computer. Lets be honest, this is a minecraft clone, and not worth the money.

I'm going to preface this review with this short statement: I "recommend" this game because I think not recommending it is too harsh. Read on if that confuses you.
I've played a lot more Minecraft in my time than I'm prepared to discuss. There's a lot wrong with that game, and FortressCraft Evolved seems to be on the right path to fixing it. I've always found creative mode in Minecraft to be dull - for me, there needs to be the chance of failure/death, no matter how slight.  I've always hated the amount of time that goes to waste just trying to mine blocks in Survival, though, and FortressCraft has taken a great direction mixing the two. I don't really appreciate that the only way you can die is freezing to death... I know you can take some form of fall damage (with a really annoying screen effect), but I don't actually know if it can kill you. But! It's Early Access, and I can appreciate that these things take time.
A few suggestions I would make, assuming that the developer(s) read(s) this:
-Portable block identification. Some way to make it not a pain to go back to "home base" and have to identify things before you can use them. I get that it's unrealistic for Steve? the wandering hobo to magically know what iron ore looks like and how to use it, but it's willing suspension of disbelief. Honestly, I would more readily believe that a space-man on what was probably a mining ship has basic earth metals committed to memory.
-Make the particle effect for "home base" visible on low graphics (that is, if we really have to have home base to begin with). There was an interesting glitch when I first started up the game that made the ship just fly off into infinity instead of crashing to ground. Since I started the game on fastest graphics, the purple light particle never showed up... unless the ship legitimately never crashed and flew across the endless map. I reset that world anyway, so we may never know.
-The way chunks load is entertaining, but I feel like that has to be taking up CPU that could be used a bit more responsibly. I don't personally know enough about this to go in depth about it, just kind of suggesting that the animation be dropped in favor of chunks "popping" into existence.
In the end, the game is solid, and I really believe it has potential. It's not going to be the Minecraft killer, but that's alright, since Minecraft is enough of a danger to itself. There's plenty of bugs to iron out, but like I already said, these things take time. All I can really hope for is that these guys aren't the Terraria team in disguise, making a quick buck and running off, leaving an orphaned game that could be much more.

THOTH is an amazing, minimalist twin stick shooter that constantly kept surprising me all the way till the end of the main 64 levels (I haven't checked the other content yet).
I don't think I've ever played a twin stick shooter before (unless some of the minigames in other games count as one) so I was a little bit worried this game would be too hard for me. But THOTH offered me a fantastic learning curve, so I've constantly experienced a loop of beginner's luck followed by tough moments and then finally beating a set of four levels. I had to take a break several times but usually what I found is that returning to the game later / next day made me play better.
The mechanics of THOTH explore vast range of possibilities and each of them puts a unique twist on the gameplay style. The game constantly forced me to refine my approach to getting through the levels. My favourite moments came from trying to understand a new set of mechanics the first time I encountered them. There aren't any words in the game (except the name/logo) so you have to learn everything through playing the game and observing the behaviour of enemies.
One of the things that made THOTH intense experience for me were the sound effects and soundtrack. It managed to set a very unsettling, almost ominous mood.
To sum it up, I've enjoyed THOTH quite a lot thanks to its simple design, clever set of mechanics and awesome audio side. If you like challenging and elegant games, you should give it a try.

1. This is a game where you are a circle that shoots other shapes.
2. A friend of mine told me he once took so much LSD, all he could see was shapes and colors. I never really believed him but I suppose if you took said dose of LSD and played
, the end result would look a lot like
. The music also sounds like some sort self-inflicted cerebral chemical abnormality.
3. This is a twin stick shooter played w/ only the two sticks. You move w/ the left stick, shoot in whatever direction the right stick is pressed. You go a bit faster when you are not shooting. This works well--elegance, simplicity and all that. It can be a bit of a mind♥♥♥♥ when you are in tight situations somehow.
4. You will be in a lot of tight situations. This game plays fast.
5. You have to beat four levels in a row to advance, the fourth of which feels like something of a boss battle. This is extremely, extremely frustrating like you wouldn't believe. Some of the boss battles might take a dozen attempts to come up w/ a strategy and to get to them you have to play the three levels before them over and over.
6. and over and over and over and over and over...
7. Frustrating isn't
bad in this case. You fall into sort of a trance repeating the levels and you naturally start challenging yourself to find the fastest way to complete them.
8. The shapes you shoot at are 3D shapes that bounce around in 3D space but you only see them on a 2D plane. This adds a certain unpredictability but it seems to be deterministic; if you input the exact same controls, you will see the exact same behavior from the game. Most games would use random number generation for this sort of unpredictability but I like this better. It also makes this an interesting option for tool assisted speed runs if you are into that sort of thing.
9. As you shoot the shapes, they gradually turn into black space. If you incompletely convert them to black space, the shapes gradually return to their original color. If you completely convert them, they still exist and can still kill you but don't block your shots from hitting the other shapes. They also get a burst of speed. Between this and the fact that your little circle moves faster when you are not shooting, a surprisingly large amount of strategy emerges.
10.
does not wait to get hard. In fact, I can't really even think of another game that gets so hard so soon after starting. By the second level of the first set of four, you are already having to start to think in terms of strategy and not just adept movement.
11. Actually, it does not even really get all that much harder from that first set of levels. Or, in any case, the difficulty curve is really gradual. Again, it is surprising how much good strategy plays a roll beyond just twitchy stick. It is better to invest your mental energy into trying to learn the dynamics of each enemy type and level than it is to worry about your increasing your manual dexterity.
12. You still need manual dexterity in spades. Don't get me wrong. There is just a lot more to it than that.
13. This is a game that gives you a lot w/ very little. I think many people will complain that this looks and feels like it should be a browser game--not that there's anything wrong w/ that. This may well be true but I think investing some time to get into
's rhythm and seeing how it ticks reveals a level of attention to detail and craftsmanship that is seldom seen in any sort of game no matter the production values.

TL;DR: Minimalist shooter with try it until you win it design that makes dying to the 'boss' levels immensly frustrating.
Admittedly, I only played this game for fifteen minutes or so, but that fifteen minutes was enough to illicit enough frustration to make me never want to play it again. Its not that its 'hard', but it is designed to be a bit random, illogical, and force you to repeat 'tests' you've already passed.
Basically, each set of levels comes in 4s. The first level introduces a mechanic (dotted lines you can't pass, boxes that shoot boxes, etc), the second and third add kinks, the fourth is a boss. After each four levels, it saves. The problem is, if you die to the boss, and you will because the mechanic of each fight is different enough that your one shot will be gone rather quickly, you have to repeat all three previous levels. The levels themselves are short, a minute or two at most, but you never feel like you've 'solved' the levels. So even after you finish one four or five times, you might still die to it because of the randomness of the bounces of the squares. So its not 'play three levels, die to a boss, repeat', its 'play a level or two, die, try again, die to first level because of random bounce, die on level three again, die on level two again, get to boss again and die'. Usually to get a few tries at a boss, I had to play the same levels a dozen times or so.
This is the shooter equivelant of forcing you to replay an entire dungeon in an RPG after dying to the boss, or replaying a full level of an FPS because you died in the last quick time event. There are older games that do this, and it was unacceptable then. When the game has so little in it that this is one of the -key- and -only- mechanics besides 'twinstick shooter'. There are no power ups, no development besides different ways to kill you. And its ten dollars...
Play Geometry Wars, play Everyday Shooter. Almost any twinstick shooter has more to it, for better value, and with better design. Don't support awful, unnecessarily frustrating game mechanics just because 'too hard = good'.

Given Jeppe Carlsen's outstanding previous works (LIMBO and 140) THOTH doesn't make as big an impact as either of those games, but more than makes up for it with more replayability than the two of them combined.
THOTH is a top-down shooter that could be described as 'minimalist Geometry Wars' or 'like Asteroids but with levels' or many other variations of 'another game but... different' but that really doesn't do it justice. You can tell from the screenshots that THOTH is a pretty simple game, visually, with a few key differences from other games of its type.
Firstly, your targets don't disappear when you shoot them, they just turn black and start chasing you even faster. Also, you progress in the game by beating levels in batches of 4, which is a really good number to choose as beating levels one at a time would make the game far too easy, but beating them in any greater quantity would be a little too difficult. Every batch introduces a new gameplay mechanic, like blocks that shoot smaller blocks at you when you defeat them, or death-lines that alternate between, um, existing or not, depending on how many enemies you've taken care of, or snakes, or teleporting circles, or a veritable mountain of other obstacles. Another thing that's great about the batches of 4 is that it allows a new gameplay mechanic to be introduced, developed a few times, presented as a real challenge, and then the process repeats anew.
There's no shortage of challenges once finished; there's a co-op mode that you can play in single player - the co-op player becomes a very persistent homing predator once killed, so it's sort of like hard mode - or, as the name suggests, in co-op. Once you beat the game, you unlock a mode of 8 random-ish procedural levels, and then 16, and then 'Lava Mode' which is the game in 2 32-level chunks with no checkpoints in which the walls kill you on contact. No shortage of challenges and no shortage of challenge in the challenges.
If I had to pick one notable flaw, it's that while the game is incredibly replayable, it doesn't hold much replay value for less dedicated players. With the exception of the 8 randomly generated levels, all other post-game challenges are incredibly difficult. So if you're not really fussed about getting achievements that fewer than 1% of players have, there's not much reason to come back.
But I close with this - I did that 'Beat all 64 levels in co-op in one sitting by yourself' challenge, and after 4 hours when I finally finished with it, I was absolutely ecstatic. I didn't just cross it off the list and think 'Well thank God that's over', I was extremely overjoyed. And I wouldn't have been if I wasn't legitimately having a fair bit of fun for those 4 hours. THOTH is simple, very fun, and extremely challenging. It's a welcome addition to Jeppe's growing library of work.

I gave this a try during the free trial they had a while ago, and after stewing over the experience for a while, I can safely declare that I will not be buying it. I'm starved for a good RTS. Strategy games like that are an old love, and that's why I gave this a try. It has potential, but it just doesn't tick the right boxes for me.
First of all, the tutorial is extremely constrictive. It refuses to let you do anything but what they want you to do. This means that anything but basic controls has to be learned in the game proper.
Although there is a skirmish mode, it's only part of the game. The conquest mode is a series of skirmishes, where instead of one victory, you'll have a series of several, where wins and losses will determine your abilities for the major part of the game, and where I spent my time.
Right now, I can say that it's broken. The controls in Conquest Mode are unituitive, and I've spent at least two minutes trying to control one of my battle fleets. Fleets at the southern end of the galaxy risk being "out of bounds", which is my way of saying impossible to select. It didn't cost me the game, but it cost me a few minutes of game time.
Victory in the game is determined either by being the first to maintain 12 victory points, or by having the most victory points at the end. How to gain victory points is mostly randomized, but holding territories for extended time is a guarantee. Outside of that, holding specific territories, successfully destroying enemy fleets or palaces, or simply playing the right card will gain you a foothold.
And the cards are something that I like the theory of, but have one fatal flaw. They're supposed to provide tactical advantages, like speeding the development of a planet, or letting a fleet move again. All I ended up with were cards that reduced all player relations towards the rogues. Haven't the foggiest idea what that's supposed to be, but they just sat there, preventing me from getting a card that could have won the game.
Conquest Mode also determines what technologies you can use. At first, you're very limited in what you can deploy in a skirmish. But, as the turns go by, you can spend technology points on techs, which you then deploy in skirmishes. To keep this in check, you can't deploy them all on the first turn. You need an equal number of technology stations installed in your bases in order to call in or construct something of a specific technology era.
And finally, the skirmishes themselves. It's very unforgiving. All you have is Etherium, a currency that you use to buy reinforcements from your own faction (rather rude). Controlling more territories means more Etherium, and more stations to increase either the number of units you can deploy, the tech level you can use, or special commands to your fleet, such as orbital bombardment. Generally, someone who grabs territory early has the upper hand, just deploy turrets wherever they're needed. Although having a tech that the enemy just can't counter is a help (using Bombers when they enemy has no AA units, for example) in the end the fastest land grab will win.
Skirmish Mode also lacks a pause button, so you spend a lot of time flicking between your landing bays and the front line. If I want to reinforce a battle with, say, a mortar infantry unit, I have to go to my nearest airport, purchase the infantry, wait several seconds for them to arrive, and then assign them to an airship, wait several more seconds, and then order them to the battle, and finally air drop them into the battle. All this is time that I need to spend keeping an eye on the current battle, because at any moment, the enemy could start construction on a turret, call in an orbital bombardment, or sound a retreat that I want to fire my own bombardment on. Either allow me to queue up orders, or give me a pause button.
This is mostly just a massive rant, because there's something about this game that just brings out the worst in me. It isn't an RTS like I'm used to, and although it has potential, it certainly isn't something that I'm interested in paying for.

The size and scope of the land of Ancaria is truly impressive. None of the areas are randomly generated, and the entire map (not including the numerous subterranean dungeons littered here and there) spans over 22 square miles of real-world distance. In a nutshell: it's freaking huge. Navigation in the overworld is seamless, and load times during transitions to the underground are very brief. All of the terrain is packed with detail and different regions have their own unique climates, inhabitants, and land features. Also, the characters, monsters, and other elements look excellent.
Sacred 2: Fallen Angel screenshot
One of the downsides, which will likely be fixed with patches, is the game's general bugginess. There are times when the pop-up map disappeared completely, making it damn tedious to navigate. Sometimes clicking on people to speak with them had no effect whatsoever, and certain actions would yield sounds but no visual or gameplay effects. In one instance, a crucial item required to proceed in the main quest was not where it was supposed to be, making it impossible to proceed. Occasionally, the direction indicator that points to the next main object disappeared completely. Most of these issues were remedied by quitting and reloading the game, but they were a nuisance when they arose.
A hack-and-slash RPG quest of massive proportion, Sacred 2 caters to the throng of players who are anxiously awaiting the eventual release of Diablo III. PC gamers who've been salivating over the prospect of the next Diablo will undoubtedly seek temporary solace in the familiar gameplay found in Sacred 2 and be willing to turn a blind eye to the title's annoying bugs and occasionally repetitious play mechanics just to get their fix. Indeed, overlook the few minor irritating aspects of the game, and you'll find Sacred 2 to be surprisingly enjoyable.

Downloaded the game 5 days ago and I have spent hours playing this game. I have played every Civil War PC game that has ever come on the market and I think this game has a lot of potential to be the best one. There are only two recommendations so I am going to go with a "thumbs up" but if there was a "so-so" button I would press that. Again, this game has the potential to be the best and it looks like the makers of this game are constantly improving it.

Pros:

Ease of Gameplay/Movement I was able to start playing this game from the moment I downloaded it. There was little to no learning curve at all. They have made the controls so easy, a caveman could do it. Its very easy to move troops around and position them where you want them to be. No Limber & Unlimber Limbering and unlimbering your artillery makes for a more realistic gameplay. That is something artillery really had to do. However, when you're in the heat of battle and being overrun by a charge, its redundant and annoying to have to keep doing that to every artillery brigade. I forgot to do it sometimes in past games. This is a detail that I am glad they left out. The AI just does it for you. It still takes a little time for them to get going but you don't have to press a button for them to do it. Multiple Scenarios, Both Historical and What If This is something most Civil War games have but it seems like this one has more "what if" options available. I have been to Gettysburg twice and know the layout well. Never heard of Benner's Hill. So I got to learn something new. Accurate All of the names, Generals and locations are accurate to the letter. Impressive when you consider the developers are all from Eastern Europe. You can tell they spent hours doing their homework on even seemingly insignificant details. Even the farms are labeled by their proper game. Fun Gameplay...At Least Initially If I were to give the gameplay a fun rating from 1-10, I would give this one a 6. Despite some faults that I will point out in a minute that annoyed me as I got into it, this is an overall fun game to play, at least for the first couple hours.

Cons

Here are some things that I think definitely needs to be fixed for this game to be great. They were not apparent during the first few hours but as time went by, got really annoying. Confederate Army Has Obvious Advantage This is a complaint that some other players have said and after playing with both armies, I totally agree. The CSA has a distinct advantage over the Union. Background: Sorry if its long but I think it needs to be said. At the start of the war, the CSA had a distinct advantage in generals and quality of soldiers. Many of the generals had experience with the Mexican War 13+ years back and the men who made up southern army handling guns from the time they could walk. What's more, people from rural backgrounds will most likely be able to handle the rigors of long marches, lack of food, lack of adequate shelter and stress much better than their city counterparts. Having said that, as the war drew on, this advantage disappeared. For one, many of the best southern generals were killed and the northern soldiers were catching up. By the summer of 1863, the quality of soldiers from the Union was pretty close to their southern counterparts. The reason the Army of the Potomac was losing battles had nothing to do with its soldiers. From all accounts, the men who were present at Fredericksburg, 2nd Manassas and Chancellorsville were as brave as you can be. It was the successive appointments of unqualified and incapable Major Generals (many of whom got their position by their connections in Washington) that were responsible for blunder after blunder after blunder. Now...back the the game. The Confederate troops are unrealistically better than the Union. Its overblow to an obvious level that gets frustrating quickly. They can withstand the worst of situations (very low moral and condition) while the Union troops seem to run at the first volley that gets fired at them. Every charge done by the CSA ends in a route for them. Pressing "charge" for any Union unit is a complete waste of time b/c it never works. They always loose the melee. The Iron Brigade and Vincent's Brigade were not the only decent units at Gettysburg. Infinite Artillery There should be a limit to the amount of shells each artillery unit has. They either need to run out until the next battle or have to resupply. The only advantage the Union army has is its superior artillery. It seems to have more artillery most of the time and can be better concentrated because of the compact interior. You can really mass artillery units together to help make up for your poor quality troops. However, the amount of artillery available is also relevant to the battle. Some may call me nitpicking but this has a HUGE IMPACT on the battle. The CSA had enough cannons but couldn't resupply them as fast as the Union. This could never be more true than during Pickett's Charge. The whole plan of General Lee was to bombard the center into smithereens and then send 15,000 into a softened center. Problem is, they ran out of artillery ammo shortly before the charge started and couldn't support the army. While they were charging on the 3rd day, the Union shooting everything you can imagine into their ranks while their guns were silent. In essence, I'm saying that if you're going to make the Confederate soldiers so much better than the Union then you need to make the Union's artillery advantage equally better than the Confederate. As the game stands, the Union has a small advantage in this department but not enough. In this game the CSA wins the 3rd day with too much ease. The Union artillery doesn't do enough to break their ranks up and the Union soldiers crack. When I'm doing Pickett's Charge as the CSA, I can put the troops on autopilot. I told every brigade to charge towards the center and won with ease. Main reason: the Unions primary advantage on this day is high mitigated. Note: I know the 3rd day is hard to replicate because no Gettysburg game has gotten it right. Sid Meier's....same thing. The artillery of the Union, as programmed, can't do enough damage and their soldiers can be easy overwhelmed. Seminary Ridge Needs To Be Further From Cemetery Hill They are way too close. They need to be distanced. One of the reasons why the 3rd day is so unrealistic is because they CSA seems to only have to charge a couple feet to get to the center line. This make the 2nd con I just mentioned more pronounced because the the Union gets a 1-3 good shoots before the Confederates are upon them. Calvery It seems awfully easy for Stuart's cavalry to to flank me from behind on the 3rd day. Custer's men don't put up much of a fight (even though they win a battle one day later) and the southern cavalry easily charges through massed volleys. I find myself having to divert an insane number of men and artillery to keep him at bay. No matter what his casualties are when I do this, he regroups after a couple minutes and charges at me again. Unrealistic! Harass. Maybe. Attack supply lines. Yes. Disrupt. Yes. Maybe I'm wrong but I never remember horse cavalry attacking the main army in massed formation like that. Bufford could be used to counter my argument but he was doing more a delaying action that anything and they were dismounted.

This game does a lot of things right. The combat is fun and does not rely too heavily on button mashing. The dodge There is a degree of skill needed to take down more powerful enemies without getting repeatedly killed or losing all of your health after one fight. The story isn't the most captivating, but it properly sets the tone and applies context to all of the action. Lastly, the art and design for this game are also excellent, evoking the fantasy of this realm. All of these factors should have combined to make a great game, but the frustrating puzzles are holding this game back.
The puzzles in this game are annoying for two reasons: they frequently involve backtracking through old areas rather than exploring new areas, and they ruin the action oriented pacing of the game. I try to avoid the Zelda comparison when talking about this game, but I can't help feel that Zelda is infinitely better at what this game is trying to do; particularly when it comes to blending the combat and puzzles. In Zelda, the combat is low-key, slow-paced and requires more decisive and timed hits (like a puzzle itself), so the puzzles keep the pace going evenly. This is different from the action heavy button-mash beatdown of Darksiders. There is nothing wrong with button-mash beatdown as a gameplay mechanic, but when I'm forced to take it slow and do a tiresome puzzle, what should be a healthy challenge becomes a tedious roadblock in my fun.
Writing this review made me sad because this game has a boatload of potential that was crippled by obnoxious puzzles. I don't recommend this game because the puzzles were more frustrating than the game was fun. If looking up a walkthrough isn't an assault on your pride then go ahead and get Darksiders, however there are not a lot of good ones for this game. As a closing note, I can't recommend this game, but parts of it were enjoyable enough for me to wonder if the sequel is better.

This game, is hands down, one of the most fun games i've played in awhile.
So, lets get to the nitty gritty. This game doesn't come with a pre-game tutorial, long explanations about what each coins ability and how to "build your deck", or explanation about the world. You've given a very short intro and then thrown into the world of Coin Crypt. My initial reaction while watching my friend play was, "Wow, this is stupid." But, after trying it out myself, I became addicted really, really fast. And, after playing through and (finally) beating the game, I have to say that this is going to be a long time favorite of mine.
The Good:
+Simple- It's so, so simple to start playing this game. Don't get it, don't worry, you will. It doesn't take long to pick up and the interface, level design, combat system and everything else is very straight forward.
+Engrossing- This little game sucks you in reallllly quick. Before you know it, you've unlocked 8 new characters and half the day is gone. And all of the hidden treasure boxes, secret tunnels, hidden bosses and fun twists keeps the game interesting.
+Controller Friendly!- Just plug in your xbox controller (or logitech/other) and get playing. Was really nice to play from the couch.
+Replayability- I don't feel like i'm trying to complete the same task over and over again with each retry. The levels present (usually) the same creeps, but there is a bit of randomization that goes on so you're not stuck having to hit the same wall over and over again.
The Bad:
-In-Game Options/Menu: So, if you want to change from fullscreen to windowed, you have to do it at "options book" in the beginning island. You can't just hit start/esc and change something on the fly. I found this really, really, really inconvienent. It's quirky, sure, but the design is poor.
-No pause during combat: Ok, I get not wanting to add a pause option since you could just keep pausing to think through you next move, but when you need to leave to go do something and you die since you can't pause, that's just bad.
-Music: The music is actually pretty decent, but the settings for it aren't. Even on the lowest setting, its pretty loud. When I was voip, I could barely hear anything outside of the games music. So, sadly, I ended up just turning it off.
Overall: 8/10

This game suffers from a very unfortunate amount of random errors, bugs and memory leaks most of which can't be fixed at all. Even though there are countles forum posts and youtube videos claiming they have a way of fixing random crashes - none of the "fixes" actually work on a x64 system (which is pretty much any PC that's not 10+ years old).
And even if you're lucky not to bump into any major crashes (some people can't even start the game) - there's always the core bug that makes the game crash 100% when it reaches aprox 1,3-1,5 Gb of RAM. It's the way the game is coded and if running on a x64 system it WILL crash due to the way it handles RAM allocation for game assets. There is no way around it.
At one point there was even a "4gb ram" fix which just breaks the .exe file nowadays so even that's not an option any more.
It's so sad since the game looks brilliantly, feels epic and the maps are HUGE and insanely detailed with amazing eyecandy effects.
So - if you're planing on playing Sacred 2 - get a x86 OS, preferably WinXP/7 because apart from crashes and mashing your head against the table - you won't have much fun :(

Best review would be a lengthy description, imo. Coin Crypt is roguelike top-down RPG w/ real-time card-based combat, and an on-map encounter system for enemies (touching an enemy in the "overworld" triggers combat). The way the card game system is done is far different from anything else I've ever come across. I suppose it would make the most sense to start by explaining how the real-time part works.
When you play a card, your character removes it from your hand, and starts to
it, during which time you cannot do anything else. Casting basically presents as a windup timer showing how long that particular played card needs until it is put into effect. When it comes down to it, casting is what really ties the combat together, and makes the real-time part viable. Cards cast quick enough to keep the feeling of real-time –combat feels like a
string of actions–, but also slow enough so you have time to think during an opponent's cast –effectively preventing it from coming down to a battle of luck and who clicks quickest. The best comparison I can give of how it
would be to say when casting is at it's very worst the combat's flow slows the same way it might when reloading your gun in an FPS, and when casting is normal I'd say combat flow is more akin to chess utilizing a stop clock –you feel pressure to be quick, but there's enough time to be deliberate, and overall strategy/planning definitely feels like the main focus and factor in winning.

However, casting is far from being the only uncommon part of the card system. That said, every unique mechanic seems to be carefully designed with each of the others in mind, chief of which are the roles cards themselves play. Cards are essentially
Not only are cards the combat medium, but cards are the loot, cards are the passive effect carriers, some cards are one-use skeleton keys, cards remaining in your deck is a secondary health bar, and –most importantly–
are currency. In line with this duel nature, used cards are not given back after battle (they are dropped when you play them), forcing you to choose a little more literally, and much more carefully,
Using cards to buy useful items and influence the island gods needs to be balanced with keeping a large enough and carefully built enough deck so you don't run out of cards. On top of this, you are forced to take only a few out of a small group of coins chest ghosts offer when you're looting a chest, so it can often be a tough choice deciding how many of the weak/low-value cards of the type you're low on (for example Heal 2 worth $5) you should take versus how many of the average/mid-value coin (like Attack 4).
Building around that duality, a lot of the other mechanics are designed in order to make deliberate, personalized deck construction and management the backbone of the game. This is also why the card game mechanics have to be so unorthodox compared to most card games. Your hand size is only 3 cards (by default), your health is only 10 (by default), and when you play a card you also draw a fresh hand. Additionally, all drawn hands will organize any duplicate cards into stacks (stacks if played will cast all the cards in that stack at once as a single cast). Having a small hand and possible stacks means trying to prevent cards that don't help your build from accumulating in your deck and not taking care not to be too prone to finding yourself choosing between using two Attack 4 cards (or w/e) on a 2/10 health monster, or letting their cast finish while you redraw and taking 4 damage.
Beyond that, it forces you to create a deliberate style of deck-build & corresponding combat style by making "use the most overpowered coins you can find" type strategy almost useless. Using lots of Steal an enemy card type cards depletes their deck to win, and so physical damage is a waste to have in your deck (most of the time), and a wasted turn could easily mean losing 40% of your health. Poison damage builds rely on overwhelming the opponent more than they can heal while trying to stay guarded, so passive cards –which usually also have a draws often effect– would (normally) get in the way of that. The thing is, there are ways to combine these kinds of cards into a useful deck, but they don't play well together if you just throw them together. Having a lot of damage cards and a few Steal cards can be useful for shield card focused enemies because you can deplete their shields quicker by just taking them (a lot of the time) than letting them keep playing them as you attack over and over, and you can augment this balance to withstand other types of enemies by having most of your deck comprised of shields in case of a bad draw, as shield health and shield time-remaining carry over between battles, so it's not nearly as much of a risk if you don't get the card type you needed. Decks have a lot of depth, esp. depending on your play style, yet coins themselves are often very straightforward.
There are 201 unique cards in the game so far, and there are tons of items, passive-power cards, blessings, and other things that all modify your stats or mechanics, often in classic RPG fashion. Using items or modifiers in tandem with particular deck builds, strategy complexity can potentially be increased to much, much further depths depending on the chosen play style. Ex. the Joker Token card with the coin pouch. When played, anything that damages the user now heals them, and anything that heals the user now damages them. Two of the status will reverse healing and damage back to normal. A coin pouch lets you store a coin from your current hand for use at any point/battle in place of one of the coins you drew. Using the saved coin also draws a new hand, and clears the quickslot. The Joker Token is one of the best coins to put in it. It can save the player from the brink of death and allow them to survive very powerful attacks, such as the Explosion Chip (Attack 20) used by the "Grandma" enemy. Furthermore, donations to gods lets up two of them bless chests and add several of their card class to your options to pick from, allowing you to more easily tune your deck to a particular play style. The more you donate, the more likely to be rarer cards of that god's type.
In addition to all of
modifiers, every one of the characters (except for the starter) have more major, unique modifiers of their own, making the game play differently for each character. For example when playing as Demon: whenever the enemy plays a card, one cursed card (that does damage to your player if cast) is added to their deck, but demon also makes all card currency values negative (so cursed coins become positive currency). Basically Demon doesn’t have to buy items or get blessings using the useful cards in his deck, and constantly makes good amounts of money from battle spoils –but the more money you save up the more chance of drawing a hand polluted with harmful cards, and you need to choose between ending battles quickly to take more of the enemy’s original cards (you [default] take 100% of their unplayed cards), or stalling to grind for cash.
Other characters have more simplistic modifiers, like Monkey: he casts more slowly than other characters, but redraws his hand at quadruple speed and always casts all of the cards in his hand. So, In order to do well as Monkey, the player must learn the effects of all the coins they carry, and be a little more frugal to make up for occasional unnecessary card casting caused by his unique traits.
All of this makes for a tight combat system with tons and tons of styles of play, and giving it an immense amount of replay value, all while remaining very intuitive and fast paced. 11/10 would build a deck again –and again –and again.

I enjoy platformers; retro platformers to be specific...  Megaman 2, Super Mario World, Donkey Kong Country and so on.  I'm sure alot of people agree with me.  But why?  Why are retro platformers considered the best?  Is it the simple yet addictive gameplay?  The music?  the innovation for the time?  The nostalgia?  I tend to believe it's all of those things and it's something most modern platformers aren't getting right...  But, in 2014, came Shovel Knight!  A modern platformer in the style of 80s retro games!  It takes everything we know and love from our favourites and blends it into something new.  On top of that, it leaves out all of the flaws from those games as well!  It's like throwing:  Mario 3's world map, Megaman's robot master system, Ducktales' cane thrust and all sorts of other cool mechanics into one.  With the addition of Plague of Shadows and Specter of Torment, the game is now ten times better!  It's the same game with a twist on the gameplay and story, enough to make you wanna replay the game time and time again.  Now, that's exactly why I love Shovel Knight so much; it's all my favourite retro games in one great homage to the golden age of platformers!

This game looks and sounds like it could literally be a Gameboy game. The sights and sounds are excellent, and it has a nice aesthetic. Also, unlike that awful Odallus game, the controls are pretty good despite their simplicity and the game being retro.
There goes the last of anything good I have to say about this game, pretty much. The entire game consists of popping bubbles that bounce, dodging the bubbles, and picking up coins and items for points. You are in a room, and it appears you remain in the same room for the entire game. You do get switched to running on a different wall of the room occasionally. Yep. Oh, and you can play for a higher score on some mode that costs you the in-game currency to play. All you get are double points in that mode, but you have one SIXTH of the health you have in normal mode.
If you die, you start the whole game over. Normally I would gripe more, such as in rogue-likes, because you don't get to progress and beat the game, but in this one, you just keep playing and getting more points. The only people I could see this game appealing to are braggarts who want to try to compete with others for high scores, and people who just want to kill time and have a nostalgic aesthetic while doing so. I really do mean "kill time," though. The game isn't very engaging, and the only persistent stuff are unlockable skins, characters, and music, though the costs are higher than I'm willing to wait to accrue, so I didn't bother unlocking the stuff.
It's not an awful game. It's just a very sparse game; so sparse that far more games that cost $5 at the current non-sale price are filled with so much more content than this one, and more fun as well. I can't recommend it.

I received this game from a friend, as he had a code and did not want the game; I decided to try it.
I'm giving Pirate Pop Plus a "not recommended" review because, for the apparent $5 price tag, what it has to offer pales in comparison to cheaper games of its caliber. The gameplay is extremely simple; you move and fire a hook upwards, which pops a bubble into smaller bubbles. You can only fire one hook at a time, which means you need to place your shots well, which would be much easier if it didn't feel like the character was sliding on ice. When you pop a bubble, the bubble splits into smaller bubbles, and when you pop
bubbles, they split into even smaller bubbles that do a fine job of blending into the background thanks to the limited color-palette and pixel art, making them hard to see and easy to lose health to.
The only incentive to keep playing the game are the unlockables, which include 3 other playable characters with different stats, as well as a vast plethora of aesthetics including the BGM, the color palette used in-game, and the colors of the virtual 'gamepad' you're playing on. All of these cost a certain amount of coins. This wouldn't be a problem if the amount of coins each thing cost was far greater than the amount of coins gained from playing. It feels like one of those classic Family Arcades where the games yield a few prize tokens each time you play, but the prizes where you cash in those prize tokens are always an absurd amount.
In conclusion, I would classify this game as a lil' retro time-waster minigame that is outclassed in many ways by cheaper games of the same genre on Steam.

I received the starter edition of R6 as a gift for my birthday last year, and I never expected to end up with nearly 400 hours (and climbing). I've never been too into more "mainstream" shooters, so my obsession with this game came as a complete surprise. Make no mistake: R6 still has an IMMENSE amount of bugs that can be frustrating to play through, but when the game goes right it goes SO right.
The highly destructible environments make for a constantly shifting and dynamic battleground, and it's insanely satisfying to use it to your advantage on both attack and defense. Mira can cleverly neglect to reinforce specific walls and watch through her one-way window gadget to go for surprise wallbangs on unsuspecting attackers. Ash can set a breaching charge on a random window barricade and then use her breaching round gadget to blow up ANOTHER window and rush in while the defenders are still unsure of what approach the attackers are taking with the multiple disorienting explosions. This brings us to the "tactical shooter / intel" aspect of the game, which is another big part of its appeal. While sometimes iffy, the sound in the game can often be just as valuable as the visuals. You can hear the attackers running around on the roof, or blowing up a wall, or sending a drone in to gather intel, and in turn plan your course of action whether it be rushing a busy attacker or simply feeding your teammates information so they can ready themselves for a push by the enemies.
On top of the incredibly fun and (mostly) skill-based gameplay, Ubisoft does a surprisingly fantastic job of updating the game both for balance of existing content and addition of new content. All non-cosmetic additions (operators and their weapon attachments) can be unlocked pretty easily by just playing the game and earning renown to purchase them, and all new maps are available to all players when they are added. Even most of the cosmetics (with the exception of digital content bundles and some select headgears) can be pretty easily unlocked with earned renown, without ever forcing you to purchase the game's premium currency. Every few months there is a new "season" that adds two new unique operators, a bunch of cosmetics, and a brand new map. In the middle of each season they push midseason reinforcements, which are sets of balance changes and reworks based on operator usage statistics and community feedback.
TL;DR: The game really is, despite its flaws, an absolutely fantastic online shooter, and I can't recommend enough that you pick it up and play it with a few friends. Rainbow Six Siege is easily a 9/10 game and the best online shooter to come out of the 2010s, rivaling even the likes of CS:GO in its continued playability and competitive balance.

Beat the game and got a few of the optional trophies (procedural 8-pack and the Bastet, which requires completing 16 in a row without dying)
THOTH is a game for people who like challenge and Arrowhead Games' offerings (Magicka, Helldivers, Gauntlet, etc.) It's a twin-stick shooter with an abstract style that reminds me of a Doesburg painting gone rogue. You must complete sets of 4 levels at a time, each with a gimmick of some sort (the first pack shows off the standard square enemy, whereas the second and third packs add deadly borders and enemies that fire cubes on death, respectively). Controls are very tight and everything flows into everything else, lowering the frustration potential. By the last few levels you have a pretty sizable variation of the types of enemies you have to fight, and there's a definite, well-designed difficulty curve between the first and the sixty-fourth level.
THOTH also features a great (albeit unmutable without volume control fondling, which may put off some) ambient soundtrack, which almost seems designed to raise the hairs on the back of your neck. It is definitely an aide to your performance, as the odd and disturbing soundtrack provides no comfort and keeps you on edge, closely observing your movements all while the undulating noises add a strange augment of focus.
Also, quick note, as I've already said; THOTH is hard. Much as the Egyptian god's tribulations in the creation of heiroglyphs likely was, there's a lot of trial and error, learning what's good and what's not and how to manipulate the AI of every shape. There's a lot going on, from environmental factors to knowing how fast that beam shoots across the playing field to keeping an eye out to prevent getting cornered. After beating the game, I felt like I learned sufficiently enough about THOTH's inner workings, but the procedural 16 and 32 level challenges proved daunting and a feat of endurance is required to get through them. I'm sure in going for these challenges I could likely double my time played in the game, so there's definitely a fair amount of replayability in knowing those levels are different every time and that there's so many you have to do to 'complete' those challenges.
Would I recommend THOTH? I got it in a Humble Bundle a few months ago - but for a reduced price I would say this game is absolutely worth it. At about 90 minutes for an experienced twin-stick player, it's a little short for the 10 dollar price tag, but a 5 dollar purchase won't hurt your wallet and'll give you a lazy afternoon's worth of entertainment. Reminds me a lot of David. in scope.

This is a great game with a good potential. However now, in it`s current state, it has two problems. First of all, it is vey, very buggy. Look at any part of the game and you will find bugs. Player falls through the floor, items cannot be moved to inventory, capacity of smelter changes randomly, sometimes items just disappear while dragging.
Second problem is balance. Prepare to wait a lot and to make many monotonous movements. Dig and recharge, dig and recharge, dig and recharge, dig and recharge, dig and recharge, dig and recharge, dig and recharge, dig and recharge. Then go to smelter and smelt for an hour. Capacity of smelter is low (and changes randomly) so you cannot just leave game and go for a walk.
Of course, there is automation in this game, everything can be automated. But you`ll spend hours and hours to craft automatic resource processing. And these hours will be very boring.
I dont recommend this game untill all bugs are fixed and long hours replaced with brief breaks.

This game is a mfer. I yell my head off when I play. Yet I'm having so much fun. This has become one of my favorite top down shooters. When you friend dies though, there is a black dot that appears and follows around the other person thats still alive, and it is an annoying circle. It usually ruins your run on levels. In some ways I like this element in some ways I hate it. I like the color choices and I LOVE the music and sounds even though they are kind of scary. The game's colours and shapes make it look simple and I like that. It looks simplistic which makes you think its a simple game. It isn't. It takes a lot of persistancy and practice to be able to beat the game and even get through the randomly generated levels. It's simple to learn but difficult to master. I highly recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of the top down shooter genre and to anyone who needs a good co-op game.
